**No daemon thread opens a path on a volume the daemon serves (2026-11-06).** A request a daemon sends to its own volume
is answered only by that daemon's receive workers. Once delivered it sits in WinFsp's processing queue, which is never
cancelled or expired (`FSP_IOQ_PROCESS_NO_CANCEL`, WinFsp v2.1 `src/sys/ioq.c:572-575`). A dying thread waits for its
cancelled IRPs, and Windows gives up on them only after 5 minutes (Microsoft Learn, "Canceling IRPs"). The volume's
control handle closes only after every thread has exited. So a daemon killed with such a request outstanding cannot
exit. A-219's probe client did this, and every daemon killed or stopped during it outlived its reap: 10 s in the
library kill oracles, 75-90 minutes in the CLI suites (`docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-daemons-own-io-on-its-volume-strands-its-exit.md`).
Anything that needs a client of a slates volume (a measurement, a check) runs that client in a child process.
- **A-190's coherent purge follows it (fixed 2026-11-06).** The command thread opened the drive under its private
  marker and wrote and read each purged range through it, so a kill inside one of those requests stranded the daemon
  the same way. The opens, writes and reads now run in the mount's purge client, a child process: a role of the daemon's
  own binary (`slates winfsp-purge-client`), started in a kill-on-close job and asked over a message pipe
  (`crates/bridge-winfsp/src/purge_client.rs`). The command thread only writes to the pipe and reads the answer, which
  a dying thread's cancellation ends at once. Proven by `a_daemon_killed_while_its_purges_open_is_delivered_exits_within_a_transaction_timeout`
  (A-190's amendment of 2026-11-06).
- **A base directory, a landing's target and a FUSE mount point (A-227).** The sweep of 2026-11-06 found three host
  paths the daemon opens itself. Each is now refused, before any open, when it lies on a mount this daemon serves, and
  every crossing below a base is checked, a successor's kept mounts included: each is recorded before any base is
  reacquired. Built on Linux, Windows and macOS (A-227; GAPS for what each platform's proof still owes).

**Base reads on macOS and Windows.** As on Linux, the daemon reads untouched base files through its own descriptor or
handle into evictable cache chunks (one copy, `pread`/`ReadFile` on the owner shard's driver) and
replies from arena pages as for any chunk. Listings use `getattrlistbulk` and
`NtQueryDirectoryFile` respectively, so a `readdirplus` of a merged directory costs one bulk call
per directory, not one `stat` per entry.

**virtio-fs and OCI attachment contract (A-9).** The guest transport is FUSE-over-virtio
served by an owned device integrated with the custom executor. Hecate's in-process libkrun
integration is the reference, not a requirement to introduce a standalone daemon with a disk
socket. The seam accepts guest-memory/queue capabilities and completion notification from the
host VMM through an in-process interface or an inherited descriptor. The harness owns VM and
container creation; Slates owns the exported attachment and filesystem service. Native host
mounts remain available without a VM. Evidence: [research/hecate-contract-review.md](research/hecate-contract-review.md) §2.

A host OCI runtime passes the established host attachment into the container mount namespace;
a Linux guest mounts the exported virtio-fs tag, and OCI containers inside it consume that guest
path. Capabilities differ by host, kernel, runtime and VMM and must be reported by `attach`
and `status`: supported transport, target-path constraints, read/write policy, sharing/cache
semantics, residency boundary and conformance evidence. Requesting an unsupported form returns
`AttachmentUnsupported{transport, reason}`. A metadata record is insufficient evidence of a
usable container path or guest device. No disk socket, image construction, target mkdir or
privilege escalation is implicit in attaching a VFS volume.

**Binding lifetime (A-28).** An OCI binding borrows the verified source mount's attachment.
Before recording it, the daemon checks the kernel source's capability against that live
bridge attachment, the requested volume, principal and rights. The binding survives the
issuing CLI's exit and daemon recovery. Explicit detach removes the binding; source-mount
removal removes its dependent bindings in the same recorded transition. A binding cannot
own another binding or mint an independent mount capability. The existing attachment-table
cap bounds these records. The runtime owns its container namespace and must finish its
use before explicit detach; removing a recipe record does not unmount a container or
establish its cache-flush boundary. A source the daemon cannot identify is refused.

> **Status (2026-09-20).** The strict real-CLI lifecycle test fails before this fix with
> two attachments instead of three after client retirement (3.57 s), then passes with
> explicit detach and dependent unmount cleanup (5.62 s). The original Docker workload's
> strict cleanup also passes in the full CLI suite (10 tests, 26.53 s). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-20-oci-binding-lifetime-is-owned-by-an-exited-cli.md`.

Device admission authenticates the consumer before creating a queue, mapping guest memory or
publishing a tag. Queue descriptors, scatter/gather ranges, arithmetic and chained lengths are
validated within derived caps before access. In-flight requests, mapped bytes, copy buffers and
replies consume the attachment's credits; cancellation and revocation reclaim them under an
owned terminal step. Separate virtqueues alone do not provide §4.9's end-to-end QoS.

DAX, if exposed, maps a range of the file's backing: an object of the attachment's own that holds
only that file's bytes, which the VFS write boundary keeps equal to the file before any change
returns, so no window is ever revoked or reused under a guest (A-163, A-168, A-195). Every page
visible to a guest must contain only bytes it is authorized to see, including page padding and
neighbouring files' bytes, which a backing holds by construction; a moved view (`advance`) refills
the backings before the guest sees anything more. A guest's stores through a writable window reach
the volume only through the VFS write boundary, at its sync points, so witness, journal, quota and
lease checks run. The baseline contract does not require DAX; a DAX capability is advertised only by
a binding a live guest has run over these backings (AC-9.7).

The same capability serves a **same-kernel** consumer — a host process, or a container or pod that shares the
daemon's kernel — with no virtual machine and no copy (A-135). A per-file copy, the kind of object a guest's DAX
window maps (A-168), is what a local reader `mmap`s directly (A-171). The agent's volume is always co-located with the agent
(its arena DRAM is on the agent's own machine, §4.1), so this path is always physically available; it is negotiated
at connect, never configured (R8, no mode switch): the daemon offers the direct map only to a peer the rendezvous
authenticated as the **same uid** (`SO_PEERCRED`, §4.7), and then only if the descriptor it would send authorizes
nothing beyond that read. **The uid is a necessary condition, never a sufficient one.** An earlier reading of this
section called a same-uid peer "its own trust domain, a peer that may read the bytes through the mount regardless";
that was wrong twice over and is corrected here. A §4.13 consumer is an untrusted process of exactly this uid holding
exactly this channel — the consumer capability exists because it is untrusted — and a descriptor is not a read: it
carries its whole object, writable, to whoever holds it. Measured, a 20 KiB read handed a peer a writable descriptor
for a 176.8 GiB content object holding every volume on the host, and a peer used it to rewrite another volume's file
(`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-a-read-handed-the-peer-the-whole-content-arena.md`). So the rule is the descriptor's own
extent and seals: the object must *be* the authorized window (offset zero, equal lengths) and must be sealed against
writing and resizing (`F_SEAL_WRITE` or `F_SEAL_FUTURE_WRITE`, with `F_SEAL_SHRINK` and `F_SEAL_GROW`). A read-only
duplicate does not qualify and must not — measured, a same-uid peer re-opens one `O_RDWR` through `/proc/self/fd`.
A different-uid or
sandboxed peer, a peer the platform cannot pass a descriptor to, and any backing that cannot meet that rule, read
through the copy path (the bulk region, §4.7) or through virtio-fs DAX; the consumer always has a correct read, and
the zero-copy upgrade is taken only where it is both safe and physically possible. Mechanism (A-171, replacing
A-135's arena hand-off): the client requests a map over the command ring; the daemon makes a copy of the file that is
the unit of authorization — a sealable memfd the size of the file's page span, at least a page — takes its own
writable map of all of it, then seals it `F_SEAL_FUTURE_WRITE | F_SEAL_SHRINK | F_SEAL_GROW | F_SEAL_SEAL`, so every
later writer is refused and the daemon's earlier map keeps writing. It fills the copy from the volume a slice at a
time (the reply is deferred to that task, as an image build's is, A-160), then sends the copy's descriptor with the
mapping id and the file length over the retained control socket by `SCM_RIGHTS` (the command ring cannot carry a
descriptor; §4.7), then the reply. The client maps the copy whole, read alone, and reads it through atomics, since the
daemon writes it at any moment. macOS has neither seals nor a control socket (A-173): there the copy is a
shared-memory object reached by two descriptors alone, its name removed as soon as both are open — the daemon's, read
and write, and one opened read alone, which is offered on the daemon's socket route (A-161) behind a fresh single-use
secret the reply carries. XNU refuses the holder of a read-only descriptor every way to write through it and sizes such
an object once, so the descriptor's access mode is the capability, judged before the offer (`confined_read_only`: read
alone, exactly the authorized length). Windows passes no descriptor (A-175): the copy is an unnamed pagefile-backed
section whose security descriptor grants no one any right (`D:P(A;;RC;;;OW)`, which also cuts the owner's implicit
`WRITE_DAC`), the daemon keeps the creator's handle, and it duplicates a read-only handle into the client's process,
whose id the claim slot carries, once the process is found to run as the daemon's user and the handle is judged as a
hostile holder would use it (`handle_route::hand_section`: exactly the authorized size, and a duplicate that writes,
one that may rewrite the descriptor and a writable view each refused `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`); the reply names the
handle's value, which the completion record leaves out. **A map may write too (A-186).** `MapWrite` names the
caller's own write attachment and resolves the file through it, as a file verb does; the copy is made writable (sealed
against resizing and new seals but not writes on Linux, its handed descriptor opened read and write on macOS, a
read-write handle on Windows whose section's descriptor refuses any wider one), judged for that access where it
leaves the process. The client's stores land in the copy, and the daemon compares the copy back into the file at the
client's `MapSync`, at its `ReleaseMap` and before its reap removes its attachments, writing each run that differs
through the attachment and publishing before it answers (A-163's compare-back, one function for both). A `Detach` with
writable maps held under it is refused `MapsHeld`. **The map is a live view of the file within its length.** The copy sits in the store's
backings beside the VMMs' (A-163), so the volume's single write boundary writes every later write, cut and growth into
it before the change returns: the client sees them as memory alone, with no request, as a shared map of a file does. A
change past the copy's length is not seen; the client maps again for it. This replaces A-135's pinned version, whose
coherence was "the version a live local map pins is held until the client drops the map": no arena block can be handed
(it holds every volume), so a pinned version would need a copy of its own anyway, and a copy kept equal by write-through
costs the same copy once and gives the client the file as it is, where a pinned copy would grow stale with no signal.
The price is a copy of each write into each mapped file's copy, and a cut that zeroes by stores over what holds bytes
(the write seal refuses the daemon's own hole punch). **Lifetime and bounds (A-172).** A copy is held for its client
from the moment it is made until the client releases it (`ReleaseMap`, `Client::release_map`) or is reaped; a hand-off
that fails in the client after the copy was made (its delivery, its claim or its map refused) gives it back before the
failure returns (A-174). A volume's
destroy or a file's last unlink only detaches its copies: they leave the write-through index, so a volume given the
prefix again once its count wraps never writes into them, but they stay held and counted, because the client's own map
keeps the object's pages, which the daemon wrote and its memory is charged for. A shard holds at most the copies its
share of the process's descriptor and mapping limits leaves room for (one descriptor and up to three mappings a copy),
and at most its fill budget's bytes; a client's share is that capacity over the clients the shard serves, those holding
its copies and the one asking, and a map past it is refused `MapShareExhausted` with nothing made. **A client of any
shard (A-188).** Every map verb names its volume and runs on the volume's shard, and the copy is held there, in that
shard's table under its client, whichever shard serves the client. The hand-off reaches the client where it is: on Linux
the copy's shard asks the client's own shard, by a cross-shard call, to send the descriptor on the client's control
socket, whose deliveries are sealed under the client's channel (A-187), and sent once: that shard records each map it
sent until its reply reaches the client, an ask after a lost answer is answered from the record, and a hand-off whose
every answer was lost keeps its copy as handed, the client's to let go (A-505); on Windows it asks that shard for the
client's process and duplicates the handle into it; macOS's offer is made on the copy's shard and claimed by the
mapping id, which names it. The reply is delivered to the client's ring on its own shard. The client's own shard runs
its reap and reaches every shard: there the client's writable maps are written back before its attachments go, and its
copies let go after. A consumer in a separate network namespace (a container on a bridge network, a pod of its own)
reaches the daemon through the rendezvous's socket file (A-187).

> **Status (local zero-copy read / A-135, 2026-10-15).** **Built and proven end to end on x86_64 Linux.** A same-uid
> client requests `MapRead` over the command ring; the daemon mints a read mapping (`Volume::dax_map_read`) and sends
> the arena block's descriptor (`Store::dax_backing`) with its metadata over the retained control socket by
> `SCM_RIGHTS` (`crates/ipc/src/rendezvous.rs` `Control::send_mapping`/`Liveness::recv_mapping`,
> `ClientEnd::recv_mapping`); the client `mmap`s it (`Client::map_read` → `MappedRead`, `crates/client/src/client.rs`).
> The server path is `crates/server/src/merge_service.rs` (`map_read`/`try_local_map`): the `SO_PEERCRED` same-uid
> gate, then `dax_map_read` + `dax_backing`, else the copy path (`read`), so the client always gets its bytes; the
> zero-copy upgrade is counted (`dax.local_map`, a non-vacuity counter). Proven by use in
> `crates/client/tests/client.rs` `a_same_kernel_client_maps_a_file_with_no_copy`: a one-shard daemon, a 20 KiB
> arena-backed file, mapped zero-copy with the bytes equal byte for byte. The whole A-135 client path is `cfg(unix)`;
> a non-Unix `MapRead` reads by copy. This path's first real descriptor map surfaced and fixed a latent arena bug —
> `block_backing` returned a region-relative offset against the whole-object descriptor, which would have mis-mapped
> the guest DAX window too (`docs/bugs/2026-10-15-block-backing-returned-a-region-relative-offset.md`).
>
> **Amended 2026-10-18 — the hand-off is refused today, and a `MapRead` reads by copy on Linux too.** The descriptor
> being sent was the arena's whole object: measured at 189,833,572,352 bytes against 20,480 authorized (9.27 million
> ×), writable, with another volume's whole file readable inside it — and a peer used it to rewrite that volume's
> file, which the ordinary read verb then served. The check now lives at the one place a descriptor leaves the
> process for a peer (`Control::send_mapping` → `confined_for_a_peer`), so no caller can skip it: the object must be
> the window (`region_off == 0`, `object_len == block_len`) and must be sealed against writing and resizing, else
> `IpcError::UnconfinedDescriptor` and the existing `LocalMap::Fallback` serves the bytes by copy. No backing
> satisfies that yet — a shard's content arena is one object holding every volume (A-64) — so the zero-copy arm is
> not taken. Restoring it needs a backing whose object is the unit of authorization, the same decision the
> message-based DAX placer waits on; the measured seal mechanism that makes such a backing safe
> (`F_SEAL_FUTURE_WRITE` after the owner's own map) is in the record. **Owed:** that decision; and the
> cross-shard owner→home descriptor hand-off (a `MapRead` whose volume is owned by another shard copies rather than
> maps for now); a prompt per-drop release (the daemon now revokes a client's maps when it is **reaped** — 3b,
> `crate::reap` over a `ClientSlot::dax_maps` list — so a dropped or dead client's read maps no longer pin versions
> toward the registry cap; a release on the client's own `MappedRead` drop would be prompter, and slates exposes no
> dax-map count yet for a reap count-assertion test — both owed); and the macOS control socket (macOS carries
> refusing `send_mapping`/`recv_mapping` stubs, so it reads by copy).
>
> **Amended 2026-10-25 (A-171) — built and proven on Linux by a real client.** A `MapRead` is answered with a sealed
> copy of the file (`slates_mem::PeerObject`; `crates/server/src/direct_map.rs`), filled a slice at a time and kept
> equal to the file by the write boundary (`ShardsBackings::insert_peer`, `BackingObject::Peer`); the client maps it
> whole and reads it through atomics (`slates_mem::PeerView`; `MappedRead::read_at`, `to_vec`, `descriptor`, which
> replace `bytes()`). The hand-off rule in `confined_for_a_peer` is unchanged in code and now met: one file's copy,
> all of it authorized, write- and size-sealed. Proven on fedora (x86_64, Linux, 2026-10-25) by
> `crates/client/tests/client.rs`, 5 of 5: zero copy asserted for a 20 KiB and a 4 MiB file and at every size from
> empty to 1 MiB; the handed descriptor's shared writable map, `write`, shrink, growth and hole punch refused `EPERM`,

> **Superseded 2026-11-01 (A-195).** The gate below is removed with every window over the arena's blocks: a guest's
> window maps its file's backing (A-168), which needs no pin, registry or revoke. Kept as the record of what was built,
> and of the escapes it closed.
>
> **Status (DAX gate, 2026-10-12).** Mapping isolation, pinning and teardown are **built in the VFS** and proven by
> use (`crates/vfs/src/dax.rs`, `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs`, 21 tests; `crates/mem/src/arena.rs` pin set, 6 tests,
> Miri-clean; recovery oracle 39/0). **Pinning:** a mapped block is pinned in the arena
> (`ChunkArena::pin`/`unpin`) — a `free` of it is deferred (bytes kept, unscrubbed) and it is never handed to another
> allocation or trimmed until the last unpin releases and scrubs it (A-99). This is the memory-level invariant a
> hardware DAX guest cannot bypass: the block a mapping names is never reused, in this volume or any other on the
> shard's shared arena, so a guest page can never fall onto another file's bytes. **Teardown:** a shard-local
> `DaxRegistry` in `Store` records every live mapping; `write`/`truncate` revoke the inode's mappings (the single
> write boundary), `snapshot` revokes writable mappings before sharing (read-only survive — the allowed
> immutable-shared case), and `destroy` revokes the whole volume's (eventual reclamation). A revoked mapping's
> hardware access is inert (the window is `munmap`'d; modeled by `Store::dax_read_raw`/`dax_write_raw`). **Rights:** a
> writable mapping copies the file up first, so no writable mapping of immutable or snapshot-shared content. The eight
> escapes an earlier experiment on this branch demonstrated — exfiltration, cross-file and cross-volume injection, a
> concurrent pile, TOCTOU, a block-move lost update, a snapshot-share corruption, and a revoke-then-reuse — are closed.
> **Still owed before DAX is advertised:** wire the gate to the virtio-fs device seam (map/revoke on admission and on
> `advance`; `crates/server/src/virtiofs.rs`); and make the registry **un-fabricable and tamper-proof across the
> fleet** — it is daemon-local RAM today and a mapping is minted here, never supplied by a caller, so no agent can
> reach or forge it, but the fleet-integrity design (a daemon-minted mapping capability, VMM-enforced teardown, and
> the version a mapping pins riding the fenced retention protocol) is recorded in `GAPS.md` and is the next step. DAX
> stays unadvertised and a DAX request is refused `AttachmentUnsupported` until both are done.
>
> **Reconciled 2026-11-06 (VFS plan Step 15).** The gate is wired to the device seam (7ce16d4c) and its registry made
> unforgeable (45937ac8, c4343670); A-195 later replaced the registry with per-file backings.

> **Amended 2026-11-01 (A-195).** No window maps the arena's blocks any more; each maps a per-file backing. Item 1's race
> has nothing left to race: no window is torn down under a guest, and a backing lives while any window maps it (the
> device keeps a backing whose window it could not unmap). Item 2's registry cap went with the registry: a guest's
> windows are bounded by its window (one a granule at most), its backings by the shard's fill budget, and its requests
> by the §4.9 credit window. Of item 3's layers, L0, L1's zones, L2 and B2 were the arena's and are removed; the backed
> route's L1 stands.
>
> **DAX multi-tenancy threat model (2026-10-14).** With the strict per-volume spatial separation above, a guest
> reaches only its own file's pinned, per-volume arena block (the inode number carries the volume prefix, distinct
> and never reused across volumes), so cross-tenant *memory* leakage — the shared-host-page-cache hazard of naive
> virtio-fs DAX — is closed by construction, not by a per-access check a hardware guest bypasses. The residuals,
> once spatial isolation holds, are low-level execution and hardware:
> 1. **Asynchronous revocation / TLB race.** When a block is reclaimed (write, truncate, snapshot, destroy,
>    takeover) the host must invalidate the guest's MMU page tables and flush every physical core's TLB *before* the
>    block returns to the pool or a new volume — a race there is the only way a neighbour could catch dirty state.
>    **Addressed:** the pin is held across the unmap. `Store::dax_revoke_pending` unregisters the mapping (the
>    hardware path goes inert, no new access authorized) but keeps the block pinned; `Store::dax_release_after_unmap`
>    unpins only after the device confirms the VMM window unmap and the cross-core TLB flush. The daemon never unpins
>    first (`crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs` `a_pending_revoke_keeps_the_block_pinned_until_the_unmap_is_confirmed`); the
>    synchronous `dax_revoke` is kept only for the no-live-guest path.
> 2. **Map/unmap-storm or page-fault DoS.** A guest cannot steal data but could try to starve the host orchestration
>    by flooding SETUPMAPPING/REMOVEMAPPING or faulting the DAX BAR. **Bounded at three levels:** the
>    mapping registry's cap is the shard's chunk budget (`DaxRegistry::new(max_chunks)`), a map past it refused
>    `NoSpace` and counted (`a_map_storm_is_refused_at_the_registry_bound`); the §4.9 credit window bounds in-flight
>    requests and bytes (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/credit.rs`); and the device serve loop is cooperative per pass,
>    so one guest's storm cannot starve another guest's **service**.
>
>    **It can, however, deny another guest a window, and an earlier version of this paragraph said otherwise.**
>    Corrected 2026-10-18 by measurement: the cap is the *shard's* and the accounting is per request, so one volume
>    re-mapping one file took all 32 slots of a 32-chunk store and the next volume's first window was refused
>    `NoSpace` (`one_volumes_map_storm_does_not_deny_another_volume`, committed `#[ignore]`d as the reproduction of
>    an open finding). Refusing a storm is a bound on *growth*; it is not fairness, and the tenant who fills a
>    shared bound is not the tenant who pays for it. A fix that returned the live window for a repeat request was
>    built and withdrawn the same day — it shared one refcounted pin between two guest windows, so the first
>    unmap would unpin a block the second still maps. **The fix that stands moves the pin from the mapping to
>    the window**: `dax_map_*` pins again on every dedup hit, so the holder count tracks guest windows rather
>    than registry entries, and the denial is closed
>    (`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-one-volumes-dax-map-storm-denies-every-other-volume.md`; this paragraph said the
>    fix was still owed until 2026-10-19, when three bugs apparently caused by it turned out to be a test
>    harness unpinning twice — the stale wording is what sent that investigation down the wrong road).
>    **The pairing callers must keep:** `dax_revoke` is the synchronous teardown and unregisters *and* unpins;
>    `dax_release_after_unmap` is phase two of the two-phase revoke, whose phase one (`dax_revoke_pending`)
>    keeps the pin. One of the two per window, never both — the arena's holder count cannot tell whose pin a
>    second unpin takes, so with two windows over one block it steals the other's.
> 3. **Rowhammer / hardware co-location.** Two untrusted tenants whose writable DAX blocks land on physically
>    adjacent DRAM rows face bit-flip risk at the silicon layer, independent of software isolation — slates cannot
>    prevent the physics and does not claim to. The hardware floor stays the host/VMM's: ECC/Chipkill, DDR4/5 Target
>    Row Refresh, and not co-locating untrusted tenants on adjacent rows. On top of that floor slates runs a layered
>    software defence whose per-event cost is bounded and whose memory footprint stays **capped** — the agentic-scale
>    answer to quarantine exhaustion (there is nothing to quarantine):
>    - **L0 — opt-in gate (built, 4b411da9; its premise corrected 2026-10-31, A-193; removed 2026-11-01 with the arena
>      windows, A-195).** Writable DAX into the arena is
>      off by default, and `Volume::dax_map_write` refuses `NotPermitted` until the owner opts in
>      (`Volume::enable_writable_dax`). **The gate bounds a guest's stores into slates' content. It does not bound
>      hammering, because reading alone hammers.** The original study corrupted nearby data "by reading from the same
>      address in DRAM", with a user-level loop of loads that flushes the cache line between them (Kim et al.,
>      ISCA 2014, abstract and §1). Project Zero's exploit rests on the same fact: "repeatedly accessing a row of memory
>      can cause bit flips in adjacent rows" (Seaborn and Dullien, 2015). So a read-only window is an aggressor too.
>      Every window a guest maps reaches the rows behind it, and each layer below must cover read-only windows as well
>      as writable ones.
>      Until 2026-10-31 this paragraph said read-only DAX "cannot hammer a neighbour". Under that premise the route
>      production serves (A-168's backings) carried none of the layers below, read-only and writable alike; its layer
>      is now the next one. Keeping writable arena DAX rare still narrows something real: B2 below can heal only
>      read-only content, since a writable block changes legitimately.
>    - **L1 for the backed route — every range a guest maps lies in huge pages with guard rows (built 2026-10-31 and
>      2026-11-01, A-193, A-194).** Since A-168, slates' own device maps per-file backings, not the arena's blocks, and the
>      Shards route maps the same objects (A-163). The layers L1, L2 and B2 below were built on the arena.
>
>      **How a backing lays out its file** (`DaxLayout`, A-194). A backing's object is cut into pages of 2 MiB, each placed
>      in one huge page where the host can.
>      - *slates' own device* tells its VMM where each piece of a window lies, so its backings are **guarded**: the file's
>        bytes lie in the interiors of consecutive pages, and the first and last chunk window of every page (64 KiB on a
>        4 KiB-paged host, `slates_vfs::content::chunk_bytes`, the slot the arena's zones held as guard rows) are held
>        empty. A guest's 2 MiB window is mapped as two pieces, each inside one page's interior (an interior is 1,920 KiB,
>        fifteen 128 KiB parts, so every 2 MiB range is exactly two pieces), and no window ever maps a guard. Each placed
>        page is then one huge page with its guard rows, CATT's shape (Brasser et al., USENIX Security 2017) as the
>        zones hold it.
>      - *The Shards route* maps by the file's own offsets, as its agreed protocol fixes (A-163), so its windows map whole
>        pages: placement without guard rows. Guard rows there need the protocol to carry pieces, which is for the Shards
>        owner to agree.
>      - Where the host cannot place a range in one huge page, both keep the file's own offsets: a guard without a huge page
>        behind it isolates nothing (`Placement::Unavailable`).
>
>      **How a range is placed.** As a range's fill finishes, before the guest's ask is answered, every page holding it
>      (two under the guard, one otherwise) is placed (`DaxObject::place_range`, through `ShardsBackings::place`, from the
>      shared DAX session in `crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`):
>      1. slates' view of the page is mapped congruent with the object, as the arena's views are (`crates/mem/src/shared.rs`);
>      2. one byte of the page is read, so the object holds a page there, since a shmem collapse of a range holding no
>         page stops at `SCAN_TRUNCATED` (`mm/khugepaged.c`);
>      3. `MADV_COLLAPSE` is asked about the view's span, and its verdict decides, as it decided for the zones.
>
>      The device then sends the window's pieces together, its ring's room asked for all of them first, answers the guest
>      on the last acknowledgement, and unmaps each piece on its own, since a vhost-user unmap must name the whole of one
>      mapped region. A piece the front end refuses fails the SETUPMAPPING, and the pieces that did map are unmapped
>      again: a window is mapped whole or not at all. While a piece's acknowledgement is owed, the serve loop answers the
>      front end's control messages too. QEMU 11.1 answers a map and then commits it, sending `SET_MEM_TABLE` and awaiting
>      the back end's answer before it reads the next request (`vhost_user_backend_handle_shmem_map`, then its memory
>      transaction's commit, `hw/virtio/vhost-user.c`). A loop that waited for the second piece's acknowledgement alone
>      waited forever: every guest test in QEMU hung on its first read until the wait served the doorbell too.
>
>      **What placement buys, and where.** A placed page is one physically contiguous, aligned 2 MiB page that holds
>      nothing of anyone else's, and under the guard a guest's window reaches only its interior: its first and last
>      64 KiB hold nothing and no window maps them, so the rows a guest's reads and stores activate are never the page's
>      edge rows. What that is in DRAM rows depends on how the memory controller spreads physical addresses over channels,
>      ranks and banks, which is undocumented and learned only by reverse engineering (DRAMA, Pessl et al., USENIX
>      Security 2016).
>      - Where 2 MiB spans several rows of each bank it touches, the page's inner rows have only its own rows beside
>        them. For example, with 8 KiB rows, 16 banks, two ranks and two channels, a row across every bank is 512 KiB, so a
>        page spans four rows a bank. Without a guard, a guest's window holds the page's edge rows, and the foreign rows
>        beside them are hammered from one side. The guard keeps the guest off those edge rows wherever a guard slot
>        covers a page's edge in each bank it touches. That holds where the interleaving lays 64 KiB in whole rows at the
>        page's ends, and it is the same bet the arena's zones made with the same slot.
>      - Where a row across every bank is 2 MiB or more, as with many channels, a placed page is less than a row of each
>        bank. It buys no row isolation then, guard or not, only a bounded, contiguous set of rows the guest can reach.
>
>      Without placement a range lay on whatever pages the fault path gave: base pages where `shmem_enabled` is `never`
>      (CI's runners), each beside whatever was there.
>
>      **Counted and visible.** A collapse the kernel declines is counted (`virtiofs.dax_placement_refused`,
>      `shards.dax_placement_refused` in the status report), and the range is served on base pages. Placements count
>      `virtiofs.dax_placed` and `shards.dax_placed`. `ShardsBackings::placed_ranges` is the live gauge, and
>      `ShardsBackings::placements` reads where each placed range lies (its PMD mapping in `/proc/self/smaps`). A placed
>      range is zeroed by stores, never a hole punch, which would split its page.
>
>      **A decline is remembered for a retry window.** A declined collapse is not free: the kernel tries to compact
>      memory first, and on adacachy at load 90 a fill step that was declined took 1,954 and 2,832 µs, where calm runs
>      placed every range. Asked once a range, a host out of huge pages would charge the shard that much for every range
>      a guest maps, and a guest churning its ranges could make it pay again and again. So a decline likely to hold is
>      remembered, the next ranges are served on base pages without asking (counted as declined), and the shard's
>      deadline keeper re-arms it a retry window after the decline (`ShardsBackings::place`, `take_declined`,
>      `rearm_placement`; A-570, the reap loop's tick until then). The kernel is asked at most once a window per shard
>      while it declines, and nothing wakes while no decline is held. A transient decline (`EAGAIN`, a page locked or
>      held for the moment) is not remembered.
>      Proven in a child process whose huge pages the kernel refuses (`PR_SET_THP_DISABLE`): three
>      ranges ask the kernel once, and a re-arm asks again
>      (`a_declined_placement_is_remembered_until_re_armed`, `crates/bridge-core/tests/dax_backing.rs`).
>
>      **The cost.** A placed page holds a whole 2 MiB, however little of it the file fills, and under the guard a range lies
>      in two pages: a one-page file mapped costs 4 MiB (2 MiB under the identity), and fifteen ranges in a row cost sixteen
>      pages, 6.7% over the file. The fill budget counts exactly the pages a backing's filled ranges lie in
>      (`DaxLayout::pages_holding`), and a range is placed only once it is filled and counted, so the placed bytes never
>      exceed what the budget counts. A VMM maps two pieces a window where it mapped one. crosvm maps each into its one
>      window arena. QEMU makes a memory region of each, so a QEMU guest without `CONFIGURE_MEM_SLOTS` meets its
>      eight-region table at half as many windows (GAPS). The pieces are not 2 MiB-aligned, so a VMM maps them with
>      base-page entries.
>      Measured with `fstat`'s `st_blocks` on adacachy (Linux 7.2.9) and on CI's x86_64 and arm64 runners (Linux 7.0,
>      `shmem_enabled` `[never]`; diagnostics run 41277950761), 2026-11-01, every range placed and none refused:
>      - a one-page file's first range and a range wholly past its end lie in four pages: 8,388,608 bytes held, 8,388,608
>        counted;
>      - a read-only window over one file holds two pages, 4,194,304 bytes; writable windows over another file's two
>        neighbouring ranges hold three, 6,291,456 bytes; the backings count 10,485,760 for both;
>      - the budget was 16,777,216 bytes.
>
>      A fill step that places its range's two pages took 387 to 579 µs on CI's runners, one sample each in debug builds
>      (BENCHMARKS).
>
>      Proven by `each_range_a_guest_maps_is_one_huge_page_within_the_fill_budget` and
>      `a_declined_placement_is_remembered_until_re_armed` (`crates/bridge-core/tests/dax_backing.rs`), the layout's
>      arithmetic (`crates/mem/tests/dax_layout.rs`), a guarded object's round trip (`crates/mem/tests/dax_object.rs`), and
>      three device tests in `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`:
>      - read-only and writable windows: each placed page one PMD page in slates' view, every piece the front end was sent
>        inside a page's interior, every guard slot holding nothing even after the guest stores across a whole window, the
>        window sharing that page keeping its bytes, and a cut keeping the pages placed;
>      - a hostile guest's churn, each range placed once however often it is mapped, and nothing left placed or held once
>        the node is forgotten;
>      - a read-only attachment's window placed with its guards empty, and its writable ask refused with nothing made.
>
>      They pass on adacachy and on CI's x86_64 and arm64 runners (diagnostics run 41277950761), every range placed.
>      Red-checked on both runners, each mutation failing on its own assertion:
>      - placement off failed all five placement tests;
>      - a placed page punched rather than zeroed failed the cut's check, the punched page reading no PMD bytes;
>      - the memo off failed "the kernel asked once for the three";
>      - the interior widened by a guard failed "`FrontPiece { fd_offset: 65536, … len: 2031616 }` reaches a guard".
>
>      Real VMMs map the two pieces: QEMU 11.1.2 with KVM passes every test of `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs` through
>      slates' own device, 5 of 5 in 9.62 s, every range placed (CI's x86_64 runner, diagnostics run 41278779089), and
>      crosvm passes the same 5 of 5 on adacachy in 33.18 s. On that box, at load 87 to 218, three windows were placed and
>      three declined and served on base pages, every guest's bytes right.
>
>      **What cannot apply to a backing, and why.**
>      - *Guard rows on the Shards route.* Its VMM maps a backing by the file's own offsets, which the protocol agreed with
>        the Shards owner fixes (`docs/wip/shards/dax-protocol.md`, A-163), so a window maps whole pages, edge rows
>        included. Guard rows there need the protocol to carry pieces, which is the owner's to agree.
>      - *Guard rows outside a page.* Memory known to lie physically beside a page cannot be had: an unprivileged process
>        can neither choose nor see it. Since Linux 4.2 pagemap zeroes the frame number without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, because
>        "information about PFNs helps in exploiting Rowhammer vulnerability" (`Documentation/admin-guide/mm/pagemap.rst`),
>        and a page larger than a PMD is hugetlb's, reserved by an administrator, which R10 refuses to require. So the
>        guards lie inside each page, at the cost of its two ends.
>      - *L2's shift.* Moving a guest's range to other rows means mapping over its live window, which the vhost-user
>        specification forbids. Unmapping first opens the zero-page gap a real guest read (A-168).
>      - *B2's net.* A read-only range's backing could be compared with the volume on the reap tick, as B2 compares the
>        arena's guarded blocks. Not built; owed (GAPS).
>
>      **The floor that remains is the host's.** It is ECC, and in-DRAM Target Row Refresh, which TRR-aware many-sided
>      patterns defeat on 13 of 42 DDR4 modules (TRRespass, Frigo et al., IEEE S&P 2020), and not placing untrusted
>      tenants on one host. Where a page spans several rows a bank, placement and the guard narrow what a guest's accesses
>      reach to rows its own page holds. They never make a guest unable to flip a neighbour's bit.
>    - **L1 — zones + guard rows (built, `crates/vfs/src/daxzone.rs`; removed 2026-11-01 with the arena windows, A-195).**
>      A tenant's writable-DAX content is shifted
>      only inside a sandbox reserved for that tenant: one transparent huge page of the content arena, **verified**
>      to have actually been given as one, cut into slots that are therefore distinct physical rows of the same
>      page, with the first and last slot held by the zone as guard rows (CATT-style, Brasser et al., USENIX
>      Security 2017) so the tenant's rows are never at the edge of its page beside a neighbour's. Without this a
>      shift moves a *virtual* address the kernel may back with the row it came from — security theatre — so
>      [`Volume::dax_migrate`] now **refuses `NoPhysicalIsolation`** on a host that cannot back a sandbox rather
>      than performing a shift that does not shift.
>      **A refused reservation is remembered.** A refusal costs 53 µs — it allocates the span, discards it,
>      walks `/proc/self/smaps` three times (a walk of the whole address space each) and faults a huge page's
>      worth — measured on fedora 6.19.10. At the 16 ms shift cadence, re-asking would burn 0.33% of a core per
>      window to re-learn the same answer, and more as the daemon's address space grows. `DaxZones` memoises the
>      refusal and the daemon clears it on its reap tick, so the host is asked at most once per volume per tick
>      and a host that frees memory still gets its sandbox within one.
>      **Unprivileged, by measurement rather than by requirement.** A hugetlb reservation would need
>      `/proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages` from an administrator, which R10 refuses to require; a transparent huge page
>      needs nothing, and whether the kernel actually gave one is a question `/proc/self/smaps` answers
>      (`slates_machine::facts::huge_backed_bytes`); `madvise` returning `OK` is not an answer (measured on
>      Linux 7.2: a 64 KiB and a 1 MiB mapping both take it and receive none).
>      The zone discards the span and faults it back, and then **asks `MADV_COLLAPSE` about that span and takes
>      its verdict** (Linux 6.1; shmem support 6.2). That call reports success only where every huge-aligned
>      region of the range it was given is PMD-mapped, *including one that already was*, so it answers about the
>      span. A whole-mapping `smaps` total cannot, and asking it that way was wrong twice over: the kernel
>      reshapes the rest of a mapping, and merges a mapping with an identical neighbour, for reasons that have
>      nothing to do with this reservation. Measured 2026-10-20 on Linux 6.12.76 (aarch64) under the DAX suite's
>      own 73 tests in parallel, with a probe at every refusal point: the commonest refusal was **no reading at
>      all** — after a merge no `smaps` entry begins at the region's base, 9–11 a run, then cached and repeated
>      16–17 — and every refusal that did read had the collapse reporting **success**, one of them while the
>      mapping's total *fell* from 14 MiB to 4 MiB as its other pages were broken up. The skips that cost "two
>      to six of the sandbox tests per run" above, and the "three runs of eight" on fedora, were this and not
>      the host declining. Asked about the span directly, the suite's loud skips on Linux went 3, 1, 0, 1, 2
>      across five runs to **0 across six**. The collapse honours the request even where `shmem_enabled` is
>      `[never]` — it is a request, not a preference. The `smaps` reading is kept, no longer fatal when absent,
>      as the leg for a kernel before 6.1 that has no `MADV_COLLAPSE` to ask
>      (`docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-sandbox-asked-the-mapping-not-the-span.md`). A reservation that cannot be backed is refused,
>      which is the only honest answer: physical contiguity is the host's to give.
>      **A window is placed from its first byte, not its first shift.** `Volume::dax_map_write` puts the block
>      on a sandbox row as it mints the window, so containment — the layer §4.6 leans on — never waits for the
>      periodic shift to arm. The cost is that a placed file holds a **whole row**: a 4 KiB file in a 64 KiB row
>      measured here. That is necessary rather than waste — a row shared with another file is precisely the
>      co-location the sandbox prevents, so a row is indivisible by construction — and it is bounded at one row
>      per writable-DAX file, which L0 keeps rare. A host that backs no sandbox serves the window with the block
>      the allocator gave it; only the *shift* refuses, because a shift is what would be theatre without one.
>      **The zone holds every slot it is not lending.** A row the zone does not hold is a row the general allocator
>      may give another volume — the co-location the zone exists to prevent — so the span is allocated whole and
>      any row that left (an ordinary delete or truncate frees a block by a path the zone does not sit on) is
>      re-claimed before the next grant. The cost is one huge page per tenant that shifts, flat and capped, which
>      is §4.6's "footprint stays capped": there is no quarantine pool to exhaust.
>      **Deployment note.** The arena is a shared memory object, so the preference that governs it is
>      `transparent_hugepage/shmem_enabled`, not `transparent_hugepage/enabled`; the `MADV_COLLAPSE` ask above
>      goes through either way, so a deployment does not have to tune that knob, but a host that cannot find the
>      contiguous memory still gets no sandbox and the shift is refused.
>      **The mapping is placed, not found (2026-10-20).** A huge page behind a memory object is addressed twice
>      over — by where it sits in the process and by where it sits in the object — and the kernel forms one only
>      where the two agree. `mmap` left to choose guarantees neither, so the sandbox was reserved only on the
>      runs where it happened to land right: measured on Linux 6.12.76 (aarch64), 13 of 16 objects began off a
>      huge boundary, `MADV_COLLAPSE` is refused `EINVAL` on an incongruent span whichever end is aligned, and
>      eight volumes over their own objects were given a sandbox 0 of 8 or 8 of 8 by address alone. The window
>      is now placed congruently when the object is mapped (`slates-mem` `shared.rs`, `Mapped`), and those same
>      eight are reserved 8 of 8 on six consecutive runs
>      (`docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-dax-sandbox-was-reserved-by-mmap-address-luck.md`).
>      **Measured across the platforms and architectures slates targets, 2026-10-19** — the whole DAX suite
>      (59 tests), the device seam (36) and the daemon (23):
>      | Host | THP | L1 sandbox | Result |
>      |---|---|---|---|
>      | macOS 15 aarch64 | none for user programs (Appendix C) | refused | 59 pass, sandbox tests skip loudly |
>      | Linux x86_64 (adacachy, `shmem_enabled=[advise]`) | 2 MiB | reserved | 59 pass, no skip |
>      | Linux x86_64 (fedora 6.19.10, `shmem_enabled=[never]`) | 2 MiB | reserved via `MADV_COLLAPSE` | 59 pass, 0–4 skips by host state |
>      | Linux aarch64 (4 KiB base page) | 2 MiB | reserved | 59 pass, device seam 36 pass, daemon 23 pass |
>      | Linux aarch64 (6.12.76, `shmem_enabled=[never]`) | 2 MiB | reserved: placed, then `MADV_COLLAPSE` | 73 DAX pass, loud skips 3,1,0,1,2 → **0 across six runs** |
>      | Linux x86_64 (7.2.9, 4 KiB page, `shmem_enabled=[advise]`) | 2 MiB | reserved: placed, advice alone sufficed (8 MiB of 8 MiB) | 73 DAX pass, **0 skips across five runs**; mem, VFS, the 41-test recovery arbiter and 87 device-seam tests green (2026-10-20) |
>      | Windows x86_64 (cross-lint, `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`) | large pages need a privilege R10 refuses | refused | clippy clean over the Windows-buildable crates |
>      A low-trust *sacrificial pool* may deliberately co-locate mutually-untrusted tenants so they absorb each
>      other's leakage rather than the host — sound only paired with B2, and not built.
>    - **L2 — moving target (built, 68b4a9c5; removed 2026-11-01 with the arena windows, A-195).** `Volume::dax_migrate`
>      relocated a writable block to a physically
>      different block under the two-phase revoke (the new block pinned and its mapping minted before the old is
>      revoked-pending, the old held until the VMM confirms the unmap), so an attacker tracking physical rows loses
>      the target; the inode follows, so non-DAX readers never see a stale block. Placement is a pseudo-random stride
>      within the bounded sandbox (`stripe_target`), so memory stays capped and deterministic — no quarantine pool.
>      Measured 242 ns/migration for a 4 KiB block (`dax_bench`), so even *unconditional* migration at the 16–32 ms
>      RowPress cadence costs <0.01% throughput; migration is meant to be *adaptive* — triggered only for blocks
>      showing a hammer signature — so honest agents run at native DAX speed with zero migration overhead. The trigger
>      must come from a signal the unprivileged daemon can see (SETUPMAPPING / fault cadence) or a privileged
>      OS-shipped broker's PEBS/IBS, since a pure direct-write hammer is invisible to the daemon; this is why the
>      strategy leans on *contain* (L1 zones) and *heal* (B2) over *detect*. slates is RAM-only, so the migration copy
>      is DRAM↔DRAM with no write-endurance cost — the PMEM-endurance concern does not apply to slates' arena.
>    - **B2 — self-healing net (built, 6922fcf2; **wired 2026-10-19**; removed 2026-11-01 with the arena windows,
>      A-195).** `Store::dax_guard` recorded a read-only
>      mapping's clean BLAKE3 and a pinned clean copy; `Store::dax_scrub` catches a flip the daemon never saw and
>      restores the block from the clean copy (`Healed`), or reports `Unhealable` if both are corrupt. Sound only
>      for read-only content (a writable block changes legitimately, so a checksum cannot tell a flip from a
>      write); read-only is the L0 default, so B2 covers the common case. The clean copy is bounded by the
>      registry cap and freed on revoke.
>      **The guard is the owner's opt-in** (`Volume::enable_dax_integrity_guard`), off by default and symmetric
>      with L0's: it costs a BLAKE3 of the block and a second copy of it per mapping, worth paying where
>      untrusted tenants share the host's DRAM and pure overhead where they do not — and slates cannot see the
>      host's other tenants, so it cannot make that call. A guard the shard has no room for is counted
>      (`DaxRegistry::guards_refused`) and the mapping served unguarded: the net is under the map, never a
>      condition of it.
>      **The net never writes through a block that is not still this mapping's.** A scrub acts only when the
>      mapping is live, its block is **pinned**, *and* the mapping is still **current** for its inode. Each
>      catches a different way an entry outlives what it describes, and the first two alone were not enough:
>      an unpinned block may already be released and scrubbed, so healing it put a deleted file's plaintext back
>      into free memory — and a released block **re-allocated to another file is pinned again**, so the pin
>      check passes while the bytes belong to someone else and a heal overwrites a live file with a dead one's
>      content. Both are the cross-tenant disclosure this gate exists to prevent, performed by its own net
>      (`docs/bugs/2026-10-19-the-self-healing-net-resurrects-a-deleted-files-plaintext.md`); both were found by
>      the four-layer chaos property, the second *after* the first was fixed. Only a `Volume` can answer the
>      currency question, so the sliced pass is `Volume::dax_scrub_slice` and the reap tick walks volumes as the
>      shift loop does. The state arises from the shared per-block pin recorded in item 2 above, which stays
>      owed; refusing to write through a stale entry is sound whatever created it.
>      **The pass runs on the reap tick** (`daemon::scrub_guarded_windows`), in cooperative slices of
>      `archive_slice_bytes` — the archive walk's budget, because this spends it the same way, BLAKE3 over
>      content under the shard's own step quantum. A flip in read-only content is invisible to slates by
>      construction, since no write explains it and no code path can notice, so looking for it on a timer is the
>      only thing that can find it. A guard whose mapping has gone is dropped as the pass reaches it, so the list
>      stays bounded without a second sweep.
>    The modern window is 16–32 ms and RowPress leaks across refresh windows, so the migration interval is derived
>    from the lowest hammer threshold, not the classic 64 ms. **The arena's four layers were built, driven and proven
>    by use** in `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs` until A-195 removed them with the arena windows (2026-11-01): L0 refused
>    writable arena DAX by default, L1 contained a writable window in a verified huge page with guard rows, L2 moved it
>    every hammer window, and B2 found and healed a flip in read-only content. The backed route, the only one now, has
>    its own placement and guard rows (above) and none of the other three, for the reasons stated there. Nothing in the set is a primitive without a caller. **The daemon→device half is settled and built** (2026-10-19). The earlier text left
>    a choice between a backend-initiated remap and "the revoke-and-refault path instead, and accept the tear"; the
>    second is taken, because the objection recorded against it no longer holds. `Volume::dax_migrate` now enqueues
>    `(inode, writable_only = true)` on the queue the device already drains every service pass
>    (`AdmittedDevice::service` → `tear_down_inode_windows`), and `writable_only` tears this inode's *writable*
>    windows only — which, since a writable map is the single-block open path, is exactly the window being shifted,
>    leaving any read-only window of the same inode alone. That was the whole of the objection ("an inode-global
>    revoke would tear every window of the inode"), written before the flag existed. The guest re-faults, its
>    SETUPMAPPING runs `Volume::dax_map_write`, and the live-window path finds the freshly-minted mapping and maps
>    the row the content moved to. Proven through the real device by
>    `a_shift_tells_the_device_so_the_guests_window_follows_the_content`, which ran (not skipped) on adacachy
>    2026-10-19. The remap was rejected for now on a measured structural ground, not a preference: under
>    `DaxPlacer::Message` a `SHMEM_MAP` parks the *guest's* chain and is finished by `complete_parked_map`, which
>    exists to answer a guest request, so a daemon-initiated map needs a second, chain-less completion arm — new
>    asynchronous state in the device's most delicate path, bought for one guest fault per shift.
>    **The trigger was built** (`daemon::dax_shift_loop`, 2026-10-19; removed 2026-11-01, A-195): once every hammer window — 16 ms, the lowest
>    of §4.6's stated 16–32 ms range — the shard shifts every live writable DAX window onto a different physical
>    row of its tenant's sandbox, unconditionally, in cooperative slices of `copy_slice_bytes` (half the
>    shard's live step quantum at the machine's measured memcpy rate) with a yield between them. Unconditional is
>    what the measurement affords: 242 ns per 4 KiB block, so a window moved every 16 ms costs under 0.01% of its
>    own throughput and nothing has to *detect* a hammer first. The round takes one snapshot of each volume's
>    writable windows and works through that — a shift mints a new mapping, so a list re-read mid-round would
>    offer the same content again and the sweep would chase its own tail.
>    **It costs an idle laptop nothing.** The hammer cadence is kept only while the shard holds a volume opted
>    into writable DAX (L0); otherwise the loop waits the liveness budget it already waits for its other periodic
>    work, so a daemon with no writable DAX adds no wakeup. The bound that buys: a volume opting in between two
>    long waits is first shifted up to one liveness budget later. Shifting is defence in depth over L1's
>    containment and the host's ECC/TRR floor, so that is bounded exposure rather than a hole; the fix is for the
>    opt-in to wake the loop rather than for the loop to poll, and it is recorded in the gap ledger.
>    The adaptive trigger from a privileged broker's PEBS/IBS — shifting only blocks showing a hammer signature,
>    so honest agents pay nothing — is the optimization on top of this, not its precondition.

> **Superseded 2026-11-01 (A-195).** The device no longer maps content blocks, so none of the revoke, recall or
> re-validation below runs: both placers map per-file backings, a moved view refills them, and a snapshot recalls
> nothing.
>
> **Status (DAX device-seam wiring, 2026-10-15).** The device side of the gate is built against the in-process
> virtio-fs seam and proven by a simulated guest (no KVM): `crates/bridge-virtiofs` serves a real
> SETUPMAPPING/REMOVEMAPPING over a `DaxCacheRegion` (the VMM cache fd overlaid with `MAP_FIXED`), and the three
> teardown obligations the body states ("mappings must be revoked before reuse or `advance` completes") are wired to
> the VFS and ride the production serve loop. (1) A write or truncate of a mapped inode enqueues a two-phase revoke
> the device drains before the block is unpinned (munmap before unpin). (2) `snapshot`/clone recalls the volume's
> *writable* windows before it freezes a shared block, refusing retryable until the device has drained — and, while
> it waits, **excluding new writable windows of that volume** (`DaxRegistry::begin_recall`; `Volume::dax_map_write`
> refuses `RecallInFlight`). The exclusion is not tidiness: without it a guest re-maps between two retries and the
> snapshot is back where it started, which a hostile guest can keep up forever. It lasts across retries, so it
> belongs to the thing that retries — the `snapshot` verb begins it and ends it on every answer but the retryable
> one, and `destroy` ends it too; the VFS revoke deliberately does not begin it, since `Volume::snapshot` has no
> moment at which the snapshot is over. Read-only windows are admitted throughout. **The wait is unbounded on
> purpose.** A lease that took the window back on lapse — the shape a write delegation uses — would be wrong here:
> a delegation is held by a cooperating client slates can refuse, while a DAX window is a page table entry in an
> unmodified guest kernel that only the VMM's `munmap` removes, and unpinning on a lapse would hand the block to
> another allocation while the guest still points at it. Closing the backend connection does not unmap it either.
> So a snapshot facing a hung VMM refuses until it can freeze safely, bounded in practice by the client's own reply
> deadline. (3) **`advance`
> revokes on the moving reader**, as the attachment lifecycle requires ("`advance` … invalidates old caches/mappings …
> cannot combine old names with new bytes"): the advancing attachment's own device re-validates its windows against the
> now-current view (`Device::revalidate_windows` → `Bridge::dax_window_current` → `Volume::dax_still_current`) and
> tears only those whose content block the new view no longer holds — the changed inodes — keeping every window onto
> unchanged, block-shared content; a device whose view did not move tears nothing, so the volume-wide kick from
> `snapshot_view::advanced` (`virtiofs::kick_volume_devices`) is self-scoping. This is eager by necessity, not taste:
> the DAX client is an unmodified guest kernel that speaks only FUSE and never sees the control-plane `advance`, so a
> lingering window would surface the old snapshot's bytes through the guest's own page table with no signal to re-map —
> a stale cross-version read only the host can prevent. The teardown is proportional to the real delta
> (`paths_changed_between`), on a rare control-plane re-pin, never a per-op cost. All of this is a no-op in production
> while DAX stays unadvertised (the FUSE_INIT flag is withheld until the tamper-proof/fleet registry and a DAX-capable
> VMM are in place) and correct the moment it is advertised. Proven by use:
> `an_advance_revalidate_tears_the_stale_window_and_keeps_the_current_one`, the step-5 and snapshot-recall cases
> (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`), and `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs`. The authorized window is the file's own
> pages — `file_len` rounded up to the window granule (`DaxCacheRegion::page`), capped at the block — not the buddy
> block's power-of-two padding; a request reaching past the file is capped to those pages and a map starting entirely
> past them is refused (`a_setupmapping_reaching_past_the_file_is_capped_to_its_authorized_pages`); the sub-file tail
> of the last page reads zero by the map-time scrub, so the surface the host shares with a guest is the file's pages
> and no more.

> **Status (slates' own device maps per-file backings for an out-of-process VMM, 2026-10-25, A-168).** For the
> message placer (crosvm over vhost-user), this supersedes the content-block windows the records below describe:
> pinning, the two-phase revoke and `reopen`-on-map now serve the fd-sharing placer and the in-process maps only (until
> A-195 removed them, 2026-11-01: both placers map backings now). A
> real crosvm guest read stale bytes, then zeros, through the old windows after another path's write
> (`docs/bugs/2026-10-24-slates-own-dax-window-shows-stale-bytes-then-zeros-after-another-paths-write.md`): a Linux guest
> keeps the 2 MiB ranges it mapped and never asks again, the vhost-user specification forbids a map over a live one,
> and crosvm's unmap leaves zero pages. A window now maps the file's backing (A-163's object, one per attachment and
> file, never moved), kept equal to the file by the volume's single write boundary, so no change ever reaches the
> window as a message:
> - a SETUPMAPPING is held while the asked ranges are filled a copy slice a turn, then sent as one SHMEM_MAP of the
>   backing (`fd_offset` the file offset), and answered on the front end's ack;
> - the front end maps every window writable when the attachment may write, so a guest's writable upgrade of a live
>   window is answered with no message;
> - the guest's stores reach the volume at FSYNC, FLUSH, RELEASE, READ, FORGET, DESTROY and the device's end, a refused
>   write-back failing the request that asked for it; beneath an overlay, a reply that could reveal the disk's change
>   waits for the refill.
>
> Built in `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/backed.rs` and `device.rs` (`Device::dax_turn`), driven by the serve loop each
> pass. Proven by eleven hermetic tests against a stand-in front end that maps what SHMEM_MAP sends
> (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`) and two unit tests of the module's parsers, on Linux x86_64; the pre-fix
> code fails the same checks (stale bytes, then the window torn), and eight mutations each fail their own test. The descriptor a VMM gets authorizes one file's bytes by
> construction, so the `udmabuf` confinement (A-138) is gone with its device dependency. **Proven through a real
> crosvm guest the same day** (G-vhost step 3, A-169's last bullet): `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs` boots crosvm

> the live map (step 4): a dead VM's unsynced stores land at the stream's end, and the daemon's death ends the VM with
> nothing synced lost; the daemon kill found A-170.

> **Status (one window kind: both placers map per-file backings, and no path maps the arena's blocks into a guest,
> 2026-11-01, A-195).** The fd-sharing placer, an in-process VMM's window that the device overlays itself, maps per-file

> (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/backed.rs`, every Unix now). It overlays each piece of a window with `MAP_FIXED` of the
> backing's object and acknowledges each at once, through the completion the message placer's acknowledgements use, so
> a window is recorded whole or refused whole. A REMOVEMAPPING restores each piece's range to the inert reservation
> before its answer. A piece whose unmap the host refuses keeps its window and its backing, which stays equal to the
> file, counted `virtiofs.dax_unmaps_refused`: each overlay splits the reservation, so a process at `vm.max_map_count`
> is refused `ENOMEM`.
>
> Everything only the arena's windows used is removed, not kept beside the backings (A-195 lists each): the VFS's DAX

> **Status (DAX: live vhost-user binding, inline files, and the at-rest-sealing limit, 2026-10-16).** The device-seam
> wiring above is now proven against a *real* VMM, inline files map, and the file-shape scope with its one hard limit
> is settled. **The message-based vhost-user DAX binding is built and proven end to end on x86_64 Linux (KVM):** a
> real crosvm guest mounts the volume `-o dax=always` and reads a 32 KiB file through an `mmap`, getting the exact
> bytes back — the read went `FUSE_SETUPMAPPING` → `VHOST_USER_BACKEND_SHMEM_MAP` over the back-end channel and slates
> mapped the content block into the guest's DAX window, not FUSE_READ (`crates/client/examples/crosvm_dax_ab`, the
> recorded A/B; the non-DAX arm reads the same file over FUSE_READ). The async map-ack park — `serve_dax` sends
> SHMEM_MAP and parks the chain, the serve loop awaits the back-end-request fd and `complete_dax_awaiting` answers the
> guest on the ack — mirrors the landing barrier, and has an in-tree hermetic proof with a stand-in front end
> (`a_message_based_setupmapping_parks_until_the_front_end_acks_then_answers_the_guest`,
> `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`). **Inline files map too:** a file whose bytes live in the inode (no
> content block) is materialized into a throwaway page block the mapping owns, exactly as a directory's entries are
> (`Volume::dax_map_read`'s inline branch over `map_owned_block`,
> `an_inline_file_is_mapped_read_only_through_a_materialized_block`); this fixed a latent bug where a materialized
> (snapshot) mapping read as permanently stale on the local-client path — `dax_still_current` compared a throwaway
> block against `file_block` and now returns `is_live` for a snapshot mapping, as the guest path (`dax_read_raw`)
> already did.
>
> **The one hard limit — multi-block files — and why.** A file larger than one chunk (`chunk_bytes`, 64 KiB on a
> 4 KiB page) reads correctly over **FUSE_READ** but is not zero-copy-DAX-mapped, because of **at-rest sealing
> (A-92/A-99)**: a sealed chunk's arena block holds AES-GCM **ciphertext** (`ChunkSeal`; a read decrypts through
> `open_into`), and `Body::Open` holds exactly one *open* (plaintext) chunk over its sealed ones — so every chunk but
> the open tail is ciphertext a guest's MMU would read raw. FUSE_READ is the copy path the body sanctions where
> zero-copy is not physically possible.
>
> **Decision (DAX maps the open frontier; one representation, no cache; supersedes both a volume-wide plaintext-at-rest
> opt-out and a decrypted-chunk cache).** A cache of decrypted chunks was considered and **rejected**: it is a second
> copy of the content and would owe coherence against every mutation (write, truncate, snapshot, advance, migrate,
> takeover) — the divergent state (staleness, invalidation races, a parallel store) slates is built to *not* have
> (single writer per volume, no global catalog, invalidate-by-revoke). DAX instead uses the chunk's *own* single live
> representation: a chunk is **open** (plaintext, the canonical bytes the inode points at) **or sealed** (ciphertext),
> and `reopen` is a transition between them, never a coexisting copy. **The rule: a DAX window exists only over a
> chunk in its open (plaintext) state; a sealed chunk falls back to FUSE_READ.** Three lifecycle transitions govern a
> window, each on machinery already built:
> - **Map.** A `SETUPMAPPING` whose offset is in the open chunk maps it (the existing DAX pin on the block, the
>   existing cap to the file's pages); an offset in a sealed chunk is refused and the guest FUSE_READs that range.
>   Because a file has at most one open chunk, the device maps **at most one chunk per file** — no
>   N-`SHMEM_MAP`-per-request and no N-ack park; it is the single-chunk map path plus a sealed-refuse gate.
> - **Write to a mapped chunk.** The existing step-5 two-phase revoke fires and the guest re-faults onto the new
>   bytes; unchanged.
> - **The chunk cools (the idle sweep would seal it).** The one new interaction, on existing tools. By default the
>   **pin defers the seal**: the DAX pin already stops reuse/free of a mapped block, and it extends to stop the
>   *encrypt*, since sealing a block the guest is reading would swap plaintext→ciphertext under its live MMU — so a
>   mapped chunk stays open for the map's life and seals when the last window drops. The exception is **growth**: if
>   the writer appends past the mapped chunk a new tail must open and the body holds exactly one open chunk, so the
>   mapped chunk is **force-sealed** — its windows two-phase-revoked first (the snapshot-recall pattern:
>   revoke-pending, wait for the device to confirm the unmap and cross-core TLB flush, then encrypt) and the guest
>   re-faults onto FUSE_READ.
>
> The only genuinely new wiring is "a pin defers a seal, and a forced seal revokes first," strictly symmetric with "a
> pin defers a free" and "a write revokes." The guest sees zero-copy over the hot/open frontier it is using and
> transparent FUSE_READ for cooled or never-touched content — DAX tracks the working set *by construction*, not by a
> store that can go stale. The cost, stated plainly: a chunk is plaintext-at-rest while a window pins it open (bounded
> by the map), the same "plaintext only while in use" A-99 already allows for an open block — no new exposure class,
> no second copy. **Owed (advertisement-gated):** the gate that maps the open chunk at a `SETUPMAPPING`'s offset and
> refuses a sealed one; the pin-defers-seal and force-seal-revoke wiring in the seal/open paths (the recovery oracle
> the arbiter); the device's sealed-refuse; and a multi-block harness A/B (the open tail zero-copy, the sealed body
> FUSE_READ). **Gated follow-on (b):** `reopen`-on-map — a read-only map of a *cold* sealed chunk could flip it
> sealed→open (the same pin/revoke, still one representation, no cache), giving a never-edited large file zero-copy
> too, at the cost of a read/map triggering a canonical state change (it allocates, decrypts, can fail `NoSpace`,
> dirties the recovery image, adds re-seal churn) — built only if a read-only-large-file zero-copy workload asks for
> it. (`GAPS.md`.)
>
> **Reconciled 2026-11-06 (VFS plan Step 15).** Every item owed here was built (9b67ce65, 5c5ee15b) and then
> superseded by A-195 (da8a7516): a window maps a per-file plaintext backing, so sealing at rest no longer meets DAX.

> **Amendment (2026-10-17): a live guest disproved the rule above; the backing is `reopen`-on-map with a learned
> re-seal hold.** Rule (a) was taken to a real crosvm guest and failed on its central premise. A guest's single
> `SETUPMAPPING` spans a whole DAX range (2 MiB at `FUSE_DAX_SHIFT`), **not one chunk**, so the device must back
> *every* chunk in the requested range — an N-map loop with an N-ack park for the message-based placer, exactly what
> (a) claimed to avoid. And a refused sealed chunk does not fall back politely: the guest's `dax=always` mmap
> **SIGBUSes**, because the range it was promised is not backed. A sealed chunk inside a mapped range must therefore
> be *backed*, not refused.
>
> Both candidate backings were built in full, on separate branches, and measured head to head (`BENCHMARKS.md`
> 2026-10-17): the **view** (a decrypted read-only throwaway the mapping owns, the canonical chunk left ciphertext)
> and **reopen** (the chunk's own representation transitioned sealed→open, decrypted in place, re-encrypted when the
> window is gone — formerly the gated follow-on (b)). Both carry a live guest's multi-block mmap byte-for-byte.
> Measured: the view costs **one byte of RAM per byte simultaneously mapped** (slope 1.0 over 256×), and a real guest
> **fills its DAX cache exactly** (an 8 MiB cache gave an 8.000 MiB high-water, a 4 MiB cache 4.000 MiB), so the view's
> cost is the whole advertised cache — 256 MiB at the harness's own setting, in a RAM-only system. Reopen costs no
> mapped-set RAM; it pays one extra AES-GCM pass per chunk per cold cycle (+0.08–0.18 s per GiB streamed) and is ~8×
> faster when the guest returns to a chunk it still holds plaintext. **Decision: reopen.** The view is recorded
> measured-and-rejected.
>
> **The re-seal hold is learned, not chosen.** A reopened chunk must be re-encrypted once its window is gone, but
> re-sealing a chunk the guest is about to ask for again pays an encrypt and a decrypt for nothing. Against a real
> guest the revoke→remap interval moved **8× (67 ms to 537 ms) for one workload merely by changing the guest's DAX
> cache**, so no fixed delay is right for every deployment. The volume therefore learns its own: the hold starts at
> zero (re-seal as soon as the window drops) and grows by one sweep each time the gate catches a re-seal the guest
> immediately undid, resetting when the volume goes quiescent so a new workload re-learns. The sweep is the hold's
> clock, so it needs no timestamp. Its ceiling is derived, not picked: the idle sweep already leaves a write's bytes
> in the clear for one to two ticks before sealing them, and a mapped read must not get a weaker at-rest guarantee
> than an ordinary write, so the hold is capped at that same window (policy may lower it).
>
> **Cost, stated plainly.** A reopened chunk is plaintext at rest while a window pins it and for at most the learned
> hold after — bounded, and never longer than a written chunk already waits to be sealed. One representation
> throughout: no cache, no second copy, no coherence to owe.

> **Status (virtio-fs, 2026-09-13).** The owned FUSE-over-virtio device exists
> (`crates/bridge-virtiofs`) and the daemon serves it on the volume's owning shard
