**A VMM with no folder sharing: the disk-image form (A-160).** A volume reaches a VM as a host mount shared in by the
VMM (`docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 item 7). Firecracker shares no folder: it has only block and pmem devices backed by
files. So a volume reaches it as an image file, and the guest's writes come back as a session's do, by a merge into a
clone:
- `slates image build ID SNAPSHOT NAME --capacity SIZE` writes the snapshot's tree as ext2 revision 1 into the file
  `image.ext2` of a new volume, which pins the snapshot (`BaseRecord::Image`);
- the guest's drive is that file read through a slates mount, writable;
- `slates image merge IMAGE NAME` reads the image at a snapshot of the image volume, as hostile input, and makes a new
  clone of the build's snapshot hold its tree. A node the build wrote, still at its number with the build's
  generation, keeps its inode, so a renamed file is renamed and an unchanged file's chunks stay shared. It is not an
  inferred merge (D-27): nothing else writes the clone, and the image's tree becomes its state.

Both verbs defer their reply to a task of the owner shard, which runs the work one unit a call in slices bounded by the
clock and releases what it made in slices after the reply. No unit's work follows a directory, a tree or a file: a
directory is read, measured and closed an entry or a block at a time, arrays grow a segment at a time, a file's
indirect blocks are computed one at a time, and the longest unit measured was 18.5 µs at 100,000 nodes on the box
(BENCHMARKS, 2026-10-24).

> **Status (2026-10-24).** Built and proven: `crates/image` (the format), `crates/vfs/src/image.rs` (the walk, the
> I/O and the merge), `crates/server/src/image.rs` (the verbs), `slates image`. A real Firecracker v1.17.0 microVM on
> the box read every node of a volume through its image, changed it, and the merge held a clone to exactly its tree
> (`crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs`, gated). Not carried: extended attributes, birth times, holes. Not yet run: a pmem
> drive (DAX on the image file). The details and the evidence are A-160's.

**A Shards microVM: the fs stream form (A-161).** Shards' VMM forwards each guest FUSE request to a backend over a Unix
stream it is handed: one request framed as a little-endian length, one reply frame back, and control asks of its own
marked by the length word's top bit (its fs device). Its VM process is App-Sandboxed on macOS and cannot open a socket,
so the backend's end reaches it as a descriptor. The daemon is that backend:
- an attach with the Shards form (a directory or the whole volume, for reading or for writing within the principal's
  rights, a write taking the lease) makes an anonymous socket pair, records the attachment (`AttachForm::ShardsFs`,
  a guest's) and serves its end on the volume's owner shard; the other end is the attachment's capability, handed to
  whoever attached. On Windows, which has no socket pair without a socket file, the pair is a duplex named pipe
  connected to itself under a fresh 128-bit name, one instance, remote clients refused, a descriptor for the owner
  alone; its server end is served by the shard's IOCP driver and its client end is duplicated into the attaching
  client's process (A-179);
- a stream end may go to a VMM where a content object may not (A-135): the daemon answers nothing on it but the one
  attachment;
- requests are answered by the shared FUSE dispatch, a durable change published before its reply as a virtio-fs
  guest's is, and the guest is revalidated, having no path for an invalidation; a `close`'s `FLUSH` publishes nothing
  of its own while the write log holds every write the shard acknowledged, as a FUSE mount's does (A-63's flush rule,
  A-399), since a successor replays them all;
- a read is answered with every byte it asks, never cut to a buffer, since a short read is the file's end to the
  guest's kernel;
- the guest's own attribute namespaces, `trusted.` and `security.`, and its POSIX ACLs are kept in the volume as its
  data and shown to no host's mount (A-290, A-302, §4.5 "Extended attributes"); an ACL's named owners are kept through
  the stream's owner view; the guest's kernel is asked to enforce its ACLs, which the shared seam keeps in step with
  the mode and gives at every create under a default ACL (A-314), and to send SETXATTR in its extended form, which says
  when an access ACL's setter is outside the file's group so the file's set-group-ID bit goes (A-378); an acknowledged
  attribute change is published before its reply;
- Shards' owner word (`trusted.shards.owner`, its value `UID:GID`) is the stream's to take, never a file's attribute
  (A-281). Shards' init sets it on a share's root as it mounts the share, so that a run of an unprivileged user can
  write the share it was given. It is read in the SETXATTR form the stream's INIT kept, the extended one where the
  guest's kernel kept `FUSE_SETXATTR_EXT`, as the dispatch reads every other SETXATTR (A-587). It is taken from the
  guest's root on the stream's root alone, and refused otherwise
  as Shards' own server refuses it: `EPERM` from any other caller, `EINVAL` on any other node or for a value that is
  no `UID:GID`. From then on the guest is shown the owner the volume keeps for the stream's root as the run's owner,
  and the run's owner as the root's, uid and gid each. The ids the guest names (a creator's, a chown's) are kept the
  other way round, so a chown and the stat after it agree and two owners never become one. Every other route sees the
  owners the volume keeps, so the host reads what the run made as its own;
- a DAX window's descriptor ask is answered with a descriptor of one shared-memory object per attachment and file,
  holding only that file's bytes (A-163). The store names the file by its volume's own prefix and its inode number
  together, since a clone, and a snapshot a device presents, shares its origin's numbers (A-166). The object is sized
  once to `2^63 − 2 MiB` and never resized. Every range an ask touches is kept equal from then on, past the file's end
  too, since a guest maps by a size another path may have cut (A-167). It is filled from the volume a
  range at a time as asked, every change of the file through any path written into it before the change returns, and
  the guest's stores written back at its FSYNC, FLUSH, RELEASE and FORGET and the stream's end. A range whose fill is
  refused or given up part-way is left uncleared: no change reaches it, it stays counted against the fill budget, and
  its next fill clears it before storing anything, since a fill skips holes and pages of zeros (A-419). So there is no revoke
  and no message to the device; the stream offers per-inode DAX (`FUSE_HAS_INODE_DAX`, `FUSE_ATTR_DAX` on files of a
  range or more) while the shard's fill budget has room. On Windows (A-180) the object is a section under A-175's
  confining descriptor, reserved at the machine's memory and committed a range at a time. It is duplicated into the
  process the ask names, once the handle that process names is shown to be this stream's own object;
- a VM's save and restore (Shards' D176 part 5; A-303): a SAVE, which the device sends while it is paused and so
  between requests, waits for the guest's stores through its maps to reach the volume, then takes a snapshot of the
  volume for the attachment's own principal, publishes it, waits on a live-shipped volume until its log is durable
  where that publication put it, as a guest's `fsync` waits (A-516; refused with its reason when it is not within the
  liveness budget), and is answered with the stream's tables, opaque to Shards and checked by a CRC-32C: the volume
  and the snapshot, the directory presented, the owner view, the form of SETXATTR the guest's kernel sends (A-378),
  and each inode the guest holds with its references and opens. A RESTORE is taken
  only as a fresh stream's first frame, onto the volume saved while unchanged since the cut or a clone of the cut's
  snapshot, presenting the same directory; the stream's attachment then holds what the saved one did, a file the guest
  held with no name left included, its guest is shown the same owners and its requests are read in the same form. A handle the restored guest's kernel kept gives its open back at its release, as one from
  before a takeover does (A-152). Anything else is refused with its reason, and changes nothing;
- a resync channel beside the stream (A-316; `slates_bridge_fuse::shards_resync`), for a stream to outlive its
  daemon on Shards' coordinator's conditions (2026-11-18): a pair made at the attach, whose first message, `Attached`,
  names the attachment and its resync token, 128 bits from the daemon's secure random and never its mount capability.
  On Linux it is a sequenced-packet pair whose device end follows the stream's on the client's control socket; on
  macOS (A-339) a stream of 28-byte messages, since a datagram pair's survivor is never told its peer has gone, whose
  device end rides beside the stream's in the socket route's confirmation; on Windows (A-427) a message-mode pipe whose
  device end is duplicated into the attaching client beside the stream's (`ShardsHanded`'s `resync`), the daemon's end
  held by the anchor's exchange before the stream serves anything and its session (with the process holding the stream,
  its id and creation time) told by `Record` before any reply that rests on a change (A-423), and whose `Resync` names
  the fresh end's handle in that process, where the successor duplicates it (A-418, A-433), since no descriptor rides a
  message there; `slates shards` hands the device end where `{resync}` stands (A-433). The daemon's end is
  held by the anchor, as a FUSE device is, and the daemon keeps its own copy while the anchor holds one (A-339: XNU's
  collector of descriptors in flight flushes a socket whose every copy rides a message), with the token, the stream's
  owner view and its kernel's SETXATTR form as its session (A-378), updated when the guest names its owner, when its
  kernel's `INIT` is answered and when a RESTORE takes a saved guest's tables, and released when the attachment ends.
  A stream whose guest maps files with DAX keeps its resync (A-365): the anchor holds each file's DAX object before its
  first descriptor goes to the device, and the shard's DAX range table in anchor RAM records each range answered and
  whether it was asked writable, a slot a range, its slots derived from the fill budget; a refusal of either gives the
  resync up, as a stream did at its first map before A-365, since the guest's stores live where only the device maps
  them once the daemon is gone. On Windows (A-448) the anchor holds a duplicate of each file's section that maps read
  and write and may ask its size, which the section's confining descriptor lets no holder widen (A-175); its hold is an
  exchange, so the answer naming the section waits for it, as a reply waits for the session's `Record`; its id is the
  backing's marked apart from every attachment's, since the Windows anchor keeps one table of ids; and the sections are
  held to a bound of their own, `shards × dax_range_slots`, past which a hold is refused `Bound` and the stream gives
  its resync up, while the attachments' mounts and resync ends keep theirs.
  A successor takes the held DAX objects back while recovery rebuilds the shard, at the very handles their backings
  had, dormant through the write log's replay (each already holds every write the dead daemon made to its ranges, in
  order with its guest's stores), and its stream ingests their writable ranges before it serves anything, wakes them so
  every change reaches them again, and answers the device's new asks with the same objects: on Windows each ask after
  the `Resync` gets the same section duplicated into the holder again, the holder's handle of the fresh stream being a
  known holder's for the claim check (A-448), and a file whose section the anchor did not hand back is asked for again
  at its next answer, never assumed held. It hands the device a fresh
  stream over the channel in a `Resync` naming the same token, and keeps its own copy of
  the fresh end until the device shows it holds its own, by its first bytes on the stream or by its end of the channel
  closing, which the stream's task watches for meanwhile (A-339: the `Resync` waits in the device's channel until the
  device reads it, and a socket whose every copy rides a message is what macOS's collector flushes); the device takes
  nothing else (default deny), resends its outstanding request whole, and asks again for its DAX descriptors; the
  successor answers a request the dead daemon published and never answered from that reply, never by running it
  again;
- the peer's close, a hostile frame, a detach, a revocation, the volume's destroy and the daemon's stop end the
  attachment one way: its references swept, its record removed, its resync channel released. A daemon's death ends
  nothing by itself: recovery keeps a Shards attachment whose resync end the anchor held (Linux, A-316; macOS, A-339)
  and serves it on a fresh stream, its owner view, its SETXATTR form and token from the hold, its references and opens
  from the image, the reply the dead daemon published and never wrote answering the request the device resends, and
  the writes it acknowledged and the lookups its guest gave back (`FORGET`, A-390) after its last publication replayed
  from the write log (A-63) as a mount's are; on Windows too (A-433), its fresh end duplicated into the holder the
  session names, checked by its creation time. On Windows, a stream with no held resync end ends at a death,
  and the writes it acknowledged after its last publication are replayed into the volume all the same (A-402). Where that log overflowed, the guest is told every file it had open may
  have lost writes, as a taken-over mount's kernel is (`LostWrites`, A-393): a handle from before the death answers its
  `flush` `EIO` until an `fsync` through it has, once. It removes any other's record, as before.

> **Status (2026-10-24).** Built and proven by use, in-process: `crates/server/src/shards.rs` (the serve task),
> `crates/ipc/src/stream.rs` (the pair), `crates/bridge-fuse/src/shards_fs.rs` (the frames and their answers),
> `Daemon::attach_shards_stream`, with seven tests against a real daemon (`crates/server/tests/shards.rs`). Over the
> wire: on Linux `attach` with `AttachRequest::ShardsFs` sends the end over the client's control socket just before the
> reply, from either shard; on macOS the reply carries a single-use secret and the client claims the end on the
> daemon's socket route, an exchange keyed by HKDF-SHA256 and sealed with AES-256-GCM (`slates_ipc::route`,
> `crates/server/src/shards_route.rs`). On Windows (A-179, 2026-10-26) the reply names the value of the pipe's client
> end, which the daemon duplicated into the client's process (`ReplyBody::ShardsHanded`); the serve loop is the same
> code over `crates/server/src/shards/end.rs`, whose Windows arm is a `slates_rt::pipe::PipeEnd`. A DAX descriptor ask
> there is answered with a section duplicated into the asking process once its claim to hold the stream is checked
> (A-180, G-shards-windows step 5). `Client::attach_shards` takes
> every form. `slates shards ID --fd N -- CMD` replaces itself with a program holding the end at
> descriptor `N`, so the attachment ends when the program's end closes. A real Shards microVM on this Mac mounts, reads and
> writes a volume the daemon serves this way (part 2: 3 of 3 boots, Shards' patch sent to its owner). DAX (part 3,
> A-163): built in `slates_mem::DaxObject`, `crates/server/src/shards/dax.rs` and `slates_vfs::shards_backing`, proven
> by use against a real daemon and, on this Mac, by a real Shards guest that maps a 3 MiB file with DAX, syncs a store
> that `slates read` then shows, and sees another attachment's rewrite in its same map (3 of 3, red-checked without
> ingest and without write-through). The details and the evidence are A-161's and A-163's. **Fixed 2026-10-25:** an
> ingest and a refill read a copy slice in one bridge call, which the volume bridge cuts at 256 KiB, so on a machine
> whose derived slice is longer (CI's ubuntu runner) a guest's stores past the cut never reached the volume at `FSYNC`
> and a refill zeroed its map past it; both now read a slice whole, and the oracle runs a whole range a slice on every
> machine (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-dax-slice-past-the-read-cap-dropped-a-guests-stores.md`).

> **Status (2026-10-26, `slates shards` on Windows, A-181).** `slates shards ID [--subtree DIR] [--read-only] -- CMD ...
> {handle} ...` attaches in the Shards form and starts CMD holding the stream end as a handle, its decimal value
> written wherever `{handle}` stands, as Shards' `--slates-fs-handle {handle}` takes it (`slates_ipc::stream::
> spawn_with`). No process replaces itself on Windows, so the command waits for CMD and exits with its code. Only CMD
> inherits the end: an inheritable duplicate exists for the one spawn, named in its handle list. Once CMD has the end,
> the command tells the daemon CMD holds it (`ShardsHolder`, judged by object against the command's own copy, A-180),
> so CMD is a known holder a VM's DAX claim is judged against, and then closes its own copy: the attachment lives
> exactly as long as CMD's end, as on Unix. CMD runs in a kill-on-close job only the command holds, so ending the
> command ends CMD, as exec's single process does on Unix. On jupiter, 2026-10-26, `crates/cli/tests/shards.rs` passes
> in each of 6 runs: a probe the command started reads a file through the handle it was named, and the daemon counts it
> added as a holder; the command exits with its program's code; the attachment ends as soon as the program closes its
> handle while the command still runs; a killed command takes its program and the attachment along.

> **Status (2026-10-27, G-shards-windows: a WHP guest maps with DAX).** A Shards microVM on Windows maps a slates file
> with DAX over the daemon's stream. On GitHub's windows-2025, against slates f71282e1 and Shards' `gpu`, the guest of
> `slates shards ID -- shards run ... --slates-fs-handle {handle} --share-window 64`:
> - maps `big` through its WHP window, whose ranges are views of the sections A-180 answers with;
> - stores through the map and fsyncs, and slates' read holds the store;
> - sees another attachment's change in its same map;
> - reads zeros past the end of a cut.
>
> It passed 3 of 3 in each of runs 40503725694, 40505101140 and 40521211082. With the window off the same guest finds no DAX (run
> 40521211082). GAPS records the pieces and what stays owed (arm64 Windows).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-281, the run's owner).** Built and proven by use. `slates_bridge_core::OwnerView` is the
> swap, its unit test reading every id both ways. `slates_bridge_fuse::shards_fs::owner_word` reads the word as
> Shards' server reads it, refusing a malformed or hostile one. The shared FUSE dispatch shows every attribute reply
> through the bridge's view and keeps every creator and chown through it (`crates/bridge-fuse/tests/shards_fs.rs`).
> On a real daemon, the stream takes the word and shows the host's files as the run's, while the daemon's NFS port
> reads the same files, and what the run made, as the host's; the word is kept on no file, and a second stream that

> stream (its `tests/slates_fs.rs`), after Shards' v0.8.0 tag and its bump of the slates revision it pins.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-290, the guest's attributes).** Built and proven by use. A stream and slates' own virtio-fs
> device keep a guest's `trusted.` and `security.` attributes as its data, read back over a second stream and after a
> daemon restart; the daemon's NFSv4.2 port, a host's FUSE dispatch and the AppleDouble view neither list nor set them,
> and a work's declaration of one is refused `Unsupported` (`crates/server/tests/shards.rs`, `virtiofs.rs`,
> `daemon.rs`; `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/shards_fs.rs`; `crates/bridge-core/tests/appledouble_view.rs`). An
> acknowledged attribute change is now published before its reply on every FUSE route.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-302, the guest's ACLs).** Built and proven by use. A stream keeps a guest's access and
> default ACLs, checked as Linux checks one, their named owners kept through the stream's owner view and read back as
> set over a second stream; a default ACL on a file is refused `EACCES`; a host's mount neither lists nor sets them
> (the codec now `crates/bridge-core/src/posix_acl.rs`; `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/shards_fs.rs`;
> `crates/server/tests/shards.rs`). They were not enforced, as Shards' own server enforces none; A-314 enforces them.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-314, the guest's ACLs enforced).** Built and proven by use, at the dispatch every guest route
> shares. A guest's INIT is answered with `FUSE_POSIX_ACL`, a host's without. Judged as a guest's kernel judges an access
> (Linux's `acl_permission_check` and `posix_acl_permission`, modelled in the test over what GETATTR and GETXATTR
> answer), a `setfacl -m u:4242:rw,u:4343:-` on a 0600 file makes it 0660 and lets 4242 read and write, 4343 nothing, the
> owning group read; a chmod 0640 through a host's mount is read back as the mask r--; a removal leaves the mode; a
> minimal ACL becomes the mode alone. A default ACL gives a file, a directory and a FIFO made under it the mode and
> ACLs Linux's `posix_acl_create` gives, the umask ignored, a symlink nothing, and a file a host's route makes there the
> same (`crates/bridge-fuse/tests/shards_fs.rs`; the rules' unit tests in `crates/bridge-core/src/posix_acl.rs`). Owed:
> a real guest's run (a Shards guest over a stream, a VM over slates' own virtio-fs device), and Shards' own server
> enforcing them too (Shards' side, after its v0.8.0 tag).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-378, the set-group-ID bit an ACL's set clears).** Built and proven by use. A guest's INIT is
> answered with `FUSE_SETXATTR_EXT` beside `FUSE_POSIX_ACL`, a host's with neither; an access ACL set in the extended

> (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`); a stream reads it from its INIT, and a restored stream, and a stream

> `shards_resync.rs`, `shards_resync_restart.rs`). Owed: a real guest's run, a non-member's `setfacl` on a

**Writeback and snapshot barrier.** Kernel/guest cache negotiation changes when writes reach
the owner. `snapshot`, `submit`, `advance`, clean `detach`, migration and archive must identify
the set of contributing writable attachments, stop admission into the closing generation,
request the supported client flush, drain accepted requests, and publish the root only after
all included writes are recorded with their bytes. New writes belong to the next generation;
no write may straddle both. A failed participant gives a typed incomplete barrier, not a clean
snapshot. Application buffers not submitted by the process remain outside this guarantee;
client `fsync` must reach the bridge and its declared durability boundary. Auto-seal of only
server-visible writes reports that narrower boundary and cannot claim to include dirty guest
pages. Mount setup and barrier latency are outside the O(1) root publication measurement.

> **Status (2026-09-21, the barrier over one registry; GAP-A9-4).** The daemon holds **one attachment
> registry per shard** (`ShardState::attachments`, the `slates-bridge-core` registry with generations
> and in-flight pins) that every transport's request on the shard's volumes rides: a mount's request is
> admitted under the registry attachment its capability maps to (`ShardState::mount_attachments`,
> admitted on the capability's first request, revoked and drained when the catalog attachment ends —
> a `detach`, the kernel's unmount (its own event since A-511), a destroy), the NFS export serving it through `Export::over` the
> shared registry rather than one it mints per request, and a guest device is admitted into the same
> registry (`bridge-virtiofs::admission::admit` takes the owner's registry; the device keeps only its
> id, and every service pass and its terminal step take the registry from the owner through
> `BridgeAccess`). `snapshot` runs `Attachments::barrier` over the volume before it freezes the root:
> every live attachment's generation closes — a request admitted before belongs to the snapshot, one
> after to the next — and a request still in flight (a consumer lost mid-request) is the typed
> `Refusal::BarrierIncomplete { attachment, generation }`, never a clean snapshot over it. The reply
> **says what the snapshot covers** (`Snapshotted.coverage: SnapshotCoverage { boundary,
> attachments_closed }`): `Complete` when no attachment could hold a write the daemon has not recorded
> (ring clients; write-through transports), `ServerVisible` when a closed attachment rides a transport
> whose kernel client buffers acknowledged writes it has not sent — the NFS client before its `COMMIT`
> — the narrower boundary this paragraph says an auto-seal must report rather than claim dirty pages;
> the FUSE writeback flush has no work left since writeback cache is refused at `FUSE_INIT` (the
> 2026-09-19 correction under "Linux"). And the attachment record no longer stays `path: None`: a host
> mount reports the mount point it established (`BindMount { attachment, path }` → `AttachForm::
> ChosenPath`, §4.4 `Binding → Bound`; `slates mount` binds after `mount_nfs` and takes the mount down
> again if the bind is refused), only its principal may bind it, an SDK attachment has no mount point
> to bind, and `status` lists the bound mounts (bounded by a mount budget, the rest counted). Proven
> by use over the real NFS socket (`crates/server/tests/nfs_mount.rs`: a snapshot before any mount is
> complete and closes nothing, over the written mount it is server-visible and closes one, the mount
> serves on under the next generation, and after the mount's end (a `detach`, the kernel's `UMNT` ending nothing since
> A-511) the next snapshot closes nothing again; a bound mount point listed, another principal and an SDK attachment refused, the detach
> unlisting it), by the device suites over the shared registry (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests`), and by
> the live kernel-mount CLI flow (`status ID` names the mount point while mounted, none after
> `umount`). Records: this entry, GAPS GAP-A9-4, `docs/wip/TBD_FIXES.md` §5.

**POSIX and transparency acceptance.** The shared operation layer must preserve hardlinks,
unlink-while-open, rename replacement/exchange/no-replace flags, symlinks, truncation/sparse
files, permissions and ownership, timestamps, error codes, descriptor lifetime, `fsync`,
shared mappings and platform locking semantics. Extended attributes, watcher events and
platform-specific flags have explicit capability contracts. Never acknowledge an ignored
`setattr` field or discard a `renameat2` flag. FUSE ABI vectors must be checked against the
kernel headers independently of the encoder; for example WRITEBACK_CACHE is bit 16, while bit
8 is FILE_OPS (audit BUG-6). Advertise READDIRPLUS only with its complete handler.

`statfs` reports logical capacity and remaining space that the physical claim can honor,
using checked block rounding; it must not derive free space from twice current usage. Base
lookups and metadata mutations go through the same overlay rules as reads and writes.
Conformance runs through actual host mounts and Linux guests, including namespace-mutating
base operations, concurrent SDK/kernel writes and invalidation loss. Source-level tests alone
cannot establish the mount guarantee. A native Windows or NFS adapter must report its actual
semantics; a Linux guest provides a separate POSIX target, not evidence for those native paths.

**The group a new object takes (A-328).** POSIX lets the implementation choose (`mkdir(2)`: the parent's group or the
creator's), and each route gives what a native file system under the kernel it serves gives, so a tool sees the same
tree over the route as on the host. FUSE and virtio-fs serve Linux kernels: System V's rule, the creator's group unless
the parent directory is set-group-ID, whose group a new object takes and whose bit a new directory takes too. The NFS
export, and the routes without a kernel, give their host's own rule, as a native NFS server does: System V's on Linux,
BSD's on macOS, the parent's group always and no inherited bit (`slates_bridge_core::GroupRule`). Measured on APFS: a
directory made in a `2755` parent reads `755`; before A-328 the macOS export gave `2755`, and a Subversion
repository's `db/revprops` differed there from the host's (CI run 44260193629).

A mount is transparent to ordinary path-based tools within the selected namespace, but remains
a filesystem boundary: `st_dev`, mount tables, cross-boundary links and EXDEV may expose it.
Attaching over an existing directory hides it in that namespace; the retained base descriptor
still serves its original contents. Other namespaces need their own attachment. Missing target
directories are refused because creating one would write disk. Full equivalence to an existing
physical volume's device identity or cross-volume rename is not promised.

**Failure matrix.** Daemon crash: Linux requests wait on the device the anchor holds until the restarted
daemon takes it back and asks the kernel to resend what the dead one read (A-61; Degraded, seconds); macOS FSKit: the extension's forwarding calls fail typed until
the daemon is back, and the extension survives because it is a separate process (Degraded; the
spike measures whether open files recover or must be reopened); macOS NFS fallback: the hard mount
waits until the restarted server answers the retried RPCs, a signal ending the wait `EINTR` (Degraded; A-229); Windows:
the volume disappears and reappears (Degraded, open handles error). Extension crash on macOS:
FSKit unmounts the volume; the daemon's state is intact; the anchor re-mounts (Degraded).
Unprivileged user namespaces disabled: Refused for the launcher form with the exact remedy. That includes
a host whose AppArmor confines them (Ubuntu 24.04's `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`): `unshare`
succeeds there, but the namespace gets no capability, so the launcher names that sysctl, or an AppArmor profile
granting `userns,` to the binary, as the operator's remedy (2026-11-05; GAPS `8a-launcher-ci`). Since A-370 slates
ships that profile and the launcher uses it only when its caller asks: asked and loaded, the namespace is made under
it and the command runs outside it; not asked, the launcher leaves a loaded profile first and the refusal is the one
above; asked and not loaded, the refusal names the profile's file and the command that loads it (below).
`allow_other` requested but not permitted: Refused with the `/etc/fuse.conf` line. FSKit module
not enabled: Refused with the exact System Settings path. Any separately selected limited
NFS form reports its weaker semantics and cannot satisfy a full-POSIX request. Base
file unreadable (permissions changed, base unmounted): Refused (`EIO` at the mount, `BaseUnavailable`
in `status`) for that entry only.

**The launcher on a restricted host (A-370).** Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 confine every unprivileged user namespace through
AppArmor (`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`): `unshare` succeeds, then the process moves into the
`unprivileged_userns` profile, which denies the namespace every capability, so the launcher can neither write its maps
nor bind, whoever writes the maps (GAPS `8a-launcher-ci`). An AppArmor profile attached to the launcher's executable
that grants `userns,` lifts this for that executable alone. Loading it needs root, so slates never loads it (R10) and
never writes `/etc/apparmor.d` (R1). Ada's decision, 2026-11-18: "Ship the profile but feature flag it so whether via
SDK (Node/Python), API, or CLI it is user enabled."
- *The profile* (`slates_client::exec::profile`) is `abi <abi/4.0>,` then `profile <executable> flags=(unconfined) {
  userns, }`:
  - It is named by the executable's real path, AppArmor's own convention. So it attaches to that path alone, two
    executables on one host never share a name, and the launcher knows its own profile by its label.
  - `flags=(unconfined)` mediates nothing else, the form Ubuntu's own `userns,` profiles take (`/etc/apparmor.d/chrome`
    on the runners).
  - A path the profile cannot name exactly is refused: one holding a character outside ASCII letters, digits and
    `/ . _ - +` (AppArmor reads several as patterns, quotes, variables or separators), or an empty, `.` or `..`
    component.
  - It ships inside every release binary and SDK package, rendered for the executable's own path
    (`slates apparmor profile`, `apparmor_profile(path)`, `apparmorProfile(path)`), not as a file naming one path: the
    profile must name wherever the binary was put. `slates apparmor check` prints the root commands that save it as
    `/etc/apparmor.d/<the path, each / a .>` and load it with `apparmor_parser -r`.
- *The flag* is `AppArmor`, off unless the user opts in: `slates exec --apparmor-profile`, slates-api's
  `ExecSpec::apparmor`, the SDKs' `apparmor_profile=True` and `{ apparmorProfile: true }`.
  - **Off:** a launcher whose thread runs under its own profile writes `changeprofile unconfined` to
    `/proc/thread-self/attr/apparmor/current` first. Its namespace then meets the host's restriction exactly as with no
    profile, and the refusal names the switch.
  - **On:** the namespace is made under the profile, then the launcher writes `exec unconfined` to
    `/proc/thread-self/attr/apparmor/exec`. So the command runs unconfined, and a namespace the command makes itself is
    restricted as any process's is. A refused write is a typed refusal, never a command run holding the grant.
- *Who is restricted.* The restriction exempts a process holding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in its user namespace (root), whose
  namespaces get their capabilities whatever the setting, so the launcher judges a refusal, and `slates apparmor check`
  its readiness, by the restriction applying to it (`Confinement::restricted_here`), not by the setting alone.
- *Who holds the grant.* A loaded profile labels every process of its executable. slates' own code uses the grant in
  the launcher alone, there only when asked, and never in the command it runs. But any user who may run the executable
  may use the grant through it (a preload or a debugger runs their code under its label), and on Ubuntu 24.04 any
  unconfined process may enter a loaded profile by `change_profile` without running it at all, as it may enter the
  user-namespace profiles Ubuntu itself loads (measured below). So loading the profile is an administrator's decision
  that every user of the host may create user namespaces, as on a host without the restriction; the profile's header
  and `docs/cli.md` say so.
- *Rejected:*
  - Entering a named profile with `change_profile` from unconfined (the `aa-exec` route). Ubuntu treats it as a bypass
    of the restriction and closes it where `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined=1`, Ubuntu 26.04's
    default. Measured, diagnostics run 44349241634: on 26.04 the kernel logs "change_profile unprivileged unconfined
    converted to stacking", the label is `slates-probe//&unconfined`, and the namespace is refused; on 24.04 (the
    setting 0) any unconfined process enters the profile and maps itself root. Path attachment needs no such
    permission.
  - A profile in enforce mode, allowing the binary what it needs and moving its children into a capability-free
    profile, as Ubuntu's `bwrap` profile does. It would confine the daemon and every verb too, and any mediation class it
    missed would break them; the exec-time `exec unconfined` gives the command the same outcome without it.

**Derived constants.** NFS fallback `actimeo` for writable volumes = k × measured GETATTR RTT
(k from the multi-process coherence test); FUSE `max_background` and congestion threshold = shard
count × per-shard in-flight budget (from measured service time); readahead = large chunk size;
FSKit forwarding batch = measured ring round trip versus per-operation handler cost (the spike's
number); attribute-return policy = always return attributes with results (the Handler API's
purpose) so the kernel needs no separate getattr.

**Worked example.** `git status` in an attached clone on Linux: after the first walk, every
`lookup`/`getattr` is answered by the kernel cache; the daemon sees `readdirplus` once per
directory and `read` for changed files; a write from the agent invalidates the file's attributes
in the kernel before the write is acknowledged, so a concurrent `git status` in another process
sees the new size. On macOS 26, the same clone is an FSKit volume: the agent's `attach` with a
chosen path mounts `slates://volume/7/attach/3` at `~/proj/build`; `cargo build` in a shell sees
a normal directory; `umount ~/proj/build` or `detach` removes it. Failure: the agent asks to
attach at `/home/u/proj/build` on Linux, which does not exist; the launcher form refuses with
`ChosenPathUnavailable{missing: "/home/u/proj/build"}` and the SDK falls back to the
root-relative path as an explicit alternative; it does not report that the requested path was attached.

**Laptop degenerate.** Identical; one root mount.

### 4.7 IPC and the provisioning fast path (D-10)

> **Test fixture correction (2026-11-02, A-31).** The armed flag precedes the client's wake-word snapshot; it is
> not a kernel-sleeper acknowledgement. An empty wake there may be coalesced, unlike a real reply that the ring
> recheck finds. The unanswered-wake fixture now waits for `wake_one` to confirm a sleeper on Linux/macOS;
> Windows' Event retains an early signal. The original deadline and reply/count assertions stay in force. The
> instrumented CI case first fails at 5.01 s; 100 corrected native Linux runs and all nine ring cases pass, as do
> all nine on macOS (0.53 s). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-02-an-empty-wake-test-mistook-an-armed-client-for-a-sleeper.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-570: the pressure hold leaves the tick).** The pressure hold's sampler (`crate::pressure`, a
> task of the control shard's) samples at its start and at the kernel's own memory-pressure reports, a stall's end among
> them (§4.2's A-570 status); a kernel that offers none has the watch refused by kind, counted. Off the tick so far:
> dead clients (A-475), staging buffers and status captures (A-522), leases, CLI attachments and destroys (A-536),
> grants, the owed audit, departed hosts and held copies (A-554), the pressure hold, NFS purges and the huge-page
> re-arm (A-570): the NFSv4 table notes what it owes as each access closes (`nfs::note_purges`), and the keeper hands
> the reaper a round at once at a start that owes purges and a retry window after any access that leaves it owing; a
> lasting decline of a huge-page placement is noted as each state borrow closes and re-armed by the keeper a retry
> window after it. Left on the tick: base hints with their delegation drain, and the idle seal.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-554: grants, the owed audit, departed hosts and held copies leave the tick; the retry window
> named).** A grant past its term ends at the first instant past it, kept by the shard's deadline keeper: the grants
> table keeps its issued grants in an index by the end of their term (`slates_land::grant::Grants`, one entry an issued
> grant, taken out at its consumption, revocation or end), so the keeper sleeps to the next grant due and its sweep
> reads the due alone, where the tick walked every grant once a window. An issue or a restore notes the earliest it
> entered, and each state borrow hands that to the keeper. A deadline its job could not end (a grant whose expiry record
> the catalog refused, a refused destroy record) is tried again the retry window on (`deadlines::retry_window_ns`,
> counted `deadline.stuck`): the shard's window of A-455, the liveness window `W` (the recovery budget by rent or buy,
> A-359) raised to the scheduler overrun the shard measured, never past the observation budget. What a shard owes the
> audit (A-265) is looked at by the keeper a retry window after the record that armed the look was owed
> (`landing::arm_owed_audit_look`, armed in `write_audit` and at the shard's start for a recovered outbox): a front
> where the look was armed is sent again (`landing.audit_resent`), and the look is armed again a window on while
> anything is owed, never while nothing is. A host the fleet let go has its clients' attachments ended (A-222) by the
> control shard's reaper, which looks when the look's inputs change: an install that changed the fleet's members
> (`FleetNode::take_members_changed`, read as each state borrow closes), an anchor learned or restarted, a peer's plane
> started (`remote_attach::look_for_departures`); a look some shard did not answer is asked for again a retry window on,
> by the keeper. A writable copy taken back after a takeover that no holder claimed (Linux, A-197) is reclaimed at its
> claim's deadline: the keeper sleeps to it (`held_copy::next_claim_deadline`) and hands the reclaim to the reaper,
> which writes the copies back. Off the tick so far: dead clients (A-475), staging buffers and status captures (A-522),
> leases, CLI attachments and destroys (A-536), grants, the owed audit, departed hosts and held copies (A-554); the
> pressure hold is next.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-536: leases, CLI attachments and destroys leave the tick).** The shard's deadline keeper
> (`crate::deadlines`) also sleeps to the lease wheel's next deadline, releasing or renewing a lapsed write lease at its
> term, and to the next CLI attachment's lapse, which the partition now keeps in an index of terms (derived from the
> records and made again at a restore), so no attachment is walked to find the lapsed. Whatever path records a lease or
> a term (a take, a renewal, a replay), the partition notes the earliest it entered and each state borrow closes by
> handing that to the keeper (`deadlines::after_borrow`). Destroys are stepped by the serve loop once woken: a takeover's
> relinquish now wakes it, as a destroy and a move's release already did, and a refused completion record is tried
> again at its own deadline, the shard's window on. A deadline still past after the keeper's pass (a job that could not
> end it) is tried again a window on, never spun on (`deadlines::armed_for`, counted `deadline.stuck`). Off the tick so
> far: dead clients (A-475), staging buffers and status captures (A-522), leases, CLI attachments and destroys (A-536);
> grants and the owed audit are next.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-522: a claim names its process; staging and status captures keep their own deadlines).**
> A claim on macOS and Windows carries its claimant's start beside its pid (the claim slot's `AT_STARTED`, the bootstrap
> layout `SLB5`): on macOS the start time the kernel keeps for the process (`proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDTBSDINFO)`, in
> microseconds), on Windows its creation time (`GetProcessTimes`). The daemon's hang-up watch is taken on that process
> alone (`ExitWatch::on_started`): macOS registers its exit note and then reads the pid's start, so a pid another process
> took before the watch reads exited at once and the dead client is retired; Windows opens the handle and checks the
> creation time. Neither route has a socket at the claim to ask the kernel for its peer (`LOCAL_PEERTOKEN`,
> `GetNamedPipeClientProcessId`); macOS's region is fetched by the Mach audit token, after the daemon seats and watches
> the client. And the reap loop's tick no longer releases abandoned staging buffers and status captures: the shard's
> keeper (`crate::deadlines`) sleeps on the timing wheel until the earliest of their deadlines, releases what is due,
> and is woken only by a deadline set earlier than the one it sleeps for. Off the tick so far: dead clients (A-475),
> staging buffers and status captures (A-522).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-475: a dead client is reclaimed at its hang-up).** The daemon no longer finds a dead client by
> a poll. Each seated client has a watch, a task of its shard that awaits the client's hang-up through the shard's
> driver: on Linux its control socket's end of stream (`EPOLLIN`, raised at the peer's close with `EPOLLRDHUP` and
> `EPOLLHUP`); on macOS its process's exit (`EVFILT_PROC`, `NOTE_EXIT`, on a kqueue the shard's kqueue awaits); on
> Windows its process handle, waited on by the system thread pool and posted to the shard's completion port
> (`slates_rt::handle_wait`). The watch registers, then tests once, so a client dead before the registration is caught
> there; it holds a descriptor of its own, which its wait borrows, so the wait is gone before that descriptor closes.
> Its report marks the client retiring (an unproven slot is ended at once) and wakes the shard's reaper, which retires
> the dead a batch at a time and idles while none is owed; each owner's cleanup call waits in that owner's own time by
> its own window (A-455's), where it was the reap cadence. A client that writes on its control socket, which no client
> does after its opening, is ended as a hang-up is. Until now every shard swept each liveness budget and asked every
> client silent for a budget whether its peer was gone, so a client killed with `SIGKILL` kept its seat, attachments and
> id for one to two budgets. The 2026-09-05 status below describes that sweep, now gone; the staging and status-page
> expiry it also ran stays on the reap loop's tick until the deadline wheel takes it. Code: `crates/server/src/hangup.rs`,
> `crates/server/src/reap.rs`.

> **Status (2026-11-06, A-230).** A CLI attachment (`slates attach`) is not the client's to take with it. It holds a
> term, the failover SLO as the write lease's, renewed by each verb that names it. It ends at the lapse with its lease,
> and a later use is refused `AttachmentExpired`. Only an SDK client's attachments end with the client, as below. Since
> 2026-11-09 only the attachment's own principal's use renews it: no record is written by an identity a request merely
> names, rather than the one its session authenticated (`use_attachment`).

> **Status (2026-09-20, A-28).** Client retirement reserves the dead client's seat and id
> until every owner shard has removed its SDK attachments. Unsent forwards are cancelled;
> read-only gathers follow already-admitted synchronous attachment verbs, and removal names
> frozen attachment ids so a delayed callback cannot remove a resumed session's new records.
> Refused cleanup is counted and retried at the existing cadence; leases retain their terms.
> The two-owner SIGKILL history passes in 3.81 s under the original lease and observation bounds.
> Fresh client identities are reserved in the control partition before handoff. Startup recovers
> the allocation floor across partitions before admitting callers; exhaustion or unpublished
> reservation refuses admission. A daemon crash cannot give a new CLI the completion key of an
> earlier CLI. The real CLI binding/crash/strict-detach history passes in 7.90 s, and the portable
> restart history additionally covers a previously admitted client that submitted no verbs.
> Both retirement and restart histories also pass in the Linux io_uring workspace run.
> The last-id/refused-fresh/restarted-session history passes on macOS in 0.98 s and in the
> five-case Linux client suite (1.51 s). Queued-forward/cancellation histories and publication
> refusal remain tracked in TBD_FIXES. The current macOS real CLI suite passes all ten cases in 28.85 s.

> **Status (2026-09-05).** Implemented in `crates/ipc` and `crates/server` (GAPS §8d, Phase 2
> tasks 3–6). As built, the failure matrix's client side: a client tells a dead daemon from a
> slow one through `Liveness` (Linux: the control socket's peer end, closed by the kernel with
> the daemon; macOS and Windows: a start stamp in the bootstrap object's header, rewritten by
> a restarted daemon and unreachable after a dead one, compared with the stamp and process id
> the answering daemon wrote into its answer, A-143), asked only after a reply has stalled
> past the deadline; the rendezvous carries the id a reconnecting client wants (a 4-byte hello
> on Linux; the claim slot's id field elsewhere) and the daemon honours it when no live client
> holds it; a client's shard is its id's residue over the partitions, so a reconnect lands on
> the partition holding its completion records. The daemon side: every shard sweeps at the
> liveness cadence, asks about clients silent for the budget (the control socket's end of
> stream on Linux; the process id probed on macOS and Windows), and reclaims a gone client's
> attachments, region, control channel and id, leaving its leases to expire by their terms
> (T-2.3 in `crates/client/tests/reap.rs`). The heartbeat slot stays the SDKs' way to be seen
> alive without a request (Phase 5); a sync client is seen through its process.
>
> Provisioning is measured end to end from the Rust client through the real rendezvous and
> rings (`crates/client/examples/provision_bench.rs`, AC-2.1, T-2.6): one client spinning
> provisions a volume at a p99 of about 25 µs against the 50 µs floor on the reference laptop;
> the 1/8/64 histogram and a parked form are recorded and ratcheted (the floor is held on the
> single-client latency; the concurrency tails are contention on shared owner shards). A verb's
> effects and its completion record are one log record (`Db::begin` … `commit`), so a crash
> leaves both or neither (AC-2.3). **Since 2026-09-18 (AUD-06) a publication that fails is the
> same:** a record that cannot be made durable — the append refused, or the log full and the
> snapshot that would carry the effects not published — rolls the transaction back (the partition
> re-derived from the segment's durable state, the effects and the completion record gone together,
> the verb refused with the typed `Unpublished` and the objects it built for the vanished record
> released), so a same-id retry re-executes rather than reading a success from memory that the next
> restart would lose; a maintenance snapshot that fails *after* a durable append is deferred and
> counted, and the commit stands (`docs/bugs/2026-09-18-unpublished-transaction-served-from-memory.md`).
> Admission is bounded (AC-2.6): a connect past the derived
> per-daemon client bound is refused `TooManyClients`, a forward to a saturated owner shard
> waits in a bounded queue and past the clients' credit is refused `Overloaded`, and a shard
> kicks another only when it is parked (a message to a spinning shard costs no syscall).

> **Status (2026-09-17, rendezvous ownership).** A client endpoint constructed from a rendezvous
> consumes the complete `Connected` value, retaining its liveness and completion resources with its
> rings. The partial region/doorbell constructor is removed. Five server fixtures and the IPC
> cross-process fixture dropped Linux's control socket with that partial constructor; the daemon
> correctly reaped their idle clients, producing false `AwaitPlaced`/`Destroy` timeouts. The two
> Linux regressions now pass in 6.24 s / 5.23 s; the timed-out verbs reply below 1 ms.
> [Diagnosis](../bugs/2026-09-17-fixture-client-drops-its-liveness-handle.md).

**Data model.**
```rust
#[repr(C, align(64))] struct Slot { seq: AtomicU64, kind: u16, len: u16, request: u64, payload: [u8; 40],
                                   stamp: u32 /* the producer's clock, low 32 bits, as it wrote the slot (A-559) */ }
struct Ring { slots: [Slot; N], head: CachePadded<AtomicU64>, tail: CachePadded<AtomicU64> }
struct ClientRegion { magic, version /* 3 */, client_id, shard: u16, cmd: Ring, cpl: Ring, wake: WakeWord, parked: AtomicU32,
                     spin_ns: u32, spin_shift: u32,
                     reply_stamp: [AtomicU64; 2] /* one per park parity; bit 63: the wake found a sleeper */ }
```
Ownership: the daemon creates the region (memfd / shm_open object / pagefile section), locks it,
and hands it to one client; the client writes only `cmd` slots and the `parked` flag; the daemon
writes only `cpl` slots and the wake word; large payloads (archive streams, big reads through the
SDK) travel through a per-client bulk region referenced by offset from a slot.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-381): a client's ring wakes only its own shard.** On macOS and Windows a client of a shard
> that has announced itself idle rings the bootstrap object's daemon-wide doorbell, and the daemon's doorbell thread
> kicks shards. It kicked every shard at every ring: at 1,000 clients over 23 shards on a Mac Studio each shard parked
> and woke about 7,500 times a second, alike on shards serving one connection and two, and the control shard ran a
> claim round for every request. A ring now marks the shard its region names (a bit a shard id in the bootstrap
> object, with a summary bit a word, so the thread reads only the words a ring touched) and a claim marks the claim
> (the header's word beside the doorbell), and the thread kicks the shards marked: the control shard only for a
> claim. The bootstrap object's magic is `SLB2`, so a client or an object of the layout before is refused as another
> layout, never served with its rings unheard. Linux clients write their shard's own kick descriptor, as before.
> Tests: `a_ring_marks_only_the_shard_it_names_and_a_claim_marks_the_claim` (`slates-ipc`) and
> `a_clients_ring_wakes_only_the_shard_that_serves_it` (`crates/server/tests/doorbell.rs`), red with the thread
> kicking every shard.

> **Status (2026-09-19, Linux rendezvous):** the control shard drains the listener and
> awaits its next one-shot driver readiness. Connections already queued or arriving during
> registration remain readable. No Linux doorbell thread polls a pending connection and
> repeatedly kicks every shard. Other platforms retain their shared-memory word watcher.
> The local delayed-accept regression fails before and passes after the change; the traced
> startup assertion remains unchanged. See the dated startup/kick-retirement bug report.

**Rendezvous.** Linux: connect to the abstract-namespace socket `@slates/<uid>/<instance>`, or, for an instance
named by an absolute path, the socket file in that path's directory (A-187); each side checks the other's
`SO_PEERCRED`; the daemon sends an ephemeral public key, the client answers with its own and its hello sealed, and the
daemon sends the region fd with `SCM_RIGHTS` beside the sealed handoff; the socket stays as the control channel, every
delivery on it sealed. macOS: `shm_open` on a name prefixed with the app group (`<team id>.slates/` plus a uid hash,
kept within the 31-character limit), `mode 0600`, so the sandboxed FSKit extension can open the
same object; the client claims a slot by CAS in the bootstrap block; an optional control socket
for streams. Windows: open `Local\slates-<sid-hash>` section and the per-slot `Local\...` Event
(DACL to the user's SID); optional named pipe for streams. Discovery: `SLATES_ENDPOINT`, then the
well-known name.

> **Status (2026-10-29, A-187): every Linux rendezvous is sealed, and a socket file reaches a workload in a network
> namespace of its own.** The exchange is daemon first and never blocks: the daemon accepts, checks the peer's user,
> sends its X25519 public key and keeps the connection among at most `BACKLOG` pending handshakes; the client's poll
> answers with its key and its hello sealed; the daemon's next round, woken by that connection's readiness, agrees,
> opens the hello and sends the handoff sealed (`slates_ipc::seal`, implemented by `crates/seal` with aws-lc-rs). A
> claimant that never sends its opening is given up at the claim wait and holds no round: before, the daemon read each
> hello with a blocking receive, and one silent claimant held every claim behind it. The client checks the listener's
> user too, since an abstract name is anyone's to bind. An instance named `<directory>/<name>` is reached at
> `<directory>/slates-rv-<name>.sock`, bound only in a directory of the daemon's user's alone, owner-only, a dead
> owner's node replaced, removed by whoever bound it. Proven on arm64 Linux (2026-10-28, in a container on this Mac):
> a client in a user and network namespace of its own (`unshare`) maps a file read and write by the direct map through
> the socket file while it finds no daemon at the abstract name, and every rendezvous test passes sealed; eight mutants
> each fail their guard. The chart takes the directory as `rendezvous.directory` and `rendezvous.hostPath`. The seal
> costs about 36 µs a rendezvous in release, and a sealed connect is about 180 µs slower at the median in a debug build
> (BENCHMARKS, A-187), once per client session. A container on a bridge network and a KIND pod of its own each wrote a
> file through a writable direct map across the socket file in CI (run 40844136550, diagnostics run 40847130881),
> red-checked. In release a sealed connect costs about 73 µs more at the median (adacachy). A namespace whose Pod Security
> profile forbids hostPath mounts the directory through a claim on a `local` PersistentVolume (A-187; the KIND leg's
> step 7).

> **Status (2026-10-27): a peer the daemon cannot see by pid is served.** Linux reports a socket peer's process id as
> the reader's pid namespace sees it, and 0 for a process outside it: a client in a container of a pod beside the
> daemon's, with no process namespace shared, which is a pod's default. rustix 1.1's `socket_peercred` cannot hold that
> 0 (its `Pid` is non-zero), and its reading was undefined behaviour, which turned every such claim into an error and an
> unanswered close. The check now reads `SO_PEERCRED` as plain integers (`crates/ipc/src/peer.rs`), and the uid is still
> the only check: a Linux client's liveness rides its control socket, so its pid is never needed there. Found by the KIND
> lane's direct leg; `docs/bugs/2026-10-27-a-peer-whose-process-the-daemon-cannot-see-was-refused-by-undefined-behaviour.md`.

> **Status (2026-10-25, A-176).** Every in-process anchor hands its daemons the rendezvous it holds, as the field's
> anchor does across the spawn (`SegmentSource::Handoff`'s `rendezvous`; `Adoption`), so nothing below a daemon's start
> reads the environment. Windows keeps a kernel object's name while any process holds it, which three defects met,
> each fixed with a failing test first:
>
> - a client's region is named afresh at every daemon start and for every region (`slates-cr-<key>-<number>`), since
>   a reconnecting client still mapped the region of the same name;
> - the owner of a rendezvous (its anchor, or a daemon run alone) holds a token only it opens, takes over an object a
>   dead owner's clients still map, and refuses a second live owner `InstanceHeld`;
> - a claim refused in an accept round ends that claim alone, on every platform, where before the round dropped the
>   clients it had already accepted.
>
> A stopped daemon also takes back the start stamp it published, so a client in its own process judges it gone, as a
> Linux client does when the control socket closes. Proven on jupiter (Windows 10.0.26200): the client binary whole,
> one test at a time, 20 of 20, its seven restart tests the first sessions to outlive a daemon restart on Windows;
> red-checked.
>
> **Status (2026-10-26, A-178).** macOS refuses a second owner of a live instance too: the owner's token there is a
> Mach bootstrap name registered at the top of the caller's bootstrap chain, which launchd gives its first registrant
> and frees when that registrant's port dies (`crates/ipc/src/owner_name.rs`). Proven on this Mac and fedora, and
> the refusal across processes on every platform; red-checked.
>
> **Status (2026-11-08, A-254).** The owner is decided before anything is created: an anchor holds the rendezvous, and a
> daemon opens its listener, before a segment is created or attached, so a start refused as a live instance's second
> owner has created and unlinked nothing, on every platform.

**Protocol.** Requests and replies are fixed-layout 64-byte slots; request ids are `(client_id,
sequence)`; the daemon keeps a completion record per client until acknowledged (RIFL), so a retry
after a lost reply returns the original result; deadlines are remaining budgets; cancellation is
a slot kind. Each slot carries its producer's stamp (A-559): the low 32 bits of the host's monotonic clock as the slot
was written, the lowest bit set so zero reads as unstamped, which whoever takes it widens back to the full reading
(`slates_ipc::slot::landed_ns`, from any reading within 2³² ns, about 4.3 s, after it). So a client knows when its
request landed in the command ring and when its reply landed in its own, not only when it took it, and a caller's
latency splits into the daemon's part and its own (`slates_machine::attribution`).

**Wake strategy.** Client: write slot, publish `tail` (release), read `cpl` head with acquire in a
loop for its wake estimate (seeded with `spin_ns`, the daemon-published measured wake cost, and
refined from the client's own parks, A-31), then clear the reply stamp slot this park names (the two
slots alternate park by park, A-199), set `parked` to that slot's value (1 or 2), fence
(`SeqCst`; the park protocol, A-44), re-check the reply (to close the race), and wait on the wake word
(futex / `os_sync_wait_on_address(SHARED)` / the Event). A call that waits while its daemon lives waits on the daemon's
departure beside its reply (A-456): Linux polls the completion eventfd and the control socket instead of the futex,
Windows waits on the Event and the daemon's process handle together, and macOS keeps the word; both look at the
daemon's liveness (its exit watch and the instance's start stamp) on a doubling schedule, since a daemon restarted
inside its own process changes only the stamp. Daemon: after writing a reply and advancing
the wake word, fence and read `parked`; if set, advance the word once more, stamp the host clock into
the `reply_stamp` slot the flag's value names (the first reply of the park only), wake (futex wake / wake by address / `SetEvent`),
mark that stamp confirmed when the wake reports it found a sleeper (Linux and macOS; Windows' Event
cannot tell, and a Linux park on the eventfd is no futex sleeper, so there the client confirms its own sleep by its
switch count across the wait, and learns nothing where the OS refuses the count, A-223, A-456), and, for SDK event
loops, signal
the completion fd (eventfd / pipe / socket) so `add_reader`/`uv_poll` fires. Where no descriptor can be
shared (macOS, Windows), a client-local bridge thread makes its pipe or socket readable after every
return from its wait while the client is armed and a reply waits in its ring: a level, never an edge
(A-44). The bridge waits where a parked synchronous call of the same client waits, and the daemon wakes one
waiter: a synchronous park raises a mark before its flag, and a bridge woken while the mark stands wakes once
more, so the parked call is never left to its deadline (2026-11-18: before, 16 to 19 of 20 parked calls beside
a running bridge slept to it). A bridge whose thread the OS refuses is refused typed, never started without
it. The client folds a
confirmed stamp inside its wait into its estimate (stamp to return). Shards poll rings while any
client has activity within the
measured idle window, then park in the driver; a parked shard is woken by the driver kick the
client sends through the control fd.

**Failure matrix.** Client crash: the daemon sees the hang-up when it happens (the control socket's
end of stream on Linux, the process's exit on macOS and Windows, each awaited through the shard's
driver; A-475), retires the client's attachments, region and id at once, and lets its leases expire
by their terms (Masked for others, Degraded for that client). Daemon crash: regions survive in the anchor; clients observe a
stalled reply and the control channel reset, reconnect, and resend with the same request ids
(exactly-once by completion records). Ring full: the client blocks on the ring (credit), never
drops.

> **Status (2026-09-22, the client ring follows Little's law).** The client ring was not sized by the formula below: `slots_per_ring` reused the runtime's inbound-ring depth, `wake.p99 / syscall.median` from one boot probe, and each client's bulk area scales with it. The probe's tail is unstable (the pod image's own profile gave wake p99 from 667 ns to 511,042 ns across runs a minute apart, often from 64 samples), so three KIND pods of one image derived 16384, 8 and 256 slots and seated 1, 1285 and 41 clients; the one-seat pod refused the lane's `bootstrap` while its readiness probe held the seat, and CI's macOS runner seated two clients and refused the restart test's third. The ring is now `next_power_of_two(requests_in_flight_per_shard)`, this Little's law value (32 slots); every pod of a two-CPU fresh-cluster run logs 32 slots and 330 client seats. Owed: the admission value rests on two stated assumptions rather than measured rates. (The wake probe's two events and unconverged tail, and `spin_ns` reading the p50, were closed on 2026-09-25: §4.1's status.) Record: `docs/bugs/2026-09-22-client-ring-sized-by-the-wake-tail-not-littles-law.md`.

> **Status (2026-09-25, A-31: the client learns its own wake).** A client spun for the daemon's boot mean for its whole life. It now spins for an online estimate seeded with that mean (`spin_ns`, weighted over about `2^spin_shift` wakes) and refined from its own parks: the daemon stamps the host clock into the region's `reply_stamp` before it wakes a parked client, marks it confirmed when its wake call reports a sleeper found (`futex_wake`'s count; `os_sync_wake_by_address_any` refuses `ENOENT` when none), and the client folds a confirmed stamp inside its wait into the estimate (`ClientEnd::wait`, `wake_samples`); a confirmation that lands after the woken client read the stamp is settled at its next wait. The region's layout goes to version 2 (a client of another version is refused by name, as before). Confirmation is not decoration: without it, a daemon replying the instant the parked flag rose taught the client 611–974 ns on Apple silicon against the boot probe's 2.0–3.3 µs for confirmed sleepers, because such a reply lands while the client's wait is being set up and the wait returns without sleeping. The same evidence corrects a benchmark: `ipc_bench`'s `ring_round_trip_parked_and_woken` row (ratcheted at 1,233 ns here) is mostly that race — of 2,000 parked trips per run only 2, 18, 11, 1 and 1 slept on Apple silicon and 1–3 on Linux (503–545 ns, against a confirmed-sleeper mean of 15–17 µs there); the bench now prints the count, and `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md` records the correction. Proven by use in `crates/ipc/tests/rings.rs` (`a_client_learns_its_wake_from_the_parks_a_reply_ended`; a client that never parked learns nothing and keeps the published window). Record: `docs/bugs/2026-09-25-wake-estimate-frozen-at-boot-and-preemptions-counted-as-long-steps.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-04, A-199: a late confirmation keeps its own stamp).** The woken client can outrun its waker:
> the daemon is preempted between its wake call and the confirmation, and the client takes its reply, sends the
> next request and arms its next park first. With one stamp that park cleared the word, so the sample was given
> up, and the late confirmation then set a bare confirmed bit on the cleared word, which refused the following
> park's stamp: one late confirmation cost two samples. Measured on adacachy, 2026-11-04, the learning case pinned
> to two busy CPUs taught 0–14 of 32 parks; in every failing run the out-of-window stamps (all zero) matched the
> given-up ones one for one. Now the region holds two stamps, the parks alternate between them, and the parked
> flag's value (1 or 2) names the slot; the confirmation is an exchange on the exact stamp the wake timed. One
> daemon serves a ring in order, so by the time the client arms a slot again the reply call that stamped it has
> returned and its confirmation is final. The region's layout goes to version 3. Interleaved, 100 runs each, the
> learning case failed 100 of 100 before and 0 of 100 after on one CPU with two busy loops, and 89 and 0 on two
> CPUs with four. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-04-a-late-wake-confirmation-cost-the-client-two-samples.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-11, A-223 sibling (d): the Windows client's wake is a confirmed sleeper's).** Windows' auto-reset
> Event cannot say whether its signal met a sleeper, and a signal set before the wait is consumed without blocking, so
> the client took any stamp inside its wait. A reply that landed between its re-check and its block was learned as an
> on-CPU handoff. Now the client reads its own context-switch count (`slates_machine::switches`) before and after the
> wait, as the shards judge their parks, and a wait across which the count did not move, or whose count the OS
> refused, teaches nothing (`wait_may_teach` in `crates/ipc/src/endpoint.rs`); Linux and macOS keep the daemon's
> confirmation. The race is rare for the client. Against a daemon replying the instant the flag rose, 11–95 of 16,384
> parks a run on CI's Windows runners never switched out, and main learned 11–48 of them a run;
> `a_reply_sent_before_the_client_blocked_teaches_its_wake_nothing` (`crates/ipc/tests/rings.rs`) reads the client
> thread's own count around each trip, and failed 10 runs in 10 on main and passed 10 in 10 with the check
> (`diag-liveness-client-4`). So the mean on main stayed a sleeper's: the parked bench form's client estimate read
> 17–33 µs on both Windows runners before and after (`Client::wake_estimate`, provision_bench's `client wake` line),
> against a published window of 8.8–9.9 µs (`diag-liveness-client-1`, `-2`).

> **Status (2026-09-29, A-42: the idle spin is opened by client activity and ends with its window).** The
> daemon set a shard "active" at its first client's handoff and nothing cleared it, so from then on every
> idle moment of the shard, however long after its clients, ended in a full idle-window spin: an idle
> solo daemon spent 1.6–1.8 % of a CPU after one client had come and gone (0.07–0.09 % before any), and
> an idle fleet pod's shard 28–62 s of CPU in 190 s. Now the server notes client work where it serves it
> (a ring request, a verb forwarded from another shard, a mount's call, a guest's pass;
> `ShardContext::note_activity`), and the shard spins only until the window that activity opened ends.
> Timers that fire after a client has gone quiet open no window of their own. The serve loop's own
> polling window, which lets a client skip the doorbell, is unchanged. The idle solo daemon measured
> 0.08–0.11 % after its client; the idle fleet pods 2.3–3.6 s of CPU in 190 s. Failing test first:
> `an_idle_daemon_parks_once_its_clients_windows_have_passed` (12 and 2 idle spins in one quiet second
> before, none after); `crates/rt/tests/idle_spin.rs` proves the window by use. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-29-an-idle-shard-spun-for-good-once-a-client-had-connected.md`.

> **Status (2026-09-29, A-44: the park protocol is fenced and the async bridges are level-triggered).** A
> reply to a client that was parking could be lost for good. The client raised `parked` and re-checked its
> ring, and the daemon wrote the reply and read `parked`, each `Release`/`Acquire` with no fence — the
> store-buffering shape the doorbell had until 2026-09-28 — so both reads could miss. The macOS and Windows
> bridges nudged their event loop on a change of the wake word, and a change seen while the client was not
> yet armed was used up, so even a later wake found "no change". The Python async lifecycle hung on the
> macOS runner (`cead594`, past 1 h 47 min), and 1 of 320 contended runs hung here with the client's loop
> in `kevent`, its bridge in `__ulock_wait2` and the shard parked. Now both halves fence
> (`slates-ipc` `park.rs`), the daemon advances the word once more before a wake, and the bridges nudge on
> a level. loom deadlocks the old protocol at interleaving 1 and explores 42,826 interleavings of the new
> one (a client, a daemon and a bridge) with no loss; 800 contended runs pass. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-29-an-async-client-waited-forever-for-a-reply-that-had-landed.md`.

> **Status (2026-10-01, A-56: an async SDK never holds its loop, and every async call ends).** AUD-29-19
> and AUD-29-20. The client's operations never wait on the daemon: `begin` is a single send attempt, the
> rendezvous a claim made at once and polled, a reconnect one step of that claim per tick. The driver
> (`crates/client/src/driver.rs`) owns every async call from submission to its end: bounded admission and
> queue, a reply deadline per call (queued calls too), recovery that resends under the calls' own ids, and
> typed ends — answered, refused, `Stalled`, `DaemonGone`, `CompletionLost`, or released when cancelled
> (Python by its task's cancel, Node by `client.cancel(promise)`).
> Both SDKs drive it from their loop's reader and one timer, and connect from the loop. A client watches the
> daemon's process (`crates/ipc/src/exit_watch.rs`), so on macOS and Windows a killed daemon is now gone
> rather than stalled. Before: the Node acceptance test hung (one queued call never ended, its timer
> re-armed every second), a fresh connect held the loop 1,002 ms, and a killed daemon's calls ended
> `Stalled`. Now every call ends and the loop's worst lateness stays under a tenth of the reply deadline, in
> the Rust driver test, the Node suite (4/4 runs) and the Python suite (4/4 runs) on macOS. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-10-01-an-async-call-could-hold-the-loop-or-never-end.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-14, A-232): a call waits while its daemon lives.** A-56's typed ends lose `Stalled`. Its rule had an
> overdue call fail `Stalled` while the daemon lived, and a stopped daemon's call stay a stall. That failed calls to
> daemons their own watchdog judged alive. At `cpu.weight` 1 beside default-weight spinners on main `29ef4521`, 10 of
> 10 runs were red on both Linux runners, 44 calls failed 2.152 to 8.929 s after sending, and no beat was withheld. Now
> every wait a call makes keeps one rule: the driver's tick, the synchronous round trip, and the wait for a slot on a
> full ring. Each reply deadline that passes asks the daemon's liveness. Gone, the client recovers or reconnects and
> fails `DaemonGone` past the reconnect budget, as before (until A-468, below: a reconnect waits while the instance's
> rendezvous has a holder, and fails at once with none). Alive, the deadline re-arms and the call waits; a stopped
> daemon's call waits until it resumes or is cancelled.
>
> The rule is safe because a daemon that will never answer is ended. An anchored (`FromEnv`) daemon is killed by its
> anchor at its lapse, within `t0 + 2·W + B + L + kill` of a wedge at `t0`, and the client's resend is answered by the
> daemon the anchor restarts. A daemon no other process can end (`Create`, `Handoff`) ends itself on its watchdog's
> stuck verdict, within `t0 + W + B + L` plus its exit, and its calls end `DaemonGone` (§4.14). `W` is the liveness
> budget, `B` the beat and `L` the lateness each line names. `ClientError::Stalled`, `defers_reply` and the driver's
> patient submissions are gone with the old rule. Measured on both Linux runners, 10 runs a shape: starved, 0 failed
> calls of 231; stuck, 40 of 40 inside their bounds. A-232's amendment and
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-13-a-live-starved-daemons-call-was-failed-stalled.md` hold the tests, the mutations and what stays
> open.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-456): a synchronous call's wait for its reply ends at the reply or at its daemon's departure,
> with no deadline.** A-232 kept the reply deadline (the liveness budget `W`, a second) as the cadence of its question:
> each deadline that passed asked the daemon's liveness, so a call whose daemon died learned it up to `W` later, by a
> clock, where the platform can wait on the death itself. Now `ClientEnd::wait_while_daemon_lives` parks on the reply
> and the daemon's process together where the platform waits on both: on Linux one `poll` of the completion eventfd,
> which the daemon writes for a parked client, beside the control socket, whose peer end the kernel closes as the
> daemon's process ends; on Windows one `WaitForMultipleObjects` on the reply's Event and the daemon's process handle
> (A-447's watch). macOS wakes a park through the wake word (`os_sync_wait_on_address`), which no wait takes beside a
> descriptor or a process, so there the park looks at the daemon's exit watch on A-443's doubling: the first look once
> the wait has lasted twice the longer of the time waited at its first park and the client's wake estimate (a look
> costs a park's timeout and a wake), each later look at twice the time waited. The looks cost the logarithm of the
> wait, and a departure is seen within the time waited. A departure is the daemon's going: on Linux its control
> socket's close (its process's end, or a stop inside the process); on macOS and Windows its process's exit, or a new
> start stamp in the instance's bootstrap object, which a daemon restarted inside its own process changes and nothing
> else. So Windows' wait takes the doubling looks' timeout too, and every look asks both (fixed the same day: the first
> form asked the process alone, and a call across a restart inside the daemon's process waited forever on macOS and
> Windows; `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-reply-wait-across-a-restart-inside-the-daemons-process-never-ended.md`). A Linux park on a
> descriptor is never confirmed by the daemon's futex wake, so the client judges its own sleep by its voluntary
> switches (`getrusage(RUSAGE_THREAD)`, `slates_machine::switches`), as Windows' parks do, and its wake estimate still
> learns. While a Linux completion bridge runs (Node's adopted descriptor), the park waits on the bridge's pipe, the
> eventfd's only reader then, and gives the pipe's level back as it ends. The synchronous round trip waits so; the
> reply deadline still paces the waits that cannot see the departure yet (the async driver's tick, the wait for a slot
> on a full ring, a delivery's read, the macOS route's claim steps), each owed in GAPS. A park a look ends (its
> timeout the look's, the daemon then found alive) is counted as its own kind, `ClientEnd::parks_ended_by_looks`, beside
> the replies and the unanswered wakes, and teaches the wake estimate nothing (A-506). The async driver's calls keep
> the same schedule (`slates_ipc::looks`, A-523): each asks the daemon's liveness at its looks, where until A-523 it
> asked at every reply deadline.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-468): a client whose daemon is gone reconnects while its instance's rendezvous has a holder,
> and fails `DaemonGone` at once when it has none.** Until A-468 a reconnect was tried for the reconnect budget (`T + W`,
> the recovery budget and the liveness window, two seconds), and a claim under a live anchor waited at most that budget
> as its restart bound. So a restart slower than two seconds (a starved start, a long recovery) failed the anchor's
> clients while the anchor was still restarting their daemon, and a client whose daemon nothing would restart waited
> out the whole budget before it was told. Now a claim carries no clock: it waits while the rendezvous's holder lives
> (`slates_ipc::begin_connect_as`), the anchor that holds the rendezvous across restarts (A-114) or the daemon that
> holds its own. On Linux the holder is the listening socket, which the anchor keeps across a restart and whose queued
