> **Status (2026-11-18, A-351: the holder's gate counts only answers that can confirm).** A holder defers a promotion
> while an answer it gave the departed owner may still feed that owner's lease, and only an answer that names the owner
> a standing can (an owner is confirmed by a standing it recognizes and superseded by none). So an answer counts toward
> the gate only when it names one (`AnswersGiven::answered`), and an answer to a host the configuration retired names
> none. A former member's last counted answer is kept until its horizon passes (`AnswersGiven::retain_members`), where
> the per-period prune had dropped it the period the member left, opening the gate while a lease built on it could still
> hold. Before, a retired owner deaf to every answer, whose probes still reached the fleet (a member that hears nobody
> condemns nobody, so it probes its suspects every period), was answered each period, and every holder deferred every
> page for as long as it probed until A-304's bound gave its objects up (the chaos nemesis's deafened owner). Now the
> gate opens a horizon after the holder's last answer to it as a member. Regressions
> `a_holder_answering_a_retired_owners_probes_still_promises_its_objects` (`crates/server/src/daemon.rs`),
> `an_answer_that_names_no_standing_never_holds_a_promotion_back` and
> `a_former_members_last_answer_holds_its_promotion_until_its_horizon` (`crates/server/src/lease.rs`).

**Authority scope.** Host failure increments the host epoch and fences every object owned by
that host. Moving one volume changes that object's ownership generation, recorded in the
configuration's moved-object exceptions, without fencing unrelated volumes. Requests and
placement records bind both scopes; cached configuration/attachment generations suffice on
ordinary writes. A region-home move also carries root-group authority. The id still routes by
creator plus these exceptions; this adds no global lookup catalog or per-write coordination.

> **Status (2026-11-18, the moved-object exceptions; the configuration's half of an explicit move).**
> `RegionalConfiguration::moved` holds, for each moved object only, its owner and the configuration version its move
> committed at, its ownership generation (`slates_db::register::Moved`). An object's line starts at its exception's
> owner, else at its creator, and a retired host hands it on along the takeover's lineage
> (`RegionalConfiguration::owner_of`). A member reports a move through the council's report stream
> (`ConfigCommand::Move`, `MovedForgotten` once the object is destroyed); the leader proposes it only when the
> configuration names the reporter as the owner, or names no owner because the object's line runs through a takeover
> that completed or one it keeps no record of (the configuration no longer keeps that successor, and a host that lost
> its authority never reports again under its id), and never for a lost line or one a kept retirement gives another
> member. An unresolved line is allowed since A-309: completion records are bounded, so the line of every volume whose
> creator's takeover completed long ago reads unresolved once its record is let go. A move that would add an exception past the bound the
> leader derives is answered `ReportOutcome::Full` and not proposed (`fleet::moved_bound`: the members times one
> member's volume slots, at the leader's size). A move back to the creator drops the exception. An exception follows
> its owner's takeover at the successor's confirmation, through a takeover carried into another's too, so no line
> starts at a retirement the configuration dropped. The encoding carries the exceptions last (the encoding itself is
> still unversioned; GAPS). Held by five tests in `crates/db/src/register.rs` (`a_move_names_the_objects_owner_and_only_its_owner_moves_it`,
> `a_moved_objects_exception_follows_its_owners_takeover_and_goes_with_its_destroy`,
> `a_moved_objects_exception_follows_a_takeover_carried_into_another`,
> `a_member_moves_an_object_whose_line_names_no_owner` and `no_member_moves_a_lost_object`, both A-309's), the council's
> `a_move_report_is_proposed_by_its_owner_and_held_to_the_bound` and the encoding's round trip and lying-count tests.
>
> **Amended the same day (A-291, the planned handoff in the daemon, §4.10 "Ownership follows the writer").** An
> exception also names the member the move took the object from (`Moved::from`) and the cohort its records sit in
> (`Moved::cohort`, carried by `ConfigCommand::Move`), until the new owner reports the move adopted
> (`ConfigCommand::MoveAdopted`, tag 10; `RegionalConfiguration::adopt_move` clears both, the ownership generation
> kept). A move back to the creator keeps an exception naming the creator, since the creator let its copy go when the
> object left and adopts it back by the same round any member does; only a takeover's successor that is the creator
> drops one. The holders' side is built: at each install a holder of a moved object's copies routes it to the
> exception's owner, so its acceptors take that owner's authority at the reconcile and a record from the old owner is
> refused; once the move is adopted, a copy outside the owner's placement is dropped (`crate::moves`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-382: a host admitted again gives up its own authority on its copies).** The host-epoch bump
> fences every object the host owned, and its re-admission yields its catalogued volumes (A-334). The same install now
> lets go every register copy the host held, as a candidate, under its own authority: the copies of the objects it took
> over before it was retired (`readmission::let_go_own_registers`, counted `fleet.readmission.registers_let_go`). Its
> takeover completed before the re-admission (`RegionalConfiguration::admits`), so each such object is its successor's.
> The configuration no longer names that successor, and the re-admission forgot the host's own routes, so nothing else
> moves those copies: kept, each refused the successor's every record `ForeignGeneration`. A live log ships only to a
> holder that holds its catalog, so the host's live copy never caught up (the chaos nemesis, CI diag 44345243646: 660
> to 796 such refusals a run). Let go, the successor's next record makes the copy afresh, as it makes any new
> candidate's, and its live log follows. The host keeps the content it holds for those objects (A-335). A volume a node
> lost to a successor, yielded or with its log fenced, ships no catalog or head record (`fleet::unplaced_heads`), since
> a copy made afresh takes the first member's record it meets as its owner's. Held by
> `every_copy_catches_up_once_the_creator_takes_its_volume_back_from_the_adopter`,
> `every_copy_catches_up_once_the_third_node_takes_the_volume_from_the_adopter` and
> `a_superseded_owner_restarted_warm_ships_no_record_of_the_volume_it_lost` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`). The
> let-go is published at once (A-415), so a warm restart does not restore the copies. Owed: the yield itself is
> memory-only (`ShardState::yielded`), so a warm restart forgets it.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-409: a lost volume's log stops by itself, and a refusal names the fence).** A volume its
> node yielded at its re-admission (A-334) ships nothing more and does no period work, as a fenced one does (A-349):
> the node knows the loss before a holder can tell it. Each verb waiting on its durability is answered
> `DurabilityPending` at the yield (`live_ship::yielded`). A holder refusing a message from a sender that is not the
> volume's acting owner answers `StaleEpoch` at the highest fence it holds the volume at, its record copy's as well as
> its live copy's (`live_ship::known_fence`), so a sender below it learns it was superseded and stops. Before, a
> re-admitted adopter's log, never fenced, sent the creator an install of its whole volume 1,714 times in one run.

**Lookup.** A volume id carries its creator host. A lookup by id routes to that host, or, when
the configuration records a takeover of that host, to the candidate that rendezvous ranks first
among the survivors of its neighbourhood at the takeover generation; an ownership or home move is a configuration exception naming the affected volume and its
authority generation. The answer comes from the current owner and is
authoritative; no global index exists. Names live in an enrolled namespace whose owner is
routable by id; the CLI resolves `namespace/name` through that owner, defaulting to its current
context. A name is not a host pathname or a bearer capability. Fleet-wide enumeration is a scatter-gather over
owners, each answer linearizable at its owner and the whole labelled with the configuration
version.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-564: an owner that cannot answer is never read as no volume).** A verb forwarded to its
> volume's owner shard was answered `NotFound` when the owner's state refused it. That happened from another node:
> `call_in_shard_time`'s `None` became `NotFound` in `named_if_unshared`. It happened on the same node too, where a
> refused owner borrow became `NotFound`. So a volume on a fenced owner read as absent. The owner's refusal is now
> answered by its kind (`call_owner`, `refusal_of_access`):
> - a fenced owner (or a retention check that fences it) answers `ConsensusRecoveryUnavailable`;
> - a call that did not run answers `Overloaded`, not started.
>
> (`a_verb_for_a_volume_whose_owner_is_fenced_is_refused_by_the_fence_never_not_found`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-volume-on-a-fenced-owner-read-as-absent.md`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-317: the location budget is the membership horizon, ended by a look begun after it).** A
> forward that does not know its volume's owner repeats the read-only location round (the direct route first, and
> again after the round) every poll interval for the membership horizon (`lease::horizon_ns`, the window in which a
> detector condemns a member, so a false death is refuted within it), on the wall from its first look, and gives up
> only once a look begun after the horizon has found no owner: a round waiting on silent peers no longer spends the
> whole budget, and a refutation the shard read while a round waited is seen before it gives up (clients' runs, nice 19
> beside two spinners a CPU: 1 or 2 calls refused in every false death under one liveness budget of wall time). The
> operator's failover SLO caps the whole on the wall. Counted: `fleet.owner_location.gave_up`, and the budget's two
> ends, `budget_spent` and `slo_ended`.

> **Status (2026-11-06, A-236: a clone's name at its name's partition).** Within a daemon a name routes by its hash to
> one partition (`owner_of_name`), where it is looked up and where its uniqueness is decided. A clone lives beside its
> origin, for copy-on-write, so when its name hashes elsewhere, the name's partition holds an alias pointing at the
> clone (`slates_db::catalog::NameAliasRecord`). A lookup by name still routes by hash, and the name's partition says
> where the name is served: its own volume, or the clone's partition through a confirmed alias (`nfs::routed`). A
> second create of the name meets the alias there and is refused `AlreadyExists`. The clone is made by a reservation
> protocol over the two partitions (`slates_db::alias`): reserve the alias, make the clone, confirm the alias. A
> reserved alias holds the name and resolves nothing until it is confirmed. A refused clone releases its reservation,
> a destroyed clone releases its alias, and a recovery reconciles every alias against the clone it names, before any
> client is admitted. Proven by a crash at every step of both protocols (`crates/db/tests/alias.rs`) and by a
> two-partition history and its one-partition differential (R8), restart included
> (`a_clone_named_on_another_partition_is_reached_by_name_and_held_once`, `crates/server/tests/recovery.rs`). With one
> partition no alias is ever made.

> **Status (2026-11-06, forwards to one owner share its session).** A forward borrowed the record session to its owner
> for its whole round trip, and the owner served one request of a session at a time. So a client node's forwards
> went one at a time: a forwarded `CreateWork` took 4.30 s at the median at 1,000 clients, against 45 µs on the
> owner. A forward waiting on a held owner shard made a forward to a free shard of the same owner wait 471.8 ms.
> Now each peer has a forward lane in the control shard's state. The waiting forwarders drive it a turn at a time,
> each turn beginning every queued forward as its own exchange on the session and taking every reply that has come;
> between turns the session is free for other borrowers. The owner runs each forwarded verb on its own task. The same
> read now takes 1.8 to 2.4 ms (`crate::forward_lane`; `forwards_to_one_owner_never_wait_behind_each_other`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-forwards-to-one-owner-went-one-at-a-time.md`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-306: a resend keeps its place in the lane).** A forward given up at its stall budget, or cut
> off by its session's replacement, is sent again by its caller under its own ids (`verbs::resolve_and_forward`). Each
> send took fresh tickets at the back of the peer's lane, so behind a backlog the lane begins more slowly than a stall
> budget a resend was given up again before it was begun, while forwards first queued after it went ahead: a read
> through a client node whose session to its owner died was refused `OwnerUnreachable` at its failover bound in 1 of 10
> runs behind a 256-client burst, and answered after 9.2 and 9.5 s in two more (load 37 to 46). A forward's place is
> now its first send's ticket, and its resends are queued there (`forward_lane::Place`): the lane begins forwards in
> the order of their first send. The same read was answered in 4.1 to 6.5 s, 10 of 10 (load 27 to 33).
> `a_resend_is_begun_ahead_of_every_forward_first_queued_after_it` and its model test hold the order, and
> `a_read_through_a_dead_session_keeps_its_place_behind_a_burst` the read
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-resent-forward-lost-its-place-in-the-lane.md`). Owed then, built by A-315 (below): a forward
> still queued was given up at its stall budget while its lane moved, so the backlog was cycled once a budget on the
> control shard.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-315: a lane's silence is judged in its shard's own time).** A forwarder gave its batch up at
> the first look past its stall budget. An origin whose control shard was kept off its CPU past a budget woke with its
> owner's replies unread in its socket, and its waiting forwarders, woken by their timers ahead of the lane's driver,
> gave those batches up to a live owner. Now a batch quiet for its budget is given up only once a turn of its lane,
> begun after the silence was first seen, has read the session's own socket empty: the record link's sessions read
> their own sockets (`Endpoint::client`), so that turn has read everything that reached the socket before. A turn that
> finds the peer with no session at all counts as one that read it empty, since a dropped session's replies never
> reach the lane (a survivor's forward to a stopped owner was otherwise held to its failover bound). The shard's
> waits in its driver (A-292's receiver rule) do not prove it here: the shard waits while another borrower (the link's
> discovery page) holds the session, and a shard kept busy by other forwards' replies rarely waits at all. A forward
> still queued, of
> which nothing was sent, counts its lane's progress as its own (a forward begun, a reply taken, bytes of a reply
> read), so a backlog that moves is no longer given up and resent once a budget (A-306's owed item). An open forward
> still counts only its own reply's bytes (the 298 forwards of 2026-11-07). Both are bounded by the failover bound from
> the forward's first send, which `resolve_and_forward` passes to every send: the lane's progress holds a queued
> forward only until then, and past it a silence is given up without waiting for the receiver. The judge
> (`forward_lane::Stall`) is pure and reads no CPU clock and keeps no poll pace, so it holds alike on every platform;
> loadtest-scale's lane poll clock (`6da9670d`, reverted from the B13 stack) assumed an idle shard's timer fires on
> time, which Windows' 15.6 ms tick breaks. Tests: the rule's unit and model tests, a queued forward behind a moving
> lane, and `a_held_origin_gives_up_no_forward_whose_reply_came_while_it_was_held` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-forward-lanes-silence-was-judged-before-its-shard-read-what-came.md`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-352: the lane under starvation, and a forward never refused below its path's floor).** At
> nice 19 beside two spinners a CPU, the two dead-session tests failed every run, and no live session was dropped and
> no forward given up silent or at its bound in any of the 20: the lane judges a silence in its own time, and what
> failed was judged on the wall. The tests now wait in the daemons' own periods, and the lane's recovery after a
> dropped session is counted in the control shard's own periods: owed within the link's redial pace and a forward's
> stall budget (`REPLACEMENT_ANSWER_PERIODS`, `state::WallAndPeriods`). And a forward's failover bound is the SLO from
> its first send, or the longest floor its path has measured where that is longer (`forward_lane::FailoverBound`,
> `path_floor_ns`): the transport's silence window, a borrower's hold, the link's redial and four probe timeouts. A
> forward through a session gone silent is answered only after the transport judges it dead and the link replaces it,
> and on a path a starved process stretched (about 9 s of silence window at a 3 s probe timeout) the 10 s SLO refused it
> first. Where the floor passes the SLO the forward runs at the floor, and the lane reports it
> (`fleet.forward.floor_past_slo`, `fleet.forward.held_past_slo`). Test:
> `a_forward_is_never_refused_below_its_paths_floor` (a 1 s SLO, below any path's silence window: answered after 2.04 s,
> refused at 1.004 s with the floor removed;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-starved-forward-lane-was-judged-on-the-wall.md`).

> **Status (2026-10-07, same-region lookups).** A lookup by id now reaches its creator from any node of the
> creator's own region, not only from another region. Before, the server forwarded only a volume homed in another
> region, and a client of another node in the owner's region was answered `NotFound` (found on two Docker
> networks, `docs/wip/GAPS.md` 2026-10-07). A forwardable read or write whose volume the owner shard's catalog
> lacks, and whose id names another creator, takes the same owner-location and forward path as a cross-region one,
> with the node's own region. It is decided on the volume's owner shard, the one shard whose catalog would hold it,
> before any completion is recorded there, and only for a local client's verb, so a forward is one hop. A volume
> this node created and no longer holds stays `NotFound` (GAP-A9-7). Attachments stay owner-local: a write from
> another node uses an attachment taken at the owner. Regression
> `a_client_of_another_node_in_the_owners_region_reads_and_writes_its_volume_through_the_owner`.
> **Amended 2026-10-10: only another member can own it.** A node alone (a laptop: the fleet of one) has no host to
> forward to. It went looking anyway, found none, and answered an id it never created `OwnerUnreachable`; the CLI's
> anchor flow expected `NotFound`. The forward is now taken only when the fleet has a member besides this node. That
> is the same rule at N = 1, not a mode switch. Regression `a_single_node_answers_an_id_it_never_created_not_found`
> (`docs/bugs/2026-10-10-a-node-alone-answered-an-unknown-id-owner-unreachable.md`).

> **Status (2026-10-07, forwarded reads read ahead in doubling batches).** A forwarded `ReadRange` is asked of the
> owner as a read-ahead window (`RequestBody::ReadWindow`, half the client's ring of pages). The origin keeps the
> window in the client's slot and answers the client's next pages from it. A read that continues where its window
> ended fetches the next windows as a batch sent at once on the owner's session, twice the last batch (Linux's
> sequential read-ahead growth). A batch is capped by:
> - what is left of the file;
> - the shard's read-ahead allowance (`DaemonConfig::read_ahead_bytes`, one session's receive bytes per peer inside
>   the fleet's receive share), which the batch is charged against before it is fetched;
> - ~~once measured, what the path delivers in one liveness budget, timed between deliveries~~ — removed 2026-10-08:
>   every batch is app-limited, so its rate sample fed the cap a loop that held a cross-region read to one window per
>   forward (97–131 s for 8 MiB on the two-network crossing, 26.5–52.2 s without it); an app-limited delivery sample
>   must not lower the estimate it feeds (draft-cheng-iccrg-delivery-rate-estimation §3.3).
>
> Joined windows must read one state of the file. A batch is given up only when it stalls (no byte for one budget),
> never at a deadline estimated from its size. Measured on two Docker networks at 100 ms one way with 3 % loss:
> 8 MiB in 28.8–33.9 s against 82.3–87.1 s for one window per forward. With ±40 ms jitter the two are even
> (125–145 s), bound by the session's congestion window (condition 7). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-10-07-a-cross-region-read-took-one-wan-round-trip-per-window.md`; regression
> `a_cross_region_read_is_served_from_read_ahead_windows_and_byte_identical` (7 forwards for 1,041 pages, where
> one window per forward took 66).

> **Status (2026-10-07, status reports each record session's congestion state).** A node's `DaemonStatus` carries
> its record session to each peer (`fleet.sessions`): congestion window, smoothed round trip, probe timeout, spurious
> losses, persistent collapses, bytes consumed and path MTU. A session out on loan (a read keeps one borrowed for the
> whole transfer) reports its state when last returned, marked `lent`. The CLI prints `fleet_session` lines, `--json`
> and MCP carry the same fields, and `docs/wip/bench/multiregion/reads.sh` prints the owner's sessions after its
> reads. This is the evidence condition 7 needs on the real crossing, whose reads gained a tenth where the simulator
> gained threefold. Regression `a_nodes_status_reports_each_record_session_with_its_congestion_state`.

> **Status (2026-10-07, a forwarded verb is waited for while the daemon lives).** A client waited one liveness budget
> for a reply, while the daemon bounds a forwarded verb by a location round (one budget) and the forward (one budget
> plus the path's tail). So a forwarded write on a live daemon inside its own bounds was reported `Stalled` at 1 s
> (reproduced with a successor answering each step 0.6 s late). Forwardability is now one rule on `RequestBody` in
> `slates-ipc` (`may_be_forwarded`), read by the server's routing and by the client's `defers_reply`. A verb the
> daemon may forward is waited for while the daemon lives, as a page read already was, and the async driver derives
> patience from the request (`Client::defers`), so the SDKs follow the same rule. Liveness stays the anchor
> heartbeat's (`daemon_gone`). Regression `a_forward_answered_within_its_bounds_is_never_reported_stalled`
> (`docs/bugs/2026-10-07-a-client-reported-a-live-daemon-stalled-mid-forward.md`).

> **Status (2026-10-07, a successor's own volume before it serves).** A node that adopted a volume's head in a
> takeover owns it before its owner shard has materialized the volume. A verb from its own client in that window
> reaches the forward path, because the catalog lacks the volume. It ran the location round, which asks the peers
> and never the node itself, and was refused `HomedElsewhere`. That refusal names another region, so it was false.
> Now, when the routing names this node the owner, the verb is refused with the owner shard's retryable
> `Overloaded`, the answer a forwarded write already gives while its acceptance waits on its owner. It is counted
> (`fleet.owner_location.owned_unmaterialized`) beside the materialization's own counters:
> `fleet.materialize.refused.*`, `.waits.*`, `.unanswered`, and `fleet.fetch.*`. The materialization's typed
> refusal had been discarded. Regressions: `a_successor_refuses_its_unmaterialized_volume_as_retryable_not_homed_elsewhere`
> (unit), and the fleet tests' successor-serves check, which failed 2 of 2 with the old answer and passes 6 of 6.

> **Status (2026-10-11, a contentless volume materializes head-only).** `owned_unmaterialized` is a *transient*
> window only if materialization eventually completes. It did not for a **contentless** volume (a scratch volume
> created but never sealed — no content manifest): `materialize_pending` dropped every `manifest=None` volume
> without building its db catalog entry, so a taken-over scratch volume stayed `owned_unmaterialized`/`Overloaded`
> forever, and a forwarded read answered false `NotFound`. Now `materialize` builds a **head-only** entry from the
> adopted head and catalog registers (no archive: `materialize_taken_over` takes `Option<&Archive>` and skips the
> restore), identical to a fresh scratch `Create`. A 1024-volume takeover reproduction served both ends at ~24/33
> periods (was: never served, 1024 dropped); the crash-at-every-step recovery oracle is 39/0. A transient false
> `NotFound` in the settle window before the successor processes the retirement was fixed in the same pass: `find`
> answers a retryable `Overloaded` for an object this node holds a copy of (a recovery candidate), never `NotFound`
> for an object that exists. `docs/bugs/2026-10-11-taken-over-scratch-volumes-never-become-servable.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-18, a taken-over volume's materialization is bounded).** Each wait of a taken-over volume's
> materialization (`fleet.materialize.waits.*`: its content, placement, catalog, catalog placement or shard; its live
> log; a refused or unanswered materialization) retried every period without end. Now each pending volume counts its
> attempts, one a period, and past the failover SLO's worth without progress (`failover_slo_ns / HEARTBEAT_NS`, the
> bound a taken-over green has had since 2026-11-09) it is given up on: its owner shard records it unrecovered, every
> verb on it answers `NotRecovered { cause: TakeoverIncomplete { waited_on } }` naming the wait (`content`, `placement`,
> `catalog`, `catalog_placement`, `shard`, `live`, `refused`), and `fleet.materialize.given_up` counts it. Progress is
> more of the head's content staged than ever before, so a large volume whose fetch is cut by its deadline each period
> is given up only once the fetch stops advancing. For a wait on its catalog register (or that register's placement)
> while the takeover round that adopted it still pages, progress is an advance of that round's pages, for a green as
> for a volume (`takeover::rounds_still_paging`, `fleet::paging_round`): a catalog register sorts after every head of
> its creator's partition and a round reads a page (about 55 objects) a member a period, so on a host with more than
> the bound's worth of pages of heads in one partition every catalog arrives after the bound, and the green bound of
> 2026-11-09 counted those waits. The wait counts only while the round stands still, so a round that never finishes
> paging cannot hold the object pending without end. A mirror-seeded volume given up is reported adopted to the
> council, unrecovered on its successor. Regressions: `a_taken_over_volume_whose_catalog_never_comes_is_refused_by_name`,
> `a_taken_over_volume_whose_content_never_comes_is_refused_by_name` (GAPS 2026-11-09, the sibling bullet), and the
> counting rule's unit tests (`a_catalog_wait_reads_its_round_only_while_the_round_pages`,
> `a_round_advances_only_when_a_member_moves_on_and_a_restart_keeps_the_count`,
> `a_wait_on_a_paging_round_is_progress_only_while_the_round_advances`,
> `a_round_pages_until_every_asked_member_has_answered_every_page`,
> `a_volumes_attempts_start_again_only_at_a_new_high_of_staged_content`).

> **Owner location (2026-09-17).** A foreign node cannot reconstruct a historic copyset from
> present membership. After its creator route stops being usable, it asks authenticated
> home-region peers through a bounded read-only exchange. A peer claims itself only when its
> held-object route names itself, it has applied the committed regional generation, and adoption
> is no longer pending. Replies bind the object, region and root version. Only the newest observed
> regional generation supplies a hint; conflicting owners at that generation refuse. The admitted
> session table bounds fanout; the existing liveness budget bounds each exchange, and the round
> retains all stragglers until their sessions return. This is location information, not a lease
> or authority grant. One successful route per live client avoids repeated discovery; a changed
> root/home, dead peer or failed forward invalidates it. No global object catalog is added.
> The actual verb is forwarded once. Its completion belongs to the executing owner; the origin
> does not turn a transient routing refusal into a permanent local completion. The five-node
> routing regression distinguishes a copyset successor from an unrelated live node, and the
> forwarded-write test requires its retry to reach the owner. Evidence and limits:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-17-remote-lookup-guesses-outside-the-copyset.md`.
>
> **Status (2026-09-29).** Two parts of this rule assumed the regional generation changes only on membership and
> takeover. Since the council settles neighbourhoods and confirms takeovers, it moves several times within a
> few periods after every takeover, so both parts refused the one owner a lookup could find. The location test
> then failed in 4 of 17 Linux io_uring rounds.
> - **"Has applied the committed regional generation."** Right after a takeover the successor's coordinator
>   period runs long, and its placement stayed a version behind its council (7 against 8) through the lookup,
>   so it refused to answer (`placement_behind`). A node now claims under its council's configuration: while
>   that holds it as a member and its route names itself. Ownership moves only when the owner is retired, so
>   the placement's lag cannot make a claim false.
> - **"Only the newest observed regional generation supplies a hint."** A survivor that had installed an
>   unrelated settlement answered "not mine" under a newer version, and the round discarded the successor's
>   claim. Only claims compete now, the newest claim winning, and conflicting claims at one generation still
>   refuse. A peer that is not the owner carries no ownership information and never takes a claim away
>   (AC-8.14: "after one stable configuration change a stale lookup refreshes once").
> - Regressions: `a_node_whose_placement_lags_its_council_still_claims_what_it_owns`,
>   `a_peer_that_is_not_the_owner_never_takes_away_a_claim`.
>
> **Status (2026-11-18, A-489).** "Replies bind the root version" refused the owner for a lookup's whole budget when the
> owner was a root learner behind the asker's root. A seat change moves the root's version (A-406), and a learner fetched
> only when its regions or its known voters looked wrong, so one that missed the change at formation never caught up.
> Main's quiet Mac Studio runs failed 2 of 3 with `OwnerUnreachable`: the successor counted `root_view_differs` once for
> each of the foreign voter's 58 and 68 rounds. The binding stands: a query under another root view is refused. A query
> bound to a newer view than the peer holds now also tells the peer that it is behind and that the asker holds the newer
> root, so the peer's root learner fetches from the asker at its next period. The asker looks again every poll interval,
> and that look is answered. Counted `fleet.owner_location.root_behind`. Regression:
> `a_location_query_bound_to_a_newer_root_sends_the_learner_to_fetch_from_its_asker`. The converse is done too (A-504): a
> refusal names the root its peer holds, where it was an empty reply, so an asker behind it counts itself behind
> (`fleet.owner_location.asker_behind`), its root learner fetches from that peer at its next period, and each look of a
> lookup asks under the root the asker holds at that look. Regression: `a_behind_askers_round_is_answered_after_one_fetch`.

> **A forward waits for the owner's session (2026-09-25).** A forward took the owner's record session once
> and, when a coordinator dispatch or a discovery page had it out, refused the client `HomedElsewhere` at
> once — though the owner was live and the route right (`fleet.owner_location.direct` counted each write),
> and though the forward's own contract said the caller retries. Right after a takeover that session is
> busiest: a write, or the retry of a write just served, was refused about once in fourteen runs of the
> copyset history. The forward now waits for the session inside its one deadline (the liveness budget),
> polled at the fleet's poll interval, and counts where a missing session was
> (`fleet.forward.session_out`, `fleet.forward.no_session`, `fleet.forward.session_never_returned`);
> the caller counts an unsent forward (`fleet.owner_location.forward_unsent`). Proven by
> `a_forward_waits_for_the_owners_session_while_it_is_out`, which holds the session out as a dispatch does
> and fails on the old forward with CI's refusal; the copyset history passed 45 of 45 after it, the wait
> exercised in 7. Owed: the location round still skips a peer whose session is out (one round answers
> `Unavailable`; a client retries past it). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-25-a-forward-refused-while-the-owners-session-was-out.md`.

**Membership.** SWIM with Lifeguard: direct probe → k indirect proxies → SUSPECT → DEAD;
suspicion timeout `max − (max−min)·log(C+1)/log(K+1)` with the originator excluded; peer
confirmation before suspicion; gossip with λ·ln(n+1) rebroadcasts under the measured per-path
MTU; a bounded local-health multiplier; randomized probe order; and, from Vivaldi network
coordinates each node learns from its own measured round-trip times and exchanges on the
acknowledgement, a per-peer RTT prediction that selects the indirect-probe relays nearest the
target, so a slow far peer is not mistaken for a failed near one. Every parameter derived from
measured RTT, loss, and convergence (`research/survey-hyperscale.md` §8.4 gives the formula per
parameter; the local-health multiplier is a small integer cap, 3×–4×, not the raw `(LHM+1)`,
which over-dilates timers under sustained probe failure).

**Deployment.** A fleet is described once, in one manifest every node starts from with its own
name: the fleet's TLS name, `f`, and each node's advertised address and operator-provisioned
certificate (§4.13 enrollment distributes these; until it does, DER files beside the manifest). A
node's member id is the leading eight bytes of the BLAKE3 hash of its certificate — the one fact
about a node every peer already holds, since it pins it — so ids agree fleet-wide without a
registry (D-14). A node's advertised port and the next are its two serve sockets — probes on the
first, records on the second — each shared by every peer through the session plane's connection-id
demultiplexer (§4.10a §8; a peer's re-dial after a lost session replaces the old session), and every
peer dials it there, so both ends of every session are computed from the same file and can never
disagree. A node behind a port mapping (a NAT's port forward, a container runtime's published ports,
the chaos harness's fault relay) also names where its own two sockets bind (`bind`: an IPv4 literal
and the base of the same block, A-277); it serves there while every peer still dials its advertised
ports, and the mapping between them is the operator's. It announces the advertised ports alone, the record
plane's too (A-330), since a peer prefers the announcement to the manifest at every later dial: announced at
its bound port, every redial of a record link went around the mapping. A manifest with fewer than `f + 1` nodes, a
repeated name or certificate, a base (advertised or bound) at the end of the port range, or an identity
the TLS stack cannot use, is refused by name at boot. A node addressed by name, and any peer enrolled under a trusted
root (it announces its address, which may be a name), is resolved at every dial through the host's nameservers, read
once at boot: `/etc/resolv.conf` on Unix; on Windows, which has no such file, the DNS servers of the network adapters
that are up and have a gateway, with `resolv.conf(5)`'s default timeout and attempts (A-490); a manifest that may dial
a name on a host with no IPv4 nameserver is refused at boot by name. The two serve
sockets are bound once, before the daemon starts (`FleetTransport::bind`, between the pure plan and the
daemon), so an address already in use refuses the start by plane and address, rather than leaving a
daemon that can never be probed. A caller that already holds its ports hands the bound sockets over
instead (`UdpSocket::adopt`, the socket-activation pattern), so a port is never released between learning
it and serving on it
(`docs/bugs/2026-09-28-a-released-test-port-was-taken-before-the-daemon-bound-it.md`). A supervising
anchor is such a caller. It binds the node's two ports once and hands them to every daemon it spawns in
`SLATES_ANCHOR_FLEET_SERVE` (as it hands over the NFS listener, §4.6), so the manifest's fixed ports are
never free between a daemon's death and its restart. The daemon refuses an inherited socket bound elsewhere
than its plan says. The manifest's seed id is a routing placeholder, never an incarnation: a record link
that learns the peer's first fresh id keeps the dial it has in flight. Only a later id change, a restart,
drops it. `status` reports the node's member id, `f`, host epoch,
the members it holds alive and the peers it has probed. A laptop has no manifest: its member id is
its machine identity's hash and it is its own one member at `f = 0` — the same code path (R8).
(A-13, `crates/server/src/deploy.rs`; proven by three real daemon processes in
`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`.)

**Slow versus stuck.** A long operation that waits on remote progress — a mirror catching up, a
put filling its quorum — is told apart from a stalled one by a progress witness (a monotone,
operation-defined measure and the time it last advanced): near its deadline, an operation still
advancing is granted a bounded extension rather than declared failed, and only a stalled one, or
one that has spent its extension budget, is left to the hard timeout. This is the per-operation
analogue of the local-health multiplier (slow ≠ dead). The statistical change-point witnesses for
noisy progress (`research/survey-hyperscale.md`, hyperscale's `health/progress_witness`) are owed.

**Placement.** The group assigns every host a neighbourhood of S hosts across distinct failure
domains from the declared tree, with S derived from the measured re-replication bandwidth
needed to restore a host's copies within the recovery budget and from the accepted loss
probability under coincident failures (Copysets); candidate holders per object are rendezvous
over the neighbourhood; a neighbourhood change moves only the objects whose candidates changed,
add before remove. The copyset count is computed at every configuration change and compared with
its bound; exceeding it is a placement bug, not a tripwire. (Implemented: `Configuration::copyset_count`
is the actual `owner_copysets` partition, `coincident_loss` its `#copysets·C(F,R)/C(H,R)` loss under a
coincident failure of `F` hosts, and `within_loss_bound(ε, F)` the check — computable from any
configuration; the operator's accepted `ε` and the coincident-failure size are the durability policy that
gates a refusal, the last wiring owed.)

**Mirroring.** Every committed record and its content is shipped to the mirror region's
neighbourhood of the owner asynchronously, in epoch and sequence order, by the same put
machinery; the mirror acknowledges at f+1 of its candidates. `mirror_age` is measured on the
home clock from the oldest home-committed record still lacking mirror acknowledgement, zero
when caught up; status also reports the mirrored prefix and observation freshness. Lost clock
or acknowledgement knowledge is unknown, not zero lag. A record count is a separate metric; `await placed(mirror)` returns when the named
snapshot's record and content are acknowledged there; elapsed time includes any backlog,
content transfer and quorum acknowledgement, not a guaranteed single WAN round trip. Region loss promotes the mirror through the root group at operator cadence; the loss
window is the mirror lag at that moment, zero for every operation that awaited the mirror.

> **Status (2026-11-07, A-243: a partition's snapshot cadence follows the partition).** The cadence was derived once at
> boot from the replay throughput recovery measured. A daemon booted fresh replayed nothing, took one byte a
> microsecond, and re-encoded its whole partition every 1 MB of log for its whole life: at 10,000 works the green's
> owner shard spent about 1,800 of 2,241 samples doing it. A partition now snapshots once the log since its last
> snapshot has taken the recovery budget's worth of replay work and is at least that snapshot's size
> (`replay::snapshot_due`). The work is timed on each commit's append and apply, the work a replay repeats per record,
> and never extrapolated from one stretch of log to the next, whose records may differ in size. So snapshot work stays
> within about twice the log it absorbs, whatever the partition's size, and `slates status` shows each shard's
> snapshots, their bytes and longest duration, the log appended, the tail's bytes and measured work, the budget and
> the floor.
> Recovery's bound changes with it (the paragraph below). The snapshot still runs whole on the committing shard's
> turn; slicing it is owed. (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-partitions-snapshot-cadence-never-left-its-boot-guess.md`.)
> **A-420 (2026-11-18):** the commits timed each record's encode in place of the decode a replay does, and a replay
> held every decoded record of its tail before applying the first, so a record that decodes dearer than it encodes
> (a thousand one-byte keys, one allocation each) replayed in more than its commits measured and the tail ran past its
> budget before the trigger fired. A commit now decodes its record as the replay will before writing it, and times
> that decode with the encode, the write and the apply; recovery decodes, applies and drops one record at a time.
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-the-snapshot-trigger-timed-the-encode-in-place-of-the-replays-decode.md`.)

**Recovery.** Node restart: the anchor segment replays the local log and `put_wal` into fresh
indexes; the node rejoins with a new ephemeral id (a restart is a join); its owned objects are
taken over by its neighbours after the membership horizon. A **warm** restart, with the anchor
retained, keeps every replica the node acknowledged: a holder acknowledges a content put only once
its shard's recovery image carrying the put is committed into anchor-owned RAM, and recovery holds
the image's replicas again, re-verified, before the node serves (A-51). A whole-anchor loss is the
RAM-fault case; that node holds nothing for others until re-replication fills it. RAMCloud's recovery-time budget is a reference, not a Slates result;
metadata takeover uses a configuration decision and phase-one exchange. A read may additionally
need content fetch and a confirmed lease; measure that complete recovery boundary. A partition's own part is decoding
its last snapshot and replaying the log after it. A snapshot comes once that log has taken the budget's worth of
replay work, as its commits measured it, and is at least the last snapshot's size (A-243). So a partition's recovery is
at most decode(P) + max(budget, the replay of P bytes of log), where P is its snapshot's size: the budget while the
partition is small enough, about twice its own snapshot's cost once it outgrows it. The commits' measure covers the
replay's work: each commit times its record's encode, its decode as the replay will decode it, its checksum and copy
into the ring, and its apply, where a replay reads, checksums, decodes and applies a record at a time (A-420). It errs
early by the encode, which bounds the replay's read, and by a preempted commit's stall.

> **Status (2026-11-17, g230: the owner's `put_wal` is its `Local` records).** No structure of its own is needed: a
> seal's snapshot record stays `Local` in the owner's partition, durable in its anchor with the rest of the log, until
> its content and its head both place; each record period's seal walk starts a seal for any head not placed
> (`fleet::sealable_head`), and the record plane re-ships every record a holder has not acknowledged from the
> partition's state. So a warm restart loses only the walk's progress, and the seal is made again from the snapshot.
> Held by `a_seal_its_owner_had_not_placed_at_a_warm_restart_places_after_it` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: the
> seal's head refused by both holders until the owner restarted over its anchor, then placed, the owner's member id
> unchanged).

**Failure matrix.** A candidate holder slow: Masked (the hedge completes the put elsewhere;
the slow holder goes on probation after the derived count and the group replaces it). Fewer than
f+1 candidates reachable: Degraded (the object stays `Local`, `placed = false` is reported;
writes continue locally). Owner loss: Degraded for the membership horizon, then Masked after
takeover, with the loss window reported. Configuration group quorum lost: Degraded (no
takeovers, no neighbourhood changes, no home moves; every owner keeps writing to its candidates
under its confirmed authority only while that authority remains valid; seals place only with
eligible quorums and admitted content). Partition of a minority: Refused for writes by owners on
the minority side once they cannot confirm membership; snapshot reads continue. Correlated loss
of all f+1 copies of a snapshot: data loss of that snapshot, documented (D-18); the neighbourhood
bound makes it as rare as the operator chose. Stale configuration on a request: Refused
(`ConfigurationStale`) with the current version; bounded refresh/retry while the request
remains live.

**Refusals.** `LeaseUnconfirmed`, `NotOwner{owner}`, `NotPlaced{scope}`, `StaleEpoch{current}`,
`ConfigurationStale{version}`, `MembershipEpochStale`, `PlacementUnavailable`, `QuorumLost`,
`DuplicateRequest{original}` (informational: the original result is returned).

**Derived constants.** f from the failure-domain tree (0 on a laptop); candidates = 2f+1; commit
at f+1; scatter width S from measured re-replication bandwidth × recovery budget and the accepted
loss probability, defaulting to the candidate floor 2f+1 — one copyset, the tightest and lowest-loss
neighbourhood — until a deployment has sized its recovery (implemented: `ConfigGroup` bounds every
neighbourhood to this width; placement and takeover route each object through the fixed-copyset
construction in `candidates_for`, so above the floor the number of copysets stays linear in S, not
`Θ(S^{2f})`, and a takeover successor is always a host that held the object — placement carries a per-host
failure-domain map so no copyset repeats a domain, defaulting to unique-per-host (each host its own); an
operator declares a node's domain with an optional per-node `domain` in the deployment manifest, threaded
to the configuration group at boot; the daemon derives S at boot as `scatter_width(D, B, T, f)` — D the
RAM content reserve, T the recovery budget, B the operator's stated re-replication bandwidth (0 by default,
so S is the floor; measuring B needs a real network, §4.10a, deferred)); hedge delay = measured p95 put
latency per
class; probation threshold = late
count over the measured window that exceeds the hedge rate's variance; detection timeout for
membership from RTT p99 × k; auto-seal cadence as before; healer cadence from the measured
put-failure rate; membership lease from heartbeat RTT p99 × k; election timeout for the
configuration group ≥ 10 × broadcast RTT p99 with the randomization span from RTT variance; the
consensus window = one append budget for each period a lost batch takes to repair, ⌈2 × broadcast RTT
tail / heartbeat⌉ (one on a loopback; `ElectionTiming::window_budget`, set each period with the timing);
SWIM period = max(k × RTT p99, scheduler quantum); gossip λ from measured convergence;
tombstone retention = measured partition-heal p99; mirror shipping batch from the measured WAN
bandwidth-delay product.

> **Election jitter is an independent draw per attempt (2026-09-28).** Each follower's timeout is
> `base + (splitmix64(id ^ attempt·γ) mod span)` periods — deterministic, but independent across nodes and
> across attempts, as Raft's randomized timeout is (§5.2, §9.3). The previous `(id + attempt) mod span` kept
> two congruent nodes congruent forever (both attempts advance together), so two survivors of a leader loss
> could split the vote every round: 19 s on the multi-region simulation until the cut healed, never with a
> permanent loss. Now a successor is elected within 3.0–3.6 s there (one seed 8.3 s, one collision round).
> Record: `docs/bugs/2026-09-28-correlated-election-jitter-livelocked-a-split-vote.md`.

> **Collection boundary correction (2026-09-20, AC-8.12).** A collector drains replies
> before judging its deadline; after a polling sleep it always returns to the receive
> loop. Judging with the pre-sleep count discarded healthy replies already queued and
> delayed the Linux hedge to 3.195–4.487 s against a 3 s hold. Simulated content and
> record histories each failed in 0.01 s before the shared correction. Content also
> retains late offer sessions alongside late put sessions, in at most two reply
> channels. This changes no deadline or extension budget. The fleet fault fixture
> selects its first candidate from the object's owner-shard configuration, including
> failure domains. Records: `docs/bugs/2026-09-20-collectors-expire-before-reading-queued-replies.md`
> and `docs/bugs/2026-09-20-hedge-test-reconstructs-the-wrong-candidate.md`.
> Verification: ten serial Linux io_uring hedge histories passed (281.630–506.180 ms);
> the full workspace passed 1,524 tests with zero failures and 14 ignored, including
> all 49 fleet histories. Strict Clippy and structural checks also passed.

**Worked example.** Two zones, f=1, host A's neighbourhood {B, C, D}: an agent on A creates a
volume; the create returns after the local append; the head record (epoch 1) goes to the two
candidates rendezvous chose from {B, C, D} and commits at the first acknowledgement beyond A's
own; the agent writes for a while (owner-local); the seal schedule seals a snapshot, its chunks
go to A's two content candidates, one is slow, the hedge sends to the third candidate, the put
commits at two acknowledgements, and the head record names the two holders that answered. Node A
loses power; B's SWIM confirms A dead; the regional group bumps A's epoch and assigns the volume
to the candidate rendezvous ranks first among {B, C, D}; that host asks the neighbourhood for A's
highest records, adopts the head, and serves; the agent's SDK reconnects by routing the id to
the new owner, its retries return their original completion records, and the volume reports a
loss window equal to the edits after the last placed seal. Failure: A wakes up and sends a head
record with epoch 1; the first holder answers `StaleEpoch{2}`; A drops the role and nothing is
applied.

**Laptop degenerate.** One node: f=0, every candidate set is the owner, every commit is a local
append, the configuration group is one self-acknowledging voter that never receives a takeover,
the mirror does not exist and `await placed(mirror)` is refused `Unsupported`, and the loss
window is the process-restart window (zero, thanks to the anchor). Same code, zero modes.

### 4.9 Wire protocol (D-15)

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-539: wire major 3).** A host's refusal code is typed by its numbering (§4.15 step 6): an errno
> field carries an errno alone, and a Win32 error code rides in a variant appended beside it. A major-2 Windows peer put
> Win32 codes in errno fields, which no append-only change can say of them, so the major is 3 and a major-2 peer is
> refused before its body is read (`crates/wire/src/header.rs`, as A-237 took major 2).

> **Status (2026-11-07, A-241: a client proves its id).** A client's id names its seat: its retained completion records,
> its attachments, every verb after. The rendezvous carries only the id a client wants, which a stranger can name, and
> a request carries its id in its slot word. So now:
> - **A session key per id** (`slates_server::session_key`): keyed BLAKE3 over the id under the node's session secret,
>   which the first daemon under an anchor makes and publishes in the supervision block, and every later one adopts.
>   The key travels only in the client's own region (its header's bytes 64 to 96, region layout 4): written by the
>   daemon for an id it issues fresh, and by a client resuming an id before its first request. `Session` carries it.
> - **Checked once a slot**, in constant time, before its first request. A slot that does not prove its id is refused
>   `SessionUnproven` with nothing recorded, and ended without retiring anything of the id's; the id is given back.
> - **A request names its own client.** One whose id names another client than its slot's is refused `BadRequest`
>   before any effect, recorded nowhere.
> Proven by `a_stranger_with_a_dead_clients_id_gets_neither_its_seat_nor_its_records` and
> `a_client_cannot_send_a_request_under_another_clients_id` (`crates/client/tests/client.rs`), each red before and
> red-checked (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-stranger-took-a-dead-clients-seat-and-planted-its-replies.md`).

> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-21).** A client's request sequence never wraps.
> - **Range and marker.** Sequences run from 1 to `LAST_SEQUENCE = u32::MAX − 1`, and `u32::MAX` is kept
>   as the session's exhausted marker, so a resume from it issues nothing.
> - **Refusal.** Past the last sequence every fresh request, including the automatic acknowledgement and
>   a rebind, is refused `ClientError::SequencesExhausted` before it is sent.
> - **What still works.** Retries of issued ids are still answered from their completion records.
> - **The transition.** New work goes through a new client, with a fresh client id and window.
> - **Arithmetic.** The acknowledgement cadence compares without wrapping. Before this, the sequence
>   wrapped to zero, which the daemon's window then met as already acknowledged
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-request-sequences-wrapped-into-acknowledged.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-19, byte sequences):** `Wire` dispatches a sequence operation to
> its element type. `u8` copies the canonical payload in bulk; structured elements encode
> and decode each field. Length prefixes, schema hashes and bytes are unchanged, and lengths
> are checked before allocation. Scalar-call counters and byte oracles guard both paths.
> The mounted fsstress trace found scalar encoding taking 442 ms of a 487 ms publication;
> bulk encoding took about 1.5 ms for a comparable image in the same debug-build environment.
> This fixes a measured source of heartbeat starvation; it is not a bound on arbitrary
> recovery image sizes. Record: the 2026-09-19 NFS heartbeat report.

**Framing.** A 32-byte header: magic (4), major (2), minor (2), flags (4), channel/class (2),
kind (2), length (4), checksum (4), request id (8); then the body. All little-endian, 8-byte
aligned; the reader checks length against the class's frame cap before allocating; the checksum
is verified before decode; bodies are canonical encodings generated by a derive with a schema hash
carried in the first body word; unknown kinds are refused; append-only evolution within a major.

**Classes.** Control (never shed), Metadata (leases, catalog), Bulk (chunks, archive streams),
Telemetry (shed first). Isolation spans admission credits, queue slots, CPU slices, arena
headroom, network frames and guest/device queues. Each unit of bulk work has a derived bounded
quantum so a large transfer cannot monopolize the executor. Reserved control capacity admits
bounded recovery work even under bulk saturation; "never shed" does not mean an unbounded
control queue. Repair and teardown carry an authenticated purpose, not a caller-selected high
priority. Measure metadata/control latency and memory under a saturated bulk producer; separate
wire labels or queues alone do not establish this guarantee.

**Configuration version.** Every fleet request carries the sender's configuration version and
every record carries the owner's host epoch; a receiver with a newer configuration refuses with
`ConfigurationStale{version}` and the current version, and a holder with a higher epoch for the
sender refuses with `StaleEpoch{current}`. Refreshes consume the operation's bounded retry
budget; the latter refusal ends the sender's authority.

**Exactly-once.** `(client id, sequence)` request ids; completion records kept until acknowledged
(the client acknowledges by advancing its sequence window, naming the ids at or below it that it
still owes); retries return the original result; provisioning is therefore safe to retry after any
failure.

> **Status (2026-10-07, the bound built).** The bound this section requires ("exhaustion refuses admission") was not
> built: a client's records grew until it acknowledged, and a client that never did grew them without end. Each
> shard now holds at most `2 × slots` unacknowledged records per client: the ring's slots in flight, the half ring
> `slates_client` acknowledges at, and one lost acknowledgement. Past that a new request is refused
> `AcknowledgementOwed { retained, bound }`, never run and never recorded; a retry of an answered id and an
> `Acknowledge` are always served (`verbs::acknowledgement_owed`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-10-07-a-client-that-never-acknowledged-grew-its-completion-records-without-bound.md`). A conforming
> client meets the refusal only while it keeps issuing new requests past the bound with an `Unpublished` id still
> unretried, which holds its acknowledgement back; it retries that id first. Regression
> `a_client_that_never_acknowledges_is_refused_at_its_bound_and_served_once_it_acknowledges`.

> **Status (2026-11-06, the watermark stops below the first request still awaited).** The client's acknowledgement
> covered every sequence it had sent, so a client with several requests in flight (any async caller; the load
> harness multiplexing logical clients over one connection) acknowledged requests whose replies had not come. Their
> completion records were then released, so a resend after a restart was answered `DuplicateRequest` for a create
> that had been applied, and a deferred verb (a fleet forward, a submit awaiting its commit) recording after the
> watermark was refused `StaleCompletion`. The watermark is now RIFL's: just below the first request with no reply
> (Lee et al., SOSP 2015), as well as below an `Unpublished` id. A client that keeps sending past an old request still
> awaited therefore meets `AcknowledgementOwed` at the `2 × slots` bound, as backpressure until that request answers
> (`slates_client` `ack_watermark`; `an_acknowledgement_never_covers_a_request_still_awaited`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-an-acknowledgement-covered-requests-still-awaited.md`).
>
> The same day it was extended to the refusals retryable under the same id. A forwarded submit whose acceptance
> outlived the owner's budget is answered `Overloaded`: the verb ran, and its completion is recorded at the commit.
> The next acknowledgement covered it, so its resend was refused `DuplicateRequest` (447 in fixtures' `f = 1`
> 1,000-client rung). An async caller's `Overloaded` or `OwnerUnreachable` id now holds the watermark below it until
> it is resent or released (`release_retryable`), within the reconnect budget, so a caller that never resends cannot
> pin it (`a_forwarded_submit_refused_overloaded_while_it_commits_is_answered_under_its_own_id`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-resend-under-its-id-was-already-acknowledged.md`).

> **Status (2026-11-17, an `Overloaded` verb is never its own completion).** `Overloaded` means the request was not
> started, so its id stays unanswered and a resend under it runs the verb. Raised inside a verb (a held copy not yet
> materialized in the takeover's settle window; a deferred verb whose task the full arena refused), it was recorded as
> the completion, and every resend under the id met it for good. `run_recorded` now leaves it unrecorded, counted
> `verb.overloaded_unrecorded`; a verb that refuses it part-way ends what it began itself, as the Shards attach ends its
> attachment (`a_resend_under_the_id_of_an_overloaded_verb_runs_the_verb`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-an-overloaded-verb-was-recorded-as-its-completion.md`). Open (GAPS): a live-shipped verb whose
> effects committed before its held-reply bound refused it, and a deferred task that ends on `Overloaded`.
>
> A-563 (2026-11-19): a deferred reply too. A reply that comes back through `deliver` is written by `retry_deferred`,
> which recorded every new one. So a read scatter's `Overloaded`, for a part not sent or not served (A-557), was the
> request's completion. It now leaves a `not_started` reply unrecorded as well
> (`a_resend_of_a_read_scatter_refused_overloaded_runs_it_again`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-read-scatters-overloaded-was-recorded-as-its-completion.md`).
>
> A-566 (2026-11-19): an operation that ran is never answered `Overloaded`. A consensus operation (a bootstrap, a
> recovery) runs on the control shard, then is published to every other shard. When a shard did not apply that
> publication, the answer was `Overloaded` naming that shard, so after A-563 the resend ran the operation again. It is
> now `DurabilityPending`. That answer says the operation ran, it is recorded, and its resend meets it
> (`a_recover_answered_after_it_ran_says_so_and_its_resend_takes_effect_once`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-consensus-operation-that-ran-was-answered-overloaded.md`).

> **Status (2026-11-08, A-252: a request waiting for a version is a durable state).** A submit whose acceptance waits for
> its version's commit was waited on in memory, so after a restart its resend under its own id found no record and ran
> again as a new version. The accept now logs `Op::CompletionAwaiting` in the transaction that appends the version, so
> the window answers `Seen::Awaiting` (never `New`) across any restart: the resend joins the wait, or is answered its
> version once it has placed. The wait counts toward the client's bound and leaves when its completion replaces it or the
> client acknowledges it. After a takeover the resend is refused retryable and nothing runs twice, but its version is not
> named, short of the failure matrix's Masked: owed as A-255 (GAPS).

> **Status (2026-11-09, A-255: a submit's completion moves with its green).** After a takeover a resend under its own id
> is answered the version it was accepted as, the failure matrix's Masked. Its completion key rides the version's chain
> entry and merge record, and the green's successor records it. The resend reaches the successor through the work's
> catalog record, which names the green: held, or learned from a location round. A version's record ships only once
> that catalog is committed, and the record plane ships the catalog at the work's creation. A merge record carries
> format version 1; another version is refused typed.

> **Status (2026-11-17, A-288: a work's route ends).** The route is kept only while the green's owner holds a completion
> it can reach: a submit forwarded from another node than the work's owner, not yet acknowledged. The merge record
> (format 2) and chain entry (version 3) name such a submit's work. The successor records the completion under it, and
> the route's adopter asks the green's owner each period and retires the route through the destroy's tombstone stages
> once none is held, or once the green is given up. Still held: a route to a green destroyed or lost while it is kept,
> one whose completion is never acknowledged, and one its adopter kept across a warm restart (GAPS).

> **Status (2026-11-07, A-245: an acknowledgement names the ids still owed).** A watermark is contiguous, so one held or
> slow request kept every later completion of its client: the owner pruned none of them, and past `2 × slots` refused
> the client's next requests `AcknowledgementOwed`. At `f = 1`, where nearly every slow submit is held, that was the
> steady state: 906,317 refused against 59,646 served on the owner shard of fixtures' 1,000-client rung, 2.46 million
> at the quiet arm's 10,000. An `Acknowledge { up_to, owed }` now covers every id the client issued and names the
> ones at or below it still owed (awaited, held for a resend, `Unpublished`): at most the ring's slots and the hold's
> cap. Every partition releases the rest and keeps the owed ones open, answerable and recordable. An acknowledgement
> closes only what it speaks for: an open id at or below its `up_to` that it does not name is closed, one above its
> `up_to` is left open, and a closed id is never opened again, so an acknowledgement that arrives late, by a scatter
> or a relay, can close only ids it covers and reopen none, and a released id is never executed twice. One naming an
> owed id above its `up_to`, or more than `2 × slots` of them, is refused whole (`BadRequest`, `ack.malformed`), never
> cut, since a cut would release ids still owed (raft). The origin relays the owed ids beside the watermark
> with a forwarded write, so the owner keeps a held submit's record too (`slates_wire::request::ClientWindow`,
> `Op::CompletionsAcknowledged`, `ClientCompletions::owed`, `ForwardedRequest::ack_owed`, `slates_client`
> `acknowledgement`; `a_client_holding_a_submit_for_its_resend_is_served_past_its_completion_bound`;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-held-request-kept-every-later-completion-of-its-client.md`).

> **Status (2026-11-05, A-216: an acknowledgement is answered once its own shard has released).** An `Acknowledge
> { up_to }` releases the client's records at or below `up_to` on every partition that may hold them. Its reply now
> promises one thing: the client's own shard has released them. The other shards' releases run as tasks the shard
> tracks (`ShardState::ack_scatters`, one entry per acknowledgement until every part is back). A part refused, or
> never sent because its shard's control channel was full, is counted (`ack.release_refused`, in `slates status`).
> It is retried by the next acknowledgement, whose watermark covers it. Before A-216 the reply waited for every
> shard. So one sync call in every half-ring paid the slowest shard's turn, and a shard held past the reply deadline
> failed it `Stalled`.
>
> Why exactly-once holds. A lagging release concerns only records at or below `up_to`. Every new request carries a
> sequence above it, since a client's sequences only grow, never wrap (`LAST_SEQUENCE`, AUD-29-21), and a new
> client never takes an id another has used (the listener assigns above every id any shard retains,
> `restore_client_ids`). So the only requests that can meet such a record are retries of ids already answered, and
> meeting their record, or the acknowledged window once it is released, is what exactly-once asks. The bound still
> holds: a release lagging on one shard is the "one lost acknowledgement" `2 × slots` already budgets for, and past
> the bound a new request is refused `AcknowledgementOwed` as before. And a lagging release is never overtaken: a
> client's later request to another shard is forwarded on that shard's control channel, the same channel and kind
> of message as the release, sent by the client's own shard after it, so it queues behind the release. A request can
> only find a release refused, which is counted.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-557: a read scatter is answered whole, or refused naming a shard whose part it lacks).** A
> listing, the grants and `DaemonStatus` gather a part from every shard. A part whose shard's state refused the borrow
> (the control shard fenced by a failed consensus publication, a retention refusal, a shard whose start failed) came
> home as an empty part, so the answer left out that shard's volumes, grants or report and read as whole. A part now
> comes home as what its shard served or as nothing, and nothing is settled as a part that could not be sent: the
> answer is `Overloaded { shard }` for the first such shard, and `scatter.part_unserved` counts it apart from a full
> control channel's refusal (`settle_unserved`; `a_read_scatter_whose_part_its_shard_refused_is_refused_naming_that_shard`,
> red before; `docs/bugs/2026-11-19-a-read-scatter-answered-whole-without-a-shards-part.md`).

**Flow control.** Credit-based, absolute offsets per stream; windows derived from the measured
bandwidth-delay product and the class's latency budget; the sender never exceeds credit; a
stalled receiver stalls only its own class.

**Transfer and cancellation.** Immutable named objects use identity, missing-set exchange,
verified ranges and resumable progress. Do not allocate a whole advertised object before its
class cap, claim and identity are checked. An unknown-length ingest uses an explicitly bounded
RAM session with per-consumer credits, checked offsets, cancellation and a terminal expiry.
A receiver distinguishes received, checksum-verified, identity-verified, placed and referenced;
only the last two imply retention under the required durability contract. Duplicate frames,
reconnects, corrupt chunks and canceled producers neither publish partial identities nor leak
session slots. Compression/decompression workspace is charged before input is accepted.
Completion records and retained response windows have bounds and acknowledgements; exhaustion
refuses admission rather than forgetting a live exactly-once obligation.

**Trace context.** The operation envelope carries a request identity for replay, optional
trace/span context for observation and optional caused-by event identity. These have different
lifetimes and cannot substitute for one another. Authentication establishes consumer and
volume tags separately (§4.13–§4.14); trace fields never authorize effects.

**Security.** Between hosts: TLS 1.3 via rustls with certificates provisioned by the operator
(bulk cost is symmetric crypto at memory speed, and no handshake sits on a hot path); on one host: peer credentials at rendezvous, no encryption.

**Refusals.** `BadMagic`, `UnsupportedMajor`, `FrameTooLarge{cap}`, `ChecksumMismatch`,
`UnknownKind`, `SchemaMismatch{expected, got}`, `CreditExceeded`.

**Derived constants.** Frame caps per class from measured MTU (per path) and class budgets;
credit windows from BDP; checksum choice: CRC32C on the control and metadata classes (hardware
instructions everywhere on the matrix), BLAKE3 identity on bulk chunks (already computed).

### 4.10 Distribution: replication under one rule, auto-seal, remote attach, ownership migration, mirroring, anti-entropy (D-14, D-16, D-17, D-18)

**Content replication.** Sealed chunks and manifests go to the owner's candidate holders under
the rule of §4.8: f+1 first, hedged to the rest of the 2f+1 after the measured p95, committed at
f+1 acknowledgements from any, the acknowledging set recorded in the head record; a chunk
already present on a candidate is never transferred again (the receiver reports its missing
set); a transfer is resumable (A-54): the offer stages the manifest on the holder, chunks travel
one per exchange and are verified and kept in that stage, the chunk completing the closure draws
the acknowledgement, and a cut transfer's next offer names exactly the verified chunks still owed;
a reader's fetch stages the same way, one chunk per exchange, and resumes from what it verified;
each holder's offer and transfer progress independently, with no wait on the slowest offer;
anti-entropy walks Merkle manifests between recorded holders and repairs only differing
subtrees; the healer replays puts that never reached f+1 from the owner's `put_wal`, and puts a
repeatedly late candidate on probation for the group to replace. The healer keeps every head naming
holders that hold its content (A-276). It re-offers a placed snapshot to exactly the holders its
placement names, all at once, and ends once each of them holds it, recording nothing: the head
already names them, and a head is never rewritten at its sequence. A holder that lacked chunks is
put exactly those, and counts one repair whenever its acknowledgement arrives, inside its round or
after the round stopped collecting at the hedge delay. A holder the placement names that has left
the fleet cannot be re-offered to, so the healer places the content on the current cohort at the
head's sequence plus one, which every holder's door admits as ahead of its records
(`content_retention::admits`), and records that placement together with the same head snapshot
advanced to that sequence, as one record; the next record period ships a head there naming holders
that hold the content. A placement naming fewer than f+1 holders is replaced the same way; at f = 0
the owner's own copy is the whole placement, and there is nothing to heal. Every heal is bounded from
its first round by its content round's whole span and one period, so its first round's every
acknowledgement is folded first; one that has not finished by then ends, counted, and a later step
heals the volume again. Cold sealed content (a
measured class by read rate, Phase 8) may be held as k+m fragments across k+m candidates instead
of f+1 copies, with hedged fragment fetches on read; the class boundary, (k, m) and the
reconstruction budget are derived, never fixed (D-O6).

**Auto-seal.** Each volume seals at its derived cadence (or on explicit `snapshot`, on `detach`,
on `archive`, and when the owner is asked to drain); publishing a server root is O(1), while
attachment flush barriers, hashing and puts have separately measured costs. An auto-seal
without a client barrier covers only server-visible writes (§4.6); the volume reports `last_placed_snapshot_age` and `mirror_age`
so an agent that needs durability can `await placed(scope)`.

> carries it as `VolumeStatus::loss`, CONTRACT 10):
> - `at_risk_ns`, `last_placed_snapshot_age` made exact: zero while the volume is exactly its newest seal placed on
>   `f + 1` hosts, or while it is live-shipped in a fleet (A-200: a write is answered at durability only once `f`
>   holders hold it); otherwise the age of that seal; with none placed, the age of the volume, which on a laptop
>   (`f = 0`) is always the case. `None`, never zero, when the time is from another boot of the clock.
> - `placed_sequence`: that seal's head sequence, the one a takeover would serve from now.
> - on a successor, `taken_over`: the epoch it serves under, the head sequence it served from, and whether from the
>   live log.
>
> Measured against the owner's own report (`a_successor_reports_the_loss_window_its_takeover_left`,
> `crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`): a seal placed, a second seal kept from placing by refusing the owner's records, a

> the successor reported serving that sequence under a later epoch; the first file survived and both later ones were

> decision for Ada), so the window is bounded.

> **Status (2026-11-05, A-222: another host's write attachment).** A client on another node attaches a volume in the
> record form, through the fleet's forward, and writes it through the file verbs; the owner records it under the
> client's host and client, ends it at a detach by volume, the client node's reap or the host's retirement, and a
> silent holder's lease at its term. Ownership migration and the snapshot's remote attach below stay owed.

**Remote attach.** An agent on node B attaches a snapshot of a volume owned by A: B routes the id
to A (or A's successor), reads the head record from A under its lease, fetches the manifest by
identity from a recorded holder (metadata only), creates a local read-only attachment record,
and serves the namespace immediately; chunk reads fault to hedged fetches by identity from the
recorded holders, verified on arrival, cached in B's arena under B's budget; a clone of a remote
snapshot is a local volume whose base chunks are fetched lazily and whose own seals go to B's
candidates.

**Prefetch.** Per base snapshot, the daemon records the ordered set of paths read within the
first window after attach (window derived from the measured attach-to-first-build interval); the
next attach of the same base prefetches that set in the background, bounded by the attachment's
budget; the policy is observe-first until a minimum number of attaches has been seen.

**Live shipping (opt-in; A-200 states the log, its acknowledgement and its takeover).** A volume created with policy `live-shipped` ships its op log to f+1
of its candidates and acknowledges writes at f+1; the backups apply entries in order and the
takeover successor is one of them, so promotion has no loss window; replica lag beyond a window
derived from the measured apply rate applies credit backpressure to that volume's writers only.
