> **A live-shipped volume conforms exactly as a plain one (2026-11-18; Windows OPEN).** The conformance suites (fsx,
> fsstress, pjdfstest) give the same verdicts over a volume live-shipped on an `f = 1` fleet as over a plain volume on the
> same host, case by case and record by record (`cargo xtask conformance compare`). That holds on macOS NFS (8,686
> pjdfstest cases) and on every Linux transport, including the daemon's own FUSE mount (8,798 cases a transport), and in
> every live run the owner's log ended durable at its head with both candidates holding it. With both candidates stopped,
> a size change waits for them and then succeeds rather than failing. CI's conformance lane runs the pair and that test
> on every push. Evidence and commands: `docs/wip/conformance.md`, the live-shipped pair; GAPS, "A live-shipped volume
> fails a waiting writer…".


**Ownership follows the writer.** Creation places the owner on the creator's host because the
writer's ring to its local owner shard is the latency floor. When write-intent attachments from
another host persist for the derived number of operations (the PNUTS rule on the origin of the
last N writes, N from the measured cost of a migration against the measured cross-host write
cost), ownership migrates there by the planned handoff: the current owner seals, the delta ships
by identity to the new host (which is usually a candidate holder already), the regional group
advances that object's ownership generation and names the new owner, the new owner runs phase
one, and the old owner's later writes are refused `StaleEpoch`. Load never moves ownership;
holder duty is balanced by neighbourhood changes; operators keep an explicit move.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-291: the explicit move is built for plain volumes; the automatic migration is not).**
> `slates move ID --to HOST` (`RequestBody::Move`; `slates_client::Client::move_volume`) runs the planned handoff
> as place, switch, adopt, release (`crates/server/src/moves.rs`):
> - **Place.** The owner refuses, each by its own `MoveRefusal`, a volume that is not a plain live one, one with an
>   attachment or lease, clones or a green that depends on it, or a snapshot other than its head, and a target that is
>   not another member of its neighbourhood (which holds the volume's sealing keys). A clone that reads no base
>   directory moves (a clone of a captured base, §4.15, or of a plain volume): its tree is archived whole, and its pin
>   on its origin's snapshot is given back when its old owner lets it go. It hands over its head (a snapshot
>   only if the volume changed since), freezes the volume (every other verb answers `Overloaded`, retryable), waits
>   until the head and catalog are placed at `f + 1` of its cohort (a live log durable at its head) and the head's
>   content is held by `f + 1` members other than itself, captures its own newest records of both registers and
>   reports `Move` with that cohort. The target's neighbourhood must cover the cohort, so the target's takeover could
>   recover the volume. An owner's own copy counts toward its content's placement only while it owns the volume (a
>   seal leaves the head held by the owner and `f` others): from the switch on, a successor of the new owner fetches
>   by identity from the hosts the head names, and a frozen copy serves no fetch. So a head short of `f + 1` others is
>   placed again first, at the next sequence on the cohort without the owner, and republished there naming the hosts
>   that took it (the handoff, `Heal::Handoff`, the healer's replace with the owner left out; `fleet.move.handoff_begun`).
>   The healer passes a frozen copy by.
> - **Switch.** The committed exception names the new owner; every node routes the volume there (a lookup asks the
>   exception's owner first), every holder takes the new owner's authority, and the old owner's records are refused.
> - **Adopt.** The new owner runs phase one by name over the recorded cohort (`MOVE_STREAM`, 29): the old owner
>   answers from its captured records, every other member from its copy; the newest of each register is re-committed
>   under the new owner's placement at the round's epoch, the volume is materialized as a takeover's successor
>   materializes it, sealed under the new owner's placement, and once that seal is placed the move is reported
>   adopted.
> - **Release.** Only then does the old owner let its frozen copy go (`Op::VolumeReleased`, no tombstone), so the
>   volume is held by `f + 1` throughout.
>
> A move's verb answers `Moving` until the switch and `Moved` from it; the old owner thaws only a move whose target
> left before any switch, or an unreported one whose records or handoff were not placed within the failover SLO
> (`MoveRefusal::Unplaced`). `a_volume_moved_to_another_member_is_served_there_and_its_old_owner_forwards`
> (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`) moves a volume between three daemons and back to its creator;
> `a_move_completes_when_its_old_owner_dies_at_the_switch` and
> `a_move_whose_target_dies_at_the_switch_is_served_by_its_successor` stop either side at the switch. The second was red
> 3 of 3 before the handoff (2026-11-18, the Mac Studio): the old owner was the target's successor, the head named it
> and the target alone, and its takeover fetched only from the dead target until it gave the volume up.
> An overlay does not move (its base stays on its source host, "Overlay volumes in a fleet"): a workspace that must move
> is a clone of a captured base (§4.15 `capture_base`), which `a_clone_of_a_captured_base_moves_and_gives_its_pin_back`
> moves between three daemons.
> Owed: the automatic migration by the origin of the last N writes (AC-8.16's other half: N is to be derived from a
> measured migration against the measured cross-host write), and a move carrying snapshots other than the head.
> A consumer drives the explicit move through the library alone (A-450): kiln moves an agent between its runners with
> its workspace volume by `Instance::move_volume` to the target's member id (its runner says the member its daemon
> serves as at every start, `Instance::member`), following `MoveProgress` until `Moved` with no clock of its own (the
> move ends itself: `Moved`, or `MoveUnplaced` once it thaws), every refusal reported by its kind and the agent left where
> it was; the target mounts the moved volume once its new owner serves it (its `Retry` pauses waited out). Its
> workspaces on the fleet's runners are clones of the folder's captured base (A-463), plain volumes the move takes; one
> capture serves the agents started over an unchanged folder, and a base goes with its last clone. A moved captured
> clone lands on its new owner against its capture (A-503): its move carries the captured state of every path it
> changed in its catalog, and the new owner keeps the moved head as its mark (§4.15's status); the mark is no snapshot
> that holds a later move back. Since A-544 every head of its own carries that record, so a workspace taken over after
> its runner's loss lands against its capture on the successor too; one whose runner died before its first snapshot
> was placed reaches the successor as an empty tree, and its landing is refused by kind.

**Green volumes in a fleet (D-27).** A green volume's owner runs its merge task; an increment's
post-state is a sealed snapshot of the work volume, placed to the work volume's candidates by
its owner before the increment is sent (the put runs at `submit` if the auto-seal has not already
placed it); the merge record is the next entry of green's ledger register: sent to all 2f+1
candidates under green's host epoch, committed at f+1 acknowledgements, and only when every
identity the new version references is placed; holders of green recompute the verdict and the
manifest identity from the record's inputs before serving the version and compare head
identities per version; a mismatch refuses that version on that holder with an alarm. Owner
loss takes green over on the candidate that rendezvous ranks first, which already holds the
ledger; increments in flight retry at the new owner by identity. Submissions from another host
route the green's id to its owner; a refusal from a non-owner names the current owner and epoch
and refresh/retry consumes the operation's bounded budget; placement refresh is single-flight
per green.

**Overlay volumes in a fleet.** A live base names an enrolled directory identity and its
serving host. Every local or remote clone retains that `BaseRef` together with the delta and
witnesses. Unchanged names, metadata and bytes continue to resolve through it; a clone must not
become a scratch volume seeded only with changed entries. An equal pathname on another host
is not evidence of source equivalence.

The base service remains on its source host; writable delta ownership can migrate by the same
fenced handoff used for other volumes while retaining this dependency. Delta replication and
mirror placement do not replicate unfetched host content. If the base host is unreachable,
available delta/pinned bytes remain readable and untouched paths return `BaseUnavailable`;
status explicitly reports partial availability and `DeltaWithLiveBase` coverage. A whole-view
availability guarantee is possible only for a `Complete` snapshot whose entire reference graph
has been captured, verified and placed. Taking over a delta never silently changes its base.

An explicit base capture (§4.15) creates that complete immutable source. Thereafter remote
clones share its manifest/chunks and fault bytes lazily from eligible holders; cloning remains
O(1) in tree size after admission. This is the preferred delta-plus-base design, not eager
whole-tree copying per agent. Capture and first-read costs are separate measurements; this
amendment claims no measured speedup.

**Placement closure.** A holder acknowledges only after reserving actual capacity and verifying
all required bytes. A version's reference graph, holder generations and placement scope must
be complete before its record can commit. A list of hashes without corresponding retained
objects does not satisfy placed-before-referenced. For a green version, holders recompute the
verdict and resulting manifest before serving; missing inputs or mismatches refuse. Repair
preserves these obligations across pressure, cancellation and membership changes.

**Mirroring across regions.** Every committed record and its content is shipped in epoch and
sequence order to the owner's neighbourhood in the mirror region, acknowledged at f+1 there;
`mirror_age` is exposed per volume; `await placed(mirror)` is the per-operation choice to wait
for it; region loss promotes the mirror through the root group; a promoted volume's owner is
chosen in the mirror region by the same rendezvous, and its loss window is the mirror lag at the
moment of loss.

> **Status (2026-10-07, mirroring in part).** A home-placed head snapshot's content is shipped to the owner's
> neighbourhood in the mirror region and recorded `SnapshotPlaced { mirror }` once `f + 1` there hold it, through
> the ordinary content rounds. A mirror holder admits only a put from a member of the object's standing home region,
> and only where its own region is that home's declared mirror. `has_mirror` comes from the manifest,
> `await placed(mirror)` answers the recorded fact, and `mirror_age` is reported per volume. Later the same day:
> - **The records.** The mirrored head and catalog records are held durably at `f + 1` mirror holders, and the
>   mirror placement waits for them.
> - **Promotion adoption.** The mirror council's leader asks every member for its mirror records, adopts once all
>   but `f` answer, and commits each object's successor (`MirrorAdopt`). The successor rebuilds the volume through
>   the takeover's materialization and serves it. A volume awaited in the mirror is read byte-identical in the mirror
>   region after its whole home region is lost and promoted.
>
> Owed: the loss-window report, `NotPlaced { mirror }` at a deadline, and the two-network proof.
> `docs/wip/mirroring.md` holds the design and the pieces.

**Failure matrix.** A recorded holder unreachable during fetch: Masked (another recorded holder,
hedged). All recorded holders unreachable: Refused (`ContentUnavailable{identity}`) for that
read, the rest of the namespace continues. Neighbourhood change mid-attach: Masked (chunks are
by identity; the head record names holders). Fewer than f+1 candidates reachable: Degraded
(seals accumulate as `Local`; reported). Owner loss of an overlay volume: Degraded
(`BaseUnavailable` on unresolved base paths; placed delta bytes remain readable and the
delta owner can be taken over without claiming whole-view availability). Green owner
loss: Degraded for the membership horizon, then Masked after takeover on a holder of the
ledger; no version is lost because none commits before placement. Holder recomputation
mismatch: Refused for that version on that holder, alarm; served from other holders. Migration
in flight when the new host dies: Degraded (the old owner keeps its epoch until the group bumps
it; the migration restarts). Mirror region unreachable: Degraded (`mirror_age` grows and is
reported; `await placed(mirror)` refuses at its deadline with `NotPlaced{mirror}`).

**Laptop degenerate.** No peers; f=0; remote attach is a local attach; prefetch still learns hot
sets; auto-seal still runs (it bounds the archive's staleness and drives dedup); migration and
mirroring have no targets and their verbs refuse `Unsupported`.

> **Status (2026-09-13).** The hedge, the healer and the cost model are built to the derived-constants

> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-18, green recovery fails closed).** A recovered green is its acknowledged
> history or nothing.
> - **Replay.** Every durable chain entry must decode and be accepted at exactly its own version, over the
>   origin's version 0, and its retention must be chargeable.
> - **Otherwise the green is fenced.** No engine is installed, verbs naming it are refused
>   `ContentUnavailable`, and the log is kept as evidence. The one verb it takes is its admin's `Destroy`,
>   the reviewed release
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-green-recovery-served-an-empty-or-shortened-history.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-43 in part, a destroy retires its replicas).** A destroyed volume's
> registers close in two stages, each an ordinary register write shipped to every candidate and committed at
> `f + 1` (`crates/server/src/tombstone.rs`).
> - **The tombstone.** It is written at one past every sequence the volume's registers used, and held
>   durably by the owner's partition until it is retired (bounded by the volume capacity). A holder that
>   accepts it releases the volume's content.
> - **The retirement.** It is written at the next sequence once *every* candidate holds the tombstone. A
>   holder that accepts it drops the volume's and its catalog's records. Waiting for every candidate is what
>   keeps a later takeover from meeting a lone live head.
> - **A takeover adopts the tombstone** and never materializes the volume. Before this a successor served a
>   destroyed volume again. The successor records the adopted tombstone on the shard the id routes to once a period,
>   and since 2026-11-18 past the failover SLO's worth of attempts (`failover_slo_ns / HEARTBEAT_NS`, as for a
>   taken-over volume or green) it gives that record up, counted `fleet.tombstone.given_up` with its last reason (no
>   shard for the partition, refused, unanswered): the adoption already placed the tombstone under the successor at the
>   quorum, so the volume is never served again, and what is lost is the retirement, which leaves the candidates
>   holding the tombstone, the safe state. The successor keeps it marked, so the volume stays known destroyed there.
>   Before, a tombstone whose partition had no shard was skipped every period, uncounted, and a refused one retried
>   every period without end.
> - **On a laptop** the tombstone retires with the destroy: there is no remote candidate to ship to.
> - **Single-value registers** (head, catalog, tombstone) keep only their newest accepted position. A
>   green's chain is a ledger and is kept whole.
> - **A stale copy the takeover reclaims** releases its content too.
>
> - **What a holder keeps** (`crates/server/src/content_retention.rs`). A manifest held for another owner
>   is kept only while one of these holds:
>   - the object's newest accepted record names it for this holder: a head naming it *and listing this
>     holder*, or any green ledger position naming it as inputs;
>   - it is the object's newest placement and ahead of every accepted record. An owner has at most one
>     placement in flight per object, and its record may follow after any delay: a green's records ship
>     strictly in version order.
>
>   Ahead content is released by events, never by time: an accepted record at or past its sequence that
>   does not name it, a newer placement, the tombstone, or the stale-copy reclaim. Superseded content and a
>   late copy the head's holder list does not name go at once. A first cut released ahead content after a
>   fixed window; under load it released a green's inputs 1.2 s after their put, before their record
>   arrived, and the submit waiting on that record never completed. It was replaced, not lengthened.
> - **The rule runs at three points:**
>   - at the door, where a put the records already supersede is refused, so the owner never counts an
>     acknowledgement for bytes the holder would drop;
>   - after every accepted record;
>   - after every put the hold accepts.
> - **Shipped content is restricted to the manifest's closure.** A put shipping a chunk its manifest does
>   not reference is refused `Unreferenced` before any chunk is decoded.
>
> - **Admission and residency.** A holder's replicated bytes live in its shard's arena, charged at their
>   block length from unpromised capacity only (`replicated` beside `retained` in the shard report). The
>   hold's index is charged to the metadata ledger at a per-entry cost derived from the standard library's
>   B-tree geometry. A put is charged whole before any chunk is verified or stored, verifies new encoded
>   chunks in one charged arena scratch block, and is refused `NoCapacity` with nothing left behind.
>
> - **Acceptance (2026-10-01).** Under churn, with one holder carrying the content and an unrelated volume's
>   promise leaving room for two seals, the holder's charge peaked at exactly its measured cap and always
>   equalled its hold's own account. Puts past the cap were refused and counted, the unrelated volume wrote
>   within its promise, freed room was reused, and destroying everything returned the hold to zero
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-a-destroyed-volume-came-back-on-takeover.md`,
>   `docs/bugs/2026-09-30-replicated-content-bypassed-admission.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-17, the catalog register class).** A volume's catalog is a register of its
> own, as §4.8 lists it.
> - **Object.** The volume id with the register-class bit (`ObjectId::catalog`). Placement and successor
>   ranking hash `placement_key()`, so the catalog shares its volume's holders and successor.
> - **Sequence.** `VolumeRecord.catalog_version`, raised by access, size and base changes.
> - **Value.** `CatalogValue`: name, size, name policy, owner, locked policy, access.
> - **Ordering.** Shipped before the head, and a head ships only once its catalog is committed.
> - **Takeover.** The successor rebuilds the volume from the adopted catalog. It locks RAM for a strict
>   volume, or refuses `BudgetExceeded` with nothing published, keeps the grants, and continues the
>   register.
> - **Class bytes.** Register values lead with a class byte. Volume ids refuse typed at the class bit
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-a-takeover-rebuilt-a-weaker-volume-and-lost-its-grants.md`).
> - **Greens (2026-11-07).** A green ships its catalog register too, and no merge record of it ships before the
>   register's current version is committed. Its successor waits for the adopted register and rebuilds the green with
>   its access list (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-taken-over-green-lost-its-access-list.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, connection credit in priority order).** A control exchange no longer waits for
> connection credit that a bulk exchange spent (the constrained-link design §5.3).
> - **The reserve.** A sender of one priority class leaves unspent one packet's stream bytes of connection
>   credit for each class above it (`class_credit_reserve`): bulk leaves two, metadata one, control none.
>   So the first packet of a more urgent exchange always finds credit, with no `MaxData` round trip.
> - **Headroom, not a cut.** The receiver advertises the bulk reserve on top of its stream window, so a lone
>   bulk stream still has its whole window (the reorder-detection minimum). The window auto-tunes so that
>   window plus reserve stays within the session's receive ceiling. Both ends derive the reserve from the
>   shape's frame cap (R8).
> - **Blocked reports** fire when any class with data waiting has no credit it may spend.
> - **Stream credit too.** An exchange binds to a stream only while the peer's stream credit leaves a slot
>   for each more urgent class (control may wait past the credit up to the limit). Otherwise it waits
>   unsequenced in the endpoint, in a queue bounded by the limit less a slot per more urgent class, and binds
>   most urgent first as credit arrives. Waiting exchanges count as blocked (`STREAMS_BLOCKED`). A ping
>   behind twice a limit's worth of bulk exchanges went from waiting for them (1,561 ms at session start)
>   to within the head-of-line bound
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-bulk-exchanges-held-the-stream-credit-a-control-exchange-needed.md`).
> - **Evidence.** On one session across a 1 Mbit/s, 40 ms bottleneck with a bulk transfer loading it, the
>   worst of twelve control pings fell from 118 ms (a 68 ms wait for credit) to 79 ms. The head-of-line
>   test's bound is now RTT + queue + two packets, down from four
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-bulk-spent-the-connection-credit-a-control-exchange-needed.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-49).** A server never amplifies toward an unvalidated address (RFC 9000 §8.1).
> - **The allowance.** Before the peer's address is validated, a server sends at most three times the bytes
>   it received from it.
> - **Validation.** The first sealed handshake fragment from the peer that opens validates it, because only
>   a peer that processed this end's flight holds those keys.
> - **Padding.** A client pads its Initial-level datagrams to the path floor, so the allowance covers a
>   reply. Fragments carry an explicit payload length, so padding is never read as flight bytes.
> - **Resuming a cut-short flight.** A flight the allowance stops resumes from a cursor at the next
>   retransmit, so a flight larger than one allowance still completes.
> - **Established sessions.** Raw handshake datagrams draw at most one answer per probe timeout.
> - **Evidence.** A silent source drew 2,499 bytes for its 1,200, against 120,351 without the limit, and a
>   talking client completed a wide-certificate flight past the allowance
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-a-server-answered-any-hello-with-its-whole-flight.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-48).** 1-RTT keys update, and their use is bounded (RFC 9001 §6, §6.6).
> - **Generations.** A session seals at most a generation's confidentiality limit, which is the AEAD's own
>   or an operator's smaller cap (`Endpoint::cap_key_usage`). Then it moves to the next generation from the
>   TLS secrets and flips the short header's key-phase bit.
> - **The update rule.** The next generation is derived ahead, so the peer recognizes an update on its
>   first packet and moves too. One previous receive key is kept for reordered stragglers, so at most three
>   key sets are held. An update starts only once the peer has acknowledged a packet of the current
>   generation.
> - **Terminal outcomes.**
>   - At the limit without such an acknowledgement, the session ends `KeysExhausted(ConfidentialityExhausted)`.
>   - Failed opens count across all keys, and at the integrity limit the session ends
>     `KeysExhausted(IntegrityExhausted)`. Below it a failure is one discarded packet.
> - **The control-plane seal** refuses past AES-GCM's 2^23-message confidentiality limit per key (the key
>   rotates by epoch) and past its 2^52-forgery integrity limit.
> - **Evidence.** A live session capped at eight packets per generation moves through thirteen generations
>   each way over forty exchanges, with every reply correct and no forgeries
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-session-keys-never-updated-or-counted.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-47).** The handshake keeps TLS's encryption levels apart (RFC 9001 §4.1.3).
> - **Initial level.** ClientHello and ServerHello cross as plain fragments.
> - **Handshake level.** EncryptedExtensions, both certificates, CertificateVerify and Finished cross as
>   sealed fragments.
>   - Each is AEAD-sealed under that level's packet keys, with its tag and a per-sender number (the nonce
>     input; retransmits re-seal under fresh numbers, so no nonce repeats) as associated data.
>   - Each level has its own stream.
> - **Receiving.** A receiver holds sealed fragments that arrive before their keys (bounded at one flight)
>   and opens them once its ServerHello yields the keys. A fragment that does not open is dropped and
>   counted, and a sealed-fragment number with no successor is refused.
> - **Before.** Both levels crossed as one plaintext stream, and an on-path observer read the
>   certificates. `crates/transport/tests/handshake_levels.rs` is red on the old flattening and green
>   now (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-the-handshake-sent-its-certificates-in-plaintext.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-27).** A session never reuses a packet number under its keys.
> - **The space ends at `2^62`** (RFC 9000 §12.3). Once it is spent, the connection sends nothing: no packet,
>   probe or confirmation, and no frame is taken from a queue. Its endpoint ends the session
>   `PacketNumbersExhausted`, and the probe plane judges that session broken and re-dials.
> - **Credit ceilings saturate.** They are `u64` on the wire and bounded by what was actually received.
> - **An oversized segment is refused.** A segment whose end is past the offset range is refused before
>   anything is recorded (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-packet-numbers-saturated-into-a-repeat.md`).
>
> **Status (2026-09-14, handshake flights fragmented).** The session plane's handshake no longer rides one datagram per flight: a flight is split into fragments that each fit the path floor (`MIN_DATAGRAM_BYTES`) and reassembled at the peer by cumulative stream offset — one CRYPTO-style stream per direction (RFC 9000 §19.6), a flight placed by the count of bytes its sender had sent before it, so a retransmit of a consumed flight is recognized by offset and never re-fed, and a stale fragment of an earlier flight can never write into the next (`crates/transport/src/flight.rs`). Fragmentation is deterministic (a retransmit resends identical fragments), every receive-loop arm is bounded, and hostile fragments are dropped typed. Proven by an oracle over 2,000 random flights and orders with duplicates and by use on the simulated fabric: a server with a wide certificate — a 2.7 KiB flight, what a chain of a leaf and an intermediate looks like — serves a dialer, its flight crossing as three fragments. This closes the truncation the roster fix exposed (`docs/bugs/2026-09-14-servers-handshake-flight-grows-with-its-roster.md`); frame coalescing for the MTU item stays owed.
> rule. A seal's content round is collected only until the measured p95 put latency and then hedged —
> the coordinator free, a slow holder's acknowledgement folded later, never dropped. The healer walks
> one placed snapshot per period derived from the measured put-failure rate, re-offering it through the
> ordinary rounds so a holder that lost content is repaired by exactly the chunks it lacks and one that
> lost nothing costs one round trip. Every chunk is stored under the §4.11 cost model over the boot
> profile's codec points, a byte's neutral worth its measured memcpy cost — at which a copy read once
> is raw, the design's hot-volume rule; the archive class's `value_of_byte` and the live pressure/load
> signals are the derivations that remain. The walk records the dedup gain and file-size distribution
> FastCDC is gated on. Record: `docs/wip/content-replication.md`. Integration found and fixed two
> defects: the hedge widened its targets on the count of rounds that had *placed* rather than on the
> clock, so a first round whose only holder was unavailable re-aimed at it until the holder returned
> (3.2 s against a 3 s hold, one run in three) — the trigger is now time outstanding since the first
> attempt (`hedge_targets`); and a progress witness reported "progressing" for a stall window after
> birth with nothing observed, granting a zero-acknowledgement round its extension — it now advances
> only on a real advance (`docs/bugs/2026-09-13-hedge-keyed-on-placed-round-count-never-widens.md`).

### 4.11 Compression, deduplication, hashing, archive (D-17)

**Cost model.** Inputs from the profile (codec throughput per level, hash throughput, memcpy
bandwidth, free memory) and from the volume (LZ4-size to zstd-size regression, expected read
count per chunk: high for attached, ~1 per re-attach for archived); per chunk: zero-detect →
Btrfs-style sampled statistics → LZ4 probe with early exit → predicted savings per level →
choose the encoding maximizing `bytes_saved × value_of_byte(pressure) − (t_compress + E[reads] ×
t_decompress) × value_of_cpu(load)`, subject to the format floor (savings must exceed the chunk's
metadata overhead). Hot volumes stay raw unless pressure raises `value_of_byte`; archived volumes
compress once.

**Dictionaries.** Trained per discovered content class from the volume's own sampled chunks
(FastCover), accepted only when a held-out sample beats the incumbent by more than the amortized
training cost; identified by BLAKE3; stored as chunks; embedded in archives; never mutated.

**Archive.** The format of `research/compression-archive-dedup.md` §2.6: header, dictionaries,
chunk records in manifest order, uncompressed manifest, seek table, trailer; streamable in one
pass; verifiable per chunk and whole; resumable by missing set; the same container is the
replication transfer unit and the clone-from-archive source. A chunk record may be a fragment
record: `{chunk identity, k, m, index, fragment identity, bytes}`; a reader
reconstructs the chunk from any k fragments and verifies the chunk identity; a fragment's own
identity verifies it in transit; fragments are content like any other and dedup by identity.

**Failure matrix.** Corrupt chunk on restore: Refused for that chunk (`IdentityMismatch`), the
rest restores. Insufficient memory to hold a compressed copy: Refused before work starts.

**Derived constants.** All from the profile and per-volume observations; the only fixed rule is
the format floor.

> **Status (2026-10-20).** The cost model above ran with no inputs in some builds and not
> others until this date. The boot profile's codec probe was compiled out wherever
> `slates-machine` was reached as a dependency — it was declared `default-features = false` on
> the workspace dependency in 2026-09-05 so a cross-target lint would resolve no C sources, and
> nothing turned `codecs` back on — so in those builds `profile.codecs` was empty,
> `codec_policy` derived `CodecPolicy::raw_only()` and `decide` returned `Verdict::Raw` for
> every chunk. A build that named `slates-machine` on the command line escaped it, so the
> release binaries (`cargo build --release --workspace`) compressed and the container image
> (`cargo build --release -p slates-cli`) did not: one source, two products, which R8 forbids.
>
> Fixing that made a codec **reachable**, not **chosen**, and the cost model above is still only
> partly implemented. `CodecPolicy` carries `value_of_byte_permille`, `value_of_cpu_permille` and
> `expected_reads`, and the archive crate's tests drive them, but no production code writes any
> of the three: `codec_policy` sets `byte_ns_scaled` from the largest memcpy point and leaves the
> rest neutral. So "hot volumes stay raw unless pressure raises `value_of_byte`; archived volumes
> compress once" does not yet hold — nothing raises it, and archived volumes do not compress.
> Measured 2026-10-20, release binary, M5 Max: the derived policy decides `Raw` for 67,500 bytes
> of highly compressible text, because a byte worth 0.025 ns at 39.6 GB/s memcpy cannot pay for
> zstd-1 at ~1.45 ns/byte. Open in GAPS §8, with the question of whether an archive's bytes
> should be valued at local memcpy bandwidth when the archive crosses a network (§4.10). Archives were valid and round-tripped, which is why no suite noticed; they
> were simply never compressed. The binary that measures the profile now asks for the probe, and
> `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs::the_shipped_binary_measures_the_codecs_its_archive_policy_chooses_from`
> gates it against the real `slates profile --json`. Write-up:
> `docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-ratio-codec-was-compiled-out-of-every-build.md`.

> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-13, AUD-29-14, AUD-29-15).** An archive is admitted before it is
> decoded or reconstructed, and only its canonical form decodes.
> - **Chunks.** A chunk's declared raw length is at most the header's `chunk_max`, and `chunk_max` is at most
>   the format's cap: `CHUNK_PAGES` (16, the content store's chunk rule) × the largest supported base page
>   (64 KiB), which is 1 MiB. A raw chunk's raw length is its payload's; an encoded chunk is smaller than its
>   raw bytes; no chunk is empty; the header's byte totals are its chunks' sums. All of it is checked before
>   decompression, so a small stream cannot demand a large allocation.
> - **Manifest.** Decoding is exact: no trailing bytes. Every name is one valid component (not empty, `.`
>   or `..`, no `/`, `\` or NUL, at most 255 bytes). A directory's names strictly increase, so there are no
>   repeats. A file's extents tile it from offset zero with no gap, overlap or empty extent, and its recorded
>   size is their length. No path is deeper than `MAX_DEPTH` (`PATH_MAX / 2`, 2,048 components). A declared
>   count is bounded by what the remaining bytes could encode, and the walk is iterative.
> - **Restore.** Restore plans the tree without reading a chunk, re-checking the same rules for trees built
>   in memory. It refuses `OverBudget` before allocating when every file's length plus one chunk's decode
>   space passes the caller's budget. It allocates fallibly and decodes each chunk once for every extent
>   that names it (`Restored::chunks_decoded`).
> - **Callers' budgets.**
>   - A takeover successor restores within the volume's bound (or dynamic maximum) and the shard's
>     admittable bytes. Over it, the takeover is refused `BudgetExceeded` with nothing published.
>   - A holder reads merge inputs within the bytes its hold admitted.
>   - Merge inputs archives are cut into page-sized chunks, the maximum they declare.
> - **Evidence.**
>   - A terabyte hole and a 256-fold repeated compressed chunk are refused one byte under their need; the
>     repeated chunk restores with one decode.
>   - Maximal and past-maximum raw lengths, lying raw lengths and empty chunks are refused typed.
>   - Trailing bytes, bad names, repeats, unsorted names, bad tilings, size mismatches and a tree one level
>     past the bound are refused typed. The bound itself encodes, decodes and restores on a test thread's
>     stack.
>   - A successor serves a hole-then-data file at its offsets and refuses a gibibyte hole under a 1 MiB bound
>     (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-archive-decoding-and-restore-trusted-declared-sizes-and-layout.md`).
> - **The producer keeps the bound.** A volume deeper than `MAX_DEPTH` is refused `TreeTooDeep` at the
>   export (`Unsupported` on the wire), never sealed into an archive no reader accepts. The bound is a
>   resource bound: restore keys entries by path, so a chain `d` deep costs `O(d²)`
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-09-30-an-export-past-the-manifest-depth-bound-emitted-an-unreadable-archive.md`).
> - **Still owed.** Restore's output is dense (AUD-29-57).
>
> **Reconciled 2026-11-06 (VFS plan Step 15).** A restore's output is sparse again (5106abc2; AUD-29-57 closed, A-55).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-441: a snapshot exported as its archive through the library).** `ArchiveExport`
> (`Instance::export_archive`, contract 38) renders a snapshot as its archive file, `ARCHIVE_FILE`, in a new volume of
> the caller's, as an image build renders an ext2 file (`crate::image`): checked at once (the volume, `read`, the name,
> the snapshot), then walked in slices by a task of the owner shard (`slates_vfs::export::SnapshotArchiver`), the
> snapshot pinned until the file is written, the volume and the request's completion committed as one atom. A consumer
> reads the file a page at a time (`read`) and keeps it where it keeps bytes (Mantle, kiln's object store, CP-T10.4).
> The archive carries every file's bytes and every entry's metadata, each chunk and the whole verified by identity on
> the way back in; its manifest identity, which the reply names, is the tree's. A snapshot whose entries still read an
> overlay's base is refused `Unsupported` (capture the base first); a merge volume's too. Owed then, both built since:
> the volume made from an archive (A-453, below) and a streamed encoder (A-459, below); until A-459 the archive was
> held whole while it was encoded, one unit of its size, then written into the file a chunk a unit.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-453: a volume made from an archive through the library).** `ArchiveImport`
> (`Instance::import_archive`, contract 40) is the export's way back. A consumer writes the archive bytes it kept into
> the root of a volume of its own as `ARCHIVE_FILE` (or names the volume an export made), and the daemon makes a new
> volume holding the archive's tree. The verb checks the archive volume, `read` on it and the name at once, then a task
> of that volume's owner shard does the rest a slice a turn, never in one long turn:
> - the file's length is admitted before a byte is read: no longer than the archive volume's class cap (every byte a
>   writer put there was charged to it, so only a file with holes is longer: refused `Malformed`), and no longer than
>   the shard's room, since the file is held whole while it is decoded (refused `BudgetExceeded`);
> - the file is read a copy slice a unit, then decoded and verified a piece a unit (`slates_archive::Decoding`: the
>   header's fixed fields at once, the whole-archive BLAKE3 at most an archive slice of bytes a piece before anything
>   past the header is decoded, then a chunk record a piece, then the manifest);
> - the new volume is admitted as a create admits one, under the archive's own name policy;
> - its tree is planned and restored (`Planning`, `Restoring`), admitted against the size the import asks and the
>   shard's room by the rule a takeover's restore follows (`verbs::restore_budget`), and laid into the volume by the
>   takeover's own `verbs::Populating`, every entry's mode, owner, times and attributes with it;
> - the volume and the request's completion commit as one atom, as an export's do.
>
> Bytes that are no whole archive are refused `ArchiveRefused { fault }` by kind, with nothing made: `ForeignMagic`,
> `Unsupported` (a newer major, flag or name policy), `Truncated`, `Corrupt` (the checksum or an identity fails),
> `Malformed` (whole and matching its checksum, but breaking the format's rules). A tree past the asked size or the
> room is refused `BudgetExceeded`, a held name `AlreadyExists`. Owners and set-id bits come back as the archive holds
> them, as a takeover's restore brings them back; a host mount the daemon makes honours no set-id bit and opens no
> device node (`nosuid,nodev`, A-94). Owed then: a streamed decoder, since the file was held whole while it was decoded,
> as the export's encoding was (built since: A-494, below); and the manifest's decode and identity in pieces (one piece
> today: the whole tree's).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-459: the export's archive is written as a stream).** An export no longer holds the snapshot's
> content or its archive whole. It walks the snapshot twice, as the streamed checkpoint counts before it encodes
> (`encode_image_into`):
> - the first walk hands each new chunk to a `slates_archive::Measure`, which keeps its identity and lengths and drops
>   its bytes (`SnapshotArchiver::advance_into`, a unit's chunks at a time). From it and the walk's manifest, a
>   `Layout` knows the header, every record's offset and the whole length before a byte is written, so the archive
>   volume is admitted exactly, as A-441 admitted it;
> - the second walk hands the same chunks, each checked against its first-walk record, to a `StreamWriter`, which
>   stages each record behind the header, then the manifest, the seek table and the trailer, folding the
>   whole-archive BLAKE3 over every byte as it is staged;
> - the stage is emptied into the archive file once it holds a copy slice (`DaemonConfig::copy_slice_bytes`: emptying
>   it is a copy into the file), a slice a turn on the owner shard, so it holds at most that and the largest item
>   staged whole after it, a record of the archive's largest chunk (`StreamWriter::bound`). Its emptyings are counted
>   (`image.archive_stage_flushes`), and a stage past its bound would be (`image.archive_stage_past_bound`, zero).
>
> The bytes are the whole-buffer encoder's (`Archive::encode`), byte for byte; that encoder is the streamed one's oracle
> in the tests and stays the encoder of a holder that keeps an archive whole (the fleet's replication). The cost is the
> second walk: the chunks' identities and compression are computed twice. Owed: the manifest's encoding is held whole
> while it is written (the tree's metadata, never its content). The import's decoder held its file whole until A-494
> (below).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-494: the import's decoder is fed its file a slice at a time).** An import no longer holds the
> archive file whole. `slates_archive::Decoding` is fed the stream in order, a slice a call, and holds nothing but what
> the archive keeps and one fixed-width field:
> - each slice is folded into the whole-archive BLAKE3 as it is fed, and framed as it arrives: a chunk record's payload
>   is copied into its own chunk once the record's declared sizes are admitted (its raw length against the archive's
>   chunk maximum, its canonical form, its payload against the stream left), the manifest's bytes into the manifest's
>   buffer once its length is admitted, and every fixed-width field (the header, a record's fixed fields, the
>   manifest's length, the seek table's magic, the trailer's pieces) assembled in a stage of one field at most
>   (`LONGEST_FIELD`, the header's 116 bytes);
> - once the stream is fed whole its checks run a piece a step, in the whole decode's order: the trailer's magic and
>   the checksum; then each chunk's payload decoded and held to its identity, so nothing a record carries is decoded
>   before the checksum holds (§4.9); then the totals, the manifest and the seek table. A record or section that breaks
>   the format is kept and refused there, so an altered stream is refused `Corrupt` whatever framing the alteration
>   broke;
> - the layout is the one every writer makes: the records from the header's end, each section where the one before it
>   ends, as the trailer's index names them. An index that names another place is refused `BadLayout` (`Malformed`).
>
> `Archive::decode` feeds a whole stream in one call, so one code path decodes either way. The import reads its file
> from where the decoder stands, a feed slice a unit, and feeds it, so it holds at most that slice and one field
> (`Decoding::bound`; a unit past it is counted, `image.archive_import_stage_past_bound`). The feed slice is derived
> (D-11): each byte is copied out of the volume, hashed and copied into its chunk, so a unit of `b` bytes fits the
> slice's half quantum when `b = 1 / (2/copy_slice + 1/archive_slice)`, both slices half the quantum at the
> deployment's measured memcpy and BLAKE3 rates. Owed: the decoded archive is still held beside the restored tree until
> the restore ends (the file's bytes less its framing), and the manifest's decode is one piece.

### 4.12 Agent surfaces (D-19)

> **Correction (2026-09-17, CLI process gate).** `run` and `exec` accept global flags before

> `slates --instance NAME run -- CMD`, which rejected its separator. The consumer and fleet
> process fixtures explicitly bootstrap their fresh groups; the fleet keeps its singleton
> root representative alive while proving regional takeover. A handshake superseded by an
> authenticated replacement is counted as `fleet.accept.replaced`, separately from actual
> handshake failures. Evidence: [CLI gate](../bugs/2026-09-17-cli-process-gate.md).

> **Status (2026-09-14, publish lane).** Both SDKs are publishable under the names §2.4 gives:

**One operation contract.** A Rust descriptor per operation defines input/output types,
authorization, side effects, replay class, cancellation, limits, refusals and documentation.
It generates the wire body, SDK surface, MCP input/output schemas and CLI help/structured
output. Each adapter tests the same behavior against it. Separate hand-maintained operation
lists are not the authority. CLI human grant operations occupy a privileged surface in this
registry and are structurally excluded from SDK/MCP exports.

**Rust client.** The ring protocol, rendezvous per OS, completion fd, request ids, typed errors.

**Embedding (A-278).** A host product that embeds slates — kiln first, then Hex — vendors it and
drives it through one Rust crate, `slates-api`, never through the `slates` command and never by
parsing its output. The crate is the client plus what was the CLI's alone: the anchor and daemon
roles, the host mount, the issuer authority, the grant's term. The CLI calls it for these, so the
command and every host start, mount and grant through one implementation.
- *No slates binary.* A host serves the roles from its own executable: its `main` hands the
  arguments after a prefix of its choosing to `role::main`, and `Instance::start` runs
  `HOST_EXE PREFIX... --instance NAME anchor`. The anchor starts its daemon from the same
  executable and prefix (the image it runs, A-145), so every process of an instance carries the
  prefix and `--instance NAME`, and a host finds exactly its own instance's processes. The start
  waits for the first answer at the anchor's heartbeat cadence while the anchor lives, and makes
  the group of an instance run alone; a host that launches the anchor under its service manager
  takes the command (`StartSpec::anchor_command`) and waits with `Instance::wait_for`, while the
  anchor lives when it holds the anchor's child and by a deadline of its own when it does not. A
  starter that has attached nothing yet asks `StartSpec::until_served` (A-366): an anchor whose
  daemons crash-loop before any of them has served (none reached its serving mark,
  `Supervisor::ever_served`) stops, exit 5, and the wait ends `StartFault::NeverServed`, since no
  client could be waiting on an instance that never answered; an anchor that has served once never
  gives its instance up (A-119), asked or not. So no host bounds its wait by a second it picked,
  which a slow start under load outlasts (kiln's 30 s at load 28, 2026-11-18). The starter
  is the launcher: under Ada's rule of 2026-11-18 (A-285 as revised, A-299) write permission
  follows each agent's mode and the launcher's authority is the instance's issuer, which the start
  is to hand its starter on every platform (owed; today the starter holds it where the anchor's
  handoff reaches it).
- *What a host holds.* An `Instance`: one held client of one running instance. A landing's
  presentation lives as long as the client that made it (A-46), so a plan an approver is shown is
  approved and landed on the same client. An `Issuer`: the launcher's authority (§4.13, A-299), the
  anchor segment's handoff, attached for the length of one proof and never kept as a secret.
- *Verbs.* Attach, the group of an instance run alone (`ensure_group`), create (an overlay over a
  host folder with a dynamic size, or scratch), snapshot, clone, destroy, list, status, drift and
  rewitness; serving as a host mount (§4.6, every platform's own mechanism; `mount::available` says
  without a daemon whether the machine can mount and what is missing, and `mount::unmount_busy` lets
  go of a mount a leftover process still holds, detached on Linux and forced on macOS and the BSDs) or as a descriptor a
  VMM takes (the Shards stream, A-161, whose guest is offered DAX per file, held through the library by
  `a_shards_stream_end_serves_the_volume_it_was_made_for`; the vhost-user socket); landing and merging under the
  caller's write mode, and
  approving exactly the manifest shown (the consumer contract below, A-299, which replaced A-278's
  `land_approved`); observation (daemon status, audit, grants, telemetry). `Instance::client` lends
  the whole typed client for the rest (a work volume's declared edits, the file verbs).
- *Refusals.* One closed `Error` whose variant is what a consumer does about it (the consumer
  contract below, A-299). None is prose alone.
- *Grant exclusion.* The SDKs and the MCP server depend on `slates-client`, not on this crate, so
  no grant verb reaches them (the structural exclusion this section asks of the registry); the
  daemon still refuses a grant kind on their channels whatever they claim.
- *Versioning.* The workspace's one version (`VERSION`), and the contract's own (`CONTRACT`, below).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-278, pieces 1 and 2).** Built: the crate with attach, the group, the
> volume lifecycle, drift, the host mount on macOS, Linux and Windows (moved from the CLI with its
> `unsafe` block), the Shards stream and vhost-user serving, landing plans, `land_approved`, the
> issuer (from the environment, as `slates grant` has it, or from a handoff's pairs), observation;
> and (piece 2) the anchor and daemon roles moved from the CLI (`role`), served by a host's own
> executable through `role::main`, with `Instance::start`, `StartSpec::anchor_command`,
> `Instance::wait_for` and `Anchor::stop`; and (A-287, g266) a landing plan's per-path entries,
> paged, `Instance::landing_entries(&plan)`; and (piece 3) `mount::available` and
> `mount::unmount_lazy` (since `CONTRACT` = 36 `mount::unmount_busy`, every Unix host). The CLI's `anchor`, `daemon`,
> `mount`, `unmount`,
> `export`, `grant`, `enroll`, `revoke`, `run` and `recover` call it. Proven by use over an
> in-process daemon (`crates/api/tests/api.rs`) and by a test binary that is itself the host
> (`crates/api/tests/start.rs`, no libtest harness: its `main` serves the roles). Owed, in order:
> an async form over a host's reactor (R6: a readiness wait and a timer over the client's driver);
> a seam trait with a simulator and a conformance suite for hosts whose rules ask for one (built 2026-11-18, A-310:
> "The seam" below).

**The seam (A-310).** A host whose rules reach every other product only through a trait that a simulator implements
and one conformance suite holds both to (Hex's `CLAUDE.md` §9; kiln's `kiln-seams`) reaches slates through
`slates_api::Volumes`: the contract's volume verbs (provision from every source, snapshot, destroy a snapshot, destroy,
list, serve to a Shards VMM, mount, unmount, detach), each with the signature and the types the `Instance` verb of the
same name has, so it is no second API. `Instance` implements it, and so does `SimVolumes`, an in-memory stand-in that
answers each verb with the outcome or the typed error an instance answers for the same request: names unique, a clone
pinning its snapshot, a green over a snapshot holding its volume (A-217), a work only over a green at its first version.
It serves no file system: a stream it hands out is a real connected pair it never answers until a detach or the volume's
destroy closes it, and a mount is a record of one. Its tables are bounded by its caller and refuse `Exhausted::Table`
past that. One flow of the verbs, every outcome and refusal asserted as its typed value, runs over both
(`crates/api/tests/api.rs`, `the_seam_conforms`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-310).** Built: `crates/api/src/seam.rs`, `crates/api/src/sim.rs`, the contract at version 9,
> and the suite over an in-process instance and over the simulator. A pinned snapshot's destroy reaches a consumer as
> `Invalid::Request` with the volume core's `Pinned` as its note, untyped; the simulator answers the same, and a typed
> class for it is owed to the contract. (Amended 2026-11-18: typed since `CONTRACT` 15, `Busy::Volume(Pinned)`, which
> the simulator answers and the suite asserts. At `CONTRACT` 30 the suite passes over an in-process instance and over
> the simulator, on a Mac Studio, kiln run r160. The seam's signatures are unchanged since 16, and the error classes
> added since reach it as they reach the instance.)

**The consumer contract (A-299).** Everything a consumer touches goes through `slates-api` (Ada,
2026-11-18): provisioning and managing volumes, serving them, landing, merging, their conflicts,
permission errors, and every other interaction. Answers are typed outcomes and failures typed
errors — closed enums a consumer matches and acts on, never strings. Kiln is the first consumer:
it builds against the contract and adds to it rather than around it.
- *Write permission.* Merging a work volume into its green (§4.16) and landing a volume onto a
  host directory (§4.15) follow the permission the user gave the harness or agent asking to write,
  a `WriteMode` per act (`WritePolicy { merge, land, require_signed_merges }`): **bypass** merges
  and writes at once; **ask** answers a typed approval request (`ApprovalRequired`) the harness
  presents, and writes once it is approved; **forbid** answers a typed refusal (`Refused`). The
  launcher (kiln passes each agent's mode) or the harness sets a policy per enrolled consumer (an
  agent's session, §4.13 "Principals") or per volume; an act follows the stricter of its caller's
  and its volume's (`WritePolicy::meet`); a subject with no policy keeps what every subject did
  before (`WritePolicy::UNSET`): its merges run at once (a change in memory) and its landings ask (a
  write to disk waits for an approval, R10). No key, signature or person-only proof decides it. An agent never raises
  its own mode: setting a policy and approving need the launcher's authority — the instance's
  issuer, handed to whoever starts the instance — which the daemon refuses on a consumer's channel,
  and an agent holds only its consumer's capability. The daemon keeps and enforces the policies
  (A-285, the owner of §4.13's grant path).
- *Outcomes.* A landing answers `LandOutcome::{Written(report), ApprovalRequired(approval),
  Conflicted(conflicts), Refused(policy refusal)}`; a merge `MergeOutcome::{Merged { version,
  verification }, ApprovalRequired, Conflicted { windows, head }, Refused}`; a rebase
  `RebaseOutcome::{Rebased { version }, Conflicted}`. A `LandingApproval` names the request, the
  presentation's id, the manifest hash it binds and a typed summary of what it writes (entries per
  action, bytes, what the filter left out); `Instance::approval_entries` lists it path by path
  (A-287). A `MergeApproval` names the work and its green, the increment's identity it binds and
  the paths it changes. `Instance::approve_landing` presents again and approves only when the
  manifest is still the one shown, and `Instance::approve_merge` merges only while the increment is
  still the one shown; otherwise each answers what holds now. Both work from any client: an
  approval is bound to what it shows, never to the client that first presented it.
  `Instance::plan_landing` presents without writing whatever the mode (the daemon's present-only
  verb), for a reviewer.
- *Conflicts are verdicts (D-26, D-27).* A landing conflict names its path, its class (§4.15 step 4's
  table: both changed, changed against deleted, deleted against changed, both renamed, both created,
  a type change, the target in use) and the bytes the volume would land there; a merge conflict its
  file, its window in base coordinates and its class (§4.16's `MergeConflictClass`), with the
  green's head the work must rebase onto. Nothing is inferred and nothing is written for a conflict;
  the consumer resolves (`read_base`, a rewrite, `rewitness`; a rebase) and lands or merges again.
- *Signed work (Ada, 2026-11-18; A-321).* A merge or a landing may carry a signature by its author's
  key (an SSH signature, `PROTOCOL.sshsig`, under the namespace `slates-work`: Ed25519 and FIDO
  Ed25519 keys) over the act's statement, which the daemon states (`Instance::merge_statement`), and
  its outcome carries how the daemon judged it: `Verified { signer }`, `Unsigned`, or
  `Invalid { reason }`, the verifier's closed reasons, under the volume's trusted signers, which the
  launcher sets (`Instance::set_signers`). The verdict is recorded with the version and read back
  (`Instance::merge_record`). A volume's policy may require signed merges; an unsigned or invalid
  merge into it is refused `SignatureRequired` even in bypass, when it would merge. Signatures never
  gate permission: the mode does. A landing's statement comes with every presentation
  (`LandingApproval::statement`, from `Instance::plan_landing` or an asked `land`), its verdict is
  judged against what it presents and again against what it writes, answered in the approval and
  in `LandingReport::verification`, and recorded on its audit records (`AuditRecord::verification`,
  `Instance::audit`); an approval carries the landing's signature on to `approve_landing`
  (`LandingApproval::signature`). Merges and landings are signed work (A-321).
- *Volumes.* One typed create, `Instance::provision(&VolumeSpec)`, for every source: an overlay
  over a host folder, an empty volume, a clone of a snapshot, a green (empty or over a complete
  immutable snapshot), a work volume over a green, which answers its green and its base version.
  Snapshot, destroy, list, a typed status (`VolumeStatus`, an overlay's base `Read` or
  `Unreadable`), an overlay's drift as typed entries (`Drift { path, kind }`, `Modified`,
  `Deleted`, `Replaced`, `TypeChanged`, apart from the entries whose re-check the host refused),
  `read` at a head, a version or an attachment's view, and serving: a host mount on bare metal, or
  a descriptor a VMM takes.
- *Errors.* `Error`'s variant is the class of thing a consumer does: `NotFound` (naming the subject
  the call named: a volume, a snapshot, a presentation, an attachment, an entry, a shard),
  `AlreadyExists`, `Denied`, `Exhausted`, `Busy`, `Stale`, `Retry { cause, pause_ns }` (the
  derived first pause; `Instance::retry_pause_ns` gives each later one), `Unavailable` (no daemon:
  start it, or report), `Unsupported`, `Invalid`, `Unusable` (destroying, not recovered, no group),
  `Elsewhere`, `Host` (with the OS's error number), `Mount`, `Start`, and `Protocol` (a fault in
  slates: report it). Every refusal on the wire maps to exactly one of them in one exhaustive table,
  so a refusal added to the wire does not compile until it is given its class. Words the daemon or
  the OS said only in prose travel as a `Note`, which is displayed and never matched.
- *Versioning a consumer pins.* No contract enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`. `slates_api::CONTRACT` is
  raised by one with every change to a type or a verb of the contract; a consumer pinning slates at
  a commit asserts the version it was written against and matches exhaustively, so at its next
  vendoring a moved contract is a failed assertion beside the compile errors of the matches it must
  extend — never a variant falling silently through a wildcard. The wire types the contract
  re-exports grow append-only (D-15) and count as the contract's where it returns them. A
  test, not review, holds the rule. `crates/ipc/tests/wire_order.rs` compares every wire enum of
  the protocol with its published tags (`tests/wire_order.txt`); `crates/db/tests/wire_order.rs`
  does the same for the records the log keeps. A variant appended is published in its change by
  the test's `--ignored` writer, which refuses to publish a moved tag. Anything else fails, naming
  the enum and the first tag that moved (since 2026-11-18, after `SubmitApproved` moved from 69 to
  71; it stays at 71). The history a consumer reads is held the same way: `CONTRACT`'s doc comment
  names what each version changed, and a doc-truth test fails a raised number without its line, a
  line out of order or one past the number (`the_contract_history_names_every_version_in_order`,
  `crates/api/src/lib.rs`).
- *Laptop and fleet (R8).* One contract and one code path: the same calls, outcomes and errors on a
  laptop instance and on a fleet node; a fleet's own refusals (`Elsewhere`, `Retry` for an owner
  not confirmed) are variants a laptop never sends.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-299, piece 4: the contract published).** Built in `slates-api`: the write
> modes, the policy and its typed refusal (`policy`), signed work's types (`signed`), the outcomes,
> approvals and typed conflicts (`outcome`), typed provisioning, status and drift (`volume`), the
> closed taxonomy with one exhaustive table over the wire's refusals, the channel's and this
> process's own faults (`error`), and `Instance::{provision, read, land, plan_landing,
> approval_entries, approve, merge, rebase, retry_pause_ns}` over today's daemon, on which every
> landing with something to write asks and the launcher approves it with the issuer; `CONTRACT` = 1,
> then 2 the same day (`Denied::Policy`, the class a policy refusal takes outside a landing or a merge,
> agreed with A-285's owner before its `Refusal::PolicyForbids` reaches the wire).
> The CLI's mount, grant, enroll, revoke, run and recover map the taxonomy to its exit codes.
> Proven by use over an in-process daemon (`crates/api/tests/api.rs`: the group missing is
> `Unusable(NoGroup)`; provisioning from each source, `AlreadyExists` naming the holder, a destroyed
> volume `NotFound` naming it; an overlay's landing answered `ApprovalRequired` with its typed
> summary, a stale approval writing nothing and answering the fresh presentation, the shown one
> `Written` and `Done`; a file changed on disk typed drift and a typed `ModifyModify` conflict with
> the volume's bytes; a merge `Merged`, a rewrite of the same bytes `Conflicted` with its window and
> the green's head, a clean work rebased and merged; signed work refused `Unsupported(SignedWork)`)
> and by unit tests of the pure parts (each refusal's class, the drift text's grammar, the summary's
> actions, the merge classes' discriminants, the policy meet). **Owed, in order:** the starter handed
> the launcher's authority on every platform (the anchor passes the segment's descriptor back on
> Linux); the daemon's side of the modes, merge approvals and signed work, with the verbs that set a
> policy and hand out a statement to sign (A-285's owner, agreed through g262's inbox); typed fields
> on the wire for drift, a presentation's conflicts, a landing's target refusal and a merge's
> versions (the work's base beside the head), replacing what the crate reads from text or asks
> again (typed audit and grant states are built, piece 6). **Lists a page at a time (A-263 to A-267, goal g247,
> `CONTRACT` = 26):** every
> list the daemon answers a reply at a time is read through the contract a page at a time — `Page { items, next }`
> from `Instance::{list_page, grants_page, audit_page, changed_since_page}`, an overlay's `DriftPage` from
> `drift_page` — or whole (`list`, `grants`, `audit`, `changed_since`, `drift`); a status's `DriftReport` counts what
> it could not carry (`elided`), and `drift` reads every entry. Proven by use (`crates/api/tests/api.rs`: 200 volumes,
> 150 changed paths, 100 drifted files and 120 audit records, each walked a page at a time and read whole).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-299, piece 5: the write modes reach the contract).** Over A-285's policy
> wire (203ad8fa): `Instance::set_write_policy(subject, &policy, &launcher)`, proven by the
> launcher's issuer, and `Instance::write_policy(subject)` (`None` while unset: merges at once,
> landings ask); a
> landing or a merge a policy forbids answers its `Refused` outcome (`PolicyRefusal { act, by,
