**Merging from the SDKs (D-27).** `submit(work_volume, evidence=None)` parks and resolves to
`Accepted{version}` or raises `MergeConflict` carrying the windows; `rebase(work_volume,
to=None)` moves the base to the head (or a named version) or raises with windows;
`advance(attachment, version)`; `versions()`, `changed_since()`; `edit(path, at, delete_len,
bytes)` declares a true insert or delete on a work volume. Whole-file writes through `write`
or through a mount are one declared operation covering the file and conflict with any
concurrent operation on it unless identical; the skills say so.

**Landing from the SDKs.** `materialize(snapshot, target, filter=None, wait=True)` returns
an awaitable landing request: awaited, it resolves to the landing report once a human has
granted the request and the landing has run, or raises `GrantRequired` at once when `wait` is
false; `status(volume)` carries the drift list's first entries and the count of the rest, and `drifted(volume)`
reads the whole list a page at a time (A-267); `read_base`, `rewitness` and `pin` are ordinary
async calls. No SDK method creates a grant.

**Python SDK.** PyO3 extension (`abi3-py312` wheels plus `cp314t` for free-threaded builds);
`async` methods return futures resolved by fd readiness (`loop.add_reader` on Unix, a socket on
Windows); zero-copy reads into `memoryview` through the buffer protocol; a sync facade; stubs and
`py.typed`; errors as a typed hierarchy mirroring the refusal taxonomy with the gRPC-style code and
errno.

**TypeScript SDK.** napi-rs addon with platform packages; Promises resolved by `uv_poll` on the
completion socket/fd; external buffers for zero-copy reads with a copy fallback; async iterators
for listings and streams; `AbortSignal` cancellation; ESM/CJS; the typed addon over the
client channel.

> **Status (2026-10-01, AUD-29-23/24).** The loopback HTTP edge runs on one slates shard with every
> bound stated (RFC 9112 line and field limits, the message bound, the daemon's derived `clients_per_shard`
> connections, and since A-523 the bound a connection gets to show the bearer, learned from the edge's own reads)
> and authorizes before dispatch: `Host` and `Origin`
> must name the loopback edge, the target is `/mcp`, the body `application/json`, and a 128-bit bearer
> token minted at start is required. Stdio lines share the message bound. A refusal ends its connection in stages
> (RFC 9112 §9.6), so the client reads it rather than a reset. Both transports are served on every platform since
> A-183 (2026-10-26). Since A-523 (2026-11-19) a connection that has not shown the bearer gets, from its acceptance,
> as long as an honest client takes to show it (RFC 6298 over the bearer holders' arrivals) and is cut off unanswered
> there; one that has shown it waits while it lives. Until then every wait ran to the client's reply deadline, a
> fixed second. Owed: servable roots enrolled by a human (§4.13); a listen stream's keep-alive period, still half
> the reply deadline.

**MCP server.** `slates mcp`: stdio and loopback Streamable HTTP; the 2026-07-28 stateless
protocol with per-request `_meta`, `server/discover`, `resultType`, `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`,
`subscriptions/listen`; dual-era `initialize` handling for the deprecation window; tools:
`slates.volume` (create with a snapshot or a host directory as base, clone, snapshot, list,
stat, resize, destroy), `slates.attach` (attach, detach, list), `slates.archive` (archive,
restore, export), `slates.fs` (read, write, list, move, delete), `slates.base` (status with the
drift list, read_base, rewitness, pin), `slates.land` (materialize, which returns `GrantRequired`
with a request id until a human grants it, and landing reports), `slates.merge` (submit, rebase,
advance, versions, changed_since, windows), `slates.status`, `slates.help`; `slates.fs` also
offers `edit` (a declared insert or delete at a position, the write an agent should prefer on a
work volume);
no MCP tool creates a grant, and the server refuses the grant kind on the MCP and SDK channels; resources: `skill://slates/<name>/SKILL.md`
and `volume://<id>/...` listings; prompts: one per skill; annotations on every tool; opaque
volume ids echoed on every call; results carry `structuredContent` with stable codes; output
bounded under the client's token limits with cursors.

**Skills.** One source tree; each skill a directory with `SKILL.md` (spec fields), `references/`
and `scripts/`; published raw by `slates skills install` into `.agents/skills/` and
`.claude/skills/` (project) and the user equivalents; over MCP as resources and prompts; through
`slates.help`; packaged as a Claude Code plugin with the MCP server; kept under the spec's size
guidance.

**CLI.** `slates daemon`, `slates status [--drift <volume>]`, `slates volume ...` (including
`create --base <dir>`), `slates attach ...`, `slates exec` (Linux launcher; `--apparmor-profile`, A-370),
`slates apparmor profile|check` (the launcher's AppArmor profile and the host's readiness, A-370), `slates archive ...`,
`slates base rewitness|pin|read <volume> [paths]`, `slates land <snapshot> --to <dir> [--filter ...]`
(plans and prints the landing manifest summary, then waits for a grant), `slates grant
<request-id> [--session]` and `slates grant --watch` (the terminal confirmation surface: prints
each pending request's manifest summary and conflicts, reads the human's answer, issues or
refuses), `slates grants list|revoke`, `slates audit [--export]`, `slates merge submit|rebase|advance|versions|windows`,
`slates mcp [install]`,
`slates skills install`, `slates profile` (prints the machine profile with derivations).

**CLI and MCP behavior contract (A-9).** Human commands accept canonical ids and unambiguous
names in the current enrolled namespace. Name lookup routes through that namespace's owner;
there is no global lookup index. Ambiguous names refuse with candidates instead of guessing.
Every verb supports `--help`; structured operations support consistent `--json`, stable error
codes and bounded pagination. Raw-byte streams use an explicit stream result. Errors name the
failed capability or resource, its observed limit, and an action that can actually resolve it.
A success includes the effective view coverage, claim, attachment form/path or guest tag,
consumer rights, placement and freshness where applicable.

The intended local flow is enroll a base, create a live overlay, clone work views, attach or
execute tools, inspect changes/drift, submit declared operations, preview a landing and obtain
a human grant. A reproducible flow explicitly captures a stable immutable base before cloning.
A guest flow binds an authorized attachment to the harness's VMM/device before reporting a
usable guest path. The same volume operations serve all flows; host capability changes the
available attachment form, not volume semantics. Endpoint/root discovery must be automatic
from the enrolled context; a required undocumented `SLATES_ROOT` is a gap. Provisioning,
mount/device setup and base capture timings are displayed separately.

MCP mutations return typed structured results and request identities; long operations expose
bounded progress and cancellation. Destructive effects and grant requirements are annotated
from the descriptor. Agent-provided tool text cannot enroll new roots, broaden a consumer's
rights or issue a human grant. Skills describe only shipped capabilities; future grammar is
clearly labelled planned. Disk installation of skill/config files cannot bypass R1/R10: it
requires an explicit user-authorized write through the granted landing path; in-memory help
and MCP resources need no installation.

### 4.13 Security and multi-user machines (D-22)

Rendezvous authenticates the host account using uid/SID or a host certificate. A daemon can
serve multiple enrolled consumers under that account, on a laptop or a fleet host with the
same authorization path; no separate shared-daemon mode is needed. Every lease and attachment
records the consumer established by that authenticated channel; volumes carry an owner
principal and an access list (read, write, admin); ids are random 128-bit values but never
authorize by themselves (possession of an id plus a valid principal and lease authorizes);
the launcher never escalates privileges; the MCP server's servable roots are enrolled by a human
through the CLI; grants for disk writes are issued by a human through the CLI or a confirmation
surface and never through the MCP or SDK channels; a landing resolves its target beneath its own
directory descriptor (`RESOLVE_BENEATH`, `O_NOFOLLOW` chains, reparse-tag checks) so no symlink or
junction planted in the target can redirect a write outside it, refuses targets the caller does
not own and targets inside a slates mount, never changes ownership of what it writes, and never
follows a symlink when removing; no code is loaded after start; every refusal is typed and counted.

**Security specification (A-8, 2026-09-05; the spec §3 of GAPS owed before Phase 2).**

*Principals.* Host credentials establish `AccountId`; a trusted enrollment establishes
`ConsumerId` and scoped rights for a workload under that account. A consumer channel is bound
at rendezvous using a capability delivered and retained outside other agents' reach, for
example an inherited endpoint from the trusted harness. Per-request identity strings and
peer uid alone cannot establish consumer identity. Between hosts, authenticated transport
also binds the delegated consumer scope. A consumer channel never carries the launcher's authority: an enrollment, a
revocation, a policy setting, a merge's approval or a grant sent on one is refused `Forbidden` whatever proof it carries
(A-285). Rights are checked before resource admission,
namespace lookup that reveals protected content, queue creation or any VFS/device effect.
Replay/session resumption preserves that binding; it cannot change the authenticated consumer.

> **Status (2026-11-07, A-237): a host account carries its host.** Every principal names the host whose account it is
> by that host's certificate anchor, a forwarded request is rescoped by its TLS session's anchor, and owner and access
> entries record (host, account), so a uid is never taken for another host's. A client of another node is refused
> `NotShared` naming the (anchor, account) a share would name. On Windows the account is still recorded as uid 0 (the
> rendezvous authenticates by the bootstrap object's mode and reads no SID), now host-qualified; naming it by its SID is
> held.

This requires a harness boundary when untrusted processes share an OS account. Slates cannot
prevent an unsandboxed same-uid process from reading other process memory or writing host files
through unrelated syscalls. It supplies scoped VFS access and grant checks; the harness owns
process isolation and capability delivery. The product must not call uid-only IPC agent
isolation. Unsupported secure enrollment refuses, instead of issuing an ambient admin channel.

*Access lists.* `Access { owner: Principal, entries: SmallVec<(Principal, Rights)> }` with `Rights { read, write, admin }`: `read` covers attach-for-read, snapshot reads, `status`, `read_base`, `versions`, `changed_since`, `export`; `write` covers attach-for-write, the mutating verbs, `snapshot`, `clone` (the clone's owner is the caller), `submit`, `rebase`, `pin`, `rewitness`, `materialize` (the grant is a separate, human-only act); `admin` covers `resize`, `destroy`, `archive`, changing the list, and revoking leases. The owner holds every right. Even a per-user daemon can host mutually isolated consumers; its access lists contain their enrolled identities. N=1 runs the same check and never grants every local process owner rights. Ids never authorize: a request names an id, a principal and (for mutations) an attachment with its lease epoch; all three must agree.

*Audit counters.* The audit log (§4.15, §4.14) records grants, manifests and landing outcomes; refusals are counted, never logged with content: `refusals{kind}` per refusal variant of §4.4's taxonomy, `forbidden{verb}` per verb, `grant_kind_refused{channel}` for the grant kind arriving on the ring or MCP channel (AC-2.8), `cross_uid_connect` at rendezvous (T-2.7), `stale_lease{shard}`, `stale_epoch`, `landing_lease_fenced` (a superseded holder refused by generation, AC-2.9). Every counter is a cache-padded per-shard `Relaxed` word summed on read (§3 of CLAUDE.md), exported through `status` with its freshness, and reset only by restart.

*Grants.* Only an authenticated human confirmation surface holds grant-issuer authority.
The daemon verifies that authority and the exact manifest hash, target identity, intended
consumer, scope and validity before accepting a grant. The issuer's protected channel is
established by trusted enrollment; running a CLI executable, claiming a control header class
or sharing the human's uid is insufficient. Ring, SDK and MCP grant kinds remain refused even
when they use a valid workload channel. Replayed, expired, revoked, retargeted or modified-plan
grants refuse before writing. Refusal to issue a grant never changes the proposed manifest.
The control transport and the VFS consumer channel have different authority, verified by the
server, not inferred from command names.

> **Status (2026-09-29, AUD-29-01).** The use of a grant now enforces what issuing it verified. A grant
> binds the landing it was presented for — the consumer by its exact principal key, the volume, the
> snapshot, and the target by its key and the opened directory's identity — and a landing whose own binding
> differs is refused (`GrantMismatch`, counted `grant_unbound.<field>`) before any write. A session grant
> covers later snapshots and manifests of its volume into its target, nothing wider. Before, the check at
> use compared only the manifest, which is equal for any same-content create-only plan. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-29-a-grant-did-not-bind-its-target-volume-or-consumer.md`.

> **Status (2026-09-29, AUD-29-06).** A grant's durable record carries its whole binding: the consumer as
> its principal, the volume, snapshot, target, and the target directory's identity. A restarted shard
> rebuilds its runtime grants from those records, in their recorded states. The durable state follows the
> engine's transition, so only a finished single-use landing consumes its grant. Before, a restart lost
> every grant and a session grant was recorded spent at its first landing. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-29-grants-were-lost-at-a-restart-and-session-grants-recorded-consumed.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-285).** Ada's rule: a grant follows the write mode the user gave the agent (bypass lands at
> once, ask answers an approval request the harness presents, a forbidding mode refuses), set by the launcher or the
> harness and never raised by the agent. The confirmation surface is whoever holds the launcher's authority, the
> instance's issuer. The write policy is owed; until it lands, grants are made as before, by the issuer's keyed hash.
> Record: A-285, GAPS (2026-11-18).

*Refusals added.* `Forbidden{verb}`, `GrantChannelRefused{channel}`,
`ConsumerNotEnrolled`, `ConsumerRevoked`, `GrantIssuerUnverified`; all are closed variants
carried through §4.4's operation refusal taxonomy. A-9 adds these requirements without claiming
that the current uid-based implementation enforces them.

> **Status (2026-09-13).** Built for one host: the issuer secret and verified grants (`596bfb0`);
> consumer enrollment, attestation, revocation and sharing (`e0d6877`). An attestation is decided by a
> pure function over the consumer's durable record — read from the partition its id names, mapped to
> the runtime shard that holds it — and binds the channel's principal; a revocation is acknowledged only
> after every shard has marked its bound slots, so "every later effect refuses" holds by construction
> rather than by scheduling (the first cut's `run_on` fan-out let the very next request through —
> measured, then fixed). Every refusal is typed and counted. Owed: the `slates enroll`/`revoke`/`share`
> verbs, the delegated consumer scope over the fleet transport, MCP servable roots against the access
> list, and the harness-owned delivery of the capability (an inherited descriptor is the
> recommendation). Record: `docs/wip/enrollment.md`.
>
> **Reconciled 2026-11-06 (VFS plan Step 15).** `enroll`, `revoke` and `share` (762bc91f) and the harness's capability
> delivery on an inherited descriptor (1e81737, 2a9d2ac, 762bc91f) are built.

> **Status (2026-09-14).** The harness delivery channel is built, as the inherited descriptor
> (`agent/consumer-capability`: `1e81737`, `2a9d2ac`, `762bc91`): a harness writes the consumer id and
> the capability, under a magic and a CRC32C, into a pipe both of whose ends are close-on-exec and
> spawns the workload so that this child alone inherits the read end (the flag cleared in the forked
> child, never in the parent; on Windows a `CreateProcessW` handle list, since the standard library
> cannot restrict inheritance); the child is told which descriptor by a number in `SLATES_CONSUMER_FD`,
> takes the record exactly once (kind checked, read without blocking, checksum before decode, closed
> and zeroed), and `Client::connect` binds the channel with `Attest` before any verb — a present but
> unusable delivery refuses typed rather than falling to the account's authority; a client holding the
> capability binds again by itself after a daemon restart before its retried verb. `slates run -- CMD`
> is the harness verb (an enrollment for the command's lifetime, revoked after unless kept), with
> `enroll`, `revoke` and `share`. Proven across real processes: the workload holds the capability in no
> argument or environment value and owns what it creates; a sibling without the delivery is the
> account; the Windows arm runs in the CI lanes. Owed: the SDKs' own spawn helpers, the fleet leg, MCP
> roots, and the Linux issuer surface. Record: `docs/wip/enrollment.md` (2026-09-14 section).

> **Status (2026-09-28).** The delivery name carries the channel's identity, not only its number. On Unix
> it is `NUMBER:DEVICE:INODE:MTIME:MTIME_NSEC`, the pipe's `fstat` after the record is written. On Windows
> it is `HANDLE:TWIN:PIPE_NAME`: two inherited handles of a pipe with a unique name, which is still a
> one-instance server/client pair. The take confirms the identity with calls that touch nothing before it
> adopts. A stale name — every process a consumer starts inherits the variable but not the descriptor —
> whose number now holds that process's own pipe or socket is refused `NotInherited`, and the descriptor
> is left untouched; before, it was read, its flags changed and it was closed. On Windows,
> `CompareObjectHandles` on the two handles runs before the name query, the one query that can wait, so
> that query never reaches a foreign handle. `NotANumber` became `Malformed`. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-28-a-stale-delivery-name-took-a-process-s-own-pipe.md`,
> `docs/wip/enrollment.md` (2026-09-28 section).

> **Status (2026-09-19, AUD-01 — the NFS edge is authorized by the mount capability alone).** The
> loopback mount serves **every** volume only through a mount capability: the attachment id and a
> random 16-byte token the access-list-checked `attach` (and a green's `attach_green`) mints, stores on
> the `AttachmentRecord` with the rights the attachment was granted — bounded by its intent, so an
> attach-for-read yields a read-only capability — and returns (`Attached.token`). A mount presents it
> in the `MNT` path `/<name>@<attachment_hex>.<token_hex>`, or `/@<capability>` for the host root scoped
> to that capability; the daemon stamps it into the root handle and every handle derived from it (file
> handle v2: version, volume, inode, generation, attachment, token) and validates it on the volume's
> owner shard on **every request** against the attachment record, so a handle self-authorizes on any
> connection and the edge keeps no per-connection state. The `AUTH_SYS` uid is never authority — it
> sets only the POSIX subject: a bare `/` lists nothing and enters nothing, a name without its
> capability is `MNT3ERR_NOENT`, a handle whose capability does not authorize its volume is
> `NFS3ERR_ACCES`, and an unbound client, a forged uid and a wrong token are refused alike. The
> attachment a host mount rides on is the **mount's** (`Consumer::Bridge`): it outlives the process
> that attached (the reaper reclaims only ring clients' attachments) and a daemon restart (recovery
> keeps a bridge's, and the attachment counter is seeded past recovered records, so the kernel's
> handles keep validating), and it ends when the kernel unmounts the mount (seen through the kernel's own unmount
> event since A-511; a `UMNT` ends nothing), with a `detach`, or with the volume's destroy — the record removed and
> the holder's last write attachment releasing the lease.
> `slates mount ID PATH [--read-only]` attaches as a host mount (`Client::attach_mount`; a write mount
> takes the write lease, D-16, refused `LeaseHeld` while another principal holds it, the read-only
> mount being the remedy) and mounts under the capability; `slates unmount PATH` unmounts and the
> kernel's unmount event ends the attachment (A-511). Proven over the real NFS socket
> (`crates/server/tests/nfs_mount.rs`: the refusals, the cross-connection read, the scoped root, every
> `UMNT` ending nothing), by the recovery crash sweep (a handle minted before a crash resolves after every
> crash point), by the handle and capability-parser hostile-input tests, and by the live kernel-mount
> CLI flow (`SLATES_TEST_CLI=1`: one attachment while mounted, the mount serving after its command's
> client was reaped, none after `umount`). The token is a bearer capability visible in the mounting
> user's own `mount` table — the user's own view on a per-user daemon; the FSKit app-group path carries
> it out of band. Records: `docs/bugs/2026-09-19-nfs-bypasses-consumer-and-volume-authorization.md`,
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-19-mount-capability-attachment-dies-with-its-client-and-the-daemon.md`.

> **Conformance adapter repair (2026-09-19).** The Linux root-NFS adapter also uses
> `Client::attach_mount` and presents the returned capability. Its guard owns attachment
> cleanup on both mount failure and unmount, and redacts helper errors. The socket regression
> proves the adapter's source mounts and its revoked source is refused on both macOS and Linux;
> this is authorization evidence, not a new claim of kernel-mount conformance. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-19-linux-conformance-mount-authority.md`.

*Content identity and sharing.* A chunk hash proves bytes, not permission to read them or ask
whether they exist. Missing-set exchange, caches, archives and dedup obey the consumer's
sharing scope and reference authorization; cross-scope existence and timing must not reveal
private data. Slates does not copy Hecate's disk-at-rest layout or salt scheme merely because
it uses content addressing. The RAM-only trust boundary and any allowed sharing are explicit.

> **Status (2026-10-04, lease reads wait).** A verb that serves an object's latest state while its owner lease is
> unconfirmed is parked, not refused (`crates/server/src/lease_wait.rs`). It runs when the lease confirms, and is
> refused `LeaseUnconfirmed` only once the lease bound passes. This is the Raft lease read (thesis §6.4) and etcd's
> `ReadIndex`. The mounted transports keep their own retry-later answers (`NFS3ERR_JUKEBOX`, held FUSE requests).
> Record: `docs/bugs/2026-10-04-a-first-mount-after-create-was-refused-lease-unconfirmed.md`.

> **Status (2026-09-30, AUD-29-45, in part).** A holder answers content requests per object, under the
> object's authority.
> - **Bound to the object.** Every offer, put and fetch names its object (`Fetch` gained it). The holder
>   decides authority from the committed configuration and its own records before any lookup or allocation.
>   - A placement needs the object's acting owner (its owner, or a departed owner's takeover successor) and
>     must land on that owner's candidates. A live log's entry (A-200) also lands on a holder the volume's
>     newest catalog record names among its live holders (A-240), though the holder's own configuration does
>     not place it yet: phase one counts the recorded holders, and a holder whose view lagged refused every
>     entry while the other was stopped (2026-11-07, `live_ship::live_admission`).
>   - A read needs the acting owner, one of its candidates, or a holder of its recovery cohort.
> - **Scoped answers.** Answers come only from what the holder holds for that object: another object's
>   chunks count as missing, cannot be leaned on by a put, and are never fetched. A refused request draws the
>   same empty reply as an unheld one, and is counted.
> - **Dedup.** Chunk bytes are still stored once across objects, with exact per-object references.
> - **Residual.** A put of a chunk another object already holds skips one allocation. That timing difference
>   is below a microsecond and masked by the verification every shipped chunk undergoes, but it is not zero.
> - **Owed.** The requesting consumer's scope across hosts is owed with the fleet delegation. Consumers are
>   separated on the host that issues the request.
> - Record: `docs/bugs/2026-09-30-content-hashes-authorized-fleet-content-requests.md`.

### 4.14 Observability (D-23)

> **Status (2026-09-09).** The chokepoint-span roster and the three distinct identity types are built
> (`slates-wire::observe`: a closed `Chokepoint` enum of the nine spans, `SpanContext` = request +
> trace + span + optional caused-by, each a separate type so a trace field never carries a
> `RequestId`'s authority; doc-truth tested). The **emission foundation** now exists: a completed
> `Span` (three-id context + a content-free bounded dimension code + monotonic start/end), a bounded
> **shed-first `SpanSink`** (a ring that keeps the most recent spans and counts every shed one — no
> unbounded growth, explicit loss), and the `ChokepointRegistry` gate. The **registration gate** (§2.6)
> is **wired into the daemon boot**: `Daemon::start` builds the roster via `registered_chokepoints()`
> and refuses to serve — typed `ServerError::ChokepointsUnregistered { missing }`, fail-closed, before
> any resource is acquired — until every chokepoint has registered its emitter, so a daemon never
> serves with a silently missing span source. **Six chokepoints now emit for real**: each shard owns
> a bounded per-shard `SpanSink` (thread-local, no lock — R2; sized to one client ring's depth), and
> emits `shard.op` (the whole verb) and `log.append` (the durable `Db::commit` within it) for every
> verb in `run_recorded`, `ring.request` (ring read → reply written) for a synchronously-served reply
> in `serve_client`/`retry_deferred`, `merge.verdict` (one increment judged) in the submit handler,
> `bridge.request` (one NFS bridge call from arrival to reply) around `serve_local` in `crate::nfs`, and
> `land.entry` (one landing entry) through a **cross-crate span seam**: the land engine's `Observer`
> trait gained an `after_entry(start, end)` callback taking primitives (so `slates-land` stays
> wire-free), the server implements it with a bounded shed-first collector (a large landing never grows
> it unbounded), and drains it into the shard's sink after the landing — the reusable pattern for the
> remaining lower-crate chokepoints. Each carries a request id (a client verb's real one, read from a
> per-verb `current_request` context deep in a verb, §4.7; a bridge call's is the default), a per-shard
> span id, a content-free label, and a trace seeded from the request word until propagation is wired.
> The held/dropped counts ride `ShardReport` to `slates status`; a non-vacuity test shows the count move
> as verbs run. The six live chokepoints are **every one active in the single-node daemon path**. The
> other three are gated not on the seam (which is built) but on their subsystems being live: a laptop
> runs no replication (`ship.record`) or consensus (`consensus.step`) at f=0, and `slates-cluster` is
> not a daemon dependency yet, so those land with fleet integration (§4.8); the archive is not wired
> into the daemon and its codec is Phase 7, so `archive.chunk` lands with §4.10 — each then through the
> same cross-crate seam. Instrumenting them before their subsystems run would be untestable code (R5).

> **Status (2026-09-13).** The registries are the documentation's source: `Chokepoint` and
> `HealthSignal` declare each entry's dimension, absence meaning, expected producer, observer and
> freshness horizon/basis, render the tables in `docs/wip/observability.md`, and doc-truth tests compare
> them byte for byte and against this section's own roster and catalog sentences. The three-id law is
> enforced by type: a span is opened only by a shard `Tracer` — a root from its request at a ring read
> or bridge call, a child within the span that caused it (same request and trace, `Cause::Span`), or
> unlinked with `Cause::Missing` when the cause crossed a boundary that carried none — and trace ids
> are minted, never derived from the request word. The ring read opens the trace; the verb, its log
> append, a merge verdict or landing entry open within it; a same-node forward carries the context to
> the owner and the origin's ring span ends when the reply is written. The export is the `Telemetry`
> verb: a per-shard drain bounded to one bulk chunk (derived at boot: 50 spans of 68 bytes past a
> 679-byte fixed part in 4096), carrying `shed_before`/`dropped_total`/`remaining`/`missing_links` as

> **Status paging (2026-09-20).** `DaemonStatus` captures one immutable schema-framed report
> per client; `DaemonStatusNext` reads bounded byte pages under that original request identity.
> The encoded report is capped by the client's reply-bulk credit and its retained allocation
> capacity is charged to the shard's metadata ledger. Page payload is the actual slot
> capacity less its encoded header. Completion, a subsequent operation, cancellation,
> disconnect or the capture's absolute failover-SLO deadline releases the retention. A late
> scatter cannot replace a newer capture. Continuations validate identity, exact contiguous
> offsets, strict progress and total length before returning the unchanged `DaemonReport`.
> An oversized capture refuses `BudgetExceeded`; a missing/expired capture refuses
> `NotFound`. Captures are ephemeral observations, never durable completion-log entries;
> a restart requires a new capture. The scalar API still returns the whole report. The
> existing scatter samples each shard independently; paging freezes its completed result,
> without promising a simultaneous cross-shard snapshot. The deadline on a lost scatter
> task remains owed. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-09-20-daemon-status-exceeds-a-reply-slot.md`.

> **Paging fixture correction (2026-09-21).** The by-use test preserves the normal bulk
> allowance for CI's eight-slot ring while dividing it into small pages. Previously it
> reduced the entire capture allowance to 1024 bytes and correctly received `BudgetExceeded`.
> The immutable-capture and cursor assertions are unchanged; the pinned regression passes
> in 0.75 s. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-09-21-ci-fixtures-count-local-work-and-shrink-status-credit.md`.

Chokepoint spans (bridge request, ring request, shard operation, log append, replication ship,
consensus step, archive chunk) with the three-id law; spans emitted asynchronously through
per-shard rings into the control shard's sink; health signals carry `(value, freshness)` and are
host-observed where possible (the anchor observes the daemon); metrics are content-free (no paths
or file contents); the machine profile and every derived constant are exported with their inputs;
per-volume counters (referenced, unique, locked, unlocked, hashing backlog, dedup hit rate,
compression ratio, lease epoch, attachments, base cache hit rate, drifted entries, watcher state;
per green: head version, merges per second, verdict p99, merge-path p99, conflict rate by
source, rebase-retry rate, base-lag p99, `StaleEpoch` refusals, holder recomputation mismatches)
are readable through the SDK and MCP status tool; the audit log (grants, landing manifests,
outcomes) is a separate append-only stream readable through the CLI, content-free except for the
paths a landing touched, which the human already approved.

**Observability specification (A-8, 2026-09-05; the spec §3 of GAPS owed before Phase 2).**

*Span roster.* Nine chokepoints, each a span with the three-id law (request identity, trace id plus span id, caused-by event identity) and a monotonic start and end: `bridge.request{op}` (a bridge call from arrival to reply), `ring.request{kind}` (a ring slot from read to reply written), `shard.op{verb}` (one verb on its owner shard, no awaits inside), `log.append{partition}` (one op-log record appended and published), `ship.record{object}` (one record or content put to its candidates, with the acknowledging count), `consensus.step{group}` (one configuration commit), `archive.chunk{codec}` (one chunk compressed or expanded), plus `land.entry{action}` (one landing entry) and `merge.verdict` (one increment judged). A span is emitted after it ends through the shard's telemetry ring (class Telemetry, shed first) into the control shard's sink; an emitter registers its name at start and the health plane refuses to serve until every name in this roster has registered (§2.6).

*Typed health and trace delivery (A-9).* Signal names form a closed registry. Every signal
specifies `AbsenceIs` (unknown or degraded as appropriate), freshness horizon, observer and
expected producer; missing/stale samples never silently mean healthy. Values may be absent
and must remain distinguishable from numeric zero. Registration does not prove live telemetry.
Bounded rings report dropped spans and missing causal links explicitly. Request identity is
for replay; trace/span identity connects work across bridges, rings, shards and holders;
`caused_by` connects causal events. Consumer and volume are authenticated tags, not substitutes
for trace context. Status exposes these definitions consistently through CLI/MCP.

*Health signal catalog.* Every signal is `(value, freshness_ns)` and host-observed where a host can observe it: `daemon.alive` (the anchor's view: the child is running and answered its last heartbeat), `daemon.restarts` (the anchor's count), `segment.generation` (the anchor segment's generation word), `shard.loop_lag_ns{shard}` (the driver's measured lateness), `shard.watch_window_ns{shard}` (the window the watchdog judges the shard by: the liveness window raised to the shard's measured scheduler overrun, at most the observation budget, A-455), `shard.tasks{shard}` (live tasks against the arena), `ring.depth{client}` (command slots pending), `client.parked{client}`, `memory.locked_bytes` and `memory.unlocked_bytes` (per shard and rolled up), `memory.pressure` (PSI slope, macOS level, Windows notification), `catalog.volumes{shard}`, `log.bytes{partition}` and `log.replay_ns` (the last replay's duration against the recovery budget), `lease.expiring` (leases within one term of expiry), `base.watcher{volume}` (live, overflowed, unavailable), `land.active` (landings in flight), `placed.pending` (records awaiting f+1), `mirror_age{volume}`, `config.version`, and the NFS service times a shard measured since boot, `nfs.local_p50_ns`, `nfs.local_p99_ns`, `nfs.local_off_cpu_p99_ns` and `nfs.forwarded_p99_ns` (so a slow client is split into the serve, the scheduler's share of it, and the cross-shard forward).

*Metric names.* One namespace, dotted, unit-suffixed, labels in braces; counters end in `_total`, histograms in `_ns` or `_bytes`. Per host: `slates.requests_total{kind,outcome}`, `slates.refusals_total{kind}`, `slates.provision_ns` (the AC-2.1 histogram: p50, p99, p999, max, spinning and parked), `slates.ring_wait_ns{client}`, `slates.wake_ns`, `slates.spin_to_park_ratio`. Per shard: `slates.shard.step_ns`, `slates.shard.batch`, `slates.shard.parks_total`, `slates.shard.kicks_total`, `slates.shard.arena_exhausted_total`. Per volume (readable through `status`): `referenced_bytes`, `unique_bytes`, `locked_bytes`, `unlocked_bytes`, `hashing_backlog_bytes`, `dedup_hit_ratio`, `compression_ratio`, `lease_epoch`, `attachments`, `base_cache_hit_ratio`, `drifted_entries`, `watcher_state`; per green: `head_version`, `merges_per_s`, `verdict_p99_ns`, `merge_path_p99_ns`, `conflict_rate{source}`, `rebase_retry_rate`, `base_lag_p99_ns`, `stale_epoch_refusals_total`, `holder_mismatch_total`. Per landing (in the report and the audit log): `entries{outcome}`, `bytes_written`, `dir_sync_ns`, `window_ns_max`, `barriers`. The machine profile and every derived constant are exported as `slates.derived{name}` with their inputs.

*Content-freedom.* No metric, span or health signal carries a path, a name or file content; the audit log carries the paths a landing touched and nothing else; a test in the observability crate asserts every emitted label against this rule.

> **Status (2026-11-06, A-228): `daemon.alive` judges a shard in its own CPU time.** The beat's writer is the daemon's
> watchdog, an owned thread pinned to no core (`crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`), not a task on the control shard. Each
> beat it judges every shard by A-65's rule (`crate::observe`'s `ShardTime`): a shard that is not parked and has
> completed no step is stuck once a whole window passes with no CPU progress (wedged: a deadlock, or a host call that
> never returns) or once it has run a window of CPU (spinning: a task that never yields). A starved shard, given a
> little CPU at a time, is alive. The watchdog withholds the beat while a shard is stuck or the control loop has ended.
> The anchor holds the beat to the window plus its own measured lateness p99 over its last 100 timed waits
> (`crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`, `Lateness`). The window is the existing liveness budget, still a fixed number (GAPS, R3
> debt). Proven by `crates/server/tests/liveness.rs`: a starved control-shard poll, which gapped the beat 1.53 s on main,
> keeps it under 0.26 s; a wedged or spinning non-control shard, which main never saw, stops it.
> **2026-11-08:** `ShardTime` itself now asks the scheduler before it ends a wait on a window with no CPU progress: a
> shard it has runnable is starved and waited for another window, so an observation or a cross-shard call no longer
> gives up on one (`an_observation_of_a_starved_shard_is_answered`, red 3 of 3 before on adacachy2).
> **2026-11-18:** it reads the shard's clock again after the scheduler answers. A thread leaves the run queue for a block
> only by running first, so only a clock read after that answer shows a shard released between the two reads, which
> ran, answered and parked before the scheduler looked; read only before it, such a shard was judged wedged and an
> observation already answered was given up (once on CI's Windows runner, where a look at the scheduler is a 3 ms
> snapshot; 1 of 32 runs of the failing tree, `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-an-observation-read-the-clock-before-the-scheduler.md`).
> **2026-11-08, the transitive wait:** a shard blocked joining another thread of the process (the FUSE notify thread,
> the landing barrier thread, the WinFsp mount thread; `slates_rt::registry::spawn_waited`) is read as that thread while
> it is runnable, so a shard waiting on a starved thread is starved, not stuck; one waiting on a blocked thread is still
> a deadlock. Before, a shard parked on a starved thread withheld the beat at 30 of 40 looks (3 of 3 on adacachy2).

> **Status (2026-11-07): a start is judged by its progress too.** Until its first beat the anchor judges a starting
> daemon by the same rule, in the daemon's own CPU time read from the OS (`slates_machine::process_clock`;
> `crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`): killed once it makes no CPU progress for a window or runs a window of CPU without beating,
> waited for while it progresses. Before, a start not beaten within the fixed recovery budget, a wall second, was killed;
> under 144 spinners on 18 CPUs the anchor killed 153 starts of 153 after each had used 16-18 ms of CPU
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-the-anchor-killed-every-start-a-busy-machine-starved.md`). On Linux the clock is the process's
> CPU-time clock: `/proc/<pid>/schedstat`, read first, is the main thread's alone
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-the-linux-process-clock-read-the-main-thread-alone.md`). At the extremes, 0 progressing starts
> were killed at 183-292 runnable processes, and a stuck start was killed at 1,001-1,294 ms on macOS, Linux and Windows.
> **2026-11-08:** the start judgment also asks the OS whether any of the start's threads is runnable
> (`slates_rt::process_runnable`), as the watchdog asks of a shard: a start whose CPU stands still a window while one of its
> threads waits for a CPU is starved and waited for. Before, a start held off its CPUs was killed ("made no progress for
> 1014 ms" on CI's Windows runner; red 2 of 2 on adacachy2 by `a_start_held_off_its_cpus_is_starved_not_stuck`).
> Since 2026-11-08 the spinning half is judged on the start's busiest thread, as the rule is a thread's: the process's
> summed CPU, held to one window, killed every start of 23 shards on a 32-CPU Studio and of 48 on an 18-CPU Mac
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-the-start-judgment-held-a-processs-summed-cpu-to-one-threads-window.md`).
> A shard's recovery still runs as one poll, which the watchdog counts as spinning past a window of CPU: GAPS holds it
> open.

> **Status (2026-11-08, A-228): a starved shard is not a stuck one.** A CPU clock cannot tell a thread held off the CPU
> from one blocked in a call: both stand still. On adacachy at `CPUWeight=1` two anchors killed live daemons on
> `shard N is wedged` lines, and the sampled shard read state `R` throughout. The watchdog now asks the scheduler about a
> shard with no step and no CPU rise (`slates_rt::registry::shard_run_readings`, one batch a beat). **Wedged** is a whole
> window in which the shard moved in no way: no CPU progress, never runnable, no wait for a CPU credited. **Starved** is
> a whole window with no CPU progress but one of the others: it goes on beating and is logged once an episode.
> **Spinning** is unchanged.
>
> | Platform | Source | Time waited for a CPU |
> |---|---|---|
> | Linux | `/proc/self/task/<tid>/stat` state and `schedstat` field 2 | Yes, credited late, so the state decides |
> | macOS | `thread_basic_info.run_state` (`TH_RUN`, on a CPU or the run queue) | None per thread: the state at each look |
> | Windows | `SYSTEM_THREAD_INFORMATION.ThreadState`, `NtQuerySystemInformation` linked at run time | None: the state at each look |
> | Miri, or an unreadable source | None | The CPU clock stands alone, as before |
>
> Proven by `crates/server/tests/liveness.rs` and the rule's replays in `crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`, red first
> (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-starved-shard-was-judged-wedged.md`). Held off its CPU for 3.0 s, the beat gapped at most
> 91.6 ms on Linux and 111.0 ms on Windows, where before it stopped for 2.01 s and 1.91 s; a shard blocked in a read
> still stops the beat within 1.08 s on both. A frozen process is still killed at its lapse. macOS could not be held off
> the CPU on demand (a full window in 1 of 20 CI runs), so there the replays carry the rule.

> **Status (2026-11-13, A-232 step 2): a daemon nobody supervises ends itself on the stuck verdict.** The watchdog knows
> from the segment's source whether an anchor in another process reads its beat (`Supervision`: `FromEnv` is anchored;
> `Create` and `Handoff`, an anchor in the daemon's own process that cannot end it, run alone), and each turn is one of
> beat, withhold or end (`Turn`, decided by the pure `decide`). An anchored daemon is unchanged: a stuck shard withholds
> the beat and the anchor kills it. A lone daemon ends its own process on the same verdict, window and
> starved-is-not-stuck rule, exit 4, so its clients see the exit as they see a kill. A starved shard, and anything found
> while the daemon stops, ends nothing. A lone daemon exits within `W + B + L` of a wedge, `L` the verdict's lateness
> its end line names (A-232's amendment has the figures and the tests).

> **Status (2026-11-14, A-232 step 5): a lapsed beat kills only a stuck daemon, never a starved one.** The watchdog marks
> every look in the segment, beating or not (`SUP_LOOKED`, offset 216 of the supervision block, zeroed at each start). On
> a lapse the anchor decides (`judge_lapse` in `crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`):
> - Looks within the lapse bound: the watchdog's verdict, killed as before.
> - No look within it: the daemon's watchdog was held off its CPU with the rest of the daemon. The anchor judges the
>   process by the start's rule, in its own CPU time, from when the looks stopped. Starved or alive, it is spared and
>   looked at every beat. Wedged (no CPU progress and never runnable, as a stopped process) or spinning for a window,
>   it is killed.
>
> Before, the anchor killed a starved daemon in 3 of 20 runs at `cpu.weight` 1 on CI. After, 0 of 20, the anchor
> sparing a silent watchdog 10 times. A daemon stopped whole is still killed, 1.88 to 2.00 s after the stop.
> A stuck shard's withhold line names the verdict's own lateness (step 2's, from the look before the shard last moved)
> and the first look's, the terms of the bound from a wedge: the verdict within `W + B + L`, an anchored daemon's last
> beat within `W + B + first`. Measured on both Linux runners and this Mac (A-232).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-305): a shard never waits on standard error.** A line written straight to standard error takes
> the lock every line of the process takes and then waits for the write. So a shard behind another thread starved while
> it held that lock, or behind a write the log's reader was slow to take, stood still a window, never runnable, and the
> watchdog judged it wedged; a lone daemon ended itself (test binaries exited 4 at daemons' starts under load, each with
> a line cut mid-write at the exit and the end line lost behind the same lock: `merge_post_state`, `merge_load`,
> `nfs_hostile`, `nfs_mount`, `nfs_writeback`, `green_checkpoint`, `fleet`, 2026-11-17, loads 40 to 50). Now a daemon
> owns a log writer (`slates_machine::log::LogWriter`), started before its shards and stopped after them, and each
> shard's thread is routed to it before anything it logs (`LogRoute::install`): a shard's line goes into the writer's
> queue, bounded at a pipe's 65,536 bytes, and the call returns at once, while the writer's thread waits on standard
> error for every shard. A full queue refuses the line, counted in `log_lines_refused`, so a log nobody drains can
> neither wedge nor end a daemon serving held mounts (the rule A-213 set for a closed one). Every other thread writes as
> before. Regressions: `a_lone_daemon_whose_log_stalls_lives_on_and_serves` (`crates/client/tests/lone_daemon.rs`:
> standard error held three windows while each shard logs; exit 4 within the stall before) and
> `a_routed_thread_never_waits_on_standard_error_and_a_full_queue_refuses` (`crates/machine/src/log.rs`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-308): a wedge is judged only over a window the watchdog watched.** The rule calls a shard
> wedged once a window passed with no CPU progress and never seen runnable, and "never seen" is sampled at each look. A
> look a window or more after the watchdog's previous one asked nothing in between: its own thread was kept off its CPU,
> as a process frozen whole or paging is, so the shard's stillness across that gap is the process's. A fleet test binary
> was ended with exit 4 on a wedge verdict that came 146 s past its window, the whole process unscheduled at 0.2 to 1 GB
> free (g231, load 62 to 131 on a 15-CPU Mac). Now such a look starts the shard's still time again (`ShardWatch::judge`),
> and a stuck shard is still judged a window after the watchdog's looks come back; the verdict's named lateness `L`
> still runs from the look before the gap, so A-232's bound `W + B + L` holds by its terms. Regression:
> `a_gap_in_the_watchdogs_own_looks_is_not_counted_as_a_wedge`. Open: a shard that stays off the CPU in the kernel (a
> page-in under that pressure, Linux `D`, XNU's uninterruptible wait) past a watched window is still judged wedged; the
> scheduler states that would tell it from a sleep are not read yet (GAPS, 2026-10-22).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-318): a poll's CPU is held to the build the daemon runs in.** A shard is spinning once it has
> run the spin window of CPU without a step, and the spin window is the budget scaled by how much slower this build runs
> compiled code than the machine runs the same work in machine code, never below the budget
> (`watchdog::spin_window_ns`). The slowdown is measured once a process (`slates_machine::build_cost`): one dependent
> chain over a page of words, `acc = acc × K + word`, compiled by this build and written in the machine's instructions
> (`asm!`, x86-64 and AArch64), timed alternately in batches past the clock's grain, the least of each kept, the two
> required to compute the same value. The watchdog's start line names the window and the measure. On CI's
> ThreadSanitizer lane, whose runtime is called at every memory access and every function's entry and exit, a poll of
> 1,054 ms of CPU ended the client tests' binary and one of 1,060 ms the server's library tests (runs 44238377555 and
> diag-b13-2), each an in-process daemon's lone watchdog ending the whole process. Measured: an unoptimized build 3.5
> times machine code (a Mac Studio), a release build 1.0 (its window the budget), and ThreadSanitizer's 17.9 to 35.3
> times on CI's runners, whose lane then passed with no spinning verdict (diag-g251-tsan, six runs of six). The wedged
> and starved judgments stay on the wall and the budget. Regressions: `a_poll_is_judged_spinning_only_past_the_window_held_to_its_build`,
> `the_spin_window_is_the_budget_held_to_the_builds_measured_cost` (`crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`),
> `a_poll_slower_than_the_budget_within_the_builds_spin_window_keeps_the_beat` (`crates/server/tests/liveness.rs`), and
> the build-cost tests (`crates/machine/src/build_cost.rs`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-356): the anchor's start judgment and a wait judged in a shard's own CPU are held to the build
> too.** The anchor measures the build in its own process, the executable its daemon runs, and judges a start's busiest
> thread against the spin window; an observation's or a cross-shard call's budget is the budget held to the build in
> CPU, its windows at most the budget on the wall (`observe::held_to_this_build`). Regressions:
> `a_starts_thread_is_judged_spinning_only_past_the_window_held_to_its_build`,
> `a_shard_in_a_slower_build_is_given_its_budget_held_to_the_build`.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-336): a shard waiting on memory while the host reports a memory stall is starved, not
> wedged.** A thread waiting on a page-in, a reclaim or a refault is neither running nor runnable, as a deadlocked one
> is, so A-228's rule judged it wedged: a lone daemon at a few hundred megabytes free ended itself (exit 4, fleet test
> binaries at 0.2 to 1 GB free on a 15-CPU Mac, 2026-11-17), and an anchor judged a daemon paging whole by the start's
> rule and killed it at its lapse. A-308 kept only the watchdog's own gaps out of the verdict. Now, at a look that
> suspects a shard, the watchdog reads the host's memory stall (`slates_machine::memory_stall`), and a still shard off
> the CPU in a wait memory shows as, while the host reported a stall since the look before, has moved, as a runnable
> one has (`watchdog::held_for_memory`); once a window passes with no CPU it is `Starved { of: Memory }`, logged with
> its kernel wait, and it beats. A stuck shard is still judged wedged a window after the stall clears. One rule on every
> platform, each reading what it can:
> - Linux: PSI's memory `some` total risen since the look before (`/proc/pressure/memory`), and the thread held in the
>   kernel past signals (`D`); a thread asleep in a futex, a poll or a sleep (`S`) is never excused. `some`, not `full`:
>   FULL holds on a CPU only while nothing there is productive, so a thread waiting on memory on a busy machine never
>   shows in it (`kernel/sched/psi.c`); a delayed thread is itself `some` on its CPU, so the total rises while it waits.
>   The thread's `wchan` names the wait in the log line.
> - macOS: `kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level` above normal (XNU's dispatch level, warning or critical); XNU reports
>   a user page fault's wait as it does a lock's, so any blocked wait counts while it is raised.
> - Windows: the low-memory resource notification signaled; any blocked wait counts (the wait reason is not read yet).
> - No reading (PSI absent, `psi=0`, a refused read, Miri): nothing excuses a still shard, as before.
>
> The anchor's start and lapse judgment run the same rule over the whole process (`slates_rt::process_run_reading`:
> runnable when any thread is; else held in the kernel when any thread is, on Linux). A shard waiting on another
> thread that is held in the kernel reads as that thread does (A-228's transitive wait). Regressions:
> `a_shard_waiting_on_memory_while_the_host_stalls_is_starved_and_wedged_a_window_after_the_stall_clears`,
> `a_shard_asleep_or_unread_is_wedged_within_the_window_however_the_host_stalls` and the rule's table
> (`crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`); `a_shard_waiting_on_memory_keeps_the_beat_while_the_host_stalls_and_stops_it_a_window_after`
> and, on Linux, `a_shard_asleep_while_the_host_stalls_stops_the_beat` (`crates/server/tests/liveness.rs`, the
> host's reading put in its place through `Daemon::inject_memory_stall`, a shard held in the kernel by a vfork's wait);
> `a_process_waiting_on_memory_is_spared_while_the_host_stalls_and_stuck_a_window_after` (`crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`);
> the readers' own tests (`crates/machine/src/memory_stall.rs`, `crates/rt/src/thread_clock.rs`). Not yet: an
> observation's and a cross-shard call's wait (`observe::ShardTime`) take the same excuse next; a shard asleep on a
> lock whose holder pages is still judged wedged on Linux (the holder is not named, GAPS); Windows' per-thread wait
> reason is not read.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-455): each shard is judged by its own window, which follows the host.** The watchdog judges
> a shard at each look against its window (`watchdog::watch_window_ns`): the liveness window `W` (A-359), raised to the
> scheduler overrun the shard measured where that is longer, never past the daemon's observation budget
> (`watchdog::WINDOW_CEILING_NS`). The overrun is how late the shard's steps ran after the waits before them, a maximum
> that forgets an eighth at each later wait (`slates_rt`'s `scheduler_overrun_ns`, mirrored in the shard's registry
> pulse). A host that keeps a shard off its CPU that long leaves it no way to show progress sooner, so A-359's floor,
> checked once at boot, is now held at every look; a quiet host's shards (an overrun of a tick or less) keep `W`. The
> spin window is the shard's window held to the build (A-318), so both judgments follow it. The ceiling keeps the
> watchdog from going blind: a wedged shard never waits again, so a spike measured just before its wedge (a process
> stopped whole and continued) would stay its window for good, and past the observation budget the daemon's own
> question to the shard already ends as a wedge's. Every verdict's line names the window it was judged by, and the
> status carries each shard's as `shard.watch_window_ns`. Regressions:
> `a_shards_window_follows_its_measured_overrun_past_the_liveness_window_and_stops_at_its_ceiling` and
> `a_shards_status_names_the_window_its_watchdog_judges_it_by` (`crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`). Not yet: the
> anchor's start and lapse judgment, the daemon's other supervision waits and a laptop's failover detection term still
> read `W` itself (GAPS).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-461): a start is judged by its silence, against the anchor's own window.** The anchor judges
> a starting daemon until its watchdog first looks (`SUP_LOOKED`), not only until its first beat, and each of its beats
> (A-312, after each unit of its work) is a step of the start's (`role/anchor.rs` `judge_start_by`): a start that keeps
> beating or progressing is waited for however long it runs in all, and a wedged one is judged by its silence, a window
> after its last beat or CPU rise. Before, the start judgment ended at the first beat, and a start wedged after it was
> found only once its beat had lapsed and its process had stood still a whole window more (A-312 recorded it, "a
> window later"). The window is the anchor's (`anchor_window_ns`): the liveness window raised to how late the anchor's
> own timed waits come back (its lateness p99), within A-455's ceiling, the watchdog's rule over the anchor's measure; a
> silent watchdog's process (A-232) is judged by the same window, and the kill lines name it. A graceful stop's bounds
> are derived too (§2.5's status). Regressions: `a_start_that_beats_is_waited_for_and_a_wedged_one_is_judged_by_its_silence`,
> `a_start_is_judged_by_the_window_its_anchors_own_waits_measure` (`crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`) and
> `a_stopping_daemon_is_overdue_by_its_own_beating_not_by_the_owners_clock` (`crates/anchor/src/supervise.rs`). Not
> yet: the anchor's lapse bound (`lapse_bound_ns`, the liveness window plus its lateness p99) and its observation
> cadence (GAPS).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-467): the anchor's lapse bound has a ceiling, and its looks keep their gaps inside it.** The
> lapse bound stays the liveness window plus the anchor's measured lateness p99 (A-228), never past the ceiling the
> watchdog holds its own windows to (A-455, the daemon's observation budget), so a runaway reading (a host paused twice
> among the last hundred waits) cannot hold a wedged daemon's lapse past it. The observation loop's longest wait is the
> bound less the anchor's own lateness p99 and a beat, never less than a beat (`Lateness::observation_gap_ns`), where it
> was half the bound. A look that comes more than the bound after the one before reads as the host having slept and
> restarts the daemon's silence (`lapsed`), so under a lateness past a window every gap of the old loop passed the bound
> and a wedged daemon was never found lapsed; now the gap stays inside the bound at the anchor's p99, with a beat to
> spare. A quiet anchor looks at a running daemon about once a window rather than twice. Regressions:
> `the_lapse_bound_is_the_window_plus_the_anchors_own_lateness` (the ceiling),
> `a_wedged_daemon_is_found_lapsed_though_the_anchors_own_looks_run_twice_a_window_late` and
> `the_loop_waits_at_most_its_gap_and_finds_a_lapse_at_the_budgets_end` (`crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-474): a watcher's own late looks are no span it did not watch.** A-308 starts a shard's still
> time again at a look that comes after a span nothing watched; that span is now a gap past the shard's window and the
> watcher's own lateness p99, capped at A-455's ceiling (`watchdog::slept_past_ns`), where it was any gap of a window.
> The watchdog keeps its looks' lateness (`watchdog::LatenessTail`, its last hundred, nearest-rank p99), each `Look`
> carries it, and the anchor's start and silent-watchdog judgments pass the anchor's own (the same tail). Before, a
> watcher whose every look ran a window late restarted a wedged shard's stillness at each look and never judged it,
> while it beat on (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-the-watchdog-never-judged-a-wedged-shard-once-its-own-looks-ran-a-window-late.md`).
> A process frozen whole is still told by its gap, a whole host's sleep a gap past the ceiling. Regression:
> `a_shard_is_judged_wedged_though_the_watchers_own_looks_run_a_window_late` (`crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`).

> **Telemetry oracle correction (2026-09-20, AC-0.11).** A drain request itself emits spans.
> The daemon integration oracle now derives convergence from the reply quota minus the
> maximum spans a drain emits, and checks progress on each batch. A four-span reply scenario
> reproduced the old count-bound failure and passes after the correction. Production telemetry
> behavior is unchanged; see `docs/bugs/2026-09-20-telemetry-drain-counts-its-own-spans.md`.

### 4.15 Disk as the source of truth: the base plane and landing under grant (D-25, D-26)

**Special names (A-26).** A landing containing FIFO/socket creation refuses before its
first host write. The current grant authorizes filesystem content, not new host IPC endpoints.
No copy-up, hashing, archive or landing step opens a host special file as regular content. A landing containing a
device node refuses the same way (A-294): a grant authorizes content, never a device on the host, and making one there
would need a privilege slates never holds (R10).

> **Containment correction (2026-09-19).** Scratch directories created by inode operations
> belong in the diverged set even without a base. Whole-target staging is removed: its hidden
> sibling and parent-directory sync escaped the grant. Step 10 now requires every write inside
> the stable target. The mounted hermeticity gate checks the landed bytes, symlink and parent
> directories as well as tracing writes; a zero-entry landing fails. See
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-19-linux-conformance-first-complete-run.md` for failing evidence and validation.

> **Status (A-9, 2026-09-05).** The read-only base seam and landing engine exist, as do
> server records, plan/refusal handling and Unix control transport/write integration. The CLI
> has `land`, grant listing and audit reads, but no `slates grant` issuance verb. Human issuer
> authentication, per-entry audit completeness and end-to-end consumer/grant tests remain open.
> Base data/metadata behavior is not fully connected to every mounted operation (BUG-5 and
> sibling audit), and restart does not yet recover complete volume contents (BUG-11).
> Historical tests in GAPS §8c/§8d were not rerun for this amendment.
>
> **Reconciled 2026-11-06 (VFS plan Step 15).** BUG-5 is swept (991c84e; GAP-A9-3), apart from the base entries' owner
> fields and the mounted conformance run. BUG-11 is closed (9c97ce6b, 5127b4b3). `slates grant` issues a grant
> (596bfb04); the Linux issuer surface stays owed (GAPS).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-287: the full entry list on demand).** Built: a presentation keeps its manifest's entries
> (moved from the plan, never copied) and the conflict classes its preliminary pass found, for as long as A-46 keeps
> the presentation; `LandingEntries` pages them to the presenting principal (`crates/server/src/landing_entries.rs`),
> and `slates_client::Client::landing_entries` joins and decodes the pages. Before, a presentation answered counts and
> conflicts only, so neither a person nor a reviewer with no mount of the volume could learn what a grant would
> write, path by path. Proven by use (`crates/server/tests/presentations.rs`: every action kind over an overlay with
> an outsider's conflict, another principal and a replaced presentation refused; a list past one page with an entry
> no page holds whole; a landed presentation's bytes as listed) and by the pager's oracle (unit tests). Not served:
> the CLI's `slates land` prints the summary alone.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-321: signed landings).** Built: `Land` and `Present` may carry an SSH signature over the
> landing's statement (`slates landing v1`, the volume, the target as the request names it with its length, the
> manifest hash; `crates/server/src/signed_work.rs`), which every presentation states in its `GrantRequired`. The
> volume's owner judges it under the volume's trusted signers against the manifest it presents, and again against the
> one a granted landing writes (`landing::landing_verdict`), records the verdict on the landing's `LandingPlanned` and
> `LandingFinished` audit records (`AuditRecord::signature`, kept by recovery as the log is) and answers it with the
> presentation and in the `LandingOutcome`; `Audit` reads it back. An asking consumer's landing keeps its signature
> through the turn into a presentation. Nothing requires a signed landing, and a signature permits nothing: a forbidden
> landing is refused signed or not, an asked one waits for its approval, a bypass one lands with an invalid signature
> recorded invalid. Proven by `crates/server/tests/signed_work.rs` (four landing tests, macOS arm64, Mac Studio,
> 2026-11-18) and the contract's `a_signed_landing_is_judged_and_read_back_through_the_contract`, each guard red alone.

> **Status (2026-11-18, the audit trail records each step once).** A granted run's finish mirrors into the durable
> log only the engine ring's records of that run: the ring's sequence when the run began (`Audit::next_seq`, kept as
> the run's `audit_from`) bounds them. Before, the finish mirrored every record the ring held for the landing's id, so
> a presented landing's plan, which its presentation records itself, was recorded twice, and a resumed landing would
> re-record its first attempt's records. Measured on the Mac Studio: a presented-then-granted landing's trail read
> plan, grant, plan, plan under the grant, validation, entry, finish; now each step once
> (`a_presented_then_granted_landing_records_each_step_once` in `crates/server/tests/presentations.rs`, red on the old
> mirror). Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-presented-landings-plan-was-audited-twice.md`.

> **Status (2026-11-18, a refused granted landing leaves its trail).** A granted landing refused at any step from the
> moment its id is decided (its target's lease, its volume, its plan or grant, its validation, its run) records, in its
> completion's atom, the engine ring's records of its attempt and then its end (`landing::record_refused`). The end is
> a `LandingFinished` whose outcome is `Refused`, or `Aborted` once the attempt wrote an entry. It names the manifest
> the attempt planned (its grant's when it planned none) and its signature's verdict against that manifest. A plan no
> grant covers ends in a presentation instead, which records itself. Before, a refused landing's trail ended at its
> grant. Since a later change the same day the landing's record reaches the same terminal state in the same atom: its
> presentation's record moves there, and a fresh id's record is made, so a restart's landing counter passes the id.
> Only a granted landing, one whose grant the shard held as it began, leaves this trail; a landing under a grant it does
> not hold is presented once planned, and refused before its plan it is a refused request (`CONTRACT` = 35). Proven by
> four tests in `crates/server/tests/presentations.rs`, three of them red before the first change and each reading the
> record's state since the second (macOS arm64, Mac Studio, 2026-11-18). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-refused-granted-landing-left-no-trail.md`.

> **Status (2026-10-01, AUD-29-62: contained base access on every platform).** The Windows base host is
> descriptor-relative like the Unix one: it retains a handle per opened directory and opens each entry with
> `NtCreateFile` relative to it with `FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`, and makes the reparse check on the object it
> opened (a link, junction or mount point is never traversed; an entry whose reparse point is its own data
> is reopened through its filter only if it is the same object). A lookup on either host names exactly one
> entry of its directory — never `..`, `.`, or a name with a separator (or, on Windows, a stream) — so no
> lookup leaves the base; the Unix host had let `..` through `O_NOFOLLOW`. Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-10-01-the-windows-base-host-re-resolved-paths.md`.

> **Status (2026-09-29, AUD-29-02).** A landing of a named snapshot lands it only while the head is still
> exactly its state: nothing but snapshots journaled since, with no record dropped
> (`Volume::unchanged_since`). A head changed since is refused `Unsupported` before any host access, and a
> snapshot the volume never had is `NotFound`. **Superseded 2026-09-30 (A-49):** a landing lands exactly the
> state it names. A named snapshot is the engine's source through plan, verdict and write, judged by the
> witnesses it froze (A-48), and the advance is relative to it: an entry the head still holds as the snapshot
> did leaves the overlay, a file the head changed since stays private and is rebased onto what landed, a head
> whiteout keeps deleting it against the landed fingerprint, and anything else waits for a later verdict. The
> head's later edits then land as replacements, not conflicts (`crates/land/tests/source.rs`,
> `crates/server/tests/snapshot_landing.rs`, red on `57a1f2f`). Still owed: an unnamed landing's durable
> records name the head snapshot while the live head lands (a catalog format version). Record:
> `docs/bugs/2026-09-29-a-landing-of-a-named-snapshot-landed-the-live-head.md`.

**Live source and complete capture (A-9).** Creating a live overlay opens and identifies its
source without walking it. Untouched paths resolve the source's current names, metadata and
bytes through validated reads; copied-up/pinned entries retain their witnessed version and
report outsider drift. This is useful for laptop agents, but does not promise an atomic tree
snapshot across unrelated reads. Every mutation of a base-derived inode, including chmod,
truncate, link, rename and xattrs, passes through the same witness/copy-up rules. Whiteouts,
opaque directories, redirects, hardlink identity and open-unlinked handles must survive both
local and remote cloning. Watcher overflow invalidates affected cache knowledge; hints alone
never prove a source unchanged. Concurrent source edits may produce a typed retry/refusal,
not fabricated metadata or silently discarded operations.

A caller requesting a complete immutable point-in-time base uses `capture_base`. Admission
first reserves capture/retention costs. The source must be quiesced by an authority that can
actually exclude all writers, or exposed through a supported immutable read facility requiring
no Slates disk write or new privilege. Enumerate and retain the complete tree, metadata and
referenced bytes from that stable source, verify identities, then atomically publish its root.
Cancel or source failure releases uncommitted capture state. A mutable source without that
facility refuses `ConsistentBaseUnavailable`; repeated stats alone cannot prove that an
arbitrary multi-file scan corresponds to one instant. Ordinary `pin` can stabilize named
entries as observed, but is not relabelled atomic whole-tree capture. Report source identity,
coverage, dependencies, bytes read/retained and elapsed cost.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-291: `capture_base` is built for a source its caller quiesces).** `RequestBody::CaptureBase`
> (`slates_client::Client::capture_base`, `slates_api::Instance::capture_base`) runs the pin's sliced walk with every
> file's bytes made the volume's own whatever their size, each large file read whole and checked against its witness
> (`DigestUnverified` when it changed under the read), and every link's target owned (`PinWalk::capture`,
> `Overlay::capture_file` in `crates/vfs/src/base.rs`). It then takes a snapshot, judges it complete with the host (no
> file left on the disk, every merged directory's base names frozen, nothing drifted or unverified), and records it
> captured (`Op::BaseCaptured`, kept in the partition's snapshot with its snapshot and dropped with it); an incomplete
> one is destroyed again and refused `ConsistentBaseUnavailable`. A clone of a captured snapshot has no base plane and
> no host (`Volume::clone_without_base`, its record `BaseRecord::Scratch`), so it serves with the folder gone and moves
> between fleet members as a plain volume does (§4.10's status). The quiescence is the caller's: kiln captures a
> commit's tree checked out where nothing else writes. Evidence: `a_captured_base_holds_every_byte_and_its_clone_needs_no_base_directory`
> (`crates/vfs/tests/base.rs`: a pin of the same tree refuses a whole archive, the capture's archives whole),
> `a_captured_base_is_kept_with_its_snapshot_and_goes_with_it` (`crates/db/tests/model.rs`),
> `a_captured_bases_clone_reads_the_capture_with_no_base_directory` (`crates/api/tests/api.rs`) and
> `a_clone_of_a_captured_base_moves_and_gives_its_pin_back` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`). Owed: admission does not
> reserve the capture's cost ahead (the volume's quota charges each file as it is made the volume's own, and a refusal
> part-way leaves what was captured as copied-up entries, which change nothing a reader sees); a large file is read
> whole in one slice (its bytes held once more while it is checked), where its windows could be read across slices;
> the report of bytes read and retained and of the elapsed cost. **A landing of a captured clone is judged against its
> capture (A-424, stage 1, 2026-11-18):** its manifest is the change of its source since the captured snapshot, found
> where the two trees part (`slates_vfs::captured::ChangedPaths`: the inode tables' changed records, each changed
> directory's entries by name, a made, removed or moved subtree walked whole, a changed file named through its home),
> and every entry is judged by content (`Judged::Content`, `slates_land::verdict::content_verdict`): its witness is the
> BLAKE3 of the bytes the capture held, the disk is hashed, a file is written or removed only where the disk still
> holds those bytes (accepted by identity where it already holds the volume's), and a directory is removed only once
> emptied; a write is bound to the object its validation found (`Landing::observed`). An outsider's change to a file
> the agent never touched is in no manifest, so it is never a conflict and never overwritten. The landing leaves the
> clone a scratch volume (no base is taken from the target), so it still moves. Owed: a later landing judged against
> what the last one landed rather than the capture (an outsider's edit of a file the agent landed and did not touch
> again is a conflict until then); a name whose kind changed lands as a removal and a making that the class order meets
> as `TypeChanged`; a symlink pointed elsewhere does not land over the old one, as an overlay's does not (GAPS, g267).
> **A captured clone that moved lands against its capture too (A-503, stage 2, 2026-11-18):** the capture stays with
> the node that made the clone, so the move carries the part of it the clone changed: before the move is reported, the
> old owner walks the capture against the head it hands over (`slates_vfs::captured::CarryWalk`, in a task of the
> volume's shard a slice at a time) and records in the volume's catalog the captured state of every path where the two
> differ (each file's BLAKE3, size, mode and Windows bits, each link's target, each directory, each name the capture did
> not hold) with the head's archive identity (`Op::CaptureCarried`, `CatalogValue::carried`). The rest of the capture is
> that head. The new owner adopts the record with the catalog and keeps the snapshot it materialized the head as, its
> **mark**, through its seal (`Op::CaptureAdopted`; the mark only when the materialized head's identity is the carried
> one and it was not rebuilt from a live log). Its landing is then judged against `CaptureBase::Carried`: the candidates
> are where the source parts from the mark and every carried path, and what the capture held at a path is the carried
> state, else the mark's, which is the stage-1 judgement exactly. A move from the new owner carries again from its mark
> and its record. A carried record whose mark this node does not hold (a takeover that rebuilt a later head) is refused
> typed, never landed as a scratch volume. **Since A-544 (2026-11-18) every head carries, not a move's alone:** a
> captured clone is born with its record (naming no head yet), each head of its own it seals is walked and recorded in
> its catalog (`crate::carry`), and its head register ships only once the record for it is in, so a takeover after the
> owner's loss adopts the newest placed head with its record and marks it as a move's new owner does, and its landing
> is judged against the capture. A head whose carry could not be walked ships without its record (the head's content
> is never held back), and a successor that adopts it, or the creation head, refuses the landing by kind; a move waits
> until the head it hands over carries its record, so a refused carry holds the move back until it is refused
> `Unplaced`, as before. A clone never sealed before its owner's loss reaches its successor as an empty tree, the
> capture's bytes included, and its landing is refused by kind (A-544's entry says what is lost). **A live-shipped one
> moves with its mark too (A-565):** its new owner rebuilds it from its live log, which the move made durable at
> exactly the head it hands over, so the rebuild is that head and is marked as a seal's is; a takeover after an
> owner's loss still marks nothing it rebuilt from a log, which may have run past the seal its head names.

**An S3 base (A-464, designed 2026-11-18; Mantle's CP-T10.5).** An overlay's base may be the objects under a prefix
of an S3 bucket instead of a host directory: kiln keeps its bytes on Mantle, Mantle keeps them in S3-compatible object
stores, and an agent's workspace over such a tree needs no copy of it on the runner's disk. The base is read-only,
live, and judged as a host directory's base is; a landing never writes S3 (a landing's target is a host directory
under a grant, as ever). Part 1, this design and its pure core, is built; the network client (part 2) and the base
host with its simulated oracle (part 3) follow, each its own piece (GAPS A-464).

*Sources* (primary, fetched 2026-11-18; tier B): S3's API reference for `ListObjectsV2`, `GetObject`, `HeadObject` and
the `Object` type (`docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_<Action>.html`); S3's user guide for object keys
(`userguide/object-keys`) and its consistency model (`userguide/Welcome`, "Amazon S3 data consistency model"); S3's
SigV4 page (`developerguide/sig-v4-header-based-auth`, with its four worked examples) and IAM's
(`IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv-create-signed-request`). AWS's SDK behaviour is tier C and flagged where used.

*What S3 promises, and what the base takes from it.*
- **Listing.** `ListObjectsV2` (`GET /?list-type=2`) returns up to 1,000 entries a page (`max-keys`' ceiling and
  default). With `delimiter=/` and a directory's prefix, a page's `Contents` are the files directly in that directory
  and its `CommonPrefixes` its subdirectories, which is the host's `list(dir)` exactly, so a directory is listed when it
  is first looked up, never the whole bucket at creation (§4.15 "Live source": a live overlay identifies its source
  without walking it). A page with `IsTruncated` true names a `NextContinuationToken`, which the next request sends as
  `continuation-token` until a page is not truncated. Keys are asked `encoding-type=url`, since XML 1.0 cannot carry
  every character a key may hold (the API reference's own reason), and decoded as form values (`+` a space: AWS's SDKs
  decode so, botocore's `unquote_plus`, tier C). Keys come in UTF-8 binary order.
- **Reading.** `GetObject` with `Range: bytes=first-last` answers `206` with the bytes and `Content-Range`; S3 serves
  one range a request. `If-Match: <ETag>` answers `412 Precondition Failed` when the object's ETag is another, and
