> - a shipment carries the record, the offer and at most one slice's verification of the chunks its targets lack, and
>   a target that cannot accept the record yet answers with what it holds: a content acknowledgement when it holds the
>   inputs whole, else the offer's missing set (`Committed::answers` hands both back to the owner);
> - each holder seeds its replica a share at a time (`merge_origin::ReplicaSeed`: the held chunks one at a time, the
>   origin decoded and the engine seeded a share at a time, the identity compared), its first slice as the record
>   arrives, so a small origin is still acknowledged in the exchange that carried it, and only while the hold still
>   holds the inputs (a green forgotten meanwhile, by its tombstone or a takeover's reclaim, installs nothing).
>
> Inputs archives are chunked at the archive's largest chunk (1 MiB), so the kernel's origin is about 1,600 extents
> rather than 100,000 to 400,000. Test: `a_green_over_a_base_places_its_origin_at_f1_a_slice_at_a_time`
> (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`). Owed: the measurement over the whole kernel; a restarted owner remakes version 0's
> inputs before it re-ships the record (A-246), since the inputs' identity is not recorded; ~~a takeover successor still
> gathers version 0 from its hold in one call (`recover_green_inputs`)~~ (since A-333 the successor adopts its replica
> and gathers nothing); a large increment's archive is still remade from its chain entry on each pass that ships it.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-313: a restarted holder rebuilds its replica from what it kept).** A warm restart keeps the
> merge records a holder accepted (its acceptor, §4.8 "Recovery") and the inputs it held (AUD-29-59), but a holder's
> replica of each green, the engine every later version is recomputed on, lived in memory alone. The restarted holder
> answered every later record `merge.out_of_order`, for good, and the owner shipped it again on every pass: at `f = 1`
> with two holders, one restart left the green one holder's answer from stalling, and a second stalled it. Now a holder
> with a green's records and no replica rebuilds it before it answers (`merge_origin::rebuild_replica`): version 0
> seeded from its held inputs as A-286 seeds it, or the empty engine of a green with no origin, then each version it
> accepted recomputed from the increment it holds, an extent gathered or a version recomputed a unit, each head compared
> with its record's identity, the records read a version at a time. The first slice runs in the exchange, so a short
> chain is acknowledged in it; a long one goes on in a task, every record answered unacknowledged meanwhile. A version
> its records lack, or inputs it no longer holds, installs nothing (counted); another identity refuses the green on the
> holder for good, as a record's mismatch does. Test: `a_holder_restarted_over_its_segment_recomputes_the_greens_next_version`
> (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: holder b restarted over its segment, holder c withholding records, so version 2
> commits only through b's rebuilt replica): with the rebuild removed, b answered version 2's record out of order 4,586
> times and version 2 never placed within 60 s; with it, version 2 placed in 2.56 s (kiln r1017; the bug record of
> 2026-11-18).

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-333: a green's takeover successor adopts its holder ledger).** The successor rebuilt a
> taken-over green beside its ledger, in one poll of each shard: version 0's inputs restored whole from its hold into one
> dense copy, every increment's too, every accepted position cloned and decoded; then the origin's bytes recorded
> (`GreenOriginated`) and every increment recorded again in its partition, and the green replayed twice. The partition's
> merge budget is a quarter of a shard's metadata reserve, so a kernel-sized origin (1.67 GB, against about 333 MB a
> shard on a 64 GB machine of 16 shards) was refused at its first record, the takeover given up at the failover bound,
> and losing the primary lost the green. Now the successor adopts what it keeps anyway (`crate::green_adopt`):
> - the partition records the green by its adoption, one operation (`Op::GreenAdopted`: the catalog record, the adopted
>   version and identity, version 0's inputs manifest), and its chain holds only the versions after it; the versions up
>   to it are the successor's holder ledger, whose records are never compacted and whose inputs are retained while named;
> - the green's engine is the successor's own replica, taken at the adopted version, advanced to it from the increments
>   the successor holds, or rebuilt from the ledger when it has none, a slice at a time, then moved by value to the owner
>   shard (`verbs::adopt_taken_over_green`), with the submit completions the ledger's records carried gathered a slice of
>   records at a time (A-255);
> - a restarted successor re-adopts it at boot, after every partition has recovered and before any client is admitted:
>   the engine rebuilt from the ledger through the adopted version (version 0 alone when a checkpoint past the adoption
>   stands, which applies onto it), then the owner shard's own chain applied a slice a call; every verb on it answers
>   `Overloaded` meanwhile, and the works over it are replayed after it. A green the ledger cannot rebuild is fenced;
> - the green's record keeps the takeover that made this node its owner (`VolumeRecord::taken_over`: the promotion epoch
>   and the adopted version), and a green's records are written at that epoch after a restart forgets `placed_heads`
>   (`merge_service::record_epoch`, as `fleet::promotion_epoch` serves a volume's, A-344). A taken-over green recorded
>   none before, so a restarted successor wrote its merge and catalog records at its own host's epoch, below the fence
>   the takeover raised at every holder, and the green's next version never committed
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-restarted-greens-successor-wrote-below-its-takeovers-fence.md`).
>
> A checkout of an adopted green compares its base by the manifest of the inputs its walked origin makes. Test:
> `a_successor_adopts_a_greens_ledger_past_its_merge_budget_and_keeps_it_across_its_restart`
> (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: three nodes at `f = 1`, each partition's merge budget 1 MiB, a quarter of the 4 MiB
> base the green's origin is walked from). Kiln r2370 on the Mac Studio, 2026-11-18, debug build: green in 4.92 s, the
> successor adopting the green (`merge.takeover.adopted` 1, the ledger's completions gathered in 2 slices) and serving
> version 0's base file, the head and a third version, then after its restart re-adopting it (`awaiting_adoption` 1, the
> replica rebuilt through version 2 in 325 seed slices, `readopted` 1) and serving a fourth version and the edit of a work
> made before the restart as the fifth; red on main's code, the takeover refused 100 times and given up
> (`NotRecovered { TakeoverIncomplete { waited_on: "refused" } }`, 880 s); red without the takeover in the green's record,
> version 3 never placed again after the restart and version 4 unanswered at the test's 60 s deadline (531 s); red with
> the works over an awaiting green rebuilt at once, the kept work answered `NotFound` (5.5 s). Owed: a successor whose
> ledger lacks records two or more versions below the adopted one (the ledger-prefix transfer of records, GAP-A9-7); a
> new candidate holder that holds nothing of the green (AUD-14's transfer to a new candidate set); the adoption's
> completions recorded in one call on the owner shard, up to each client's bound per client.

> **Status (2026-11-06, A-235: the record plane runs when there is merge work).**
> The merge record plane ran once per coordinator period (100 ms), putting a version's inputs at one period and its
> record at the next, so every answer at `f > 0` waited at least one period, and usually two. One submit at a time on an
> idle three-node fleet at `f = 1` took 208 to 647 ms, and at 1,000 clients every accepted submit was answered
> `Overloaded` (`docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-submit-at-f1-waited-for-the-coordinators-period.md`). Now an enqueued version, an
> input newly placed, or a record newly acknowledged with versions still pending nudges the coordinator. It runs the
> merge plane at once, between its periods, and the council, root, seals and heads keep the period. A version's inputs
> are put only to the holders whose next record it is: a holder keeps only its newest placement ahead of its records, so
> a later version's inputs had released a lagging holder's next. Median answer now 2.7 to 4.4 ms on the debug build.
> Still owed: pipelining, more than one version to a holder per pass.

> **Status (2026-11-04, A-202: a submit's cost follows what it changed).** A work holds only the files it changed
> since its base and reads the rest from the green's history there; an accept moves its base and clears that, in
> O(1). The deriver composes over the base restricted to the journal's paths, and the merge record's identities are
> made only for a record that goes to holders. An increment's identity names its work and its base, as the data model
> below says (it had left both out, and a second work's identical edit was answered with the first work's version;
> `docs/bugs/2026-11-04-the-same-edit-from-two-works-was-one-increment.md`). Since A-202 (2026-11-05) the head
> identity is a set hash over the green's entries, brought up to date when read, so a record at `f > 0` costs what its
> version changed. Since part 3 (2026-11-06) a clean rebase returns only what the work changed over the head.

> **Status (2026-11-07, A-242: the history is copy-on-write, and an increment carries what it adds).**
> - **The history.** The engine kept a whole copy of a file per version that changed it, and charged the whole
>   previous file to each submit. A version now holds pieces of shared chunks (`crates/merge/src/history.rs`): the
>   bytes it added and its piece list. That is the "Splice" below, done in the engine's history.
> - **The increment.** Its post-state laid out each edited file's whole final content, zero-filled but for the runs,
>   and the seal read each run at its op's base-coordinate offset. A run after an earlier length change in the same
>   file therefore merged zeros into the green. The post-state now holds only the runs, each read from where the
>   work's file holds it (`increment::compose_volume_planned`).
> - Measured on CI: behind a held floor, 64 versions of 64-byte overwrites of a 1 MiB file under a 16 MiB budget,
>   16 of 64 accepted before and 64 after. The corruption's test: the green's head was `cd\0\0`, now `cdXY`.
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-greens-history-kept-a-copy-of-every-file-per-version.md`,
>   `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-run-after-a-length-change-merged-zeros.md`.)

> **Status (2026-11-08, A-257: a chain entry records what its verdict resolved, and recovery applies it).** A
> checkpoint at the floor can pass the base of an entry left above it, and recovery re-judged each entry at its base,
> which a restored green no longer holds: the entry was refused and the green fenced, every acknowledged version
> unreadable (every restart of the load harness's state, 2026-11-08).
> - The durable entry is now the increment as submitted, byte for byte, then the effects its verdict resolved it to
>   (content by reference to its post-state; a splice whose ops were not mapped by its path alone), then a digest.
>   Recovery applies the effects unconditionally (`slates_merge::chain_entry`, `Green::apply_recorded`). The position
>   of a checkpoint no longer matters to replay, and a straggler pins nothing.
> - A merge record's inputs are still the increment as submitted (`inputs_of`): holders ("Apply on holders") and a
>   successor (`recover_green_inputs`; since A-333 the replica it judged them into as a holder) judge it afresh, so a
>   wrong resolution on the owner cannot reach them.
> - Integrity: the digest on every entry; the head identity recorded and compared at every checkpoint, at every
>   version whose record goes to holders, and at the head wherever one is recorded (`GreenFence::IdentityDiverged`).
>   At f = 0 the entries after the last checkpoint are checked by digest alone: a divergence there is found at the
>   next recorded identity, not at its own version (an identity at every f = 0 accept cost 287-363 µs against a
>   35-42 µs verdict). The oracle (`crates/merge/tests/chain_replay.rs`) compares identity at every version.
> - Cost: 789 bytes an entry against the increment's 611 (+29%), and 4-5 µs on the p50 of an accept over a base behind
>   the head (32 to 36-37 µs; p99 within noise). Layout 6; a version-5 segment is refused, and a green already fenced
>   by a wrong checkpoint stays fenced.
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-checkpoint-passed-a-retained-entrys-base-and-recovery-fenced-the-green.md`.)

> **Status (2026-11-06, A-238: a green's chain is checkpointed at its reachable floor).** The partition kept
> every accepted increment for good, and the "fold into checkpoint deltas" below had no durable form.
> - Now, after each accept, the owner checkpoints the chain at the floor. The floor is the oldest version a live work
>   or pin names, kept below any merge record still waiting for placement. The owner checkpoints once the increments
>   to fold reach the size of the checkpoint they replace (`Op::GreenCheckpointed`, `slates_merge::checkpoint`).
> - Recovery restores the green from its origin and the checkpoint and replays only the increments after it.
> - A base below the checkpoint is no reader's and is answered `UnknownBase`. It is not mapped through deltas that
>   are gone, so "every base back to green's origin" now holds back to the checkpoint.
> - Under a 256 KiB cap, a green whose work kept up took 200 versions where it was refused at 31.
>   (`docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-greens-chain-kept-every-version-it-ever-took.md`.)

> **Status (2026-11-04, A-201: a green's head lands through a checkout).** `checkout GREEN VOLUME ATTACHMENT
> --snapshot N` writes the green's head into the volume it was created from (the server's overlay of the directory
> it lands into), checked to be that base and unchanged since, and `land` lands the volume under a grant; a green
> itself is still refused `land`. Proven by `crates/server/tests/checkout.rs` (a real daemon over a real directory:
> two merged pushes and an overlapping one refused with its window; the granted landing writes every merged byte; an
> outsider's edit of a merged file is the presentation's only conflict; a wrong or moved base refused; three of three
> red with the base check and the writes removed), by `crates/cli/tests/fs_server.rs` (two fleet nodes through the real
> binary: presented and unwritten under an unset policy; since 2026-11-18 landed on the server's disk under the write
> policy its launcher set, A-285: bypass in the one `slates land`, ask once the launcher approves exactly the presented
> manifest, on macOS arm64 and Linux x86_64 and arm64; and with the server node in its own Linux container, landing into
> the volume attached to it, in CI's Linux CLI step), and across two machines on 2026-11-05: a client on Linux pushed
> to a green on a macOS server, whose human granted the landing at its anchor, and the merged files landed on the
> server's disk (GAPS). The stop at the presentation on a Linux server (no grant from its CLI, A-201) is gone for the
> launcher's path: the policy the launcher set, never a person's proof, decides the write (A-285).

**Role.** Let many agents work on clones of one shared volume and fold their work back into it
with no locks, no last-writer-wins, and no inferred merge. Each agent's work becomes an
increment of declared operations; the green volume's merge task maps the increment through
everything accepted since the agent's base version, decides a pure verdict, splices accepted
operations into a new version by extent surgery, and commits the version as the next entry of
the green's fenced ledger register. Conflicts are byte-exact windows the agent rebases against. This is hecate's merge architecture
in slates' ownership model; the departures and their reasons are in D-27 and
`research/merge-engine.md` §2.

**Data model.**
```rust
struct Chain /* per green volume, on its owner shard */ { head: Version, records: Art<Version, VersionRecord>,
             deltas: Art<Version, Handle<CanonicalDelta>>, checkpoints: Vec<(Version, Handle<CanonicalDelta>)>,
             last_changed: Art<PathKey, Version>, seen: Art<IncrementId, (Version, VerdictSummary)>, task: MergeTask }
struct VersionRecord { version: Version, snapshot: SnapshotId, manifest: Option<Blake3>, increment: Option<IncrementId>, host_epoch: u64, at: Monotonic }
struct Increment { id: IncrementId /* blake3(work_volume, base, post_state, ops_doc, filter) */, work_volume: VolumeId,
                   base: (VolumeId, Version), post_state: SnapshotId, ops_doc: Blake3 /* a sealed chunk */, filter: FilterId,
                   evidence: SmallVec<Blake3> /* opaque to slates */ }
struct OpRecord { kind: u8, flags: u8, path: u64, at: u64, len: u64, src: u64 }   // 34 bytes, little-endian, written field by field (version 2, A-621)
enum OpKind { Overwrite, Extend, Truncate, Insert, Delete, Create, Unlink, Mkdir, Rmdir, Rename, Link, Symlink, SetMode, SetXattr, RemoveXattr, Mknod }
struct OpsDoc { header: WireHeader /* magic, version 2, path and op counts as u64 */, paths: PathTable /* path → bytes, sorted, unique */, ops: [OpRecord] }
struct CanonicalDelta { version: Version, ops: Handle<OpsDoc>, effects: Art<PathKey, RangeSet> /* per path: ranges touched and size shifts */ }
struct MergeRecord { green: VolumeId, version: Version, increment: IncrementId, verdict: VerdictSummary, manifest: Blake3, host_epoch: u64 }
struct ConflictWindow { path: PathKey, mine: (u64, u64), theirs: (u64, u64), theirs_version: Version, class: MergeConflictClass }
enum MergeConflictClass { Overlap, AnchoredInDelete, SamePositionDiffering, RenameRename, CreateCreate, DeleteModify, ModifyDelete, TypeChanged, MetaMeta }
```
Ownership facts: the chain lives on green's owner shard; an increment's ops document and
post-state are sealed chunks and a snapshot on the work volume's owner shard, readable from any
shard by handle while pinned (D-7); the merge record is an entry of the green's ledger register
(a partition log append on a laptop; a record sent to the green's candidate holders in a fleet,
§4.8); nothing in this plane is shared mutable state.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-621: a work names as many paths as it declares).** An op's path index is 64 bits, in memory
> and on the wire, and the ops document's header counts its paths and operations in 64 bits (`crates/merge/src/ops_doc.rs`,
> version 2; the chain entry, which writes an op's record the same way, version 5). So a work names as many paths as
> its caller's admission allows, with no fixed cap: a kernel tree's first push (about 97,000 files) is one work. Until
> then an index was 16 bits, and interning answered `u16::MAX` for every name past the 65,535th, so the 65,536th and
> every later name aliased one path. The deriver's index lookup, the verdict's reading of a rename's or an attribute's
> index, and the server's laying-in of an attribute's value narrowed the same way, the last silently skipping the
> value. Interning looks a name up in an ordered map, so a table of n names costs O(n log n) comparisons, where the
> scan it replaced cost O(n²); a test counts them. A table naming a path twice is refused at decode (`DuplicatePath`):
> read as the first, every later index would name the path after its own. A version 1 document, and a version 4 chain
> entry, are refused `BadVersion`, never read under the other layout. The golden vectors are version 2's, derived by
> an independent encoder and BLAKE3 that reproduce version 1's vector from version 1's layout.

**Declared operations (the journal, §4.5).** Every mutation is declared at the boundary where it
happens: through a mount, `write(off, len)` is `Overwrite` (or `Extend` past the end) and
`truncate` is `Truncate`; through the SDK, `edit(path, at, delete_len, bytes)` is `Delete` then
`Insert` with true positions; namespace calls are themselves. Each record carries the file's
previous version so composition is exact. Bytes are never in the journal.

**Composition at seal (the deriver).** Per path, the declared operations since the base version
compose by interval algebra into a net op set relative to the base version's content:
overlapping overwrites merge into one; an insert followed by an overlapping delete cancels or
splits; a truncate cancels operations beyond the new length; a rename maps the path of later
operations; a create followed by an unlink cancels; a whole-file rewrite (truncate to zero and
write, or write-and-rename) composes to one `Delete` of the base length and one `Insert` of the
new bytes. Composition of declared operations is arithmetic on facts; comparing file states to
reconstruct operations is inference and does not exist in slates. The same journal yields the
same ops document on every platform (its identity is the test). Paths under the work volume's
excluded subtrees are left out; the filter id is part of the increment identity. The composition
needs every record since the base: when the journal's retention has dropped any of them, the
derivation is refused `JournalIncomplete` (naming the sequence it needed and the oldest the journal
holds), never composed from what is left (`Volume::records_since`; 2026-11-05). A rename's destination the work edited
after the rename carries those edits on the move: the verdict maps them through the source's deltas onto the bytes the
rename moves, an edit meeting one of them an overlap conflict, and the chain entry records them with the copy, so
replay and a rebase restate them after the `Rename` (A-547).

**Position mapping.** Through the canonical deltas in (base, head], one direction, per path: an
intervening size-changing operation at position p with delta d shifts the increment's ranges
that lie strictly after p by d; ranges that overlap an intervening effect range are handed to
the verdict; a rename in an intervening delta remaps the increment's paths beneath it. Maps
compose: `map(a..c) = map(b..c) ∘ map(a..b)`. Deltas older than the derived retention fold into
checkpoint deltas by the same composition, which is exact, so every base back to green's origin
maps at O(log) checkpoint lookups plus the raw deltas after the last checkpoint. (Since A-238 the durable
checkpoint is the green's state at its reachable floor, and a base below it is refused `UnknownBase`: no live reader
names one.) A holder's replica folds where its owner's engine had folded when it made the merge record the holder
holds (the record names the floor), so no replica keeps more history than its owner (A-385).

**The verdict, two pure passes.** Inputs: the mapped increment, the effect ranges of the
intervening deltas, and the referenced immutable content. Pass one: a sweep line over the
increment's ranges and the intervening effect ranges per path, O((n+m) log(n+m)); disjoint
ranges are `Accept`; same-range candidates are listed for identity checks; everything else is a
`Conflict` with its class: overlap or containment; an edit anchored inside an intervening
delete; same-position differing inserts; rename against rename; create against create with
differing content; delete against modify in either direction; a type change; differing mode or
xattr changes on one path. Fetch, outside the pure core: the candidates' bytes by handle. Pass
two: memcmp; equal bytes are `AcceptIdentical`, unequal are `Conflict`. Neither pass performs
I/O, reads a clock, draws randomness, or calls the system allocator (a lint and a test enforce
it). Fast path: if `last_changed[path] <= base` for every path in the increment, the verdict is
`Accept` with no range work at all; this is what a basis buys, and it never decides a conflict. An operation marked
node-exclusive (`NODE_EXCLUSIVE`, the high bit of `OpRecord.flags`; §4.17.4 item 3, A-542) is judged whole instead: any
change to its path after the base, in any dimension, is a `Conflict`, never accepted by range or by identity, as a stock
Subversion client's commit needs. A `Copy` (A-586) is always judged so, as an addition: its destination's tree must be
absent at the head and unchanged after the base, and its source's tree unchanged after the version it copies.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-612: a work never changes bytes it did not see).** Two rules the verdict now keeps, each a
> defect A-596's oracle found:
> - *A file removed after the work's base is deleted, whatever stands at its path now.* The green records the last
>   version that removed the file at each path (`Green::file_removed`): an unlink, a rename away, or a rename onto it,
>   which removes the file it replaces. Replay rebuilds it, and it is never folded. A work based before it that edits the
>   path is delete against modify (`DeleteModify`), and one that renames it is rename against rename (`RenameRename`),
>   though a file was made there again, renamed onto it, or moved onto it beneath a directory's rename. Before, the
>   verdict mapped the work's ops through the replacement's one-insert delta and spliced them at the new file's end, and
>   a rename moved the replacement.
> - *A truncate removes the bytes it saw.* In a net op set it is a removal of base bytes, `[at, at + len)`, reaching the
>   base's end: a hunk over base bytes, as the interval algebra composes it (`slates_vfs::algebra`), judged by its span
>   with the edge rule. Mapped to a head that grew past that span after its base (an append at the end), it is the delete
>   of its span (`at_head`), in a submit, a rebase and a rename's edits, so the append is kept and the version's delta
>   states exactly what left. Before, the splice cut to the head's end and removed the append, a lost update.
>
> The sweep's other cases already held, judged by the spans in both directions: an overwrite ending at the cut, an
> insert at the cut and an append past it kept beside a truncate; an overwrite inside the cut span or a shorter
> truncate a conflict; the same truncate identical. Tests: `crates/merge/src/engine/unseen_bytes_tests.rs`; A-596's
> oracle generates both cases again (`engine/reanchor/tests.rs`).

**Splice.** For each accepted operation the new version's entry for that path gets an extent
list built from the base version's extents with the operation's range replaced by a reference
into the increment's post-state chunks (`Extent{src: Chunk{chunk, off}}`, sub-chunk offsets
allowed), so no byte is copied; directory operations apply to current-epoch nodes under the
birth-epoch rule; the result is one snapshot, version N+1, whose manifest identity the
background hasher computes, or the merge task computes at once (O(changed)) when a fleet needs
it before commit. The increment's post-state snapshot stays pinned by the merge record until the
version is superseded and its deadlist processed; cross-shard chunk references are acquired in
one batched message per increment (§4.8).

**Commit.** The merge record `{green, version, increment, verdict, manifest, host_epoch}` is the
next entry of green's ledger register: on a laptop an append to the partition log in the
anchor segment; in a fleet a record sent to green's 2f+1 candidate holders under the owner's host
epoch, committed at f+1 acknowledgements, refused by any holder that has seen a higher epoch for
that host, and issued only when every identity the version references is placed. The reply is `Accepted{version}` or `Conflict{windows}`. An
increment id already in `seen` returns its original result (the completion record holds the
reply); retries are always safe. A signed submit's verdict rides the version's chain entry and the green's accepted
record, a checkpoint keeping it once it folds the entry (A-321): the version's provenance, read back by `MergeRecord`
and answering every later reply that names the version. A green that is a member of a repository commits each version
as an entry of the repository's register, which one step can share with the repository's other greens' versions, its
namespace and its own state (§4.17.1 shared piece 2, A-603).

**Apply on holders (fleet).** Every holder of green's version N+1 recomputes the verdict and the
manifest identity from the record's inputs before serving the version to any attachment, and
compares its head identity with the record at every version; a mismatch refuses that version on
that holder, fatal-and-loud, before any read. On a laptop the owner is the only holder and no
second computation exists; that is the derived N=1 case, and the differential test proves the
fleet path computes the same answers. A holder reads a version's inputs from its content hold extent by extent, as
the inputs were cut, so inputs that repeat a chunk's bytes (one chunk named at several extents) read as the file
they are; what the recomputation holds of them, the gathered bytes and the increment decoded from them, is charged to
the holder's shard's budget before a byte is reserved and released once it has recomputed, and a record whose inputs
the shard cannot admit waits, counted `merge.inputs_over_budget`, as one whose inputs are not yet held (A-383).

> **Status (A-247, 2026-11-08).** A green's works are served on the partitions their names hash to, and only the verdict
> and a first read of a base file are the green's: a verb that needs either is parked on the work's shard and resumed
> by the owner's answer (`crates/server/src/work_home.rs`). Each work's base is held by a durable floor on the green's
> partition. Across nodes (a work on the creating client's node) is not built.

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-513: a work replayed through its green's owner is found again after a lost answer).** At
> recovery a work whose green lives on another partition is replayed through the green's owner, every ask in its
> target's own time. Every ask may lose its answer after it ran, and the pass took the work's shard's list of such
> works, so one lost answer left all of them unbuilt for the daemon's life: unserved, every change they acknowledged out
> of reach (against A-207 and the recovery rule above, "unserved until it has"), and each floor holding its green's
> checkpoint at its base. The list is now read, never taken (`verbs::unbuilt_works`), each ask is made once more after
> a lost answer (`daemon::ask_once_more`), and the install ends the work's record on its shard, so a second ask changes
> nothing (`verbs::install_replayed_work`). *Done by A-533 (2026-11-19):* a work whose asks go unanswered twice keeps
> its record and answers `Unpublished`, never recorded as the request's completion, and its shard asks its green's
> owner again as clients are let in, by messages each shard runs when it next runs: no timer, and no wait holds the
> admission.

**Submission.** `submit(work_volume, evidence?)`: seal the work volume (drain open extents,
compose the net op set, chunk; in a fleet, place the snapshot to its candidate holders now, at
f+1 acknowledgements, if the auto-seal has not), build the increment, send it to green's owner: the same shard is a call, another
shard a cross-shard message, another host the wire, routed by the green's id to its current
owner with the piggyback rule (a refusal from a non-owner names the current owner and epoch;
placement refresh is single-flight per green). The caller parks and resumes with the verdict. A work volume with
`stream = true` submits at every auto-seal; an agent that wants a review boundary submits
explicitly. A green with `require_evidence` refuses increments without evidence references. A submit may be signed
work (A-321): it carries an SSH signature over the merge's statement (the work, its green, its base and the increment's
identity, which a held submit hands the signer), judged on the green's owner under the work's and the green's trusted
signers once the increment is built, recorded with the version and answered; a work or a green whose policy requires
signed merges refuses one that did not verify when it would merge (`SignatureRequired`). A signature never permits a
merge: the write modes do (A-285).

**Edit and submit in one request (A-225).** `edit_and_submit(work_volume, path, at, delete_len, bytes, evidence?)` is
`edit` and then `submit`, in one request: the work's owner applies the edit exactly as `edit` does and, when the edit
is accepted, submits exactly as `submit` does. Both run inside the one durable step and under the one completion record
of the request, so a restart replays both or neither and a retry answers from the record. Its reply is the edit's
refusal when the edit is refused (nothing is submitted, as a client that saw `edit` refused would not submit), else the
submit's reply: the same verdict, the same conflict windows, the same refusals. `edit` and `submit` stay separate verbs
because they are separate operations (an agent edits many times and submits once); the combined verb is for a client
that does both, and saves it one round trip, which across machines is the whole of a request's cost.

**Rebase, the only corrective path.** `rebase(work_volume, to = head)`: map the work volume's
pending operations (since its base) through the canonical deltas up to `to`; if every operation
is `Accept` or `AcceptIdentical`, re-base the clone to `to` by extent surgery (its root becomes
version `to`'s root with the mapped pending operations re-applied), O(pending operations), and
the work volume's base becomes `to`; if any is `Conflict`, return the windows and change nothing.
The agent reads green's bytes for each window (a read of the named version), rewrites its own
bytes, and calls `rebase` again. A rebased increment has a new identity; deduplication never
blocks it. Rejects are non-blocking; the merge task never stalls on a conflict.

**Rebase off the owner (A-273): measured and rejected (A-528).** A work's rebase and its base reads at a named
version are the green's owner's: a work's shard asks them of the owner's shard (A-247, A-388), which answers them on
its one thread beside the verdicts. A-273 tried keeping a replica of the green on each shard that holds its works (the
engine made from the owner's, fed the owner's versions and folds in order, its content the owner's sealed blocks read
in place), so a rebase and a read at a version the replica held were answered on the work's own shard. It was built
whole (steps 1 to 4 in the engine; A-457, A-465, A-473 and A-502 on the shards) and lost the 1,000-client A/B twice:
accepted submits' p99 at a 20 ms think 61 to 89 ms against 0.81 to 13.6 ms without the replicas (r406), then, with the
feed moved off the submit's path, head reads and submits 26 to 57 ms at p50 against at most 1.27 ms, and every kind
worse at p99 (r100). A-528
removed it whole, with no flag and no dormant path: the owner-shard path is the design (BENCHMARKS, "A green's replicas
on the shards that hold its works: measured and rejected").

**Attachments and versions.** Mounts and SDK attachments of green pin a version;
`advance(attachment, version)` re-pins and invalidates exactly the paths the manifest diff
between the two versions names (O(changed) by structural sharing); no attachment's view changes
without `advance`; `status(green)` reports the head, the attachment's version, and
`changed_since(version)` from the change index (the paths each version changed, A-264) so a work volume learns early
which of its pending paths green has moved under (awareness, never load-bearing).

**The state's maps, and a green made at another green's version (A-534; §4.17.1 item 4).**

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-534).** Built in the engine: `crates/merge/src/ptrie.rs` (the tree), `crates/merge/src/dims.rs`
> (the eight maps), `crates/merge/src/engine/branch.rs` (`Lineage`).
>
> **Status (2026-11-19, A-618).** Two rules of the state. The root, the empty path (the server keys a volume's `/` so),
> is always present for modes and attributes: the deriver composes them and the engine lands them, which a push's head
> needs (§4.17.1 "A push is a work" item 3) and an agent's `chmod` or `setxattr` of a mount's root declared to a refusal
> before. And a removed file or directory takes its mode and attributes with it once nothing stands at its path, as a
> special node's did: they are the inode's, so a path made again starts without them (`Green::drop_metadata`; a rename
> or a file made again within one version keeps them). The removal is recorded as any change is (the history keeps the
> values, the identity and the verdict's change index see it).
>
> **Status (2026-11-19, A-575).** The server holds a repository's greens in one lineage on the repository's partition
> (`crates/server/src/greens.rs`): a verb lends a member's engine out of its lineage for one borrow (`Lent`) and every
> other lend of that lineage meanwhile is refused and counted; a member's destroy retires it at once and gives what
> only it held back a node a unit under the shard's slice (`Lineage::retire`, `Release`, `repository::run_releases`);
> a recovery rebuilds members in the order they joined, a branch by branching its source again at its version. A green
> standing alone is served as before, and `CreateGreen { base }` still walks its base.
>
> **Status (2026-11-19, A-586).** Built in the engine: `Copy` (`OpKind` 16), a path's tree copied by reference and
> recorded once at its destination (`crates/merge/src/engine/copy.rs`; the "Copies" bullet below). Owed: a checkpoint
> of a green holding a copy, a rebase that restates one, a copy from a version its source changed after, and a copy
> onto a path its own increment removes (the A-586 entry).

- **The maps.** A green's current values (files, IPC nodes, directories, modes, symbolic links, hard links, attributes,
  and the reverse map of hard links) are eight persistent radix trees keyed by the path's bytes (Morrison's PATRICIA,
  JACM 1968). Each tree's nodes live in an arena and count their holders. A change copies the nodes on its key's path
  that another holder names (path copying, Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator and Tarjan, JCSS 1989), at most one a byte of the
  key, and changes in place the ones only its own map names, so a green no other green shares pays what an ordered map
  paid. A prefix is one node, so a subtree grafts under another prefix by reference, which §4.17.4's `Copy` builds on;
  a tree's byte order is the string order every encoding relies on. A file's bytes are a block counted by the nodes
  naming it, so copying a node never copies a file. A walk assembles each key from its edges, so readers that list paths
  hand out owned strings. An attribute's key is its path with each NUL escaped, two NULs, then its name, which keeps
  the order of `(path, name)` pairs and makes one path's attributes one prefix.
- **One history rule.** A key with no history has held its current value since version 0. A key's first recorded change
  first records, at version 0, the value it held, when it held one; a key that appears records only its appearance.
  Every reader of a key at a version answers from its history when it has one and from its current value when it has
  none, and the readers that list a version list the current keys and the history's together. A green seeded from its
  origin therefore records no history for the origin's keys (until 2026-11-19 each had a version-0 entry, which held
  every origin file's bytes a second time), and a green made at another's version starts with none.
- **Copies (A-586).** `Copy` copies a path's tree at a version (Subversion's copy-from revision) to an absent
  destination, by reference in every map, when the source's tree did not change after that version, so the head's tree
  is the version's. It is recorded once, never key by key: an appearance record at the destination (the version, the
  source, the source's version), one entry of the change index and one `last_changed` entry for the destination, which
  stands for its tree. A key reads by the latest copy above it while it holds what that copy gave it (its own last
  change, if any, is older): its current value from the copy's version on, its own history before. Its first change
  after the copy records, at the copy's version, the value the copy gave it, as the one history rule records a key's
  first change at version 0; a change in the copy's own version records none. Its last change for the verdict is the
  later of its own and the copy's, and an edit declared against a base before the copy that replaced its file is a
  conflict. The set hash adds one entry a copy (its destination, source and source version), which stands for every
  entry the copy brought: the sum is the state's entries plus each copy's entry less the entries of the tree it copied,
  O(1) a copy and recomputed alike by every holder that applies the same versions. A branch made before a copy cuts the
  copy's tree from its maps (`Ptrie::cut`, a graft's inverse) and takes the copy's entry out of its identity.
- **A lineage.** Greens made from one another's versions share their maps' arenas through a `Lineage`, which owns the
  arenas and lends them to one green for the length of one call, so every node has one owner and nothing is shared by
  pointer (R2). `branch(from, v)` forks `from`'s eight roots (one count each), sets back in the new green every key whose
  value at `v` differs from the head's (the paths named by the change index in `(v, head]`, each value read from its
  history), and moves the head identity to `v` by the same keys, an entry out and an entry in (A-202's set hash). The
  new green's version 0 is `from`'s `v`; its histories, last-change indexes and change index start empty. A retire gives
  the green's holds back and frees what no other green names; a retired green's handle is a typed miss.
- **The bound.** With E the change index's entries in `(v, head]`, c the paths they name, L the longest of them in
  bytes, n the keys a history map holds and B the bytes of the changed files at `v` and at the head, a branch costs
  O(E + c·(L + log n) + B), plus bringing `from`'s identity to its head (the keys changed since it was last read, which
  any read pays): O(1) at the head, O(the changed paths) behind it, never a walk of the tree. Refusals: a version past
  the head is `PastHead`, one below the fold floor or the checkpoint the green was restored at is `Folded` (its values
  are no longer reconstructible), a retired handle is `Stale`.
- **Evidence** (`cargo test -p slates-merge --lib`, the Mac Studio, 2026-11-19, 22 of 22). The oracle,
  `every_branch_reads_as_its_copy_over_every_history`: generated histories over a lineage (works of every operation
  kind at the head and behind it, branches of any green at any version it reconstructs, branches of branches, folds,
  retires), each green fed with a copying reference, a green seeded from a copy of its source's whole state at the
  branch's version; after every step every green reads as its reference at every version it reconstructs (bases, files,
  lengths, pages, path bases, metadata, the change index against its model, the checkpoint, the identity against its
  recount, the retained figures) and as it read when each version was its head; each branch visits no node of any map
  (the walk counter, the non-vacuity count) and sets back exactly the keys whose value at its version differs from the
  head's; and a lineage with every green retired holds no node and no block. The cost test: a green of 10,000 files
  branched at version 1 of 3 visits no node, sets back the 4 keys changed after it, and makes fewer nodes than those
  keys have bytes and three each; branched at its head it sets back and makes nothing. Every dimension is set back
  once in its own test (10 keys at version 1, 5 at version 2, none at the head). Red on a copy of the tree with the
  reverts taken out, with a walk added, and with the version-0 entry of the one history rule taken out: three of the
  five branch tests fail each time.

**Failure matrix.** Green owner restart: Masked (chain, deltas and `seen` replay from the log;
in-flight submissions retry by identity). Green holder restart: Masked (the holder keeps the merge records it accepted
and the inputs it held, and rebuilds its replica from them a slice at a time before it recomputes the next version,
A-313; since A-404 from the durable checkpoint it keeps at the newest version its owner's records name committed, so it
recomputes only the versions after it). Green owner loss in a fleet: Degraded for the
membership horizon, then Masked after takeover on a candidate that holds the ledger (the successor adopts its own holder
ledger and replica, whatever the origin's size, and a restart of it re-adopts them at boot, A-333). Work volume owner loss before
`submit`: the volume's loss window (D-18) applies to the unsubmitted work. Submitter crash after
commit: the retry returns the original result; the version stands. Merge record with a stale
host epoch: Refused (`StaleEpoch`) at the first holder, never applied; the stale owner drops the
role. Holder
recomputation mismatch: Refused for that version on that holder, alarm, served from other
holders (Degraded); persistent mismatch is a bug signal that fails CI. Unknown base (green
destroyed, or a version of another green): Refused (`UnknownBase`). Ops document or post-state
unavailable: Refused (`ContentUnavailable`), retryable. Increment above the derived size budget:
Refused (`IncrementTooLarge{limit}`); the SDK splits by path. Evidence required and absent:
Refused (`EvidenceRequired`).

**Refusals.** The merge entries of §4.4's taxonomy plus `StaleEpoch`, `ContentUnavailable` and, for a volume that
requires signed merges, `SignatureRequired` (A-321).

**Derived constants.**

| Constant | Formula | Anchors |
|---|---|---|
| Delta retention before folding | measured base-lag p99 (versions) × safety, capped by the delta memory budget | base-lag histogram per green; budget from §4.2 |
| Checkpoint spacing | the version count where measured mapping cost through raw deltas exceeds mapping through one folded delta | per-delta mapping cost samples |
| Increment size budget | ops records such that measured per-record verdict cost × records stays under the merge-path budget | per-record cost; the ratcheted merge-path p99 |
| Stream cadence | the auto-seal cadence of §4.8 | mutation rate; loss-window SLO |
| Submission deadline | measured merge-path p99 × k | merge-path histogram |
| Placement refresh | single-flight per green; bounded refresh/retry using the returned configuration version | refusal timestamps and operation deadline |
| Last-changed index budget | paths touched per green × (key + version) | per-green path counts |

**Worked example.** Green G is at version 42 (a 300k-file repository). Agents A, B and C each
clone it as a work volume. A uses the SDK `edit` on `src/lib.rs`: delete 40 bytes at offset 412,
insert 45; B's editor rewrites `src/main.rs` whole, which composes to one delete of the base
length and one insert of the new bytes; C edits `src/lib.rs` at offset 400 for 60 bytes. A
submits: `src/lib.rs` last changed at version 39, so the fast path accepts without range work;
version 43 references A's chunk for the new bytes and G's chunks around it; the merge record
commits; A's reply is `Accepted{43}`. B submits with base 42: `src/main.rs` last changed at 41,
fast path, `Accepted{44}`. C submits with base 42: `src/lib.rs` changed at 43, so the increment is
mapped through delta 43 (a size shift of +5 after offset 452) and the sweep line finds C's
[400, 460) overlapping A's effect range [412, 457): `Conflict{[src/lib.rs: mine (400, 60),
theirs (412, 45) at 43, Overlap]}`; nothing is written. C reads version 44's bytes for the
window, rewrites its edit, calls `rebase(to = 44)`, which maps C's remaining operations and
accepts, and resubmits: `Accepted{45}`. Failure: G's owner is paused for longer than the
membership horizon while a merge record for version 46 is in flight; the regional group has
bumped that host's epoch and assigned G to a candidate that holds version 45; the stale record
is refused `StaleEpoch` at the first holder and never applied; the paused owner drops the role
on resume; the submitter's retry lands at the new
owner and returns `Accepted{46}`.

**Laptop degenerate.** One shard: a green and all its works share a partition, and every ask of the owner is a direct call in the verb's own step (A-247). One node: the merge record is a partition log append, placement is local,
the holder set is the owner, every arrow in the submission is an in-process call, and the
merge path is microseconds.

**Integration points.** §4.4 (roles, verbs, refusals), §4.5 (declared operations, per-inode
versions, the deriver's inputs), §4.6 (`EROFS` on green mounts; invalidation on `advance`), §4.8
(chains, deltas, last-changed index, merge records as ledger entries), §4.10 (placed before committed;
holder recomputation; submission across hosts), §4.12 (`slates.merge`, `edit`), §4.15 (the
landing verdict shares the class vocabulary; entry-level for the disk side because the disk
declares nothing), Part 6 (the merge oracle and the purity lint).

### 4.17 Version-control servers: git, Mercurial and Subversion over greens and works (D-28)

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-497).** Designed; nothing is built. The section has four parts. §4.17.1, the shared mapping,
> and §4.17.2, git (g261, A-497's second part), are written here, and §4.17.3, Mercurial (g291, A-499); §4.17.4
> Subversion (g292) follows as its own amendment, and every server builds on §4.17.1 without redefining its terms.
> The reading notes, with every source's revision and the lines quoted, are `research/vcs-servers.md` (Mercurial's in
> `research/mercurial-server.md`).

**Role.** slates serves stock git, Mercurial and Subversion clients over each tool's own protocols, as a hosting server
does: clone, fetch, push, branches, review, protected branches, hooks and access control. The repository lives in
slates instead of in the tool's files on a disk, and the merge engine of §4.16 is the server's write path: a branch is
a green, a push is a work submitted to it, and the verdict is the push's answer. What this is meant to buy (each claim
is unproven until measured by the method below):

- no disk on the path (R1): a repository is held in RAM and replicated as every green is (§4.10), and it reaches a disk
  only through a landing under a grant (§4.15);
- one copy of every byte: file contents, the tool's objects, every branch, every fork and every checkout share content
  by identity (§4.11);
- a checkout is a mount: any version of any branch is a volume that an agent or a build attaches on the provisioning
  path (R9), with nothing copied out of the repository;
- no inferred merge anywhere (§2 ban 11, D-27): a server-side merge, a rebase or a stacked change is the verdict's
  accept, identical or conflict with byte-exact windows, never a three-way text merge;
- a push's answer is durable when it is given: the merge record commits at f+1 holders before the client hears "ok"
  (§4.16 "Commit").

#### 4.17.1 The shared mapping onto greens and works

**Terms.** Each row is one concept in each tool, the slates object it becomes, and where the server's own section
decides the details.

| Concept | slates | git (§4.17.2) | Mercurial (§4.17.3) | Subversion (§4.17.4) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repository | a repository record (§4.8) and its greens | a repository | a repository | a repository |
| Branch: a name whose value a push moves | a green | each ref (`refs/heads/*`, `refs/tags/*` and every other ref) | each bookmark, and each head of a named branch (one green a head, §4.17.3) | the whole repository: one green whose version N is revision N; a branch is a directory in it |
| Push | a work submitted to the green; the verdict is the push's answer | `receive-pack`'s update commands | `unbundle`, with its heads check | `commit`: the request and its editor drive |
| What the client says it saw | the work's base | each command's old value | the `heads` argument, or the `check:heads`, `check:updated-heads` and `check:bookmarks` parts | the base revision of each path the drive touches |
| Stacked changes; a rebase | a chain of works | a series of commits reviewed in order; a server-side rebase | a stack of draft changesets: topics, a chain of works (§4.17.3) | §4.17.4 decides |
| A review request and the requests built on it | a work held for review; works over works | a pull request and its stack | a topic, or a bookmark the policy marks for review (§4.17.3) | §4.17.4 decides |
| Objects | content in the volume store, deduplicated by identity, indexed by the tool's id | blobs, trees, commits and tags | changesets, manifests and file revisions | node revisions, their contents and revision properties |
| History of a branch | the green's chain of versions | the successive values of the ref (the server's reflog) | the successive values of the bookmark or head | the revision sequence |

**The repository and its greens.**

> **Status (2026-11-18, A-515).** The record and its namespace are built in the metadata database
> (`crates/db/src/repository.rs`, the records in `catalog.rs`, five operations of the log): a repository's name is
> unique on its partition; a name binds a green of the repository's own partition that no other name binds; an empty
> name or one holding a NUL byte is refused; retiring a name leaves its green, so binding it again restores the
> branch; destroying a repository leaves its greens; a destroyed green leaves its name; a partition rebuilt from its
> snapshot answers the same. A model test holds the namespace to these rules over generated histories. Owed: the
> verbs that create repositories and their greens (with the namespace riding one register with the greens, item 3,
> shared piece 2) and the record's replication in a fleet (shared piece 2). A green made at another green's version
> without a walk is built in the engine (A-534, below).
>
> **Status (2026-11-19, A-534).** Item 4's engine half is built (§4.16 "The state's maps, and a green made at another
> green's version"): a green's current values are persistent radix trees, and `Lineage::branch` makes a green whose
> version 0 is another green's version `v` by forking them and setting back what changed after `v`, O(the changed
> paths), never a walk. Owed: a branch made through the register (shared piece 2); a green at a commit that is no
> version's head (that commit's tree has no state to fork until the object store of piece 3 holds trees); and
> Subversion's `Copy` on the same maps (§4.17.4, A-542). Since A-614 the object store holds trees,
> and a green made from a commit that is no version's head is git's receive-pack create (§4.17.2 piece 6).
>
> **Status (2026-11-19, A-575).** The repository verbs are built (`crates/server/src/repository.rs`; the wire's
> `CreateRepository`, `CreateBranch`, `BindBranch`, `RetireBranch`): a repository and its root (a new empty green, or an
> unbound green of the partition joining as it stands) bound to its default branch; a branch made at a version of
> another through `Lineage::branch` and bound; a name bound again to a member, which restores a retired branch; a name
> retired with its green kept (item 5). They route to the partition the repository's name hashes to; they are the
> owner's until the policy of piece 7; every refusal is typed, and each verb judges what a later record could refuse
> before its first, since a refused verb's records commit with it. Each member's membership is a record of the
> partition (`MemberRecord`: its repository, and whether it is the lineage's root or made at which version of which
> member), carried by the partition's snapshot, held to the rules by a model test, and a recovery rebuilds members the
> way they joined. A branch can be made only at a version its source's durable checkpoint has not passed, and a live
> branch keeps its source's checkpoint and history from passing that version (`merge_service::reachable_floor`): what a
> long-lived branch costs its source is that history, bounded by the source's retention budget. Owed: a branch's base
> recorded as a delta against its source's checkpoint, which ends both.
>
> **Status (2026-11-19, A-603: shared piece 2 built on the owner).** A repository's register is built in the metadata
> database (`crates/db/src/repository.rs`, the entry's guard in `crates/db/src/repository/entry.rs`;
> `Op::RepositoryAdvanced`). One entry commits, as one durable step, any of: several of the repository's greens'
> versions (several of one green too, a stack landed whole), greens joining its lineage, its namespace's changes, and its
> own state (Mercurial's phase roots and obsolescence markers, §4.17.3 decisions 3 and 4), with that state moved beside a
> push or alone. Its checks are read at its position, before any of its own changes: a green's head (`check:heads` and
> `unbundle`'s heads), and the exact names under a prefix (so no head was added or retired). The entry commits all of
> it or none: each item is judged against what the items before it left, guard then apply, and a refusal is typed
> (`OutOfOrder`, `CheckFailed` and `StateChanged` naming the item, or the namespace's and the lineage's own). Every
> change of a repository takes the register's next position, whichever operation records it (A-515's and A-575's
> operations, a member's version recorded alone, a member's destroy), so one position names one state of the
> repository. The server's verbs and every member's version now record entries (`crates/server/src/repository.rs`,
> `version_record`). The state is charged to the partition's merge budget; a partition snapshot carries the register;
> a recovery rebuilds it, and the entries' versions replay into each green's chain as any version does. A model test
> runs generated histories through a database over a real anchor segment, crashing it at random points, against the
> rules kept over plain maps; its census meets every kind of entry, refusal and recovery. Owed: (1) the push that makes
> an entry of several greens: its works are judged all before any commits (§4.16's verdict split into a judgment and its
> commit), then one entry carries them, with piece 4's works from a client's push. (2) The fleet half: the register as
> one ledger object of the repository's candidates (§4.8), its record the entry with each version's merge record value,
> committed at f + 1; every holder recomputes every version of an entry before it acknowledges, all or none, and a
> mismatch refuses the repository on that holder; a takeover adopts whole entries; and the repository record's own
> replication rides it (A-515's owed half). Until then each member's version still ships on its green's own register,
> so in a fleet an entry of several greens is atomic on its owner and not across a takeover of it.

1. A repository is a record in the metadata database (§4.8): its name, its tool, its object format (git's SHA-1 or
   SHA-256, Mercurial's node format, Subversion's revision numbers), its policy (below), its default branch, and its
   namespace, from each branch's name to its green.
2. Every green of one repository carries the repository's partition in the high bits of its id, as an attachment id and
   a landing id carry their owner's (`crates/server/src/shards.rs`, `landing.rs`). So a repository's greens share one
   owner and one ledger register, and one register append commits several greens' versions together. git's atomic push
   ("Either all refs are updated or none" [B: gitprotocol-capabilities `atomic`]) and a Mercurial push that adds
   changesets and moves bookmarks are each one durable step, with no coordination call on the write path (§2 ban 10).
   Repositories spread across the fleet; one repository's greens serialize on its owner shard. §4.16 gives each green a
   register of its own; a register shared by a repository's greens, whose entry carries one or more of their merge
   records, is the change this needs (shared piece 2; built on the owner by A-603, its fleet half owed: status above).
3. The namespace changes ride the same register: creating a branch, deleting one and moving the default are entries
   of it, so two clients creating one name race on one append and one of them is refused (built, A-603: every change of
   a repository takes one position of its register).
4. Creating a branch creates a green whose origin is a version of another green or one commit of the tool, shared by
   identity, so creating it costs no walk of the tree. (The engine makes a green at another green's version without a
   walk since A-534, §4.16; the verb, `CreateGreen { base }`, still walks its base until piece 1's repository verbs use
   it.) The new green records where it started (the green and version, or the tool's commit), which is the base a
   review request between the two branches later uses.
5. Deleting a branch retires its green: the name leaves the namespace, and the chain is kept for the retention the
   policy names, so a deleted branch can be restored as a server's reflog allows.
6. A tag is a green whose policy refuses any version after its first; the policy may allow a tag to move (git lets a
   forced push move one).

**A version.** Version N of a green is one value of the branch, and holds three things:
- its tree: the snapshot of the files at the branch's head, so attaching version N is a checkout of it;
- its head: the tool's name for what the branch names (git's commit id, Mercurial's changeset node, and for
  Subversion the revision number, which is N);
- the tool's objects that the version brought, each held as content (below).

The chain is the history of the branch's values, which a server keeps as its reflog. Version N+1's head descends from
version N's unless the policy allows a rewrite (a non-fast-forward push in git, a forced push in Mercurial); a rewrite
is one more version, and the chain itself is never rewritten.

**Objects: one copy, indexed by the tool's id.**
1. Every object's raw bytes, the bytes the tool hashes to name it, are content in the volume store, chunked and
   deduplicated by BLAKE3 identity (§4.11). A file's bytes in a version's tree and the tool's object for that file
   (git's blob, Mercurial's file revision, Subversion's file contents) are the same content, so a checkout costs
   metadata and no bytes.
2. Wire forms are derived and never the truth: a git pack (zlib and deltas), a Mercurial bundle or changegroup and
   Subversion's svndiff windows are computed from the raw objects for a transfer and cached by the identity of what
   they encode. A damaged cache entry is dropped, never repaired.
3. A repository keeps an index from the tool's id to the object's kind, length and content identity. The index belongs
   to the repository and lives on its owner, reached by the repository's id: it is not a global catalog (§2 ban 12).
   It is kept as immutable sorted tables that are content themselves, so a fork shares its parent's tables by identity
   and adds only rows for its own objects. Each server's section gives its layout.
4. The objects a push brings are held by the work, not by the green, until the verdict commits. This is the quarantine
   git's `receive-pack` keeps: objects "are placed into a temporary "quarantine" directory ... and migrated into the
   main object store only after the `pre-receive` hook has completed. If the push fails before then, the temporary
   directory is removed entirely" [B: git-receive-pack]. A refused push leaves nothing behind; the work releases what it
   held.
5. Every object is checked on arrival: the server hashes it as the tool does, and a push holding an object whose bytes
   do not hash to its claimed id is refused, typed, before any of it is indexed.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-581).** Shared piece 3's core is built as a pure crate, `slates-vcs` (`crates/vcs`), which the
> three servers' object pieces build on:
> - **Content** (`content.rs`, items 1 and 4): an object's raw bytes are kept once, named by BLAKE3, whichever tool,
>   push or repository brought them; a repeated put counts a holder and stores nothing, and the identity is always the
>   store's own hash. No content is longer than the content plane's window, which the owner derives (D-6's chunk,
>   sixteen base pages, `slates_vfs::content::chunk_bytes`) and gives the store. An object longer than that is cut at
>   the offsets a volume cuts a file's bytes at and named by lists of its windows' identities up to one root, admitted
>   whole or not at all, so an object's windows and a checkout's are one identity each. A window is named by plain
>   BLAKE3, as a volume's sealed chunk and an archive's chunk are; a list and a table by BLAKE3's key-derivation mode
>   under contexts of their own, so a pushed window can never be read as a list's identities or outlive a table's hold
>   on its rows. A content is held by count and freed with its last holder (a freed list gives back what it named),
>   within a budget the owner derives from its shard's memory (§4.2), which the indexes' tails and fences are charged
>   against too. Within a window, identity is whole-object, the deduplication D-6 chose first (whole-file deduplication
>   captures about three quarters of block-level deduplication's gain [A: Meyer and Bolosky, FAST 2011]).
> - **Tables** (`table.rs`, item 3): rows sorted by key, each naming in its own bytes the contents it holds, encoded as
>   bytes that are content (`slvcstb1` magic, the row count, 64-bit offsets, then the entries), at most one window
>   each, so a table is named, shared and checked by its identity. Bytes from anywhere are opened with the frame, every
>   entry and the keys' order checked and every fault refused by kind (§4.9).
> - **The index** (`index.rs`, item 3): a tail (an ordered map) over runs of tables, the log-structured merge tree's
>   shape [A: O'Neil et al., Acta Informatica 1996]. A run is tables in key order whose ranges do not meet, found by
>   their first keys (fences), so a lookup reads one table a run. An id names one object for ever, so a key is in one
>   layer at most and an insert of a held key is `Identical` or refused `RowDiffers`. The table's size and the tail's
>   length are derived, never counted in rows: a table is one window, and the tail is due to seal once its rows no
>   longer fit one table, sealing its full tables and keeping the last one's rows. A fork seals its parent's tail,
>   holds each table once more and copies the fences: no table written, no row copied. A merge reads the newest `j`
>   runs this index alone holds into one; runs a fork shares are never merged, and read as this index's own again once
>   no other index holds them.
> - **The merge point** (`rule.rs`): learned, one rent-or-buy problem for each `j`. The index counts, for each lookup,
>   the runs it visited and how many of those it alone holds; the owner times its lookups, inserts and merges. The rent
>   toward merging the newest `j` is the time spent on the visits that merge would save (`min(p, j) - 1` for a lookup
>   that visited `p`); its price is the last merge's measured time a row (before any, what building the tail cost);
>   the largest `j` whose rent has reached its price is due: the ski-rental break-even, within twice an offline
>   optimum's cost [A: Karlin et al., Algorithmica 1988]. So two small runs are merged long before the visits to a
>   large run under them pay for rewriting it. §4.17.3's and §4.17.4's index rows read this rule.
> - **Arrival** (`arrival.rs`, items 4 and 5): the tool's naming is a parameter (`Naming`, with its own id and refusal
>   types: git's `slates_git::object_name::name_of`, which refuses an input its SHA-1 collision detection flags,
>   `CollisionAttack`; Mercurial's node rule over its parents, the context), checked before a byte is stored. A
>   mismatch is `IdMismatch`, a refusal `NotNamed` with the tool's own reason, one id brought twice with other bytes
>   `Collision`. A push's objects are held by its quarantine, committed into the index as one step whose every row,
>   content and byte of room is checked before any is applied, or abandoned with nothing left. An object row is the id,
>   its root content, and its kind and length.
>
> Evidence (`cargo test --locked -p slates-vcs --lib`, 29 of 29, the Mac Studio, 2026-11-19, at ca821c3a6; `cargo fmt
> --check` clean): an oracle over 300 generated histories of arrivals with lies among them, commits, abandons, raw
> inserts, lookups, seals due and whole, merges of any number of runs, timed merges the rule calls due, forks and
> releases over four repositories and three pushes on one store, a ten-window object among them whose window is another
> object. After every step each repository reads as a plain map, no table is longer than the window, every named content
> is held with the bytes the oracle's own statement of each object's layout gives, no content is held that nothing
> names, and the store is empty once all is released. Beside it: one content across tools; an object past a window
> arriving as its windows and read back through its row; a tool's refusal carried with its reason; a fork writing no
> table; two repositories sealing the same rows sharing one table; a merge reading only its own runs; the seal due
> exactly when the tail's rows no longer fit one table; two small runs merged with the large run under them left as it
> was; budget refusals; hostile tables. Thirteen mutations of the code each turned one to four tests red (A-581).
>
> Owed: one content index for this store and the volumes' sealed windows, so a checkout and a blob are one copy (piece
> 4, with Phase 7's per-shard content index; a green's blocks keep their own bytes today); a merge, a seal, a release and
> an abandoned push sliced under the shard's budget (each is one call here, linear in its rows); the store and each
> repository's index on the owner shard, fed the shard clock's times, with each tool's naming implemented (git's over
> `slates_git::object_name`, Mercurial's node), in each server's pieces; content-defined cuts of tables, so identical
> rows written apart share tables, and of the large-file class (D-6), each gated on a measured gain; pruning what no
> branch reaches; the wire forms cached by identity (item 2); content placed and replicated by identity in a fleet
> (§4.10).

**A push is a work.**

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-618: shared piece 4 built in the engine).** `slates_merge::push::build` makes a client's push
> into the work items 2 to 4 state. It compares the base version's tree and the pushed tree entry by entry by the ids
> the tool named them by, read through `PushObjects` (tree entries, a blob's length, a blob's bytes; a store implements
> it, git's over `slates-vcs` in §4.17.2 piece 5), on an explicit stack; a subtree whose id is the base's is never read,
> so a push costs the directories on the paths it changed (counted: trees read, blobs read, subtrees skipped). It makes
> the operations item 2 names: a changed file replaced whole (`Truncate` then its bytes, which the deriver composes into
> one `Delete` of the base length and one `Insert`), `Create`, `Unlink`, `Mkdir` before what a directory holds, `Rmdir`
> after it, `SetMode` 0755 for an executable and 0644 for a file that stops being one, `Symlink`; and item 3's head, one
> `SetXattr` of `slates.vcs.head` on the root, the empty path, which the deriver and the engine now hold always present
> (§4.16). It composes them against the green's base, lays the post-state from the pushed blobs, charges every
> operation, queued step and byte against the caller's room as it is made (a file's length before its bytes), and
> refuses typed: a base the green does not hold, an object the store cannot give as its kind, a name or a link target
> slates cannot hold, a name twice in a tree, a submodule link (its special node kind is §4.17.2 item 5's, owed), a path
> that changes kind (the deriver's composition is owed, GAPS §8f), a work past its room (which bounds a push of any
> size: an ops document names as many paths as its work declares since A-621, and a push of 70,000 paths lands as one
> work), and a base the green disagrees with. Item 4's client-fidelity test runs after every push of generated
> histories, and found that a removed file or directory left its mode and attributes in the green, so a path made again
> took them (a file deleted and pushed again as plain kept the deleted one's mode 0755); a removed file or directory now
> takes its mode and attributes with it, as a special node's did (§4.16). Owed: git's tree entries mapped onto
> `PushObjects` by git's store (piece 5) and the receive-pack verb that submits the work (§4.17.2 piece 6); submodule
> links; kind transitions; one copy of a pushed blob's bytes shared by the store and the green (A-581's owed content
> index); the post-state assembly shared with the server's (`verbs::assemble_post_state`), so the two never lay a
> document out apart.
1. **Its base** is the version whose head is the value the client says it saw. In git that is each command's old value:
   the server must "validate each reference that is being updated that it hasn't changed while the request was being
   processed (the obj-id is still the same as the old-id)" [B: gitprotocol-pack]. In Mercurial it is the heads the
   client observed, which the server uses "to detect race conditions" [B: hg wireprotocol `unbundle`], or bundle2's
   `check:heads`, `check:updated-heads` and `check:bookmarks` parts [B: hg bundle2]. In Subversion it is the base
   revision of each path the editor drives, and a working copy mixes revisions, so one commit names a base per path:
   the server checks each path against its own base (the out-of-date test, item 5) and builds the work on the version
   current at that check, so the verdict then catches whatever lands after it. A value that no version of the green
   ever held (git's old value naming a commit inside an earlier push, say) is answered as the tool answers a ref that
   moved, before any work is built.
2. **Its declared operations** are what the client declared, read at the granularity the client declared it. git and
   Mercurial push snapshots, so a push declares which content now stands at each path: for each path whose content
   identity differs between the base version's tree and the pushed head's tree, the work holds one `Delete` of the base
   length and one `Insert` of the new bytes (the whole-file replacement §4.16's deriver makes of a whole-file rewrite);
   `Create`, `Unlink`, `Mkdir` and `Rmdir` for what appears or vanishes; `SetMode` for the executable bit; `Symlink`;
   and a special node for an entry with no file form (git's submodule link; §4.17.2). Subversion's editor declares
   each changed file, and the work holds the same whole-file operations for it. This reads identities the client
   computed: no bytes are compared and no edit position is guessed, so D-27's never-diff clause holds. A push that moves
   a branch across several commits is one work: its post-state is the new head's tree, and the commits in between are
   objects of the version it makes.
3. **The head operation (git and Mercurial).** Each such work also sets the green's head: one `SetXattr` of the
   reserved attribute `slates.vcs.head` on the green's root, to the new head's id. Two works that both move the branch
   meet on that one attribute, and §4.16's verdict then answers what the tools answer: the same new value is
   `AcceptIdentical` (that push already happened), and a different one is a `MetaMeta` conflict (another push came
   first). A Subversion work sets no head: Subversion lands a commit made against an older revision when its paths did
   not move, so its versions advance without a compare-and-swap on the whole repository. A work the server itself turns
   into the tool's objects (item 4) carries no head operation either, or two such works on one version would conflict on
   it: the server makes the commit after the verdict, records it with the version (its time and author taken from the
   merge record, never from a holder's clock), and every holder recomputes it from the record (§4.16 "Apply on
   holders").
4. **The client-fidelity rule.** A stock client must end where it thinks it is. After its push is accepted, every path
   it changed holds exactly the bytes it sent, and the branch names exactly the head it computed: git and Mercurial
   name each commit by a hash of its content, so any change the server made would be a different commit, and
   Subversion's client records each file it committed as being at the new revision with its own bytes. So a stock
   client's work is decided at whole-file granularity, which the operations of item 2 give; it is never merged into
   byte ranges it did not send. Byte-range accepts, where two edits to one file both land, are for works the server
   itself turns into the tool's objects: an agent's work through the SDK or a mount, a server-side merge of a review
   request, a server-side rebase. The server makes the new commit, changeset or revision, and clients fetch it. What
   the server makes needs what a client's commit carries: a message, which such a work's submit must carry, and its
   principal's name and address in the tool's form (git's author and committer, Mercurial's `Name <address>`), which
   the principal's record holds (§4.13). A submit to a green of a repository without a message, or by a principal with
   no such identity, is refused typed (`MessageRequired`, `IdentityRequired`) before any work is built.
5. **The answers.** For each tool:
   - git: the push's old value is the green's head, and whether each command is a fast-forward is the policy's check
     (`receive.denyNonFastForwards` [B: git-receive-pack]), made after the admission hooks and before the verdict.
     Accept and identical are `ok <ref>`; a conflict on the head is `ng <ref>` with the reason git gives for a ref that
     moved ("someone pushed in the meantime" [B: gitprotocol-pack]). §4.17.2 names every answer's words.
   - Mercurial: the heads the client saw are the green's heads; accept answers the push response's change in heads
     [B: hg wireprotocol `unbundle`], and a conflict answers the abort its heads check calls for (§4.17.3).
   - Subversion: a commit whose paths did not change since their base revisions is accepted and answered with
     `commit-info` and the new revision [B: ra_svn `protocol`, `commit`]; a path changed since its base revision is a
     conflict, answered as Subversion's out-of-date error (§4.17.4). Here the verdict is Subversion's own commit rule:
     it merges a transaction into the newest revision node by node and fails a file "whenever source, target, and
     ancestor are all distinct node revisions" [B: svn_fs.h `svn_fs_merge`], and it calls a path out of date when its
     base revision "is less than the last-changed-revision of the path" [B: svn_fs.h `svn_fs_lock_many`], which is the
     negation of §4.16's fast path (`last_changed[path] <= base`). Subversion's exact rule is §4.17.4 item 3's, FSFS's
     commit-time merge, and it is stricter than §4.16's verdict over whole-file operations: it accepts no identical
     replacement, a directory whose properties changed meanwhile conflicts with any change beneath it, and a
     directory's last change is its subtree's.
6. **A base that is no version.** A review request or a merge may need a base that is a commit inside an earlier push,
