> `svn_time_from_cstring` and APR read them), `rev-proplist`, `rev-prop`, `check-path`, `stat`, `get-mergeinfo` (A-605's
> catalog) and `get-iprops`, each writing what `svnserve` writes: the trivial authentication request first, refusals
> with Subversion's numbers and messages, an unknown command refused, malformed parameters ending the connection.
> Held to transcripts of stock `svnserve` 1.15.0 answering stock `svn` 1.15.0 and scripted clients
> (`crates/svn/fixtures/reads`, recorded by its `make-fixtures.py` through a relay, each file's SHA-256 in
> `SHA256SUMS`), property lists compared as sets: `svnserve` writes them in APR's per-table seeded hash order, three
> recordings gave three orders, and slates writes them in name order. Its second part's first slice (2026-11-19):
> `get-dir` (the node's and the entry properties, the dirent fields asked for, the ancestors' properties) and
> `get-locations` (`svn_repos_trace_node_locations` over the index: the closest copy by FSFS's youngest copy root, its
> source, the same line at the same path), with `svn info` of a file and `svn proplist --show-inherited-props` replayed
> whole. Owed: `get-file`, `list`, `log` with merged revisions, `get-location-segments`, `get-file-revs`,
> `get-deleted-rev`, then `svn mergeinfo --show-revs`; read access by the authorization rules (A-606).

**Role.** slates serves stock Subversion clients (the `svn` command line of the 1.x line, and TortoiseSVN and SVNKit,
which speak the same protocols) as `svnserve` and Apache's `mod_dav_svn` do: over `svn://` (the ra_svn protocol on TCP),
`svn+ssh://` (the same protocol through an SSH tunnel) and `http://` and `https://` (mod_dav_svn's WebDAV/DeltaV and its
HTTPv2). A repository is one green whose version N is revision N, and a branch is a directory in it (§4.17.1's row). A
commit is a work submitted to that green; the verdict is Subversion's own commit rule; and a client ends exactly where
`svnserve` would have left it (§4.17.1's client-fidelity rule).

*Sources* (primary, read 2026-11-18; notes §1). Subversion's `1.14.x` branch at `d434dc14` (2026-11-01): the ra_svn
protocol (`subversion/libsvn_ra_svn/protocol`), the HTTP notes (`notes/http-and-webdav/http-protocol-v2.txt`,
`webdav-protocol`), the svndiff format (`notes/svndiff`), FSFS's design (`subversion/libsvn_fs_fs/structure`), the
filesystem, repository, mergeinfo, properties and error headers, the locking specification, and the test suite's
README, tier B; and the code that decides what the documents leave open, tier C: the commit editor
(`libsvn_repos/commit.c`), FSFS's commit-time merge (`libsvn_fs_fs/tree.c`), the svndiff codec
(`libsvn_delta/svndiff.c`, `libsvn_subr/encode.c`, `compress_lz4.c`), the ra_svn parser (`marshal.c`), the hooks
(`hooks.c`), log's
access rule (`log.c`), and the two servers (`svnserve/`, `mod_dav_svn/`).

*1. What a Subversion server presents, and where each part lives.* A client sees a repository as a filesystem with
history (notes §5): numbered immutable revisions, revision 0 an empty root; unversioned revision properties; named
transactions that become revisions; node-revisions with ancestry; a changed-path list per revision; locks.

| Subversion | What the client reads or sends | In slates |
|---|---|---|
| Repository | a UUID, a root URL, revisions 0 to N | §4.17.1's repository record, with its UUID, and its one green |
| Revision N | an immutable tree | green version N; version 0 of a Subversion repository is an empty root directory |
| Revision properties | `svn:author`, `svn:date`, `svn:log` and any others; changeable through a hook | the revision-property table (item 6): a commit's values recorded with its version, a change an entry of the repository's register |
| Transaction | a named mutable tree on a base revision, with properties | a work on the green, based on the head when the commit began (item 3) |
| Node-revision | kind; text with its MD5 and SHA-1; properties; created revision and path; predecessor; copy source and copy root; mergeinfo count | a row of the Subversion index (item 2), its text and property list held as content by identity |
| Changed paths of a revision | path; add, delete, replace or modify; kind; text, property and mergeinfo changed; copy source | the revision's changed-path rows, recorded from the commit's own editor drive |
| A copy: a branch, a tag | `add-dir` or `add-file` naming a copy source | a declared `Copy` in the green that shares the source by reference (item 3) |
| Lock | path, token, owner, comment, creation and expiry | the lock table (item 7) |
| `svn:mergeinfo` | a versioned property | a property like any other, indexed per version for its queries (item 8) |

Files hold Subversion's repository-normal bytes, exactly what `svnlook cat` prints: end-of-line and keyword
translation (`svn:eol-style`, `svn:keywords`) is the client's, never the server's. A node's properties are one sorted
property list, held as content and named from the node by the reserved attribute `slates.svn.props`, so a large
`svn:mergeinfo` costs one reference per node and one copy in the store (§4.17.1 "Objects"). A symbolic link is what
Subversion stores, a file with `svn:special` and the text `link TARGET`, and the executable bit is the property
`svn:executable`. Holding Subversion's model as it is keeps every byte and property a client committed exactly as it
sent them; a translated view for agents (a link as a link, `svn:executable` as a mode) would be a view over this
storage, not the storage, and is not part of this section.

*2. The Subversion index* (§4.17.1 "Objects" item 3, this tool's layout). It lives on the repository's owner, as
immutable sorted tables that are content plus a mutable tail, and every row is a function of the green's versions and
their commit records (item 3), so replicas (A-273) and holders (§4.16 "Apply on holders") compute it and never receive
it.
- *Revisions:* per revision, its changed-path rows sorted by path, and its transaction's name.
- *Nodes:* per node-revision, by its created path and revision: kind; text identity (BLAKE3, the green's content) with
  the MD5 and SHA-1 clients check; size; property-list identity; predecessor and its count; copy source and copy root;
  the node's identity (where it was born) and its copy identity, assigned by FSFS's rules (notes §5; `structure`,
  "Copy-IDs and copy roots"; `tree.c` `get_copy_inheritance`): a creation takes its parent's copy identity and copy
  root, a copy gets a fresh copy identity and is its own copy root, a change through the node's own created path keeps
  its copy identity, a change of a never-copied node through a copied directory (a lazy copy) takes that directory's,
  and a change of a copied node through another path (a soft copy) takes a fresh one; so the three answers of
  `svn_fs_node_relation` (unchanged, common ancestor, unrelated) come out as FSFS's; and whether the node has
  `svn:mergeinfo`, with the count of such nodes at and beneath a directory (FSFS's `minfo-here` and `minfo-cnt`).
- *History:* per path, the revisions at which a node-revision was created there, deletions included. FSFS makes a new
  node-revision of every directory above a changed node (notes §5, "bubble-up"), and of the root in every revision,
  even one that changes nothing (`transaction.c` `create_new_txn_noderev_from_rev`), so a directory's list holds every
  revision that changed anything beneath it. The created revision of a path at revision R, which the out-of-date test,
  `stat` and `svn:entry:committed-rev` all read, is one search in that list: its last entry at or before R, a deletion
  meaning absent, unless a directory above the path was added, copied to, replaced or deleted after that entry (each
  path keeps a list of those changes too). Then the latest such change decides: a deletion, or an addition without
  history, leaves nothing at the path, and a copy sends the question to the same place beneath the copy's source, in the
  source's revision. So a path beneath a branch answers its trunk node-revision until it changes on the branch, as FSFS
  shares it. §4.16's `last_changed` is a file's own last change; a directory's last change in Subversion's sense is its
  subtree's, which this list keeps.
- *How a revision's rows are applied:* in path order, parents first, against revision N - 1, each as FSFS applies the
  editor call it records (the path's directories opened and made mutable from the root down, then the entry made,
  copied, deleted or changed). That is what FSFS's commit leaves for every commit it accepts: `merge()` refuses a
  directory both sides changed unless both kept its node and copy identities ("not a direct modification"), and points
  its predecessor at the newer revision's (`svn_fs_fs__dag_update_ancestry`). FSFS makes nodes mutable in its drive's
  order, and a stock client sends file texts last; the oracle replays every generated revision in random drive orders
  and finds every identity, copy root and predecessor equal to path order's, the decisions where order could matter
  among them (A-553).

*3. A commit is a work, and its verdict is FSFS's commit rule.* (§4.17.1 "A push is a work" items 1, 2 and 5, made exact
for Subversion.)
1. **The transaction.** A `commit` (ra_svn), a POST to the me resource (HTTPv2) or a MKACTIVITY (HTTP v1) opens a work
   on the green, based on the head at that moment: version B, the transaction's base. Every per-path test of the drive
   compares with B, as Subversion's commit editor compares with its transaction's root (notes §6). start-commit runs
   first (item 9). The transaction's name is B, a `-` and the work's id in base 36, which keeps to the letters, digits,
   `-` and `.` that `svn_fs.h` promises.
2. **The drive.** Each editor command is checked when it arrives, then declared on the work:
   - `open-file`, `delete-entry`, and a property change on a directory, each carrying the client's base revision R of
     that node: out of date (`E160028`) when R is below the node's created revision at B, and no such revision
     (`E160006`) when R is past B (`commit.c` `check_out_of_date`); `delete-entry` of a path absent in the work and
     `add-file` or `add-dir` of a path present in it (unless its parent was copied in this transaction) are out of date
     too.
   - A copy (`add-dir` or `add-file` with a copy source): the source must lie in this repository, the principal needs
     read on it (recursive for a directory) and write on the target and its parent (item 10); declared as `Copy`.
   - A text change (`apply-textdelta`, its windows, `close-file`): the base checksum must equal the stored MD5 of the
     path's text in the work, the svndiff windows are applied as they arrive against that text (one window at a time,
     each at most 102,400 target bytes, notes §4), the result's MD5 is taken as it is written and must equal
     `close-file`'s (`E200014` otherwise), and the path's change is declared as one whole-file replacement (§4.17.1
     item 2). The windows' source copies say which byte ranges of the new text are the base's own, so the new text's
     extent list references those base extents rather than copies of them (§4.16 "Splice"). That decides storage only,
     never the verdict: the client's delta is not read as an edit.
   - A property change: refused as Subversion refuses it (`svn_repos__validate_prop`: regular properties only; a
     translated `svn:` property UTF-8 with no CR; `svn:date` a date; `svn:mergeinfo` in its grammar; `E125005`,
     `E200020`), else declared as one replacement of the node's property list.
   - Every operation of a Subversion work is *node-exclusive*: the verdict judges it as touching the whole node, never
     by byte range and never by identity (item 3.3). An agent's work and a server-side merge keep §4.16's byte ranges
     (§4.17.1 item 4).
3. **The verdict.** `close-edit` submits the work; pre-commit runs over its post-state (item 9); the merge task judges
   it against the versions in (B, head]. The rule is FSFS's merge at commit (`tree.c` `merge()`, notes §6), stated on
   the index:
   1. a file the work changed (its text or its properties) that also changed in (B, head] is a conflict, even when
      both made the same change ("If any of the three entries is of type file, declare a conflict");
   2. for a name both sides changed: a double delete, a delete against a change, a replacement on either side ("even an
      identical replacement") and an addition on both ("two additions are not auto-mergeable") are conflicts, and a
      directory changed on both sides otherwise is judged entry by entry, by these rules, beneath it, when both sides
      kept its node and copy identities; a directory of a branch that no revision changed since the copy takes the
      branch's copy identity when first changed inside it (a lazy copy, `get_copy_inheritance`), so two works that
      change different files beneath it conflict there, as they do in FSFS (A-592);
   3. a directory on the path from the root to any node the work changed whose property list changed in (B, head] is a
      conflict (FSFS refuses the source's property change of a directory both sides changed beneath);
   4. a directory whose property list the work changed is a conflict when its names, or their node or copy identities,
      changed in (B, head] (`compare_dir_structure`); a change that keeps an entry's identities is no conflict, and, as
      in FSFS, the first change of a file inside a branch, which takes a fresh copy identity, counts;
   5. otherwise the work is accepted: the new version is the head with the work's nodes, node by node, as FSFS's tree
      merge takes each entry changed on one side alone from that side.

   An accept answers `commit-info` (the new revision, its `svn:date` and `svn:author`, and post-commit's words if it
   failed); a conflict answers FSFS's own `E160024` "Conflict at '<path>'", which the client reports as out of date. No
   identity accept: the client records each node it committed as created at the new revision, so accepting an identical
   change on top of someone else's would leave the client's `svn:entry:committed-rev` naming a revision in which the
   server holds no change of that node, and `svnserve` would have refused it. *Raised with A-497's owner:* §4.17.1
   items 2 and 5 state Subversion's commit as §4.16's verdict over whole-file operations, whose second pass accepts an
   identical change and which knows neither rule 3 nor rule 4 nor a directory's subtree-wide last change; this section
   states the exact rule, and §4.17.1 needs only to point here.
4. **Locks at the verdict.** Before it accepts, the merge task reads the lock table for every node the work changes,
   deletes or moves away. A modified path meets its own lock. A path the work adds, deletes or replaces meets every
   lock at or beneath it, as FSFS's `verify_locks` checks: a lock kept through its file's deletion can stand beneath a
   path added later. A lock held by another principal is `E160039`, checked first. A lock whose token the commit did
   not present is `E160037`, wherever in the commit the token was presented. A commit with no principal that meets a
   lock is `E160034`. The first lock that fails answers, in the order FSFS's `verify_locks` meets them: the changed
   paths in Subversion's path order, a path's children right after it, so `/t/a/b` before `/t/a-b` (A-617). An accept
   releases every presented lock whose token and owner match, paths it did not change
   among them, unless the client asked to keep them. The check and the release are in the verdict's one step on the
   owner, so no lock changes between them (A-602).
5. **What the version records.** The revision's changed-path rows as the drive declared them (add; delete; replace, a
   delete and an add of one path in one drive; modify; text changed when `apply-textdelta` came; properties changed;
   mergeinfo changed; the copy source), the transaction's name, and the initial revision properties: `svn:author` the
   authenticated principal's name (never the client's word), `svn:log` and the client's other properties from the commit
   (`commit-revprops`, or the transaction's properties over HTTP), and `svn:date` the merge record's time, as §4.17.1
   item 3 rules for every object the server makes. They are one content object named by the version's increment, so the
   version and its Subversion record are one durable step, and every holder recomputes the index from them.
6. **After.** post-commit runs and only observes (item 9).
7. **A transaction's life.** Over ra_svn the work lives with its connection: `abort-edit`, a refused drive or a
   connection that ends releases it. Over HTTP a transaction outlives requests: DELETE, its MERGE or its idle bound
   (the table) releases it, and a request naming a released one is answered `E160007`, no such transaction.

*4. Reads.* They run on any shard holding a replica of the green (A-273, A-465), never on the merge task's turn.
- **update, switch, status `-u`, diff, checkout and export** (the reporter): the client reports its working copy
  (`set-path`, `link-path`, `delete-path`, each with a revision, `start-empty` and a depth), and the server drives its
  editor from that state to the target revision. A subtree reported at R and wanted at T whose history list has no
  entry in (R, T] is skipped whole, as FSFS skips equal node-revision ids. Otherwise the change index (A-264) names
  exactly the paths changed in (R, T] beneath it, walked in the editor's depth-first order. A changed file goes out as
  an svndiff from its text at R to its text at T made from the two extent lists: an extent both share is a source copy,
  an extent only T has is new data. Windows keep the format's limits (at most 102,400 bytes of source view and of
  target, source views never sliding backward), and a shared run outside the window's admissible source view goes out
  as new data. Checksums come from the node rows, entry properties (`svn:entry:committed-rev`, `committed-date`,
  `last-author`, `uuid`, `lock-token`) from the node rows, the revision-property table and the lock table. A path the
  principal may not read goes out as `absent-file` or `absent-dir` when the client announced `absent-entries`, and is
  left out otherwise.
- **checkout** is a report of "start-empty at T" on its root: every node is added, and each file's text goes out as
  new-data windows read in place from its chunks (§4.17.1 "Objects": the file's bytes are the content; nothing is
  copied into a buffer to be sent).
- **log**: per path, the history list gives revisions newest first, crossing copies unless `strict-node` is set; the
  revision rows give changed paths; the revision-property table the properties. Each revision is shown at the
  principal's access level (notes §7: none; partial, `svn:date` and `svn:author` with the readable changed paths only;
  full). `include-merged-revisions` reads the mergeinfo changes the revision's rows name.
- **blame** (`get-file-revs`): the file's history across copies, and for each revision its properties, its property
  changes and its text's svndiff from the previous revision's text, made from the extent lists as above. The client
  computes the blame.
- `get-locations`, `get-location-segments` and `get-deleted-rev` read the history lists and copy sources; `get-file`,
  `get-dir`, `stat`, `check-path`, `list` and `get-iprops` (each ancestor's property list) read the node rows;
  `rev-prop`, `rev-proplist` and `get-latest-rev` the revision tables; `get-dated-rev` is a binary search over the
  revisions' `svn:date`, as `svn_repos_dated_revision` searches (`rev_hunt.c`).
- `replay` and `replay-range` (svnsync, svnrdump) drive the editor with one revision's changes from its rows and the
  deltas above.
- `get-mergeinfo` (item 8).

*5. The wire.* Every connection is a task on a shard of slates' own runtime (D-9, R6); nothing blocks a shard.
- **ra_svn.** The item codec (grammar in notes §2; built, A-531) parses bytes in whatever pieces they arrive, resuming
  where it stopped, with every length checked before a byte is held, against bounds the caller derives and the codec
  never fixes: the bytes an item may take (the connection's memory share, the table; a string's declared length is
  checked against it at its `:`), the longest word (the longest a stock 1.14 parser accepts, 24, since no peer can send
  a 1.14 server a longer one; the protocol text's 31 is older), the deepest list (the deepest prototype the server
  reads), and the item count (the bytes bound over the two bytes the smallest item takes, and the memory a parsed item
  costs); a number is at most 2^64 - 1, refused exactly past it.
  The greeting is `svnserve`'s, version 2 with the capabilities `edit-pipeline`, `accepts-svndiff2`, `absent-entries`,
  `commit-revprops`, `depth`, `log-revprops`, `atomic-revprops`, `partial-replay`, `inherited-props`,
  `ephemeral-txnprops`, `file-revs-reverse` and `list`, without
  `svndiff1`: a sender uses zlib only for a peer that announced `svndiff1` (`marshal.c`, notes §2), so slates never
  receives it and never needs zlib, and it answers clients older than 1.10 in version 0. `mergeinfo` is announced in
  `repos-info`. An editor drive follows the protocol's early-error rule: an error is written as soon as it is known,
  on a send that never blocks the task, and the rest of the drive is read and dropped until `abort-edit`.
- **svn+ssh.** sshd starts `svnserve -t` as the logged-in user; slates installs that command as one of its own (a CLI
  verb under the name `svnserve`), which speaks ra_svn on its standard input and output and relays to the daemon
  through its client channel, and the server takes the SSH login as the principal (the `EXTERNAL` mechanism).
- **HTTP.** HTTPv2 for clients from 1.7 (notes §3): OPTIONS with the `SVN-*` headers and stubs; GET with
  `X-SVN-VR-Base` answered as an svndiff; PROPFIND and PROPPATCH; the REPORTs; POST to open a transaction; PUT, MKCOL,
  COPY and DELETE against it with `X-SVN-Version-Name` for the out-of-date test; MERGE; LOCK and UNLOCK. DeltaV's
  version-1 resources for older clients follow it as their own piece. HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive and pipelining; XML
  bodies parsed with every cap checked before anything is held, as A-464's listing parser does; TLS through rustls over
  aws-lc-rs, the workspace's one cryptographic library. Responses use svndiff 2 for a client that lists it in
  `Accept-Encoding`, else 0; slates never advertises `svndiff1`, so no client sends it in a PUT (notes §3).
- **svndiff** (built here, `slates-svn`): versions 0 and 2 (version 1 is refused, never having been offered).
  Decoding makes every refusal Subversion's decoder makes (notes §4: the header; views and sections past their caps;
  overflowing sums; a source view sliding backward, judged as Subversion judges it, only for a window with a source
  view, against the previous window whatever its view; each instruction decodable, nonzero, inside the target, the
  source and the new data, a target copy starting before the position; the target filled and the new data used exactly;
  a compressed section's length, limit and result), and one it does not: an integer encoded past 64 bits, which
  Subversion's decoder truncates. The encoder writes minimal integers and the short length form, and refuses a window
  the decoder would refuse. The reference applier, byte by byte with a target copy's overlap repeating, is the oracle.

*6. Revision properties.* A table on the repository's owner, by revision. A commit's values are recorded with its
version (item 3.5). A change (`change-rev-prop`, `change-rev-prop2`, or PROPPATCH on `!svn/rev/N`) is an entry of the
repository's register (§4.17.1), ordered with the versions and replicated with them: validated as a commit's are; gated
by pre-revprop-change, whose absence refuses every change (`E165006`, Subversion's default, notes §7); compared with
the old value the client sent (`atomic-revprops`, `E160049` on a difference); then applied; post-revprop-change
observes. A read sees the newest entry.

*7. Locks.* Each lock is an entry of the repository's register: the path, a token (`opaquelocktoken:` and a UUID, drawn
on the owner before the append so every holder replays the same token), the owner (the principal), a comment, and its
creation and expiry times. An expiry is judged when the lock is used, against the owner's clock, never in a holder's
replay. `lock` and `lock-many` (with stealing), `unlock` and `unlock-many` (with breaking), `get-lock` and `get-locks`
follow the locking specification (notes §7): only a file is locked; a current revision given with the request must not
be out of date (`E160042`); pre-lock, post-lock, pre-unlock and post-unlock run around each. A lock is data the verdict
reads, not a lock in the sense of §2 bans 1 and 10: nothing ever waits on it and no coordination call is made; a commit
that meets another principal's lock is refused at once. `svn:needs-lock` is a property whose meaning is the client's.

Stated with A-602, beyond Subversion's own rules:
- **An expiry, once judged, is recorded.** FSFS removes an expired lock it meets under its write lock. Here the guard
  that meets one records its removal: a lock request replaces it, an unlock answers `E160041` and removes it, and an
  accepted commit removes every expired lock its check met. So the judgment stands on every holder whatever its
  clock says.
- **A refused commit records nothing.** FSFS removes the expired locks its walk met before the refusing one, in a hash
  table's order, which leaves which it removed unspecified. Here none is removed, and the next use judges each again.
- **The table's room is the owner's**, derived from its shard's room (item 12). A lock request whose paths could take
  the table past it first lets go of every expired lock. A new lock past the room is then refused `E160000`, which is
  the closest error Subversion has.
- **A comment or a token is the whole string the client sent.** C stops at a NUL; here a comment holding one is
  `E130004` and a token `E160037`.
- **Release in the verdict's step.** `svnserve` releases a commit's locks after the commit; here release is in the
  verdict's step (item 3.4).

*8. Mergeinfo and merges.* `svn:mergeinfo` is a property whose value must parse (notes §7). `get-mergeinfo` answers it
explicit (the node's own), inherited (the nearest ancestor's, each source path extended by the relative path, its
non-inheritable ranges dropped, `svn_mergeinfo.h`) or nearest-ancestor, and with descendants finds the nodes with
mergeinfo beneath a path by the per-directory counts, never entering a subtree that holds none. `svn merge` is the
client's: it asks for mergeinfo, logs with merged revisions, location segments and diffs, merges text in its working
copy and commits the result as any commit. The server never merges file contents (§2 ban 11).

*Branches, tags, stacks, rebases and reviews* (what §4.17.1 leaves to this section).
- A branch or a tag is a directory made by a copy of any path at any revision; Subversion has no other kind. Policy
  protects a path prefix (`/trunk`, `/tags/**`) as §4.17.1's policy protects a green's name pattern: who may commit
  under it, whether a directory under `/tags` may change after the revision that made it, what evidence a commit under
  it needs.
- The client has no stacked changes and no rebase: `svn update` merges the repository's changes into local edits, in
  the client. On the server a stack is a chain of held commits (below), and a rebase of a held commit maps its
  node-exclusive operations through the revisions since its base: a path changed meanwhile is a conflict naming it;
  otherwise the work moves to the new base.
- A review request takes one of two forms. *The branch form* is Subversion's own practice: the change lives on a branch
  made by a copy, the review record names the branch's path and its revisions, and landing it is the author's
  `svn merge` and commit, or a server-side merge when every path the branch changed is unchanged on the target since the
  branch was made: one revision on the target that holds the branch's texts and properties for those paths and the
  `svn:mergeinfo` the client's merge would record, judged node-exclusively, so a path changed on the target is a
  conflict naming it. *The held form* is review before commit: under a path whose policy requires review, a commit is
  held as a work instead of being submitted, and is answered as a pre-commit refusal (`E165001`) whose words name the
  review; approving it submits the work under item 3 and makes the revision, and the author's next `svn update` meets
  its own edits as the incoming change. A held commit built on another is a work over a work (§4.17.1).

*9. Hooks* (§4.17.1's hook rule). start-commit (the repository's path, the user, the client's capabilities joined by
`:`, the transaction), pre-commit (path, transaction; on standard input `LOCK-TOKENS:` and a `path|token` line per
presented token), post-commit (path, revision, transaction), pre- and post-revprop-change (path, revision, author,
property, action `A`, `M` or `D`; the new value, or the old one, on standard input) and the four lock hooks, each with
`hooks.c`'s arguments (notes §7). A hook's standard input is a pipe, never Subversion's temporary file (R1). A stock
hook reads the transaction with `svnlook -t TXN REPOS`, so slates installs its own `svnlook` (the subcommands hooks use:
`author`, `cat`, `changed`, `date`, `diff`, `dirs-changed`, `filesize`, `history`, `info`, `lock`, `log`, `propget`,
`proplist`, `tree`, `uuid`, `youngest`) first on the hook's `PATH`, answering from the work or the revision through the
client channel and never from a disk, and REPOS is the repository's configured directory. A refusing pre-hook's
standard error is the client's message (`E165001`); post-commit's becomes `commit-info`'s `post-commit-err`.

*10. Who may do what.* The transport proves the principal (§4.13): over `svn://` the SASL mechanisms `ANONYMOUS`,
`CRAM-MD5` and, through the tunnel, `EXTERNAL`; over `https://` a TLS client certificate or Basic credentials inside
TLS; over `svn+ssh://` the SSH login. `CRAM-MD5` needs the server to hold the shared secret or its keyed-MD5
"contexts", which "must both be protected" alike (RFC 2195 §2 and §4), so slates holds the contexts, never the
cleartext, as §4.15's S3 credentials are held: in RAM on the owner and the anchor, never on disk. The exchange is
`svnserve`'s (`serve.c` `construct_server_baton`, `auth`; `cram.c`; built, A-599), stricter on three inputs no stock
client sends: a CRAM-MD5 response holding a NUL is malformed, as `cram.c` finds every such response; an `EXTERNAL`
token is compared whole, where `strcmp` stops at a NUL; and a list deeper than the handshake's prototypes is refused at
its third level, where `svnserve` reads 64. `svn://` carries no
encryption, so it is served on loopback alone unless the repository's policy names another interface; `svn+ssh://` and
`https://` are the encrypted routes. Path rules are Subversion's authorization file (notes §7: per-repository and global
sections, globs from 1.10, users, `@groups`, `&aliases`, `$anonymous`, `$authenticated`, `*`, `~`; 1.14.1's combining of
global and per-repository rules), compiled per file identity into a path trie per principal and consulted for every
path the server sends (absent entries, log's access levels, `get-file`, `get-dir`) and every path a commit changes
(write on the path and its parent; recursive write to delete or replace a directory; recursive read of a copy source).
A principal with read on the whole repository and no rule beneath meets one comparison and no per-path check.

> **Status (2026-11-19, A-606).** Built: authorization (`slates-svn`'s `authz`, piece 10). The rules file, and a
> separate groups file, are read as `svn_config__parse_stream` reads them and their sections, groups, aliases and
> entries taken as `authz_parse.c` takes them; groups are resolved without being expanded. Each principal's rules in a
> repository are compiled into Subversion's tree of path segments and walked with its precedence: the deepest matching
> level, then the rule defined last; a later `**` eclipsing the rules beneath it; 1.14.1's choice between a global and
> a repository rule for one path. Answers are read, write or none at a path, beneath it (`svn_authz_recursive`) and
> anywhere (`svn_authz__get_global_rights`). A principal whose rules all give one access is answered by one
> comparison, counted. Every refusal is typed, with its line and its Subversion error. Held to Subversion's own authz
> tests (`authz-test.c` with `authz.rules` and `authz.groups`, and the authz tests of `repos-test.c`), APR's
> `apr_fnmatch` table, the documentation's files, and a naive oracle over generated rule sets. Where 1.14.x's code
> departs from its own documentation, the documentation is followed and each case is a named test:
> - the root has no segments (`lookup` walks `/` as one empty segment, so `[:glob:/*]` decides the root there);
> - a suffix pattern leaves the segment as it was for the other rules of its level (`lookup` reverses it in place);
> - `[//x]` is refused (Subversion takes it for the root).
>
> Owed: the server's questions (piece 7: every path sent, every path a commit changes); the file read from the
> repository (`authz-db` as a `^/` URL) and compiled per file identity; `svnserve`'s `force-username-case`; and
> `mod_authz_svn`'s questions with HTTP (piece 13).

*11. Large files.* No file is held whole anywhere on the path: a commit applies one window at a time, taking the MD5 and
the content identity as it writes; a read streams windows from chunks; content is chunked and deduplicated (§4.11, D-6),
the large-file class by content-defined chunking, so a copy or a branch of a large file costs a reference. Locks and
`svn:needs-lock` serve files no one can merge.

*12. Every tunable, learned* (§4.17.1's rule: an estimator, its inputs, when it updates, its derived bounds, and a first
value from the first request's own inputs, never a literal).

| Tunable | Estimator | Inputs | Updates | Bounds | First value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compress a window (svndiff 2) or send it stored | the argmin of predicted time: stored bytes over the connection's delivery rate, against LZ4's time plus compressed bytes over that rate | the connection's delivered bytes a second; the shard's LZ4 bytes a second; the compression ratio of the repository's content class (D-17) | every window sent | a choice of two; stored for a peer that did not announce svndiff 2 | the first window is compressed and timed, which gives its own ratio and rate |
| The cap on a path, a property value or a log message | the connection's share of the shard's admittable memory, divided among the connections served now (A-188's share) | the shard's room (§4.2); live connections | every connection that opens or closes | the shard's admittable room; refused `E210009` past it | the share when the connection is accepted |
| Socket send and receive buffers | the connection's bandwidth-delay product | its measured round trip and delivery rate | every window | the connection's memory share | the first exchange's round trip and rate |
| A hook's deadline | §4.17.1's (A-597): the tail of that hook's own finished runs by RFC 6298's estimator (`LearnedWait`), with Karn's rule for runs cut short and the bound doubled after a run cut at it; a regression on the commit's size (paths and bytes), the prediction plus the largest residual seen, takes its place only once measurement shows a hook's run time following the size | that hook's own past runs | every run | never past the requesting client's own liveness (its connection) | none on a hook's first run but the client's liveness |
| An idle HTTP transaction's bound | the longest gap seen between two requests of one transaction that went on to commit | the gaps of committed transactions | every commit over HTTP | the shard's room for held works: past it the longest-idle goes first | none until a transaction has committed; the room alone |
| The index's table size and tail seal (§4.17.1's rule, A-581) | derived, never learned: a table is one window of the content plane (D-6's chunk, from the base page), and the tail seals its full tables once its rows no longer fit one | the store's window | each insert | the window; a row too long for a table of its own refused `RowPastWindow` | the window |
| The index's merge point (§4.17.1's rule, A-581) | for each `j`, merge the newest `j` runs only this index holds once the time lookups spent on the visits that merge saves reaches its predicted time (rent or buy, one problem for each `j`; the largest due `j`) | each lookup's visits, counted by the index; the times the owner measured for its lookups, inserts and merges | each timed batch and each merge | the shard's room, which every table, the tail and the fences are charged against | before any merge, what building the tail cost a row |
| The wire-form cache (§4.17.1 "Objects" item 2: svndiff windows of hot versions) | keep what saves the most time per byte held: re-use rate times the encode time saved, over bytes | hits and encode times | every hit | the shard's room | empty |

The window size is not a tunable: windows are as large as the format allows (102,400 bytes), which every stock decoder
accepts and which costs the fewest headers. Long reads (log, checkout, blame, replay) are sliced under the shard's
per-iteration budget (§4.3), and the replicas that serve them are A-273's and A-473's.

*13. The order-of-magnitude target* (§4.17.1's method, for Subversion; main measures and records it).
- **Competitors.** `svnserve` 1.14 in threads mode with its default cache, and Apache httpd 2.4 with `mod_dav_svn` 1.14
  at its defaults, each over FSFS format 8 made by `svnadmin create`, warm, on the same machine: the repository on tmpfs
  as their best case, and on the SSD as deployed.
- **Dataset.** The load tests' kernel tree (Linux v7.4-rc1, `6628e7d4`) as a Subversion repository: (a) the tree
  imported as one revision under `/trunk`; (b) the first-parent history from v7.3 to v7.4-rc1 replayed one commit a
  revision (author, date and message as revision properties) by a recorded command that uses only `git` and `svn`, then
  `svnadmin dump`; (c) a branch copied from `/trunk` with 10 and 100 revisions on it. The one dump is loaded by
  `svnadmin load` into FSFS and by slates' load verb into slates, and each repository's own `svnadmin dump` must equal
  the dump byte for byte before any timing (the fidelity gate).
- **Operations,** from the stock client: checkout of `/trunk` at the head; update after 1, 10 and 100 revisions; commit
  of 1 file and of 100 files, and 100 commits in a row; `log -v` of the last 1,000 revisions and `log` of one path;
  `blame` of a file with a long history (`MAINTAINERS`); merge of the branch into a trunk working copy and its commit;
  and update and commit with 1, 8 and 64 clients at once.
- **Measures.** Wall time at the client; the server's CPU time and peak memory; throughput under concurrency; and the
  server's own share: the time from a request's first byte to its answer's last, taken at a recording relay between the
  client and each server, since a checkout's time is mostly the client's own (its files and its SQLite working copy). A
  commit's comparison names its durability: FSFS answers after its writes reach its disk; slates answers after the
  merge record commits at f+1 holders in RAM (§4.16), at f = 0 the anchor's RAM.
- **Where the gain should come from** (each a hypothesis until measured): no delta chain to rebuild a text (FSFS stores
  skip-deltas; slates holds the text's extents); an update that visits only the changed paths (the change index) rather
  than comparing directories level by level; deltas made from extent lists rather than by comparing bytes; a
  checkout's bytes written from their chunks; no lock file and no disk write on a commit's path; and requests from many
  clients served by every shard at once, where `svnserve` gives each connection its own process or thread. "An order of
  magnitude" is claimed per operation only where it was measured.

*14. The interop proof* (main runs it).
- **Subversion's own suite** (`subversion/tests/cmdline`, notes §9) at 1.14.x, every script run with
  `--url=svn://127.0.0.1:<port>` and again with `--url=http://127.0.0.1:<port>` against a slates server whose root is
  the suite's `svn-test-work` directory, with `--bin` naming a directory that holds the stock 1.14 client tools and
  slates' own `svnadmin` and `svnlook` (the administration verbs, a piece below). The suite makes each repository with
  `svnadmin create PATH` and writes `PATH/conf` and `PATH/hooks` itself, so slates' `svnadmin create` makes the
  repository's green and its directory skeleton, the latter written under the launcher's write policy (a landing, R10),
  and the server reads `conf/` and `hooks/` there, read-only. Expected failures are the tests of FSFS's own files and
  maintenance (`svnadmin hotcopy`, `pack`, `upgrade`, `recover`, `svnfsfs`, the format tests), on a reviewed list that
  only shrinks; every other test must pass.
- **A differential run:** the same scripted session of stock-client operations against `svnserve` and against slates,
  over one dump, the clients' working copies then compared whole (bytes, `svn status`, `svn info -R`,
  `svn proplist -R -v`) and both repositories' `svnadmin dump` compared.

*Failure matrix* (beyond §4.17.1's). A client gone during a drive: the work is released and nothing commits (over HTTP,
at its idle bound). The owner lost after `close-edit`: the submit retries by the increment's identity (§4.16); a client
that heard nothing finds its revision by `svn update`, which brings its own edits back as the incoming change. A text or
base checksum that differs: `E200014`, the work released. A malformed item or svndiff: refused with its code (`E210004`,
`E185000` to `E185005`, `E200046`) and the connection closed, as `svnserve` closes it. A hook past its deadline:
refused, naming the hook. A lock in the way: refused as item 3.4 says. A holder whose recomputed index differs: as
§4.16, fatal and loud.

*Refusals*, each in Subversion's words and number (derived from `svn_error_codes.h`, notes §6): out of date at the drive
`E160028`; conflict at the verdict `E160024`; no such revision `E160006`; no such transaction `E160007`; a lock held by
another `E160039`, a bad token `E160037`, already locked `E160035`, no such lock `E160040`, out of date for a lock
`E160042`, an expired lock `E160041`, no principal `E160034`, a directory to lock `E160017`, a path to lock the head
lacks `E160013`, a lock comment XML cannot carry `E130004`, a negative expiry `E200004`; a revision property's old value
differs `E160049`; hook refused `E165001`; revision properties not enabled `E165006`; post-commit failed `E165007`; not
authorized `E170001`; unreadable `E220001`, unwritable `E220004`; checksum `E200014`; property value `E125005`;
mergeinfo `E200020`; malformed `E210004`; unknown command `E210001`; request too large `E210009`; svndiff `E185000` to
`E185005`; LZ4 `E200046`. §4.17.1's typed refusals map onto these.

*Worked example.* Repository `kernel` is at revision 1,200. Carol's working copy mixes revisions: `/trunk` at 1,190 and
`/trunk/kernel/sched/core.c` at 1,195. She commits an edit of `core.c`: the work's base B is 1,200, and `core.c`'s
created revision at 1,200 is 1,195, so it is not out of date. During her drive Dan's commit lands as 1,201, changing
`/trunk/kernel/fork.c`. At Carol's `close-edit` the verdict reads (1,200, 1,201]: `core.c` did not change there, and no
directory above it changed its properties, so she is accepted as revision 1,202, whose `core.c` references her base's
extents wherever her delta copied them. Eve then commits `core.c` from base 1,195: its created revision at B = 1,202 is
1,202, so `open-file` answers `E160028`, "File '/trunk/kernel/sched/core.c' is out of date"; she updates and commits
again, as revision 1,203. Frank finishes a merge by setting `svn:mergeinfo` on `/trunk`. His working copy is at 1,203,
so B is 1,203 and `/trunk` is up to date (its created revision, which counts everything beneath it, is 1,203). During
his drive Gina's commit lands as 1,204, changing `/trunk/README` in place: `/trunk`'s names and their identities are
unchanged, so Frank is accepted as 1,205; had Gina added a file directly under `/trunk`, rule 4 would answer `E160024`
"Conflict at '/trunk'". Failure: the owner dies after Frank's `close-edit` and before any answer. If the merge record
had committed at f+1 holders, the takeover's successor serves revision 1,205 (§4.16), and Frank, whose client reported
the lost connection, finds his own change in it at his next `svn update`; if it had not, nothing committed, and he
commits again.

*Laptop degenerate.* One node: the repository's green, its index and its register on one partition, every hook a local
process, every arrow an in-process call; the code is the fleet's (R8).

*Integration points.* §4.17.1 (everything above builds on it), §4.16 (node-exclusive operations, `Copy`, works), §4.8
(the repository's register: revision properties and locks as its entries), §4.10 (placement and replication of the
green, the index recomputed), §4.11 (content identity, chunks, content-defined chunking), §4.12 (the CLI's `svnadmin`,
`svnlook` and `svnserve` verbs), §4.13 (principals, secrets), §4.14 (a counter per verb and per refusal code), §4.15
(the repository's directory read, read-only; a dump loaded from a disk read as a base; an export by landing), Part 6
(the suites).

*Pieces that follow* (in order, each one piece with its own tests, after §4.17.1's shared pieces it needs).
1. The svndiff codec (built here).
2. The ra_svn item codec (built, A-531): the resumable parser and the writer, with the protocol's examples as golden
   vectors and hostile input (a word too long, nesting too deep, a number past 64 bits, a string past its cap, a stream
   cut anywhere).
3. The engine's node-exclusive operations (built, A-542) and `Copy` that shares a subtree by reference (its maps built,
   A-542 part 1: `graft` of the source's `subtree` at the destination in every map; the engine's operation built,
   A-586: one record a copy, read by the latest copy above a key, one identity entry a copy; owed from it: the
   checkpoint, the rebase, a copy from a changed source's older version, and the replace with history).
4. The Subversion index, with its oracle: a naive filesystem replaying the same revisions must give equal created
   revisions, histories, relations and mergeinfo counts (built, A-553; its tables as content and their fold are the
   object store's, §4.17.1 shared piece 3).
5. The commit rule as a pure function, with its oracle: a transcription of FSFS's `merge()` over generated histories
   must give the same accept or conflict, and the same conflicting path (built, A-592, with the drive's out-of-date
   test, the lock table's check after the merge, and `verify_locks` in the oracle).
6. The administration verbs: `svnadmin create`, `load` and `dump` (the dump format; its codec built, A-593),
   `setrevprop`, `setlog`, `info`, `uuid`, `youngest`; the dump round trip is their gate.
7. The ra_svn server: the greeting and authentication (built, A-599: `handshake`, held to stock 1.15.0's sessions);
   the plain reads; the reporter (update, switch, status, diff, checkout); commit; log, locations, segments, file
   revisions, deleted revision, replay; revision properties.
8. Locks (built, A-602: the table, the guards of its verbs and the verdict's check, with FSFS's lock rules as its
   oracle). 9. Mergeinfo queries (built, A-605; the eligible and merged revisions owed with piece 7's segments and
   log). 10. Authorization (built, A-606: the file, its evaluation, a naive oracle). 11. Hooks and `svnlook`.
   12. The `svn+ssh` tunnel command.
13. HTTPv2 with TLS and its authentication, then DeltaV version 1. Its first part, the bodies as codecs, is built
    (A-609); of its second, `list-report`, `file-revs-report`, PROPPATCH, LOCK's request and the update-report drive are
    built (A-627), and the replay drive, LOCK's answer and LOCK and UNLOCK onto the lock table are owed.
14. Review: held commits, the branch form's server-side merge, stacks of held commits.

Then main runs the suite over both URLs, the differential run and the order-of-magnitude measurements.

## Part 5 — Phased implementation plan

Rules for every phase: nothing is stubbed and left; each phase ends with running, tested code
and a recorded benchmark baseline; every constant lands with its derivation table; the gap ledger
(`docs/wip/GAPS.md`, created in Phase 0) is updated in the same change as any acceptance or
tripwire. Acceptance criteria are numbered AC-<phase>.<n>; test cases T-<phase>.<n>. "Expect"
lines state the observable outcome an implementer must see.

### Phase 0 — Foundations: workspace, machine profile, memory, runtime, wire

**Goal.** A workspace that enforces the rules by construction, plus the four crates everything
else stands on, each measured on the reference machines.

**In scope.** Cargo workspace with the lint wall; `slates-machine` (profile), `slates-mem`
(slabs, handles, arenas, buddy allocator, segmented arrays, locking), `slates-rt` (executor,
timing wheel, rings, drivers for io_uring/epoll, kqueue, IOCP, and the simulation driver),
`slates-wire` (framing, canonical bodies, schema hash, credits); the release matrix and CI from
Appendix B; the gap ledger.

**Out of scope.** Volumes, bridges, database, SDKs.

**Ordered tasks.**
1. Create the workspace from Appendix B (toolchain pin, edition 2024, lints, `panic = "abort"`,
   CI with fmt/clippy/test, the nine-target release workflow as a dry run). Add the structural
   test that walks the dependency graph and fails if `std::fs`, `std::net`, `Arc`, or `Rc` appear
   outside the allow-listed crates. Add the grep-based literal check that fails on numeric
   literals in tuning positions (a `#[derived("formula", anchors)]`-style attribute or a
   `derived!` macro marks the allowed ones).
2. `slates-machine`: implement every query and microbenchmark of Part 4.1 with Kalibera-Jones
   stopping; produce the profile struct and its JSON export with derivations; cache it in a
   segment keyed by host identity (Linux memfd, macOS shm_open, Windows section); re-measure on
   power-state events.
3. `slates-mem`: `Handle<T>`, `Slab<T>`, `ChunkArena` with buddy allocation over locked regions,
   segmented arrays, per-shard free lists with message-passing frees, the RAM-only locking
   sequence with reporting, and the pre-fault batch scheduler; huge-page requests per region
   after pre-fault where the profile shows benefit.
4. `slates-rt`: task arena, `RawWaker` encoding, intrusive run queue, hierarchical timing wheel,
   per-shard inbound rings, cross-shard wake kicks, the three OS drivers with a common completion
   seam, and the simulation driver (seeded time, randomness, sockets, rings); structured
   cancellation (parent-tracked children); the bounded-work watchdog counter.
5. `slates-wire`: the 32-byte header, canonical `#[derive(Wire)]` bodies with schema hash,
   append-only evolution checks (trybuild), credit windows, CRC32C, golden vectors, hostile-input
   tests.
6. Audit compio's request path for `Arc` and driver seams (one page in the gap ledger); confirm
   `LocalWaker` status on 1.98.
7. Record the Phase 0 benchmark baseline (ring round trip per core pair, task spawn/wake cost,
   timer accuracy, slab alloc/free, buddy alloc/free, frame encode/decode) and set the ratchets.

**Worked examples.**
- On the author's laptop, `slates profile` prints page 16384, line 128, 18 cores (6 Super, 12
  Performance), lock capacity 108.8 GiB, wake p99 (measured), memcpy curve, hash 
  and codec throughput, and the derived shard count (5 = 6 Super cores minus one control) with
  the formula beside each number.
- A cross-shard wake: shard 2 wakes a task on shard 4 by writing `(slot, generation)` into shard
  4's ring from shard 2 and writing shard 4's eventfd; shard 4's driver returns from `io_uring_enter`,
  drains the ring, and runs the task; the whole path is one cache-line transfer plus one syscall.
- Failure example: a container refuses `io_uring_setup`; the driver probe records it and the
  shard runs on epoll; the profile marks `io_uring = unavailable(EPERM)`.

**Acceptance criteria.**
- AC-0.1 The structural test fails the build when a forbidden symbol is introduced in a core
  crate (catches: disk fall-through and `Arc` creep).
- AC-0.2 Every numeric literal in a tuning position carries a derivation attribute, verified by
  the literal check (catches: magic numbers).
- AC-0.3 `slates profile` completes within the wall-time bound on all nine targets and reports
  intervals for every measurement (catches: unmeasured constants; slow boots).
- AC-0.4 Slab and buddy allocation never call the system allocator after start (allocation
  counter feature proves zero calls on the hot path) (catches: hidden allocation).
- AC-0.5 Locked-bytes reporting matches what the OS reports (`/proc/self/status` VmLck, macOS
  wired count, Windows working set) within one page class (catches: pretend locking).
- AC-0.6 The executor runs the same task program on all three OS drivers and the simulation
  driver with identical observable results (catches: driver divergence).
- AC-0.7 loom passes on the ring and handle cores; Miri passes on `mem`, `rt`, `wire` unit tests
  (catches: memory-model and UB bugs).
- AC-0.8 Frame decode refuses every hostile corpus input without panic or over-allocation
  (catches: parser DoS).
- AC-0.9 The N=1 differential harness exists and passes for the runtime's public API (catches:
  mode creep).

**Test cases.**
- T-0.1 (unit) Allocate every slot of a slab, free them in random order, reallocate; expect no
  duplicate handles, every stale handle refused.
- T-0.2 (property) Buddy allocator: random alloc/free sequences; expect no overlap, coalescing
  restores the full region, fragmentation bounded by the buddy guarantee.
- T-0.3 (concurrency, loom) SPSC and MPSC rings under all interleavings of one producer and one
  consumer (and two producers); expect FIFO, no lost or duplicated slots.
- T-0.4 (error) Lock capacity exhausted mid-boot; expect the profile records the capacity, the
  diagnostic control surface starts, and volume admission refuses `LockCapacityExceeded`;
  no successful claim is backed by unlocked memory and no panic occurs.
- T-0.5 (edge) A 32-bit target with a 2 GB address space; expect region reservation caps derived
  from `ullAvailVirtual`, and a request above it refused with `BudgetExceeded`.
- T-0.6 (benchmark) Ring round trip per core pair; expect numbers within the profile's interval
  and a ratchet recorded.
- T-0.7 (fault) Kill a shard thread's driver mid-wait (simulation driver injects); expect the
  shard's tasks are cancelled with terminal completions, no leak, counters incremented.
- T-0.8 (hostile) Frames with `length = u32::MAX`, truncated headers, bit flips; expect typed
  refusals.
- T-0.9 (timer) 10,000 timers with random deadlines; expect firing order and accuracy within one
  wheel tick derived from the profile.

**Exit criteria.** All AC pass on Linux and macOS in CI and on Windows nightly; baselines
recorded; the gap ledger lists the compio audit result.

**Risks and fallbacks.** io_uring differences across kernels (probe and fall back); Windows
IOCP driver complexity (keep the seam small; WinFsp integration comes in Phase 4).

**A-9 required acceptance and regression cases (open; 2026-09-05).**

| Acceptance | Test | Required behavior | Do X, expect Y |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC-0.10 | T-0.10 | All allocator and temporary-operation costs are bounded and charged to usable locked capacity. | Exercise fragmented/non-power-of-two regions, exhausted locks and saturated bulk/parse work; expect honest admission refusals and bounded control progress, with no uncharged growth. |
| AC-0.11 | T-0.11 | Health absence and trace identity retain their declared meaning. | Drop a producer and overflow telemetry; expect typed unknown/degraded freshness and loss markers, while request, trace/span and caused-by identities stay distinct. |

### Phase 1 — Volume core (single node, in-process API)

**Goal.** The copy-on-write filesystem as a library: namespace, inodes, content, snapshots,
clones, accounting, journal, tested against a model and the host filesystem, with no bridge and
no server.

**In scope.** `slates-vfs`: directories (small/indexed), inode slab, extent lists, open extents,
seal, birth-epoch CoW with deadlists, snapshots, clones, destroy, quotas (bounded and dynamic),
name-equivalence policies, hard links, symlinks, rename semantics, the per-volume op log and
journal; the executable model and the differential harness; the base plane of §4.15 (`slates-base`:
read-only host access, listings, witnesses, whiteouts, redirects, copy-up, drift with watcher
hints behind the driver seam) and the landing engine (`slates-land`: manifest, verdict, per-OS
write primitives, ramp, syncs, advance, resume), driven through the in-process API against
RAM-backed target directories (tmpfs, an APFS RAM disk, an NTFS RAM VHD).

**Out of scope.** Hashing/dedup (Phase 7 wires the identity pass; Phase 1 leaves `identity =
None`), bridges, IPC, database replication.

**Ordered tasks.**
1. Data model and the volume state machine of Part 4.4/4.5 on one shard's arenas.
2. Directory operations with the adaptive representation and the measured cut-over (start with
   the profile-derived value; record it).
3. Inode slab, monotonic inode numbers, generation on reuse, POSIX attributes with ns timestamps.
4. Content: open extents, page-multiple growth, CoW at chunk granularity, holes, seal into fixed
   chunks (CDC stub disabled until Phase 7).
5. Snapshots and clones by birth epoch with deadlists; destroy as cooperative slices.
6. Accounting: `referenced_bytes`, `unique_bytes`, bounded reservations, dynamic growth policy
   fed by a pluggable pressure source (the real one lands with the daemon in Phase 2).
7. The op log and journal with the bounded retention formula.
8. The executable model (a map with POSIX rules and declared nondeterminism) and proptest
   state-machine tests; the differential harness against tmpfs (Linux) with the equivalence policy.
9. Baselines: create/lookup/readdir/write/read/rename/snapshot/clone/destroy costs versus tree
   size; write amplification per mutation.
10. `slates-base`: the base directory descriptor; listings through the bulk calls with the
    fingerprint-keyed cache; merged and opaque directories; `Body::Base` with descriptors;
    whiteouts and redirects; copy-up with the witness and the small/large class split; the racy
    rule; drift checks on read, on `status`, and on hints; watchers (inotify, FSEvents,
    `ReadDirectoryChangesW`) behind the driver seam with the overflow-to-recheck path; `read_base`,
    `rewitness`, `pin`. The crate's lint wall forbids every write-capable syscall.
11. `slates-land`: the manifest and its canonical hash; the pure verdict function with an
    exhaustive table test; the landing state machine; the per-OS entry writer (temporary, swap,
    verify, undo; reflink where probed; sparse and preallocation; timestamps); ordering by class;
    the online concurrency ramp; sync strategies; advance; crash resume and sibling sweep; the
    target-contained per-entry writer; the exchange fallback with the
    reported window. Grants and leases are stubbed by an in-process record in this phase and
    become database records in Phase 2.
12. The landing oracle: an executable model of (disk, overlay, witnesses) whose verdicts and
    post-landing disk state the implementation must match on every generated history, including
    outsider edits injected between validation and write.
13. Baselines: listing cost per directory size per OS; copy-up cost per class; drift check
    cost; landing throughput versus `cp -r` and `git checkout` of the same delta; verify and swap
    cost per entry.
14. Declared operations (D-27): the journal records `{at, len, prev_version}`; per-inode version
    counters; the SDK-level `edit` operation in the in-process API; the deriver (composition by
    interval algebra into the fixed-layer ops document) with its determinism test; the interval
    algebra as a pure module with property tests against a reference applier.

**Worked examples.**
- Snapshot of a volume with 2 million files: one record; the next write to `src/lib.rs` copies
  the nodes from the root to `src` (say 4 nodes, ≈ 3 KiB) and allocates one open extent; the
  snapshot still reads the old bytes.
- Clone then destroy the clone after writing 100 files: destroy walks the clone's deadlist
  (100 chunks and ≈ 400 nodes), releases them, and leaves the origin untouched; `unique_bytes`
  of the origin is unchanged.
- Failure: `link("a", "d/")` where `d` is a directory returns `EPERM`; `rename("d", "d/e")`
  returns `EINVAL`; a bounded volume at its quota refuses a 1-byte append with `ENOSPC` and the
  file's size is unchanged.
- Overlay: create over a 300k-file tree on tmpfs returns in one call with no walk; a lookup of
  `src/lib.rs` loads one listing (one bulk call); a write copies it up (one `fstat`, one read,
  one BLAKE3); an outsider then overwrites the file on tmpfs; `status` lists it as drifted; the
  landing verdict for it is `Conflict(ModifyModify)` and nothing is written.
- Landing: a scratch volume with 1,000 files lands into an empty tmpfs directory; the plan has
  1,000 creates; the writer ramps in-flight depth until throughput plateaus; every file is
  exchanged into place after its data sync; the report lists 1,000 `Written`; a second landing of
  the same snapshot plans 1,000 `Skip` (identical by hash) and writes nothing.

**Acceptance criteria.**
- AC-1.1 The model-based suite passes 10^6 generated operations per CI run with shrinking enabled
  (catches: semantic drift).
- AC-1.2 The differential suite against tmpfs agrees on every abstract state under the reviewed
  policy (catches: POSIX divergence).
- AC-1.3 Snapshot and clone are O(1): measured cost is independent of tree size across 10^3,
  10^5, 10^6 files (catches: hidden copies).
- AC-1.4 Write amplification per mutation is bounded by depth × fanout entries and by one page
  multiple of content (catches: whole-file or whole-directory copies).
- AC-1.5 Memory per file and per directory entry stays within the derived budget (a formula from
  struct sizes and the cut-over), verified on the scale trees (catches: bloat).
- AC-1.6 Inode numbers are never reused within a volume and survive snapshot/clone/re-open of the
  same volume (catches: build-cache breakage). Across a daemon takeover too since A-150 (2026-10-22): a number is handed
  out only under a published reservation, so a successor starts past every number a client may hold.
- AC-1.7 `referenced_bytes` and `unique_bytes` equal the model's exact values after every
  operation (catches: accounting drift).
- AC-1.8 Destroy of a 10^6-file volume runs in bounded slices without stalling other volumes on
  the shard beyond the per-iteration budget (catches: bounded-work violations).
- AC-1.9 Create over a base directory costs one directory open regardless of tree size (10^3,
  10^5, 10^6 entries); memory after create is independent of tree size (catches: hidden walks).
- AC-1.10 The overlay holds exactly the diverged entries: after any generated history, the set
  of overlay entries equals the model's diverged set, and every diverged file carries a witness
  equal to the disk state at its copy-up (catches: over- or under-materialization).
- AC-1.11 Drift is never absorbed: after any outsider edit to a witnessed entry, the agent's
  reads return the agent's bytes and `status` reports the drift; reads of unpinned large-class
  extents after an in-place overwrite return `BaseDrift`, never torn bytes (catches: silent
  adoption; torn reads).
- AC-1.12 The verdict function is pure and matches the table in §4.15 for every generated
  (witness, disk, overlay) triple, including all conflict classes; no landing writes while any
  entry's verdict is `Conflict` (catches: merge creep).
- AC-1.13 Landing atomicity: under the oracle with outsider edits injected at every step and
  crashes injected at every instruction, every entry on disk is old or new, every `Written`
  entry's hash equals the overlay's, every compare-and-swap loss is undone and reported, and a
  re-run is idempotent (catches: torn files; silent overwrites; non-idempotent resume).
- AC-1.14 Landing cost is proportional to the delta: plan time and disk bytes written are
  independent of the base tree size across 10^3 to 10^6 entries (catches: tree walks at
  landing).
- AC-1.15 The deriver is deterministic and exact: the same journal yields a byte-identical ops
  document on every platform, and applying the net op set to the base version reproduces the
  sealed post-state byte for byte on every generated history (catches: split-brain derivation;
  lossy composition).

**Test cases.**
- T-1.1 (property) Rename cycles, rename over non-empty directories, rename of a file over a
  directory; expect the POSIX errno the model predicts and no state change on failure.
- T-1.2 (edge) Names that fold equal under the volume's policy (`README` vs `readme` on a
  case-fold volume; precomposed vs decomposed `é`); expect `EEXIST` and a single entry.
- T-1.3 (edge) Sparse file: write at offset 10 GiB in a dynamic volume; expect one window charged at
  the buddy block it takes (one page for a one-byte write; at most a chunk — A-16), holes read as
  zeros, `referenced_bytes` = `allocated_bytes` = one page.
- T-1.4 (edge) Truncate to a non-page boundary then extend; expect the tail page zero-filled
  (the clang zero-fill reliance).
- T-1.5 (error) Dynamic volume growth denied by the pressure source; expect `ENOSPC` with a
  pressure event and no partial write.
- T-1.6 (concurrency, shuttle) Two simulated agents interleaving clone-and-write on the same
  base; expect each clone's view independent and the base unchanged.
- T-1.7 (benchmark) 190k-file create burst (a `cargo build` trace replay); expect throughput and
  amplification within ratchets.
- T-1.8 (robustness) Directory with 61,067 entries; expect lookup within the derived bound and
  readdir order canonical.
- T-1.9 (fault) Simulated allocator refusal during a rename; expect the rename fails atomically
  (both names intact) and the refusal is typed.
- T-1.10 (property, base) Random overlay histories over a random base tree with random outsider
  edits; expect the oracle's diverged set, witnesses, drift list and verdicts match after every
  step.
- T-1.11 (edge, base) A base file modified in place within the timestamp granularity without a
  size change (the racy case); expect the racy rule re-hashes and the drift is detected.
- T-1.12 (edge, base) `rm -r` of a 40k-entry base directory then recreate two files inside;
  expect one opaque whiteout, two overlay entries, a merged listing that shows exactly two
  entries, and a landing plan with one recursive removal and two creates.
- T-1.13 (fault, base) Watcher overflow injected (`IN_Q_OVERFLOW`, `MustScanSubDirs`, zero-byte
  `ReadDirectoryChangesW`); expect a full re-check, no missed drift, `status` reporting
  `watcher: overflowed`.
- T-1.14 (concurrency, landing) An outsider thread rewriting target files at random while a
  landing runs; expect every loss detected at the swap, exchanged back, reported
  `Conflict(TargetInUse)`, no outsider write lost, no agent write silently applied over one.
- T-1.15 (fault, landing) Crash at every instruction of the writer under the simulation driver
  and with real `kill -9` on tmpfs; expect old-or-new per entry, a hidden sibling sweep on
  resume, and an idempotent re-run.
- T-1.16 (edge, landing) Target filesystem without exchange (a mocked `EINVAL`/`ENOTSUP`);
  expect the fallback path, the window measured and written into the outcome, and the Degraded
  cell reported.
- T-1.17 (benchmark, landing) Land a 10k-entry delta into a 10^6-entry tree; expect time
  proportional to 10k and within the ratchet versus `cp -r` of the same delta; the ramp's
  settled depth recorded.
- T-1.18 (property, deriver) Random sequences of overwrites, extends, truncates, inserts,
  deletes, renames, creates and unlinks on random files; expect net-apply ≡ raw replay, every
  `src` valid, and composition order-insensitive where the algebra says it is.
- T-1.19 (edge, deriver) A whole-file rewrite by truncate-and-write and by write-and-rename;
  expect both compose to one delete of the base length plus one insert, with identical ops
  documents.

**Exit criteria.** AC-1.* pass; baselines recorded; the equivalence policy document reviewed.

**A-9 required acceptance and regression cases (open; 2026-09-05).**

| Acceptance | Test | Required behavior | Do X, expect Y |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC-1.16 | T-1.20 | Clone preserves delta, witnesses and complete base reference; coverage never overstates immutability. | Clone an overlay with edited and untouched files, mutate the live source, and read both; expect isolated edited bytes, accurate untouched state and explicit live coverage. Capture a quiesced source, change it later, and expect stable complete bytes; refuse atomic capture of an uncontrolled mutable source. |
| AC-1.17 | T-1.21 | Base metadata mutations and digest caches obey the same witness rules as content writes. | Run lookup-before-readdir, chmod, truncate, rename, links, xattrs, unlink-open and watcher overflow against a host oracle; expect correct metadata/bytes, stable witnessed entries, and no stale clean digest. |

### Phase 2 — Local server, database, IPC, anchor process, Rust client

**Goal.** Agents on one machine provision volumes through the ring protocol in under 50 µs
(client spinning), with the catalog, leases, accounting, and op logs surviving daemon crashes
through the anchor process.

**In scope.** `slates-db` partitions (indexes, log, completion records, leases, timing wheel, grants, landing
leases, landing records, the audit log), `slates-ipc` (rendezvous per OS, rings, wake words, completion fds), `slates-server`
(admission, lifecycle verbs, the control shard), the anchor process (`slates anchor`), the Rust
client, `slates` CLI verbs, the `slates.status` data.

**Out of scope.** Bridges (volumes are reachable only through the client API), replication, MCP,
SDKs.

**Ordered tasks.**
1. The anchor: create/attach the shared segment; hold the profile and the op logs; supervise the
   daemon (start, restart on exit, hand back held fds later in Phase 3/4).
2. Partition data model and indexes; the op log in the segment; replay on start; snapshots of
   partition state into the segment on a cadence derived from measured replay throughput and the
   recovery budget (since A-243: once the log since the last snapshot has taken the budget's replay work, as each
   commit's append and apply measure it, and is at least the last snapshot's size).
3. Rendezvous per OS; ring regions; wake words; the completion fd; peer authentication.
4. The lifecycle verbs of Part 4.4 through the server, with completion records (exactly-once),
   leases with epochs, attachments (client form only), quotas fed by the real pressure sources.
5. The Rust client with spin-then-park and request ids; the CLI.
6. The provisioning histogram benchmark and the ratchet; crash-recovery tests.
7. The register protocol at f=0: every head, chain version, lease and catalog entry is a
   register written by its owner under a host epoch; the configuration oracle is the local
   partition with one voter; `await placed(region)` returns after the local append; `placed`
   and `mirror_age` exist in every reply from the first version so the fleet parts of Phase 8
   change no interface.
8. Grants and landings through the server: `GrantRecord`, `LandingLease`, `LandingRecord`, the
   audit log in the segment; the control-channel-only grant kind (refused on the ring); `slates
   land`, `slates grant`, `slates grant --watch`, `slates grants`, `slates audit`; the
   request-then-await flow with deadlines; session grants tied to the client session.

**Worked examples.**
- `slates volume create scratch --bounded 4GiB` from the CLI: rendezvous (one-time), request in
  a slot, reply in a slot; the CLI prints the id and the path it will have once a bridge exists.
- Daemon killed with `kill -9` while 200 clients create volumes: the anchor restarts it; the
  op log replays; clients' retries return their original completion records; no volume is
  duplicated or lost.
- Failure: a client from another uid connects to the rendezvous; `SO_PEERCRED` (or the DACL)
  refuses; nothing is created.

**Acceptance criteria.**
- AC-2.1 Provisioning p99 from the Rust client, spinning, under the ratcheted floor (initially
  50 µs) on the reference Linux and macOS machines; the parked form measured and reported
  separately (catches: hot-path regressions).
- AC-2.2 Zero filesystem entries created by the daemon, anchor, or client during the suite under
  the write tracer, except the documented one-time mount point (Phase 4) and entries inside a
  granted landing target during that landing (catches: hermeticity leaks).
- AC-2.3 Crash-recovery: after `kill -9` at any instruction (simulation and real), every
  acknowledged operation is present and no unacknowledged one is partially present; retried
  requests return original results (catches: durability and idempotency bugs).
- AC-2.4 Leases: a write with a stale epoch is refused and never applied; lease expiry and
  takeover follow the derived term (catches: fencing bugs).
- AC-2.5 The N=1 differential test passes for every verb against the simulated cluster stub
  (catches: modes).
- AC-2.6 Admission: 10,000 concurrent clients on the reference machine stay within the task
  arena and ring budgets; refusals are typed (catches: unbounded growth).
- AC-2.7 Recovery time within the derived budget for a catalog of 10^4 volumes and 10^6 log
  records (catches: slow replay).
- AC-2.8 No grant can be created through the ring or MCP channels: the kind is refused with a
  typed error and an audit counter; a grant created through the CLI is bound to the manifest
  hash and a landing whose plan changed is refused with `GrantMismatch` (catches: agents granting
  themselves; stale approvals).
- AC-2.9 One holder per target: two sessions landing into one directory serialize on the lease;
  a superseded holder's next write is refused at the chokepoint by generation (catches: disk
  split-brain).
- AC-2.10 The audit log replays after `kill -9` with every grant, manifest and outcome present
  and nothing partial (catches: lost accountability).

**Test cases.**
- T-2.1 (error) Create with a name that exists; expect `AlreadyExists` and the original's id in
  the reply.
- T-2.2 (edge) Two clients race to take an expired lease; expect exactly one succeeds with
  epoch+1 and the other gets `LeaseHeld`.
- T-2.3 (fault) Kill the client mid-request; expect the daemon reclaims the region and the
  lease after expiry; other clients unaffected.
- T-2.4 (fault) Kill the daemon between log append and reply; expect the client's retry returns
  the completion record built during replay.
- T-2.5 (chaos) Clock jump on the host; expect leases use monotonic time and no lease is
  wrongly expired or extended.
- T-2.6 (benchmark) The provisioning histogram with 1, 8, 64 concurrent clients; expect the p99
  ratchet holds and the p999 is reported.
- T-2.7 (security) Cross-uid connect; expect refusal and an audit counter.
- T-2.8 (edge, Windows) Client parks; expect the Event wakes it and the socket signals the event
  loop; measure the wake cost and record it.
- T-2.9 (hermeticity) The tracer run, now asserting zero writes outside granted targets.
- T-2.10 (security) An SDK client and an MCP client each attempt to create a grant; expect typed
  refusals and the audit counter.
- T-2.11 (edge) A session grant, then the session ends mid-landing; expect the current entry
  finishes, no further entry starts, `Partial` with the reason, and the grant `Expired`.
- T-2.12 (fault) Kill the daemon between `LandingValidated` and the first write; expect on
  restart the landing is `Aborted` with zero entries written, the lease released, and the grant
  still `Issued` for a re-run bound to the same manifest.

**Exit criteria.** AC-2.* pass on Linux and macOS in CI, Windows nightly; the ratchet recorded.

**A-9 required acceptance and regression cases (open; 2026-09-05).**

| Acceptance | Test | Required behavior | Do X, expect Y |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC-2.11 | T-2.13 | An admitted bounded claim remains spendable despite all competing allocations. | Reserve a claim, then race other shards, dynamic volumes, snapshots, caches, copy-up and pressure for capacity; expect competitors to refuse before stealing it, and every within-entitlement write to succeed. Repeat through resize, cancellation, destroy and restart. |
| AC-2.12 | T-2.14 | Daemon restart preserves acknowledged content and its atomic completion. | Write bytes and metadata, snapshot/clone an overlay, kill the daemon at publication boundaries and retry the same request; expect identical bytes, witnesses, roots, claims and result ids, or an explicit incomplete-recovery refusal where no acknowledgement was promised. |
| AC-2.13 | T-2.15 | Distinct consumers sharing a uid cannot use each other's VFS or grant rights. | Enroll two consumers through a trusted harness, forge/replay ids and channel labels, revoke one and reconnect; expect refusal before any protected lookup, allocation or mutation. A workload invoking the CLI cannot mint grant authority. |

### Phase 3 — Linux bridge (FUSE) and the launcher

**Goal.** Ordinary Linux programs see volumes at `<root>/<volume>` and at chosen paths through
`slates exec`, with kernel caching and explicit invalidation, and pass the conformance and
workload suites.

**In scope.** `slates-bridge-fuse` (own driver, `FUSE_INIT` negotiation, per-shard channels,
io_uring queues on 6.14+, invalidations, splice/registered buffers), root-mount establishment and
fd handoff through the anchor, `slates exec`, the conformance and workload harnesses on Linux.

**Ordered tasks.**
1. The driver: request framing, reply writes, notifications; one channel per mount on its owner shard (A-62);
   the io_uring command path with fallback; negotiation of splice, readdirplus,
   `EXPLICIT_INVAL_DATA`, `EXPIRE_ONLY`, `INC_EPOCH` (writeback cache refused: the kernel would own
   sizes and times a volume changes through other attachments, §4.6 "Linux", 2026-09-19).
2. Mount establishment with the new mount API when permitted, `fusermount3` otherwise; the fd
   held by the anchor; restart handoff.
3. The `Bridge` trait implementation in the core; inode `(no, gen)`; invalidation on every
   mutation visible through another attachment; `fsync` semantics; `statfs`.
4. `slates exec`: user+mount namespace, recursive-private root, bind mount, exec; AppArmor
   detection and the exact remedy message; slates' AppArmor profile for a restricted host, used only when the caller
   asks (A-370).
5. Conformance: pjdfstest, fsx, fsstress in CI; xfstests generic and LTP nightly; the reviewed
   expected-failure list.
