  4, and the step stranded to its 25-minute timeout), green under the fix with the whole WinFsp CLI suite (diag-slabs-9,
  run 42163139554: 14 passed on each runner), red again with the check removed (diag-slabs-10, run 42163139568).
- **Built on macOS (2026-11-06).** Four tests over real NFS mounts on jupiter, no daemon killed under a mount: a base and
  a landing target on the daemon's own mount refused `OwnMount`; after an orderly restart (`SIGTERM`: the daemon drains,
  the anchor holds the mount and starts a successor), a base on the kept mount refused `OwnMount`; and a base the kept
  mount came to cover is not rebuilt, its log naming the daemon's own mount. 4 passed in 31.6 s. With the successor's
  learning removed, the restart test got "no reply within 1000000000 ns" and the reacquire never finished; the two
  bind-time tests still passed.
- **The kept mounts on Linux.** A daemon stopped in order ends its FUSE connections (its mount then answers `ENOTCONN`,
  run 42167684399), so a Linux mount is kept only across a killed daemon, whose device the anchor holds (A-61); the
  Linux tests kill it, and macOS's stop in order. On ubuntu-latest (diag-slabs-13, run 42170240376) the five A-227 tests
  passed, and the CLI's whole Linux flow, 85 passed. With the kept mounts learned after the reacquire, the old order
  (diag-slabs-14, run 42170240677), `a_base_a_kept_mount_covers_is_not_reacquired_through_it` failed: the successor never
  finished reacquiring the covered base.
- **The kept mounts on Windows.** `a_base_a_held_drive_covers_is_not_reacquired_through_it` points a directory symbolic
  link under a base at the drive (`mklink /J` refuses a WinFsp drive: "Local volumes are required") and kills the
  daemon. Under the fix (diag-slabs-13, run 42170240452) every A-227 assertion held on both runners: the successor
  served the held drive, the covered volume was not rebuilt, and the drive still listed `project`; with the drive
  detached by its attachment, the whole WinFsp CLI suite passed, 15 on each runner (diag-slabs-15, run 42171800738).
  With the held volume
  recorded at its adoption, the old order (diag-slabs-14, run 42170240630), no successor served after the kill on either
  runner.

### A-198 — A WinFsp mount outlives its daemon: the anchor holds the volume's control handle, the drive's link and the mount's ledger, and the next daemon serves the held volume (accepted 2026-11-01, Step 9 of the VFS and DAX plan; built and measured 2026-11-02)
Applied in the same change to: GAPS (gap 2 of the platform inventory). The build applies it to §4.6 "Windows",
`docs/wip/platforms.md`, `crates/anchor`, `crates/server` and `crates/bridge-winfsp`, each in its own change.
Source checks and remaining proof obligations are recorded in `docs/wip/research/winfsp-takeover.md` (2026-11-02).
The source-derived design and its corrections are realized by the implementation below; the live measurements
and failed-then-passing oracles distinguish those results from the initial source inferences.
- **Hold transport built and proven (2026-11-02, Step 9.2).** `crates/anchor/src/handles.rs` defines the bounded,
  CRC32C-checked channel messages and inherited-handle handoff; aliases of a handle or entry id are refused before
  adoption. `held_windows.rs` implements the message-mode pipe and duplication; `supervise_windows.rs` integrates it
  with the shared supervisor. A successor receives a fresh channel and explicitly listed inheritable duplicates,
  while a pending acknowledgement remains bounded to one. The child joins the anchor's kill-on-close job at creation.
  - `tests/handles_windows.rs` drives a held event across a sender's death, an excluded inheritable event, the
    no-hold lifetime contrast, and the real supervisor: the child publishes its record only after acknowledgement,
    and the successor uses the same live event and reads that record. Each child has a distinct successful exit code
    so libtest selecting zero tests cannot pass the fixture; the parent owns and reaps each process.
  - `cargo +1.98.1 test -p slates-anchor --test handles_windows -- --nocapture --test-threads=1`: three passed on
    jupiter. On CI, three passed in each of three runs on x86_64 and arm64, with native clippy, documentation and the
    full anchor/IPC regression suites green (run 41399665112). A separate diagnostic tree discards the duplicates
    instead of holding them: the unchanged positive oracle fails on both architectures, `left: 0, right: 1`
    (run 41399840638). The diagnostic mutation is absent from the implementation.
  - The initial fixture selected `sender` where libtest required `sender_role`; the failure and sibling sweep are in
    `docs/bugs/2026-11-02-a-windows-hold-test-ran-no-child-test.md`. Integrity and aliasing tests failed against the
    unchecked draft before the channel checks were added.
  - **Applied in the same change to:** §4.6's status, GAPS gap 2, the source record, `crates/anchor` (formats,
    transport, Windows spawn, supervision and process tests), `crates/ipc` (shared environment builder, explicit
    spawn API, cross-process duplication, process polling and message-mode pipe pair), `crates/cli` (open the Windows
    hold before the first spawn), CI's Windows test steps, and `unsafe-budget.toml` (anchor 6 → 10, IPC 105 → 109;
    the old six-site job-assignment implementation is replaced by IPC's existing creation-time job attribute).
  - The live WinFsp hold is now wired (Step 9.3 below). The transport tests alone establish no live-mount,
    in-flight-request or second-daemon criterion.
- **What a daemon sends never ends supervision (2026-11-05, audit step 3).** A message the hold channel refuses, or a
  reply it cannot write, is counted in `Supervisor::handle_refusals` and dropped, and the holdings are untouched, as the
  Unix device hold counts its refusals. `Supervisor::step` can no longer fail on the channel. A message of no bytes is a
  short message, not "nothing waited"; a long one is malformed, and its remainder is refused too. The log says each
  distinct refusal once (`handles::RefusalLog`, a table of 64), since logging on a change of kind still grows without
  bound when two kinds alternate. Held by `crates/anchor/tests/handles_windows.rs`: 20 bad messages between two real
  holds give 0 anchor exits, 20 refusals, 2 log lines and both holds inherited live, on CI's Windows x86_64 and arm64
  (run 41976042550; red on the old sources in run 41974533851). A live drive is not sent bad messages, since only the
  daemon reaches the channel. Record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-03-one-malformed-hold-message-ended-the-windows-anchor.md`.
- **Live mount wiring (2026-11-02, Step 9.3).** The server awaits the anchor's `Held` before committing a WinFsp
  attachment, and its normal detach awaits `Released` before deleting the file system. The mount owns its temporary
  DOS link directly. A successor retains a matching attachment, substitutes the inherited control handle and volume
  name into fresh DLL dispatcher state, and resolves per-open generation/slot tokens from the held RAM ledger.
  A recovered bridge handle uses a slot index outside the bounded local store; zero is a valid fresh handle, and the
  collision oracle against the real store failed before the draft zero sentinel was replaced.
  The ledger's header is immutable; recovery derives its new epoch from valid live frames without rewriting shared
  memory. A torn frame is quarantined, never recycled. The first round covers the ledger's live home names.
  - Initial diagnostics run 41415062574 lost zero drives of twenty on each Windows architecture. The final oracle
    also requires the old handle's first read after adoption, the mapped view following a fresh SDK write before an
    uncached read, and a counted successful read through a restored context. Diagnostics [41422186336](https://github.com/hyper-light/slates/actions/runs/41422186336) lost zero drives of twenty on both architectures; every iteration required a restored-context read, and the last daemon counted four. All five live WinFsp tests, 36 bridge tests, 32 active anchor tests, native clippy and Windows docs passed on each runner. With only the control-handle hold omitted, the unchanged oracle failed its first post-kill read with Windows error 995 on both runners ([41422382101](https://github.com/hyper-light/slates/actions/runs/41422382101)); the still-held link alone left a dangling drive letter.
  - `crates/bridge-winfsp/src/opens.rs` has five recovery/reuse/torn-frame tests; the complete native bridge suite
    passes 36 tests. The recovery-with-no-writes test failed against the draft header rewrite before it was removed.
    `held.rs` checks lengths before decoding the handoff and refuses malformed drive names, flags and UTF-16.
  - **Step 9.3's remaining obligations, completed by Step 9.4 below:** in-flight request settlement with safe hint
    handling; close/cleanup publication; foreign and second-daemon refusal; retained kernel names for the A-158 set,
    including aliases; and acknowledged normal-shutdown hold release. The twenty-kill history alone did not
    establish these. Cleanup now checks the open's identity before deleting a current name; a replacement is refused
    stale and preserved. Its real-bridge regression first deleted the replacement and now preserves it.
  - **Applied in the same change to:** §4.6's status, GAPS gap 2, `platforms.md`, the bug record, `crates/anchor`
    (release acknowledgement), `crates/ipc` (clear inherited flags), `crates/mem` (unnamed held sections),
    `crates/bridge-winfsp` (owned link, held dispatcher and open ledger), `crates/server` (hold, recovery and serving),
    `crates/cli/tests/winfsp.rs` (the live oracle), and `unsafe-budget.toml` (bridge 112 → 104, IPC 109 → 110,
    server 6 → 7; net six fewer sites).
- **What it answers.** A WinFsp mount dies with its daemon (A-177: "the file system is the dead process's own, so
  recovery ends its record"), where a FUSE mount is held by the anchor (A-61). WinFsp deletes a volume at the cleanup
  of its control file object, that is when the last handle to it closes (`src/sys/volume.c`, `FspVolumeDeleteNoLock`,
  which asserts `IRP_MJ_CLEANUP`), and the daemon held the only handle. The drive letter goes the same way:
  `FspMountSet_Drive` (`src/dll/mount.c`) makes the `\??\X:` link a temporary object and keeps its handle, so the link
  dies with its last handle. WinFsp v2.1, the source read on 2026-11-01.
- **What the anchor holds.** Per WinFsp mount, three handles. The daemon sends their values on the hold channel; the
  anchor duplicates them out of its live child and acknowledges the hold before the attachment record commits.
  Windows does not attach handles to a channel message as Unix's `SCM_RIGHTS` does, so sending the values alone is not
  enough. The three handles are:
  1. the volume's control handle, which keeps the volume;
  2. the drive link's handle, which keeps the drive letter;
  3. the mount's ledger: an unnamed section backed by the paging file (nothing on disk, R1) that the daemon writes as it
     serves.

  A detach, a destroy or a stop releases all three before the file system is deleted, so a mount that ends still loses
  its volume and its drive at once. **Superseded by A-369 (2026-11-18):** two handles, the control handle and the
  ledger; the drive is a Mount Manager drive the volume keeps, so no link is held. **Corrected by A-206 (2026-11-04):** this sentence was not true of a release the
  anchor refused or did not answer.
- **The drive is the daemon's own.** The daemon defines the drive letter itself, as `FspMountSet_Drive` does: it calls
  `DefineDosDeviceW` with `DDD_RAW_TARGET_PATH`, opens the link with `DELETE`, makes it temporary and keeps its handle.
  It no longer calls `FspFileSystemSetMountPoint`, so the handle is the daemon's to duplicate. A successful mount
  releases its own link handle at teardown; the temporary link disappears when its final owner closes it. Only a
  partially failed construction removes its exact definition explicitly. Thus a dead or replaced daemon cannot
  remove the anchor-held drive. The DLL's `MountPoint` stays null, so deletion owns no drive definition.
  **Superseded by A-369 (2026-11-18):** the daemon asks WinFsp's driver for a Mount Manager drive on the volume
  (`FSP_FSCTL_MOUNTMGR`), which lives as long as the volume does, so a dead or replaced daemon still cannot remove the
  anchor-held drive, and Windows resolves its files' final paths, which it does for no drive `DefineDosDeviceW` made.
- **The next daemon serves the held volume.** It inherits the three handles and nothing else (A-183), with the held
  records naming each mount.
  - For each restored WinFsp attachment with a held volume, it calls `FspFileSystemCreate` with the mount's parameters.
    That call builds the file system and the DLL's dispatcher state, whose thread-local key is made there and nowhere
    else (`src/dll/fs.c`, `InitOnceExecuteOnce`).
  - It then closes the throwaway volume that call made, and puts the held handle and the held volume's name in the
    structure's public fields. `FSP_FILE_SYSTEM` is public, and WinFsp's header asserts its size (792 bytes on 64-bit,
    `winfsp.h`).
  - The owned receiver transacts on that handle, invoking the initialized DLL operation table for each checked
    request. The driver checks no caller process (`src/sys/volume.c`, `FspVolumeTransact`). The original DLL receive
    pool is replaced so recovery can settle a captured batch before any fresh receive.
  - A killed daemon cannot stop the volume first. The owned receiver never calls `FspFsctlStop0`; its owner joins
    it before closing this process's copies. The anchor's duplicate still owns the same control file object.
- **Each open's context survives.** Each open's context (`UserContext2`, kept per file object: `src/sys/create.c`,
  `FileDesc->UserContext2`) becomes a slot in the ledger, where it was a pointer into the daemon.
  - The slot holds the open's record: the bridge's handle, the inode and generation, and whether it is this process's
    purge open (A-190). A successor reads every record its predecessor left.
  - A request on an open from before the takeover names its file through its record. Reads and writes address files by
    identity (`slates_bridge_core::Bridge::read`), so the file is all they need. Its close releases the bridge's handle
    by the file's inode, which a successor does not hold in its store, so it gives back an open the recovery restored
    (A-152, A-148: `release_restored_open`).
  - The per-file-node word (`UserContext`) cannot carry the file. WinFsp shares a file node by name and keeps the first
    open's value (`src/sys/file.c`, `FspFileNodeOpen`, which inserts the node by its name and takes an existing one), so
    after another path replaced an open file a new open of its name would read the replaced file's inode.
  - A dead daemon's purge open keeps its mark, so a purge write queued at the kill is still dropped, never applied.
  - The ledger holds one slot per open the bridge allows (`MAX_OPEN_HANDLES`), with a typed refusal past it.
- **Requests in flight at the kill.**
  - Requests the kernel queued while no daemon served wait in WinFsp's pending queue, and the successor serves them.
  - Those the dead daemon had taken remain in the processing queue until a response names their hint
    (`FspIoqEndProcessingIrp`). **Source correction, 2026-11-02:** `driver.h` defines
    `FSP_IOQ_PROCESS_NO_CANCEL`; `ioq.c` sets their timestamp to infinity and excludes them from timeout removal.
    The earlier timeout claim was wrong. A request lost between transact and an operation guard can hang indefinitely.
  - A guard-only journal is therefore rejected. Request recovery must retain the receive buffer at the transact
    boundary and distinguish a response returned by a callback from one accepted by the driver. The live taken-read
    oracle failed first, then passed with the replacement receiver below; the twenty-kill history alone does not
    establish in-flight settlement.
  - Replaying an arbitrary saved hint is also unsafe: it is an IRP address, and another dispatcher can take a new
    request at that address after the first response completed. Missing hints being ignored (`FspVolumeFastTransact`,
    "BOGUS") does not solve address reuse. The replacement must prevent that ambiguity before replay, and settle
    cleanup and close effects once. Exact source and the test boundary are in `research/winfsp-takeover.md`.
  - **Replacement receiver (2026-11-02, Step 9.4).** One owned receive worker uses the public
    direct-output batch FSCTL, with its fixed receive buffer in the anchor-held unnamed ledger section. The driver
    copies into that output before placing an IRP in processing. Adoption waits for complete predecessor exit,
    including that process's own I/O completion. The DLL still supplies the operation table; its heap receive loop
    is replaced, not retained beside another path.
  - Responses are sent without receiving a new batch. The worker settles its entire captured batch before any new
    receive, and recovery does the same before normal serving. No second receiver can put a reused hint into
    processing meanwhile. A response saved before the driver accepted it is then safe to send again: the original
    IRP remains in processing, or a recycled address is merely pending and does not match.
  - Live diagnostics [41472709500](https://github.com/hyper-light/slates/actions/runs/41472709500) settle one counted
    captured read in 0.33 s on x86_64 (`windows-latest`) and 0.17 s on arm64 (`windows-11-arm`). The same tree loses
    zero drives of twenty on each architecture, with four restored-context reads in its final iteration. The run's
    conclusion is `cancelled`; both takeover jobs had finished these tests first. (Corrected 2026-11-03 by the audit
    of this step's record: the two times were given the wrong way round.) That partial result still exposed the
    renamed-view failures corrected below; the final untraced verification is 41484542209.
  - A complete saved response has a CRC32C and is recorded before sending. Without one, a buffer-bearing operation
    is refused STATUS_CANCELLED, never replayed through a dead process's buffer or token handle. Cleanup and close
    settle by checked open identity. Pending open contexts are tied to the still-outstanding request; a context never
    handed to the kernel is retired, while a saved successful open response is completed. Successful opens and closes
    publish their reference changes. Recovery reconciles the attachment's restored open counts with its live ledger
    contexts so a kill between ledger retirement and root publication cannot release a sibling open or pin an orphan.
    A saved successful rename is also replayable: the driver's completion uses its original kernel-owned name buffer,
    not an old user buffer. Before sending that result, the receiver updates one held context's kernel name per shard
    turn. Replaying the saved success resumes a partially completed name update after another death.
  - Intentional unmount still waits for the anchor's Released before stopping the volume and removing the drive.
    Dropping a worker closes its stop channel, waits for its current finite control transaction and joins, then closes
    only its own copies. The control wait is the API's minimum admitted TransactTimeout, 1000 ms; this is distinct
    from processing-request expiry, which is disabled. It never stops the anchor-held volume or removes a successfully
    acquired temporary drive link. The successor can resume the retained batch as after a kill.
- **Coherence at takeover.** The successor must tell Windows of changes the dead daemon never told it of. The held
  ledger records the original kernel name of every open, including each alias; it does not reconstruct that name
  from the file's current namespace home. Each slot has two generation-checked UTF-16 name versions with CRC32C,
  published one complete version at a time. The unnamed sparse section reserves the admitted open/path caps and
  commits touched ranges only. Recovery seeds one context per owner turn from these records.
  **Corrected by A-206 (2026-11-04):** a record's cap is the longest name the WinFsp driver passes, not 1,024 units.
  - Every WinFsp cache hangs off an open file node, including the Cache Manager's own file-object reference
    (`bridge-winfsp/src/notify.rs` and WinFsp's `FspFileNodeInvalidateCachesAndNotifyChangeByName`). The first round
    therefore notifies and purges every held kernel name, covering the A-158 set Windows can still cache. All aliases
    of one inode are covered. A current namespace walk cannot substitute for that set after an SDK rename.
  - A purge carries both that name and the file's stable identity. Its drive opens use a mount-specific restricting
    SID in a less privileged copy of the daemon's own token; the receiver checks the PID and marker before resolving
    the target by identity. Ordinary lookups still use the namespace, so an old removed name stays absent.
  - A bounded Begin/End channel is woken by an owned event even when Windows refuses an open before a callback.
    The receiver drains it while its overlapped control call is pending and before each callback. This replaces the
    callback-only drain that could block the publisher. A failed wake/wait is typed, and the control call is settled
    before any error can free its borrowed buffer. The callback-free oracle fails after 10 s when the event signal
    is omitted and passes with it (41480713447; 41480565373). The latter run still exposed a separate lost volume wake.
  - After each delivered round, including an empty one, the mount registers its waker at the delivered generation
    before parking. Its earlier ready check registered nothing; after an SDK rename with no open directory, an empty
    round otherwise left the next file write unheard until another kernel request. Stage trace 41482946787 records
    `names=1 records=0`, then the delayed write round only after the failed test's pathname lookup. The unchanged live
    rename oracle failed first; the final untraced verification is recorded below.
- **Final Step 9.4 verification (2026-11-02).** Diagnostics
  [41484542209](https://github.com/hyper-light/slates/actions/runs/41484542209), commit
  `a7e5bce5c4ec70c9773a434887cc66c9b865a90e`, pass without operation traces on x86_64 and arm64:
  - Nine live CLI tests each: zero lost drives of twenty; each original-handle read is counted and returns the
    successor's bytes; the original mapped view follows before an uncached read can refresh it. The final daemon
    counts four restored reads. The live and killed renamed-view cases pass with one and two completed purges/echoes
    respectively, with no refused or kept purge and the removed public name still absent.
  - One counted captured read settles in 0.15 s and 0.19 s respectively, alongside a successful fresh successor read.
    Its unchanged oracle first hung for 10.14 s per architecture (41437374883). All six new duplication/DACL/owner
    requests are denied; a second daemon is refused with Windows error 183, CLI exit 4, while its owner still serves.
  - All 54 native bridge tests, all 32 active anchor tests, native clippy and private Windows docs pass. The CLI
    histories take 41.51 s and 21.76 s. Mac formatting, workspace clippy, xtask and private workspace docs pass in
    92.15 s. The earlier no-control-hold red-check loses the drive on both architectures (41422382101).
  - The three native Windows CI lanes run the bridge recovery suite with the driver enabled and the live CLI history.
    Captured-batch, saved-response, torn-name, slot-reuse, private-path and reference-reconciliation oracles, plus
    the native token-copy oracle, remain beside the real-process cases.
  - **Applied in the same change to:** §4.6's status and A-190's private-open recognition, GAPS, platforms, the source
    record and bug records; `crates/bridge-winfsp` (receiver, capture, original names, private identity purge, lifecycle),
    `crates/server` (reference reconciliation, serving and volume-wake registration), `crates/vfs` (restored counts),
    `crates/mem` (unnamed sparse sections), `crates/ipc` (creation-time process descriptors), `crates/anchor` and
    `crates/cli` (holder confinement and process oracles), CI and the unsafe budget (bridge 104 → 130, IPC 110 → 113;
    the named Win32 FFI sites and the removed DLL receive/guard sites are listed at those definitions).
- **A second daemon is refused.**
  - A held handle passes only by inheritance, to the anchor's own next daemon.
  - Another unprivileged process could take it only by duplicating it out of the anchor or the daemon, which needs
    `PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE` on that process. So each sets its own security to refuse that right to every other process of
    the user, through an owner-rights entry as A-175's sections use. The anchor's existing child-process handle lets it
    duplicate out of that child; the child is given no process handle for duplicating into the anchor.
    The child's descriptor is applied by CreateProcessW before its first instruction; dedicated CLI holders protect
    themselves before acquiring held resources. Existing handles and an enabled debugger privilege are outside this
    new-open policy. Diagnostics 41432451084 and 41432477849 verify the same unprivileged probe with and without it
    on both architectures (the test disables privileges only on its own thread and checks restoration).
  - A second daemon on the instance is refused by the rendezvous's owner (A-176, A-178).
- **Tests** (Step 9.2 to 9.4; the live mount runs on CI's Windows runners only, since jupiter has no WinFsp):
  - the hold across real processes on Windows: duplicated in, inherited by the next daemon only;
  - the daemon killed 20 times under an open handle and a mapped view: the drive stays, each next read through the
    handle returns the file's bytes, and the view follows a change made after the takeover, on x86_64 and arm64;
  - a red-check with the volume handle not held, which loses the drive;
  - a request in flight at the kill, answered or refused typed;
  - a process that is not the anchor's child duplicating a held handle (refused), and a second daemon on the
    instance (refused).
- **Rejected.**
  - Answering in-flight requests by WinFsp's timeout alone: the minimum pending timeout is 60 s, but processing
    requests do not expire at all (`FSP_IOQ_PROCESS_NO_CANCEL`). This cannot settle a taken request or close.
  - The per-node word for the file (see above).
  - Rebuilding the successor's handle store from the ledger (`Slab::insert_at`): the bridge's release already settles a
    predecessor's handle by its file, as for FUSE, so a rebuilt store would only duplicate that accounting.

### A-199 — A client's reply stamps alternate by park, so a late confirmation is never lost (accepted 2026-11-04)

A-31's client learns a wake only when the daemon's wake call confirms a sleeper, and it said a confirmation that
lands after the woken client read the stamp is settled at its next wait. Under load it is not: the waker is
preempted between its wake and its confirmation while the woken client runs on, takes its reply, sends the next
request and arms its next park, which cleared the one stamp. The late confirmation then set a bare confirmed bit
there, so the following park's stamp was refused too. Replace the one stamp with two: the client's parks
alternate between them, the parked flag's value names the park's slot (1 for slot 0, 2 for slot 1; zero is not
parked, and any other armed value names slot 0, so a hostile client chooses only which of its own slots is
stamped), and the daemon confirms by an exchange on the exact stamp it wrote. One daemon serves a ring in order,
so the slot a park arms was last stamped by a reply call that returned before the reply the client took since.
An unconfirmed stamp is held in its slot until that slot is armed again, then given up. The async path arms slot
0 and times nothing. Rejected: a client-side sleep signal (a futex wait's zero return), which macOS's wait does
not give, and would make the two platforms learn by different rules.

Applied in the same change to: §4.7 (data model, wake strategy, status); `slates-ipc` (region layout version 3,
`REPLY_STAMP_SLOTS`, `PARKED_STAMP_SLOT_ZERO`/`ONE`, `ClientRegion::reply_stamp(slot)`, `ClientEnd::wait`'s park
and settle, `DaemonEnd::reply`'s stamp and confirmation) and `crates/ipc/tests/rings.rs`; GAPS. Evidence:
`docs/bugs/2026-11-04-a-late-wake-confirmation-cost-the-client-two-samples.md`. A client and a daemon of
different layout versions refuse each other by name; no consensus rule or capability changes.

### A-257 — A green's chain entry records what its verdict resolved, and recovery applies it (accepted and built 2026-11-08)

A checkpoint at the reachable floor (A-238) can pass the base of an entry left in the chain, and recovery, which judged
each entry again at its base, refused it and fenced the green. Holding the checkpoint below every retained base never
folds under steady concurrency; carrying the deltas down to it is not enough, since a verdict reads files' lengths and
bytes at the base. So the decision is recorded where it is made: the verdict at accept is the guard, the entry its
result, and recovery applies it (`crates/db/src/partition.rs`'s guard-then-apply). The merge record's inputs stay the
increment, so holders keep their independent judgement. Integrity at f = 0 between checkpoints is the entry's digest;
the head identity is compared at checkpoints, holder-bound versions and recorded heads.

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.16: its status ("Commit").
- GAPS: the load-test blockquote (W3's recovery).
- `crates/merge`: `chain_entry.rs` (new), `Green::submit_resolved`, `Green::apply_recorded`, `Checkpoint::head_check`
  (encoding version 2).
- `crates/server`: `verbs::submit`, `record_accepted`, `replay_green`, the takeover's chain; `merge_service::inputs_of`,
  `checkpoint_green_when`, `record_goes_to_holders`, `GreenFence::IdentityDiverged` (and `NotAccepted` removed).
- `crates/anchor`: `LAYOUT_VERSION` 6.
- Tests: `crates/merge/tests/chain_replay.rs` (new), `crates/server/tests/green_checkpoint.rs`.
- Bug record: `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-checkpoint-passed-a-retained-entrys-base-and-recovery-fenced-the-green.md`.

### A-252 — A request waiting for a version to commit is a typed durable state, so a resend after a restart never runs again (accepted and built 2026-11-08, fixtures' primary-kill rung; supervisor's two changes to the first cut)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.9: its status of 2026-11-08.
- GAPS: the load-test blockquote.
- `crates/wire/src/request.rs`: `Seen::Awaiting`, `ClientWindow::await_version`, `awaiting_entries`; `retained` counts a wait.
- `crates/db`: `Op::CompletionAwaiting` (appended), `AwaitingCompletion`, `ClientCompletions::awaiting` (appended).
- `crates/server`: `merge_service::stage_awaiting` (the `Accepted` arm, ahead of the append) and `serve_awaiting`; the
  `Seen::Awaiting` arms in `serve`, `run_forwarded` and `await_deferred_completion`.
- The tests: fixtures' restart test and the still-waiting and takeover cases (`fleet.rs`),
  `a_wait_and_its_transaction_are_one_durable_step` and the owed model's wait step (`model.rs`), the window's unit tests.
- **What was there.** At `f > 0` the wait for a version's commit was in memory, and the version's append and the work's
  reset were durable. A restart lost the wait, and a resend under its id ran again as a new version.
- **The rule.**
  - A request that ran and waits for a version is `Seen::Awaiting`, never `New`: answered that version once it has
    placed, else joined to the wait, and never run again.
  - The wait is logged in the transaction that appends the version, staged first, so the two are one durable step and a
    failure fails the accept.
  - It counts toward the client's bound and leaves when its completion replaces it or the client acknowledges it.
  - It is a type, not reply bytes, so no reply encoding can be mistaken for it, and recovery and snapshots carry it by
    type.
  - After a takeover the resend is refused retryable and nothing runs twice, but the version is not named. That falls
    short of §4.16's failure matrix (Masked after takeover) and is owed as A-255, not accepted here.
- **Measured.** The bug record (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-submit-resent-after-its-owner-restarted-was-applied-twice.md`):
  the rung's 109 to 4,261 oracle failures fall to 0 on every run that finished. 7 of 18 runs stalled on W3's checkpoint
  fence, which is independent of this rule (A-257).

### A-286 — Version 0 of a green over a base is made, shipped and seeded a slice at a time at `f > 0` (accepted and built 2026-11-17, g232)

§4.16 "Commit" names a version's inputs in its merge record and places them at `f + 1` before the record commits, and
"Apply on holders" recomputes the version from them. For a green over a base, version 0's inputs are its origin: every
byte of the base snapshot in the origin's canonical encoding. At `f > 0` the owner made them in one poll (the held
snapshot walked again, encoded and archived; A-217) at the green's creation and again on every pass of the record plane
until version 0 placed. A-244's shipment carried them whole in one message, and each holder restored, decoded and seeded
them in one poll. Over the whole Linux kernel (97,229 files, 1.67 GB) each of those is seconds of one shard's poll, past
the watchdog's verdict on a shard that holds its CPU that long (A-232), so the load test's one primary and two replicas
could not set the kernel up at all. No fleet test had a green over a base, so none of it had run.

Replace it, keeping A-244's one path:
- **Made once, a share at a time.** The owner makes version 0's inputs in a task of the green's shard: the held snapshot
  walked a unit at a time, its canonical bytes written a share at a time into an archive that cuts and hashes chunks as
  the bytes arrive, and the origin's identity hashed from the same bytes and checked against the one the green recorded.
  A taken-over green's recorded origin bytes are cut the same way. Version 0's record is enqueued once they are made, and
  nothing of the green ships before. The archive is kept until every candidate holds version 0.
- **Shipped in bounded parts.** A shipment carries the record, the offer of its inputs and at most a shipment's bound of
  the chunks its targets lack. The bound is what a holder verifies in one slice, half a step quantum at the measured
  BLAKE3 rate, and at least one chunk always goes. A target that cannot accept the record yet answers with what it holds
  of the inputs: a content acknowledgement bound to them when it holds them whole, else the content plane's missing set
  for the offer, asked again after the shipment's chunks. The owner keeps each target's missing set, ships each group of
  targets what it lacks, and nudges the record plane when an answer shows progress. An ordinary increment is far below
  the bound and still crosses whole in one exchange.
- **Seeded a share at a time.** A holder seeds its replica of version 0 from the held chunks, read one at a time, the
  origin decoded and the engine seeded a share at a time, and the head identity compared with the record's. The seed's
  first slice runs as the record arrives, so an origin that seeds within it is acknowledged in that exchange; a larger
  one goes on in a task, and every record of the green is answered with the content acknowledgement until it is done.
  A seed installs its replica only while the hold still holds the inputs: a tombstone or a takeover's reclaim forgets
  everything held for the green and drops its replica, and a seed past reading the hold that installed after that
  would keep a whole origin nothing removes.
- **Inputs chunked at the archive's largest chunk.** That is 1 MiB, the most any reader admits (AUD-29-13), where the host
  page made a kernel-sized origin 100,000 to 400,000 extents and a 6 to 23 MB manifest. At 1 MiB it is about 1,600
  extents and 90 KB, small enough to offer in every shipment and to read in a slice. Neither page nor chunk size is a
  wire constant: a holder keys held inputs by the manifest identity the owner computed.

Rejected: placing a large version's inputs through the content plane's own put ahead of its record (A-244's removed
path), which is a second path chosen by size. Also rejected: one whole-archive shipment with a longer deadline, which still
holds each holder's shard for the whole verification and decode. Also rejected: offering the manifest only once per
target, since the holder can then name what it lacks only by keeping the offer, while at 1 MiB chunks the offer costs
little.

Applied in the same change to: §4.16 (status); A-217 (owed); A-244's shipment (bounded); GAPS; `slates-cluster`
(`Committed::answers`; `ContentHold::held_manifest`, `held_chunk`); `slates-server` (new `merge_origin`: `InputsBuilder`,
`OriginInputsJob`, `ReplicaSeed`, `seed_version_zero`; `merge_service`: `inputs_archive` at the archive's largest chunk,
`MergeShardState::origin_inputs` and `seeding`, `PendingMergeRecord::lacking`, `ship_version`, `ship_groups`,
`cut_shipments`, `ShipInputs`, `shipment_bound`, `record_inputs_answers`, `inputs_held`, `insert_pending`,
`corrupt_if_faulted`, `HeldWalk::into_walked`, the removal of `walk_held_origin`; `fleet::serve_merge_shipment`); the
unit tests (among them `a_seed_whose_green_is_forgotten_meanwhile_installs_nothing`, red with the install's hold check
removed) and `a_green_over_a_base_places_its_origin_at_f1_a_slice_at_a_time`. No change to a record's format, the
content messages or the shipment's framing.

### A-246 — A restarted owner re-enqueues the merge records its chain holds (accepted 2026-11-07)

AUD-11 answers a submit at `f > 0` once its version's record commits at the quorum. The records an owner owes and the
submits waiting on them were in memory only, and a restart rebuilt greens from their chains without them, so a version
appended before a crash and not yet placed was never shipped again. Replace that: the restart's replay of each green
(`verbs::replay_green`) yields every replayed version's record fields with the green's head identity there. Those are
version 0 when no checkpoint stands for it, then each chain entry. The owner enqueues them as pending records, placed
from the configuration it holds when it ships. A holder that already applied a version re-acknowledges it from its
acceptor, so re-shipping what was already placed costs one exchange a version and changes nothing.

Rejected:
- Persisting each record's placement. That is a durable write per commit, to save a re-ship only after a restart.
- Asking the holders for their heads before shipping. That is a new exchange whose answer the re-acknowledgement
  already gives.
- Re-enqueueing on a takeover too. A takeover adopts its placed head under the promotion epoch and keeps that path.

Applied in the same change to: §4.16 (Commit status); `slates-server` (`verbs::replay_green`, `rebuild_green`,
`rebuild_recovered`; `merge_service::ReplayedVersion`, `enqueue_recovered_record`, `enqueue_record_with`); the fleet
test; GAPS. Evidence: `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-version-appended-before-its-owner-restarted-never-committed.md`. No wire,
layout or capability change.

### A-244 — A merge record carries its inputs, so a version commits in one exchange (accepted 2026-11-07)

A-235 woke the record plane per event, but a version still crossed five hops: a nudge, the inputs' offer, their transfer,
a second nudge, the record. A submit at `f = 1` cost 6.7 ms at p50 quiet, against goal 4's 1 ms. Replace the separate
inputs put. A record ships with its inputs whenever a target lacks them, as one merge shipment on the record's own
stream: the record, then the content exchange's offer and every chunk. The holder serves the content frames through the
content plane's own path (authority, retention at the door, the verified hold), then recomputes and accepts. Its one
acknowledgement binds the record and places the inputs. Placed-before-referenced holds by construction, because a
holder that does not hold the inputs a record names refuses it (`merge.inputs_unheld`). Also: a holder's retention rule
reads only the ledger position at the sequence a held input was placed for, since a green's inputs are placed at their
version's sequence. Rejected: keeping the put and sending it concurrently with the record, which is two paths for one
fact and a record that can reach a holder before its inputs do. Also rejected: a larger content window, which leaves
the second nudge and the second exchange.

Applied in the same change to: §4.16 (Commit status); §4.10 content retention (the module doc); `slates-cluster`
(`commit_record_sent_as`); `slates-db` (`Acceptor::value_at`); `slates-server` (`merge_service::carries_inputs`,
`encode_shipment`, `decode_shipment`, `ship_record`, `fold_acknowledgements`, `INPUTS_CARRIED`, the removal of
`put_inputs`; `fleet::serve_merge_shipment`, `serve_content_request`; `content_retention::named`); the fleet and unit
tests; GAPS. Evidence: `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-versions-inputs-and-record-took-five-hops.md`,
`docs/bugs/2026-11-07-retention-decoded-every-merge-record-per-put.md`. Wire: the merge record stream's payload is now a
shipment. A holder of an older build fails to decode it and answers nothing, so a mixed fleet refuses safely.

### A-255 — A submit's completion moves with its green, and a resend reaches the green's successor through its work's catalog (accepted and built 2026-11-09; loadtest-scale's route, fixtures' gate, the supervisor's three constraints)

Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/merge`: `chain_entry` version 2 carries `Completion { origin, client, sequence }`.
- `crates/anchor`: `LAYOUT_VERSION` 7.
- `crates/server`:
  - `MergeRecordValue::completion` and its format version (`RECORD_MAGIC`, `RECORD_VERSION` 1, `RecordRefused`);
  - `record_taken_over_completions`;
  - `CatalogValue::work_of`, `fleet::owed_merge_catalogs` and `owed_adopted_work_catalogs`;
  - `verbs::locate_work_green`;
  - `owner_location::locate_work_of` and `Reply::work_of`;
  - the record plane's gate (`PendingMergeRecord::work`, `fleet::catalog_committed`, `MergeWork::ShipWorkCatalog`,
    `works_owing_catalog`).
- The tests named in the bug record, GAPS, and §4.16's status.

- **What was there.** A-252 made a waiting submit a durable state of the owner's partition. After a takeover the
  resend was refused `OwnerUnreachable` without end. The completion window died with the owner, and the resend routes
  by its work's id, which no survivor owns: a work's head is never placed.
- **The rule.**
  - RIFL §3: "If the object migrates, then the completion record must move with it." For a merge the object is the
    green. The submit's completion key rides its version's chain entry and merge record, which holders replicate.
    The successor's adopted chain answers a resend under that key with its version at once. The key lives as long as
    the record, under W2's retention, and has no separate table.
  - The route is the work's own replicated catalog register, which names its green. It needs no global catalog (D-14),
    no client wire change and no id format change. A request for a work no member owns goes unchanged to the green's
    owner. An origin holding no copy of the catalog learns the green from a location round of the catalog's holders.
  - The green's owner answers only the completion under the request's own key and refuses anything else `NotFound`. A
    key copied into another session is refused at its origin's door (A-SEAT).
  - A version's record ships only once its submitting work's catalog is committed, so no holder holds a completion
    without its route. The record plane ships that catalog at the work's creation, and on demand. A work on another
    shard than its green (A-247) meets this on its own shard before its verdict is asked (A-298).
  - The successor never runs a resend whose key its chain does not hold. A work no member owns has no work to run against,
    so the green's owner refuses it `NotFound`. It answers only from the chain it adopted whole, to the quorum's head
    (`takeover::adopt`), so a version committed at the quorum whose answer was lost is answered, never run again
    (`a_submit_whose_answer_was_lost_with_its_owner_is_answered_its_version_by_the_greens_successor`).
  - A merge record carries its own format version. Another is refused typed, never decoded by a second path (§2.7).
- **Measured.** A submit made right after its work's creation: median 1.59–1.64 ms against 1.25–1.29 ms without the
  work's catalog, on an idle Mac Studio, 2026-11-09. While the catalog waited for the coordinator's period it was
  109 ms. The bug record has the arms.
- **Open.**
  - A second loss of the green's owner needs the ledger-prefix transfer (GAP-A9-7).
  - The cross-region case is owed a test.
  - ~~The route has no end for a work whose owner died~~: ended by A-288 (2026-11-17). A route is kept while the
    green's owner holds a completion only the route can reach, then its adopter retires it.

### A-288 — A work's route ends once its green's owner holds no completion the route can reach (accepted and built 2026-11-17; amends A-255; the supervisor's option A)

Applied in the same change to:

- `crates/db`: `CompletionRecord::work` (appended); `Partition::completions_routed_by`, kept beside the windows and
  released by the acknowledgement that releases the completion.

  - `MergeRecordValue` format 2 (`SubmitCompletion::work`); `record_taken_over_completions` records the work;
  - `work_route` (the keeper, its question on fleet stream 25, and the retirement);
  - `takeover::record_adoption` wakes the keeper, and `forget_owner_on_every_shard`;
  - `fleet::retire_shard_tombstones` drops the owner's own copies of a retired object's registers.
- The test `a_works_route_ends_once_the_greens_owner_holds_none_of_its_completions` (red on main 7c6faee27 and
  dbf53afa2: retired false, counted 0; green with the fix, both routes retired, counted 2), §4.16's status, GAPS, and
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-a-works-route-was-never-retired.md`.
- The second piece, the same day: `work_route::held_completions` answers for a green its shard holds `unrecovered`, and
  `work_route::nudge` is public for a test that plants a route. The test
  `a_route_to_a_green_its_successor_gave_up_on_is_retired` (red: the route kept, all 111 questions refused).

- **What was there.** A-255 made a work's catalog record, which names its green, the route a resend of its submit
  takes after the work's owner is taken over. Its adopter keeps it placed (`fleet::owed_adopted_work_catalogs`). Nothing
  ever retired it: only a volume's owner writes its tombstone, and a work never comes back to have one. Every work alive
  at an owner's death was held by its adopter and every holder for as long as the fleet ran, a store with no bound
  (CLAUDE.md §2 item 8).
- **The rule.**
  - A route is kept exactly while the green's owner retains a completion that a resend can reach only through it.
    RIFL keeps a completion until its client acknowledges it, and moves it with its object (Lee et al., SOSP 2015, §3),
    so the route lives as long as those records.
  - Only a client on another node than the work's owner reaches its completion through the route. A client of the
    owner's own node resends to that node, which answers from the records it made, since its partition still holds the
    work. If the node is gone, so is the client. So a merge record names the submit's work only for a forwarded submit.
    This is what ends the commonest route, a work its own owner's clients submitted from.
  - The green's successor records each such completion under its work, durably (`CompletionRecord::work`). Its
    partition counts what each work still has (`Partition::completions_routed_by`), and the acknowledgement that
    releases the last ends the count.
  - The route's adopter asks the green's owner every record period, for the works whose routes it keeps, whether any is
    still held (`work_route::Question`, fleet stream 25). Only the green's shard answers, and only once its count is
    final: once it serves the green, or holds it `unrecovered`, since a takeover given up after the failover SLO's
    attempts recorded no adopted completion and never will. A green pending materialization, owned elsewhere or not
    found gives no answer, and the route stays.
  - A work answered "none" moves from the adopter's pending catalogs to its pending tombstones, at sequence 1, where the
    work's own destroy would have closed its registers. AUD-29-43's two stages then drop every holder's copy. When the
    tombstone retires, the owner drops its own copies of both registers too: a successor had kept its takeover's
    acceptors and its placement of an adopted catalog for good, for a destroyed taken-over volume as well.
  - The keeper is its own task, parked while its node keeps no route, so a slow question never holds the record
    plane's coordinator and an idle node takes no wakeup for it. A question names at most as many works as fit one
    fleet frame (71). An owner that leaves one question unanswered is not asked its green's others that period, so a
    pass spends at most one liveness budget on it, however many routes lead there.
- **Rejected.**
  - (B) A cap per adopter, the oldest route retired first. It refuses a resend that could have been answered.
  - (C) Leaving the store unbounded.
  - Counting every adopted completion, a local client's too. That is the literal "holds no completion", but a local
    client's completion of a dead owner is never acknowledged. Its route would never end, for the commonest work.
  - Judging a completion by whether the council still holds its client's node as a member. A restarted node is a new
    member, and its old id is retired before the new one is admitted (`fleet::LearnedOutcome::Restarted`, from
    reading). A route retired in that gap refuses a resend its surviving client is owed.
- **Open.**
  - A green destroyed (a given-up one too, which is then neither served nor `unrecovered`), or lost to a second
    takeover it cannot survive (GAP-A9-7), while a route to it is kept leaves that route held: the green has no owner
    to answer.
  - ~~A green its successor gave up on keeps a route to it~~: ended the same day. Its shard answers for a green it
    holds `unrecovered`, from its partition's count (`a_route_to_a_green_its_successor_gave_up_on_is_retired`).
  - A completion its client never acknowledges keeps its route, as it keeps the record itself. This covers a client of
    another node that died, and one that never writes to the green again. Only an acknowledgement or a client lease
    ends either, and RIFL's client leases are not built.
  - An adopter that restarts warm gets its holder copies back but not the routes it kept (`pending_catalogs`), so it
    neither re-places nor retires them. This is A-255's own gap, found by reading; no test shows it yet.
- **Wire.** A merge record of format 1 and a chain entry of version 2 are refused typed. An older segment is refused at
  layout 8. A peer of an older build does not answer the route's question, which it does not know, so the route stays.

### A-254 — The owner of an instance is decided before anything is created (accepted 2026-11-08)
Applied in the same change to: §4.7 (the rendezvous's status), GAPS, `crates/cli/src/anchor.rs` (`run`),
`crates/server/src/daemon.rs` (`Daemon::start_with_fleet`), `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` and `crates/server/tests/daemon.rs`
(the tests below), and `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-refused-second-anchor-unlinked-the-live-instances-segment.md`.
- **What was wrong.** A-176 and A-178 made the rendezvous refuse a live instance's second owner, but both start paths
  created their segment first. On macOS a shared-memory name is the user's, a creation unlinks any holder's, and the
  creator's drop unlinks the name again, so a refused second anchor or lone daemon took the live instance's segment name
  with it. The live anchor's next daemon could not attach (`shm_open` `ENOENT`) and looped until the anchor was restarted.
- **The rule.** A start decides that it owns the instance before it creates anything: the anchor holds the rendezvous, and
  a daemon opens its listener, ahead of the segment and the content object. A refused start has created nothing, so it
  unlinks nothing and a running instance is untouched.
- **On every platform, though two hid it.** Linux's segment has no name (a memfd), and on Windows a live section's name
  refuses the second creation. Both took the same wrong order; all three now take one.
- **What it does not change.** The owner's token on each platform, the adoption of a held rendezvous (A-114), and what a
  client sees: a daemon opens its listener a few steps earlier in its start, and a claim waits for it as before.
- **Proven** on this Mac by two tests that failed on the old order: `a_refused_second_anchor_leaves_the_live_instance_its_segment_and_its_bytes`
  (across processes: a live anchor and its daemon, a second anchor refused, the daemon killed, its successor adopting the
  segment by name and reading the file back) and `a_refused_second_daemon_leaves_the_live_ones_segment_in_place`.

### A-275 — A volume symlink is a Windows symbolic link: the WinFsp drive serves reparse points (accepted 2026-11-09, the supervisor's pick)
Applied in the same change to: A-209 (amended: REPARSE and SYMLINK), §4.5 (the inode's kept Windows bits), §4.6 (the
Windows conformance status), §4.8 (image version 26, delta version 9: 27 and 10 when built on 2026-11-09, which left
26 and 9 to A-270; A-275 landed first, on 2026-11-17, so it took them), GAPS, `docs/wip/conformance.md`, the winfstest
list (`docs/wip/conformance/expected-failures/native-windows-winfsp.winfstest.txt`, 355 to 382 entries) and its record,
`crates/vfs` (`inode::WindowsAttributes::LINK_DIRECTORY`, `kept`, `from_image`; `IMAGE_VERSION`, `DELTA_VERSION`),
and `crates/bridge-winfsp` (`symlink.rs`; the reparse slots, `GetSecurityByName`'s walk and `file_info`'s tag in
`host.rs`; the slots and exports in `ffi.rs`).
- **What was missing.** The drive served no reparse point, so every `CreateSymbolicLinkW` answered
  `ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION`, a link made on Linux showed on Windows as a reparse point Windows could not follow, and
  winfstest's `t/reparse/02.t`, `03.t` and `t/streams/04.t` stopped at their first link. Git for Windows
  (`core.symlinks`) and npm make links this way.
- **The rule.** A volume symlink is the Windows symbolic link; there is no second kind of link. The drive sets WinFsp's
  `ReparsePoints` (bit 4 of `VolumeParams`, `fsctl.h` v2.1) and fills its four reparse slots. Windows follows a link
  through WinFsp's own resolver (`FspFileSystemResolveReparsePoints`, and `FspFileSystemFindReparsePoint` when a path's
  walk fails, as memfs's `GetSecurityByName` does), which asks the shard for each component's link by name without
  following it. `FSCTL_GET_REPARSE_POINT` is answered with an `IO_REPARSE_TAG_SYMLINK` buffer made from the volume's
  target. `FSCTL_SET_REPARSE_POINT` with a symbolic link's buffer, on the empty file or directory `CreateSymbolicLinkW`
  has just made, replaces it with a volume link at its name, keeping its attribute bits; `FSCTL_DELETE_REPARSE_POINT`
  turns a link back into an empty file or directory. Generic reparse data (every other tag) is its own change, owed
  after named streams; it still answers `STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST`, as every reparse request did before.
  **Since A-438 (2026-11-18)** the map between a volume link and its buffer lives in `slates_vfs::host::windows_link`,
  shared by the drive and the landing's Windows writer, which lands each volume link in this form.
- **1. A link's type.** A Windows link is typed: a directory link carries `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY` and is removed by
  `RemoveDirectory`, a file link by `DeleteFile`. A volume symlink is untyped.
  - A link Windows made keeps the type it was created with: the empty object `CreateSymbolicLinkW` made is a directory
    for `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY`, and the link that replaces it keeps `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY` in A-262's
    `Inode::windows`, whose kept set admits that bit for a symlink alone (`WindowsAttributes::LINK_DIRECTORY`). It
    reports `DIRECTORY | REPARSE_POINT` (0x410), a file link `ARCHIVE | REPARSE_POINT` (0x420), as `t/reparse/03.t` and
    `02.t` expect.
  - A link POSIX made has no type and is presented as a file link, whatever its target is, and stays one when its target
    changes type. This is how Samba presents a link opened as itself (`fdos_mode` reports `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT`
    for `S_IFLNK`, never `DIRECTORY`; samba master 9ae24f2f, `source3/smbd/dosmode.c` 729-746). WSL types a link by its
    target only when it makes the NT link itself, and only for a target that exists (release notes, build 17046;
    microsoft/WSL 2183822c, `test/windows/wsl/DrvFsTests.cpp` 160-191); Git for Windows makes a typeless link a file link
    and recreates it as a directory link once its target exists as one (`compat/mingw.c`, `create_phantom_symlink`,
    `process_phantom_symlink`), which on this drive sets the bit as any directory link does. The type decides only how
    the link is removed and listed: WinFsp follows a file link into a directory, "contrary to NTFS" (its traverse check
    in `src/dll/security.c`, and its resolver, which reads no link's type), so nothing a POSIX link names fails to
    resolve on the drive. Deriving the type from the target at each lookup was rejected: it costs a resolution per link
    in every listing, and Windows keeps a name's information until told (`FileInfoTimeout` infinite), so a target's
    change of type would leave the link's reported type stale with no notification to correct it. Promoting a link the
    drive finds pointing at a directory, as Git for Windows promotes its own, was rejected too: the drive would write the
    volume on a lookup, which a read-only attachment refuses and which a publication would then carry; Git for Windows
    promotes by recreating the link with `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY`, which the drive keeps. When a target later
    changes type, no link's type follows it: a POSIX link stays a file link, and a Windows link keeps the type it was made
    with, as on NTFS.
- **2. Separators (R8: one volume, one meaning).** A relative target is stored with `/` and presented to Windows with
  `\`, as Git for Windows writes a link (`mingw_create_symlink`) and reads one (`normalize_ntpath`), and as WSL's DrvFs
  does both ways (`drvfs.c` 3524-3570). A Windows link relative to the drive's root (`\x\y`) is stored as the path to the
  same object from the link's own directory (`../../x/y` for a link at `\a\b\link`), which resolves to that object on
  every platform; Windows reads it back in that form. This is a stated difference: POSIX has no form relative to a
  volume's root, so a moved link of this form reaches what its path names from its new directory, where NTFS keeps it
  naming `\x\y` (`a_link_relative_to_the_drives_root_follows_its_directory_when_moved`: moved one directory deeper, the
  link reaches `\a\x\y`). `CreateSymbolicLinkW` never makes this form (it makes a rooted target absolute); only a
  program that writes the reparse buffer itself does. Every other target is presented as given and resolves only where
  it means something: a POSIX-absolute one (`/usr/bin`) is shown to Windows unchanged with flags 0 and resolves to
  nothing on the drive; a Windows-absolute one keeps the Win32 path of its `\??\` substitute (`C:\x`, or `\\srv\share\x`
  for `\??\UNC\srv\share\x`), which Linux and macOS read unchanged and do not resolve. Any other absolute NT form
  (`\??\Volume{…}\`, `\Device\…`) has no Win32 path and is refused `STATUS_IO_REPARSE_DATA_INVALID`. The lossy case: a
  POSIX name holding `\`, which Windows takes for a separator, so `a\b` reads on Windows as two components and `C:\x` as
  a drive path; neither reaches what Linux meant, and Windows cannot name such a file in any case. Samba sends a
  relative target's `/` unchanged (`read_symlink_reparse`, `source3/smbd/files.c` 859-922); slates converts, since its
  drive is followed by WinFsp's resolver, which splits at `\` alone.
- **3. Privilege: NTFS's rule.** Making or removing a symbolic link asks for `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege`, unless
  Developer Mode is on (Microsoft Learn, CreateSymbolicLinkW, `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_ALLOW_UNPRIVILEGED_CREATE`, which Git
  for Windows passes, `adjust_symlink_flags`). WinFsp's own check (`ReparsePointsAccessCheck`, `SeSinglePrivilegeCheck`
  in `src/sys/fsctl.c` 231-240, v2.1) was measured refusing Developer Mode's unprivileged create: a token with no
  privilege, the flag passed and Developer Mode on (`AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense` 1), answered
  `ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD` (diagnostics run 42712321599). memfs, airfs and WinFsp's FUSE layer leave the check off, which
  would make the drive looser than NTFS. So the drive judges it:
  - WinFsp passes the caller's token only on a Create or Open (`Req.Create.AccessToken`; no FSCTL carries one). Only for
    one that could become a link does the receiver read it: from user mode, opening a reparse point itself
    (`FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`, as `CreateSymbolicLinkW` opens the object it makes a link) and asking an access a link's
    set needs (`FILE_WRITE_DATA`, `FILE_APPEND_DATA`, `FILE_WRITE_ATTRIBUTES`, or a generic or maximum right granting
    one; `Request::could_become_a_link`). Every other open costs no token query. The receiver reads the token's
    privileges while WinFsp keeps it live, and keeps the open as one that may make a link if the token holds the
    privilege enabled, as NTFS's check asks (`crate::dispatcher::may_link`). That table is bounded by the drive's open table, since each entry is one
    of its live opens, and an entry is dropped at its Close; an open a successor restored after a takeover has none, and
    is judged unprivileged unless Developer Mode is on.
  - A symbolic link's set or delete is allowed if its open was kept so, or if Developer Mode is on, read from the registry
    at the set. Otherwise it answers `STATUS_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`, which Windows reports as `ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`,
    NTFS's answer.
  - Stated deviations from NTFS. (a) WinFsp never passes `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_ALLOW_UNPRIVILEGED_CREATE` to a file
    system, so under Developer Mode the drive allows a program without the privilege that sets a link's buffer itself
    (`FSCTL_SET_REPARSE_POINT`) without that flag, where NTFS may refuse it. A `CreateSymbolicLinkW` caller never meets
    this: `CreateSymbolicLinkW` itself refuses a caller without the privilege that did not pass the flag, before any file
    system is asked, so on its path the drive answers as NTFS in every case measured (a token with no privilege, the
    flag and Developer Mode each off and on: `ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD` three times and the link made once, on the
    drive and on the runner's NTFS alike, diagnostics run 42715955734). (b) The privilege
    must be enabled in the token at the open, where NTFS asks it enabled at the set. `CreateSymbolicLinkW` enables it
    around its whole operation, before its create, so on that path the two agree; a program that never enables it is
    refused, as on NTFS. Only a program that enables it after its open and before its `FSCTL_SET_REPARSE_POINT` is
    refused where NTFS allows it: stricter, and safe (`a_raw_link_set_needs_the_privilege_enabled_at_its_open`).
    (c) A link set through an open made without `FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT` or a write access, or through one a
    successor restored after a takeover (which kept no token), is judged as one without the privilege: allowed under
    Developer Mode alone.
  - Measured on the runner by `a_link_by_a_caller_without_the_privilege_and_the_flag_is_refused` (`ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`,
    no link left), `a_link_is_made_by_a_caller_holding_the_symlink_privilege`, and
    `a_link_without_the_privilege_follows_developer_mode_with_the_unprivileged_flag` and
    `a_raw_link_set_needs_the_privilege_enabled_at_its_open`, on the final build (diagnostics run 42720006662), with
    Developer Mode on and then off: `CreateSymbolicLinkW` without the privilege and without the flag, 1314 and 1314;
    with the flag, made and 1314; with the privilege, made; a raw set with the privilege held but disabled, made (the
    deviation (a)) and 1314; enabled before its open, made and made. The NTFS control (the same token and
    flags on the runner's own disk, Developer Mode off and on) gave the same four answers as the drive. The daemon holds no privilege (R10).
- **4. Absolute targets and SymlinkEvaluation.** The daemon never follows a link. WinFsp's driver completes every link
  its resolver returns by rewriting the file object's name and answering `STATUS_REPARSE` with `IO_REPARSE`, for a
  relative link (prefixed with the volume's name) and an absolute one alike (`src/sys/create.c` 893-996, v2.1), so the
  I/O manager reopens the new name under the caller's token and is never handed an `IO_REPARSE_TAG_SYMLINK` to evaluate.
  The drive is a local disk file system (`FILE_DEVICE_DISK_FILE_SYSTEM` without `FILE_REMOTE_DEVICE`,
  `src/sys/volume.c`); Windows reports it a "Fixed Drive" (`fsutil fsinfo drivetype`). Measured on the runner (diagnostics
  run 42712321599): the evaluation classes are L2L and L2R enabled, R2L and R2R disabled; a drive link to
  `\\localhost\C$\Windows\win.ini` is followed. With `fsutil behavior set SymlinkEvaluation L2R:0` (which `fsutil behavior
  query` then reports DISABLED) the drive link was still followed, but so was the same link on the runner's NTFS, so the
  setting did not take effect on the running system and the run cannot tell the drive from NTFS there; the reason the
  drive would not apply it either is WinFsp's rewrite, read in its source above.
- **The stored form's cost, and the format bump.** The directory bit lives in the inode's existing `u16`: no inode,
  wire, archive or layout change. But an earlier reader would drop the bit without a word and show a directory link as
  a file link, so the image (version 26) and the delta (version 9) are bumped, and a reader of another version refuses
  them typed rather than read them as its own (the version-refusal tests in `crates/vfs/tests/checkpoint_log.rs`). FUSE,
  NFS and FSKit read and make links as before and never see the bit.
- **Crash behaviour.** A set or delete is one shard request that removes the object and makes its replacement, then
  publishes once (§4.8, D-18): no publication shows the name missing or holding both, so a crash leaves the old object or
  the link, never neither.
- **Limits, each answered by its status.** The print name is derived, not kept. A file with bytes cannot become a link
  (`STATUS_DIRECTORY_NOT_EMPTY`). A link holds no bytes of its own: a write or read through a handle opened on the link
  itself is refused (`ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`; NTFS and memfs keep a data stream beside a reparse point;
  `t/reparse/02.t` cases 15 and 16, listed SYMLINK-DATA). The open that set the link keeps the object it opened, now
  unlinked, as a POSIX open of an unlinked file does; WinFsp drops what Windows cached of the name after the set
  (`FspFsvolFileSystemControlReparsePointComplete` invalidates the node's information), so the next open finds the link.
- **What winfstest says** (diagnostics run 42695804063, windows-latest, 733 cases): the links let 105 cases run that
  never ran. With the 3 listed cases they unlocked (02.t:1, 03.t:1, streams/04.t:9), 78 pass and 30 are listed, none a
  defect: 02.t 39 of 41 (15 and 16, SYMLINK-DATA), 03.t 26 of 26, streams/04.t 13 of its cases 9 to 49 (28 listed
  STREAMS, each through a `name:stream` path). The list goes from 355 to 382, recorded from diagnostics run 42720006662 on the final build (733 cases, 382
  expected, 0 unexpected, 0 listed-now-passing).
- **Proven** by `symbolic_links_made_through_the_drive_are_followed_and_read_back` and
  the three privilege tests and `a_link_relative_to_the_drives_root_follows_its_directory_when_moved`
  (`crates/cli/tests/winfsp_semantics.rs`, on CI's Windows
  runner; the first red on main, `ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION` at the first `CreateSymbolicLinkW`, and red with the four
  reparse callbacks removed, `Incorrect function.` at the first `CreateSymbolicLinkW`, diagnostics run 42712321599), `a_symlink_keeps_the_directory_bit_that_makes_it_a_windows_directory_link`
  (`crates/bridge-core/tests/volume_bridge.rs`; on main the reply read 2 where 18 was set),
  `windows_attributes_survive_an_image_and_a_rebuild` (`crates/vfs/tests/recover.rs`; with the old image mask the
  rebuilt volume read 2, not 18), the version-refusal tests, the buffer's ten tests in `crates/bridge-winfsp/src/symlink.rs`
  (its layout built field by field from MS-FSCC 2.1.2.4; hostile buffers refused; the separator rule and its lossy case),
  and winfstest judged against the 382-entry list.

### A-268 — A device node is refused as a file system without device nodes refuses it: EPERM, after the name and the directory (accepted 2026-11-08)
> **Superseded by A-294 (2026-11-17).** A device node is made; `NFS3ERR_PERM`/`NFS4ERR_PERM` now answers only a caller
> who is not root asking for a device other than a whiteout, after the taken name and the unwritable directory this
> amendment ordered.

Applied in the same change to: A-26 (its device refusal's answer), the condition-4 status (§4.6), GAPS, the record
`docs/bugs/2026-09-19-pjdfstest-special-files-and-nfs-limits.md`, and `crates/bridge-nfs/src/procedures.rs`
(`Export::refuse_device_node`; NFSv4's CREATE reaches it through MKNOD).
- **What was wrong.** A MKNOD of a block or character device, and NFSv4's CREATE of one, answered `NFS3ERR_BADTYPE`
  (`NFS4ERR_BADTYPE` over v4), the status RFC 1813 §3.3.11 names for a type the server does not make. The Linux client
  maps both to its internal `EBADTYPE`, errno 527, which reached every program as "Unknown error 527": 331 cases of a
  full pjdfstest run over NFSv4, and the same over NFSv3 (CI run 42498995934 and a CachyOS run, 2026-11-08). It was
  also answered before the name was looked at.
- **Why EPERM.** On a local Linux file system a device node needs privilege (`CAP_MKNOD`, checked in `vfs_mknod`), and
  slates never holds privilege (R10), so `EPERM` is what a local file system gives this same caller. RFC 1813's
  `BADTYPE` describes a server that lacks the type, which is not slates' reason, and Linux turns it into a
  kernel-internal errno that leaks to programs.
- **The rule.** Slates makes no device nodes (A-26), so it answers as a local file system that cannot hold one, in the
  order Linux's `vfs_mknod` checks: a taken name is `EXIST` (an exclusive create over NFS skips the client's own lookup,
  so only the server can say so), a directory the caller may not write is `ACCES`, then `PERM`, which a client reports
  as `EPERM`, what `mknod(2)` answers when "the filesystem containing pathname does not support the type of node
  requested".
- **What it does not change.** A-26's boundary (no device node is made, on any path), FIFOs and sockets, and every
  reviewed list: no pjdfstest case expects `EPERM` from a device `mknod` (each failing one expects success, or `EEXIST`
  on a name the case before failed to make), so every listed case still fails, now reading `EPERM`.
- **Proven** by `a_device_mknod_is_refused_eperm_as_a_file_system_without_device_nodes_refuses_it` and
  `a_device_mknod_is_told_its_name_is_taken_or_its_directory_unwritable_first` (`crates/bridge-nfs/tests/procedures.rs`),
  `a_device_create_is_refused_eperm_and_a_taken_name_eexist_first` (`crates/bridge-nfs/tests/v4.rs`), each red on the old
  MKNOD with 10007, and through the Linux kernel's NFSv4 client by `a_device_node_is_refused_eperm`
  (`crates/server/tests/nfs_v4_kernel.rs`, as root on CI).

### A-262 — The volume keeps Windows' attribute bits beside the mode, and a file's read-only state is its mode (accepted 2026-11-08; the drive, the volume and the Windows base plane built; a Windows landing and the merge owed)
Applied in the same change to: §4.5 (the inode), §4.6 (the Windows conformance status), A-209 (amended: ATTRIBUTES),
GAPS, `docs/wip/conformance.md`, the winfstest list
(`docs/wip/conformance/expected-failures/native-windows-winfsp.winfstest.txt`, 373 to 355 entries), `crates/vfs`
(`inode::WindowsAttributes`, `Volume::set_windows_attributes` and the overlay's, the image v23 and delta v6 layouts),
`crates/bridge-core` (`NodeAttr::windows`, `SetAttr::windows`, the owner rule, the AppleDouble view's refusal), the
FUSE, NFS and FSKit bridges (each sets none), and `crates/bridge-winfsp` (the attribute decisions in `lib.rs`; create,
overwrite, `SetBasicInfo`, `CanDelete` and rename in `host.rs`).
- **Why A-209's reason no longer covers them.** A-209 left the bits out because "the volume's permission is POSIX's
  mode": one permission model. That holds for `READONLY` alone. `HIDDEN`, `SYSTEM`, `ARCHIVE`, `OFFLINE` and
  `NOT_CONTENT_INDEXED` are metadata, not permissions, and Windows tools rely on them: Git for Windows hides `.git`
  (`core.hideDotFiles`), Explorer hides by them, and backups and `robocopy /A` read `ARCHIVE`. The drive answered
  their `SetFileAttributes` success and kept nothing.
- **The rule.**
  - A file's `READONLY` is its mode's write bits, the one model. Setting it clears every class's write bit; clearing it
    gives the owner's back. The drive reports `READONLY` for a file its owner may not write. This is WSL DrvFs's mapping,
    and Samba's `map readonly`, so a POSIX tool sees what Windows set and the reverse.
  - The other bits, and a directory's `READONLY` (Windows gives it no permission: Explorer reads it as a display
    hint, and the mode keeps its POSIX meaning), are kept as metadata in `Inode::windows`, a `u16` at Windows' values.
  - A file the volume makes is `ARCHIVE`, as NTFS and WinFsp's memfs mark every file they make. A create applies the
    caller's word with `ARCHIVE`; an overwrite's supersede takes the caller's word and a plain overwrite adds it to the
    file's, each with `ARCHIVE`; `SetBasicInfo` replaces the word, `INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES` leaving it as it is.
  - The Win32 rules on top: a read-only file refuses its delete (`STATUS_CANNOT_DELETE`, `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`) and a
    rename replacing it (`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`). Setting the bits asks for the owner or root, as a mode change does.
- **What it costs.** No inode grows: the `u16` sits in the two bytes of tail padding (measured with `offset_of!`;
  `Inode` stays 168 bytes, `cargo run -p slates-vfs --example tree_heap` reads 260, 275 and 293 heap bytes per entry for
  npm, pip and cargo trees, before and after). The image's inode gains two bytes (layout version 23, the delta's 6), with
  a reviewed golden vector (`an_inode_images_encoding_is_its_golden_vector`). WinFsp's wire already carries the word.
- **What other platforms do with them.** NFS, FUSE and FSKit expose none and set none. A Linux or macOS landing carries
  them in the volume and applies none; a Windows landing applies them since A-451 (below). An overlay reports none of them for a
  file whose disk attributes it never read: no bit, so `NORMAL`, or `READONLY` from the mode. Since stage 3's base half
  an overlay of a Windows directory reads them from its disk; an overlay of a Linux or macOS directory has none to read.
- **Each stage's state.**
  - **Stage 1, built 2026-11-08:** the volume, the image (layout 23), the drive, the list (373 to 355).
  - **Stage 3's base half, built 2026-11-08:** the Windows base plane reads them. A fingerprint carries the disk's bits
    apart from its mode (`Fingerprint::windows`, image layout 24, delta 7, `a_witness_encoding_is_its_golden_vector`), and
    the Windows base reports a POSIX mode by DrvFs's mapping (`windows_mode_and_bits` in `crates/base/src/lib.rs`: a
    directory `S_IFDIR | 0o755`, a file `S_IFREG | 0o644`, `0o444` when `READONLY`, a reparse point `S_IFLNK | 0o777`).
    An untouched base entry reports the disk's bits, and takes an outsider's change to them at its directory's relist,
    as it takes an outsider's `chmod`
    (`an_untouched_base_file_reports_the_disks_windows_attribute_bits_and_follows_their_change`, `crates/vfs/tests/base.rs`),
    and on CI's Windows runner through an overlay of a real directory mounted as a drive
    (`an_overlay_of_a_windows_directory_keeps_its_files_read_only_state_and_attributes`, `crates/cli/tests/winfsp.rs`:
    an ordinary file is writable and deletable, an `attrib +R` one refuses both, an `attrib +H` one reads hidden).
    It also fixes what stage 1 would have exposed: the Windows base had reported the attribute word itself as the mode, so
    an ordinary file (`ARCHIVE`, `0x20`) read as `0o040`, which the drive would have reported read-only and refused to
    delete (`docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-windows-base-files-mode-was-its-attribute-word.md`).
  - **Stage 3's landing half, built 2026-11-18 (A-451):** a Windows landing gives each file, directory and link it
    makes the bits the volume keeps for it, a file's `READONLY` still its mode's, reads the word back and refuses the
    entry `EOPNOTSUPP` where a bit did not take; a directory link lands as a directory link. The manifest carries the
    bits, so a grant binds them. Linux and macOS landings carry the bits in the volume and apply none. Since A-458 (the
    same day) a change of a file's bits or mode alone lands too, as a metadata entry with no byte rewritten; until then
    it landed nothing.
  - **Stage 2, owed when works are mountable:** the merge's metadata dimension, the bits merged as the mode is, accept,
    identical or conflict, never inferred (D-27). No work can set the bits today (below), so no merge can drop them.
- **Invisible to the merge and the landing until then (checked 2026-11-08).** A work's increment is composed from the
  operations declared through the SDK (`WorkState::journal`: edits and declarations, `WorkOp`), and no `WorkOp` carries
  the bits, so no work can set them and two increments can never differ in them alone; a mounted work would be derived
  from its volume's journal, and the volume's ops document carries none of them
  (`windows_attribute_bits_are_invisible_to_the_ops_document_until_the_merge_carries_them`, `crates/vfs/tests/derive.rs`:
  a bits-only work derives the unchanged document byte for byte, and a rewrite derives the same with or without them).
  A landing ignored them without error until A-451 carried them
  (`a_landing_carries_windows_attribute_bits_and_writes_the_same_bytes`, `crates/land/tests/oracle.rs`: §4.15's worked
  example with the bits on an edited, a created and an untouched base file lands `Done` and leaves the same bytes,
  writing as many entries as without, the edited and created files holding the bits).
- **Proven** by `windows_attributes_survive_an_image_and_a_rebuild` and the golden vector (`crates/vfs/tests/recover.rs`),
  `setattr_keeps_the_windows_attribute_bits_for_each_kind` (`crates/bridge-core/tests/volume_bridge.rs`; red with the
