  bridge's setter removed: the file reported 32 where 6 was set), `windows_attribute_bits_ask_for_the_owner`, the
  drive's decisions unit-tested in `crates/bridge-winfsp/src/lib.rs`, and on CI's Windows runner by
  `a_files_attributes_are_kept_and_its_read_only_state_refuses_a_delete` (`crates/cli/tests/winfsp_semantics.rs`) and
  winfstest against the shortened list.

### A-260 — An NFSv4 open or delegation holds its file, so a file removed while open is preserved (accepted 2026-11-08)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (NFSv4 state, "An open holds its file"), GAPS, `docs/wip/conformance.md`, the
NFSv4 pjdfstest list (`docs/wip/conformance/expected-failures/native-linux-nfs4.pjdfstest.txt`, `tests/unlink/14.t:4`
struck), `crates/vfs` (`RefOwner::NfsState` and its settle), `crates/bridge-nfs` (`files::Holding`, `FileState`'s and
`Delegations`' queues, `Backend::preserves_unlinked`, OPEN's result flags), and `crates/server` (`nfs_state::hold`,
`hold_recovered`, `release_attachment`; the recovery and `end_attachment` call them).
- **What was wrong.** An NFSv4 open lived only in the owner's file state and held nothing in the volume, so a REMOVE
  reclaimed an open file at once and its handle answered `NFS4ERR_STALE`. The Linux client keeps POSIX's
  unlink-while-open by renaming such a file aside (`.nfs<fileid><counter>`) unless the server answers its OPEN with
  `OPEN4_RESULT_PRESERVE_UNLINKED`, which this server never did: every tool that removes a file it holds open (git,
  editors, sqlite) left a `.nfs*` name in the volume until the close, a name a landing would carry. pjdfstest listed it
  as `unlink/14.t:4` (NFS-OPEN).
- **The rule.** Every open and delegation holds one volume reference on its file from the commit of its record to the
  commit of its end's, owned by `RefOwner::NfsState(attachment)`. The journal is the holds' only record, and a
  recovery takes them again from it before reclaiming unheld files. An attachment's end gives its holds back. The OPEN
  reply carries `OPEN4_RESULT_PRESERVE_UNLINKED` from a server whose backend holds (the daemon's), and not from the
  standalone server's.
- **Why a third owner kind.** A kernel's references (a FUSE mount's, owned by its attachment) are carried in the
  recovery image and settled by their attachment's survival; NFSv4 state is journaled and must be counted from its
  journal. One count for both would let a recovery double a hold, or reclaim a file a FUSE kernel still holds.
- **What it does not change.** The wire of the state extension procedures and of the journaled records, the recovery
  image, NFSv3 (stateless: its client's silly rename stays, NFS-OPEN on the NFSv3 lists), and how a client's state ends.
- **Proven** by `a_file_removed_while_open_over_nfsv4_serves_until_its_last_close`,
  `..._serves_across_a_daemon_restart` and `..._is_freed_when_its_clients_lease_lapses`
  (`crates/server/tests/recovery.rs`, each red on the old server: `NFS4ERR_STALE` at the first GETATTR by handle; the
  restart one red again with the recovery's re-take removed, and the lease one with a purge's give-backs removed, its
  file's 65,536 bytes kept), `every_open_and_delegation_takes_one_hold_and_gives_it_back_at_its_end`
  (`crates/bridge-nfs/tests/v4_delegation.rs`), and through the Linux kernel's v4.1 and v4.2 clients by
  `an_unlinked_open_file_keeps_serving_with_no_silly_rename` (`crates/server/tests/nfs_v4_kernel.rs`; with the
  daemon's promise turned off, the kernel's client renamed the unlinked open file to `.nfs000100000000000b00000009`,
  2026-11-08, Linux 7.2), the unlinked-open leg of `nfsv4_opens_and_locks_survive_a_daemon_restart`
  (`crates/cli/tests/nfs_v4_restart.rs`, across a `SIGKILL`), and pjdfstest's `unlink/14.t:4` over the NFSv4 transport
  (6,972 passed and 1,798 failed against the struck list, every failure listed). Record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-an-nfsv4-file-removed-while-open-was-reclaimed-at-once.md`.

### A-259 — The WinFsp drive reports and keeps the creation time a caller sets (accepted 2026-11-08)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the Windows conformance status and its stated differences), A-53 (amended),
GAPS, `docs/wip/conformance.md`, the winfstest list
(`docs/wip/conformance/expected-failures/native-windows-winfsp.winfstest.txt`, 374 to 373 entries),
`crates/bridge-core` (`NodeAttr::btime`, `SetAttr::btime`, the access rule, the volume bridge and its read-only view),
`crates/bridge-winfsp/src/host.rs` (`SetBasicInfo`, `file_info`), the FUSE, NFS and FSKit bridges (each sets none), and
the record `docs/bugs/2026-11-05-winfstest-found-win32-semantics-the-drive-broke.md`.
- **What was missing.** The volume keeps a birth time per object (A-53, `Volume::set_times` takes one), but the bridges'
  attributes carried none. WinFsp reported the change time as every object's creation time and dropped the creation
  time `SetFileTime` set, so winfstest's `t/base/06.t` case 5 was listed as CREATION-TIME, one of A-209's five stated
  differences.
- **The rule.** A bridge's attributes report the volume's birth time, and a `setattr` may set it. Only a host whose API
  sets a creation time asks for one (WinFsp's `SetBasicInfo`, from `SetFileTime` and `SetFileInformationByHandle`);
  POSIX has no call that sets a birth time, so the FUSE, NFS and FSKit bridges never set it. Setting it is an explicit
  time, so it asks for the owner or root, as an explicit access or modification time does (`setattr_denial`); a read-only
  view refuses it, as it refuses every time.
- **What it does not change.** The wire and the archive (the birth time was already in both, A-53), FUSE, NFS and FSKit's
  answers, and the other stated differences (ATTRIBUTES, SECURITY, REPARSE and SYMLINK, STREAMS).
- **Proven** by `setattr_sets_and_reports_a_birth_time` (`crates/bridge-core/tests/volume_bridge.rs`; with the volume
  bridge passing no birth time, as before, the reply read back 1794155205189903000 instead of the 333 set),
  `a_creation_time_asks_for_the_owner` (`crates/bridge-core/src/access.rs`; with the birth time out of the owner check,
  a writer who is not the owner was allowed), and on CI's Windows runner by
  `a_files_creation_time_set_through_the_drive_is_kept` (`crates/cli/tests/winfsp_semantics.rs`) and winfstest judged
  against the shortened list.

### A-235 — The merge record plane runs when there is merge work, and a version's inputs go only to holders whose next record it is (accepted 2026-11-06)

§4.16 "Commit" ran the record plane only on the coordinator's period, so a submit at `f > 0`, answered once its record
commits, waited one to two periods (208 to 647 ms at `f = 1`), against goal 4's 1 ms. Replace that: an owner shard
nudges the coordinator when it has merge work it can do now, which is a version enqueued, a version's inputs newly
acknowledged, or a record newly acknowledged with versions still pending. The coordinator runs the merge plane at once
between its periods, and everything else keeps the period. Only events that make new work nudge, so an unanswering
holder adds no passes. Put a version's inputs only to the candidates whose first missing record is that version. Hedging
them to every candidate gave a lagging holder two placements ahead of its records, and content retention keeps only the
newest of those, so it let go of the one its next record needed. Rejected: a separate shipping task per version as live
shipping uses (A-200). The owner's acceptor and the holders' sessions belong to the coordinator, and a second
dispatcher would contend for both. Also rejected: a shorter period, which charges every node the council's and the
heads' work more often to buy what an event gives for free.

Applied in the same change to: §4.16 (Commit status); `slates-server` (`merge_service::nudge_record_plane`, `nudged`,
`MergeShardState::nudged`, `put_inputs`'s recipients, `fleet::pace_running_merges`); the fleet test; GAPS. Evidence:
`docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-submit-at-f1-waited-for-the-coordinators-period.md`. No wire, layout or capability change.

### A-234 — A joint write's sub-quorum cohort needs every member, and pending merge records follow the current placement (accepted 2026-11-06)

A bootstrap installs a one-candidate placement on the bootstrapping node and settles its neighbourhood as itself, so
a green made there before the council grows was enqueued under that placement and then, re-placed, met a joint
placement whose settled cohort has one member. Joint writes required `f + 1` of each cohort, which a cohort of one
can never give at `f = 1`; nothing committed and the neighbourhood change never settled. Replace the rule: each
cohort of a joint write commits at `f + 1` of it, or at every member when it has fewer (`Quorum::committed_within`),
and pending merge records are re-placed from the owner's current configuration each period, as head records are.
Safety: a takeover's phase one needs `max(cohort − f, 1)` promises of a cohort (`Quorum::recovery`), and a commit in a
sub-quorum cohort is held by all of it, so one promise meets it; every reader of a placement judges through
`Placement::placed_with`. Rejected: refusing writes until the council has formed, which leaves the deadlock for any
object placed before then and fixes neither half. Reviewed by raft-chaos (2026-11-06).

Applied in the same change to: §4.8 (Neighbourhood changes, status); `slates-db` (`Quorum::committed_within`,
`Placement::placed_with`, `Quorum::recovery`'s doc); `slates-server` (`merge_service::PendingGreen::retarget`); the
fleet and CLI tests; GAPS. Evidence: `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-submit-in-a-three-process-fleet-is-never-answered.md`. No
wire, layout or capability change.

### A-197 — pmem over a handed copy: a socket route for every pmem VMM (accepted and built on Linux x86_64 2026-11-01, Step 6 of the VFS and DAX plan; Firecracker on arm64 owed)
Applied in the same change to: A-186 (the copy's length), GAPS, `crates/ipc` (`protocol.rs`: `MapWrite`'s `granule`;
`stream.rs`: `spawn_bound`), `crates/server` (`direct_map.rs`: the granule checked and the copy sized by it;
`verbs.rs`), `crates/client` (`map_write`'s granule, `page_bytes`; the granule test in `tests/client.rs`), `crates/cli`
(`args.rs`: the `pmem` verb, `{pmem}` and `{len}`; `verbs.rs`: `run_pmem`; `signal.rs`: the signal relay;
`tests/pmem.rs`, new), and `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-ipc` 104 → 105, `slates-cli` 5 → 7). The takeover (Step 6.2):
`crates/anchor` (`held.rs`: the copy kind, its bound and `ENV_COPIES`; `supervise.rs`), `crates/mem`
(`PeerObject::adopt`), `crates/vfs` (`ShardsBackings::adopt_peer`), `crates/ipc` (`Liveness::watch`,
`ClientEnd::daemon_watch`), `crates/client` (`Client::daemon_watch`), `crates/server` (`held_copy.rs`, new;
`anchor_hold.rs`, `config.rs`: `held_copy_bound`, `daemon.rs`, `direct_map.rs`, `reap.rs`, `state.rs`, `verbs.rs`:
recovery keeps a held copy's writer and takes its copy back before the write log's replay), `crates/cli` (the
launcher's watch on its daemon; `anchor.rs`). The real VMMs (Step 6.3): `crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs` (each pmem
test over both backings) and `tests/vm/mod.rs` (`Guest::expect_line`). The hostile guests (Step 6.4):
`crates/guest-probe` (`protocol.rs`: `device`, `storm`, `sweep`, the `stormed` reply and `sweep_value`; `guest.rs`),
`crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs` (three tests over a handed copy), `tests/vm/mod.rs` (`Guest::last_line_holding`)
and CI's image-form step (seven tests). The matrix (Step 6.5): `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (Firecracker's, Cloud
Hypervisor's and QEMU's socket-route cells), §4.6 (the DAX matrix's status) and CLAUDE.md.
- **What it answers.** A pmem VMM reached a slates volume only through a host mount: Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor and
  QEMU map an image file shared as a virtio-pmem device's memory, and the file was a path through a slates mount (the
  image form's pmem route, A-160, A-165, A-189). Firecracker has no folder sharing at all, so its socket-route cell was
  impossible. A-186's writable copy is what a pmem VMM needs instead of a path: a descriptor that authorizes changing
  one file's copy and nothing else, which the daemon keeps equal to the file as every other path changes it.
- **The launcher.** `slates pmem ID FILE --fd N -- VMM [ARG ...]` (Linux) takes its own write attachment of the volume,
  maps FILE to write, and runs the VMM as its child with the copy at descriptor N. `{pmem}` in the VMM's arguments
  names the copy as `/proc/self/fd/N` (Cloud Hypervisor's `--pmem file=`, QEMU's `memory-backend-file,mem-path=`),
  `{fd}` as N, `{len}` as its length (QEMU's `size=`); a Firecracker configuration file names `/proc/self/fd/N` in its
  `path_on_host` itself, since the launcher never rewrites a file.
  - **2 MiB multiples.** `MapWrite` names a granule, a power of two of at least the page, and the copy is the file's
    length rounded up to it; the launcher asks 2 MiB. Firecracker's virtio-pmem "requires for the guest exposed memory
    region to be 2MB aligned" and pads a shorter backing with anonymous pages it never syncs (its `docs/pmem.md`);
    Cloud Hypervisor refuses a backing that is not a 2 MiB multiple (`size % 0x20_0000 != 0`, its
    `vmm/src/device_manager.rs`); QEMU takes any page multiple. So the whole region a guest sees is the copy, and the
    part past the file's end is the copy's too: never written back, as A-186 holds for a copy's last page. A granule
    that is not a power of two of at least the page is refused `BadRequest` before anything is made.
  - **Sync points.** The guest's stores land in the copy. They reach the file when the launcher compares the copy
    back: at each SIGUSR1 (`map_sync`) and at the VM's exit, when it lets the map go (the last compare-back). **The
    guest's own flush never reaches slates**: a virtio-pmem flush is the VMM's `msync(MS_SYNC)` of its backing
    (Firecracker's `docs/pmem.md`; QEMU's persistence asks the guest's `fsync` or `msync`), and a copy has no file to
    write to. A store the guest flushed and the launcher has not yet compared back is in the copy alone.
  - **No VM outlives its map's holder.** The launcher must stay the VMM's parent to hold the map and compare it back, so
    it cannot replace itself with the VMM as `slates shards` and `slates vhost-user` do (`slates_ipc::stream::exec_with`,
    whose reason is a waiting parent's kill leaving the program running). It spawns the VMM bound to itself instead
    (`spawn_bound`): Linux's parent-death signal (`PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`, SIGKILL) ends the VMM when the launcher's thread
    ends, and a child whose parent died before the signal was set ends itself before the exec. The daemon's reap of the
    launcher's client then compares the copy back, as for any client that dies holding a writable map (A-186).
  - **Signals.** The launcher waits on the VMM's pidfd and on a self-pipe its signal handler writes, never on a timer:
    SIGUSR1 is a sync; SIGINT and SIGTERM are passed to the VMM, whose end the launcher then answers as an exit. It
    exits with the VMM's code (128 and the signal for a VMM ended by one), and fails when the last compare-back was
    refused.
- **Proven so far** (adacachy: Linux 7.2.9, x86_64; 2026-11-01), by use:
  - `crates/client/tests/client.rs`, `a_writable_copy_is_its_files_length_rounded_up_to_its_granule`: a 100 KiB file
    mapped with a 2 MiB granule shows 2 MiB; its sync writes the store at the start and not the one past the end; the
    page granule maps the page span; granules of three pages and of half a page are refused. On macOS and Linux.
  - `crates/cli/tests/pmem.rs`, three runs of three tests each passing, with this test binary as the VMM: the copy is
    2 MiB and the VMM maps and sees 2 MiB; a SIGUSR1 wrote the VMM's page and the file held it; the VM's exit released
    the map, writing the second page and nothing past the end; the launcher's SIGKILL ended the VMM and the reap
    compared its page back; SIGTERM reached the VMM, the release wrote its page and the launcher exited 143.
    Red-checked in a copy of the tree: without the parent-death signal the VMM was alive 20 s after its launcher's
    kill; with SIGUSR1 answered by no sync, the sync wrote 0 bytes of 4,096.
- **The copy survives a takeover** (Step 6.2). A-186's maps ended with their daemon: their records were the process's,
  and recovery drops every SDK client's attachment ("the SDK's client attaches again"), so a successor answered a
  holder's sync `NotFound`, and a guest's later stores never reached the file nor another path's change its map.
  - **The anchor holds each writable copy** with a 16-byte record (the file's inode and the writer attachment; the
    volume, the client and its principal come from the attachment's record, the length from the sealed object), sent
    before the copy is handed to its client, released when it is let go: a new kind on A-61's hold channel, under its
    own bound (`shards × direct_maps_per_shard`), handed to each daemon the anchor spawns in `SLATES_ANCHOR_COPIES`.
  - **The successor takes each back while recovery rebuilds its shard.** It keeps the writer attachment, as it keeps a
    FUSE mount whose device the anchor held; checks the object (sealed against shrinking, growing and new seals, not
    against writes, a whole number of pages: `PeerObject::adopt`); adopts it at the exact slot and generation its
    backing had (`ShardsBackings::adopt_peer`, over the slab's `insert_at`), so the map id its client holds names it
    again; and holds the map under its client. Adoption precedes the write log's replay (A-63), so every write the
    replay applies is written into the copy by the volume's write boundary, as every change is. (Amended 2026-11-18 by
    A-389: the copy is kept dormant through the replay and woken after it. It already holds every write the dead daemon
    made, in order with its client's stores, and the replay written into it wrote a logged write over a store the
    client made after that write.)
  - **The holder claims it.** A client reconnects under its own id; `slates pmem` watches its control socket for its
    daemon's departure (`Client::daemon_watch`, `POLLRDHUP`) and syncs at once, which reconnects and claims the map. A
    map no holder claims within the client's reconnect budget (recovery 1 s + liveness 1 s), counted from the shard's
    start, is written back through its kept attachment and let go with it, as a dead client's maps are reaped:
    `dax.local_map_unclaimed_reclaimed`.
  - **What it does not hold.** A change neither published nor logged when the daemon died, which the write boundary had
    written into the copy, is in the copy and not in the successor's file; the next sync writes it back as the guest's
    own, the bytes the guest's map already showed. Linux alone: a macOS copy keeps a second descriptor the anchor does
    not hold, and Windows' anchor does not yet hold writable copies.
  - **Proven** (adacachy, 2026-11-01): `crates/cli/tests/pmem.rs`, `a_pmem_vmms_copy_survives_a_daemon_takeover_with_
    its_unsynced_store` — the daemon killed under the stand-in VMM's unsynced page, the launcher's resync after its
    departure wrote the page through the successor, a later SIGUSR1 synced through it, and an SDK write after the
    takeover showed in the VMM's map; and `a_copy_no_holder_claims_after_a_takeover_is_written_back_and_let_go` — the
    daemon and the launcher killed together, the successor wrote the unclaimed page back, counted once. Six of six in
    each of three runs at load 46 to 52. Red-checked in a copy of the tree: with no hold sent to the anchor, and with
    recovery taking no copy back, the takeover test found no resync within 20 s; with nothing reclaiming, the unclaimed
    page never reached the file. `PeerObject::adopt` takes back a held copy's bytes both ways and refuses an unsealed
    object and a read-only copy (`crates/mem/tests/peer_object.rs`); the hold channel's copy kind crosses whole, keeps
    its bound and refuses malformed handoffs (`crates/anchor/src/held.rs`, 4 tests). The recovery oracle 43 of 43, the
    anchor's suites and the client's on Linux; the client package once ran eight of its tests `Stalled` past the 1 s
    reply deadline at load 50, and passed whole in each of three runs after.
- **Through real VMMs** (Step 6.3). `crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs` runs each of its three pmem tests twice: over the
  image file through a slates mount, and over a copy `slates pmem` hands the VMM at descriptor 3, with no host mount in
  the VMM's path (Firecracker's `path_on_host`, Cloud Hypervisor's `--pmem file=` and QEMU's `mem-path=` each name
  `/proc/self/fd/3`). Over the copy the test sends the launcher SIGUSR1 where over the mount the guest's flush writes,
  and holds what only the copy does: the guest's store is not in the host's file until the launcher's sync; after the
  guest's own flush slates holds exactly the bytes it held before the store; when the daemon is killed under the live
  map, the launcher's resync writes the store the guest left unsynced through the successor, and the copy the anchor
  held serves the guest on; and a VMM killed under its launcher has its unsynced stores compared back at its exit
  (`released:`), the launcher exiting 137 as its VMM did.
  - **Proven** (adacachy: Linux 7.2.9, x86_64; 2026-11-01): three of three in each of three runs with Firecracker
    v1.17.0 and Cloud Hypervisor v54.0, over both backings, 30 to 42 s a run at load 21 to 37; the resync wrote 498
    bytes each time, the quarter of the patch the guest left unsynced less the two bytes the file already held as the
    patch's byte. QEMU 11.1 (CI's guest image, from Debian's trixie-backports) on CI's ubuntu runner: three of three in
    each of three runs, 31 to 32 s a run, the resync 498 bytes each time (diagnostics run 41307486734). Red-checked in
    a copy of the tree: with the guest mounting `dax=never` over the handed copy alone, the test failed at the DAX
    check (`map docs/sub/b.bin → Mapped { dax: false }`, exit 101), on adacachy with Firecracker and on CI with QEMU.
- **A hostile guest** (Step 6.4). Three tests of `guest_image.rs` play a guest over a handed copy that the launcher and
  the daemon must survive, each through a probe command made for it.
  - **A write past the image's end stays in the copy.** The copy is the file's length rounded up to 2 MiB, so the
    guest's pmem device runs past the file's end. Over a 31 MiB image the guest wrote 64 KiB through its block device
    at the image's end (32,505,856) and at the copy's last 64 KiB (33,488,896 of its 33,554,432 bytes), each read back
    from the device with its cached pages dropped, so from the copy itself. After the launcher's sync (42 to 52 bytes,
    the mount's metadata, within the file) and after the VM's end, the image kept its length, alone in its volume,
    slates held none of those bytes, and the merge changed nothing. Two guards hold it, each enough alone: a
    compare-back stops at the file's length when it began (`direct_map.rs`), and compares only as far as the file's
    bytes reach (`write_back_runs` in `crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`). Red-checked in a copy of the tree:
    with the first removed the second held and the test passed its checks; with both removed the launcher's sync wrote
    131,124 bytes, the two runs and the metadata, and the image grew to 33,554,432 bytes, which the test refused.
  - **A flush storm asks nothing of slates.** The guest stored the patch and synced its map 10,000 times over, each
    sync a flush of its device, in 241 to 795 ms. The daemon's served requests (every client request records its
    completion) rose by what a `slates status` read costs alone, no map was synced, and slates held none of the stores;
    the launcher's one sync then raised both counts and put the patch in slates. Served requests count no FUSE request,
    so the bytes are the check that no flush wrote through any path: red-checked over the image file through a mount,
    the same storm left the patch in slates and the test refused it.
  - **A guest killed mid-store leaves each byte compared back or lost.** The guest swept the large file's whole pages
    (196,608 bytes) a byte at a time, sweep after sweep, each sweep's byte one more than the last's; the launcher synced
    until a sync wrote at least half a sweep's bytes, so the guest was storing; then the VMM alone was killed. Its
    launcher's compare-back at the VM's exit wrote what the guest had changed since the last sync (all 196,608 swept
    bytes each time on adacachy, where it had swept on), and the launcher exited 137; a second guest read one sweep's byte up to the point the kill reached and the sweep before's
    after it, exactly, as x86's in-order stores leave them; the file's last part, the other files, the image's length
    and the other volumes were as they were. Each of the six kills landed mid-sweep (sweeps 42 to 227, at bytes 4,204
    to 147,662). Red-checked with a release that lets the copy go without comparing it back: it wrote 0 bytes, which
    the test refused. arm64 may make stores visible out of order, so there the test holds each byte past the point to
    the sweep's byte or what was there; and a kill during the first sweep would leave the file's own bytes past the
    point, which the test takes as the sweep before's.
  - **Proven** (adacachy, 2026-11-01): the seven tests of `guest_image.rs`, the three above among them, seven of seven
    in each of three runs with Firecracker v1.17.0 and Cloud Hypervisor v54.0, 52 to 73 s a run at load 23 to 33.
    QEMU 11.1 on CI's ubuntu runner: seven of seven in each of three runs, 50 to 51 s a run (diagnostics run
    41310124785); its storms took 811 to 850 ms, each kill landed mid-sweep (sweeps 136 to 189, at bytes 3,670 to
    168,301), and each release at the VM's exit wrote 192,600 to 196,608 bytes.
- **The matrix** (Step 6.5). With no host mount in a pmem VMM's path, the copy `slates pmem` hands it is a socket
  route: Firecracker's cell on Linux x86_64 turns from impossible to proven, Cloud Hypervisor's from impossible to proven
  for an image (its fs device has no window, so a file tree still has no such route), and QEMU's, proven by slates' own
  device (A-189), gains the same route for an image (`docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8).
- **Owed** (GAPS): Firecracker on arm64 over a handed copy (Step 6.6, on the nested arm64 KVM host Step 7 builds); a
  writable copy across a takeover on macOS and Windows.

### A-196 — A guest's write through slates' own device or a Shards stream is answered once every FUSE mount of its volume has been told, and the device serves on while the reply waits (accepted and built 2026-11-01)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 ("Cache posture": the paragraph on when a mount is told), Phase 3's AC-3.3, A-191
("What it does not change"), GAPS (the AC-3.3 entry's owed guests), `crates/bridge-virtiofs` (`device.rs`: the told hold
— `hold_replies_for_told`, `hold_or_publish`, `settle_told`, `told_oldest`, a pass's `Serviced::published`, and the
module's note on `FUSE_INTERRUPT`; `admission.rs`: the same through the admitted device, and a pass notifying a queue
only for the replies it published; `backed.rs`: a held request's journal mark and a held reply's owed record;
`serve.rs`: `BridgeAccess`'s told wait, the loop's race of its doorbell, a request and the oldest held reply's wait or
bound, `TOLD_ABANDONED`), `crates/server` (`told.rs`: `told_through`, `parked`, `count_settled`; `virtiofs.rs`: the
bridge's told wait on the owner shard; `shards.rs`: a stream's reply flushed only once its record was told), the tests
(`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/serve.rs` and `tests/admission.rs`; `crates/server/tests/shards.rs`, with
`tests/common/fuse_map.rs`, new, the map reader A-191's test had kept to itself; `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs` and
`tests/vm/mod.rs`), and CLAUDE.md.
- **What was open.** A-191 holds the reply of every writer outside FUSE that holds no kernel lock until every FUSE mount
  of its volume has been told. A guest's write through slates' own virtio-fs device (in-process or `slates vhost-user`)
  or a Shards stream was still answered as soon as it was applied (GAPS, the AC-3.3 entry), so a host process reading the
  file through a FUSE mount right after the guest's write returned could see the old bytes. The device's loop answered
  its requests in order, so holding one reply would have stalled every request behind it.
- **The rule for slates' own device.** Before the device serves a request it notes its volume's journal head
  (`Bridge::seen`, the journal `told::mark` notes). A request whose serving made a newer record owes every FUSE mount of
  the volume that record. The device keeps its reply aside, its chain and its credits with it, and goes on serving the
  guest's later requests; the loop publishes it once every mount has been told through the record. Virtio allows this:
  "Device is not generally required to use buffers in the same order in which they have been made available by the
  driver" (virtio 1.2 §2.6), and the device never offers `VIRTIO_F_IN_ORDER` (§2.7.9; `OFFERED_FEATURES` is
  `VIRTIO_F_VERSION_1` and the protocol-features bit). Only the told wait completes out of order:
  - a request held for the ingest of the guest's DAX stores (a sync's write-back) keeps its order, and its reply, which
    covers the records the ingest wrote, waits for the mounts after it;
  - a reply that waits for the owner's barrier (D-18) is published only after the barrier, then waits for the mounts.
- **How the loop settles.** After every pass, and whenever the oldest held reply's wait or its bound wakes the idle loop
  (the loop races its doorbell, a request and that one wait), it publishes each held reply whose mounts were told, and
  each that has waited the bound: A-191's half the liveness budget, 500 ms, counted from the first settle that saw the
  reply. A reply past the bound is published all the same and counted `fuse.told_overdue`: never held for good. A reply
  already told when its pass ends — always, on a volume no FUSE mount holds anything of — is published at the pass's
  end, uncounted, so a pass's write replies go out together after it rather than one by one. A pass notifies a queue
  only for the replies it published, and a settle for the ones it published, so the guest is never woken with nothing
  new in its used ring.
  - **Bounded.** The held replies are at most the sum of the device's queue sizes, each one of the guest's descriptor
    chains; a reply past that is published at once. One wait is parked at a time, the oldest held reply's.
  - **Switched on by the settling loop alone** (`serve_loop` calls `hold_replies_for_told`), so no other caller of the
    device can strand a reply.
  - **Counted** on A-191's ledger: a reply that waited, `fuse.told_waits`; one published at the bound,
    `fuse.told_overdue` as well. A reply still held when the device ends — its guest gone, or the device revoked — goes
    unsent with every other reply in flight at an end, its write applied, counted `virtiofs.told_abandoned`.
  - **Interrupts.** The device still answers `FUSE_INTERRUPT` `ENOSYS`: a held reply is a request already applied,
    which an interrupt could not undo, waiting at most the bound.
- **The rule for a Shards stream.** Shards' VMM sends one request at a time on a stream and reads its reply before the
  next (one lock across the frame's write and the reply's read: Shards' `crates/vmm/src/devices/virtio/fs/mod.rs`,
  `Slot::ask`), so nothing queues behind a held reply. The stream's reply frame is flushed only once its record has been
  told, the serve task awaiting A-191's `told::wait` as an SDK verb's held reply does. A request held for the ingest of
  the guest's DAX stores takes its mark when it is held, so what its sync writes back is covered.
- **Where the wait runs.** The device and the stream serve on the volume's owner shard, which serves the volume and all
  its FUSE mounts (A-191), so the wait is a parked waker on that shard, woken as a mount is told further or ends, and
  the shard serves on.
- **Found on the way.** The first build notified a queue for every chain a pass served, held replies included, so a
  pass whose only reply was held woke the guest with nothing in its used ring. The daemon's vhost-user tests, whose
  front end reaps once per interrupt, found it on Linux (`crates/server/tests/virtiofs.rs`, "a used element after the
  interrupt", two tests of 23); the pass now counts what it published (`Serviced::published`), and an admission test
  holds it on every host.
- **Proven** (adacachy: Linux 7.2.9-2-cachyos, x86_64, 32 cores, crosvm 0.1.0, `fusermount3`, 2026-11-01, load 24–36
  unless stated):
  - **Through a real guest** (`crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs`): a guest mounting the tag with `dax=never` wrote a page
    200 times while a host process mapped the file read-only through a `slates mount`, reading the map as memory alone
    the moment each write returned. 0 of 200 first reads were stale on an anchor of one shard and 0 of 200 on two, in
    each of three runs, every write's reply counted waiting and none overdue. In the two runs that printed it, a write
    took 1.9 and 1.6 ms at the median and 40 and 68 ms at p99 on one shard, 2.4 and 2.0 ms and 43 and 56 ms on two, as
    the test saw it, the serial console's carriage included.
  - **In QEMU** 11.1.2 with KVM, on CI's x86_64 runner (diagnostics run 41292937267): 0 of 200 on one shard and on two,
    every write waiting and none overdue, a write's median 4.1 and 4.9 ms; every test of `tests/guest_vhost.rs` passed,
    8 of 8.
  - **Red-checked**, a copy of the tree whose device holds nothing: 1 of 200 first reads stale and no write waiting
    through crosvm (one shard, load 205), and 0 of 200 in QEMU. Few or none, because the guest's close of the file (its
    `FLUSH` and `RELEASE`) and the console give the mount's round time before the test reads; the counted waits, 0
    against 200, are the check that cannot miss, and failed the copy both times.
  - **Hermetic** (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/serve.rs`, a stand-in FUSE mount whose round is held; macOS and Linux):
    the write's reply was published at 202.3 ms, past a 200 ms bound, counted overdue, while a read the guest sent after
    it was published at 195 µs. Red-checked: the copy whose device holds nothing fails it.
  - **A Shards stream** (`crates/server/tests/shards.rs`): 0 of 200 first reads stale, 200 waits, none overdue, on
    adacachy and on CI's x86_64 and arm64 runners (Linux 7.0, diagnostics run 41292937267); the copy whose stream waits
    for nothing read 196, 191 and 141 of 200 stale there.
  - **The notification**, `a_pass_notifies_a_queue_only_for_the_replies_it_published` (`tests/admission.rs`); the copy
    that notifies for every chain served fails it on adacachy and both CI runners, and fails three of the daemon's
    vhost-user tests.
  - **Chaos.** Hermetic: the guest killed while its write's reply waits ends the loop at once, not at the bound, with
    its wait on the mount gone, every credit restored, the reply counted abandoned and the write applied; the daemon
    stopped while the reply waits takes the wait with it. Through crosvm: 12 guests killed at 12 points across their
    write's round trip, in each of two runs — every page held all of one write or all of the other (3 and 4 of 12 cut
    writes applied), every device ended and let its attachment go, and the host's map came to show what the volume
    held. None of the 24 landed inside the hold (`virtiofs.told_abandoned` 0), which lasts about a mount's delivery
    (median 82 µs, A-191) of a round of 2–35 ms. In QEMU one of 12 did: its reply was counted abandoned, its write was
    applied, and the map showed it 256 µs later (4 of 12 cut writes applied). The hermetic test is what holds that case
    every time. And 6 daemons killed under a guest's write, in each of two crosvm runs and one QEMU run, and taken over
    by the anchor's successor: every page whole (1, 1 and 2 of 6 applied), the host's map through the mount the
    successor took over showing the successor's page within 2.7–5.2 ms through crosvm (its first run's figures) and
    276–396 µs in QEMU, and the next guest's writes told before they returned.
  - Every test of `tests/guest_vhost.rs` passed through crosvm and QEMU (8 of 8), the DAX tests included with the hold
    on; the virtio-fs suites, the server's virtiofs (23 of 23), shards, fuse_told and recovery suites and the client's
    shards suite on adacachy and both CI runners, where A-191's SDK and NFS cases still read 0 of 200 stale; Linux
    clippy `-D warnings` for `slates-bridge-virtiofs`, `slates-server`, `slates-client` and `slates-cli`, every target;
    the Linux doc gate.
- **Cost.** Not measured apart. A held reply waits for the mount's notify thread as an SDK write does (A-191: p50 about
  +12 µs with a mount, nothing without), and a guest's round through the console is milliseconds, so the test's round
  times cannot show it. Owed (GAPS).
- **What it does not change.** A write through a FUSE mount (A-191's window). A retry of a held request is answered from
  its completion record at once. A guest's DAX stores reach the volume at its sync points, as before (A-168); the sync's
  reply now waits for the mounts like a write's.

### A-195 — One window kind: the fd-sharing placer maps per-file backings as the message placer does, and every path that mapped the arena's blocks into a guest is removed (accepted and built 2026-11-01)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the DAX rule restated for backings; a status for the one window kind; the DAX
gate's, the device-seam wiring's and the 2026-10-16 binding's records, and the open-frontier decision with its
amendment, marked superseded; the threat model's arena layers L0, L1's zones, L2 and B2 marked removed, its first two
residuals restated for backings, and the backed layer's wording no longer leaning on the zones), GAPS (the 2026-11-01
entry; the gate checklist of 2026-10-18 and the gate's 2026-10-12 entry marked superseded), `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`
(the `dax_bench` and `dax_backing_ab` sections retired), `crates/vfs` (`dax.rs`, `daxzone.rs`, `tests/dax.rs` and the
examples `dax_bench.rs` and `dax_backing_ab.rs` removed; `volume.rs`: the store's registry and zones, the writable-DAX
and integrity-guard opt-ins, the revokes on write, truncate, snapshot and destroy, the reseal machinery and the
pin-defers-seal check removed; `content.rs`: reopening in place, relocation and resealing removed; `error.rs`:
`RecallInFlight` and `NoPhysicalIsolation` removed; `shards_backing.rs`: `of_file`; tests), `crates/mem` (`arena.rs`:
the pin API and `block_backing` removed; `region.rs`: `backing_fd`, `backing_base`, `collapse_huge` and
`huge_backed_bytes` removed; `error.rs`: `ExtentRefusal::NotPinned` removed; `shared.rs`: the placed mapping's and the
huge-page advice's docs; tests), `crates/machine/src/facts.rs` (`huge_page_bytes`'s doc), `crates/bridge-core` (the
`Bridge` trait's seven content-block methods and `DaxState::registry` removed, with their implementations in
`volume_bridge.rs` and `scoped.rs`; `dax_backing.rs`: `Refused::Busy` removed; the scoped mount's confinement test moved
onto the backed session), `crates/bridge-fuse` (the busy refusal's errno removed; docs), `crates/bridge-virtiofs`
(`backed.rs` on every Unix; `device.rs`: both placers through one backed path, the fd-sharing placer's pieces overlaid
and acknowledged at once, `view_advanced`, `dax_window_store`, `dax_overlays`, and the content-block windows, their
teardown, the revoke drain and the remap rollback removed; `dax.rs`: `DaxCacheRegion::check_window`,
`DaxPlacer::window_fits`; `admission.rs`: the revoke wrappers and `dax_window_revokes` removed, `view_advanced`,
`dax_window_store`, the in-process gate's stated reason; `serve.rs`: the backed turn, the end's ingest and the counts on
every Unix, a kick a moved view; `capability.rs`: the reason; tests: the backed fixture takes a placer, every backed test
runs over both, a property test, and the admission test through the serve loop's entry points), and `crates/server`
(`daemon.rs`: the shift loop and the scrub pass removed, the reap tick re-arming placement alone; `config.rs`:
`DAX_SHIFT_CADENCE_NS` and the shift's mention in the copy slice removed; `verbs.rs`: the snapshot's recall removed;
`direct_map.rs`: the exclusion with an in-process writable window removed; `shards/dax.rs`: `shards.dax_busy` removed;
`virtiofs.rs`, `snapshot_view.rs`: the advance kick's docs).
- **Decided by A-168**, for the day an in-process VMM ships: an fd-sharing window maps per-file backings as the message
  placer's does. Built now, so production has one window kind and no path maps the arena's blocks into a guest.
- **How the fd-sharing placer maps.** A SETUPMAPPING is held while its ranges fill a copy slice a turn, exactly as for
  the message placer. The device then overlays each piece of the window (two under the guarded layout, A-194; one under
  the identity) with `MAP_FIXED` of the backing's object, and acknowledges each at once through the completion the
  message placer's acknowledgements use. A window is recorded whole or refused whole (`EIO`, the pieces that did map
  unmapped again). A REMOVEMAPPING restores each piece's range to the inert reservation before its answer. Both placers
  lay backings out guarded where ranges can be huge, since the device names each piece's place either way; the ingest,
  the refill, placement and the fill budget are the same code for both.
- **Removed, not layered** (CLAUDE.md banned item 7): everything only the arena's windows used.
  - The VFS's DAX gate (`slates_vfs::dax`): the mapping registry; maps of the open frontier, of directories and of
    inline files; the arena's pins and the two-phase revoke; `reopen`-on-map and its reseal; the snapshot recall and its
    exclusion (`RecallInFlight`); the revokes on write, truncate, snapshot and destroy; B2's guards and scrub.
  - The writable-DAX opt-in (L0) and the integrity-guard opt-in.
  - L1's zones (`slates_vfs::daxzone`) and L2's shift (`dax_migrate`, `NoPhysicalIsolation`).
  - The daemon's DAX loops: the shift loop, awake every 16 ms while any volume had writable DAX, and the scrub pass on
    the reap tick. The shard's perpetual-task count (`LOOP_TASKS_PER_SHARD`, five) had never counted the shift loop.
  - The arena's pin API, `ChunkArena::block_backing`, and the region accessors only those used.
  - The `Bridge` trait's seven content-block methods, the device's content-block map paths, its revoke drain and remap
    rollback, and admission's revoke wrappers.
  - The backed session's refusal of a file an in-process guest mapped writable (`Refused::Busy`, `shards.dax_busy`) and
    the direct map's matching exclusion: no such window exists any more.

  14,237 lines of code and tests removed and 2,805 added (`git diff --shortstat`, 2026-11-01, before the docs).
- **Kept:** the backed route whole (A-163, A-168, A-193, A-194); every shared object's congruent placement and the
  huge-page advice, which a backing's views use (`crates/mem/src/shared.rs`); `region::collapse_huge`, which a placement
  asks.
- **What a moved view does now.** A snapshot reader's `advance` marks the device's backings stale, so each refills from
  the new view before its guest sees anything more. No window is torn, for either placer.
- **What the in-process seam still refuses.** Admission refuses DAX over the in-process seam (`DaxNotEstablished`), and
  the capability report advertises none there. Isolation and teardown hold there by the same construction as over
  vhost-user now, but no in-process VMM has run a guest over it, and a simulated driver cannot close a transport
  guarantee (AC-9.7). The stated reason was "until mapping isolation, pinning and teardown have been established", which
  this change made false; it now says what is missing.
- **The unsafe budget** is unchanged: slates-vfs 0 of 0, slates-bridge-virtiofs 3 of 3, slates-mem 61 of 61
  (`cargo xtask unsafe`).
- **Proven** 2026-11-01 (§4.6 status): macOS's suites, CI's x86_64 and arm64 runners with both placers, three
  red-checks of the fd-sharing placer, and real VMMs: the virtio-fs suites 72 of 72 on macOS and 85 of 85 on each Linux
  runner (diagnostics run 41283211879), every range placed for both placers there; QEMU 11.1.2 with KVM, `guest_vhost.rs`
  5 of 5 in 11.87 s, and crosvm on adacachy 5 of 5 in 11.40 s at load 181 to 387. Each red-check fails its own
  assertions on both runners (diagnostics run 41283778280): each piece overlaid at the window's own offset rather than
  its place in the object, a REMOVEMAPPING that leaves its overlays, and a moved view that refills nothing.

### A-194 — slates' own device lays its backings out guarded: the first and last chunk window of every page held empty, and each guest window mapped as two pieces from page interiors (accepted and built 2026-11-01)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the backed route's layer: the layout, what it buys, its cost, its limits),
GAPS (the 2026-10-31 entry), `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md` (the placement's cost under the guard), `CLAUDE.md` (the
canonical example), `crates/mem` (`dax_object.rs`: `DaxLayout`, `DaxPiece`, `DaxPieces`; `DaxObject::create` takes a
layout, its offsets go through it, `place_range` places every page a range lies in, `placed_pages`, `page_pmd_bytes`;
the host's huge-page fact asked once; `tests/dax_layout.rs` new, `tests/dax_object.rs`, `tests/dax_section.rs`),
`crates/vfs/src/shards_backing.rs` (`BackingObject::layout`, `PagePlacement`, `placed_pages`; its tests),
`crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs` (`DaxBackingSession::with_layout`, `layout`, `guarded_layout`, the charge in
pages, `offer` by layout; its tests), `crates/bridge-virtiofs` (`backed.rs`: `BackedPiece`, `window_pieces`, the held
map's pieces, `file_range_fits` by layout; `device.rs`: pieces sent together and acknowledged, a refused piece undoing
the window, an unmap per piece; `vhost_user.rs`: `has_room_for`; `serve.rs`: control messages served while map acknowledgements are owed;
`tests/device.rs`: the stand-in front end maps a window's pieces), and `crates/server` (`virtiofs.rs`: the guarded offer;
`shards/dax.rs`: the identity offer).
- **Corrects A-193**, which rejected guard rows for backings as impossible and a guard by splitting each range as not
  worth its cost, for three reasons, none of which holds:
  - "it breaks the identity layout the Shards protocol shares": only the Shards route's VMM maps by the file's own
    offsets. slates' own device names every SHMEM_MAP's descriptor offset itself, so its backings can lie as it chooses;
  - "a guard's worth in rows depends on the memory controller's undocumented interleaving": true, and equally true of
    the arena's zones, whose one-slot guard §4.6 L1 already takes on the same bet;
  - "it costs memory": the step asked for exactly that, a defense whose memory cost is measured and bounded by the fill
    budget. The cost is two pages for a range alone and sixteen for fifteen in a row, not the double A-193 assumed.
- **The layout.** A guarded object holds the file in the interiors of consecutive 2 MiB pages, the first and last chunk
  window of each page (64 KiB on a 4 KiB-paged host, the zones' slot, `slates_vfs::content::chunk_bytes`) held empty. An
  interior is 1,920 KiB, fifteen parts of 128 KiB, and a guest range is sixteen, so every range is exactly two pieces,
  never three (`a_guest_range_is_two_pieces_inside_page_interiors_under_a_guard`). Neighbouring ranges share the page
  between them, a window mapping only its own range's part. The layout is `guarded_layout()`, asked once a process:
  guarded where the host places a range in one huge page, the identity elsewhere, since a guard isolates nothing without
  one.
- **The device.** A SETUPMAPPING's pieces are sent together after the ring's room is asked for all of them, so a window
  is never half sent for want of room; the guest is answered on the last acknowledgement. A refused piece fails the
  SETUPMAPPING with `EIO` and the pieces that did map are unmapped, so a window is mapped whole or not at all. An unmap
  goes a piece at a time, since vhost-user requires an unmap to name the whole of one mapped region.
- **Found by QEMU 11.1's guest tests, fixed in the same change:** QEMU answers each SHMEM_MAP and then commits it,
  sending `SET_MEM_TABLE` and waiting for the back end's answer before it reads the next request
  (`hw/virtio/vhost-user.c`). The serve loop waited for the second piece's acknowledgement and served nothing else, so
  all five tests of `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs` hung at the guest's first read (diagnostics run 41277950761). The
  wait now races the doorbell and serves the front end's control messages (`drive_dax_acks`), and a kick it drains
  meanwhile gets another pass. One piece a window never met this, since the loop's wait ended at the first
  acknowledgement; crosvm sends no table on a map.
- **What it costs.** A one-page file mapped holds 4 MiB, not 2 MiB. The fill budget counts the pages a backing's filled
  ranges lie in, so placed bytes never exceed what it counts. A VMM maps two pieces a window; QEMU makes a memory region
  of each, which halves the windows a guest has before QEMU's eight-region table without `CONFIGURE_MEM_SLOTS` (owed,
  GAPS). The pieces map with base-page entries, not the PMD entry a whole aligned range could take.
- **Kept:** the Shards route's identity layout (its protocol fixes it), and with it placement without guard rows there.
- **Measured and proven** 2026-11-01, on adacachy (Linux 7.2.9) and on CI's x86_64 and arm64 runners (Linux 7.0,
  diagnostics run 41277950761):
  - every range placed;
  - each placed page one PMD page in slates' view;
  - every piece inside an interior, every guard slot empty after the guest's stores across a whole window;
  - each object exactly its pages, counted alike: 8,388,608 bytes for two lone ranges, 4,194,304 and 6,291,456 for one
    range and for two neighbours;
  - four red-checks, each failing on its own assertion: placement off, a placed page punched, the memo off, and the
    interior widened into a guard.

  Real VMMs: QEMU 11.1.2 with KVM, `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs` 5 of 5 in 9.62 s, every range placed (diagnostics
  run 41278779089, after the deadlock below was fixed); crosvm on adacachy, 5 of 5 in 33.18 s, three windows placed
  and three declined on the loaded box, every guest's bytes right.

### A-193 — Reading alone hammers: §4.6's read-only premise corrected, and every range a guest maps over a backing is placed in one huge page (accepted and built 2026-10-31)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (Rowhammer: L0's premise corrected; the backed route's layer, its cost, its limits
and the floor beneath it; the layers' summary), GAPS (the 2026-10-13 multi-tenancy entry's L0, and a 2026-10-31
entry), `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md` (what a placement costs in memory and in a fill step), `CLAUDE.md` (the placement as a
canonical example, with its gotchas), `crates/mem` (`dax_object.rs`:
`Placement`, `DaxObject::place_range`, `placed_ranges`, `placed`, `range_pmd_bytes`, and a placed range zeroed by
stores; `shared.rs`: `RangeView::collapse_huge` and `pmd_bytes`; `region.rs`: `collapse_huge` shared within the crate,
saying whether a decline is transient; `lib.rs`), `crates/vfs/src/shards_backing.rs` (`BackingObject::place_range`,
`ShardsBackings::place` with its memo, `rearm_placement`, `placement_declined`, `placements_asked`, `placed_ranges` and
`placements`, `RangePlacement`; `volume.rs`: the writable-DAX gate's comment corrected), `crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs` (each range placed as its fill finishes;
`Counts::placed` and `placement_refused`) with `tests/dax_backing.rs`, `crates/bridge-virtiofs` (`backed.rs`:
`virtiofs.dax_placed` and `virtiofs.dax_placement_refused`; `tests/device.rs`: three tests, the stand-in front end's map
placed congruent with the object, its unmaps acknowledged, and the forget test's REMOVEMAPPING body corrected), and
`crates/server/src/shards/dax.rs` (`shards.dax_placed`, `shards.dax_placement_refused`), and
`crates/server/src/daemon.rs` (the reap tick re-arms the placement memo).
- **Corrects §4.6's L0.** It said a writable mapping is the only DAX mode a guest can hammer, and that read-only DAX
  cannot hammer a neighbour. The primary sources say otherwise:
  - Kim et al. corrupted nearby data "by reading from the same address in DRAM", with a user-level loop of loads that
    flushes the line between them (ISCA 2014);
  - Project Zero: "repeatedly accessing a row of memory can cause bit flips in adjacent rows" (Seaborn and Dullien,
    2015).

  The gate still bounds a guest's stores into the arena. It bounds no hammering.
- **Adds the backed route's layer.** The windows production serves map per-file backings (A-168; the Shards route maps
  the same objects, A-163), and L1, L2 and B2 were built on the arena, so every window production served carried no
  Rowhammer layer. Each range of a backing is now placed in one huge page as its fill finishes, before the ask is
  answered: slates' view placed congruent with the object, one byte read so the object holds a page there, and
  `MADV_COLLAPSE` asked about the view's span. A placed range is 2 MiB of contiguous memory of its own; where 2 MiB
  spans several DRAM rows of each bank, foreign rows lie beside it only at its two ends (§4.6 says where it buys less).
- **Placed after the fill, never before.** A fill that fails part-way unmarks its range and gives its charge back, and a
  huge page placed before it would stay resident and uncounted. Placed last, a placed range is always a filled one,
  which the budget counts as 2 MiB, so the placed bytes never exceed what the budget counts. The price is a collapse
  that copies the pages the fill stored, rather than stores into a page placed first.
- **A declined collapse is served on base pages, counted, never refused.** A guest's access fails with its
  SETUPMAPPING: `fuse_iomap_begin` returns `fuse_setup_new_dax_mapping`'s error to the access itself (`fs/fuse/dax.c`),
  with no fallback to the queue. A defence that refused there would turn a fragmented host into a guest that cannot
  read its files. The refusal shows in the status report (`virtiofs.dax_placement_refused`,
  `shards.dax_placement_refused`), so an operator sees where the layer did not apply.
- **A placed range is zeroed by stores.** A cut over it punched its pages, which splits a huge page (`mm/shmem.c`), so a
  cut stores zeros over its whole pages instead, at the cost of the bytes zeroed.
- **A decline likely to hold is remembered until the reap tick.** A declined collapse charges the shard the kernel's
  compaction effort first: 1,954 and 2,832 µs a fill step on adacachy at load 90. So `ShardsBackings::place` remembers a
  decline other than `EAGAIN`, serves the next ranges on base pages without asking, and the daemon's reap tick re-arms
  it beside the arena zones' memo. A host out of huge pages is asked at most once a tick per shard, and a guest churning
  its ranges cannot make the shard pay the compaction again and again. Proven in a child process whose huge pages the
  kernel refuses (`a_declined_placement_is_remembered_until_re_armed`).
- **Rejected** (the first and third overturned the next day by A-194, which builds guard rows inside each page: their
  reasons did not hold; rows outside a page and L2's shift still cannot apply):
  - *guard rows* in the range, since a Linux guest maps each range whole, `inarg.len = FUSE_DAX_SZ`, 2 MiB
    (`fs/fuse/dax.c`), so its rows include the page's edge rows;
  - *guard rows* beside it, which need memory known to lie physically beside the page: an unprivileged process sees no
    frame number since Linux 4.2 (`pagemap.rst`: "information about PFNs helps in exploiting Rowhammer vulnerability"),
    and a page larger than a PMD is hugetlb's, reserved by an administrator (R10);
  - *a guard by splitting each range* over the middles of two huge pages: twice a placed range's memory, the identity
    layout the Shards protocol shares broken (A-163), and a guard whose worth in rows depends on how the memory
    controller interleaves channels, ranks and banks, which is undocumented and learned only by reverse engineering
    (DRAMA, Pessl et al., USENIX Security 2016);
  - *L2's shift*, which needs a map over a live window: the vhost-user specification forbids it, and unmapping first
    opens the zero-page gap a real guest read (A-168).
- **Measured** on adacachy (Linux 7.2.9, x86_64, 4 KiB pages, `shmem_enabled` `[advise]`) and on CI's x86_64 and arm64
  runners (Linux 7.0, `shmem_enabled` `[never]`; diagnostics run 41271016248), 2026-10-31:
  - every range the tests filled was placed, 2 of 2, 3 of 3, 1 of 1 and 2 of 2, none refused, except one adacachy run
    at load 90 whose kernel declined both;
  - each object held exactly its placed ranges' bytes by `fstat`'s `st_blocks`: 4,194,304 against 4,194,304 counted, and
    2,097,152 and 4,194,304 against 6,291,456 counted, of a 16,777,216-byte budget;
  - a fill step that places its range took 193 to 359 µs on CI, a declined one 1,954 and 2,832 µs on adacachy (BENCHMARKS).
- **Proven** by `each_range_a_guest_maps_is_one_huge_page_within_the_fill_budget` (`crates/bridge-core/tests/dax_backing.rs`)
  and three device tests (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`):
  - `every_window_over_a_backing_is_one_huge_page_read_only_or_writable`, which reads each placed range's PMD mapping in
    slates' view and in the front end's map, and holds it across a cut;
  - `a_hostile_guests_churn_over_placed_backings_is_served_as_before_and_leaks_nothing`;
  - `a_read_only_attachments_window_is_placed_and_its_writable_ask_refused`.

  With the memo's test, they pass on adacachy and on both CI runners. Red-checked on both runners, each mutation failing
  on its own assertion: placement off failed all five placement tests; a placed range punched rather than zeroed failed
  the cut's PMD check; the memo off failed "the kernel asked once for the three". The tests skip loudly where a host's
  PMD page is not a range, or where its kernel declined every placement. macOS gives user programs no huge page
  (Appendix C), and Windows' large pages need a privilege R10 refuses, so placement there is `Placement::Unavailable`.
- **Owed:** B2 over read-only backings (compare each with the volume on the reap tick, as B2 compares the arena's
  guarded blocks). Found on the way and reported, not changed here: the arena zone's guard slot (`GUARD_SLOTS`, one
  64 KiB slot) is sized in bytes, and what a guard of bytes is worth in rows depends on the same undocumented
  interleaving; a 64 KiB slot may hold less than one row across the banks it touches.

### A-192 — An NFS v3 write-back that would put stale bytes back over another path's newer change is refused: the winner of Ada's A/B against sync-point coherence (accepted and built 2026-10-31)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the macOS fallback: a stale write-back is refused, with its status), GAPS (the
macOS writable maps entry, settled), `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (the macOS bare-metal mount-route cell),
`docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` (the footprint as a canonical example, with its gotchas), `crates/server`
(`nfs_writeback.rs`, new, with its unit test; `nfs.rs`: an id and a footprint for every connection, both moved with it
between shards, a WRITE judged before it is served, a READ's bytes and a call's own records noted after it;
`nfs_tls.rs`: a session's footprint; `xshard.rs`: `run_on_waiting`; `state.rs`, `daemon.rs`, `lib.rs`;
`tests/nfs_writeback.rs`, new), `crates/bridge-fuse`
(`coherence.rs`: an empty range clipped to nothing), `crates/cli/examples/nfs_writeback_ab.rs` (new), and three records
in `docs/bugs/` (2026-10-31: the byte states' empty range, a connection's end sent to every shard, a keeper that took
a newer tracker); in a second commit the same day, `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` (the dirty-page test through Apple's
client, on CI's macOS runner), `crates/server/tests/common/client.rs` (new: the client helpers on every platform, so the
write-back suite builds on Windows) and
`docs/bugs/2026-10-21-a-dirty-shared-map-page-overwrites-a-later-write-through-another-path.md` (its macOS side,
decided); in a third, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the three Windows NFS steps run the write-back suite).
- **What was open.** An NFS v3 client writes a dirty page back whole: the program's stores and the rest of the page as
  it was fetched. Through Apple's client a page dirtied through a shared map and not synced while another path replaced
  the file came back over the replacement, and the replacement's 16,384 bytes were lost (3 of 3, diagnostics run
  40821794698). NFS v3 has no recall, and Apple's NFSv4.1 recall returns the delegation without flushing, so the
  client cannot be made to flush first (GAPS). The open question was what the server does with such a write-back.
- **How it was decided.** Ada asked for the routes built in isolated worktrees, A/B tested, and the winner picked on
  robustness (adversarial edge cases, fault tolerance) and performance (throughput, resource consumption). Arm A was the
  status quo: maps coherent at sync points, the stale write-back applied. Arm B refuses it. Applying the write-back
  except its stale bytes was not an arm: it is an inferred merge (banned item 11), which Ada's answer did not
  authorize.
- **The rule (arm B).** The server keeps, per connection, A-140's byte states for each file the client touched: a READ
  makes the bytes it returned fresh as of the journal's head, the connection's own changes refresh what they wrote,
  another path's change makes earlier-fetched bytes stale, and a byte never fetched is absent, so a write made without
  reading is applied. A per-volume tracker's consumer task, parked on the volume's change generation and reading the
  journal as a reader of its own (A-157), feeds every change into every connection's states as it is made; each
  tracker has exactly the task spawned for it. A WRITE whose stale bytes differ from the file's bytes now is refused
  whole, `NFS3ERR_IO`, and nothing of it applied; stale bytes equal to the file's are applied. Where the states cannot
  tell (a file lost for room, a journal overrun) the WRITE is refused too. The states are charged to the metadata
  ledger. A connection carries a footprint, the shards its READs and WRITEs were served on, and however it ends its
  states are dropped there and only there.
- **Robustness.** The adversarial suite (`crates/server/tests/nfs_writeback.rs`, driving the export with a hand-rolled
  client as a cache does): arm B 6 of 6, arm A 2 of 6. Arm A failed every case of a stale page against another path's
  write — the SDK's replace, a second client's write, a cut the stale page brought back to 32,768 bytes, a volume of
  either shard — each silently; both arms applied every write-back nobody overtook (alone, beside another client's page,
  after a refetch, a blind write, an identical rewrite) and answered hostile offsets. Through Apple's client (macOS
  26.6.2 on CI's runner, diagnostics runs 41230091726 and 41233122465), in each order of a store and another path's
  write — the measured order, the same with no `stat` before the `msync`, and the other path first — arm A lost the
  other path's write in every run (9 of 9) and arm B kept it in every run (9 of 9); the measured order is now a test of
  the CLI suite on CI's macOS runner (`a_dirty_shared_map_page_never_undoes_a_later_write_through_the_nfs_mount`; with
  the refusal disabled it fails with 16,383 of 16,384 bytes the page's stale copy, on this Mac's own client), and
  the suite's five other mapped-mount tests, which write through a map around other paths' changes, pass through
  Apple's client with the rule in place. The Windows NFS server judges alike: the suite passes 7 of 7 on jupiter one test
  at a time (236 s), as CI's three Windows lanes now run it. The hostile NFS suite, interleaved
  on fedora-2 under its caps (`CPUWeight=1`), passed 8 of 8 in each arm at load 72–139 with arm B as landed. An earlier
  series at load 24–63 found the keeper defect below in arm B, and failed the broken-connections test the same way in
  both arms once each (`SYSTEM_ERR` to an honest client, A's daemon reporting its shard starved 1.6 s): main's, not
  this change's. In that series arm B also stalled the stale-handle test's attackers once for its whole 2 s window
  (0 attempts), a test in which arm B does nothing but look its tracker up and find none; 0 of the other 13 runs of
  each arm did.
- **Performance** (`docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`). In process (`nfs_writeback_ab`), nothing measurable while quiet (the Mac's
  median write-back +0.8 %). While another connection writes, +2 to 3 % a write-back at the median and the least, a
  heavier tail, and up to 10 % fewer write-backs a second on the loaded Mac (2.6 % on fedora-2 at best): every change is
  fed into every tracking connection's states, work arm A does not do. Peak memory +0.3–0.9 %, CPU +1–3 %. Through
  Apple's client, no difference outside the runner's spread (a 64 MiB write and `fsync` a median 0.230 s in A and
  0.190 s in B, five runs a side).
- **Its limits.** Apple's client tells the program nothing of a refusal: `msync` and `close` answered 0 in every case. So
  a program's stores in a refused page go without a word. When they came before the other path's write, that is the
  order of events; when they came after, through a page the client had not refetched, they were the newer write and
  are lost, the case only a byte-level merge could keep. A program that needs both kept maps through the socket route
  (A-186). A daemon restart started the states empty, so a page fetched before it was not judged; A-231 carries them.
- **Found and fixed on the way**, each failing a test first, each recorded in `docs/bugs/`:
  - The byte states panicked on an empty range, which an NFS WRITE of no bytes reached and no FUSE kernel sends: a
    release daemon would have aborted on it.
  - A connection's end went to every shard, whatever it had read: a control message on each other shard's channel per
    connection, outside the bound the channel is sized by (33 of 33 ends in the new test; now 1 of 33, the one
    connection that read both shards' volumes).
  - A keeper that ran only after its tracker closed took the volume's next tracker as its own, and one of the two was
    never woken again (fedora-2's `9 live before, 16 after`; the unit test leaked 8 of 8 rounds' keepers).
  - And arm B's consumer task outlived its last connection until the volume changed again; a closed tracker wakes it.

### A-191 — A writer outside FUSE is answered once every FUSE mount of its volume has been told (accepted and built 2026-10-30)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 ("Cache posture": the paragraph on when a mount is told), Phase 3's AC-3.3, A-139
and A-140 (their residual), A-141 ("Why writers never wait instead"), GAPS, `crates/bridge-fuse` (`channel.rs`:
`ServeState::told_through`, the takeover round's `takeover_out`), `crates/server` (`told.rs`, new: the wait, its bound
and its counters; `fuse.rs`: `told_through` over a volume's mounts, the parked writers woken as a mount is told further
or ends; `verbs.rs`: `run_recorded` holds a recorded verb's reply, `serve_forward` awaits a cross-node verb's; `nfs.rs`:
an NFS call awaits its own; `direct_map.rs`: a write-back's reply; `lease_wait.rs`: a parked verb's late reply;
`state.rs`, `daemon.rs`, `lib.rs`), `crates/server/tests/fuse_told.rs` (new), and `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`.
- **What was open.** AC-3.3 read "every mutation invalidates before it is acknowledged". Since 2026-10-21 a mount's task
  tells its kernel as soon as another path changes the volume, but that was after the writer's reply: a shared map read
  an SDK write's bytes 52–193 µs after the reply (median 82 µs), so a reader of the mount right after the write
  returned could see the old bytes (GAPS, the AC-3.3 entry, closed by this amendment).
- **The rule.** A writer that holds no kernel lock — a verb over the typed channel (the SDKs, the CLI, MCP and the merge
  plane's verbs, all run by `verbs::run_recorded`), an NFS call, a direct map's write-back — notes its volume's journal
  head before it runs. Its reply then owes every FUSE mount of the volume the newest record it made: each mount must
  have been told through it. A mount's told point is its coherence cursor, held back while a round is out (that round's
  records are told only once its write to the device returns) and while a restored mount's takeover round is unsent or
  out; a mount whose first round has not run holds nothing and owes nothing (`ServeState::told_through`). The reply waits
  on the volume's owner shard, which serves the volume and all its FUSE mounts, parked and woken as a mount is told
  further or ends, so the shard serves on: a verb's reply is held and sent by a task, an NFS call's task awaits it, and
  a verb forwarded from another node awaits it on the owner before its exchange answers. A reply that cannot be held
  (the held replies at the shard's client credit, or no task) is answered at once and counted `fuse.told_unwaited`.
- **The bound.** Half the liveness budget, 500 ms (`told::TOLD_WAIT_NS = LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS / LATE_BEAT_SHARE`): the
  longest the daemon lets one of its own shards go unheard before it logs a near miss, so a live mount told late on a
  loaded machine still holds its writer, and a writer held to it keeps half its client's reply deadline (the same
  liveness budget; past it the client reports the verb stalled). Past the bound the writer is answered, its change
  already applied and published, and the late mount counted `fuse.told_overdue`. This answers A-141's objection: a
  mount whose round is blocked in its kernel holds each writer at most the bound, never for good.
- **Why a write through FUSE does not wait.** A request through one FUSE mount holds its kernel's locks on what it
  touches — a read's or a write's pages, a lookup's directory — until the daemon answers it, and another mount's
  notification needs that mount's own locks. Two mounts each with a request in flight on one file, each reply waiting
  for the other mount's notification, would wait on each other until the bound: the 2026-10-17 amendment's deadlock,
  across two mounts. So a write through a FUSE mount is answered at once, and the volume's other FUSE mounts are told
  just after, as before. AC-3.3's text states the window: a write through one mount reached a read-only map of the file
  through the other after a median of 22–35 µs (p90 43–74 µs, worst 2.6 ms) in three runs of the change's release build
  and 1.7 ms (worst 40 ms) in a fourth taken at a busier moment; the build without the wait, whose FUSE writes take the
  same path, measured 21–29 µs (p90 24–34 µs, worst 263 µs) in four runs interleaved with them (fedora-2, Linux 6.19,
  load 17–25). A debug build measured 237 µs.
- **Proven** (fedora-2: Linux 6.19.10, x86_64, 32 cores, `fusermount3`, 2026-10-30), `crates/server/tests/fuse_told.rs`:
  - **Red-checked**, a copy of the tree whose writers never wait (`told::owed` answering nothing), release builds,
    interleaved with the change: after an SDK write on one shard 7 and 4 of 50 first reads of the maps were stale,
    then 7 of 200 (on two shards, where the reply travels home first, 1 of 50); after an NFS WRITE 11, 13 and 10 of
    50, then 58 of 200. The mount is often told before the writer's own thread has woken to read, which is why so few:
    the test runs 200 writes, and one shard is its sharpest case.
  - **With the change**, four runs of the release build and one of the debug: every first read after an SDK write and
    after an NFS WRITE showed the write — 0 of 50 a case in four runs, then 0 of 200 (the one-shard SDK case in the last
    three) — the daemon counting a wait per write, none overdue and none unheld.
  - **The bound**, a copy of the tree whose mounts are never told (`told::told` answering false), five writes each:
    every write was answered after the bound, `fuse.told_overdue` counting each (13 writes in 6.70 s, setup's
    included), and no read was stale, since the mounts were in fact told well within it.
  - The FUSE-to-FUSE window, the same test's third case: 50 of 50 and 199 of 200 first reads stale, as designed.
  - Linux clippy `-D warnings` clean for `slates-bridge-fuse` and `slates-server`, every target.
- **Cost** (`docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`): an SDK write to a volume a FUSE mount reads now waits for the mount's notify thread: with the mount, its p50 rose from about 28 µs to about 40 µs and its p90 from about 35 µs to about 53 µs; with no mount it is unchanged, about 13 µs (fedora-2, `write_round_ab`, release builds differing only in the wait, interleaved three times, load 19–20).
- **What it does not change.** A write through a FUSE mount (the window above). A guest's write through slates' own
  virtio-fs device or a Shards stream, answered by its device's loop in order, was not held yet (held since A-196,
  its device completing the held reply out of order). WinFsp
  mounts are Windows' and never share a daemon with FUSE mounts. A retry of a held request is answered from its
  completion record at once.

### A-190 — A mapped view through the WinFsp mount follows another path's change: the mount purges views through WinFsp's own coherent purge (accepted and built 2026-10-30; an experiment Ada asked to build and measure)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 ("Windows" and its status; the DAX matrix's A-164 status), A-177 (its decision by
the run, superseded), `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (the bare-metal Windows mount-route cells, and the Shards Windows
cell's reason), GAPS, `crates/bridge-winfsp` (`purge.rs`, new: the plan, pure and tested on every host; `host.rs`: an
open this process made unbuffered taken as a purge, its writes answered without being applied and its cleanup publishing
nothing, and the mount thread's purge after a round Windows took; `ffi.rs`: `FspFileSystemOperationProcessIdF`,
optional; `notify.rs`: `open_names`, `open_inodes`), `crates/server` (`winfsp.rs`: `purges_owed`, the purge counters),
`crates/machine` (`Facts::allocation_granularity`), `crates/cli` (`tests/winfsp.rs`: the view must follow, and the
purge must be counted), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-bridge-winfsp` 104 → 111).
- **What it answers.** A process's mapped view of a file through the WinFsp mount kept its pages after another path's
  change (A-177, measured on CI's x86_64 and arm64 runners), and while the view stood a read through any other handle
  was stale too. WinFsp purges a notified file with `CcPurgeCacheSection` (`src/sys/file.c`), which "will not purge
  mapped files" (Microsoft Learn). WinFsp's non-cached write purges first with `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache`
  (`src/sys/write.c`, `FspFsvolWriteNonCached` calling `FspFileNodeFlushAndPurgeCache`), which Microsoft documents as
  invalidating user mapped views. A-177 listed three candidates and called the cell impossible; this is a fourth, which
  needs no change to WinFsp.
- **The mechanism.** After a notification round Windows took, the mount's thread opens each changed file Windows holds
  open through the drive, unbuffered and write-through, and writes the changed range, widened to whole sectors and
  clipped to the file's last sector, in pieces of the machine's allocation granularity, from a zeroed buffer. WinFsp
  flushes the file's dirty pages (a program's stores reach the volume as its writes), purges the range from the cache
  and invalidates every view of it, so a view's next touch reads the volume. The write reaches the host on an open the
  host knows as its own and is answered with the file's attributes, never applied; the open's cleanup publishes nothing.
- **Why a purge cannot write a file (A-198 correction, 2026-11-02).** The command thread opens the drive under a
  less privileged copy of its own token carrying a mount-specific restricting SID. A fresh Create must match that
  marker, the daemon PID and the one bounded pending purge before the host resolves it by file identity. The original
  cached name reaches the same kernel node even after an SDK rename; ordinary callers still use the namespace and
  cannot open a removed old name. Every write through the authenticated context is an echo. This replaces the old
  PID/unbuffered heuristic, which could also discard an embedding application's ordinary unbuffered write. The
  receiver reads the checked Create directly; no optional process-ID export or alternate path remains. The historical
  `winfsp.purges_unavailable` counter remains zero; private-context setup errors end the mount with a typed failure.
  `ReadOnlyVolume` only reports the flag (`src/sys/volinfo.c`); the host's private open needs no writable attachment.
- **Proven** on CI's Windows runners, diagnostics run 41133474977 (slates 78483e80, this change on 405b2d83; WinFsp
  2.1.25156), `crates/cli/tests/winfsp.rs` 4 of 4 on each:
  - x86_64 (`windows-latest`, job 124330034742): the view followed the SDK's change at the test's second poll, 20.8 ms
    (the poll is 20 ms); a read through a handle opened after it followed in 169.5 µs; the daemon counted 1 purge made
    and 1 purge write answered without being applied; after the view and every handle closed, a fresh open read the
    change in 493.5 µs, where A-177 measured 3.03 s.
  - arm64 (`windows-11-arm`, job 124330034878): 20.5 ms, 169.6 µs, 1 purge and 1 write dropped, and 492.6 µs.
  - Red-checked in the same run (job 124330034929): with the server planning no purge, the view kept its first byte for
    10 s (`Some(65)`, the old `A`), a read through a handle was stale for 10 s too, and the test failed.
  - The plan's tests (`purge.rs`, 4, on every host): a change widened to whole sectors, never past the file's last
    sector, extreme offsets without overflow, and a range cut into pieces that cover it exactly.
- **Its limits.** A cut under a live view leaves the view's pages past the new end: Windows refuses to cut a file a view
  maps, and a cut through another path cannot be shown to it. A program's store and another path's write to the same
  page race, as any two writers of one page do; the flush the purge makes writes the program's page first.
- **What it does not change.** The notification rounds (they still drop what Windows caches through handles), the
  mount's other requests, and every other transport.
- **Amended 2026-11-01 (Step 8 of the VFS and DAX plan): a purge is read back, and one Windows did not take is made
  again.** In main's Windows job the view once stayed stale for 10 s (run 41148561681, 2026-10-31). Beside two CPU
  spinners a core and two I/O loops it stayed stale in 9 of 200 iterations on the x86_64 runner and in none of 200 on
  arm64 (diagnostics runs 41326838360 and 41327264613). Each stale iteration made its purge, had its write dropped by
  the host and refused nothing, and no read of the file reached the host after it; each of the 95 passing iterations of
  the second run saw one. `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache` reports a page it could not invalidate as
  `STATUS_CACHE_PAGE_LOCKED`, a success status, and WinFsp's `FspFileNodeFlushAndPurgeCache` turns it into
  `STATUS_SUCCESS`, so a purge Windows did not take looked like one it took.
