  - **The check.** After each piece's write the purge reads the piece back through a cached open of the file and
    through its own unbuffered open. A page Windows dropped is read from the host both times, so the two reads agree; a
    page it kept answers the cached read with its old bytes. A piece whose reads differ makes the purge untaken, counted
    `winfsp.purges_untaken`. A write that lands between the two reads makes them differ too, which costs one more
    attempt, never a stale view.
  - **The retry, and its bound.** The round stays taken. Only the untaken purge is owed again
    (`slates_bridge_winfsp::retry`). Its first attempt waits one tick of the mount's pacing (the heartbeat over the
    fleet's polls a period, 10 ms), and each next attempt waits twice as long as the one before. The task sends a
    due purge to the mount thread as a purge-only command, one command (a round or a purge) out at a time, and waits
    for the next due time or for any wake, so a wait never holds up a request.
    - A purge is given up, counted `winfsp.purges_kept`, once its next attempt would come later than the volume's
      request timeout after Windows first kept its page: 300 s, WinFsp's default, now set in the volume's parameters so
      the horizon follows the pending queue's budget. **Source correction (A-198, 2026-11-02):** processing requests
      never expire (`FSP_IOQ_PROCESS_NO_CANCEL`), so this deadline does not prove no I/O still holds a page. The kept
      outcome is a finite retry policy and is counted; a program's own page lock can also outlive it.
    - With a 10 ms tick that is at most 14 attempts. The list holds at most one purge per open handle
      (`MAX_OPEN_HANDLES`); an untaken purge past it is given up and counted kept.
    - The first form of this fix put the round's cursor back and made the whole round again a tick later, without a
      bound, as a deferred round is. It re-told every record, re-purged every file of the round, and a page a program
      keeps locked would have been purged at full rate forever. It was replaced before it landed.
  - **Applied in the same change to:** §4.6 ("Windows" and its status), GAPS, `crates/bridge-winfsp` (`purge.rs`:
    `PurgeTarget`, `PurgeOutcome`, `purge_through`, tested on every host against a modelled file whose locked pages a
    purge cannot drop; `retry.rs`, new: `PurgeRetries`, the doubling waits, the horizon and the bound, tested on every
    host; `host.rs`: `DriveFile`, the purge's open made for reading too, each purge's outcome in `Purged`, the
    purge-only command, the volume's request timeout set), `crates/bridge-core` (`MAX_OPEN_HANDLES` public),
    `crates/server` (`winfsp.rs`: the retries, `winfsp.purges_untaken`, `winfsp.purges_kept`,
    `winfsp.purge_retries`), `crates/cli` (`tests/winfsp.rs`: the purge count awaited, the untaken and kept purges
    printed), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-bridge-winfsp` 111 → 112, for the `ReadFile`), CLAUDE.md (the WinFsp
    example's gotchas) and `docs/bugs/2026-11-01-a-winfsp-purge-windows-did-not-take-left-a-mapped-view-stale.md`.
  - **Measured after,** the fix as it landed (diagnostics run 41336524903 unless named):
    - x86_64, the reproducing load: 0 of 200 views stale. In 10 iterations Windows kept a page at the first purge:
      9 were taken at the first retry and 1 at the second, and none was given up. The view followed in 460 ms at the
      median, 752 to 1,059 ms where a purge was retried; a read through another handle followed in 0.26 ms.
    - arm64, the reproducing load: 0 of 100 views stale, no purge untaken. That load kept no arm64 view stale before
      the fix either (0 of 200), so the load was raised. Beside 40% of memory held and touched every 2 s, the code
      before the fix kept 1 of 100 views stale (run 41346373137, iteration 44: the purge made, its write dropped, no
      read after it), and the fix kept 0 of 100 (run 41346376630). Four spinners a core and four I/O loops of 256 MiB,
      with no memory held, kept no arm64 view stale either before the fix or after it (0 of 100 each), so on arm64
      what keeps the page goes with the memory manager's own work.
    - A heavier load (60% of memory held and touched every 200 ms, four spinners a core, four I/O loops of 256 MiB)
      kept 2 arm64 views stale before the fix (run 41332842815), but it starved the daemon: its heartbeats came 5 to
      7 s late against the anchor's 1 s budget, and 65 of 96 iterations stalled at setup. It measures overload, not
      the purge.
    - The first form, which owed the whole round again: 0 of 200 views stale on x86_64, with 5 purges untaken and each
      taken at its first retry (run 41332247673).

- **Amended 2026-11-06 (the rule of §4.6 Windows): the purge's client leaves the daemon's process.** The command thread
  had made the purge's opens, writes and reads itself, on a volume its own process serves. A request delivered to the
  receiver sits in WinFsp's processing queue, never cancelled (`FSP_IOQ_PROCESS_NO_CANCEL`), so a daemon killed inside
  one could not exit while the anchor held the volume (the sibling in
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-06-a-daemons-own-io-on-its-volume-strands-its-exit.md`).
  - **The mechanism.** Each mount has a purge client (`crates/bridge-winfsp/src/purge_client.rs`): a child process, a
    role of the daemon's own binary (`slates winfsp-purge-client`; the bridge's tests run their test binary), started at
    the mount's first purge in a job that kills it when the daemon's handle to the job closes, and asked over one message
    pipe. It answers its start with a ready byte once it has made its token, then each request (the range, the piece and
    the full drive path) with one outcome byte. A child that does not answer is let go, its purge refused, and the next
    purge starts another. With no client program installed (`purge_client::install`), a purge is counted
    `winfsp.purges_unavailable`.
  - **Recognition.** The mount makes the private marker and hands it to the child, which builds its own restricted token
    with it (`PurgeToken::with_marker`). Each published purge (`purge_intents::Intent`) names the child's process id, and
    the receiver takes a Create as the purge's only from that process with the marker; with no purge published, or from
    any other process, a Create is a program's. Every other rule of the A-198 correction stands.
  - **Why no other mechanism.** WinFsp purges a mapped file's pages only on a non-cached write; every way to reach
    `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache` is a request on the volume, so whoever makes it must not be a daemon thread.
  - **Proven** (diagnostics, 2026-11-06, WinFsp 2.1.25156, both of GitHub's Windows runners), by
    `a_daemon_killed_while_its_purges_open_is_delivered_exits_within_a_transaction_timeout`: a serving process retains
    the purge's open unanswered and is killed, and must exit within one transaction timeout (1,000 ms).
    - Main's code (run 42155020781, `diag-slabs-1`): red on both runners. The killed server had not exited at the
      bound (`exited None after 999.95ms` on x86_64, `1.0042s` on arm64). With the anchor's hold then released it still
      did not, since its own control handle closes only at its rundown, so the fixture's 10 s reap failed and the step
      ran out its 20 minutes.
    - The fix (run 42155196630, `diag-slabs-2`): the killed server exited in 1.74 ms on x86_64 and 2.89 ms on arm64;
      the bridge's suite 77 of 77 on each, the CLI's WinFsp mount suite 13 of 13 on each (the purge counted done and
      echoed by the child, none unavailable; a cached read followed the SDK's change in 20.2 and 20.7 ms, and a fresh
      open after the view in 408 and 537 µs), and `winfsp_semantics` 7 of 7 on each.
    - Red-check, the in-process open put back over the fix (run 42155197023, `diag-slabs-3`): red again on both
      runners (`exited None after 1.0047s` on x86_64, `1.0130s` on arm64), the reap failing the same way.
  - **Applied in the same change to:** §4.6 (the rule's A-190 bullet), GAPS, the bug record, `crates/bridge-winfsp`
    (`purge_client.rs`, new; `host.rs`: the purge asks the child, the drive helpers moved out; `dispatcher.rs`:
    `PrivateOpens::authenticate` compares the intent's process; `purge_intents.rs`: `Intent`; `purge_token.rs`: the
    marker's text and `with_marker`; `tests/support/host.rs`: the purger role and the oracle), `crates/cli`
    (`main.rs`: the role; `daemon.rs`: the install).

### A-189 — QEMU 11.1 maps the window of slates' own device: its generic vhost-user device takes the end by number, and the back end takes the memory tables QEMU sends as it maps (accepted and built 2026-10-29)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the DAX matrix's status and its list of what the platforms rule out), A-164 (the
same list), `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (the VMs table's QEMU, Kata and crosvm arm64 rows), GAPS, `docs/cli.md`,
`crates/cli` (`args.rs`: `{fd}`; `verbs.rs`: `exec_vmm`; `tests/cli.rs`; `tests/guest_vhost.rs`: every test in each VMM
the environment names, and QEMU's command line), `crates/bridge-virtiofs` (`vhost_user.rs`: `set_mem_table` under
running rings, `ObjectIdentity`), `crates/server` (`tests/virtiofs.rs`: the test of QEMU's tables;
`tests/common/guest.rs`: a chain whose payload lies in another region), `ci/guest/Dockerfile` (QEMU from
trixie-backports, fuse3), `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the live-guest lane's QEMU leg), and
`docs/bugs/2026-10-29-qemus-memory-table-after-a-map-ended-slates-own-device.md`.
- **Shutdown diagnostics (2026-11-02).** Main CI 41487560076 passes 19/20 jobs but its eight `guest_vhost` cases
  fail at clean poweroff in two attempts, after their functional histories finish. `Guest::quit` previously stopped
  reading after the probe's Done reply, hiding the VMM's final stderr. The shared harness now retains bounded final
  output after observing exit. A real-process oracle fails before that drain (0.03 s) and passes after (0.02 s), on
  adacachy under the recorded resource cap. The clean-exit and data assertions are unchanged. This exposes the
  QEMU shutdown cause: the backend closed control after the first ring stop, before QEMU could stop the second.
  A-169's 2026-11-02 correction keeps control through suspension and drains the specified ring before reporting
  its device-owned position. All eight guest histories pass in the existing QEMU image on adacachy (28.23 s).
  Records: `docs/bugs/2026-11-02-a-vmm-exit-hid-its-final-diagnostic.md` and
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-02-stopping-one-vhost-ring-closed-the-control-connection.md`.
- **What it answers.** The DAX matrix ruled QEMU out on both routes: upstream's vhost-user-fs device has no window
  property, and the window is the front end's to offer. That holds of QEMU's vhost-user-fs-pci, which has no window in
  11.1 either, and was wrong of QEMU. 11.1.0 is the first release whose generic vhost-user device
  (`vhost-user-test-device-pci`, user-creatable since 10.2) asks the back end for its shared-memory regions
  (`VHOST_USER_GET_SHMEM_CONFIG`, request 44), makes them a PCI BAR, and maps each `VHOST_USER_BACKEND_SHMEM_MAP`
  (request 9) into it: QEMU 6608dca74ecf, "vhost-user-device: Add shared memory BAR", 2026-06-03; `vhost-user.rst` at
  v11.1.0. slates' back end already speaks those numbers for crosvm (protocol feature 22, requests 44, 9 and 10). Debian
  ships QEMU 11.1.2 in trixie-backports. The device is `-device
  vhost-user-test-device-pci,chardev=slates,virtio-id=26,num_vqs=2,config_size=40` over guest memory from a shared
  memfd backend.
- **The end by number.** `slates vhost-user` named the device's end only as `/proc/self/fd/N`, which crosvm takes and
  QEMU would connect to as a path. `{fd}` names it by number, as QEMU takes an inherited socket: `-chardev
  socket,id=slates,fd={fd}`.
- **The tables QEMU sends.** QEMU puts every shared memory section that has a descriptor in the memory table it sends
  the back end (`hw/virtio/vhost.c` `vhost_section`), so each map it places comes back as a new `SET_MEM_TABLE` under
  running rings, and each unmap as one without it. The back end refused any table under configured rings, so the first
  run ended the device at the guest's first map (diagnostics run 40874255591; the bug record). A table under configured
  rings is now taken when every region a configured ring lies in is still in it unchanged: the same object, by device
  and inode, at the same guest and front-end addresses, from the same offset. A kept region keeps its mapping, a new
  one is mapped, a dropped one is let go; a table that moves or drops a ring's region is refused, as before. With the
  window's ranges in its table, the device reads and writes a request's buffer that lies in the window, as a guest's
  `O_DIRECT` read into or write from a mapped file's pages makes one.
- **Its bound.** Without `VHOST_USER_PROTOCOL_F_CONFIGURE_MEM_SLOTS`, QEMU sends at most 8 regions
  (`VHOST_MEMORY_BASELINE_NREGIONS`). Past them its own commit fails and the back end keeps the table it has, so the
  guest's maps work and a request buffer in a range past the eighth region is refused. The incremental form
  (`ADD_MEM_REG`, `REM_MEM_REG`, up to QEMU's 512 slots) is owed (GAPS).
- **QEMU's mount route is the image form.** QEMU has no virtio-fs device of its own: its vhost-user-fs-pci has no
  window, and virtiofsd, the back end that would serve a host mount through one, has no DAX in any release (its "feat:
  add DAX support", merge request !318, open since 2026-06-03, unmerged on 2026-10-29). Its virtio-pmem serves A-165's
  image form as Firecracker's does: QEMU maps the image file, through a slates mount, shared as the device's memory
  (`memory-backend-file,share=on`), and a guest's flush is QEMU's `fsync` of the file (`hw/virtio/virtio-pmem.c`). QEMU
  builds virtio-pmem for x86 machines only (`hw/i386/Kconfig` selects `VIRTIO_PMEM_SUPPORTED`, `hw/arm/Kconfig` does
  not), and the arm `virt` machine's NVDIMM needs a firmware boot with ACPI and passes no guest flush to its file, so an
  arm64 QEMU guest, Apple silicon's included, has no mount route. Kata: its QEMU driver asks
  vhost-user-fs-pci for a `cache-size` (govmm `qemu.go`), a property upstream's device has never had, so neither route
  reaches a Kata guest. Windows: QEMU builds no vhost-user there (`meson.build`: "vhost-user is not available on
  Windows"). macOS: QEMU builds vhost-user only when asked (`--enable-vhost-user`), which Homebrew's 11.1.3 does not
  ask, and slates' vhost-user back end is Linux's (memfds and eventfds), so that cell is owed. crosvm on arm64, corrected
  in the same change: its x86_64 gate is in its own fs device (`devices/device_virtio_fs/src/lib.rs`), the mount route;
  its vhost-user front end maps a back end's region on any architecture, so slates' own device under crosvm on arm64
  is owed, not ruled out.
- **Proven** (2026-10-29), every test of `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs` in QEMU 11.1.2 from trixie-backports
  (Debian 1:11.1.2+ds-3~bpo13+4), Debian's 6.12 kernel, the static probe as `/init`: on x86_64 with KVM (CI's
  `ubuntu-latest`, diagnostics run 40876474403, job 123456468150: 5 of 5 in 11.88 s) and on arm64 under QEMU's own
  emulation (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`, which has no KVM; the same run, job 123456468166: 5 of 5 in 23.17 s). The live-guest
  lane's own suite passes on the new QEMU too (the same x86_64 job, 23 of 23: pjdfstest's 8,798 cases with no unlisted
  failure, fsx, fsstress, the roster's workloads identical on slates and on the guest's RAM). Each guest maps the session's file with
  `dax=always` and holds every change of every path as memory alone, its stores reaching the session at sync, at close
  and at the VM's death, never past the file's end, over generated histories (123 ingests held and 51 runs ingested in
  one). Red-checked in the same run with the device offered no window: all 5 refused at the guest's mount
  (job 123456467863). The device's own test of QEMU's tables (`crates/server/tests/virtiofs.rs`
  `a_front_end_that_puts_each_placed_map_in_its_memory_table_keeps_its_device`) failed before the change on adacachy and
  passes after, with the virtio-fs suite 23 of 23, bridge-virtiofs's suites and the five crosvm tests unchanged. The
  image form in QEMU 11.1.2 with KVM: `crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs` 4 of 4 in 11.67 s (diagnostics run 40883925064,
  job 123482449569), red-checked with the guest mounting `dax=never`, the three pmem tests failing at their DAX check
  (job 123482450208); on arm64 the same QEMU has no `virtio-pmem-pci` (job 123482450147), and the drive form passed
  there. The Firecracker leg of the same test, after its refactor into one leg per VMM, 4 of 4 on adacachy.
- **Cloud Hypervisor's mount route is the image form too** (2026-10-30, Ada's go for its binary on the box): its
  virtio-pmem device (`--pmem file=…,discard_writes=off`) maps the image file shared, and the same test passes 4 of 4 in
  Cloud Hypervisor v54.0 on adacachy, red-checked with `dax=never`. Its `--serial tty` reads input only from an
  interactive terminal (`vmm/src/serial_manager.rs`), so the harness gives it a pseudo-terminal
  (`Guest::spawn_on_terminal`); its disks need `image_type=raw`; and its guest powers off, since it reboots a guest
  that restarts. Its fs device has no DAX, so slates' own device gets no window there.

### A-188 — A client of any shard is handed a direct map: the copy held on its volume's shard, the hand-off through the client's own (accepted and built 2026-10-29)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the same-kernel direct map paragraph), A-186 (its owed item), GAPS,
`crates/server` (`direct_map.rs`: `ClientMaps` and `DirectMapState::held`, the share counted over the clients served,
holding and asking, `Fill::begin` taking the principal, the three hand-offs reaching the client's shard, `deliver_to`,
`write_back_held` and `let_go_held` replacing `write_back_for_reap`, `give_back`; `xshard.rs`: `task_within`;
`reap.rs`: each shard's maps written back before its attachments go and let go after; `state.rs` and `daemon.rs`: the
slot's `direct_maps` removed; `config.rs` doc), `crates/client` (`tests/client.rs`, `tests/reap_map.rs`), `crates/cli`
(`tests/cli.rs` doc), `CLAUDE.md`.
- **What it answers.** A copy was handed only to a client of the volume's own shard: the copy and its write-through
  live where the volume does, and the client's slot, which held the copy and the channel it went over, lives where the
  client is served, its id's residue over the shards. So in a daemon of N shards a writable map was served to about one
  client in N, and every other client's read map fell back to the paged copy: the direct map, A-171's zero-copy read and
  A-186's write, was a one-shard feature. Every map verb already names its volume and runs on the volume's shard.
- **The hold moves to the copy.** A map is held on its volume's shard, in that shard's table under its client id, with
  the principal its write-back is checked under, whichever shard serves the client. `MapSync`, `ReleaseMap` and the
  detach's `MapsHeld` read that table where they run. A client's share of a shard's copies is counted over the clients
  the shard serves, those holding its copies, and the one asking: a superset of the clients it served before, so a
  share is never larger than it was.
- **The hand-off reaches the client.** Linux: the copy's shard asks the client's own shard, the reply route's, by a
  cross-shard call, to send the descriptor on the client's control socket, since a delivery is sealed under the
  client's channel and only that shard may seal on it (A-187); the reply follows once that shard answers, so the
  descriptor is waiting when the client reads the reply, as before. Windows: the copy's shard asks the client's shard
  for the client's process and duplicates the handle into it. macOS: the offer is made on the copy's shard, where any
  client claims it by the mapping id, whose high bits name the shard (A-173 already found offers there). The reply is
  delivered to the client's ring on its shard, as an image build's is (A-160).
- **The reap reaches every shard.** The client's own shard runs its reap and visits every shard in turn: there the
  client's writable maps are written back before its attachments go (A-186), then its copies are let go. A write-back
  is sliced, a copy slice a turn, so it runs as a task on its shard: the new cross-shard call `task_within` awaits a
  task's result where `call_within` awaits a closure's. A write-back that does not end within the reap's deadline
  defers the reap, which is retried, rather than removing an attachment its stores still need.
- **Proven** (2026-10-29): on a two-shard daemon a client of the shard that does not own the volume maps a 20 KiB file
  read-only, zero-copy, then read and write, its sync writing exactly the differing bytes, which another client reads,
  every copy given back after (`a_client_of_another_shard_maps_a_file_read_and_write`); the cross-shard read test now
  demands zero-copy on every volume; and a client of the other shard killed with unsynced stores has them written back
  by its reap through the volume's shard, the copy let go there
  (`a_killed_client_of_another_shard_has_its_writable_maps_stores_written_back`). macOS (this Mac): the client suite
  32, reap 1, reap_map 4, the server's direct-map, cross-shard and reap unit tests 6, the Shards suite 26; Linux
  x86_64 (adacachy): clippy of the server and client, the client suite 31, netns, reap 1, reap_map 4. Each new test
  failed before the change: the read maps fell back to copies and the writable map was refused `MapUnavailable`.

### A-187 — A client in its own network namespace reaches the daemon through a socket file, every rendezvous sealed (accepted 2026-10-28; built and proven 2026-10-29)
Applied in the same change to: §4.7 (the rendezvous paragraph and its status), GAPS, `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (the
Docker and Kubernetes socket-route cells), `crates/ipc` (`seal.rs`: the interface, `Role`, `Class`, `install`, `fresh`;
`rendezvous.rs`: the Linux address (`node`, `bind_node`, `owner_only`), the daemon-first exchange (`Handshake`, the
round's `sweep`, `serve`), the client's `Claim` stages, sealed deliveries, `Listener::pending`, `Served::Pending`;
`error.rs`: `SealRefused`, `HandshakesFull`; `tests/support/toy_seal.rs`, the stand-in both test kinds share), the new
`crates/seal` (aws-lc-rs: X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, RFC vectors and golden messages), `crates/server`
(`daemon.rs`: the seal installed before the listener opens; the rendezvous wait also on pending handshakes and their
deadline), `crates/client` (`install_seal`; `tests/netns.rs`), `crates/cli` (the probe's `reach` mode; the bridge-network
container test), the chart (`rendezvous.directory`, `rendezvous.hostPath`) and `xtask/src/kind_direct.rs` (step 6, a pod
of its own).
- **What it answers.** The DAX matrix's Kubernetes and Docker socket-route cells are proven only for a workload in the
  daemon's network namespace: a container of the daemon's pod, or `docker run --network host`. Linux's rendezvous is an
  abstract socket, which the kernel scopes to a network namespace (unix(7)), so a pod with a namespace of its own, or
  a container on a bridge network, cannot reach it. A socket file can be reached through a mount, and Ada authorized
  socket files for DAX when what crosses them is encrypted end to end and at rest (2026-10-22).
- **The address.** When the operator names a rendezvous directory, the daemon's listener is a socket file there instead
  of the abstract name, and a client given the same directory connects to it; with none, the abstract name, as now.
  The address is configuration, like the instance's name, and carried by it: an instance named by an absolute path,
  `<directory>/<name>`, is reached at `<directory>/slates-rv-<name>.sock`, any other at the abstract name; the protocol
  over either is one. The directory must be the daemon's user's alone (owned by it, no permission for group or
  others), checked before the bind, as macOS's route checks its directory; the node is owner-only, a node a dead
  daemon left is found unanswered and replaced, a live owner's is refused as the abstract name's is (`EADDRINUSE`),
  and it is removed by whoever bound it: the anchor, which holds the listener across daemon restarts as it holds the
  abstract one (A-114), or a daemon run alone. A workload mounts the directory read-only, so it can connect but cannot
  replace the node: a Unix socket's connect asks only the node's permission, which a read-only bind mount leaves.
- **Every rendezvous is sealed**, abstract or file, so there is one exchange and no plain mode: each side sends an
  ephemeral X25519 public key, both derive one key per direction by HKDF-SHA256 from the shared secret, salted with
  both public keys, and every later message (the hello, the handoff, every delivery) is sealed with AES-256-GCM under
  its direction's key at a counter nonce, its kind as additional data. A descriptor rides beside its sealed message
  (`SCM_RIGHTS` carries kernel objects, not bytes). Each side checks the other's user by `SO_PEERCRED` as the daemon
  checks a client's now. Nothing crosses at rest: a socket file holds no bytes.
- **Where the seal lives.** `slates-ipc` builds for targets with no C toolchain (CI's cross-lint), so it takes the seal
  from its caller through a small interface, and a crate of its own implements it with aws-lc-rs, the one crypto
  library (A-66); the daemon and the client supply it. A second crypto library in ipc was the alternative, rejected for
  A-66's reason.
- **The exchange never blocks either side.** The daemon speaks first: it accepts, checks the peer's user, sends its
  public key and keeps the connection pending; the client answers with its public key and its hello sealed, in one
  send; the daemon's next round, woken by that socket's readiness or the earliest pending deadline, agrees, opens the
  hello and sends the handoff sealed. A round reads each pending handshake once. At most `BACKLOG` handshakes are
  pending, one more is refused `HandshakesFull` (its socket closed, which its client retries), and one whose opening
  has not come within the claim wait is given up. The client checks the listener's user as the daemon checks the
  client's, since an abstract name is anyone's to bind.
- **Proven** (arm64 Linux in a container on this Mac, rust 1.98.1, 2026-10-28; the Mac and the Windows and musl cross
  lints the same day):
  - the seal's 8 tests (RFC 7748 and RFC 5869 vectors, golden messages, tampered, replayed and reordered messages
    refused);
  - the ipc crate's 29 module tests and the rendezvous suite's 22, every exchange sealed: a silent claimant given up
    at the claim wait while an honest claim beside it connects, a forged opening refused asking for no region, an
    unsealed, forged, unknown or dropped delivery refused with its descriptor closed, a process with no seal claiming
    nothing, a listener of another user refused by the client (run as root), a shared directory refused, a dead
    owner's node replaced and a live one's kept;
  - a client in a user and network namespace of its own (`unshare --user --map-current-user --net`) mapping a 64 KiB
    file read and write by the direct map through the socket file, its sync writing the 42 stored bytes back, while
    its claim on a daemon at an abstract name this process reaches finds none;
  - the client suite's 30 tests, `reap_map` and `reap`, over the real seal.
- **Red-checked:** eight mutants each fail their guard: the socket file read as an abstract name (the namespaced
  client finds no daemon), no give-up, no check of the listener's user, the hello used unopened, a delivery parsed
  unopened, the rendezvous wait blind to pending handshakes (every connect took 1.001 s to 1.012 s, against a bound of
  100 ms), any directory accepted, a live owner's node replaced.
- **Measured** (adacachy, x86_64, Linux 7.2.9, load 60 to 132, 2026-10-29; debug test binaries, so a release figure
  is owed): `~/a187-ab/ab.sh` builds A (ce36e9aa, unsealed) and B (844792e3, sealed) each in its own target and runs
  their `a_connect_is_answered_within_a_tenth_of_the_claim_wait` alternately, three times each, 200 connects to a fresh
  one-shard daemon a run. The least connect of each run was 90, 73 and 97 µs unsealed against 228, 254 and 226 µs
  sealed; the median 178, 169 and 195 µs against 357, 369 and 367 µs; the 99th percentile 5.1 to 10.6 ms against 5.9
  to 6.9 ms, the loaded box's own. So the exchange adds about 160 µs at the least and 180 µs at the median to a connect
  in a debug build: three X25519 operations in sequence and half a round trip more. In a release binary the seal
  itself, one whole exchange with both sides' operations, costs about 36 µs at the least on both an M5 Max and a Ryzen
  9 9950X3D2 (`cargo run --release -p slates-seal --example seal_cost -- 2000`; BENCHMARKS, "What sealing the rendezvous
  costs a connect"). A connect happens once per client session, never per request, so R9's provisioning floor is
  untouched.
- **Proven in containers and pods** (2026-10-29): the bridge-network container test on CI's x86_64 and arm64 lanes,
  `synced=43 released=0` through the socket file while a container on a bridge network finds no daemon at an abstract
  instance (run 40844136550); and the KIND direct leg's step 6, a pod of its own on pod 0's node finding no daemon at the
  abstract socket, then pods of their own writing the file and writing through it by a writable direct map through the
  node's directory mounted read-only, `differing=37 synced=37 released=0 whole=true`, on x86_64 (the same run, job
  123347393577) and on arm64 (diagnostics run 40847130881). Red-checked on arm64 with the socket file read as an
  abstract name: step 6's pod of its own and the bridge container were each refused "daemon unavailable". Linux x86_64
  ran the ipc, client and namespace suites on adacachy the same day (29, 22, 30 and 1 passed).
- **A namespace that forbids hostPath** (Pod Security's restricted and baseline profiles) reaches the directory through
  a claim instead: an administrator's `local` PersistentVolume names the node's directory, a claim in the namespace binds
  it by name, and the pod mounts the claim read-only, a `persistentVolumeClaim` volume, which the restricted profile
  allows; the kubelet mounts it, and nothing privileged of slates' own is involved. A CSI driver, the other way, would
  be a privileged node plugin of slates' own, which R10 rules out. Proven by the KIND leg's step 7 on x86_64 (run
  40855180817) and arm64 (diagnostics run 40855403394): the namespace refuses a hostPath pod ("violates PodSecurity
  \"restricted:latest\": restricted volume types"), then its pods write the file and write through it over the claim,
  `differing=37 synced=37 released=0 whole=true`.
- **Measured in release** (adacachy, load 31 to 42, 2026-10-29, the same interleaved A/B in release builds): the least
  connect of each run 24.1, 25.2 and 24.1 µs unsealed against 69.7, 79.4 and 72.7 µs sealed, the median 43.2, 45.7 and
  41.0 µs against 115.9, 117.5 and 116.9 µs: the exchange adds about 48 µs at the least and 73 µs at the median, of
  which about 36 µs is the seal's own crypto and the rest the half round trip more.
- **Run on CI since 2026-10-29:** CI's runners refuse an unprivileged user namespace (AppArmor's
  `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns`), so the `unshare` tests skipped there loudly, and the impostor test, which
  needs root, skipped too. The Linux lanes now lift the restriction for their own runner and run the impostor test as
  root in a container, a skip failing the step; all three passed on x86_64 and arm64 (diagnostics run 40876479984).

### A-186 — The direct map maps a file read and write: the client's stores are compared back into the file at its sync points (accepted 2026-10-28)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the same-kernel direct map paragraph and its status, the DAX matrix status), GAPS, `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8, `crates/mem` (`dax_object.rs`: `PeerAccess`, `PeerObject::create` taking it, `PeerObject::access` and `read_write_handle`, `PeerWriteView` on every platform, `within_view`; `tests/peer_object.rs`, `tests/peer_section.rs`), `crates/ipc` (`protocol.rs`: `RequestBody::MapWrite` and `MapSync`, `ReplyBody::MapSynced`, `Refusal::MapsHeld`, appended; `rendezvous.rs`: `Mapping`, the Linux judge by access and its writable test; `route.rs`: `confined_map`, replacing `confined_read_only`; `handle_route.rs`: `confined_section` and `hand_section` by access), `crates/vfs` (`shards_backing.rs`: a writable copy's ranges marked writable, `is_attached`, `BackingObject::peer_handle` replacing `read_only_handle`), `crates/bridge-core` (`dax_backing.rs`: `write_back_slice` and `WroteBack`, the one compare-back, which the ingest now calls), `crates/server` (`direct_map.rs`: `HeldMap`, `map_write`, `map_sync`, `Sync`, the writable release, `write_back_for_reap`, `defer_task`, `complete` shared; `fs_verbs.rs`: `with_writer`, `writable_file`; `verbs.rs`: the verbs' dispatch, the detach's `MapsHeld`, the refusal's ledger name; `reap.rs`; `state.rs`), `crates/client` (`MappedWrite`, `map_write`, `map_sync`, `release_map_write`; `tests/client.rs`, `tests/reap_map.rs`).
- **What it answers.** A-164 defines DAX as reading and writing a file's bytes in place. With no VM (bare metal, a
  container, a pod) the socket route's direct map read alone (A-171, A-173, A-175), so writing in place had only the
  mount route, and Windows has no mount route that maps (A-177). A writable direct map gives every platform both.
- **The mechanism: A-163's, for a process.** The daemon makes the same per-file copy, writable
  (`slates_mem::PeerAccess::ReadWrite`), fills it a slice at a time, and hands it as the read-only copy is handed. The
  client's stores land in the copy. The daemon compares the copy back into the file at the client's sync points, with
  the compare-back a Shards guest's stores take (`slates_bridge_core::dax_backing::write_back_slice`, one function for
  both). Each run where the copy differs from the file is written through the map's attachment, a copy slice a turn,
  and the shard publishes before the reply, as a file verb does. The write boundary keeps writing every other path's
  change into the copy, as for a read-only copy. The copy being written back from is passed over while its runs are
  written (`ShardsBackings::suppress`), or the bytes the comparison read would land back in the copy over a store made
  since.
- **What the copy authorizes.** Its bytes, and nothing else about it:
  - **Linux:** sealed against shrinking, growing and new seals, but not against writes;
  - **macOS:** the handed descriptor is opened read and write before the name goes, and XNU refuses a second sizing
    whatever the mode;
  - **Windows:** the peer is handed a duplicate that maps read and write, and the section's descriptor refuses any
    wider one (rewriting the descriptor, extending the section).

  Each is judged for that access where it leaves the process (`confined_for_a_peer`, `confined_map`,
  `confined_section`). A read-only copy keeps its access: it refuses a writable handle, and its judge refuses a writable
  object.
- **Coherence and durability.** A store reaches the file at the client's `MapSync`, at its `ReleaseMap` (whose reply
  then reports that write-back), and before its reap removes its attachments. So a store outlives its client's process,
  as a store into a shared map of a file does. Other paths see a client's stores after its sync, as they see a guest's
  (A-163) and a mount's mapped stores after write-back. The client sees every other path's change at once, through the
  copy. A store past the file's end within the copy's last page is not the file's and is never written (since A-197
  the copy is the file's length rounded up to a granule its client names, the page or 2 MiB for a pmem VMM, and the
  same holds for all of it past the end). A later write
  over a store not yet synced wins, in the order the writes reached the copy.
- **Authority.** `MapWrite` names the caller's own write attachment, and resolves the file through it, its scope
  applied, by the check every file verb takes (`crate::fs_verbs::with_writer`). Each write-back slice takes that check
  again, so an attachment that ends stops the write-back. A `Detach` of an attachment with writable maps held under it
  is refused `MapsHeld`, as a file system with files open refuses to unmount. A copy detached from its file (the volume
  destroyed, the file's last link and open gone) is never compared back, since its inode number may name another file
  by then: its stores reach nothing, as a deleted file's do.
- **An in-process guest's writable window and a writable map exclude each other,** as a Shards backing and such a
  window do (A-163): the guest's stores go to the file's block past the write boundary.
- **Rejected:**
  - **A copied fallback** (read the file, let the client change a buffer, write it back): it could not keep the bytes
    another writer changed meanwhile, so a writable map the daemon cannot hand is refused `MapUnavailable`.
  - **Writing back at every other path's read of the file:** each such read would pay a comparison (0.70–1.14 ms per
    mapped MiB, A-163) on behalf of a client that has not asked for its stores to be durable.
  - **Ending the map with its attachment:** a detach would drop stores silently. Refusing the detach keeps every store
    to an explicit end.
- **Proven:** Linux x86_64 (adacachy, Linux 7.2.9, 4 KiB pages), macOS arm64 (this Mac, macOS 26.4.1, 16 KiB pages)
  and Windows x86_64 (jupiter, Windows 10.0.26200), 2026-10-28. `crates/client/tests/client.rs` runs 8 tests over a
  real daemon on each:
  - the sync writes exactly the bytes that differ;
  - another path's write reaches the map, and the other writer's bytes are kept;
  - a store past the end is not written;
  - a detach is refused while a map is held, and a release writes back;
  - the map follows its file across a rename, and reaches nothing once the file is gone;
  - the authority check refuses a missing attachment, a read attachment, a directory and a missing file;
  - what the map hands changes one file's bytes and nothing else: exactly the mapped length, no neighbour's byte in it,
    a resize refused (Linux `EPERM`, macOS `EINVAL`), a new seal refused (Linux), a wider duplicate refused (Windows
    `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`);
  - a store made during a sync is never undone (Linux: about 130,000 stores over 200 syncs, 3 runs of 3; macOS:
    1,251,963; Windows: 209,504).

  `tests/reap_map.rs` kills a client holding unsynced stores and finds them in the file after its reap. From a Docker
  container on adacachy (`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`, `a_container_maps_a_slates_file_read_and_write_by_the_direct_map`),
  the container's process stores 43 bytes through its map, syncs and releases, and the host reads them in place. From
  a Kubernetes pod (GitHub's `ubuntu-24.04-arm`, the KIND direct leg's third probe) and from a Windows process-isolated
  container (`windows-2025`, Nano Server, its daemon beside it), a client stores 37 bytes, syncs, releases and reads
  them back (`differing=37 synced=37 released=0 whole=true`, diagnostics run 40816955827), each red-checked in the same
  run with a write-back comparing nothing. `slates-mem`'s
  `peer_object.rs` holds the writable object alone, 9 of 9 on Linux and 8 of 8 on macOS, and `peer_section.rs` the
  writable section, 4 of 4 on Windows. The rendezvous judges writable hand-offs. Clippy is clean on all three.
- **Red-checked** on the box, eleven mutants, one at a time in a separate tree and target, each failing the test that
  guards it (and three on jupiter, after the list):
  - the sync comparing nothing;
  - the reap writing nothing back;
  - a writable release letting go unsynced;
  - a detach not refused;
  - no write-through into a writable copy;
  - both end-of-file guards gone (the comparison's end and the volume read's short tail; either alone keeps the store
    out);
  - a read attachment allowed to write;
  - the write-back written through into its own copy: 84 of 158,498 stores undone over 200 syncs;
  - a writable copy sealed against writes;
  - the writable judge without `F_SEAL_SEAL`;
  - the read-only judge passing a writable copy.

  On jupiter, a writable handle handed with `WRITE_DAC`, and a section made under the default descriptor, were each
  refused unconfined at the hand-off (`MapUnavailable`); that section with the writable judge passing everything was
  caught by the hostile test (a duplicate that may rewrite the descriptor granted). The detached-copy guard is not
  red-checkable without a volume prefix handed out again: the attachment's check and the inode's own absence refuse
  first.
- **Owed then, built since (A-188, 2026-10-29):** a client of another shard than the volume's was handed no copy: a
  read fell back to the paged copy and a writable map was refused `MapUnavailable`, so in a daemon of N shards about one
  client in N was served. Every map is now held on its volume's shard under its client, whichever shard serves it.
  - Nothing more by platform: CI's run of 4552995b (40816824486) ran the 8 writable-map client tests on its native
    arm64 lanes, Linux (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`: 159,669 stores over 200 syncs, none undone) and Windows (`windows-11-arm`,
    with the writable section test), all passing, and its x86_64 KIND lane's pod wrote through its map
    (`differing=37 synced=37 released=0 whole=true`).
- **Found after the first push, each fixed failing test first:**
  - **A long write-back reported stalled.** CI's ThreadSanitizer lane slowed a 4 MiB map's release past the client's
    one-second reply deadline, and the client answered `Stalled` while the daemon finished: `defers_reply` named
    `MapRead` but not `MapWrite`, `MapSync` or `ReleaseMap`, whose replies are deferred the same way
    (`docs/bugs/2026-10-28-a-writable-maps-long-write-back-was-reported-stalled.md`).
  - **A wait with no time left refused on macOS.** The test for the first, a client with a 1 ms reply deadline, met
    `os_sync_wait_on_address`'s refusal of a zero timeout (`EINVAL`) as `OsRefused`; the wake word's wait now reads the
    word for a zero timeout, as a futex answers it (`docs/bugs/2026-10-28-a-wait-with-no-time-left-was-refused-on-macos.md`).

### A-176 — A Windows daemon restarts under its clients: names that no restart repeats, an owner's token, and a claim's refusal kept to itself (accepted 2026-10-25)
Applied in the same change to: §4.7 (the rendezvous's status), A-114 (adoption handed over in process; its Windows sentence corrected), A-175's owed line, GAPS, `crates/ipc` (`rendezvous.rs`: `Adoption`, `Listener::open` taking it, `Round` and `Served`, the Windows owner token and takeover, the stamp taken back at a listener's drop; `wake.rs`: `Event::create_new`; `error.rs`: `InstanceHeld`; `tests/rendezvous.rs`), `crates/server` (`daemon.rs`: `SegmentSource::Handoff`'s `rendezvous`, `region_name_key`, `CLAIMS_REFUSED`, the accept loop's refusals), `crates/cli` (`anchor.rs`), every in-process anchor of the tests (`crates/client/tests/{client,consumer,driver}.rs`; `crates/server/tests/{common/anchor,fleet,seal,recovery,attach_forms,shards,virtiofs}.rs`; `daemon.rs`'s warm-restart test), `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (both x86_64 Windows lanes run the client binary whole, one test at a time), `CLAUDE.md`, and three bug records.
- **What was found.** The client binary's six restart tests had never run on Windows. Run on jupiter (Windows 10.0.26200, 2026-10-25), each failed at its second daemon's start, `CreateFileMappingW` refusing `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS`. Windows keeps a kernel object's name while any process holds it and cannot unlink one, and beneath that one failure lay a harness gap and three defects.
- **The harness: the tests played the anchor's segment but not its rendezvous.** So each daemon made its own, and the second met the first's bootstrap object in the surviving client's doorbell. The field's anchor holds the rendezvous (A-114), and every in-process anchor now does too, handing it to each daemon it starts as `SegmentSource::Handoff`'s `rendezvous` (an `Adoption`). The environment variable a spawned daemon reads would have reached every daemon of a test process, so nothing below a daemon's start reads the environment any more; `SegmentSource::FromEnv` reads it at the start.
- **A reconnecting client was refused, so a Windows restart cost every client its session** (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-windows-client-could-not-reconnect-after-a-restart.md`). The daemon named a client's region `slates-cr-<instance>-<client id>`, a reconnect keeps its id (§4.9), and the client still maps its old region, so Windows refused the name and the session ended `DaemonGone` where AC-2.3 says it resumes. Each region is now `slates-cr-<key>-<number>`: a 64-bit key derived with a keyed-hash domain of its own from the issuer secret every start mints, and the region's number in that daemon. The number wraps; a repeat can meet only a region made 2^32 regions earlier, and refuses that one connection, typed. The name takes 35 of the claim slot's 40 bytes.
- **A claim's refusal cost its round every client it had accepted, on every platform** (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-refused-claim-dropped-its-rounds-accepted-clients.md`). The round returned the refusal and dropped the clients it had accepted and already answered. Now each claim served is `Served::Accepted` or `Served::Refused`; a refusal is answered to its claimant, handed to the caller and ends that claim alone (counted `CLAIMS_REFUSED`). Only a failure of the rendezvous itself ends a round, which keeps what it accepted (`Round::ended`).
- **No daemon of an instance could start on Windows beside a client of its dead owner** (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-windows-instance-could-not-start-beside-a-dead-ones-client.md`). This hit a daemon run alone, or an anchor started again after its predecessor died. The owner (the anchor that holds the rendezvous, or a daemon run alone) now holds a token: a named Event created only if no live process holds one, which no one else opens, so its name lives exactly as long as its owner. Holding it, an owner takes over an object it finds: its layout checked, its claims readied as a restarted daemon readies them, nothing published and no anchor named. A second owner of a live instance is refused `InstanceHeld`. macOS kept its unlinking create, with an empty token, until
  A-178 gave it a token of its own.
- **One in-process semantic made the same everywhere: a stopped daemon takes back its start stamp.** The macOS and Windows listener's `Drop` takes back the stamp, by exchange so a successor's stays. With the anchor holding the object, a stopped daemon's stamp stayed published, and a client in the daemon's own process, whose exit watch sees no exit, judged it alive for good (`crates/client/tests/driver.rs`'s death phase found it once the driver's anchor held the rendezvous). A Linux client learns the same from its control socket closing.
- **Proven** on jupiter, 2026-10-25: the client binary whole, one test at a time, 20 of 20, its seven restart tests the first sessions to outlive a daemon restart on Windows; the driver 2 of 2; the rendezvous 12 of 12. The same suites pass on this Mac (rendezvous 11 of 11, client 21, driver 2, consumer 3, recovery 41) and fedora (rendezvous 12, client 20, driver 2, consumer 3, recovery 43; `slates-ipc`, `slates-server`, `slates-client` and `slates-cli` linted). Red-checked on jupiter: the old region name fails the session test again, with the daemon's own log line, and a token taken by a plain create-or-open let a second owner in. Red-checked on fedora: the old round fails the round test again.
- **Rejected for now: handing a Windows client its region by handle duplication.** A region with no name would also close GAP-A9-9's same-uid access to a ring on Windows, but it reshapes the claim slot's answer. Per-start names fix the restart and leave GAP-A9-9 where it was.
- **Not changed here: macOS took a live owner's name over** (an owner unlinked the name it found), so two daemons of one instance could run side by side there, each with its own clients. Closed by A-178.
- **Owed:** replies that stall on Windows with many daemons at once in one process. They are oversubscription (GAPS): each in-process daemon sizes itself from the whole machine, Windows charges commit when memory is made, and the test process met the commit limit, aborting on an allocation of 873,462,528 bytes. One test at a time runs clean.

### A-177 — The daemon serves a WinFsp volume at a drive letter and tells Windows of every other path's change (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 ("Windows (own thin WinFsp binding)" and its status; the DAX matrix's A-164 status), the DAX matrix (`docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8, the Windows x86_64 mount-route cell), GAPS, README (the Windows capability row), `crates/bridge-winfsp` (`host.rs` rewritten: requests to the owner shard, `MountThread`; `ffi.rs`: the exports found at run time; `notify.rs`, new; `build.rs` and `tests/mount.rs` removed), `crates/bridge-core` (`delivery.rs`: `Coherence` and `Delivered` moved from `slates-bridge-fuse`), `crates/server` (`winfsp.rs`, new; `transports.rs`: WinFsp offered where its library loads; `verbs.rs`: the WinFsp form's establishment, deferral, end and recovery; `daemon.rs`: `EndWinFspMounts`), `crates/ipc` (`AttachRequest::WinFspMount`, `UnsupportedReason::WinFspNotInstalled`, appended), `crates/db` (`AttachForm::WinFspMount`, appended; `daemon_mount_point`), `crates/client` (`attach_winfsp`), `crates/cli` (`mount`/`unmount` on Windows; `tests/winfsp.rs`, new), `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (both x86_64 Windows lanes), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-bridge-winfsp` 86 → 104), `xtask/src/capabilities.rs`, and two bug records.
- **What was there.** The WinFsp host served only a volume it built and owned itself (its live test's scratch volume), `slates mount` refused on Windows, and the daemon reported the transport `BridgeNotWired` (research f17). Nothing else could change a file under a Windows mount, so there was nothing to tell Windows.
- **Built: the owner shard serves the mount.** `attach` with the WinFsp form defers its reply to the mount's task on the volume's owner shard. An owned mount thread creates the file system, defines the drive and starts WinFsp's two dispatcher threads, off the shard. Each callback sends its request over a bounded channel to the task and wakes it (§4.3: "WinFsp requests arrive on WinFsp's threads and are routed to the owning shard"). The task serves one request a turn through the shared operation layer, under a registry attachment, behind the live-tree fence. A namespace or size change, a write (A-379), a flush, or the close of a handle that changed its file publishes before its reply. The attachment is recorded with the reply once the drive is mounted. A drive letter has nothing beneath it, so every end of the attachment removes the drive.
- **Built: Windows is told.** `FileInfoTimeout` is infinite (§4.6, as designed), and the volume's free space has a zero timeout: no notification names it. Before each request, and whenever the volume's generation moves, the task runs the FUSE mount's coherence rounds (now `slates_bridge_core::delivery`). It hands Windows one `FspFileSystemNotify` round naming what Windows holds open: Windows caches only what hangs off an open file node (WinFsp `src/sys/file.c`). A round a rename's lock defers (`STATUS_CANT_WAIT` at a zero-timeout begin) or WinFsp refuses puts the cursor back. WinFsp processes a round in a work item of its own (`FspVolumeNotify`, `src/sys/volume.c`), so the shard never waits on a kernel lock.
- **Decided: the library is found at run time, not linked.** Linked, a daemon could not start on a Windows host without WinFsp. Loaded as WinFsp's own `FspLoad` loads it, the daemon starts everywhere, and the form is refused `WinFspNotInstalled` where the library is absent (run on jupiter, which has no WinFsp, 2026-10-25).
- **Two defects found on the runner by a request log, both fixed** (run 40251802164). A paging write (`ConstrainedIo`) was applied whole, so a 62-byte file grew to its 4096-byte page; it is now clipped to the file's size, as WinFsp's `memfs` clips it (`docs/bugs/2026-10-26-a-paging-write-through-winfsp-grew-a-file-to-its-page.md`). And since the host was first written, every open of a file was handed the first open's context, so a second open freed that context twice (`docs/bugs/2026-10-26-a-winfsp-file-opened-twice-freed-its-first-context-twice.md`); the mount now takes per-handle contexts (`UmFileContextIsUserContext2`). A file's last close now writes its pages back before its publication (`FlushAndPurgeOnCleanup`): before, a Windows program's write reached the shard only at the cache manager's lazy write-back.
- **Proven** on CI's Windows runner (Windows Server 2025, WinFsp 2.1.25156), run 40252840969, the CLI tests 3 of 3 (`crates/cli/tests/winfsp.rs`): Windows programs create, write, read, list and delete through the drive, and `slates read` returns their bytes; a cached read through a handle opened before an SDK write follows it in 20.7 ms (20.5 and 20.5 ms in runs 40249524066 and 40250856246). Red-checked twice with the mount handing Windows empty rounds (runs 40249528145 and 40250871529): the cached read stayed stale for 10 s and the test failed.
- **Decided by the run: a mapped view does not follow** (superseded 2026-10-30 by A-190: the mount now makes WinFsp purge
  coherently, and the view follows; the measurements below stand). The view held its first byte for 10 s in every run. WinFsp's notification purges with `CcPurgeCacheSection` (research f8, `src/sys/file.c`), which "will not purge mapped files" (f9, Microsoft Learn); only `CcCoherencyFlushAndPurgeCache` invalidates user-mapped views (f9), and WinFsp does not call it (f10). So the DAX matrix's Windows mount-route cell is impossible through WinFsp. Worse, while the view stands a read through any other handle is stale too, and after the view and handles closed a fresh open read the change only 3.03 s later (GAPS: "A file mapped through the WinFsp mount…").
- **Owed:** a scoped (`--subtree`) and a read-shared WinFsp mount; arm64 Windows; the takeover cases are proven by A-198 (Steps 9.3–9.4); the attribute and AppleDouble-like calls (§4.6 status).

### A-179 — The Shards route on Windows rides a duplex named pipe, which the runtime serves by completions (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to: §4.3 (the drivers' status), GAPS, `crates/rt` (`pipe.rs` and `pipe_state.rs`, new;
`iocp.rs`, its pipe table and completion key; `driver.rs` and `shard.rs`, the pipe calls; `afd.rs`, `dos_error`
shared; `tests/pipe.rs`, new), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-rt` 73 → 84). This change is the runtime's half.
The route's half (2026-10-26, G-shards-windows step 1) was applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (the Shards form's bullet and status), A-161's report entry, GAPS;
- `crates/ipc`: `stream_pipe.rs` (new: `slates_ipc::stream` on Windows, the pair, `name_of`, `read_waiting` and
  `write_waiting`), `lib.rs`, `handle_route.rs` (`hand_stream`, `adopt_stream`; the duplication and the adoption
  shared with a section's), `protocol.rs` (`ReplyBody::ShardsHanded`, appended; `DescriptorRouteNotBuilt`'s doc);
- `crates/server`: `shards.rs` (built on every platform; Windows' hand-out; `deliver_handoff` split by platform;
  `end_stream` ends a stream once; `owner_shard`, moved from `virtiofs.rs`), `shards/end.rs` (new: the daemon's end per
  platform, one seam), `shards/dax_refused.rs` (new: Windows' DAX arm, every descriptor ask refused `ENOSYS`),
  `shards/dax.rs` (`Then` and `Done` moved to the parent), `verbs.rs`, `state.rs`, `daemon.rs`, `lib.rs`,
  `transports.rs` (Windows offers the form), `Cargo.toml` (the FUSE codec on every platform);
- `crates/client`: `client.rs` (`StreamEnd` on Windows, the `ShardsHanded` arm), `tests/shards.rs` (run on Windows;
  hostile frames, a destroy, a revocation, a second process refused the pipe);
- the workspace `Cargo.toml` (`Win32_Security_Cryptography`), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-ipc` 79 → 94), `ci.yml`,
  and `docs/bugs/2026-10-26-a-destroyed-volumes-stream-was-ended-again-each-teardown-pass.md`.
- **Why a pipe.** The Shards form hands a microVM's virtio-fs device a stream with nothing on disk (A-161, R1).
  Windows has no `socketpair`. An AF_UNIX socket at an abstract address binds and listens, but its connect is refused
  `WSAEINVAL`, so the only AF_UNIX pair is one made through a socket file. A duplex named pipe under a fresh name needs
  none. Measured (Shards' PM M340: jupiter, and GitHub's windows-2022 and windows-2025 runners, 2026-10-26):
  - the pair costs 9.9 to 14.3 µs at p50, against an AF_UNIX pair's 0.6 ms;
  - once connected, a second client or server instance is refused `ERROR_PIPE_BUSY`;
  - a reader gets every byte at its writer's exit, where AF_UNIX loses what is unread;
  - every handle to an end names the pipe;
  - its round trip is the shorter on every host, 0.6 to 0.9 times loopback TCP's on the runners.

  Throughput is not why: it is two to eight times TCP's on jupiter and 0.7 to 1.8 times on the runners. The Shards
  owner agreed the interface: `--slates-fs-handle V`, duplicated into the confined VM process by its spawner.
- **Why completions, and how ownership holds.**
  - Pipes report their I/O when it finishes, and the AFD reactor gives readiness to sockets alone. So each end holds
    at most one read and one write in the kernel, each in a leaked block reclaimed exactly once: at its completion,
    which always comes through the port (no `FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS`), or at once when the kernel
    refused it, which posts nothing.
  - A block names its end by handle value and generation, so a completion for a released end frees its buffer and
    wakes no one.
  - The handle is never lent out: overlapped I/O issued on it elsewhere would deliver a pointer the driver does not
    own. What an owner needs beyond reading and writing is a method: `PipeEnd::disconnect` cuts the peer off without
    closing the end, as `shutdown(Both)` does a socket.
- **Proven:**
  - `pipe_state`'s tests, every sequence of ten events six deep (10⁶): each delivered byte taken once and in order,
    each waiter handed back by its completion, and nothing started after the end.
  - On jupiter, `crates/rt/tests/pipe.rs` passes 6 of 6, 3 runs: a round trip; a write ten times the pipe's buffers
    to a reader that waits, whose would-block path is signalled, not slept on; a peer gone (the end of the stream, and
    a write refused as `ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE`); 64 KiB taken a byte at a time; an end dropped with a read in the kernel
    and a new end after it; a disconnect waking its reader.
  - `slates-rt` is clean under clippy `-D warnings` on macOS and on Windows.
- **The route.** The daemon makes the pair (`slates_ipc::stream::pair` on Windows): a duplex named pipe under
  `\\.\pipe\slates-shards-` and 32 hex digits from `BCryptGenRandom`, with `FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE`, one
  instance, `PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS` and the descriptor `D:P(A;;GA;;;OW)`, connected at once by the daemon's own
  open of the client end, which asks `SECURITY_ANONYMOUS` so the server end cannot impersonate its holder. Both ends
  are overlapped and neither is inheritable. The pipe buffers one largest frame each way, so a frame's write completes
  without its reader: with the system's default of zero every write waited for its reader, and this module's own
  round-trip test hung on jupiter. The server end becomes a `PipeEnd` on the volume's owner shard, and the serve loop of
  `crates/server/src/shards.rs` runs unchanged over `shards/end.rs`, the one seam whose arms read, write and end a
  socket or a pipe. The client end is kept under the attach's request word as Linux keeps its socket end. As the reply
  goes to the client, `deliver_handoff` duplicates the end into the client's process (`handle_route::hand_stream`,
  which judges the process to run as the daemon's user) and writes the value into `ReplyBody::ShardsHanded`. The record
  keeps zero, so a reply replayed after a restart names no handle. The client adopts it (`adopt_stream`). No
  descriptor rides a pipe, so a DAX descriptor ask is refused `ENOSYS`, and no file is offered for DAX, until step 5
  builds Windows' window (built 2026-10-26, A-180).
- **Proven (route), 2026-10-26:**
  - On jupiter: `slates-ipc`'s stream tests (a round trip each way; a second client refused `ERROR_PIPE_BUSY` and a
    second server refused; a dropped end read as the end, every byte before it delivered; a fresh name per pair);
    `crates/client/tests/shards.rs` 7 of 7 in each of 3 runs, over the handle the daemon duplicated in:
    - the FUSE history on two volumes, one served on the client's own shard and one on the other (`INIT`, `CREATE`,
      `WRITE`, `LOOKUP`, `OPEN`, `READ`, `FLUSH`, `RELEASE`, `RENAME`, `UNLINK`, each checked through slates' own
      verbs);
    - two scoped streams, each reaching only its own directory;
    - hostile frames (a length of `u32::MAX`, one past the largest frame, a frame cut in its length word and one cut
      in its body by the peer's close), each counted by its kind, with the volume's attachments back to zero;
    - a detach, a destroy and a revocation each ending the stream and its record;
    - a second process refused the attachment's pipe by name, `ERROR_PIPE_BUSY`, and the stream serving on after.
  - Unchanged on Unix: the same client tests pass on macOS (its 6) and on Linux x86_64 (adacachy, its 7), and the server's Shards suite passes on macOS (26) and Linux (21, one ignored). `slates-ipc`,
    `slates-server` and `slates-client` are clean under clippy `-D warnings` on all three.

### A-180 — Windows answers a Shards DAX ask with a confined section duplicated into a process that proves it holds the stream (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the Shards form's DAX bullet and status), A-179's route line, GAPS,
`docs/wip/shards/dax-protocol.md` ("Windows"), `crates/mem` (`dax_object.rs`: `DaxObject` on Windows, a reserved
confined section viewed and committed a range at a time; `dax_object_bytes`; `prepare_range` on both platforms;
`tests/dax_section.rs`, new), `crates/machine` (`Facts::memory_total`, `Facts::page_bytes`), `crates/vfs`
(`shards_backing.rs`: `handed_to_vmm`, `prepare_range`, `HandedObject`; `volume.rs`: the size refusals read
`dax_object_bytes`), `crates/bridge-core` (`dax_backing` built on every platform: the answer is a `HandedObject`, a range
readied before its fill; the page size from `slates-machine`, so no `rustix`), `crates/bridge-fuse` (`shards_fs.rs`:
`descriptor_claim`, `descriptor_handle_answer`; `bridge.rs`: the DAX errno maps on every platform, `EACCES` public),
`crates/ipc` (`handle_route.rs`: `claim`, `Claimant`, `hand_to_claimant`; `error.rs`: `NotAHolder`), `crates/server`
(`shards/dax.rs` serves both platforms, `shards/dax_refused.rs` removed; `shards.rs`: the stream's holders and claimant,
`tell_holder`), `crates/client/tests/shards.rs` (the Windows DAX tests), `ci.yml` (the Shards step's comment),
`unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-mem` 60 → 61, `slates-ipc` + 4).
- **What was there.** Since A-179 a Windows stream refused every DAX ask `ENOSYS` and withheld per-inode DAX at `INIT`,
  because no descriptor rides a pipe.
- **The hand-off.** The ask carries two more fields, agreed with the Shards device's author: the asking process's id
  and the value there of its stream handle (38 bytes). Once its fill is done the object's section is duplicated into
  that process, and the answer carries the duplicate's value. The duplicate maps read alone, or read and write for a
  writable ask, and may query its size. The section is made under A-175's confining descriptor, so no holder can widen
  a duplicate, a rewrite of the descriptor included.
- **The claim check, by object and not by name.** Before anything is made or filled, the named handle is duplicated
  into the daemon and must be the same object as a known holder's handle (`CompareObjectHandles`). The known holders are
  the attaching client, whose handle the attach duplicated and whose owner shard is told of it, and the last claimant
  that passed. Anything else is refused `EACCES`, counted, and nothing is put into the named process. The goal named
  the pipe's name as the test. Measured first (jupiter, Windows 10.0.26200, 2026-10-26): on a synchronous pipe with a
  read pending, `FileNameInfo`, `NtQueryObject(ObjectNameInformation)` and `FileModeInformation` each hung past 3 s,
  because a synchronous file's queries wait on its lock. `CompareObjectHandles`, `GetFileType`, the object's type and
  the duplicate's close each answered at once. So a name check would let any asker hold the shard by naming a
  synchronous handle of any same-user process. The pipe allows one instance, already connected, so the object check
  refuses and grants exactly the claimants the name check would. Its cost: a holder must still hold its handle at the
  first claim, so `slates shards` names its child as a holder (`ShardsHolder`) before it closes its own copy (A-181).
- **The object's size, derived.** A section's making costs in proportion to its size, reserved or not. Measured on
  jupiter the same day: 2^48 bytes took 3.3 ms and 12,001 pages of commit, 2^53 took 129 ms and 358,807 pages, and
  2^62 or more was refused `ERROR_NO_SYSTEM_RESOURCES`. So Windows sizes it to the machine's physical memory in whole
  ranges (`dax_object_bytes`). A RAM-only volume's file holds no more bytes than that, so only a hand-made sparse file
  passes it, and a change taking a backed file past it is refused `EFBIG`, as Unix refuses past `2^63 − 2 MiB`.
- **Committed a range at a time.** A reserved page faults any view until it is committed, so each range an ask covers is
  committed whole before its fill begins (`prepare_range`), past the file's end and over holes too. A commit is the
  section's, so the VMM's views need no commit of their own. Committed pages stay charged until the backing ends,
  within the fill budget's one range per range filled. Windows gives no committed page of a section back, so a zeroing
  is stores of zeros.
- **One code path.** The backed session and the stream's DAX module are the Unix ones. Only the parse of the ask, the
  claim and the hand-off are paired `#[cfg]` functions.
- **Fixed on the way: Windows base file times saturated, so no outsider's edit was ever seen**
  (`docs/bugs/2026-10-26-windows-base-file-times-saturated-so-no-outsider-edit-was-seen.md`). The Windows host kept
  every time as nanoseconds since 1601, which pass `i64::MAX` for any date after 1893. So every modification, change
  and birth time was `i64::MAX`, measured by the guest's `GETATTR` and by instrumenting `follow_live_disk`, and
  `now_ns` saturated too. Every host time is now nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, as on Unix:
  `crates/base/src/windows.rs`, with `crates/base/tests/host.rs`
  `a_files_times_are_unix_nanoseconds_and_an_in_place_edit_moves_them`, which failed on jupiter before the fix and runs
  on every host.
- **The last check, closed with A-185 (2026-10-26).** The step asked for a write through another slates attachment
  to show in a mapping after the compare-back's refill. Within a volume such a write reaches every map by write-through
  before it returns (tested). Across volumes it reaches the disk only by a landing, and a landing places a new file
  rather than writing in place, so an existing map keeps the replaced file as POSIX does; Ada chose to prove the fresh
  map: `a_write_through_another_attachment_landed_on_the_disk_reaches_a_fresh_map` lands overlay B onto the directory
  overlay A maps, A's old node answers `ESTALE` and keeps the old bytes, and A's name, looked up again, maps the landed
  bytes. The refill itself is proven by an in-place edit (`a_section_of_an_untouched_base_file_is_refilled_with_an_
  outsiders_edit`). Built for it: landing on Windows (A-185).
- **Rejected: the pipe's name, as the goal stated it** (above: it lets an asker hold the shard). **Rejected: the
  daemon keeping a duplicate of the client end as the reference.** Any handle keeps the pipe's client open, so the
  stream would never end when its VM did.
- **Proven** on jupiter (Windows 10.0.26200), 2026-10-26:
  - `crates/client/tests/shards.rs` 10 of 10 in each of 3 runs, among them the three DAX tests against an in-process
    daemon. Four hostile claimants each get `EACCES`, counted `shards.dax_claim_refused`, with the named process's
    handle count the same before and after, and the stream serving on: a process holding another attachment's pipe,
    one holding an event and no pipe, a value naming nothing, and a process that has exited. A genuine claimant names
    a second handle of its own stream, a different value of the same object, and maps the section it is handed. The
    section holds exactly the file's 8,292 bytes and zeros to the end of the range. The claimant stores into it and
    sends `FSYNC`, and slates' own read returns the stored bytes. A write through another attachment shows in the map
    at once, and still after a request on the stream, and the guest's next `FSYNC` (the compare-back) leaves it
    standing in the volume and the map. A duplicate that may rewrite the descriptor is refused `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`.
    The backing is held while the attachment lives (one, 2 MiB charged) and let go, its charge given back, when the
    attachment ends (`Daemon::dax_backings_held` back to zero).
  - The refill, beneath an overlay over a real directory in the build output: a read-only section of an untouched base
    file shows the host's in-place edit by the reply to the guest's next `GETATTR`, every other byte as it was,
    `shards.dax_refilled` counted. Its first run found that no Windows overlay had ever seen an in-place edit: every
    base file's times were `i64::MAX` (fixed on the way, below).
  - `crates/mem/tests/dax_section.rs` 2 of 2: a section of 132,766,498,816 bytes (63,308 ranges, the machine's
    memory) whose first and last ranges each side reads and stores; a read-only and a writable duplicate each refused
    `WRITE_DAC`, and the read-only one refused a duplicate or a view that writes.
  - Red-checked in a scratch tree: the claim check passing everyone handed the section to a holder of another pipe
    (`Ok(192)` where `EACCES` was asserted); an owner-all descriptor granted the widening duplicate in both tests;
    ranges never committed killed the test process (`STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION`); and an ended stream that let nothing go
    kept its backing (`(1, 2097152)` where `(0, 0)` was asserted). The refill test failed 3 of 3 before the fix below.
  - Measured, release build, 3 runs of 41: a section's making takes 4 to 16 µs at p50 (53 µs at most) once the
    process has made one confined section. The first confined section a process makes, a peer's or a DAX one, costs
    592 to 837 µs (the descriptor's conversion), which the first ask's shard pays (GAPS).
  - macOS: the Unix DAX suites pass unchanged (`slates-server --test shards` 26 of 26, `slates-vfs --test
    shards_backing`, `slates-mem --test dax_object`, `slates-bridge-core`, `slates-bridge-fuse`).

### A-185 — Landing runs on Windows: a handle-relative NTFS writer, and NTFS's renames in the engine's move check (accepted 2026-10-26; landed 2026-11-18)
Applied in the same change to: §4.15 (a status), A-180 (its last check), A-262 (its landing half's status), GAPS,
`docs/wip/ci-matrix.md`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (both Windows lanes), the bug record of 2026-11-08 (the earlier
finding), `crates/land` (`src/os_windows.rs`, new: the Windows seam; `src/lib.rs`; `Cargo.toml`, `windows-sys`;
`src/engine.rs`, `same_object_after_a_move`; `tests/os.rs`, `tests/os_escape.rs` and `tests/os_removal.rs` on Windows,
their symbolic-link cases on Unix, and three new tests in `tests/os.rs`; `tests/common`, `write_file_with_mode`;
`examples/land_bench.rs`, its OS rows on every platform), `crates/base` (`src/windows.rs`: `walk_dir` with the
own-drive refusal, `WalkRefusal`, `drive_of`, the handle accessors and adoption, `entry_fingerprint`; `tests/host.rs`: the
junction helper's backslashes), `crates/server` (`src/landing.rs`, `src/image.rs` and `src/landing_entries.rs` without
a Unix gate; the landing and lease fixtures, `common::client::channel_account`, and `presentations.rs`, `lease.rs`,
`snapshot_landing.rs`, `landing_fairness.rs`, `presentation_fairness.rs`, `write_policy.rs`, `checkout.rs` and
`signed_work.rs` on every platform, a channel's account read from the daemon where they asked `getuid`), `crates/client`
(`tests/presentation.rs` on every platform; `tests/shards.rs`, the landing-to-fresh-map test), `crates/cli`
(`tests/winfsp.rs`, a landing target on the daemon's own drive), and `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-land` 4 → 22).
- **What was there.** `slates-land`'s write seam was Unix-only and the server refused every landing on Windows
  (`Unsupported { feature: "landing" }`), so no landing test ran there and no Windows lane ran the daemon's unit tests,
  two of which asked for a landing until they moved to `crates/server/tests/presentations.rs`. Ada's rule (2026-10-26):
  every function works on every platform. Another session built the writer on 2026-10-26 on jupiter (Windows
  10.0.26200) and left it uncommitted (`agents/windows-land-wip`, `dcd74474`); on 2026-11-18 it was ported onto main,
  1,985 commits on, and finished.
- **The writer.** Every verb is relative to a handle the base host holds, never a path, as on Unix:
  - creates by `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_CREATE` and the parent's handle as `RootDirectory`, so a name, link or
    junction already there refuses the create;
  - the rename that never replaces by `NtSetInformationFile(FileRenameInformationEx)`, POSIX semantics and never
    `REPLACE_IF_EXISTS`. Win32's `SetFileInformationByHandle(FileRenameInfoEx)` refused a name relative to
    `RootDirectory` with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` (measured on jupiter, Windows 10.0.26200);
  - removals by `FileDispositionInfoEx`, POSIX semantics, the read-only attribute ignored;
  - writes through the temporary's own file (`seek_write`), never a duplicated handle per write;
  - a file's mode as its `READONLY` bit alone, set where the mode has no write bit and cleared where it has one
    (A-262), every other attribute bit kept (`attributes_for_mode`);
  - a batch's barrier as each file's `FlushFileBuffers` on ⌈√n⌉ threads, off the shard (A-132). A directory's sync
    goes through the directory opened again, an empty name relative to its own handle, with `FILE_ADD_FILE`:
    `ReOpenFile` with `GENERIC_WRITE` was refused `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`.

  NTFS has no atomic exchange of two names, so the capabilities say so and the engine moves the old entry aside
  first. A symbolic link is refused `EPERM`: Windows makes one only through a path (`CreateSymbolicLinkW`) or with a
  privilege, and slates writes through handles and asks for no privilege (R10).
- **Containment.** The target is walked from its drive's root one component at a time with `FILE_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`,
  refusing `..`, a link, a junction or a mount point (`slates_base::walk_dir`), and must be owned by this process's
  user, compared by security identifier. A target on one of this daemon's own WinFsp drives is refused `OwnMount`
  before any open (A-227), as the Unix walk refuses a component on one of its mounts: the walk refuses every name
  surrogate, so the drive the path names is the only volume it can reach, and its DOS device is asked of the object
  manager, never of the volume.
- **What the engine met on NTFS** (each measured, then fixed):
  - The base host's fingerprint carried the raw attribute word as the mode, so the engine read a witnessed directory
    as a file (`Conflict(TypeChanged)` on the worked example's tree removal; jupiter, 2026-10-26). A-262 fixed the same
    bug for the base plane on 2026-11-08 (`windows_mode_and_bits`), before this landed, and the writer reads its
    mapping; its bug record now carries this finding.
  - NTFS gives a file renamed onto a name another file left moments before that file's creation time (tunneling),
    and the engine's fallback does exactly that, so every replacement was undone `TargetInUse`, the birth time the
    only other difference (jupiter, 2026-10-26). A moved object is now judged on the device, the file index, the size,
    the mtime, the mode and its attribute bits, the birth time set aside with the ctime and owner
    (`same_object_after_a_move`, one check where three sites had their own).
  - A rename sets `ARCHIVE` on the file it moves, and a backup clears it from every file it has copied, so a witnessed
    file without it could never be moved aside and found the same: with the bit compared, such a file's replacement was
    undone `TargetInUse` and the landing ended `Partial` (red-check on CI's windows-latest, run 44367207034). The move
    check sets the bit aside with the birth time, and a moved file that differs from its witness in any field still has
    its bytes compared (`a_file_whose_archive_bit_a_backup_cleared_is_replaced_by_a_landing`).
  - The writer gave each file its mode by writing the attribute word whole (`NORMAL` or `READONLY`). The rename that
    places the file sets `ARCHIVE` again, so a landed file held it either way (red-check: the word written whole lands
    the same, run 44367207034); the writer now sets or clears `READONLY` alone, A-262's rule, every other bit kept
    (`attributes_for_mode`; `a_landed_file_keeps_its_archive_bit_and_takes_read_only_from_its_mode` holds the mapping).
  - An elevated process owns nothing it makes by its user: Windows makes the token's default owner the owner of a
    process's new objects, and an elevated administrator's is the Administrators group (the owner CI's runner gave a
    directory it made: `BUILTIN\Administrators`). The writer compared a target's owner with the token's user alone, so
    on CI's runners every landing into a directory the test made was refused `TargetNotOwned`
    (`OwnedByAnother`; presentations 0 of 6 on windows-11-arm, run 44364587413). The owner may now be the token's user
    or its default owner (`TokenOwner`): a directory this process made is its own however it ran, as a root daemon's
    is its own on Unix.
- **What a landing means for a DAX map** (A-180's last check, decided with Ada). A landing never writes a file in
  place (R1's old-or-new): it places a new file at the name. So a guest holding the old file open keeps its bytes,
  as POSIX does (measured: its `READ` returned them), and a node with no descriptor held answers `ESTALE` (A-151);
  the guest looks the name up again and maps the new file, which holds the landed bytes. A refill follows a change
  made in place on the disk only.
- **Still owed.** A symbolic link in a Windows landing (no unprivileged, handle-relative way to make one); a reflink
  (`FSCTL_DUPLICATE_EXTENTS_TO_FILE` on ReFS); A-262's landing half, applying the volume's other attribute bits. And
  the seam's numbering: it reports the refusals the engine tells apart by POSIX numbers (`EEXIST`, `ENOSPC`,
