  `EOPNOTSUPP`, `EPERM`) and every other one by its Win32 code, so a Win32 code equal to one of the engine's numbers
  (`ERROR_NOT_SAME_DEVICE` 17, `ERROR_BAD_COMMAND` 22, `ERROR_OUT_OF_PAPER` 28, `ERROR_TOO_MANY_SESS` 69,
  `ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER` 122) would read as that POSIX refusal. None of the writer's calls is known to answer one;
  a typed refusal at the seam, rather than a number, would close it on every host.
- **Proven** (2026-11-18) on CI's windows-latest and windows-11-arm, on main 53353e5e8 with this change merged (run
  44371955995):
  - `slates-land` whole on NTFS: the oracle 30 of 30, `os.rs` 9 of 9 (the real kill test, T-1.15, and the three new
    tests among them), the escape oracle with junction and hard-link swaps before every seam call, and the removal
    oracle with real outsider saves; 62 s and 87 s with the build;
  - `slates-server`'s unit tests one test at a time, 368 passed and 3 ignored, in 9.68 s and 16.64 s;
  - the landing suites through the daemon, one test at a time: `presentations.rs` 10 of 10 (the two landing tests the
    unit tests once held among them), `checkout`, `landing_fairness`, `lease`, `presentation_fairness`, `signed_work`,
    `snapshot_landing` and `write_policy`, all passing;
  - the client's `presentation.rs` (the presenter killed by `TerminateProcess`), the landing-to-fresh-map DAX test
    (`crates/client/tests/shards.rs`), and the MCP surface with `slates.land.materialize`;
  - a landing target and a base on the daemon's own WinFsp drive refused `OwnMount` before any open (run 44376034930).

  macOS (the Mac Studio) and ubuntu-latest: the land suite whole (71 tests), the daemon's landing unit tests,
  `presentations.rs`, `write_policy.rs` and `signed_work.rs` (runs 44367197015 and 44371955995). Red-checked on
  windows-latest (run 44367207034), each mutation alone: the move check comparing `ARCHIVE` undid the backup-cleared
  file's replacement (`Undone(TargetInUse)`, the landing `Partial`); the owner compared with the token's user alone
  refused all three new tests' targets (`TargetNotOwned`); and the attribute word written whole changed nothing a test
  sees (the placing rename sets `ARCHIVE`). The own-drive refusal's red-check (the walk without its drive check) is
  filed for main's run, not yet read. The 2026-10-26 red-checks on jupiter stand: a rename that may
  replace failed the removal oracle; a walk that follows a junction failed the escape test; a placement made a no-op
  failed the fresh-map test.

### A-181 — `slates shards` on Windows starts its command holding the stream end as a named handle, and waits for it (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the Shards form's Windows status), GAPS, `crates/ipc` (`win_spawn.rs`, new: the
handle-list spawn moved out of `delivery.rs`, now with a job list, a kill-on-close job and the console-event handler;
`delivery.rs` spawns through it; `stream_pipe.rs`: `spawn_with`, `HandedChild`; `tests/stream_spawn.rs`, new),
`crates/cli` (`args.rs`: `HandOffKind`, `HandOff`, `HANDLE_PLACEHOLDER`, both forms parsed on every host; `verbs.rs`:
`run_shards` over `hand_to`, paired per platform, and `exec_vmm`'s Windows arm, which no longer compiled once A-179
gave `StreamEnd` values there; `tests/shards.rs`, new; `Cargo.toml`: the FUSE codec a dev-dependency on every
platform), `ci.yml` (the Windows lanes), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-ipc` + 5); and, in a second change the same
day, `crates/ipc` (`protocol.rs`: `RequestBody::ShardsHolder`, `ReplyBody::ShardsHolderAdded`,
`Refusal::HolderPending`, appended; `stream_pipe.rs`: `HandedChild::let_go_of_end`), `crates/server` (`shards.rs`:
`add_holder`; `verbs.rs`), `crates/client` (`Client::tell_shards_holder`, resent through `call_through_transient`;
`tests/shards.rs`: the hostile holder test), and A-180's claim bullet.
- **What was there.** `slates shards` replaced itself with its command, the end at `--fd N`, on Unix alone. A-179 gave
  Windows the stream, so its `StreamEnd` became a handle and the Windows arms that matched it as empty no longer built.
- **Why a named handle, not a number.** A Windows process cannot choose the value a handle gets in another process, so
  the command is told it in its arguments, where `{handle}` stands. The Shards device's author agreed the interface:
  `--slates-fs-handle V`, V decimal, which the spawner checks is a pipe and not one of its own standard handles, then
  makes non-inheritable and duplicates into its confined VM.
- **Why inheritance through a handle list.** A handle duplicated into a child after it is created has a value the
  child's command line could not have named. An inherited handle keeps its value, so an inheritable duplicate is made
  first and named in the arguments, and `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST` gives the child that one handle and its
  standard three, so nothing else inheritable reaches it (the consumer delivery's spawn, now shared). The standard
  library cannot set the attribute on the pinned toolchain (`windows_process_extensions_raw_attribute`).
- **Exec, emulated.** On Unix the command is CMD, so a supervisor's kill ends CMD and the attachment. Here CMD is
  created inside a kill-on-close job (`PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST`, a member from its first instruction) whose only
  handle the command holds, so the kernel ends CMD when the command ends by any means; Shards' VM nests its own job
  beneath. Ctrl-C reaches every process on the console, so after the spawn the command answers console events as
  handled (a handler, never `SetConsoleCtrlHandler(NULL, TRUE)`, whose ignore flag children created later inherit) and
  leaves the shutdown to CMD.
- **The command names CMD as a holder, then closes its copy, as the plan states.** A-180's claim check compares a
  VM's handle with a known holder's by object, the attaching client's first, because a name query on a synchronous
  pipe handle with a read pending hung past 3 s (jupiter, 2026-10-26). Closing the command's copy at once would leave
  the stream with no live known holder, and a VM's first DAX ask would be refused `EACCES`. So once CMD has the end,
  the command sends `ShardsHolder { volume, attachment, pid, handle }` naming CMD's process and handle. The stream's
  shard judges it by `claim` against the holders it knows, the command's own copy still open among them, records CMD
  (`dax::record_holder`, which keeps the first holder and the latest), and only then does the command close its copy.
  A true claim adds no authority, since CMD holds the stream already; a false one is refused `Forbidden` and counted.
  A daemon that will not take CMD fails the run: the command drops CMD's job, which ends CMD, and exits 4.
- **Found by the first test: the request can overtake the attach's own holder record.** The attach records its
  client as the first holder by a task it queues on the stream's shard as it replies, and a request sent at once met
  no holder, 3 of 3 on jupiter (counted `shards.holder_unknown`, as the diagnosis named it), so it was refused although
  true. The daemon now answers a stream with no known holder `HolderPending` (counted `shards.holder_pending`), having
  recorded nothing, and the client sends again through `call_through_transient`, the bounded, backed-off resend it
  already uses for `OwnerUnreachable`, within its reconnect budget. A command that starts CMD first takes
  milliseconds, and never met it in its runs.
- **Rejected: the command keeping its copy until CMD exits,** built first in b16bac34. It needed no new request, but
  the attachment then outlived CMD closing its end early, which the plan rules out and Unix does not do.
- **Proven** on jupiter (Windows 10.0.26200), 2026-10-26, against the tree with A-180 beneath it, as committed:
  - `crates/ipc/tests/stream_spawn.rs`, 1 of 1 in each of 6 runs. A program writes through the handle its arguments
    name and exits 7, and `wait` returns 7. The end stays open after the program has gone while the launcher holds
    its copy, and closes once the launcher lets go. A child the standard library starts afterwards, told the value,
    finds no handle there naming the pipe, while an inheritable copy, the contrast, is found. A dropped launcher's job
    ends a program that never exits on its own. No placeholder is refused `Layout`, and the end is closed.
  - `crates/cli/tests/shards.rs` with `SLATES_TEST_CLI=1`, 1 of 1 in each of 6 runs, a real anchor and daemon:
    - a probe started by `slates shards` mounts the attachment over `{handle}` (INIT, LOOKUP, OPEN, READ, RELEASE) and
      reads the file's bytes; the daemon's `shards.holder_added` moves by one; the attachment is gone after the
      probe's exit;
    - the command exits 7 with a silent program;
    - the attachment ends while a program that closed its handle still runs, with the command still waiting;
    - a `TerminateProcess` of the command takes a program that never exits on its own, and the attachment, along;
    - a missing volume exits 1, a program that cannot run exits 4 and leaves no attachment, and `--fd` or no
      `{handle}` exits 2.
  - `crates/client/tests/shards.rs`, 11 of 11 in each of 3 runs, among them the new hostile holder test: this
    process's own handle is taken (after one `HolderPending` in each run), another pipe's handle and a value naming no
    handle of the stream are refused `Forbidden`, a missing attachment `NotFound`, and the stream serves throughout.
    On Unix the request is refused `Unsupported` (macOS).
  - The consumer delivery, whose spawn moved, passes `crates/ipc/tests/delivery.rs`. Clippy `-D warnings` and the
    documentation step are clean over the Windows lane's crates, the binary and both of its Windows test targets.
  - **Red-checked** on the same copy, one mutant at a time:
    - the inheritable duplicate never closed fails the hand-off test (the end outlives its launcher);
    - no job fails it, and fails the CLI test's kill case;
    - the launcher's copy closed with no holder named fails both;
    - the command never letting go fails the CLI test (the attachment outlives the closed handle);
    - the daemon recording a holder without judging it fails the hostile holder test (another pipe's handle taken);
    - the client not resending on `HolderPending` fails it too.
  - The first run of the no-job mutant passed the CLI kill case: the holder then waited on its standard input, and that
    read returned once the command died, so the holder exited by itself. The holder now parks for good, so only the
    job can end it, and the mutant fails.

### A-184 — The NFS server, and with it the network export, runs on Windows: a connection's inbox frames requests where no receive low-water mark exists (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to:
- the design: §4.6 (the export's status);
- the records: `docs/wip/platforms.md` (the export, fleet and container rows), GAPS (`8a-platforms`, and gap 2's
  owed work);
- `crates/server`:
  - `lib.rs`: the NFS modules ungated; `anchor_hold` paired with a Windows arm, `anchor_hold_windows.rs`, new;
  - `Cargo.toml`: `slates-bridge-nfs` on every platform;
  - `nfs.rs`: the framing pair `head`, `want`, `consume` and `closed_mid_record`, the Windows `Inbox`, migration
    carrying it, the thread clock paired;
  - `config.rs`: the NFSv4 caps on every platform, and `inode_reserve` one function over a paired
    `guest_listing_entries`;
  - `state.rs`, `daemon.rs`, `verbs.rs` and `fleet.rs`: the NFS state, the transport's start, the publication's call
    records and replies, the service times, and the export listener on every platform;
  - `tests/nfs_hostile.rs` and `tests/nfs_tls.rs`: run on every platform;
- `crates/rt`: `tcp.rs` (`TcpStream::read_now`);
- `ci.yml`: both x86_64 Windows lanes run the two suites.

- **Why.** Ada's rule (2026-10-26). The NFS server is the network export on every platform: `slates export`, a fleet
  node's export, and the way in for Docker Desktop's Linux containers and WSL2. Its gate was the runtime's TCP, built
  by A-182. Windows' local mount stays WinFsp: this serves other machines and virtual machines, it mounts nothing
  here.
- **What Windows refused, and the shape that answers it.** The first Windows run ended 15 of the hostile suite's 17
  tests at their first call: the client read `WSAECONNABORTED` or `WSAECONNRESET`.
  - **Cause.** A connection waits for a whole request by setting the receive low-water mark to the record's length
    (A-113), and Windows' TCP refuses `SO_RCVLOWAT` (A-182). The connection ended rather than spin, as its rule says,
    at its first `want(1)`.
  - **No equivalent exists.** Winsock refuses `MSG_WAITALL` with `MSG_PEEK`, and the AFD reactor's readiness is
    level-triggered. A request cannot wait whole in the kernel there: a connection peeking half a record would wake
    at once, every time.
  - **The Windows arm.** A connection reads what is queued into its own inbox, two records long as the kernel buffer
    is on Unix, and parses whole records there. It consumes each once its reply is sent, and sees a close as the end
    of stream it is. Once the queue is drained, each wake brings new bytes, so waiting never spins. The inbox moves
    with the connection to its volume's owner shard, carrying the call that moved it.
  - **What it gives up.** A-113's survival of a daemon's death: a request read into the inbox dies with its daemon.
    On Windows so does the connection, since no anchor holds it (gap 2), and the client resends on its next
    connection. NFSv4.1's call records (A-127) still answer a retry exactly once. Holding Windows connections across a
    restart must carry the inbox's bytes with the socket.
- **The inode reserve on Windows.**
  - **Before.** It was zero: "no transport here hands out an inode number a client keeps across a restart".
  - **Now.** The export is such a transport, since an NFS client keeps its file handles across a server restart. So
    the reserve is the NFS term there.
  - **The guest term** stays zero on Windows: a guest's stream ends with its daemon, since no anchor holds it.
    `guest_listing_entries` is the paired place where holding it adds the term.
- **Also on every platform now:** the NFSv4 caps, the publication's NFS call records and held replies (Windows
  published none before), the NFS service times, and a fleet node's export listener. That listener's adoption from an
  anchor stays Unix (gap 2).
- **Measured and left out:** Windows charges a thread's CPU time a scheduler tick at a time (15.6 ms), too coarse to
  split a call of microseconds. So the off-core share of a local call is not recorded there, rather than recorded as
  its whole wall time.
- **Proven** (2026-10-26):
  - **Windows x86_64 (jupiter):**
    - `nfs_hostile` 17 of 17. Its honest clients write and read back their own files while breakers send partial
      records, oversized markers and garbage, abort mid-call and replay tampered handles; the volume lives on the
      shard the listener is not on, so every connection moves with its inbox.
    - `nfs_tls` 8 of 8.
    - Run 17 at once, every test stalled a reply past its one-second deadline: each starts a daemon sized from the
      whole machine, as the client suite's did. So CI runs them one test at a time.
  - **Red:** before the inbox, 15 of 17 failed with the connection aborted or reset at its first call.
  - **macOS arm64:** `nfs_hostile` 17 of 17, `nfs_tls` 8 of 8, the recovery oracle 41 of 41.
  - **Linux x86_64 (adacachy, capped, load 70):** `nfs_hostile` 17 of 17, `nfs_tls` 8 of 8, the recovery oracle 43
    of 43; clippy on the server, the runtime and the CLI.
  - **Lints:** clippy `-D warnings` on `slates-server` (all targets) and the `slates-cli` binary for Windows
    (`cargo xwin`, and natively on jupiter), and on macOS.
- **Owed:**
  - A real Linux kernel client mounting a Windows export: Docker Desktop's machine through `host.docker.internal`, or
    WSL2.
  - What owner a Windows export presents: a provisioned root's group is 0 there (`verbs::creator_gid`), where Unix
    takes the creator's.
  - The arm64 Windows lane, which builds no server.

### A-183 — The MCP HTTP edge is served on every platform, a refusal ends its connection in stages, and no Windows socket is inherited or shared (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to:
- the design: §4.3 (the sockets' status), §4.12 (the HTTP edge's status), and A-182 (its exclusivity proof, corrected
  below);
- the records: `docs/wip/platforms.md` (the MCP and fleet rows, the order of work), GAPS (`8a-platforms`), and a bug
  record (`docs/bugs/2026-10-26-the-mcp-edges-refusal-was-erased-by-a-reset-on-windows.md`);
- `crates/mcp`: `lib.rs` (the edge ungated) and `http.rs` (`refuse`, `drain`);
- `crates/cli`: `verbs.rs` (`slates mcp --http` on Windows) and `Cargo.toml` (`slates-rt` on every platform);
- `crates/rt`:
  - `netsys.rs`: `exclusive_socket`, which now makes the datagram socket too; an adopted datagram socket taken out of
    inheritance; `shutdown_write`;
  - `tcp.rs`: `TcpStream::close_write`;
  - `tests/udp.rs` and `tests/tcp.rs`: a test that a child keeps no copy, and the exclusivity tests rebuilt on the
    case that tells the two apart;
- `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-rt` 96 → 95) and `ci.yml` (`slates-mcp` linted and documented in the Windows lanes).

- **Why.** Ada's rule (2026-10-26): every function on every platform. The HTTP edge stood on A-182's TCP; once that
  was built, the edge's own `cfg` was the only thing keeping `slates mcp --http` off Windows.
- **The edge on Windows: one code path.** The gates are gone. The first Windows run of the MCP test found a bug the Unix
  stacks had hidden:
  - The edge refused a request on its head (a body past the bound) and closed with the body still arriving.
  - The close reset the connection, and Windows' reset discarded the `413` the client had not yet read: the client
    read `ConnectionAborted`.
  - RFC 9112 §9.6 says any stack may do this. So every refusal inside a served connection now ends it in stages: the
    refusal, a half-close, the client's remaining bytes read and dropped within the edge's deadline, then the close.
- **No Windows socket is inherited or shared.**
  - **Before.** The datagram socket was made by `socket()`, which Winsock makes inheritable. Any process a daemon
    started kept the fleet port after the daemon closed it: the standard library's spawn inherits every inheritable
    handle, `unsafe-budget.toml`'s `slates-ipc` note. It also lacked `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE`.
  - **Now.** Both kinds are made by one `WSASocketW` with `WSA_FLAG_NO_HANDLE_INHERIT`, and `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE`
    set before any bind. An adopted datagram socket has its inheritance cleared, as an adopted stream socket does.
    Its sharing is its creator's, since the option only takes effect before a bind.
- **What exclusivity defends, measured.** Jupiter, Windows 10.0.26200, 2026-10-26, one user. Every pair of a first
  socket (default or exclusive; on `0.0.0.0` or `127.0.0.1`) and a second (plain or `SO_REUSEADDR`; on either
  address), for UDP and TCP. Both protocols behaved the same:
  - a second bind of the address the first holds is refused either way: plain `WSAEADDRINUSE`, `SO_REUSEADDR`
    `WSAEACCES`;
  - a second bind of the wildcard address beside a first on loopback succeeds either way;
  - only beside a first socket on the wildcard address does the option tell. There a plain loopback bind of the same
    port succeeds against a default socket and takes the traffic addressed to loopback; against an exclusive one it is
    refused `WSAEACCES`.
- **Corrects A-182.** Its exclusivity test bound both sockets to loopback, so it would have passed without the option.
  The datagram twin's red-check exposed this: it passed against a mutant without the option. Both tests now bind the
  first socket to the wildcard address and the second, with no option, to loopback.
- **Proven** (2026-10-26):
  - **Windows x86_64 (jupiter):**
    - `tests/tcp.rs` and `tests/udp.rs` 11 of 11 each.
    - Red-checked with one mutant made without the inherit flag and without the option: exactly the four new or
      rebuilt tests fail. Each kind's child test fails `WSAEADDRINUSE`, and each exclusivity test fails because the
      loopback bind was accepted.
    - The MCP test runs through the HTTP edge, the `413` now read whole. It stops at landing: `slates.land.materialize`
      answers `Unsupported` on Windows until the Windows landing lands, which is in progress (G-shards-windows step
      5's owner).
    - Before the staged close, the same test failed with `(Err(ConnectionAborted), "")`.
    - `cargo clippy -D warnings` clean on `slates-rt` and `slates-mcp` (all targets), the `slates-cli` binary, and its
      two Windows tests.
  - **macOS arm64:** the MCP test whole (1.75 s); `tests/tcp.rs` 10 of 10 and `tests/udp.rs` 11 of 11. The child test
    is red-checked there with close-on-exec removed: `EADDRINUSE`.
  - **Linux x86_64:** `cargo clippy -D warnings` on the three crates; `tests/tcp.rs` 10 of 10 and `tests/udp.rs` 11 of
    11; the MCP test whole.
- **Corrected the same day (CI on 8233f875):** both kinds' child test failed on GitHub's Ubuntu runner with the port
  still bound right after the spawn, in both lanes that ran them, and passed on jupiter, macOS and adacachy.
  - **Cause, from the kernel's source:** Linux v6.11 releases a vfork parent, and so the standard library's
    `posix_spawn`, in `exec_mmap` (`exec_mm_release` → `mm_release` → `complete_vfork_done`). `begin_new_exec` reaches
    `do_close_on_exec` only after that (fs/exec.c, kernel/fork.c). So for a moment the spawned child still holds every
    close-on-exec descriptor.
  - **Why only CI showed it:** Linux master closes them first. adacachy's 7.2 kernel passed 50 of 50 even with both
    processes pinned to one CPU.
  - **The fix:** the tests now wait for the child's own first line, which only a child past its exec prints, before
    closing the socket. The property is unchanged: a child never runs code holding the socket.
  - **Red-checked:** close-on-exec removed, the test still fails `EADDRINUSE`.
- **Siblings, not done here:**
  - The accept loop's `503` to a connection past the bound still closes at once, since the loop must not wait. A client
    that has already sent its request can read a reset there. Staging that close needs a bounded set of shedding
    tasks (GAPS `8a-platforms`).
  - Linux could make a socket close-on-exec as it is made (`SOCK_CLOEXEC`), where the seam set the flag after
    `socket()`, so a process another thread started in between inherited the socket for its life. Done the same day:
    `netsys::new_socket` and `accept4` on Linux; macOS has no such atomic form.
  - The MCP test joins the Windows CI lanes once landing runs on Windows.

### A-182 — The runtime's TCP is built on every platform: one code path over the socket seam, Winsock 2 and the AFD reactor on Windows (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to: §4.3 (the sockets' status), §4.6 (the MCP server's status), `docs/wip/platforms.md`
(new: every function by platform, with this as gap 1's close), GAPS (`8a-platforms`, new), `crates/rt` (`netsys.rs`,
its stream half on both arms and three refusal helpers; `tcp.rs`, cfg-free over the seam, its hand-off named
`from_owned`/`into_owned` over `OwnedStream` where it said `from_fd`/`into_fd`; `lib.rs`, the module ungated; `udp.rs`,
`into_owned` on every platform; `tests/tcp.rs`, run on every platform, five tests added), the renamed callers
(`crates/server` `nfs.rs`, `fleet.rs`, `daemon.rs`; `crates/cli` `anchor.rs`; `crates/anchor` `supervise.rs`,
`tests/anchor.rs`), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-rt` 84 → 96), and `ci.yml` (the three Windows lanes run
`tests/tcp.rs`).
- **Why.** Ada's rule (2026-10-26): every function works on macOS arm64, Linux and Windows on amd64 and arm64. The
  runtime had no TCP on Windows (`#[cfg(not(windows))] pub mod tcp`), so every TCP service was missing there: the MCP
  HTTP edge, the NFS network export, a fleet node's export, and with the export Docker Desktop's and WSL2's way in.
  This is what each of them stands on; each is built on it next (`docs/wip/platforms.md`).
- **Shape.** The async logic stays in `tcp.rs`, and the calls are the seam's, as `udp.rs`'s are: the Unix arm is the
  `rustix` and `libc` code `tcp.rs` held, moved unchanged; the Windows arm is Winsock 2. The AFD reactor already armed
  a socket's accept, disconnect, abort and connect-failure edges, so readiness needed nothing new.
- **Where the platforms differ, each answers for itself:**
  - whole sends: macOS and the BSDs (`SO_SNDLOWAT`); Linux and Windows answer `NotOffered` (a non-blocking Winsock
    send may take part of its bytes);
  - a receive low-water mark: Unix keeps one; Windows' TCP provider refuses `SO_RCVLOWAT`, and the refusal is
    returned, not hidden (the A-113 peek-whole-record design needs another wait on Windows, for the export's turn);
  - the peer's close: Linux `TCP_INFO`, macOS `TCP_CONNECTION_INFO`, Windows `SIO_TCP_INFO`;
  - a Windows stream socket is made with `WSA_FLAG_NO_HANDLE_INHERIT` (Unix's close-on-exec), an accepted or adopted
    one has inheritance cleared, and every one binds with `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE`, so no other process can take a
    listener's connections by binding its port with `SO_REUSEADDR` (Microsoft Learn).
- **Proven** (2026-10-26):
  - Windows x86_64 (jupiter, Windows 10.0.26200): `crates/rt/tests/tcp.rs` 10 of 10, among them a refused connect
    reported typed, the peer's close seen in Windows' own record, a peeked request left queued until discarded, the
    low-water mark refused typed, and a second socket's `SO_REUSEADDR` bind of a listener's port refused `WSAEACCES`;
    CI's Windows doc step clean.
  - Linux x86_64: `tests/tcp.rs` 9 of 9 and the NFS server's hostile-client suite 17 of 17 over the moved calls.
  - macOS arm64: `tests/tcp.rs` 9 of 9, the NFS hostile suite 17 of 17, the anchor's 15 of 15.
  - Clippy `-D warnings` on macOS (the workspace), Linux x86_64 and arm64, and Windows x86_64 and arm64 (`slates-rt`);
    format, `cargo xtask check` and CI's doc step clean.
- **Measured and set aside:** the vectored-run test expected the 8 MiB run back `Completed` after a short send, a Unix
  kernel's buffer bound. Windows' AFD took the whole run in one `WSASend` on loopback (`Whole`), so there the test keeps
  the byte-for-byte check and the completion path is covered by the same code's Unix runs.
- **Siblings found:** the Windows datagram socket is made by `socket()`, which Winsock makes inheritable, and binds
  without `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE`, so a local process could share a fleet node's UDP port. Closed by A-183, which also
  found this amendment's exclusivity test vacuous (both sockets on loopback) and rebuilt it.

### A-178 — macOS refuses a second owner of a live instance's rendezvous: the owner's token is a Mach bootstrap name (accepted 2026-10-26)
Applied in the same change to: §4.7 (the rendezvous's status), A-176 (its macOS sentences), GAPS, `crates/ipc` (`owner_name.rs`, new; `rendezvous.rs`: the macOS `Owner`, `owner_token_name` and `take_ownership`; `lib.rs`; `tests/rendezvous.rs`: the second-owner test now also macOS's, and a cross-process one on every platform), `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-ipc` 70 → 79), `CLAUDE.md`, and a bug record (`docs/bugs/2026-10-26-a-second-owner-took-a-live-macos-instances-rendezvous-over.md`).
- **What was wrong.** On macOS an owner of an instance's rendezvous (its anchor, or a daemon run alone) unlinked whatever object held the bootstrap object's name and made its own, a live owner's too. So a second anchor, or a second daemon run alone, took a live instance over: new clients reached the second, the first kept the clients it had, and the two served one instance with separate state. Linux refused the second at the abstract address, and Windows at the owner's token (A-176), whose sweep found this one.
- **Why a bootstrap name.** The token must end with its holder and touch no disk. No lock can be taken on the shared object itself: measured 2026-10-26 on macOS 26, `flock` on a POSIX shared-memory descriptor answers `ENOTSUP` and `fcntl` record locks `EBADF`. A Mach bootstrap name is launchd's: its first registrant wins, and it is free the moment its holder's receive right is gone. Measured unprivileged: a second process refused (1100) and a second registration of the same process refused (1101) while the first held it; 200 of 200 registrations made right after a holder dropped its right accepted at once (the worst 0.105 ms); 20 of 20 made right after a holder killed with `SIGKILL` was reaped accepted (the worst call 10.25 ms). A SysV semaphore held with `SEM_UNDO` would be machine-wide too, but names a set by a 32-bit key other software draws from, and a crash leaves the set behind.
- **Where.** At the top of the caller's bootstrap chain, the namespace that is its own parent: the widest one the user's processes register in, so the user's every login session meets one token, as they meet one shared-memory name. Measured from a GUI session: a chain three deep, a registration accepted at every level, and a name registered in the parent refused to a second process both there and in its own namespace. The name is `com.slates.owner.<uid>.<16 hex digits of a BLAKE3 of the rendezvous's name>`, within a bootstrap name's 128 bytes whatever the instance's name.
- **D-10 holds.** D-10 lost Mach messages as the request transport, since rings beat message passing. The token sends no message: one registration in an owner's life, ended by its holder's drop or death.
- **Proven** on this Mac: the second-owner test, run on macOS for the first time (a second daemon run alone and an anchor beside a daemon run alone refused `InstanceHeld` while the first owner lives, the rendezvous free once it is gone, a second anchor and a daemon run alone beside an anchor refused); and a new cross-process test (`a_second_process_is_refused_a_live_instances_rendezvous`), since the server answers a second process otherwise than a second registration of one. The rendezvous suite passes 14 of 14 on this Mac and on fedora, and `slates-ipc` is linted on all three platforms (Windows on jupiter). Red-checked on this Mac with a token that never meets a holder (a fresh name at each claim): both tests fail.
- **Owed:** the token's reach measured beyond one GUI session: an ssh login's parent namespace, and the one a launchd job is given (CI's macOS runner, which runs both tests, is one).

### A-170 — A clone's copy-up copies an open extent its origin owns; only its own is sealed in place (accepted 2026-10-25)
Applied in the same change to: `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs` (`Volume::make_current_inode`), `crates/vfs/src/content.rs`
(`ChunkStore::copy_open`), `crates/vfs/tests/content_in_place.rs` and `crates/server/tests/recovery.rs` (the new tests
below), `crates/vfs/tests/retained_bytes.rs` (the clone's retention rule restated), the A-134 note in §4.3's status,
GAPS, and `docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-clones-copy-up-sealed-its-origins-open-extent-behind-its-image.md`.
- **Changes the copy-up every mutation begins with.** Before, a version born in an earlier epoch had its open extent
  sealed in place, and the shared old record was rewritten to the sealed body so that every view of it saw the seal.
  Now only a version this volume owns (born after its clone origin) is sealed in place. A clone's copy of a version
  its origin owns takes a copy of the open extent, born at the clone's epoch, and the origin's record, and so the
  image the origin publishes, is left exactly as it was.
- **Why.** The rewritten record was the origin's: its head and its snapshot use it. The clone marked only itself
  dirty, so the origin stayed clean (`Volume::is_clean`), and a barrier, which records only a volume that is not
  clean, left the origin's last image naming the open extent. The seal had freed that block, the trimmed tail always
  and the whole of it where a cipher moves the bytes (A-118, A-99), and a later allocation took it. Recovery then
  either refused every volume of the shard (two images naming one block differently, at A-64's all-or-nothing claim:
  the daemon kill of G-vhost step 4, 2 rounds of 3 on the box) or rebuilt the origin's file from the freed block,
  which reads zeros (the new restart test with the fix reverted).
- **Price.** A copy of at most one chunk per file a clone changes whose last window was open in its origin's snapshot,
  made at the clone's first change of that file (a write, a truncate, a metadata change). The copy is the clone's, so
  the clone's own snapshot retains it, where it once shared the origin's sealed chunk.
- **Rejected:**
  - sealing every open extent when a snapshot is taken: it shares with no copy, but needs a complete list of open
    extents (a recovered one is in neither of the idle sweep's sets) and an answer for a block a DAX map pins, and it
    puts O(open files) of seals into the snapshot verb;
  - keeping the in-place seal and having the origin publish: a store-wide register of records sealed by another
    volume, aware of lineage through clones of clones, with a lifecycle of its own. More cross-volume coupling, the
    pattern that failed.
- **Proven:** `a_clones_first_write_to_a_file_it_shares_with_its_origin_leaves_the_origins_image_true` and
  `a_clones_first_write_to_a_sealed_volumes_shared_file_leaves_the_origins_image_true` (`content_in_place.rs`; without
  and with a cipher) and `a_clones_rewrite_of_a_file_its_origin_holds_open_survives_a_restart_beside_the_origin`
  (`recovery.rs`, through a daemon and its restart). Red-checked with the in-place seal restored: the first two fail
  at the claim (`RecoveryIncomplete`), the third at the origin's bytes (zeros). The whole vfs suite (43 test binaries)
  and the recovery suite (41 tests) pass. On the box, the daemon-kill chaos test, which failed 2 rounds of 3, then 3 of
  4, passed 5 of 5 at the same timing.

### A-169 — An out-of-process VMM attaches slates' own virtio-fs device by the attach verb (accepted 2026-10-25)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the guest form over the ring), `crates/ipc/src/protocol.rs`
(`AttachRequest::VhostUserFs`, appended), `crates/bridge-virtiofs` (`VhostUserSeam::adopt_for`; `serve::until_revoked`
and `abandon`; the admission's DAX gate opened for the inherited-descriptor binding), `crates/server` (`virtiofs.rs`
`attach_verb`, the handed device's task, `reconcile_unrecorded`, the per-inode DAX offer; `verbs.rs` the form's
dispatch; `shards.rs` the end handoff shared), `crates/client` (`attach_vhost_user`, `VhostUserDevice`), `crates/cli`
(`slates vhost-user`), the tests named below, GAPS, `docs/cli.md`.
- **Adds the form.** `attach(volume, intent, VhostUserFs { tag, subtree, dax_window })` on Linux, on the volume's owner
  shard inside the verb's transaction: the checks first (the transport offered, the rights for the intent, a snapshot
  only for a read, the tag, the window a power of two of at least one 2 MiB range, room for the device and its end);
  then a socket pair, the device's seam over this process's end, the view, the write lease, the record, the device's
  loop slot and its task, each given back when a later one is refused. The other end goes to the client over its
  control socket just before the reply, as A-161's Shards end does, and is the attachment's capability. macOS and
  Windows refuse the form `AttachmentUnsupported`/`BindingNotBuilt` before any effect.
- **The consumer is named, not read from the socket.** A pair this process made reports this process as its peer, so
  the seam is adopted for the principal the verb authenticated (`VhostUserSeam::adopt_for`); the peer-credential
  `adopt` stays for an in-process harness that hands in a socket its VMM already holds.
- **No handshake bound.** The device is recorded and reachable by `detach` before its front end speaks
  (`serve::until_revoked` races the negotiation against the loop's revoke), and it ends when the VMM's end closes: the
  VM exited, never started, or closed it. A VM's boot is not slates' to bound (§4.6 "The harness owns VM and container
  creation"), and a front end that never speaks holds only its own attachment, within the shard's device bound.
- **Ring lifetime corrected 2026-11-02.** GET_VRING_BASE stops the specified queue, waits for every chain it took to
  have a published used element, then returns the device's next available index. Started/stopped is independent of
  enabled/disabled; SET_VRING_KICK restarts a ring. With every ring stopped, the device is suspended: no new DAX turn
  writes guest memory, and control messages still work. Socket close, not the first or last ring stop, ends the
  device. This replaces the backend's wrong first-stop hangup, exposed by QEMU's queue-1 EOF and eventfd abort in
  main CI 41529944478. Applied together to `bridge-virtiofs` (`virtqueue`, `device`, `admission`, `serve`,
  `vhost_user`), the server's real-socket tests, `virtiofs.md` §6, A-189, GAPS and
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-02-stopping-one-vhost-ring-closed-the-control-connection.md`. The two-stop test fails before
  the fix (0.28 s) and passes after (0.27 s); the DAX in-flight/restart test passes (0.64 s), all 24 server cases pass,
  and all eight real QEMU guest histories pass (28.23 s), adacachy, 2026-11-02. Evidence: QEMU's vhost-user protocol,
  Ring states / Suspended device state / GET_VRING_BASE, and `hw/virtio/vhost.c::do_vhost_dev_stop`.
- **A restart resumes or ends the device (corrected 2026-11-03).** The ring-lifetime correction left a restart
  served from the layout and index the device was admitted with: after admission, `SET_VRING_NUM`, `SET_VRING_ADDR`
  and `SET_VRING_BASE` only updated the seam's record, though QEMU's `vhost_virtqueue_start` sends all three before
  every kick (its base is the last available index, zero after a guest reset). Now a drained stop's index becomes the
  ring's base; only a stopped, answered ring takes new settings (a running ring moved is refused); and a kick
  restarts a ring only over its admitted layout at the index it stopped at, which is QEMU's restart after a pause
  or a stop. A driver that started over opens a new FUSE session that the device cannot take over in place, since
  the old session's references and windows would stay behind; its restart is refused and ends the device, so a reset
  is a new device. Owed: an in-place reset that sweeps the old session and re-admits every queue. Three tests fail on
  the old seam and pass after (`a_vhost_ring_restarted_after_a_guest_reset_is_refused_not_served_from_its_old_ring`,
  `a_running_vhost_ring_cannot_be_readdressed`, `a_vhost_ring_whose_stop_awaits_its_chain_cannot_be_moved`); the
  virtiofs suite passes 28 of 28, adacachy, 2026-11-03, and main CI's live QEMU lane passes (41732529738). Record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-03-a-restarted-vhost-ring-was-served-from-its-old-layout.md`.
- **Live-fixture inheritance corrected 2026-11-02.** The ring fix exposed the live QEMU harness clearing CLOEXEC
  in its parent: sibling VMs inherited each other's frontend sockets, hiding peer close. It now changes that flag
  only in the intended child's pre_exec. A two-child real-exec EOF test fails first (20.04 s), then passes (0.00 s);
  the live mount/device-end case and fsx/fsstress case pass concurrently (6.74 s, adacachy). Applied together to
  `crates/server/tests/virtiofs.rs`, GAPS and
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-02-a-live-vm-test-exported-its-socket-to-sibling-vms.md`. Device and guest-exit assertions are
  unchanged; no serial execution masks the lifetime rule.
- **DAX.** The window's size is the request's; the device offers per-inode DAX while the shard's fill budget has room,
  and the admission's DAX gate is open for this binding, whose windows map per-file backings (A-168). The in-process
  binding's gate stays closed.
- **A rolled-back attach serves nothing:** a device whose record the rollback removed is revoked and its end dropped
  (`virtiofs::reconcile_unrecorded`, beside A-161's).
- **`slates vhost-user ID [--tag NAME] [--subtree DIR] [--read-only] [--dax-window SIZE] -- VMM ...`** replaces itself
  with the VMM, the end kept at the descriptor it arrived at (so it displaces nothing the VMM was handed by its
  caller) and named where `{socket}` stands, as `/proc/self/fd/N`, which crosvm takes as an inherited socket. No
  socket file exists anywhere (R1). A VMM with no `{socket}` is usage.
- **Proven** on Linux x86_64 (fedora, 2026-10-25): `crates/server/tests/virtiofs.rs`
  (`the_vhost_user_form_hands_the_client_a_socket_end_that_drives_a_guest_on_either_shard`: a stand-in front end
  negotiates over the delivered end and the guest's file reads back through the client, on both shards;
  `a_vhost_user_device_detached_before_its_front_end_speaks_closes_its_end`;
  `the_vhost_user_forms_refusals_are_typed_and_leave_nothing_behind`: `NotFound`, four `BadRequest`s, a green's
  `Unsupported`, a read-only consumer's `Forbidden` and its read-only attach with no lease;
  `a_guests_dax_window_shows_another_paths_write_and_its_store_reaches_the_volume_at_fsync`: the whole route through
  the daemon's real serve loop with no VM — the front end negotiates the shared-memory features, reads the window's
  size and hands over the back-end-request channel; the guest's SETUPMAPPING is answered only after the front end
  places and acknowledges the map; the client's rewrite shows in the window, the cut tail zero; the guest's writable
  upgrade is answered with no message; its store is in the volume by its FSYNC's answer); `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`
  (`slates_vhost_user_names_the_devices_socket_end_in_the_vmms_arguments_and_ends_with_it`, a real anchor); the CLI's
  parse tests. macOS: `the_vhost_user_form_is_refused_by_kind_where_vhost_user_is_not_built`. Red-checked: negotiating
  without the revoke race fails the detach test; the DAX gate left closed fails the route test. A real crosvm guest is
  G-vhost's step 3.
- **Also repaired (CI red on 1d86208e):** `DaemonConfig::copy_slice_page_bytes` takes the profile's base page
  (`DaemonConfig::page`) rather than rustix, which the server does not link on Windows; and the backed module's own
  doc is its only doc, so its intra-doc link resolves on Linux, the only platform that builds it.
- **Proven through a real guest (G-vhost step 3, 2026-10-25):** `crates/cli/tests/guest_vhost.rs`, gated like
  `guest_dax.rs`. `slates vhost-user SESSION --dax-window 8MiB -- crosvm run --vhost-user type=fs,socket={socket} ...`
  boots a guest whose probe mounts the tag `dax=always` and maps a file of a session (a clone of a snapshot of an
  origin; a guest's writes land in the session itself, so nothing is merged after). Each check holds the guest's map
  (read as memory alone) and the session (read through slates) to a model of the design's rules, byte for byte:
  - another path's change is in the map the moment its writer is answered: a `slates mount` write across a page, the
    SDK's whole-file write, a growth past the end the guest knows on its last page, zeros over a cut (where the mount
    route's guest hangs: virtiofs.md §8 item 7), and a growth past the last page once the guest maps again;
  - the guest's stores reach the session at its `msync` and at its close without one; a store past the file's end
    never does, and a later extension over it zeroes it in the session and in the guest's map (POSIX.1-2024 `mmap`:
    "the system shall never write out any modified portions of the last page of an object which are beyond its end");
  - the origin keeps its own bytes, and its later write never reaches the session's map (A-166);
  - generated histories (three fixed seeds, 80 steps each) mix all of it: 73 stores, 11 of them past the end, 16
    syncs, 52 mount writes opening 14 holes, 16 SDK writes, 12 size changes, 30 new maps and 44 checks.

  Green 3 of 3 on adacachy (host and guest Linux 7.2.9-2-cachyos, crosvm 1c8d17a85) in a capped user unit, 1.63–4.79 s
  a run at load 24–140; the histories' device counted one map sent, one upgrade answered with no message, 123 requests
  held for ingests and 51 to 58 runs ingested across the rounds. Red-checked from a scratch copy, each mutation failing at its own check: no write-through (the map as the
  mount's write is answered holds the seed); no ingest (the session by the sync's answer lacks the store); no window
  (the guest's `dax=always` mount refused: `mount virtiofs tag slates at /mnt: Invalid argument (os error 22)`). The
  red-check also found the probe cutting its last reply short, fixed (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-the-guest-probes-last-reply-was-cut-short.md`).
- **The VM and the daemon killed under the live map (G-vhost step 4, 2026-10-25),** in the same file:
  - **The VM killed** with unsynced stores: the stream's end ingests them, all but a store past the file's end, while a
    mount write racing the end keeps its bytes, and a second guest maps what the first left. Red-checked: with no ingest
    at the stream's end, the dead guest's stores are missing.
  - **The daemon killed:** the device's stream ends with it (a guest's attachment does not survive a restart, A-161).
    crosvm then ends the VM, since it takes a vhost-user back end's hangup for a crashed device (exit 0). Every byte the
    guest synced and every acknowledged write survives, the unsynced store does not, recovery removes the device's
    record, and a fresh VM through the successor sees the session.
  - **The bug it found:** a clone's copy-up had sealed its origin's open extent behind the origin's image, so the crash
    lost the whole shard (A-170). A VM that outlives its device's daemon is owed to a later goal.

### A-168 — Slates' own virtio-fs device maps per-file backings for an out-of-process VMM (accepted 2026-10-25)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (a status block before the 2026-10-16 record), `crates/bridge-virtiofs`
(`src/backed.rs` new; `src/device.rs`, `src/admission.rs`, `src/serve.rs`, `src/dax.rs`, `src/vhost_user.rs`,
`src/lib.rs`; `src/udmabuf.rs` removed; `tests/device.rs`, `tests/serve.rs`), `crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`
(`begin_ingest_all`, `mark_all_stale`, `len`), `crates/bridge-fuse/src/bridge.rs` (`dax_refused_errno`,
`dax_failure_errno`, shared with the Shards route), `crates/vfs/src/shards_backing.rs` (`mark_backing_stale`),
`crates/vfs/src/dax.rs` and `volume.rs` (the re-map claim corrected), `crates/server` (`virtiofs.rs`, `config.rs`
`copy_slice_page_bytes`, `shards/dax.rs`), `unsafe-budget.toml`, GAPS, virtiofs.md §8, and the bug record above.
- **Changes §4.6's message placer.** A SETUPMAPPING is no longer served by pinning the content blocks of its range and
  sending a `udmabuf` of each. The file's backing (A-163) is filled over the asked range, a copy slice a turn, and sent
  as one SHMEM_MAP with the file offset as its offset; the guest is answered on the ack. Nothing the daemon does to the
  file reaches a window as a message: the write boundary keeps the backing equal before any change returns.
- **Why not the alternatives** (kiln research 01a171bff4bd73c6bea625793fb5f821, 12 findings, each graded A):
  - re-pointing a window onto the inode's new blocks needs a map over a live map, which the vhost-user specification
    forbids, and unmap-then-map opens the zero-page gap a real guest read;
  - writing in place into the mapped block fails because content moves (an open block that grows is copied to a larger
    one, an idle one is sealed) and one block never covers a guest's 2 MiB range;
  - a revoke-and-refault never refaults: a Linux guest keeps its mapped ranges and never asks again.
- **The price of giving up zero copy.** The content-block window mapped slates' own bytes. A backed window maps a copy,
  so:
  - the file's bytes in every range a guest maps are copied once from the volume, a copy slice a turn, and nothing past
    its end: a full 2 MiB range at the box's measured memcpy rate (the daemon's boot profile on adacachy, 2026-10-25:
    19,337,055,392 and 11,966,135,495 bytes a second in two runs) is about 110 to 175 µs, in slices of 31,045 to
    44,340 bytes;
  - its bytes are resident twice while the guest maps them, once in the volume and once in the backing, bounded by the
    shard's fill budget;
  - every write is copied again into each backing that maps its range, before it returns;
  - each ingest compares the ranges asked writable with the volume and writes back only the runs that differ.

  It buys a window that never moves under a guest that never re-asks, with no message on any other path's change.
- **Writable at the front end.** Every window is mapped writable when the attachment may write. A guest's upgrade of a
  read-only range is a SETUPMAPPING over the live window (`fuse_upgrade_dax_mapping`); it is answered with no message.
  The guest's page tables keep read-only mappings read-only, and an ingest compares only ranges asked writable.
- **Durability** follows A-163: the request that asks for the guest's stores (FSYNC, FLUSH, RELEASE, READ, FORGET,
  DESTROY) is held, unserved, while they are written back, published before its reply, and answered the write-back's
  refusal where its asker reads one. The serve loop ingests every writable backing after its last pass and before the
  terminal step, waiting out a fence, and lets the backings go only then.
- **Counted in the owner's status** (added 2026-10-25 with G-vhost step 3): after every pass, and once after the
  terminal step, the serve loop adds what each count moved to the owner's status counters (`BridgeAccess::count`), so
  `slates status` shows a guest's use of its window while the device runs: `virtiofs.dax_maps_sent`, `_maps_kept` (a
  SETUPMAPPING answered with no message), `_unmaps_sent`, `_unmaps_refused`, `_ingests_held`, `_replies_held`,
  `_backings_released`, `_asks_answered`, `_runs_ingested`, `_ingest_refused`, `_refilled`, `_refill_refused`,
  `_refill_writable` (`backed.rs` `BackedCounts::named`). They are the real guest test's non-vacuity witnesses, and the
  stand-in route test holds their exact values (one map, one upgrade with no message, one held FSYNC, one run, one
  backing let go); removing the report fails it at the first.
- **Beneath an overlay** a reply that could reveal the disk's change (the base plane marked a backing stale while
  serving it) is held until the backing is refilled. A snapshot device's advance marks its backings stale, so each is
  refilled from the new view; no window is torn.
- **Bounds.** One request is held at a time (the device serves nothing past it); windows are bounded by the guest's
  window; backings by the shard's fill budget; the outstanding ring by the region's pages plus one. A SETUPMAPPING's
  window must be whole granules inside the region and its file range must start at a granule inside the object.
- **The fd-sharing placer, decided in this change.** It keeps pinned blocks for now: no in-process VMM is wired, and
  the L1/L2 DAX defenses are built on its pinned blocks. By the same sources its revoke leaves a guest at a `PROT_NONE`
  hole it will not re-ask for, so before an in-process VMM ships it takes the backed route or is retired (GAPS).
- **Proven** on Linux x86_64 (fedora, 2026-10-25) by eleven hermetic tests in `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`
  against a stand-in front end that maps what SHMEM_MAP sends, and two unit tests in `backed.rs`. The rest of the
  crate's suites, the server's virtiofs, shards and attach-form suites, and Linux clippy pass. A real crosvm guest
  proved it the same day, killed under its live map included (A-169's last two bullets).
- **Red-checked.**
  - The pre-fix code (411c243d, on adacachy with `/dev/udmabuf`) ran the coherence checks in the old API: its map
    covered 4,096 of the 2,097,152 bytes asked; a write after the file outgrew its block was not in the map
    ("AAAAAAAAAAAA"); and the next pass's revoke drain sent SHMEM_UNMAP for the range the guest held.
  - Eight mutations of the new code, each failing its own test: no write-through; no ingest hold; no refused errno; no
    refill hold in the service pass; none after the owner's barrier; the front end mapped writable only as asked; no
    ingest at the end; no release at FORGET.
- **Removed:** the message placer's `udmabuf` confinement (A-138) and its two unsafe sites, since a backing's descriptor
  authorizes one file's bytes by construction; the tests premised on it, and on pinned windows under the message
  placer, went with it.

### A-167 — A range a guest maps past a file's end is kept equal like any other (accepted 2026-10-25)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the Shards stream's DAX bullet), `crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`
(`covered` and the module's account of an ask), the test `a_range_asked_past_the_files_end_takes_a_later_write_into_it`
in `crates/bridge-core/tests/dax_backing.rs` (new), GAPS,
`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-range-mapped-past-the-files-end-missed-later-writes.md`.
- Changes A-163's fill: an asked range covers every range it touches, past the file's end too, where the fill copies
  nothing. Before, an asked range was clipped to the file's size, so a range wholly past the end was never marked
  filled and write-through passed it by.
- Why: a Linux guest maps the 2 MiB range holding the offset it touches by its own idea of the size (`fs/fuse/dax.c`,
  `fuse_iomap_begin` declines only at `pos >= i_size`), which another path's cut makes stale. Such a guest then read
  zeros through its map after a later write into the range, for as long as it held the mapping, since it never asks
  again for a range it holds. Proven by the test above, which failed before the change.
- Cost: such a range counts against the fill budget like any filled range, which is what a guest can store into.
- Unchanged: a whole-file ask; the ingest, which compares only up to the file's end; the 25 Shards tests.

### A-166 — A DAX backing names its file by volume and inode number together (accepted 2026-10-25)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the Shards stream's DAX bullet), `crates/vfs/src/shards_backing.rs` (the registry
keyed by volume prefix and inode; every query and write-through names both), `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs` and
`crates/vfs/src/base.rs` (the write boundary and the base plane pass their own volume's prefix), `crates/vfs/src/dax.rs`
(`dax_map_write`'s exclusion), `crates/bridge-core` (`DaxState::volume`, the backed session), the test
`a_change_of_a_clone_never_reaches_a_backing_of_its_origin` in `crates/vfs/tests/shards_backing.rs`, GAPS,
`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-clones-change-reaches-its-origins-dax-backing.md`.
- Corrects A-163's "one object per attachment and file": an inode number names a file only within a volume. A clone
  shares its origin's nodes and their numbers (`Volume::clone_of`), and a snapshot a device presents is such a clone in
  the same store. The registry kept backings by number alone, so a write of either volume reached the other's guest's
  map. Found while reusing the backings for slates' own virtio-fs device (goal G-vhost); proven by the test above,
  which failed before the fix with the clone's bytes in the origin's backing.
- The key is the volume's own prefix (`Volume::prefix`), never the one an inherited number carries: each volume and
  each view in a shard is given its own (`verbs::volume_config`).
- Unchanged: the protocol, the bounds, the write-through and the ingest; the 25 Shards tests pass as before.
- Reported, not changed (the bug record's sibling sweep): write-log replay routes a record by its number's prefix; the
  in-process gate's recall counts a clone's windows on inherited files under the origin; `has_writable_of` keys by
  number alone (an over-refusal); prefix allocation wraps at 65,535 with no check against live volumes.

### A-165 — Firecracker maps a volume's image with DAX through virtio-pmem (accepted 2026-10-24)
Applied in the same change to: `crates/guest-probe/src/guest.rs` (module loads, the device node's wait, the block
mount's file system and `dax=` keys), `crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs` (three pmem tests beside the drive test, which
now shares their setup), `crates/cli/tests/vm/mod.rs` (an initramfs that carries modules; the daemon's and the VM's
kills, shared), `crates/cli/tests/guest_dax.rs` (those helpers moved out), `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (the Firecracker
row, the matrix's Firecracker cell, the pmem paragraph), §4.6 (the DAX matrix status), GAPS, `docs/cli.md` (an image a
crashed guest left). The evidence is kiln research 01a171864dfb7057a3dc0aee87b29280 (12 findings, graded from their
sources).
- **What it answers.** A-164 left Firecracker's mount route owed. Firecracker has no virtio-fs, but since 1.14 it
  presents a host file to its guest as a virtio-pmem device: it maps the file shared, as a range of the guest's
  physical memory, and carries out a guest's flush as an `msync(MS_SYNC)` of the file (its `docs/pmem.md`). The image
  A-160 builds, read through a slates mount, is that file, so nothing in the daemon changes. The guest's DAX reads,
  writes and maps reach the image file's pages in the host's cache, and the host's cache writes them back into the
  volume.
- **The guest.** It mounts `/dev/pmem0` as ext4 with `dax=always`.
  - ext4's driver mounts the ext2 image; ext2's own DAX was removed for Linux 7.2. DAX needs the 4 KiB block A-160's
    format already has.
  - A distribution's kernel builds virtio-pmem and the nvdimm drivers behind it as modules: on the box's 7.2.9 there are
    nine, from `asn1_encoder` to `nd_pmem`, by `modules.dep`. The test carries them in the initramfs from the guest
    kernel's module directory. The probe loads them with `finit_module`, which decompresses them in the kernel, then
    waits for the device node on an inotify watch, since libnvdimm registers its namespaces asynchronously.
  - Firecracker v1.17.0's configuration must name `drives` even when it attaches none.
- **What DAX is here, by test.**
  - A store through the guest's map is in the image file, read through the slates mount, before the guest syncs: it is
    the file's own page in the host's cache.
  - A write through the slates mount shows in the guest's map, the guest touching memory alone.
  - The guest's sync, which Firecracker carries out as its `msync`, writes the guest's stores into the volume, read
    through slates itself.
- **Chaos.**
  - **The daemon killed with `SIGKILL` under the guest's live map.** The anchor's successor serves the restored mount,
    with A-158's round: 13 inodes invalidated and 3 epochs bumped a run. The guest's unsynced store is in the image after
    the takeover, the host's next write shows in its map, and the merge is exact.
  - **Firecracker killed with an unsynced store.** The store is the file's own page, so it reaches the volume when the
    dead VMM's file closes.
    - The guest never unmounted, so `slates image merge` refuses the image `NotClean`. It still refuses it after a
      second guest mounts and cleanly unmounts it: ext4 without a journal clears the clean flag at mount and writes back,
      at unmount, the state it found.
    - `e2fsck -fy` through the mount makes the file system clean. Its one repair is the `lost+found` it creates, which
      A-160's images do not carry. The merge takes it as a new directory, as it would take any orphans e2fsck recovered
      there.
- **Evidence (2026-10-24).** On the box: Linux 7.2.9 x86_64, Firecracker v1.17.0, the box's own kernel as the guest's.
  Every run was in a capped `systemd --user` unit, at load 38–84 on 32 cores.
  - The pmem test: green 5 of 5 in rounds of the whole image-test binary on the committed code, and 6 runs before.
    - The guest booted to ready in 157–652 ms, the nine module loads included.
    - The host's write reached the guest's map in 8–13 µs.
    - The merge was exact: 2 made, 1 moved, 1 removed, and 4,123 bytes written (the patch's page and the new file).
  - The takeover test: green 10 of 10 on the committed code (5 alone, 5 in whole-binary rounds), and 7 runs before. The
    host's write reached the guest's map 83–3,351 µs after the takeover.
  - The crash test: green 5 of 5 on the committed code, and 4 runs before.
  - The drive test (A-160), sharing the new setup: green in every round.
  - Red-checked, each mutation failing at its own check:
    - without DAX: the map is not DAX;
    - without DAX and without that assertion: the store is not in the host's file;
    - without the guest's sync: slates lacks the guest's last store;
    - the crash test with a clean quit for the kill: the merge is not refused;
    - the crash test with no store: slates lacks it;
    - the takeover test with no unsynced store: the image lacks it.
- **Does not change:** A-160's format, build and merge, or the drive route.

### A-164 — What DAX means in each environment, and the cells the platforms rule out (accepted 2026-10-24)
Applied in the same change to: `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 (the DAX matrix, which replaces the route table's DAX column),
§4.6 (its DAX status), GAPS. The evidence is kiln research 01a17143717a7556a52f40f1d5a0e1b2 (19 findings, each graded
from its sources) and 01a171494952772991b9bc668b5d89f0 (the 10 the matrix rests on).
- **The definition.** DAX is a consumer reading and writing a file's bytes in place, through memory mapped onto them and
  coherent with every other path, rather than copying them through a read or a write call. What maps them depends on
  the environment:
  - **a VM or microVM** (QEMU, crosvm, Kata, Firecracker, a Shards microVM): the guest maps host bytes through its
    device's DAX window (virtio-fs) or a pmem device, with no guest page cache between;
  - **no VM** (bare metal, a Docker or OCI container, a Kubernetes pod on runc): a process maps the file;
  - **a Kubernetes VM runtime** (Kata): as a VM.
- **The two routes** (Ada, 2026-10-22), each defined per environment in the matrix:
  - **the mount route:** the volume mounted on the host (FUSE on Linux, NFS on macOS, WinFsp on Windows), shared in by
    the environment's own mechanism with its own DAX. With no VM, the host kernel's cache holds the pages a process's
    map reaches;
  - **the socket route:** slates' own device or descriptor, reached over a socket (A-161's handoff; socket files allowed
    when what crosses them is encrypted end to end and at rest). With no VM, a same-kernel process maps slates' own
    memory with no copy (A-135).
- **Ruled out by the platforms**, each on the platform's own source:
  - upstream QEMU's vhost-user-fs device has no DAX window property, and virtiofsd has no DAX, so a QEMU guest gets no
    file tree with DAX from QEMU's own device, and Kata, which drives that device, has neither route. **Corrected
    2026-10-29 (A-189):** this line ruled QEMU out on both routes. QEMU 11.1's generic vhost-user device offers slates'
    own device its window (proven on x86_64 and arm64), and QEMU's virtio-pmem serves the image form on x86_64
    (proven; QEMU builds it for x86 machines only);
  - Cloud Hypervisor states that virtio-fs DAX is not available;
  - crosvm's own fs device offers DAX on x86_64 only (its vhost-user front end has no such gate: A-189);
  - Apple's Virtualization framework documents no DAX window for its virtio-fs device, so Docker Desktop's containers on
    macOS map through the VM's cache (unconfirmed: the evidence is documentation that says nothing);
  - WSL2 reaches Windows files over 9P, which has no window (unconfirmed: search summaries only).
- **Possible and owed**, each a goal in the stack:
  - Firecracker by virtio-pmem over the image file (1.14 and later). The guest mounts the ext2 image with the ext4
    driver, since ext2's own DAX has been removed from Linux;
  - VMs attaching slates' own device out of process (crosvm on Linux x86_64);
  - the no-copy direct map on macOS and Windows;
  - the mount route's maps on each platform, in a container and in a pod;
  - Shards' own window over the macOS mount.
- **Proven so far:** crosvm over a slates mount (Linux x86_64, 4 of 4); a Shards guest over the daemon's stream (macOS
  arm64, 3 of 3 twice, A-163); the same-kernel direct map (Linux x86_64, A-135).
- **Why this definition.** A DAX that meant only virtio-fs's window would leave the goal's environments without a VM
  without a meaning. One that meant any `mmap` would count a copy into a guest's page cache as DAX. What the VMs and
  microVMs share with bare metal is the consumer mapping the bytes in place, coherently, and that is the definition.

### A-163 — A Shards guest maps a file from a copy slates keeps equal to the volume (accepted 2026-10-24)
Applied across 1675dc0c, ba0f8ef0, b3a3a07c, 8f0e1b2b and 2d2cee52, and in the same change to: §4.6 (the Shards stream's
DAX bullet and its status), GAPS, `docs/wip/shards/dax-protocol.md` (agreed with the Shards owner), BENCHMARKS (three
sections), and Shards' patch series (six patches on its `gpu` ff01fe0b3, the range on the ask among them, with its
owner for review).
- **Adds §4.6's Shards DAX.** Shards' device asks the backend for a file's descriptor at each `FUSE_SETUPMAPPING`, and
  maps each range from its own ask's descriptor (D189). slates answers with a descriptor of one shared-memory object per
  attachment and file (`slates_mem::DaxObject`). On Linux it is a memfd sealed against growing, shrinking and further
  seals; on macOS a POSIX shm object whose random name is unlinked at once. It holds only that file's bytes, so it
  authorizes nothing else (A-135's rule). It is sized once to `2^63 − 2 MiB`, the largest file a guest can have,
  sparse until touched, never resized: Shards' window follows a file's size by `fstat`, and a size that never changes
  gives it nothing to follow. Ranges are filled from the volume a copy slice a turn as they are asked, holes skipped.
- **Coherence is write-through, before acknowledgment** (`slates_vfs::shards_backing`, at the volume's one write
  boundary). Every change, whatever its transport, is written into each backing's filled ranges before it returns: a
  write's bytes, the hole an extension opens and the part a truncate cuts zeroed, an edit's shifted tail copied again.
  Writes go through slates' own mapping, never `write(2)`, which would wake Shards' inotify watch. Beneath an overlay
  (D-25):
  - a writable ask copies the file up first (§4.6 DAX rights), so an outsider's edit is drift, never the guest's store;
  - an untouched file's backings are refilled when the base plane adopts a disk change, before the reply that reveals
    it;
  - `rewitness` refuses a file mapped writable (`DaxMapped`).
  An in-process writable map and a backing exclude each other.
- **Durability is ingest at the guest's sync points.** At FSYNC, FLUSH, RELEASE, READ and FORGET of a file mapped
  writable, and at the stream's end, the request is held while the object is compared with the volume over the ranges
  asked writable. Each run that differs is written through the attachment's bridge and published before the reply. A
  write-back the volume refuses answers the request's errno.
- **Bounds (R3).** The fill budget is the shard's content reserve (`shard_content_layout().arena`), one copy of all it
  can hold. A backing counts a range for each it filled, at least one. Past the budget, a fill is refused `ENOMEM` and
  files stop being marked DAX.
- **Measured** (BENCHMARKS, M5 Max):
  - ingest: 0.70–1.14 ms per mapped MiB, after a chunked comparison beat a byte-at-a-time one by 30–42%;
  - write-through: 117 µs per MiB per backing, 3.7 times the write itself (8-byte atomic stores into shared memory);
  - a real guest's synced store shows in `slates read` 261–581 ms after the guest's word (the read process's own cost).
- **Rejected,** each with its reason in the protocol note:
  - the revoke protocol (a doorbell, REVOKES and REVOKED asks, a stage-2 unmap and remap), which would make every
    writer wait on a VM;
  - an object resized with its file (macOS refuses a second `ftruncate`; a peer able to resize could shrink it under
    slates' mapping);
  - doubling with a swap at growth;
  - a fresh copy per ask;
  - a Linux udmabuf over the arena's blocks.
- **What zero copy would need:** a per-file content object, since a descriptor authorizes its whole object and the
  arena holds every volume. That would end block sharing across files and volumes (clones, snapshots); not taken.
- **Proven:**
  - by use against a real daemon: 25 tests in `crates/server/tests/shards.rs` and 7 in
    `crates/vfs/tests/shards_backing.rs`, including model tests over generated histories, each red-checked;
  - on CI's Linux, the object's tests and the stream's;
  - on this Mac, a real Shards guest under `slates shards`, 3 of 3, red-checked without ingest (the host reads old
    bytes) and without write-through (the guest never sees the change).
- **Owed:** Shards' review of the six-patch series (its sixth, the range on the descriptor ask, written by slates for
  review as the owner offered); the zero-copy question above, if a measurement ever makes the copy matter.
- **Corrected 2026-10-25: a slice is read whole.** The ingest's compare and the refill each read a copy slice in one
  bridge call, and a bridge answers at most its read cap a call (the volume bridge's `MAX_READ`, 256 KiB). The compare
  took a capped call for the file's end, so a guest's stores past the cap were never written back while `FSYNC`
  answered 0; the refill padded a capped call with zeros and stored them into the map. Only a machine whose derived
  copy slice exceeds the cap shows it (CI's ubuntu runner on `d71ce235`, run 40211222944); every development machine
  derived one within it, so the oracle never read a slice the bridge cuts. Both now read through `read_whole`, call
  after call until the slice is read or a call reads nothing; the Shards tests run each case with the machine's slice
  and with a whole range a slice. Slates' own virtio-fs device (A-168) shares the session and the fix
  (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-a-dax-slice-past-the-read-cap-dropped-a-guests-stores.md`).

### A-162 — A copy-up's witness is racy only while the file's own timestamp tick is open (accepted 2026-10-24)
Applied in the same change to: §4.5 (copy-up), `crates/vfs/src/base.rs` (`copy_up`, and `rewitness` the same day),
`crates/vfs/tests/base.rs`
(`a_witness_taken_after_an_edit_made_since_the_listing_is_racy_only_while_the_edits_tick_is_open`,
`a_rewitness_inside_the_files_tick_is_racy_and_a_same_tick_edit_is_caught`), GAPS,
`docs/bugs/2026-10-24-a-copy-up-judged-its-witness-racy-by-the-listings-time.md`.
- Changes §4.5's copy-up: the witness's racy flag is decided by the host's clock at the copy-up's own `fstat` (racy when
  `now − mtime` is within the filesystem's timestamp granularity), no longer by the directory listing's read time. The
  witness's fingerprint is that `fstat`; whether a later edit in the same tick could hide from it is a question about
  that moment, as git's racy-clean rule asks it of the time a stat was recorded [B: git racy-git].
- Why: a file edited after its directory was listed has an mtime later than the listing's read time, and the old
  subtraction saturated to zero: racy, for good. Every later drift check of such a witness hashed the whole file through
  its descriptor, so every read of an unpinned range did. Found by the Shards route's refill (A-161's part 3), which
  read a 3 MiB file in 76 slices, each re-hashing the whole file: a refill of one range took past the test's 5 s wait in
  a debug build.
- Unchanged: T-1.11 (a file copied up in the tick it was written is racy, and its in-place edit is caught by
  re-hashing); the listing racy rule for directories (§4.5), which is about the listing's own read.
- `rewitness` follows the same rule (fixed the same day, failing test first). It had recorded every witness not racy,
  so a same-tick edit after a rewitness was caught only by a later fingerprint change.
- Owed, reported: a racy witness stays racy even after a re-hash at a time past its tick has confirmed it, so a
  genuinely racy large file (a coarse-granularity filesystem) still hashes whole on every drift check.

### A-161 — A Shards microVM's fs device is served by the daemon over an anonymous stream (accepted 2026-10-24)
Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/ipc/src/stream.rs` (new): the anonymous pair, its send, receive and end;
- `crates/bridge-fuse`: `shards_fs.rs` (the control frame and its asks, `split_frame`, `answer`, `refuse`,
  `read_ceiling`, the refusals in Shards' forms), `bridge.rs` (`reply_error` and `takes_reply`, now shared by the FUSE
  channel and the virtio-fs device, whose private copies are gone);
- `crates/db/src/catalog.rs`: `AttachForm::ShardsFs`, appended;
- `crates/rt/src/readiness.rs`: `writable` is public;
- `crates/server`: `shards.rs` (new), `state.rs`, `daemon.rs` (`EndStreams`), `verbs.rs` (`end_attachment` ends a
  stream; `scoped_or_whole` and `release_unrecorded_lease` shared with the FUSE mount), `virtiofs.rs` (`owner_shard`
  shared), `Cargo.toml` (the FUSE codec a Unix dependency); the test `tests/shards.rs` (new);
- (step 2) `crates/ipc`: `protocol.rs` (`AttachRequest::ShardsFs`, `AttachTransport::ShardsFs`,
  `UnsupportedReason::DescriptorRouteNotBuilt`, `Conformance::SimulatedShardsDevice`, appended), `rendezvous.rs` (the
  delivery envelope, `Control::send_stream`, `Liveness::recv_delivery`, `ControlDelivery`), `endpoint.rs`;
  `crates/server`: `shards.rs` (`attach_verb`, the handoffs, the destroy and rollback hooks), `verbs.rs` (the attach
  form, `send_reply`, `send_forward`, the destroy's wait), `transports.rs` (the report's entry); `crates/client`
  (`attach_shards`, `ShardsStream`, deliveries matched by what the reply names) and `tests/shards.rs` (new);
- (step 3) `crates/ipc`: `route.rs` (new, macOS), `error.rs` (`RouteRefused`, `RouteRefusal`), `protocol.rs`
  (`ReplyBody::ShardsOffered`, appended), `Cargo.toml` (aws-lc-rs on macOS); `crates/server`: `shards_route.rs` (new),
  `shards.rs` (the platform's hand-out), `daemon.rs` (`start_shards_route`, `SHARDS_ROUTE_BOUND`), `transports.rs` (the
  route's fact), `state.rs`; `crates/client` (`attach_shards` claims an offer); the tests; `unsafe-budget.toml`
  (`slates-ipc` 47 → 48, the `confstr` call); `xtask` (the route's socket node in `slates-ipc`'s host-path reason);
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-24-a-stream-end-arrived-flushed-by-the-kernel-in-flight.md`;
- (step 5) `crates/bridge-fuse`: `shards_fs.rs` (the blocking helpers removed, the module doc rewritten),
  `tests/shards_fs.rs` and `examples/shards_fs_bench.rs` (on `split_frame` and `answer`), `examples/shards_fs_serve.rs`
  (removed); `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`, `docs/wip/shards/`, `docs/wip/virtiofs.md`;
- (step 4) `crates/ipc`: `stream.rs` (`exec_with`, `FIRST_HANDED_NUMBER`), `route.rs` (the received end made
  close-on-exec), `tests/stream_spawn.rs` (new); `crates/client` (`attach_shards` on every platform, `StreamEnd`, the
  delivery steps as paired functions; the Windows refusal in `tests/shards.rs`); `crates/cli` (`slates shards`:
  `args.rs`, `verbs.rs`, `main.rs`; `tests/cli.rs`; the FUSE codec a Unix dev-dependency); `crates/server` (`shards.rs`,
  `verbs.rs`: unit structs where a platform prepares or carries nothing); `crates/conformance` (`trace.rs`, `record.rs`,
  `matrix.rs`: the daemon's socket node, a class of its own) and `xtask` (the hermeticity run names the route's node);
  `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the Windows refusal test on both Windows lanes); `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-ipc`
  48 → 49, `exec_with`'s `pre_exec`); `docs/cli.md`, `docs/wip/conformance.md`; `tests/stream_exec.rs`;
- §4.6, GAPS.

- **What it answers.** Shards' fs device forwards each guest FUSE request to a backend over a Unix stream it is handed
  (Shards' `gpu` branch at 0e8f2d6f, `crates/vmm/src/devices/virtio/fs/mod.rs`, read 2026-10-24):
  - a request is a frame, a little-endian length then the request, and every request gets one reply frame back, an
    empty one for a request that takes no reply;
  - the device's own asks are control frames, the length word's top bit set: its backend's tables for a snapshot of
    the VM and their restore (its D176), and a file's descriptor for a DAX window's mapping (its D189), answered as a
    `shards_ipc` message;
  - the VM process is App-Sandboxed on macOS, so an unsandboxed spawner connects and hands it the descriptor.

  The daemon was not that backend: a one-file example served a volume outside it (2026-10-21). Now an attach with the
  Shards form makes a socket pair with no name and nothing on disk (R1), records the attachment as a guest's, and
  serves its end on the volume's owner shard until it ends.
- **Why a stream end may go to a VMM.** A descriptor handed to a peer authorizes its whole object (A-135), so the
  content object is never handed to a VMM. A stream end carries only the conversation the daemon answers on it, which
  is one attachment's: the end is the attachment's capability, with the rights and the directory the attach recorded.
- **How it is served.** Each frame's length is bounded by the largest frame (`MAX_WRITE` and a page of headers) before
  anything is allocated for it. A request is answered through a transient `VolumeBridge` (a `ScopedBridge` for a
  directory) under the attachment's registry entry, with its own open-handle map. A change that must survive a restart
  publishes the shard before its reply, as a virtio-fs guest's does (AUD-29-82); a refused or uncaptured publication
  answers `EIO`, and what the reply granted is given back. The guest is revalidated, having no invalidation path. A
  reply the peer has not read waits for the end's writability before the next request is read, so a peer that never
  reads holds one reply, never a queue. A shard serves at most its client seats of streams (`clients_per_shard`).
- **A read is never cut short.** A short read is the file's end to a FUSE client, which then shrinks the size it
  caches. A guest asks for up to its page count in its own pages, and `INIT`'s count follows the host's page, so a
  guest with larger pages than its host asks more than the count suggests. The reply buffer grows to the read asked, up
  to the most any guest can ask (`read_ceiling`: the count `INIT` names, or the kernel's default 32, in 64 KiB pages),
  and falls back to one largest frame once the reply is out. A read past the ceiling is answered `EIO`.
- **The control asks are refused in Shards' forms.** slates keeps no tables a VM's snapshot can carry, and a file's
  descriptor would be the content object (A-135): a snapshot's or a restore's ask is answered with a control frame
  whose first byte is not zero and its reason, a descriptor ask with a `shards_ipc` message of kind 1 carrying Linux's
  `EOPNOTSUPP`. A share served by slates is launched without a DAX window until part 3's backing exists. (Amended
  2026-11-18 by A-303: a SAVE is answered with the stream's tables and a RESTORE takes them; A-163 had answered the
  descriptor ask.)
- **How it ends.** The peer's close, a frame refused as hostile, a stream error, a detach, a revocation, the volume's
  destroy and the daemon's stop all end it one way: the references the guest still holds are swept (a guest sends no
  forget per reference at its end), the registry entry revoked and drained, the descriptor closed, the record removed.
  Anything but the stream ends the stream first (`shutdown` on the daemon's end), so the task wakes on its own
