  readiness. A record a dead daemon left is ended by recovery, as every guest's is.
- **Evidence, 2026-10-24.** `crates/server/tests/shards.rs` drives a real daemon over the end a VMM would be handed,
  checking every change through the daemon's NFS port:
  - a guest's history (`INIT`, `CREATE`, `WRITE`, close, `LOOKUP`, `OPEN`, `READ`, `FORGET`, `RENAME`, `UNLINK`) is
    the volume the host sees, bytes crossing both ways;
  - a read-only stream refuses every change and nothing lands;
  - a scoped stream serves its directory as its root, and its `..` is itself;
  - a closed end ends the attachment and releases the lease; a detach ends the stream;
  - an acknowledged close survives a daemon restart, and the stream does not;
  - a closed stream gives back the bytes of a removed file its guest still held;
  - Shards' control asks are answered in its forms; a request with no header gets an empty frame, a body too short
    for its opcode `EIO` and an unknown opcode `ENOSYS`; a length past the bound (`u32::MAX` among them), a control
    frame with no ask, and a frame cut short by its peer's close end only their own stream, each counted by its kind
    (`shards.frame_refused`, `shards.frame_truncated`), while another on the volume keeps serving.

  Seven of seven pass on macOS arm64 and on Linux x86_64 (the fedora runner, epoll), where a peer's write after the
  daemon ends its side answers `EPIPE` at once and macOS takes it until the descriptor closes (both asserted in
  `crates/ipc/src/stream.rs`). Red-checked on macOS: without the sweep the bytes stay referenced (262,144 → 262,144);
  without the barrier the restarted daemon has no file; with the detach hook disabled the guest's read waits out its
  five seconds; with a close mid-frame taken for a clean one the truncated count stays 0.
- **Found on the way, recorded in GAPS, not changed here:** a read-only attachment grants a write-mode open and answers
  each write `EPERM` on every FUSE transport, and NFS answers `PERM`, where a read-only file system answers `EROFS` at
  the open (fixed 2026-11-08, §4.6 "A read-only attachment is a read-only file system"); `INIT`'s page count follows the host's page, so a 4 KiB-page guest of a 16 KiB-page Mac is told 16 pages,
  64 KiB a request, a quarter of the largest write.
- **Over the wire on Linux (2026-10-24, part 1 step 2).** `attach` takes `AttachRequest::ShardsFs { subtree }`. On the
  volume's owner shard, inside the verb's transaction, the stream is made and served as above and its end kept under
  the request's word (`ShardState::stream_handoffs`, bounded by the requests a shard's clients may have in flight). The
  end goes to the client over its retained control socket by `SCM_RIGHTS`, just before the reply is written
  (`verbs::send_reply`, the one place every reply is written), and only with the `Attached` reply that names it: a
  rolled-back verb's refusal drops it, and the stream, seeing its peer gone, ends its attachment. A forwarded attach
  carries the end home to the client's shard with the reply (`verbs::send_forward`); an attach is never forwarded across
  nodes (a volume homed elsewhere is refused `HomedElsewhere`), so a descriptor never leaves its machine.
  - Every control-socket delivery now opens with a kind word (`ControlDelivery`: a content map, A-135, or a stream end),
    so neither is taken for the other. The client takes the delivery its reply names (a map's id, a stream's
    attachment) and drops any other, closing its descriptor: before, a map delivered for a request whose caller had
    given up could answer the next map read.
  - The destroy ends a volume's streams and its teardown waits for them, as for its guest devices, so each sweeps its
    references while the volume is whole; a rolled-back attach's stream is ended and its end dropped
    (`reconcile_unpublished_effects`).
  - The transport report carries the form (`AttachTransport::ShardsFs`): offered on Linux, its evidence the simulated
    device (`Conformance::SimulatedShardsDevice`), refused `DescriptorRouteNotBuilt` on macOS and Windows.
  - Evidence: `crates/client/tests/shards.rs` on a two-shard daemon, a volume on each shard, so one end is made where
    the client is and the other comes home with a forwarded reply; the history checked through slates' own reads and
    writes; two scoped ends of one volume each reaching only its own directory, the read-only one changing nothing; a
    detach ending the stream; on macOS, the refusal by kind with nothing left behind. The control socket's envelope is
    tested in `crates/ipc/src/rendezvous.rs`: three deliveries of two kinds in order, and a delivery of an unknown kind
    or the wrong length refused with its descriptor closed.
- **macOS: the socket route (2026-10-24, part 1 step 3).** macOS has no control socket, and a descriptor reaches an
  unrelated process there only through a Unix socket with a name, so the daemon listens on one socket file: in the
  user's own temporary directory (`confstr(_CS_DARWIN_USER_TEMP_DIR)`, checked to be the user's alone, never `/tmp`),
  named by a hash of the instance, made owner-only, removed when the daemon stops, and a node a dead daemon left found
  unanswered and replaced. Socket files are authorized for this when what crosses them is encrypted end to end (Ada,
  2026-10-22).
  - The attach keeps the end as an offer on the volume's owner shard with a fresh 256-bit secret, and replies
    `ShardsOffered` with the secret. Since A-492 the offer is the requesting client's and waits for its claim while that
    client lives: it goes when claimed, withdrawn (its attachment ended) or let go when the reaper retires its client
    (`shards_route::let_go_of_client`); until then it expired after two liveness budgets on a timer.
  - The claim: the client's hello (version, attachment, its nonce), the daemon's nonce, then per-direction keys by
    HKDF-SHA256 from the secret salted with both nonces, the client's proof and the daemon's confirmation each the
    attachment sealed with AES-256-GCM (the transcript as additional data, each key sealing one message at nonce
    zero). The owner shard checks the proof and retires the offer, so the secret never leaves it; the end goes by
    `SCM_RIGHTS` with the confirmation, which the client opens before it trusts the end. Since A-512 the owner first
    claims the offer for the exchange and answers copies of the ends, keeping them until the exchange settles the
    claim (`shards_route::settle`): retired once the client has its ends, claimable again when the hand-over failed. An
    answer lost on its way back then loses nothing: the exchange asks once more and is answered the same claim, and no
    other exchange can take the offer meanwhile.
  - Bounds: a shard's exchanges at its client seats (`Busy` past them), each waiting on its client while the client's
    connection lives (A-492; one liveness budget until then), the socket being the user's alone; every
    refusal is one byte naming its kind and every ending is counted (`shards.route_*`, `shards.route_claimed` the
    route's non-vacuity counter). The crypto is aws-lc-rs's, a dependency of `slates-ipc` on macOS only, so the
    crate's cross-lint targets keep no C dependency.
  - **Found by the hostile test: a passed end could arrive flushed by the kernel**
    (`docs/bugs/2026-10-24-a-stream-end-arrived-flushed-by-the-kernel-in-flight.md`). XNU's collector of descriptors in
    flight flushes a socket whose every reference is in a message (`unp_gc` → `sorflush`); the daemon closed its copy
    right after the send, so 4 of 20 claims at load 35-47 received an end whose reads answered end of file and whose
    `SO_RCVBUF` read 0. Now the daemon keeps its copy until the client closes the route after its receive, and the
    client refuses a flushed end `Flushed`. `every_end_handed_over_arrives_live_while_sockets_churn` claims 48 ends
    while another thread opens and closes sockets: 16–40 of 48 flushed before the fix, none after; the route tests
    passed 30 of 30 at load 49–55.
  - Evidence: `crates/client/tests/shards.rs` (the history from both shards, two scoped ends, a detach) passes on macOS
    through the route; `crates/server/tests/shards.rs` drives the wire by hand: a wrong secret, a proof replayed from
    another connection, a message cut short, one of another version, bytes after the proof, a silent stranger, each
    refused by kind and counted with the offer left to its honest claim, which succeeds once; a second claim and an
    expired offer find none, the expired offer's attachment ending; the socket exists only while its daemon runs,
    owner-only, the only entry named for the instance. The protocol's unit tests (`route.rs`): an exchange holds only
    under its own secret, nonces and attachment, every tampered byte fails, a hostile hello is refused.
  - What it does not change: the secret is as private as the client's ring, which on macOS a same-user process could
    open by name (GAP-A9-9), and that process could read the ring's file contents as well.
  - **Version 2 (2026-10-25, A-173).** The route carries a direct map's copy too, so the hello names the offer's kind
    (a stream end, a map's copy) beside its id, both bound into the additional data, and a shard keeps each kind's
    offers apart: a secret or proof for one kind never claims the other. The labels read `slates route v2`; a version 1
    hello is refused `Malformed`.
  - **An offer never outlives what it offers (2026-10-25).** An attachment that ends before its end is claimed (a
    detach, a revocation, the volume's destroy) withdraws the offer as its stream ends, counted `shards.route_withdrawn`;
    before, a later claim was handed an end whose other side was closed
    (`docs/bugs/2026-10-25-an-ended-attachments-stream-offer-stayed-claimable.md`).
- **The CLI (2026-10-24, part 1 step 4).** `slates shards ID [--subtree DIR] [--read-only] --fd N -- CMD` attaches the
  volume in the Shards form, announces the attachment, and replaces itself with the command, the end at descriptor `N`
  (3 or more), so a Shards spawner, or a test, gets a working end without linking slates (`shards run … --slates-fs-fd
  N`). The client is closed first and only the copy at `N` goes into the command, so the attachment lasts exactly as
  long as the command's end; and the process a launcher started is the command itself, its pid, signals and exit code
  the command's, so a supervisor that ends it ends the attachment.
  - `slates_ipc::stream::exec_with` makes its own copy of the end close-on-exec and places one at `N` with `dup2` in
    `pre_exec`, just before `execvp`; a failed exec is refused (exit 4) and the end closes as the process exits.
  - **Replaced the same day: the command first spawned the program and waited** (`spawn_with`). A launcher that killed
    the process it started killed only `slates shards`, and the program kept its end and its attachment (kiln's Sandbox,
    which launches and supervises VMs, described that shape on 2026-10-24). `a_killed_launch_ends_its_attachment`
    failed on it: the process spawned was not the program (pid 14084, the reader 14086). It passes on the exec. Found
    in `spawn_with`'s review before it was replaced, and moot now: the standard library learns of a failed spawned
    `exec` through a pipe whose write end could take a free `N`, which the child's `dup2` then closed, so a missing
    program was reported spawned (at the lowest free number plus one, 6). An exec makes no such pipe.
  - macOS has no `MSG_CMSG_CLOEXEC`, so the client makes the end it receives on the route close-on-exec at once.
  - Windows: `attach_shards` compiles on every platform; off Unix the end's type (`StreamEnd`) has no values, the
    delivery steps refuse as unexpected replies, and the daemon refuses the form by kind
    (`AttachmentUnsupported`, `DescriptorRouteNotBuilt`), the reason its transport report gives. `slates shards` there
    sends the attach and prints the refusal (exit 1). Both Windows CI lanes run
    `the_shards_form_is_refused_by_kind_where_no_route_hands_a_handle`.
  - Evidence: `slates_shards_hands_a_program_a_working_stream_end_and_the_attachment_ends_with_it`
    (`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`) runs a real anchor: a reader, the test binary re-invoked under `slates shards --fd 7`,
    mounts the attachment over descriptor 7 (`INIT`, `LOOKUP`, `OPEN`, `READ`, `RELEASE`) and prints what it read,
    byte-equal to the file; the attachment it ran under is gone once it exits; a program that exits 7 exits 7; a program
    that closes its end and waits sees its attachment gone while it still runs; the process a launch spawned is the
    program, and a `SIGKILL` of it ends the attachment; a missing volume is refused (exit 1), a program that cannot run
    fails (exit 4) with its attachment ended, and `--fd 2` is usage (exit 2). `crates/ipc/tests/stream_exec.rs`: a
    process replaced by `sh` hands it the end at 5, and the end closes while `sh` still runs once it closes its 5;
    red-checked, without the close-on-exec of `exec_with`'s own copy the read waited out its 10 s.
  - Step 2's evidence on Linux (adacachy, 2026-10-24): `crates/client/tests/shards.rs` 3 of 3, `crates/server/tests/
    shards.rs` 7 of 7; with the control-socket send withheld in `deliver_handoff`, all three client tests failed at the
    attach (`Ipc(DeadlineExceeded)`), and passed again restored.
- **Found on the way (2026-10-24).**
  - CI's Linux and Windows lanes stopped compiling at 285ce936 and 7dad728d: a platform with nothing to prepare or carry
    used `()` (`shards::Prepared` on Linux, `verbs::Carried` on Windows), and clippy refuses binding or passing a unit
    value (`let_unit_value`, `unit_arg`). Neither branch was linted before the push: `slates-server`'s C dependency
    (aws-lc-sys) does not cross-build from the Mac, so its Linux branch lints on a Linux host and its Windows branch
    only on Windows. Both are unit structs now; the Linux branch is linted clean on adacachy, the Windows one by CI.
  - CI's macOS hermeticity run counted the route's socket node outside (run 40104138955: its `create`, `setmode` and
    `unlink`, all by the daemon). The tracer now knows the daemon's own socket node as a class of its own, named by the
    route's path function and allowed only its making, mode and removal by the daemon
    (`only_the_daemons_making_mode_and_removal_of_its_socket_node_are_allowed`, which fails with the call-kind check
    removed). CI's next macOS run (40118981721, `105b8b4d`) judged 61 write-capable calls: 23 inside the granted
    target, 35 on RAM-only objects, 3 on the socket node, 0 outside — the route writes no other file.
- **Step 5, in part (2026-10-24).** The one-file example server and the blocking `serve`, `serve_one`,
  `read_shards_frame` and `write_shards_frame` it ran on are removed: nothing in the daemon used them, and `serve_one`
  dispatched without `answer`'s reply framing and read ceiling. `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/shards_fs.rs` now drives a
  guest's mount and read, and the hostile lengths (a literal `u32::MAX` among them), through `split_frame` and `answer`
  on every platform; `examples/shards_fs_bench.rs` times them (BENCHMARKS, 2026-10-24: GETATTR 125 ns, READ 4 KiB
  250 ns, CREATE p50 291 ns at best, no dearer than before).
- **Linux's handoff under its collector, measured (2026-10-24).** The daemon still closes its copy of an end right after
  the send. `every_end_delivered_arrives_live_while_the_kernel_collects_descriptors_in_flight` attaches 48 times while
  another thread drops unreachable cycles of descriptors in flight, each release scheduling Linux's collector: 10 of
  10 runs on Linux 7.2.9 (load 49) delivered every end live, 8,192–12,976 cycles dropped during each. Why, from memory
  of `net/unix/garbage.c` and not re-read for this: Linux's collector keeps a descriptor that sits in the queue of a
  socket something outside the messages still holds, as the client holds its control socket; XNU's flushed one in the
  same window. Evidence of absence under that stress, not a proof.
- **CI, part 1's code complete (2026-10-24):** run 40123120384 at `50d6ef80`, 19 of 19 jobs green on macOS, Linux and
  Windows (the Linux `cargo test --workspace` and CLI flow with the exec, TSan over `stream_exec` and the churn test, the
  macOS hermeticity run with the socket-node class); the state before the exec, `105b8b4d`, was 19 of 19 too (run
  40118981721).
- **Part 2: a real Shards microVM over the daemon (2026-10-24).** Shards' `--slates-fs-fd` and its boot test, ported
  from their old base onto Shards' `gpu` (`b12ec23d`) as a patch series the Shards owner applies (they asked for a
  patch; slates writes nothing to their repository):
  - `--slates-fs-fd` takes `Slot::attach`'s answer;
  - the testguest writes, syncs and reads back a file after reading one;
  - the boot test drives the slates daemon. It starts `slates anchor`, writes `hello`, runs
    `slates shards ID --fd 3 -- shards run … --slates-fs-fd 3 …`, and reads the guest's file back through `slates read`.

  On this Mac (HVF, arm64) the test passed 3 of 3:
  - 54.7 s on the first run, which built the musl testguest and fetched the kernel; then 1.36 s and 1.22 s;
  - the console of one run showed the VM running 50.8 ms and the guest printing `SHARDS-TEST PASS`, with the host reading
    back what the guest wrote.

  Red-checked: with `--read-only` the guest's create is refused (`EPERM`) and the test fails, so the writes go through
  the attachment and its rights. The series is `~/.cache/slates-scratch/shards-part2-patches/` on this Mac, sent to
  the Shards session.
- **Owed:** Shards applying the series to its repository, and a DAX window over a backing that authorizes only the
  attachment's bytes (part 3).

### A-160 — A volume's disk-image form: ext2, written in bounded steps, read back as hostile input (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/image` (new): `format.rs`, `tree.rs`, `layout.rs`, `write.rs`, `read.rs`, `error.rs`; the tests
  `round_trip.rs`, `layout.rs`, `hostile.rs`, `e2fsck.rs`;
- the workspace manifest and `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-image = 0`);
- GAPS (the owed item "Firecracker's disk-image form", now in progress);
- (2026-10-24) `crates/guest-probe` (a block-device guest: list, write, patch, rename, remove, mkdir, flush; the VM
  ended by reboot under Firecracker), `crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs` and the real-VM harness both guest tests
  share, `crates/cli/tests/vm`;
- (2026-10-24) `crates/vfs/src/image.rs` and `tests/image.rs`; `crates/server/src/image.rs`, the create and clone
  verbs split into admission and recording (`verbs.rs`), `BaseRecord::Image` in `crates/db/src/catalog.rs`, the
  pin reconciliation and the destroy's unpin; the protocol's `ImageBuild`, `ImageMerge`, `ImageBuilt`, `ImageMerged`
  and `ImageRefused`; the client's `image_build` and `image_merge`; `slates image build` and `slates image merge`;
  `docs/cli.md`; `DaemonConfig::copy_slice_bytes` (formerly `dax_shift_slice_bytes`, generalized to every
  copy-bound slice);
- (2026-10-24, every unit bounded) `crates/image`: `segments.rs` (new), `tree.rs` (segmented tables, entries in one
  array, a stepped close and release), `write.rs` (a directory measured a block a unit, groups counted a group a unit,
  nodes without data passed a node a unit, a file placed a group's run a unit, records packed in place, bitmaps by
  bytes), `layout.rs` (`Map::indirect_at`, `Allocator::take_run`), `read.rs` (descriptors read on first use, records
  read an entry a unit); `crates/vfs`: `dir.rs` and `dirtree.rs` (`DirNode::next_entry`, `TreeCursor`), `image.rs`
  (the walk through the cursor, the merge's phases); `crates/server/src/image.rs` (the release in slices after the
  reply); the tests `crates/vfs/tests/image_cost.rs` (new) and those the API changes touched;
  `crates/vfs/examples/image_bench.rs`; `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`, `docs/wip/GAPS.md`, `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 item
  7, and §4.6.

- **What it answers.** Firecracker shares no folder with its guest. It has no virtio-fs, only block and pmem devices
  backed by files (its v1.17.0 docs, read 2026-10-23), so a volume reaches a Firecracker guest only as an image file
  holding a file system (`docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 item 7). The guest's writes come back by reading that file system
  out of the image and merging what changed into a clone, slates' usual session.
- **The format.** ext2 revision 1: 4 KiB blocks, 256-byte inodes, and only the `filetype`, `sparse_super` and
  `large_file` features, the set `mkfs.ext2 -O ^resize_inode,^dir_index,^ext_attr` makes.
  - Every Linux guest mounts it read-write, through the ext2 driver or the ext4 driver that serves ext2 on kernels
    built with `CONFIG_EXT4_USE_FOR_EXT2`.
  - Its large inodes carry nanosecond times, and its 4 KiB blocks are the page size DAX on a pmem device needs.
  - ext4 was not chosen: nothing here needs a journal, extents or checksums, and each would be more for the reader to
    distrust. A format of slates' own was not either: the guest's kernel must mount the image with no driver slates
    ships.
  - No `lost+found` is made: `e2fsck -fn` passes without one, so the guest sees exactly the volume.
- **Writing** lays the whole image out first: the geometry, a single allocation cursor through the groups' data areas,
  and each node's blocks in ext2's classic order (each indirect block before the data it maps). It then writes in
  steps a caller bounds. One tree and one identity always make the same bytes.
- **Reading** treats the image as hostile: the superblock must be what the writer writes and cleanly unmounted, each
  group's structures must lie inside it, every block pointer inside the file system, and every directory record must
  fit its block. The walk refuses a directory named twice (a cycle) and holds its entries to the caller's bound.
- **Evidence (2026-10-23).**
  - Generated trees round-trip exactly at the format's precision (proptest, 96 cases a run). The oracle is not
    vacuous: dropping the high 16 bits of each uid fails it at once, shrunk to one directory owned by uid 65536.
  - The block map fills its slots once each with every indirect block first, through the triple-indirect level.
  - The determinism gate holds, and the golden digest is the same on macOS arm64 and Linux x86_64.
  - 43,264 single-bit flips of the superblock, the first group descriptor, the root inode and the root directory block
    each give a tree or a typed refusal; each targeted corruption is refused by its own kind.
  - `e2fsck -fn` passes every written image, and `debugfs` lists every directory and reads files as written (e2fsprogs
    1.47.4 on the box). Each link count raised by one fails it.
- **What the differential found.**
  - A writer bug: group descriptors ran 36 bytes, not 32, so every group past the first was misread. A round trip whose
    inodes span groups was red before the fix and green after, and the reader now refuses a group's structures outside
    it.
  - An e2fsprogs bug: e2fsck 1.47.4 deadlocks in pass 5 (`pthread_mutex_lock` under `io_channel_set_options`, from
    `ext2fs_rw_bitmaps`) when it would write a fix to an image opened read-only, and ignores the `SIGTERM` meant to
    stop it. Each e2fsprogs run is bounded with `timeout --kill-after`.
- **Not carried:** extended attributes, birth times (the change time stands in), and holes (a sparse file takes its
  length; its zero blocks are left unwritten). Times outside 1901–2446 are refused.
- **Bounded steps for the daemon (2026-10-23).** Every piece of work is a step a caller bounds by bytes:
  - the builder plans only the geometry when made; it measures each node's blocks, holds the total to the capacity
    and places them a node a step before it writes a byte;
  - the reader keeps no hold on its source (each read is handed it), and its walk reads a directory a block a step and
    an entry a step;
  - one checker grows every tree a directory at a time (`TreeGrower`), so no step pays for a whole tree; the batch
    `TreeBuilder` grows its tree through it.

  Tests: walking in the smallest steps reads the same tree as a whole walk, every round trip, with no step reading
  past one unit's bytes; 2,000 FIFOs take at least two layout steps each before the first write.
- **The build's generation.** Every written inode carries `i_generation` 0. A guest's kernel gives an inode it
  allocates a generation of its own. Linux's ext2 counts up from a random start per mount: `ext2_new_inode` sets
  `inode->i_generation = sbi->s_next_generation++`, and `ext2_fill_super` sets
  `sbi->s_next_generation = get_random_u32()`. Its ext4 driver draws one at random: `__ext4_new_inode` sets
  `inode->i_generation = get_random_u32()` (torvalds/linux master, read 2026-10-24). So an inode at its written
  number with generation 0 is, but for a 1 in 2³² chance, the node the writer put there. A merge keeps that node's
  identity through renames and rewrites.
- **The volume's side (2026-10-24; `crates/vfs/src/image.rs`).**
  - The build walks a snapshot depth first, each directory's entries in its canonical order (its folded names'
    hashes, §4.5, a function of the names alone; name order until the 2026-10-24 change below), so one snapshot always
    walks to the same tree, node for node. It writes the image into a file of another volume, each directory's
    entries in name order. A volume over a host directory is refused, since its snapshot may still read the disk.
  - The merge makes a clone of the build's snapshot equal to the tree the image holds. It is not an inferred merge
    (D-27): the clone starts at the image's base, nothing else writes it, and the image's tree becomes its state. A
    node at its written number with the build's generation keeps its inode in the clone. A renamed file is renamed,
    not copied, and an unchanged file's chunks stay shared. Identity is a hint only: every name, attribute and byte is
    compared and set, so a node taken for the wrong one still ends as the image holds it.
  - The phases, an item a step: prepare the tables and identify; under folded names, index the image's entries; plan
    (an entry kept stays; one whose name the image gives to another node is moved aside into a staging directory,
    made only when needed under a name sought a counter a step); attach, depth first from the root (rename an old
    name, link, or create); remove what is left (files first, then directories from the last walked down); unstage;
    settle each node's size, differing pages, permissions, owner and times (the change time set from the image).
    A merge of an unchanged image changes nothing.
  - Tests (`crates/vfs/tests/image.rs`, 2,000 cases each on 2026-10-24, green):
    - generated volumes round-trip through their images;
    - an unchanged image merges as no change, every byte compared;
    - generated guest histories merge to the edited tree with every build node at its inode, the report exact;
    - images renumbered throughout merge to their tree;
    - each kind of change takes its own path;
    - what a volume cannot hold is refused by kind.

    Turning identity off fails the three identity tests.
  - **What the oracle found first:** the remove phase took nodes from the last walked down, and a file is numbered
    where it is first met. A hard link in a directory walked later was still there when that directory was removed,
    which was refused `NotEmpty`. The seed is kept in `image.proptest-regressions`, red before the fix and green after.
- **The daemon's verbs (2026-10-24; `crates/server/src/image.rs`).**
  - `ImageBuild` makes a new volume whose root holds `image.ext2`, the snapshot's image. `ImageMerge` makes a new
    clone of the snapshot an image volume was built from, holding the image's tree.
  - Each verb checks the volume, the right (write, as a clone needs), the name and the snapshot at once. It then
    defers its reply to a task of the volume's owner shard, as a granted landing does (AUD-29-03). The task steps the
    work in slices of `copy_slice_bytes` (half the live step quantum at the measured memcpy rate), yielding between
    them. A retry while it runs joins it.
  - The new volume is outside the registry while it is made, so no client attaches a half-built image or a
    half-merged clone. Its record, its publication and the request's completion record commit as one atom. A refusal,
    or a task that ends early, discards the volume and gives back its credits and its pin.
  - Pins: the image volume's catalog base, `BaseRecord::Image { volume, snapshot }`, pins the snapshot as a clone
    pins its origin. Recovery counts it with the clones (`reconcile_clone_pins`), and the image volume's destroy
    releases it. An image volume shares no record with its snapshot, so recovery rebuilds it as a scratch volume, not
    a clone. The merge's clone carries a lineage edge, as every clone does.
  - The merge reads the image file at a snapshot of the image volume taken when it starts, so a running guest cannot
    change the image under it. The snapshot is recorded nowhere and destroyed when the merge ends; recovery trims
    one a crash leaves. The image is trusted for identity only when its file system's UUID is the image volume's own
    id, which the build gave it; any other image merges by names and bytes alone.
  - The image volume takes the source's size class at the image's size, rounded up to whole chunks. A write is
    charged its chunk window (§4.5), so a guest can fill every block; growing the file to the image's length costs
    nothing until written.
- **Evidence (2026-10-24).**
  - `crates/client/tests/image.rs`, against a daemon in the test process, macOS arm64 (256 KiB chunks) and Linux
    x86_64 (64 KiB chunks):
    - an image is built, read back through the client as ext2 and found to hold every file;
    - a guest's edits written into it (a rename, a chunk rewritten, a deletion, a new file at the freed inode number
      under a new generation) merge with the report exact (7 kept, 1 made, 1 moved, 1 removed) and the bytes written
      the new file's and the one changed chunk's;
    - the refusals are typed and make no volume;
    - the image volume pins its snapshot until it goes.
  - `crates/server/tests/recovery.rs`: the pin survives a restart, and is red with image bases left out of the
    reconciliation.
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`, through FUSE mounts on the box (Linux 7.2.9, e2fsprogs 1.47.4), green 3 of 3:
    - the daemon's image passes `e2fsck -fn` through the mount, and `debugfs` reads every file;
    - `debugfs -w` edits through the mount (a rename, a block rewritten in place, a new file, a deletion, a new
      directory) leave it passing `e2fsck`;
    - `slates image merge` reports 2 made, 1 moved, 1 removed, with a chunk and 17 bytes written, and the clone's
      mount holds exactly the edits.
  - The first run of the CLI test found that debugfs leaves a new inode's generation zero. A file made right after a
    deletion takes the freed number and is merged as the deleted file renamed and rewritten: harmless, since the clone
    still holds the image's tree, and impossible under a kernel. The test makes its new file first.
- **A sibling fixed on the way:** a clone refused for want of a fresh volume id discarded itself but kept its pin on
  the origin's snapshot. The split clone verb releases the pin on every refusal (`publish_clone`).
- **A real Firecracker microVM (2026-10-24; `crates/cli/tests/guest_image.rs`).** Firecracker v1.17.0 ran on the box:
  the release binary, its tarball's SHA-256 `06094a11…e558` matching the release's checksum file, and the binary
  checked against `SHA256SUMS`.
  - It booted the box's own 7.2.9 kernel, unpacked to ELF by `scripts/extract-vmlinux`. That kernel's virtio-mmio is a
    module, so the guest's disk comes over virtio-pci (`--enable-pci`). It ran with `--no-api` (no socket) and its
    configuration in a slates volume.
  - The initramfs, the guest probe as `/init`, lived in a slates volume. The disk was the image file read through a
    slates FUSE mount, as a writable virtio-blk drive whose flushes are written through (`cache_type: Writeback`).
  - The guest mounted the disk as ext2 through its ext4 driver, and listed every node with an FNV-1a digest of its
    bytes. It found the volume's tree exactly: directories, a file of three chunks and more, a hard link and a
    symbolic link.
  - It then patched a file inside its second chunk, renamed one into another directory, removed one, wrote a new
    file, made a directory, flushed, listed its own changes and ended the VM by rebooting (`reboot=k`).
  - `slates image merge` reported 7 kept, 2 made, 1 moved, 1 removed and 65,563 bytes written: the patch's one
    64 KiB chunk and the new file's 27 bytes. The clone, read through its own mount, held exactly the guest's tree.
  - The guest booted to its probe's ready in 191–207 ms. The test ran green 3 of 3, and was red with the merge's chunk
    writes disabled. The crosvm guest tests share its harness (`tests/vm`) and stayed green, 3 of 3.
  - Later runs found Firecracker's exit on the guest's restart a race: 1 of 18 at load 46–53 exited 1. The kernel's
    `reboot=k` pulses the keyboard controller's reset for about a millisecond, then falls through to a triple fault
    (`native_machine_emergency_restart`). When Firecracker's main thread stops the vCPU later than that, the vCPU's KVM
    shutdown exit is one Firecracker v1.17.0 leaves unhandled (`UnhandledKvmExit("Shutdown")` → `GenericError`). The
    test accepts that exit only when the console shows the guest's restart and Firecracker's `Shutdown` line, read
    after the VM's last output is drained. Forced with `reboot=t` it passed, the merge after it intact.
- **Slices bounded by the clock (2026-10-24).** The daemon first bounded each slice by 256 KiB of charged work
  (`copy_slice_bytes`). Measured with `crates/vfs/examples/image_bench.rs`, those slices ran 230 µs to 1.5 ms when
  the scheduler left them alone, ten to sixty times the box's 24 µs (half its 47.5 µs step quantum). A unit's cost
  is not its bytes: a walked entry is charged about 80 bytes and costs about 450 ns.
  - The daemon now runs each phase one unit a call, until half the live step quantum has passed
    (`DaemonConfig::copy_slice_ns`, a granted landing's share), so a slice overruns by its last unit at most. A unit
    longer than a whole slice is counted (`image.units_past_budget`).
  - The merge's unit is the store's page, not its chunk. Comparing a whole 256 KiB chunk took about 40 µs on macOS
    arm64, longer than a slice. A page compares and writes in about 1 µs at p99, and only differing pages are
    written, so a chunk with no differing page is still never written.
  - The tests' byte counts follow: one page and the new file's bytes.
- **Every unit bounded (2026-10-24).** `image_bench` gained the extremes, a directory of 20,000 and of 100,000 entries
  and a tree of 100,000 nodes, and reports each unit's least time over five rounds. A slice's wall time could not tell
  a unit's cost from the machine's: setting aside slices the process was switched out or faulted in hid exactly the
  units that allocate. On the Mac at load 32–38, before:
  - the snapshot walk opened a 100,000-entry directory in one unit of 12,035 µs, every name copied and sorted;
  - the tree grower closed it in one of 540 µs, and measuring it for the image took one of 175 µs;
  - a node vector's doubling took 271 µs at 16,384 nodes;
  - the merge's step from identifying to planning took 70 µs at 100,000 nodes, its tables made whole;
  - a bitmap block, set a bit at a time, took 42–60 µs;
  - releasing a finished merge and its builder was one drop of 4.4–14.9 ms at 100,000 nodes.

  Now:
  - the walk reads a snapshot's directory an entry a unit through a cursor into the directory itself
    (`DirNode::next_entry`, `TreeCursor`), which nothing changes while the snapshot lives. A reading that ends short
    of the directory's count is refused, since a missing entry would make the merge remove it;
  - a directory closes an entry a unit, every directory's entries in one array, each directory's together;
  - every table grows a segment at a time and never moves (`slates_image::Segments`);
  - a directory is measured a block of entries a unit, the groups' blocks in use counted a group a unit, a file placed
    a group's run a unit and its indirect blocks computed one at a time (`Map::indirect_at`); a directory block's
    records are written in place, and a bitmap's bytes filled whole;
  - the reader checks a group's descriptor when an inode of the group is first read, not every group at the open;
  - the merge sizes its tables a slot a unit, takes each entry's offset from the tree, indexes folded names an entry a
    unit, seeks a staging name a counter a unit, and attaches depth first from the root with a stack as deep as the
    tree;
  - a finished build's or merge's trees, tables and walks are released in slices after the reply, 64 pieces a unit
    (`shed_in_slices`), a plain table a segment at a time.

  The image bytes are unchanged (the golden digest held). `crates/vfs/tests/image_cost.rs` holds every phase's worst
  step at 16,384 files to its worst at 2,048 by allocator count, through the release; it failed in every phase before.
  The longest unit after: 18.5 µs on the box (a release unit at 100,000 nodes) and 22.9 µs on the Mac at load 55–67
  (BENCHMARKS, 2026-10-24). The walk's new order changes which inode each node takes, not what a merge keeps:
  identity is the written number, read back from the image. The client test now orders its guest's tree by the
  numbers it read.
- **Owed:** a pmem drive under Firecracker (DAX on the image file). Two costs are not a unit's and are recorded as
  such: the refusal message of a merge names its path by scanning each parent's entries (once, as the merge stops),
  and the new volume's publication inside the completion atom is the publication path's cost (§4.8), not the image's.

### A-159 — The bootstrap header no longer carries the daemon's process id (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/ipc/src/rendezvous.rs` (macOS and Windows): `AT_DAEMON_PID` and its write in `Listener::open` removed; the
  header's layout names those four bytes padding;
- GAPS §8a-sdk-stamp and `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-client-whose-claim-crossed-a-restart-judged-the-live-daemon-gone.md`.

- **What it answers.** Since A-143 a client judges the daemon that answered its claim by the stamp and process id in
  the answer, never by the header. The header's copy of the pid was still written by every daemon and read only by
  clients built before A-143: a write kept for older versions, which CLAUDE.md's rule 7 bans. `docs/publish.md` ships
  one version, so no shipped pairing reads it.
- **What stays.** The header's start stamp (a client's `begin` and `daemon_gone` read it as the instance's current
  daemon) and the holding anchor's pid (A-114) are unchanged and keep their offsets; the removed field's bytes are
  padding, so no other field moved.
- **Evidence.** By use on macOS: `slates-ipc` 46 tests and `slates-client` 22 tests pass without the write, the A-143
  restart test and the client's reconnect and reap histories among them. The arm64 Windows cross-lint of `slates-ipc`
  is clean.

### A-158 — A restored mount tells its kernel what its predecessor may not have (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (a mount taken over by a restarted daemon; the held device's status);
- `crates/bridge-fuse`:
  - `src/init.rs`: `InitNegotiation::kernel_minor`;
  - `src/session.rs`: `Session::kernel_bumps_epoch`, bit `1 << 2` of format 1, `EPOCH_MINOR`;
  - `src/notify.rs`: `Notify::IncEpoch`, `inc_epoch`;
  - `src/channel.rs`: the takeover round (`takeover_told`, `Takeover`, `TakeoverSlice`), `ServeState::slices_within`,
    `owes_takeover_round`, `take_takeover_counts`;
- `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs`: `Volume::replayed`, `mark_replayed`, `visit_takeover_inodes`;
- `crates/bridge-core`: `Bridge::takeover_inodes` (`lib.rs`, `volume_bridge.rs`, `scoped.rs`, and the test bridge in
  `crates/bridge-fuse/tests`);
- `crates/server/src/fuse.rs`: the wake while a slice is owed, the slice budget (`TAKEOVER_SLICE_PERMILLE`), and the
  counters `fuse.epoch_bumped`, `fuse.epoch_unsupported`, `fuse.takeover_invalidated`;
- `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`: `replay_one` marks the inodes the replay names;
- the tests:
  - `crates/bridge-fuse/src/session.rs`: the 8 golden sessions, and a kernel offering 7.44 recorded as able to bump;
  - `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/abi.rs`: `the_epoch_notification_is_a_bare_header`, and the code in the header table;
  - `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/takeover_round.rs`: the whole set in slices, each inode once; a kernel before 7.44;
  - `crates/vfs/tests/recover.rs`: the set names the owner's references and the replay's inodes and nothing of another
    owner; walked in slices it is the whole set;
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`: the replacement, rename and chaos tests across kills;
- GAPS and `docs/bugs/2026-10-23-a-change-a-dead-daemon-never-delivered-outlives-the-takeover.md`.

- **What it answers.** A change reaches a mount's kernel about 82 µs after its writer's reply (A-142's measurement). A
  daemon that died in between had made the change durable and never told the kernel, and the successor's journal starts
  empty, so nothing named it. Under the `Invalidated` posture the kernel's names, attributes and pages live until
  invalidated, so the old bytes and names were served indefinitely. Reproduced 4 of 4 on Linux 7.2.9.
- **Why this set.** Every acknowledged change is durable before its reply. A kernel holds state older than a change
  only for an inode it looked up before it, and that change's publication recorded the reference, which the recovery
  gives back. A logged FUSE write is in no publication, so the replay notes its inodes, landed or refused. The set is
  therefore the owner's restored references (and any taken since) and the replayed inodes. The route that would carry
  the delivered cursor or the kernel's holdings across the takeover was not taken: it is anchor traffic on every round.
- **Names.** A name renamed or removed away belongs to no inode the successor can list. `FUSE_NOTIFY_INC_EPOCH` (FUSE
  7.44, Linux 6.16) bumps the connection's epoch, so every dentry stamped before fails its next revalidation. The
  kernel answers a notification by its own version, not the agreed one (it took `FUSE_NOTIFY_RESEND` on connections
  agreed at 7.31), so the session records the minor the kernel offered. A kernel before 7.44 would answer the code
  `EINVAL`, which the notify thread takes for a device refusal, so it is not sent there and is counted instead.
- **Slices.** The set can be tens of thousands of inodes, and each message is built on the serving thread. So a slice
  takes at most half the shard's live step quantum and at least one inode, walked in inode order from where the last
  ended; each costs only what it visits. An inode looked up after the takeover, below where the walk stands, is fresh,
  and one forgotten needs nothing, so a set that changes between slices loses nothing. The mount turns at once while a
  slice is owed and no round is out, and the round's return wakes it otherwise, so a takeover never spins its shard.
- **Evidence.** On the box, with load 15–82 from other sessions:
  - the two kill-in-window tests are red on their final text with the change's files at the previous commit, and
    green 3 of 3 runs, every takeover bumping the epoch once and invalidating 2 inodes;
  - the chaos test is green 3 of 3 runs, 13 inodes in every round, and red at its first cycle without the change;
  - the socket-pair test gives each inode once, in 40 slices at a zero budget. Resuming the walk at its cursor rather
    than after it re-sends the last inode forever; an unbounded slice sends all 41 at once. Both turn it red.
- **A test premise.** Under load the mount's round for another path's create reached the kernel after the test had
  looked the new file up. It dropped that name, and the kernel evicted the unused inode. So the kernel held nothing to
  leave stale, and the set rightly named only the root. The tests now wait until the mount's journal reader is at the
  head before caching, and hold the file open.
- **Not in this change.** A dirty pre-takeover page is still judged fresh as of the mount's start (A-156). An effect
  served before its publication can outlive a crash in a kernel. An outsider's base change in the gap stays in a kernel
  that looked the file up after the last publication. Kernels before 7.44 keep renamed-away names. Each is a GAPS
  entry.

### A-157 — The journal keeps what a live reader still needs, growing from the metadata ledger (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.5 (Journal retention; the derived constants);
- §4.6 (a mount that falls behind the journal);
- A-141 (an overrun now needs a refused growth or a reader silent past its liveness);
- `crates/vfs/src/journal.rs`:
  - readers carry a patience;
  - `OpLog::append` takes the shard's metadata ledger and grows the budget for a record a live reader still owes;
  - `grown` and `growth_refused`;
- `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs`:
  - `Volume::record` takes the ledger, at all 24 of its call sites (`volume.rs`, `base.rs`, `xattr.rs`);
  - `open_journal_reader` takes the patience;
  - `journal_grown`;
- `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`:
  - `JOURNAL_SHARE_PERMILLE` and `journal_bytes_for` replaced by `journal_floor_bytes` (one page) at creation and
    recovery;
  - `release_slot_credits` returns the growth;
  - the journal report gains `grown_bytes` and `growth_refused`;
- `crates/server/src/fuse.rs`: a FUSE mount's reader is opened with the daemon's liveness budget as its patience;
- `crates/ipc/src/protocol.rs`, `crates/cli/src/verbs.rs`, `crates/mcp/src/lib.rs`: the report's two fields;
- the tests:
  - `crates/vfs/src/journal.rs`: `retention_keeps_what_a_live_reader_needs_as_the_model_does`;
  - `crates/bridge-core/tests/invalidation.rs`:
    - `a_live_readers_records_are_kept_by_growing_from_the_ledger`;
    - `a_reader_past_its_patience_pins_nothing_and_overruns`;
    - `a_growth_the_ledger_refuses_overruns_its_reader_and_is_counted`;
- the module docs of `crates/bridge-core/src/changed.rs` and `crates/vfs/examples/create_heap.rs`;
- GAPS.

- **What it answers.** §4.5 derives the journal's budget as the mutation rate times the longest subscriber lag times
  the record size. The code took a fixed 10‰ of the quota instead, citing a ratification the ledger never held
  (R3). Measured on real workloads, the largest backlog any round found was 39,424 bytes, where a 1 GiB volume's share
  was 10,737,418 (BENCHMARKS, 2026-10-23). And a volume under 3.76 MiB held less than that backlog.
- **The rule.**
  - The journal's budget starts at a one-page floor, reserved with the volume's records.
  - While an incoming record does not fit, the oldest record leaves only if every open reader has read past it, or if
    it has waited longer than the patience of the reader still owing it.
  - Otherwise, once an append, the budget grows by the shortfall, reserved from the shard's metadata ledger.
  - A refused growth keeps the budget, drops the oldest record, and is counted. The reader that owed it overruns
    (A-141).
  - A FUSE mount's patience is the daemon's liveness budget: a reader silent that long is not keeping up with a live
    daemon, and is presumed gone.
  - The budget never shrinks while the volume lives. Its growth is returned at teardown, as a dynamic volume's byte
    growth is. A rebuilt journal starts at the floor.
  - Writers never wait.
- **Why it is the formula.** By Little's law, the records a reader has yet to read are the mutation rate times its lag.
  The journal holds exactly those, and grows to the largest such backlog a live reader ever had. So the budget is the
  product, measured at the moment of need rather than estimated. The Disruptor's producers track their consumers'
  sequences so the ring never wraps past an unread entry. This ring grows instead of making its producers wait.
- **How close it follows.** A reader's point is the start of its round in flight, since a refused round is gathered
  again from there (A-141). So the journal keeps that round's batch until the next round begins, and the budget is at
  most two consecutive backlogs, or the floor. Measured on the box (BENCHMARKS, 2026-10-24):
  - git clone, cargo build and the SDK ring each ended at 4,096–16,896 bytes, every one within twice its largest
    backlog and 8 of 9 within a page of it;
  - no overrun and no refused growth;
  - the share would have reserved 10,737,418 bytes for each of those 1 GiB volumes.
  Advancing the point when a round's delivery is confirmed would halve the worst case. It is not taken at tens of
  kilobytes.
- **Why first the borrowers.** Two things leaned on the journal's depth:
  - the byte states, whose bound was its capacity: charged to the ledger since A-155;
  - a restored mount's lazy adoption, which read it back to the mount's start: tracked from the start since A-156.
  With both moved off it first, a smaller journal costs neither.
- **Proven.**
  - The oracle compares retention, budget, growth and refusals with an independent model after every step of 2000
    histories, with the ledger's commitment equal to the growth. While nothing was refused, it checks directly that no
    record a live reader owes within its patience has left. With growth disabled it fails at a shrunk two-record case.
  - The bridge tests show:
    - a live reader's records kept by growing, with no overrun;
    - a reader past its patience overrunning;
    - a refused growth counted and overrunning.

### A-156 — A restored mount tracks the files the last publication counted open from its start (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (a mount taken over by a restarted daemon);
- A-147 (lazy adoption kept only for opens no publication counted);
- `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs`: `Volume::restored_open_files`;
- `crates/bridge-core`: `Bridge::restored_open_files` (`volume_bridge.rs`, `scoped.rs`, the test bridge in
  `crates/bridge-fuse/tests`);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/coherence.rs`: `Coherence::begin_at`;
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs`:
  - `adopt_restored`, run once at a restored mount's first turn (`ServeState::adopt_restored`);
  - `drop_released_restored`, at the release of a handle the mount never saw opened;
- the tests:
  - `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs`: `a_released_pre_takeover_files_states_go_once_nothing_of_it_is_open`;
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`: `a_restored_mounts_counted_files_are_tracked_from_its_start_past_the_journals_reach`;
- GAPS.

- **What it answers.** A-147 adopted a restored mount's file only when a request named one of its handles. It read the
  journal back to the mount's start for the changes the file had missed. Once the journal no longer reached back, the
  file was lost and its write-backs were refused. With a journal that keeps only what a live reader needs (the plan
  "Journal budget derived", step 4), that would be soon after any activity.
- **The rule.** At a restored mount's first turn:
  - it tracks every file the volume restored opens of for its owner (A-152's counts) as fresh as of that moment;
  - it starts its rounds at the same head, so they feed each file every change after it.
  The same assumption A-147 made of an adopted file, fresh as of the mount's start, is now made of every counted file
  at once. No journal record from before is ever needed.
- **What stays lazy.** A handle opened after the last publication is in no count. Its file is still adopted when a
  request names it, from the journal's records since the start, as A-147 did. A publication that counts every open
  promptly would close that window, at the cost of a publication per open (not taken).
- **The release.** When a handle the mount never saw opened is released, and nothing of its file is open on the mount
  any more, the file's states go. Otherwise they would outlive the handles, and a later open would inherit them (a lost
  file's refusals among them), though that open dropped the kernel's cached pages.
- **Evidence.** On the box (Linux 7.2.9), with this change's files restored to the previous commit:
  - setup: a 256 KiB volume (a one-page journal), a mapped file, an unlink publishing its open, a `SIGKILL` and the
    anchor's successor;
  - then 50 SDK replacements of another file, each consumed by the mount's round, and a store through the map;
  - before: `msync` answered `EIO`;
  - with the change: it succeeds, with no overrun and no write-back refused as unknown, and slates holds the store.
  The existing A-147 test passes unchanged.

### A-155 — A mount's byte states are charged to the metadata ledger, not bounded by the journal (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (the write-back rule's refusals);
- A-140's bound (superseded);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/coherence.rs`: `PageStates` keeps the ranges it holds and the room the ledger admitted, a
  file whose update would pass the room is lost (`take_lost_for_room`), and the per-call bound is gone;
  `RANGE_BYTES`, `MOST_ADDED_BY_AN_UPDATE`, `most_added_by_an_ambiguous_read`;
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs`: `make_room` before each update that can add ranges, a page of ranges per
  reservation; `ServeState::states_charged`;
- `crates/bridge-core`: `Bridge::admit_states` (`volume_bridge.rs` reserves from the shard's metadata ledger;
  `scoped.rs`; the test bridge in `crates/bridge-fuse/tests`);
- `crates/server/src/fuse.rs`: `release_states` in `ended` and `drop_devices`; the counter `fuse.states_lost_for_room`;
- the tests:
  - `coherence.rs`: the byte-state oracle now grows a just-sufficient room before each event and requires no
    file lost; `a_full_room_loses_only_the_file_being_updated`;
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`:
    - `a_mapped_files_write_back_survives_more_scattered_changes_than_the_journal_holds_records`;
    - `a_fuse_mounts_byte_states_are_charged_while_it_lives_and_returned_when_it_ends`;
- GAPS.

- **What it answers.** A-140 bounded each file's byte states by the journal's capacity: the budget over a record's
  fixed size. The states are in no way the journal's records, and they were charged to no ledger (§4.2: "an
  uncharged heap allocation cannot sit outside the bound"). The bound was only borrowed. The journal's budget is
  becoming the measured product (the plan "Journal budget derived"), which on a quiet volume is the one-page floor.
  A file would then be lost past about 51 ranges instead of the 850 an 8 MiB volume's share allowed. A file another
  path changes in scattered places while a mount holds it open, mapped or for writing, needs more than that.
- **The rule.** A mount's byte states are charged to the shard's metadata ledger at `RANGE_BYTES` a range, as the
  journal charges a record its fixed size.
  - Before an update that can add ranges, the mount grows the states' room by that update's most:
    - two for an update of one range;
    - one per run an ambiguous read covers.
    The room grows a page of ranges at a time, so a mount asks the ledger once a page of states.
  - An update that would take the ranges held past the room loses its file, as the old bound did, and is counted
    (`fuse.states_lost_for_room`). So a file is lost only when the ledger refuses.
  - The mount's owner returns the charge when the mount ends. The room never shrinks while the mount lives, as the
    journal's budget will not.
- **Why it is exact.** The oracle grows the room before each event by exactly the event's stated most, and no history
  of 2000 loses the file. A stated most below an update's real growth would lose it and fail the comparison with the
  per-byte model.
- **What it costs.** One ledger reservation per page of ranges (128 at 4 KiB, 32 bytes each). The unused room stays
  under a page per mount.
- **Evidence.** On the box (Linux 7.2.9), with step 2's files restored to the previous commit:
  - the scattered-changes test's `msync` answered `EIO` (30 single bytes a kilobyte apart through a second mount, on
    a 256 KiB volume: 60 ranges, past the one-page journal's 51);
  - the charge test read 89,902 bytes committed before the mount and while it lived.
  With the change, both pass. The scattered-changes test asserts no overrun and no file lost for want of room, and the
  charge test asserts the committed metadata back where it was once the mount ended. The full slates-cli suite passes
  twice (61/61), and bridge-fuse passes 135 tests in 19 suites.

### A-154 — A release of an open a publication counted is published before its reply (accepted 2026-10-23)
Applied in the same change to:
- A-61 ("What the kernel kept") and A-152;
- `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs`:
  - `committed_opens` and `releases_unpublished`;
  - `close_for` sets the flag;
  - `restore_references` and `sweep_attachment` keep `committed_opens` in step;
  - `unreserved` became `awaits_publication`;
- `crates/vfs/src/delta.rs`: `mark_published` commits the open counts (`commit_opens`);
- the hook renamed from `numbers_unreserved` to `awaits_publication`:
  - `crates/bridge-core` (`Bridge::awaits_publication`, `volume_bridge.rs`, `scoped.rs`);
  - `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/device.rs`;
  - `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`, `fuse.rs` and `nfs.rs`;
  - the test bridges in `crates/bridge-fuse/tests`;
- the tests: `crates/bridge-core/tests/takeover_release.rs` (`a_handle_released_after_the_last_publication_leaves_no_open_behind`,
  `a_release_of_an_open_no_publication_counted_waits_for_nothing`);
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-23-a-release-the-dead-daemon-answered-after-the-last-publication-came-back-as-an-open.md`.

- **What it answers.** A-152 restores the opens an image counted and gives one back at each release of a handle the
  successor never issued. It covered a handle opened after the last publication, but not one released after it. The
  kernel never resends a release its daemon answered, so a daemon that answered one and died before publishing left
  the image counting an open that nothing would ever give back. A-152's own end-to-end test found it under load on
  the box, about one full-suite run in five. The kernel's background `RELEASE` of a `CREATE` handle had queued behind
  the file's write-back, and the `UNLINK`'s barrier published three opens where two handles were left.
- **The rule (D-18).** After every reply, each recorded attachment's live opens of a file are at least the opens the
  committed publication counted.
  - A release that leaves fewer marks the volume as awaiting a publication (`Volume::awaits_publication`, the hook
    A-150 made for unreserved inode numbers).
  - The transport's reply then waits for the owner's barrier.
  - A crash before that reply leaves the `RELEASE` unanswered: the kernel resends it, and it consumes the restored
    open.
- **Why the bound holds.** A successor restores the committed count, and the kernel's later releases consume restored
  opens while any are left. So the opens nothing will give back number max(0, committed − live), which the rule keeps
  at zero.
- **What it costs.** Only a release of an open a publication counted waits. The kernel sends a regular file's
  `RELEASE` after `close()` has returned, so the wait costs the daemon one publication and the application nothing. An
  open and release both since the last publication leave the count where it was, and wait for nothing
  (`a_release_of_an_open_no_publication_counted_waits_for_nothing`).
- **Left open:** a `FORGET` processed after the last publication leaves its lookup reference counted in the image, and
  the kernel never resends a `FORGET` either. It has no reply to wait behind; it stays under A-61's stated limits, as
  a bounded leak (GAPS). **Closed 2026-11-08 by a1b44bb1:** each `FORGET` is logged beside the writes (A-63), and a
  successor gives it back in its place (§4.6, "A `FORGET` after the last publication is logged").
- **Evidence.** See the bug record's verification.

### A-269 — Through a read-only NFS attachment, what ACCESS decides answers `EACCES`: v3's open for writing, and a path truncate and `access(W_OK)` over v3 and v4 (accepted 2026-11-08, the supervisor's decisions)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 ("A read-only attachment is a read-only file system");
- `crates/bridge-nfs/src/procedures.rs` (`access_result`, `change_refusal`, `extension::CHANGE_ALLOWED`, `state_io`),
  `crates/bridge-nfs/src/v4/compound.rs` (`check_open_access`), `crates/bridge-nfs/src/v4/v3call.rs` (`status_only`);
- the tests: `crates/server/tests/nfs_read_only_kernel.rs`, and `a_write_through_a_read_only_export_is_refused`
  (`crates/bridge-nfs/tests/procedures.rs`);
- GAPS; `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-read-only-attachment-was-not-a-read-only-file-system.md`.

- **What §4.6 said.** A read-only attachment refuses every change as POSIX's read-only file system does: `EROFS`, at the
  open for an open for writing and at every mutating verb.
- **What it says now.** It still does, over every transport, with the exceptions ACCESS decides. Over NFSv3 an open for
  writing answers `EACCES`, and every change that reaches the server answers `EROFS`. Over NFSv3 and NFSv4 a path
  `truncate(2)` and `access(2)` for writing answer `EACCES`. Every other refusal over NFSv4, the open's included, is
  `EROFS`.
- **Why.** NFSv3 has no OPEN: a client decides `open(2)` from the ACCESS reply. Linux asks every ACCESS bit in one call
  and caches the answer (`fs/nfs/dir.c` at v6.8, `nfs_do_access`, lines 3201–3207), and reports a bit the server did
  not grant as `-EACCES` (lines 3219–3221). The only other answer a server has is an error on the ACCESS call itself,
  which that one call carries for every bit, so it would refuse reads and lookups too. Over NFSv4 a regular file's open
  skips ACCESS (`nfs_permission`, lines 3286–3288) and the server's OPEN decides, so `NFS4ERR_ROFS` reaches the
  application as `EROFS`. Measured through the kernel's own clients on CI: v3 `EACCES` for `O_WRONLY`, `O_RDWR` and
  `O_RDONLY|O_TRUNC`, v4 `EROFS` for each (diag-slabs-43, run 42517769901); every other change `EROFS` over both
  (conformance's read-only run, 42498995934; the kernel test's create probe re-runs it). EROFS at a v3 open
  would need a kernel mount made read-only (`-o ro`), which a read attachment under a writable mount is not.
- **The truncate, and why the write bit stays withheld over v4 too (the supervisor's decision (a), 2026-11-08).** A path
  `truncate(2)` checks write permission before any SETATTR, and Linux's `nfs_permission` sends a regular file's write
  without an open through ACCESS on v4 as on v3, so it answers `EACCES` over both (conformance's run on this fix,
  diag-conformance-32, run 42523564648: v3 10 of 14 `EROFS` with the three opens at the limit, v4 13 of 14; the other in
  each is `truncate/10.t`). Granting the write bits in v4's ACCESS would turn the truncate into `EROFS` but make
  `access(W_OK)` report a read-only file writable to every caller that checks first (`test -w`, editors, git): a wrong
  answer, where `EACCES` is a refusal. Linux's own server gives a Linux client exactly these answers for a read-only
  export: `fs/nfsd/vfs.c` (Linux v7.4-rc1) `nfsd_permission` (about line 2871) answers `nfserr_rofs` to any write,
  attribute or truncate access on a read-only export or mount, and `nfsd_access` (about line 855) treats `nfserr_rofs`,
  `nfserr_acces` and `nfserr_perm` alike: "simply don't 'or' in the access bit". So `access(W_OK)` and the truncate are
  `EACCES`, and every WRITE and SETATTR is `EROFS`, from the incumbent too. (The knfsd lines are the supervisor's
  reading of loadtest-scale's dataset tree; `fs/nfs/dir.c` at v6.8 is read here.) A local read-only file system answers
  `access(W_OK)` `EROFS` from the mount's own flag, which no NFS server can reach through ACCESS.
- **Evidence.** GAPS, the read-only attachment's entry; the bug record's "Found by conformance".

### A-256 — A base directory recovery cannot reacquire costs only its own untouched entries (accepted 2026-11-08, the supervisor's confirmation)
Applied in the same change to (the code and tests in 4db8c179, this entry and A-153's pointer after them):
- §4.8 ("Required persistence and protocol invariants");
- `docs/wip/recovery.md`;
- `crates/vfs/src/base.rs` (`BasePlane::unavailable`) and `crates/vfs/src/base_recovery.rs` (`BasePlane::recover`,
  `image`);
- the tests:
  - `crates/vfs/tests/base.rs`: A-153's guard as it now stands,
    `an_overlay_whose_base_directory_another_replaced_never_serves_the_other` (it was
    `an_overlay_whose_base_directory_another_replaced_is_refused`), and
    `an_overlay_whose_loaded_base_directory_was_removed_recovers_and_refuses_only_that_directory`;
  - `crates/server/tests/recovery.rs` `an_overlay_whose_base_directory_was_removed_serves_its_own_files_after_a_restart`;
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` `an_overlay_whose_base_directory_was_removed_serves_its_own_files_through_a_kept_mount`;
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-11-07-a-removed-base-directory-refused-the-whole-volume-at-recovery.md`.

- **What A-153 said.** A directory another directory replaced is not the same source, and is refused: the restart
  refused the whole volume (`RecoveryIncomplete`), and the guard test named that. It left open a loaded directory
  removed after the last publication, which refused the whole volume the same way.
- **What it says now.** A recorded directory recovery cannot reacquire as the same one, gone from the disk, unreadable,
  or another at the path, costs only its own untouched entries.
  - The volume recovers.
  - Those entries refuse `BaseUnavailable{path, errno}` (`ENOENT` when the host says only that it is not there).
  - The volume's own entries in that directory serve.
  - The next image keeps the directory's record, so a later recovery tries it again.
- **What it does not change.** A-153's identity rule (device, inode number and birth time) still decides whether a
  directory is the recorded one. Another directory is never substituted for it: reopening a path alone cannot substitute
  another base. Only the price of a failed reacquisition changed, from the whole volume to that directory.
- **Why.** §4.8's failure matrix already gives the runtime rule in its row "Base directory unreadable or gone": refused
  `BaseUnavailable` for untouched entries under it, witnessed and pinned entries serving. Recovery was harsher than that
  row, and one directory removed beneath a base cost the user every file the volume held, its own writes included (the
  bug record).
- **Not covered.** A directory that comes back while the daemon runs stays unavailable until the next restart.
- **Evidence.** See the bug record and GAPS (A-153's "Open, found here", closed).

### A-153 — A recovered base directory is judged by its identity, not its entries (accepted 2026-10-22)
**Amended by A-256 (2026-11-08):** a directory recovery cannot reacquire, replaced or removed, now costs only its own
untouched entries rather than the whole volume; the identity rule below stands.

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.8 ("Required persistence and protocol invariants");
- `docs/wip/recovery.md`;
- `crates/vfs/src/inode.rs` (`Fingerprint::same_object`) and `crates/vfs/src/base_recovery.rs` (`BasePlane::recover`);
- the tests:
  - `crates/vfs/tests/base.rs`: `an_overlay_recovers_after_an_outsider_changed_its_base_directories_since_its_image`, the
    guard `an_overlay_whose_base_directory_another_replaced_is_refused`, the no-birth-time case, and
    `an_unvisited_overlay_recovers_its_verified_source` (whose second half had asserted the refusal);
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` `a_takeover_recovers_an_overlay_whose_base_directory_an_outsider_changed`;
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-takeover-refused-an-overlay-whose-base-directory-an-outsider-had-changed.md`.

- **What it answers.** Recovery reopened each base directory the image recorded and required its whole fingerprint to
  match. That includes the times and size any change to the directory's entries moves. So an outsider's edit beneath a
  loaded directory at any time since the last publication made a takeover refuse the whole volume. Reads publish
  nothing, so that window can be hours. Measured on the box: "volume basechanged not rebuilt", and the held mount
  answered nothing.
- **The rule.** §4.8 asks for the same source identity, and a directory's identity is its device, inode number and
  birth time (`Fingerprint::same_object`, the three fields A-151's `FileTag` digests).
  - A directory whose entries changed is the same source, and recovers. Its listing is read again on first use, as
    every recovered listing is. An untouched entry beneath is checked at that first listing (A-151), and a witnessed one
    by its drift rule.
  - A directory another directory replaced is not the same source, and is refused, as §4.8 says.
- **Without birth times** the device and inode number decide. A directory replaced by one that took its number is then
  taken for the recorded one, but serves no wrong bytes:
  - its untouched entries are renumbered at the first listing (A-151);
  - its witnessed files show drift;
  - only a whiteout there could hide one of the new directory's names.

  Refusing would cost the volume whole for what is otherwise an ordinary edit.
- **Left open:** a loaded directory removed after the last publication still refuses the whole volume (`open_source`
  fails). §4.8 allows `RecoveryIncomplete` there, but the failure matrix's runtime rule (`BaseUnavailable` for that
  directory's untouched entries, overlay entries serving) is the robust form (GAPS).
- **Evidence.** See the bug record's verification.

### A-152 — A handle a dead daemon issued gives back its open at its release (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- A-61 ("What the kernel kept");
- `crates/vfs/src/recover.rs` (`InodeReferences::opens`; image layout 21), `delta.rs` (`ReferenceChange::opens`, both
  encoders and the applier), `volume.rs`:
  - `restored_opens` and `release_restored_open`;
  - `attachment_open_count`;
  - `restore_references` takes the open count and refuses more opens than references;
  - `open_for` and `close_for` record a changed reference;
  - `sweep_attachment` drops the owner's restored opens;
- `crates/bridge-core/src/volume_bridge.rs`: every handle `open_handle` issues is counted open (a created file's and a
  directory's too), and a release of a handle this bridge never issued gives back a restored open;
- the tests:
  - `crates/bridge-core/tests/takeover_release.rs` (four);
  - `crates/vfs/tests/recover.rs` (the open counts through a delta; more opens than references refused);
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` `the_handles_a_dead_daemon_issued_give_back_their_references_at_release`;
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-handle-opened-before-a-takeover-gave-back-nothing-at-its-release.md`.

- **What it answers.** After a takeover the successor serves the releases of handles the dead daemon issued, from a
  fresh handle store that never issued them. Such a release gave back nothing, by design: the image counted an
  attachment's lookups and opens together, so the successor could not tell whether an open's reference had been
  restored, and dropping one could take a lookup reference instead. So every pre-takeover handle's open reference
  stayed until the mount ended. A file unlinked while open was never reclaimed, and its bytes stayed charged. Measured
  on the box: 1,048,576 bytes still referenced 10 s after both descriptors of an unlinked 1 MiB file had closed.
- **The rule.**
  - Every handle is an open, whatever opened it: a file's `OPEN`, a `CREATE` and an `OPENDIR` alike. Until now only
    `OPEN` counted one, so a created file's or a directory's handle left nothing to give back.
  - The image and the delta carry each recorded attachment's open count beside its references. An open takes a
    reference, so more opens than references is a corrupt image, refused.
  - A recovery gives the opens back as restored opens. The release of a handle the successor never issued consumes
    one restored open of its file and attachment, closing it and dropping its reference, while one is left. With none
    left, nothing is given back.
- **Why it never reclaims a file the kernel still holds.** The kernel cannot forget an inode it holds open, so a
  publication that captured an open reference also captured a lookup reference, and that holds the file until the
  kernel's `FORGET`, whichever handle's release consumes a restored open. Restored opens are counts, as references are,
  so it does not matter which handle a release is taken for. That covers three cases:
  - a handle opened after the last publication left nothing in the image, so its release consumes at most a sibling's
    restored open, and all releases together never more than the image restored;
  - the successor's own handle under a reissued value (A-148) balances the same way: two releases give back two opens;
  - a release repeated gives back nothing more.
- **A consequence for A-151.** Restored opens count toward `Volume::is_open`, so a detached base file keeps a descriptor
  the successor reopened for a pre-takeover handle, where before it was closed and the handle refused.
- **Rejected:**
  - restoring the dead daemon's handle table exactly (by value, through anchor RAM): exact, but every `OPEN` and
    `RELEASE` would then write anchor RAM, and nothing observable needs the values once opens are counted;
  - tagging each daemon's handle values with an incarnation, so a successor never reissues one: it tells a reissued
    value apart, but the counts already balance without it.
- **Evidence.** See the bug record's verification.

- **2026-11-07, U10 (the supervisor's option 2): what a successor cannot count is kept until the mount ends.** A handle
  the dead daemon issued after its last publication is in no image, so its successor reclaimed the file when it left the
  namespace, and the handle's next read was refused. Now a volume names the FUSE mounts that survived the takeover at
  recovery (`Volume::settle_recovered_references`'s `held_mounts`, from the server's surviving mount records), and while
  any of them lives, a file made before the takeover (an inode below the volume's counter then, A-150) that leaves the
  namespace with no reference the successor knows is kept as an orphan (`takeover_kept`): charged to the volume's quota,
  so a write past it is refused `NoSpace`, counted in `slates status` (`takeover_kept`), and reclaimed when the last such
  mount ends (`Volume::end_takeover_holder`, from the attachment's end: Linux sends `FUSE_DESTROY` only to fuseblk and
  virtio-fs mounts, so the sweep alone never ran for an ordinary one). A file made after the takeover, and every file outside a takeover, is reclaimed at its
  last close as before. This replaces A-152's "reclaimed at the kernel's forget" for pre-takeover files on a surviving
  mount: the successor cannot know a handle no publication counted is not still open.
  - **2026-11-09, never kept for a mount that forgot it.** A `FORGET` comes only once the kernel holds nothing of the
    inode, no handle included (a handle holds a lookup), so a file whose last reference went back with a mount's
    `FORGET`, live or replayed from the write log, is reclaimed at once unless another mount that survived the takeover
    may still hold it (`Volume::forget_for`, `keeps_for_takeover_besides`). Found by
    `the_lookups_a_dead_daemon_was_given_back_after_its_last_publication_stay_given_back` (a1b44bb1's replayed
    `FORGET`): with the first U10 rule it failed on both Linux arches (diag-bug-sweep-27, run 42515180074), the file kept
    until the mount ended; after, 3 of 3 on adacachy2. A-152's five takeover tests, which end with the kernel's `FORGET`,
    expect the reclaim at the forget again, as they did before U10, and the real-mount release test the bytes back once
    both descriptors close. A file is kept only while the successor cannot know: unlinked while a handle no image
    counted may be open.
  - `a_file_a_handle_no_publication_counted_may_hold_is_kept_until_its_mount_ends` (`crates/bridge-core/tests/
    takeover_release.rs`): the file unlinked after the takeover still read through the uncounted handle, counted kept,
    and reclaimed when the mount ends; a file made after the takeover reclaimed at once.
  - `a_restart_loop_cannot_grow_the_kept_files_past_the_quota`: each takeover keeps one more file, the loop is refused
    `NoSpace` with the volume's bytes never past its quota, and the mount's end frees them all.
  - A-152's five takeover tests now hold the file to the mount's end, each asserting every reference given back first,
    as does the real-mount release test (`the_handles_a_dead_daemon_issued_give_back_their_references_at_release`,
    `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`, Linux), which U10's first commit left expecting the bytes at the last close. Updated to
    the rule, it found that the first commit never freed a kept file at a real unmount: red on both Linux arches
    (`diag-bug-sweep-21`, run 42463819520, 1,048,576 bytes still referenced), where the in-process tests had called the
    sweep directly.
  - Red-checked: with no held mount named, the uncounted handle's file is reclaimed and the loop never meets the quota.

### A-151 — An untouched base file is bound to the disk file it was made from (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.5 (the inode-number rule, the failure matrix, a status note) and A-61 ("What the kernel kept");
- `crates/vfs/src/inode.rs` (`Fingerprint::birth_ns`; `BaseBody::file` and `FileTag`);
- `crates/vfs/src/base.rs` (`prune_unloaded`, `names_another_file`, `release_detached`, `refresh_unloaded`,
  `descriptor`; `Listing::restored`), `base_recovery.rs`, `recover.rs` (image layout 20), and `host/sim.rs` (birth
  times, `replace_file_with_number`, `close_files`, `without_birth_times`);
- `crates/base/src/unix.rs` (`statx` on Linux, `st_birthtime` on macOS) and `windows.rs` (the creation time);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/bridge.rs` (`StaleHandle` answers `ESTALE`);
- the tests:
  - `crates/vfs/tests/base_identity.rs`;
  - `crates/server/tests/nfs_mount.rs` `an_nfs_handle_of_a_base_file_an_outsider_replaced_never_reads_the_new_file`;
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` (the takeover test, now refused `ESTALE`, and its control without a takeover);
  - `crates/bridge-core/tests/invalidation.rs` (a replaced file is a new inode);
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-base-file-opened-before-a-takeover-read-the-file-an-outsider-put-at-its-name.md`.

- **What it answers.** A relist kept an untouched base inode on its file only when the inode was open in this process
  and the descriptor it held named a file other than the listed one; otherwise the inode was refreshed in place onto
  whatever file the name now named, and its next read opened the name with no check. Neither fact survives a daemon,
  and the inode recorded nothing that does. Measured on the box: after a takeover, the successor's relist saw
  `open=false held=false`, refreshed inode 281474976710658 from disk inode 50547211 onto 50547213, and the descriptor
  opened before the takeover read the outsider's bytes. NFS keeps no open state, so its clients met the same refresh
