  with no takeover at all.
- **The rule.** An untouched base inode is bound to the disk file it was made from. When the disk gives the name to
  another file, the name becomes a new entry: the old inode leaves it, open or not, held by its references, and serves
  the file it was made from only through a descriptor it holds; without one it is refused `StaleHandle` (`ESTALE`). A
  replaced file gets a new number, as on a real filesystem; base symlinks have worked this way since 2026-10-08.
  - **The identity** is the device, the inode number and the birth time, digested to 56 bits in seven bytes the base
    body had as padding (`Inode` stays 168 bytes). The birth time is what tells a file from one that took its number:
    ext4 and XFS hand a freed number to the next file, so two editor saves in a row put the first save's number back at
    the name. A held descriptor still decides by device and number, since a number it holds cannot be reused.
  - **A descriptor opened by name** must find the inode's file, else it is closed and refused. That also closes the
    race between a lookup and an open across an outsider's replacement.
  - **Descriptors.** A detached inode that no handle holds open has its descriptor closed at once: nothing reads it
    without opening it again, and that open is refused. So a replaced file the kernel merely caches holds none of the
    host's descriptors until its last reference goes.
  - **A filesystem that records no birth time.** A recovered volume cannot rule out a reused number there, so the first
    listing of each directory it restored gives its untouched entries new numbers, and until then none is opened by
    name. ext4, XFS, btrfs and tmpfs on Linux, APFS and NTFS record one; the box's tmpfs and btrfs report it
    (`stat -c %W`, 2026-10-22).
- **`ESTALE` at the FUSE edge.** `StaleHandle` fell to `EIO` there, against A-61's text and the volume core's own name
  for it. `ESTALE` is what an NFS server answers for a file that is gone, and Linux repeats a path walk that meets it
  with revalidation, so a stale cached name finds the disk's file.
- **Rejected:**
  - publishing open counts with the references (the earlier GAPS note): an `OPEN` is answered before any publication,
    so the count misses opens in that window unless every open is logged; once the descriptor is gone, a count still
    cannot tell that the name was replaced; and NFS keeps no opens;
  - the device and inode number alone: the two-saves reuse passes for the opened file
    (`a_number_the_filesystem_reused_never_passes_for_the_file_a_recovered_handle_opened` is red without the birth
    time);
  - the change time in place of the birth time: an in-place edit, which keeps the file, would renumber it.
- **What it leaves** (GAPS): a pre-takeover handle that A-147 adopted is not counted open; a node id the volume no
  longer holds answers `ENOENT`; recovery refuses an overlay whose loaded base directory changed after its last
  publication.
- **Evidence.** See the bug record's verification.

### A-150 — An inode number goes out only under a published reservation (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- AC-1.6 (its status) and D-4's realized form (§4.5);
- `crates/vfs/src/volume.rs`:
  - `Store::inode_reserve`, `Store::counters_low` and `RESERVE_TOP_UP_SHARE`;
  - `Volume::counter_ceiling`, `recorded_counter` and `unreserved`;
  - `next_no` takes the store;
- `crates/vfs/src/delta.rs` (the delta's roots and its streamed encoding record the ceiling; `mark_published` raises
  it), `recover.rs` (the image and its streamed encoding record it; a rebuild asks for a top-up), `base.rs` and
  `xattr.rs`;
- `crates/bridge-core` (`Bridge::numbers_unreserved`);
- `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/device.rs` (a chain waits for the barrier while numbers are unreserved);
- `crates/server/src/config.rs` (`inode_reserve`, derived), `daemon.rs`, `verbs.rs` (`relieve_deferred` tops up;
  `publish_shard` clears the flag; `numbers_unreserved`), `fuse.rs` and `nfs.rs` (the reply's barrier);
- the tests:
  - `crates/vfs/tests/counter_reserve.rs`;
  - `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` `a_node_id_handed_out_before_a_takeover_never_names_another_file_after_it`;
  - the vfs model oracle, run with a nonzero reserve;
  - the virtio-fs fixtures model a committed publication;
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-takeover-reissued-inode-numbers-the-kernel-still-held.md`.

- **What it answers.** A volume's counter was durable only in a publication, and a successor restored it from the
  last one. `LOOKUP`, `READDIRPLUS` and `OPEN` number base entries and publish nothing, and nothing publishes
  periodically. So the kernel learned numbers no publication recorded, and a successor issued them again.

  A FUSE node id is the inode number with generation 0, as is an NFS file handle's. So a handle opened before a
  takeover named whatever the successor numbered next. Measured on the box: the dead daemon gave `first.txt`
  3659174697238530, the successor gave `second.txt` the same number, and the first file's old descriptor read the
  second file.
- **The rule.** Handing out an inode number is an effect a client keeps across a restart, so it follows D-18: a reply
  that carries a number the committed publication does not reserve waits for the publication that does.
  - A publication records the counter plus the store's reserve, never below the last ceiling. The live ceiling rises
    to that value only when the publication commits (`mark_published`, the bracket A-64's arena capture uses).
  - A number at or past the live ceiling is unreserved. The FUSE reply, the NFS reply and a guest's chain then run the
    owner's barrier first.
  - The per-work hook (`relieve_deferred`) publishes before a unit of work once a volume's reserve falls under half,
    so those barriers are rare. A rebuilt volume asks for that top-up before its first unit of work.
  - A successor restores the counter at the recorded ceiling: it skips at most one reserve of numbers and reuses none.
- **The reserve (R3).** It is derived, and the boot log names it. It is the most numbers one unit of work can issue,
  times the top-up share, so a top-up at half leaves a whole unit reserved. The most is a directory listing filling the
  largest reply a transport serves with its smallest entries: the guest's reply cap over the smallest `fuse_dirent`, or
  the NFS message cap over the smallest `entry3`. That is 262,144 on the box, against 2^47 numbers per volume.

  Windows records no reserve. No transport there hands a client a number it keeps across a restart: there is no host
  mount, and the SDK names files by path.
- **What the first build missed.** The daemon publishes through the streamed encoders (`encode_publication`), not the
  struct builders, and only the builders recorded the ceiling at first. The vfs fixtures run with a reserve of zero,
  where the two counters coincide, so the model oracle's streamed-equals-built check passed. Temporary logging on the
  box showed the successor rebuilding from an image that recorded 2.

  Now both encoders record the ceiling. The model oracle runs with a nonzero reserve and fails when either encoder
  writes the live counter. The reservation model publishes through the streamed path.
- **Rejected:**
  - a barrier on every reply that hands out a number: a publication per `LOOKUP`;
  - refusing past the ceiling: a FUSE `LOOKUP` answered `EAGAIN` reaches the application.
- **Evidence.** See the bug record's verification.

### A-149 — A readiness wait names its own descriptor (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.3 ("Drivers": the readiness seam's status);
- `crates/mem/src/handle.rs` (the interest word beside `Encoded`'s layout; `pack` refuses the marked slots);
- `crates/rt/src/interest.rs` (new: the shard's readiness registrations), `shard.rs` (`register_interest`,
  `take_interest`, `forget_interest`, and one `deliver` for every path that turns a word into a wake; the arena bound),
  `registry.rs` (a same-shard wake delivers), `readiness.rs` (`Ready` answers only for its own registration);
- `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/serve.rs` (the doorbell wait races the shard's requests explicitly);
- the tests:
  - `crates/rt/tests/readiness.rs` (two descriptors raced on the OS driver and on the simulation; a deadline
    raced against a readiness wait);
  - `crates/server/tests/fuse_idle.rs`;
  - `a_revoke_request_ends_a_loop_parked_on_an_idle_guests_doorbell` (`crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/serve.rs`);
  - the interest table's and the layout's unit tests;
- CI (the Miri step runs the simulated race);
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-readiness-wait-took-any-wake-of-its-task-for-its-own.md`.

- **What it answers.** A driver's completion carried the waking task's word and nothing else, so a readiness future,
  once registered, answered ready on any wake of its task.
  - The FUSE serve loop races its device against its change signal. A change made through another mount fired the
    signal; its wake was read as the device's, and the loop read nothing, never drained the signal, and was woken
    again at once. A daemon serving two FUSE mounts of a volume used a whole core from the first write on (397 of
    400 ticks over 4 s, about 92,000 empty wakes every 2 s, measured on Linux 7.2.9).
  - A deadline raced against a bare readiness wait (`futures::within`) could never be reported: the deadline's own
    wake was taken for readiness.
- **The rule.**
  - A registration hands the driver an interest word instead of the task's: the owning shard in the shard field,
    the slot field's top 15 bits marked, then the direction and the descriptor. No task's slot reaches the marked
    range.
  - The shard keeps one record per descriptor and direction: the task waiting, its own token, and whether its
    descriptor fired. A later registration of the key replaces the earlier, as the drivers themselves do, so the
    table never holds more than twice the descriptors the process may open.
  - Every path that turns a word into a wake decodes interest words: both completion harvests, a same-shard wake (the
    simulation's fabric wakes through the registry), and a word from another shard. A readiness future answers ready
    only when its own record fired; a wake from anywhere else leaves it pending.
  - A ready answer that finds nothing to read is still possible (another reader took the data first), so callers
    keep retrying their syscall and awaiting again.
- **What leaned on the old behaviour.** The virtio-fs device loop's doorbell wait was interrupted by a revoke (a
  `detach`, a destroy) or a drain kick (a `snapshot` recall) only because the request's wake passed for a doorbell
  kick. Its wait now races the shard's requests explicitly. Without that, a loop parked on an idle guest's doorbell
  kept serving a detached device until the guest kicked again. The sweep of every other consumer and every stored
  waker found no other: the transport's loops, the deadline races, the rendezvous accept loop and the landing's
  barrier wait each wait on their own state.
- **Rejected:** probing the descriptor with a zero-timeout `poll(2)` on each wake. It attributes as exactly, at one
  syscall per wake on every socket and device; the interest word costs a map lookup.
- **Evidence.**
  - The two OS-driver tests were red before the fix on macOS (kqueue) and Linux (epoll), with `left: Quiet`,
    `right: Signalled`. With a registration counted as fired on any wake (the old behaviour), all three go red again,
    the simulated race included.
  - `fuse_idle` was red ("86 of 100 clock ticks in the 1s after the mounts had served the write") and is green. After
    a write through one of two mounts, the busier shard had used 2 clock ticks in all, over a 6 s trace in which no
    request arrived.
  - The virtio-fs revoke test was red with the runtime fix alone and is green with the explicit race.
  - Miri is clean on the memory and runtime tests CI runs, and on the simulated race.
  - On the box, these suites stay green: the runtime, memory, virtio-fs, client, NFS, FUSE, CLI (51 of 51) and guest
    (3 of 3) suites.

### A-148 — A release frees a handle only of the file it names (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 ("What the kernel kept" across a takeover);
- `crates/bridge-core/src/volume_bridge.rs` (`release` checks the handle's file; `LostWrites` keys issued handles by
  value and file);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/bridge.rs` (`serve_release` and the lost-reply reclaim resolve the node as the open did);
- the tests:
  - `a_release_of_a_reissued_handle_value_never_closes_the_successors_handle_for_another_file`;
  - `a_lost_write_reaches_a_pre_takeover_handle_whose_value_the_successor_reissued`
    (`crates/bridge-core/tests/volume_bridge.rs`);
  - `releasing_the_root_directory_frees_its_handle_round_after_round` (`crates/bridge-fuse/tests/volume_bridge.rs`);
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-after-a-takeover-a-reissued-handle-value-closed-another-files-handle.md`.

- **What it answers.** A mount taken over (A-61) is served with a fresh handle store, which starts at generation 0 as
  its predecessor's did, so it reissues the values its predecessor issued. A release of a handle the kernel opened
  before the takeover could find a handle the successor had since issued for another file, under the same value. It
  closed that one: an unlinked file still open was reclaimed under its handle, and its read answered `NotFound`. The
  same reuse hid a pre-takeover handle's lost-write report, its `fsync` answering success.
- **The rule.** A release frees a handle only when the handle's file is the file the release names; any other value
  is a handle this daemon never issued for that file, released as a no-op, as §4.6 already said. So a release must
  name the node its open resolved: a `RELEASEDIR` of the root (node id 1) names the root's inode. The lost-write record
  knows the successor's handles by value and file.
- **What it leaves.** A pre-takeover handle's release still frees nothing. Its open's reference is durable only once
  published, so the successor cannot tell whether it restored it, and dropping one it did not restore would take a
  lookup reference instead. That is a bounded leak until the mount ends (GAPS).
- **Evidence.**
  - The two seam tests were red (`Err(NotFound)`; `Ok(())` for the report) and are green. The first goes red again
    without the file check.
  - The root-release test is red without the resolve (`EMFILE` at the third open) and green with it.
  - The bridge, NFS, CLI (51 of 51) and guest suites stay green.

### A-147 — A mount taken over by a restarted daemon adopts the files its kernel opened before (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (the write-back rule);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/coherence.rs` (`WritableOpens` keyed by handle and file; `PageStates::adopted`);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs` (`ServeState.adopts_unseen_handles`, `adopt_unseen_handle`, `note_read`,
  `written_handle`; a release names its file);
- the tests:
  - `a_store_made_after_a_refetch_lands_through_a_mount_taken_over_by_a_restarted_daemon` (`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`);
  - the guest takeover test (`crates/cli/tests/guest_dax.rs`);
  - three unit tests in `coherence.rs`;
- GAPS;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-mount-taken-over-by-a-restarted-daemon-dropped-a-store-made-after-a-refetch.md`.

- **What it answers.** A restored mount's byte states began only at writable opens it saw, so a file its kernel opened
  before the takeover stayed untracked. Its re-fetches went unrecorded, and its write-backs were judged against every
  change since the mount's start. A store made after a re-fetch of bytes another path had changed was kept back and
  lost: its `msync` succeeded, and the map showed it. Found by the guest test with a daemon killed under a live DAX map,
  and reproduced without a VM, each 3 of 3.
- **The rule.** On a mount taken over from a daemon that died, a `READ` or `WRITE` that names a handle the mount never
  saw opened adopts the handle and its file:
  - every byte is fresh as of the mount's start;
  - the journal's changes to the file since then are applied;
  - the file is lost (write-backs refused) if the journal no longer reaches back.

  From there the file is judged like one opened on this mount, and forgotten at its last release. A handle is known by
  its value and its file together, since a successor's fresh handle store reissues its predecessor's values.
- **What it leaves.** The start point is the fallback's, the journal head at the mount's first request, so the
  successor's write-log replay (A-63) is not counted against the mount's own writes. Changes the dead daemon made and
  never delivered remain the takeover gap (GAPS).
- **Evidence.** The CLI test was red 3 of 3, is green 3 of 3, and goes red again with adoption turned off. The guest
  takeover test is green across the kill. bridge-fuse's suites, the CLI suite (51 of 51) and the other guest tests stay
  green.

### A-146 — A change drops from a mount's cache only the bytes it touched (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (the cache posture);
- `crates/bridge-core/src/lib.rs` (`CachedBytes`, the type of `Invalidation::Inode`'s `data`);
- `crates/bridge-core/src/volume_bridge.rs` (`journal_bytes`; a directory's and the base plane's invalidations name
  `CachedBytes::ALL`);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs` (`notified_range`, `TO_THE_END`) and `crates/bridge-fuse/src/abi.rs` (a doc line);
- the tests: `a_content_change_owes_its_kernel_the_bytes_it_touched_not_the_whole_file` in
  `crates/bridge-core/tests/invalidation.rs`, whose other expectations now name exact ranges too, and
  `a_change_through_another_path_drops_only_the_pages_it_changed` in `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/coherence_mount.rs`;
- `virtiofs.md` §8 item 7 (the crosvm run that found it), `BENCHMARKS.md` (the A/B), GAPS.

- **What it answers.** Every content change through another path was sent to each mount as
  `FUSE_NOTIFY_INVAL_INODE` for the whole file. The kernel dropped every cached page of the file, after writing back
  every dirty one. A guest's DAX map of a file shared through the mount lives in that cache, so one changed byte made
  the guest re-fetch all of it. Found running a real guest under crosvm over a slates mount: with a 128 MiB map, the
  guest's next scan after each one-byte change took a median of 273 ms, against 0.2–0.3 ms warm.
- **The rule.** An invalidation names the bytes the change touched:
  - an overwrite, or bytes appended past the end: exactly those bytes;
  - a truncate: everything from its new length;
  - an insert or a delete: everything from its point, since the rest shifts;
  - a metadata change: no bytes;
  - a directory's listing, a base witness or drift, and an overrun: the whole file, having no byte range.

  The FUSE transport hands the kernel that range as `off` and `len`, and the kernel drops the pages holding it, a whole
  folio at a time. A range the ABI's signed offsets cannot express is sent as the rest of the file from where it can
  still be named; dropping more is never stale.
- **Why it is safe.** The write-back rule (A-140, A-144) judges each byte against the journal's records, never against
  what an invalidation laundered. A dirty page outside a changed range keeps its bytes and is judged when it is written
  back. Both real-mount chaos tests pass unchanged.
- **Evidence.** The real-mount test: before, the untouched middle block lost 512 of its 512 pages; after, none. The
  A/B in `BENCHMARKS.md`: the scan after a change went from a median of 273 ms to 0.45 ms, with the cold scan
  unchanged.

### A-145 — The anchor starts and restarts its own image, never a path (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §2.6 (status note);
- `crates/anchor/src/supervise.rs` (`Supervisor::new` takes no program; `own_image`'s paired `identity` and `command`);
- `crates/anchor/src/error.rs` (`OwnExecutable`, `ExecutableReplaced`);
- `crates/cli/src/anchor.rs`;
- `crates/cli/src/daemon.rs` (`name_this_process`);
- the tests: `crates/anchor/tests/anchor.rs`, and the new
  `a_daemon_killed_after_its_anchors_executable_is_replaced_restarts_from_the_anchors_own_image` in
  `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`;
- GAPS (the 2026-10-21 tripwire);
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-an-anchor-restarted-its-daemon-by-a-path-an-upgrade-can-replace.md`.

- **What it answers.** The supervisor ran `Command::new(path)` at every start, the path taken once from
  `current_exe()`. After an upgrade in place, a daemon killed or crashed was restarted from the new file, or refused
  `ENOENT`.
  - **By hand, on the box:** an anchor whose binary copy was deleted printed `daemon spawn refused (code Some(2))` at
    the restart and exited, ending the instance.
  - **The red test:** an anchor whose link was replaced by a script restarted the script into a crash loop, and no
    daemon answered within 20 s.

  This is the 2026-10-21 tripwire's message. Whether it was that event's trigger is not shown.
- **The rule.** A supervisor's daemons run its own executable, and each start runs the image it runs.
  - **Linux:** `/proc/self/exe`, with `argv[0]` the path, and the daemon renames itself, since the kernel would name it
    `exe`.
  - **The other Unix systems:** the path, only while its device and inode are the ones recorded when the supervisor
    was made. Otherwise the start is refused `ExecutableReplaced`, and the anchor ends saying so. A replacement inside
    the check-to-spawn window is not caught.
  - **Windows:** owed. A running file there can only be renamed aside, and std has no stable file identity.
- **Evidence:** the red test above, green after the change. Verification is in the bug record.

### A-144 — A READ through an `O_DIRECT` handle is ambiguous, and a write-back over what it left unknown is refused (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6 (the cache posture's write-back rule);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/request.rs` (`ReadIn::flags`, the handle's open flags from `fuse_read_in`);
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/coherence.rs`:
  - the byte state is three-way (`Byte`: fresh, stale, unknown);
  - `PageStates::read_ambiguously`;
  - `stale_after` answers `None` over an unknown byte;
  - the oracle's model and a case-by-case test;
- `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs` (the READ arm, `may_bypass_the_cache`, and `pending_changes`, shared with the
  write-back judgment);
- the tests:
  - `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/coherence_mount.rs`: `a_direct_read_does_not_make_a_cached_page_fresh`, and the
    harness asks that hold the mount's rounds;
  - `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/common/mod.rs`: `FailingGather` forwards the rule's inputs;
  - the ABI and codec vectors;
- GAPS ("`O_DIRECT` reads");
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-direct-read-made-a-stale-cached-page-fresh.md`.

- **What it answers.** A-140 counted every READ of a file open for writing as a fetch, making its bytes fresh at the
  head. A direct READ is answered from the volume and leaves the kernel's cached page as it was. One direct read of a
  page another path had just changed therefore marked the stale cached copy fresh. A store into that copy was then
  written back, and the write-back was applied whole, reverting all 4,096 bytes of the other path's acknowledged write.
  Reproduced on the box (kernel 7.2.9), 3 of 3, against the same steps without the direct read, which kept the stale
  bytes back.
- **The rule.** A READ through a handle whose open flags carry `O_DIRECT` (or a body too old to carry flags) is
  **ambiguous**: it is a direct read or a fill of the kernel's copy (a fault on a map of the handle, a buffered
  fallback), and nothing on the wire tells which.
  - Bytes fresh after the records not yet consumed are fresh either way, and stay so.
  - Every other byte it covers becomes **unknown** as of the read's head.
  - A fetch, or the mount's own later record, makes an unknown byte fresh. Another path's later record makes it stale,
    as both readings are then.
  - A write-back over an unknown byte is refused `EIO`, as one the states cannot tell. It is loud: neither reading
    may be guessed.

  "Always a fetch" silently undid another path's write. "Never a fetch" would silently keep back a process's real
  store into a page it had just filled.
- **Evidence.**
  - The mount test is red before the change: all 4,096 bytes reverted, 3 of 3. After it, the write-back is refused and
    the replacement survives.
  - The oracle's three-way model, with generated ambiguous reads, fails when the read is counted as a fetch.
  - On the way, the in-process harness was found never to have run A-140: its wrapping bridge did not forward
    `data_changes` or `journal_capacity`, so every map write-back there was refused unknown.
  - **Chaos over a real mount** (`generated_map_stores_direct_reads_and_other_writes_never_revert_another_paths_write`,
    added after). It runs three seeds of 80 steps over a three-page shared map: stores, the mount's own `pwrite`s,
    another attachment's runs, direct and buffered reads, and rounds held and released. After every sync, each byte
    must hold the other path's latest write or a mount write made after it. On the box it is green 3 of 3, and every
    seed exercises both outcomes: 55–346 bytes kept back, and 1–2 write-backs refused unknown.
  - **Red-checked by mutation.** With A-144 reverted, a byte read the file's original value although the other path
    had written it ten steps before (step 56). With A-140's keep-back removed, that happened at step 23.

### A-143 — A client judges the daemon that answered its claim (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.7 (the liveness status) and A-114;
- `crates/ipc/src/rendezvous.rs`, the macOS and Windows module:
  - the claim slot's answering-daemon stamp and pid (`AT_ANSWERED_STAMP`, `AT_ANSWERED_PID`);
  - `write_answerer` and `read_answerer`;
  - `Listener::stamp`;
  - `Claim` keeps no stamp;
  - `open_bootstrap`;
- `crates/ipc/tests/rendezvous.rs` (one test, and a child role);
- GAPS §8a-sdk-stamp;
- `docs/bugs/2026-10-22-a-client-whose-claim-crossed-a-restart-judged-the-live-daemon-gone.md`.

- **What it answers.** On macOS and Windows a client tells a dead daemon from a slow one by the bootstrap header's
  start stamp and the daemon's process. It recorded the stamp when its claim *began*, and took the process from the
  header when the claim *completed*. Since A-114 a claim that begins during a restart is answered by the next daemon.
  That client therefore held the dead daemon's stamp and the live daemon's process. The first reply that stalled
  afterwards read "gone", so a call to a live, silent daemon ended `DaemonGone` after the reconnect budget instead
  of `Stalled`.

  The process had the mirror race. An answering daemon that died before its answer was read left the client
  watching its successor's process while holding the dead daemon's region, so every call would have stalled and
  the client would never have reconnected.
- **The rule.** The daemon names itself in its answer: its start stamp and its process id, written into the claim
  slot's spare bytes while it holds the slot `ANSWERING`, and published with `READY`. The client builds its
  liveness from those, never from the header. An answer whose stamp is zero names no daemon (a daemon of another
  version, against `docs/publish.md`'s one version), and it is refused `Layout` after its slot is freed.

  Linux needs no change: its liveness is the peer of the connection the daemon accepted.
- **Evidence.**
  - **By use, on macOS.** The SDK over a real anchor and daemon. Stop the anchor, kill the daemon, call; resume the
    anchor; then stop the new daemon and call again. Before: `DaemonGone` 3 of 3. After: `Stalled` 3 of 3. Without
    the anchor stop the result was `Stalled` 3 of 3 both times.
  - **Root cause, logged.** A claim that began on stamp `…213142448000` was answered while `…215559132000` was
    published.
  - **The red test.** `a_claim_begun_before_a_restart_judges_the_daemon_that_answered_it_alive` fails on macOS
    before the change and passes after. It passes on Linux, whose code this change does not touch.

### A-142 — One notify thread per FUSE mount, not one per invalidation round (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the 2026-10-17 amendment's notify thread); `crates/bridge-fuse/src/channel.rs`
(`Notifier` replaces `NotifyThread`; `Round`, `Outcome`, `write_round`; `ServeState::notifier`; `deliver_owed`; two
tests); `crates/cli/examples/write_round_ab.rs` (new); `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`.
- **Changes the 2026-10-17 amendment.** A mount's invalidation rounds are still written off the serving thread, one
  round at a time, with the cursor put back on a refused write. What changes is the thread. One is started with the
  mount's first round and kept: rounds reach it over a channel of one, and outcomes come back over a channel of one.
  Dropping the notifier closes the channel and joins the thread after the round in flight. It used to be a new
  thread for every round, started on the owner's shard.
- **Why.** Every change made through another path runs a round on each mount of the volume, so the shard paid a thread
  start (p50 16–20 µs on the box) per change per mount, and the next request waited behind it. Through the
  optimization hierarchy: the thread is needed; one per round is more than needed.
- **Evidence (measured, `BENCHMARKS.md`).** The bare-metal box, interleaved builds differing in this file alone, 12
  phases each: a mounted volume's SDK write p90 fell from a median of 23.3 µs to 15.1 µs, against 13.3 µs with no
  mount. The p50 does not move, since the writer is answered before the round runs.
- **Proven.**
  - A round whose write blocks leaves the owner free, and a second round goes through the same thread. Red-checked:
    joining the thread after each round fails the second hand-off, with `EIO`.
  - A notifier dropped with a round out returns, its thread joined.
  - Regression on the box: workspace clippy and the doc gate clean; `coherence_mount`, `owner_turn`, the CLI map,
    truncation and eviction tests, `fuse_mount` (3 of 3) and recovery (41 of 41) green.
- **Bounds.** One thread per mount, idle in its channel between rounds, and at most one round and one outcome in
  flight: the same peak as before.

### A-141 — A mount that falls behind the journal is told everything, and drops what its kernel holds (accepted 2026-10-22)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (cache posture); `crates/bridge-core` (`Invalidation::Everything`; the overrun
check in `VolumeBridge::invalidations`; `ScopedBridge` passes it through); `crates/bridge-fuse` (`coherence.rs`
`KernelHolds`; `bridge.rs` `KernelChange`/`kernel_changes`; `channel.rs`: the holdings fed as each reply reaches the
kernel, an `Everything` expanded in the round, `fuse.journal_overruns`); `crates/server/src/fuse.rs` (the counter);
tests in `bridge-core/tests/invalidation.rs`, `bridge-fuse/tests/kernel_changes.rs` and `coherence_mount.rs`, and
`cli/tests/cli.rs`; GAPS; the bug record.
- **Changes §4.6.** The journal keeps a bounded share of the quota. A mount whose cursor has fallen behind its
  retention can no longer be told which names, attributes and pages changed. Walking from the oldest record still held
  skipped the rest, and the kernel kept serving them. The gather now reports an overrun, `Invalidation::Everything`,
  and the mount invalidates everything its kernel holds, then resumes from the head:
  - every node it references, with an attribute-and-data invalidation, and the root;
  - every name it holds, with an entry invalidation, expire-only where negotiated.

  The mount knows what its kernel holds by following the FUSE lookup protocol as each reply reaches the kernel:
  - entry replies add a lookup and a name, and `FORGET` gives lookups back;
  - its own unlinks and renames take names away or move them;
  - an invalidation of a name takes it away, since a later use is a new lookup.
- **Why writers never wait instead** (the alternative weighed in the bug record). Holding the journal for a lagging
  mount would make writers wait on mounts. That is the AC-3.3 machinery, and a mount whose round is blocked in its
  kernel would hold every writer behind it. (Since A-191 a writer outside FUSE does wait, for each mount's told point
  rather than the journal, and at most half the liveness budget, so a blocked round holds a writer only that long; the
  journal's retention is unchanged.) Pushing changes to each mount as they are journaled would keep a second
  record of every change beside the journal. An overrun costs one burst of notifications and a cold kernel cache, and
  only when the bound is reached.
- **Evidence.** One SDK client pipelining a ring of writes onto a volume with a one-page journal left a FUSE mount
  serving an acknowledged write's old bytes for 10 s, 2 runs of 33. A trace showed the change's records evicted before
  the mount's gather ("since 7, oldest 16").
- **Proven.** See the bug record's verification.
- **What it does not change.** Rounds within retention, the byte states (an overrun already loses them: A-140 refuses
  their write-backs `EIO`), and the journal's budget, which stays as the ledger records it.

### A-140 — A cache write-back is judged by byte states the mount keeps as it consumes the journal (accepted 2026-10-22)
> Its masked apply superseded 2026-11-07 by A-248 (Ada's decision, "Refuse, like NFS"): a stale write-back whose stale
> bytes differ from the file's is now refused whole, `EIO`. The byte states below, and how they are fed, stand.

Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (cache posture); A-139 (its basis superseded); `crates/bridge-core`
(`changed.rs` `DataChange`/`data_change`; `Bridge::data_changes` replaces `Bridge::changed_since`; `volume_bridge.rs`,
`scoped.rs`; `tests/data_changes.rs` replaces `tests/changed_since.rs`); `crates/bridge-fuse` (`coherence.rs`
`PageStates` replaces `FetchPoints`, `OwnRecords::took`; `channel.rs`: the states fed at each round's gather, at the
mount's own requests and at reads, and judged at write-back); `crates/server/src/fuse.rs` (the two counters' meaning);
`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` (two tests); GAPS; the bug record; `docs/wip/virtiofs.md` §8 item 7.
- **Changes §4.6 and A-139's basis.** For each file open for writing on a mount, the mount keeps, for every byte, the
  journal point its kernel's copy is as of and whether another path changed it since. A fetch makes its bytes fresh at
  the head. The mount's own record refreshes the bytes fetched before it, and another path's record marks them stale.
  The states are fed from the records the mount's invalidation rounds already walk, so no record older than the
  mount's cursor is ever needed. Once every record through the cursor is consumed, the points at or below it can no
  longer be told apart by any record to come; they are raised to it, which merges the ranges they split. A write-back
  is judged by the states within it, plus the few records after the cursor applied to a scratch copy. A file whose
  states would need more ranges than the journal's capacity is lost, and so is every file when the mount falls behind
  the journal's retention. A lost file's write-backs are refused `EIO`, counted, until its last writable release.
- **Why A-139's walk was replaced (measured-and-rejected).** A-139 walked the journal back from each page's fetch
  point. The journal keeps a 10‰ share of the quota, about 850 records for an 8 MiB volume, and a long-lived map has
  an old fetch point. That is exactly what DAX keeps. `a_long_lived_maps_write_back_survives_unrelated_activity_past_the_journal`
  (a store, 2,000 SDK writes to another file, then `msync`) failed 2 runs of 3 on A-139, `msync` answering `EIO`.
- **Why the raise.** Every fetch is stamped with the head at that moment, so a map faulted in a page at a time while
  the volume is busy would keep one range per page. The bound on ranges would then refuse it, which is the DAX case
  again. The raise is exact: a record still to come is later than the cursor, so it treats every point at or below
  the cursor alike.
- **Why a fetch and an own write may reset bytes, and nothing else.** Linux 6.12 keeps each write-back in the inode's
  in-flight tree until the daemon answers it (`fs/fuse/file.c:2124`, removed at `:1931`). A cache read (`:872`,
  readahead page by page at `:1020`) and a write (`:1141`) wait on that tree before they are sent, so no older copy of
  their pages can arrive after them. The end of an invalidation round resets nothing: a write-back copied out before
  it can still be in flight (A-139's evidence).
- **Proven.** See the bug record's verification.
- **What it does not change.** The write-back's routing, the masked apply and the write log's applied parts, the first
  writable open's cache drop, the residual race (AC-3.3; narrowed by A-191 to a store concurrent with another path's
  call), and every other transport.
- **Owed, stated in the ledger.**
  - A mount restored across a daemon restart has files whose opens predate the daemon. They have no states and are
    judged from the mount's start against every record since, as under A-139, so a long-lived one is refused past
    the journal's retention.
  - `O_DIRECT` reads were found by reading the source on 2026-10-22, not reproduced. On the wire a direct READ looks
    like a cache READ, but it leaves the cached page in place. Counting it as a fetch can therefore clear a staleness
    that page still holds, in the window before the round's invalidation reaches the kernel. This has been present
    since A-139.

### A-139 — A cache write-back is applied only where it is not stale, judged by its page's fetch (accepted 2026-10-21)
> Basis superseded 2026-10-22 by A-140: the walk back from each page's fetch point below needed records the journal no
> longer held for a long-lived map (2 runs of 3 refused `EIO`, measured). The rule itself superseded 2026-11-07 by A-248
> (Ada's decision, "Refuse, like NFS"): a write-back is no longer applied outside its stale bytes but refused whole. The
> evidence of the bug stands.

Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (cache posture); `crates/bridge-core` (`changed.rs`, `Bridge::changed_since`,
`Bridge::journal_capacity`); `crates/vfs/src/journal.rs` (`OpLog::oldest_seq`, `OpLog::capacity`); `crates/bridge-fuse`
(`coherence.rs` `OwnRecords`/`WritableOpens`/`FetchPoints`, `channel.rs`, `bridge.rs`, `request.rs`, `abi.rs`);
`crates/server/src/fuse.rs` (the write log's applied parts, two counters); `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`; GAPS; the bug
record.
- **Changes §4.6.** A FUSE `WRITE` carrying `FUSE_WRITE_CACHE` is the kernel's cached copy of a page coming back. It is
  applied except over the bytes another path changed after the page's fetch (the journal walked from the page's fetch
  point, the mount's own records since excepted), and answered whole. A file's first writable open on a mount drops
  the kernel's cache of it. Where the journal no longer holds the changes since a page's fetch, the write-back is
  refused `EIO` and counted.
- **Evidence.**
  - The bug (`docs/bugs/2026-10-21-a-dirty-shared-map-page-overwrites-a-later-write-through-another-path.md`):
    measured 2026-10-21, a dirty map page's write-back reverted 4,095 of 4,096 bytes of a later SDK replacement on
    Linux, and 16,383 of 16,384 on macOS.
  - The mechanism, in Linux 6.12's source: an invalidation launders dirty pages (`mm/truncate.c:651`,
    `fs/fuse/file.c:2477`).
  - Why rounds cannot judge it: FUSE writes back from a temporary copy and ends the page's write-back at once
    (`fs/fuse/file.c:2092`), so a stale copy reaches the daemon after the round that should have covered it. The
    round-based mask was built first and still failed 9 of 10 runs; it is kept on record as measured-and-rejected in
    the bug record.
- **Proven.** See the bug record's verification: the failing test red with the rule disabled and green with it, the
  shrink test, the unsynced chaos history, the walk's and the fetch points' oracles (each red-checked), and by-use
  tests of the walk (`Unknown` past eviction included) and of the FUSE side.
- **What it does not change.** Invalidation delivery; `write(2)` through a FUSE mount, which is write-through and never
  masked; and any other transport. macOS NFS v3 cannot carry it, since it has no write-back mark and no callback: open
  in the ledger.
- **Residual, stated.** A store into the very bytes another path is changing, made after its page's fetch and before
  the change is delivered, is kept back: two writers racing on the same bytes. Since A-191 a writer that holds no
  kernel lock returns only after every mount was told, so a store made after its call returned lands on the new page;
  only a store concurrent with the call, or with a write through another FUSE mount, still races.

### A-138 — A guest's DAX window is handed out as a descriptor covering only that window (accepted 2026-10-19)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (DAX), `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/udmabuf.rs` (new), `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/device.rs`, `crates/mem/src/shared.rs`, `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`, `unsafe-budget.toml`, GAPS (gate row 1), `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-the-message-based-dax-map-hands-the-vmm-the-whole-arena.md`.
- Changes §4.6: the message-based DAX placer narrows the arena's descriptor to the authorized window with a Linux `udmabuf` before sending it. `fd_offset`/`len` scoped the request; now they scope the descriptor too. The fd-sharing placer maps in-process and hands out nothing, so it is unchanged.
- Why: `Store::dax_backing` handed the front end the arena's whole shared object — measured 64× the authorized window, with another tenant's blocks inside it. Three options were on record and each gave something up (a per-tenant backing cuts against A-64; a per-mapping copy is the view arm measured and rejected at slope 1.0; fd-sharing-only forfeits the crosvm route). `UDMABUF_CREATE` is a fourth that gives up none of them: it returns a descriptor over a memfd range, pinning the existing pages rather than copying, so confinement, zero-copy and A-64's layout all hold.
- Evidence: proven before it was built, unprivileged on Fedora 6.19 — the window maps its own bytes and refuses both the whole object and any offset past itself, survives `SCM_RIGHTS` to another process, takes `MAP_FIXED` into a VMM-reserved region with the hole restorable afterwards, and a write through it reaches the arena's pages. Then in-tree: the SETUPMAPPING test maps what the front end was sent and asserts one byte past the window is unmappable, red-checked by handing back the arena descriptor (it fails on exactly that assertion).
- Consequences: `slates-mem` creates every shared object with `ALLOW_SEALING` and `F_SEAL_SHRINK`, which `UDMABUF_CREATE` requires — nothing in slates shrinks an object, so the seal costs nothing today and binds the future not to. A host without `/dev/udmabuf` gets a **refusal**, never the wide descriptor; the device is not a privilege under R10 (it is the one the VMM already uses) but DAX over the message-based placer now follows host configuration. `slates-bridge-virtiofs`'s unsafe budget rises 3 → 5 for the ioctl and the descriptor it returns.
- What it does not change: the fd-sharing placer, the arena's layout (A-64), the pin/revoke discipline, or the advertisement gate — DAX stays behind `DaxNotEstablished`, and the live crosvm leg is still owed.

### A-137 — A lookup miss is `ENOENT` again: a negative entry's invalidation is not proven (accepted 2026-10-19)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (cache posture), `crates/bridge-fuse/src/bridge.rs`, `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/dispatch.rs`, BENCHMARKS.md (c3c0024b's table), GAPS, `docs/bugs/2026-10-19-linux-6-19-refuses-the-entry-invalidation-slates-swallows.md`.
- Changes §4.6: a lookup miss is answered `ENOENT` and is no longer a cached negative entry (node id 0 with the directory's lifetime), which it had been since `c3c0024b`. Positive entries, attributes, pages and listings are unchanged.
- Evidence: Linux 6.19.10 refuses `FUSE_NOTIFY_INVAL_ENTRY` for a negative dentry with `ENOENT` and goes on answering from it, so a name another attachment creates is never seen through the mount; the same code passes on 6.12 (x86_64 userspace on both, so not an architecture difference). Six causes were eliminated by measurement first, including a true drop rather than an expire, and an invalidation of the parent inode — no notification clears it. A runtime degrade cannot rescue it either: by the time a refusal is observed the kernel already holds the entry with an unbounded lifetime.
- Why the rule decides it rather than a preference: §4.6 already required "proven invalidation delivery" for an infinite lifetime, and delivery for this case is now disproven on a shipping kernel. R4 does not allow the cost to be weighed against it.
- Cost, measured: five interpreter starts over a mount (a workload built of repeated misses) cost 273 daemon reads with the negative entries and 310 without — **+14%**, two interleaved rounds, non-overlapping, Fedora 6.19, 2026-10-19. The earlier −28% figure covered negative entries, kept pages and listings together; the other two are untouched.
- Proven: `coherence_mount` and `owner_turn` go from red to green on 6.19, with `fuse_mount` 3, `nfs_mount` 38, `cli` 33 and the bridge-fuse lib 13 unchanged.
- What it does not change: the `Invalidated` posture itself, the invalidation machinery, or any other transport (a virtio-fs guest already got lifetime 0).

### A-136 — Linux runs on epoll; the io_uring driver is removed (accepted 2026-10-18)
Applied in the same change to: D-9 (decision text and evidence tier), §4.3 (Drivers, Loop, the readiness follow-up, the 2026-09-19 driver-retirement follow-up), `crates/rt` (`driver.rs`, `lib.rs`, `epoll.rs`, `readiness.rs`, `tests/reclaim.rs`, `Cargo.toml`), the workspace `Cargo.toml`, `unsafe-budget.toml` (slates-rt 75 → 73), `docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md` (the A/B that decided it).
- **What changed.** `os_driver` on Linux now builds the epoll driver unconditionally; `DriverKind::IoUring`, the probe, the per-shard ring build and `crates/rt/src/uring.rs` are gone, as is the `io-uring` dependency. Removed rather than demoted behind a flag: banned item 7 is replace, do not layer, and a dormant second driver is exactly the "just in case" path that rule forbids.
- **Why — what it bought, measured for the first time.** D-9 had chosen io_uring citing `DEFER_TASKRUN`+`SINGLE_ISSUER` "for jitter" at evidence tier B, with no number anywhere in the project. The A/B (two binaries differing in one line, interleaved, each arm verified by descriptor) found the win real but confined: **io_uring +13% at the parked p50** (65.4 vs 73.9 µs) and +9% at the parked p99, against **epoll +23% at the 8-client spinning p99** (1.56 vs 2.02 ms) — and the spinning path is the one R9's sub-50 µs gate measures. slates only ever issued two opcodes through a ring, `PollAdd` and `Nop`, which is epoll's job.
- **Why — what it cost.** (1) Attack surface: io_uring is ~60% of Google's kernel VRP submissions, disabled in ChromeOS, restricted on Android, removed from their production servers; openSUSE ships `kernel.io_uring_disabled=2`; Docker and containerd dropped it from their default seccomp profiles — so a growing share of deployments ran the *less*-exercised driver anyway. (2) A real liveness bug: rings are locked memory, so a host near `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` (default 8 MiB) ran out partway through a many-shard start and `io_uring_setup` returned `ENOMEM`, failing the shard and with it the daemon. That is what made the Linux recovery oracle fail a random, differing subset of its tests on roughly every other run — clean source and modified source alike, which is why it read as load for so long.
- **What it does not change.** kqueue, IOCP and the simulation driver are untouched; the `Driver` seam, its paired-`#[cfg]` shape and every readiness contract are the same. The one Linux driver still carries `register_readable`/`register_writable` (the trait's doc had gone stale claiming the completion-native drivers refused them; corrected in the same pass).
- **Evidence:** `BENCHMARKS.md` "io_uring against epoll on Linux" (2026-10-18, 32-core cachyos, interleaved, arms verified by descriptor; the box was loaded 13→29 so only the p50 rows carry signal, and a quiesced re-run is owed to tighten the parked figure — it does not change the direction). Verified after removal: the daemon holds `eventpoll=4, io_uring=0` for 4 shards; `slates-rt` suites green; the recovery oracle 41/41 on four consecutive runs where it had been failing a differing subset every other run.

### A-229 — The macOS NFS mount is hard, so a writer waits under backpressure (accepted 2026-11-06, Ada's choice)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (macOS fallback options, failure matrix), T-4.5, `crates/bridge-nfs/src/client.rs`
(`MountArgs` clears `NFS_MFLAG_SOFT`), `crates/cli/src/mount.rs` and `crates/cli/examples/slates_mount.rs` (the
`mount_nfs` options), `crates/cli/tests/live_fleet.rs`, GAPS.
- **Changes §4.6:** the loopback NFS mount was `soft,intr`; it is `hard,intr`.
- **Why:** A-200 says holders that do not answer make the writer wait: backpressure, never a false success. On a soft
  mount macOS's own NFS client ends any call it has waited on for about a minute, whether the daemon holds the reply
  or answers `NFS3ERR_JUKEBOX`, so no daemon design can keep a writer waiting there. Measured: with both candidates of a
  live-shipped volume stopped, a size change through the mount failed `ETIMEDOUT` after 57.2 s (57.1 s in conformance's
  run); hard, the same call waited through the stop and succeeded once the candidates resumed (90.6 s and 102.4 s, the
  candidates resumed at 75 s; `a_writer_on_a_macos_mount_waits_for_stopped_candidates_rather_than_fail`).
- **What keeps it escapable:** `intr` lets a signal end a waiting caller (`EINTR`), and a forced unmount ends a mount
  whose daemon is gone. Since A-113 the anchor holds the listener and every accepted connection across a daemon restart,
  so a restart is a slow reply, which a hard mount waits through where a soft one failed it.
- **Cost:** a mount whose anchor is gone for good blocks the programs touching it until they are signalled or the mount
  is force-unmounted. Tests unmount (forced if refused) before they stop any daemon (`MountPoint`, `KernelMount`).
- **What it does not change:** Linux's mounts (FUSE; conformance's own NFS options), Windows, or the daemon's answers:
  a stable reply still waits for durability up to the liveness budget and is then answered "try again", which the hard
  mount retries.

### A-258 — A handshake gives up on time, not on a peer's resends; a dialer past its confirmation redials at once; an accepting end that abandons says so, sealed (accepted 2026-11-08)

The fleet formed in 40 to 72 s instead of about a second on a loaded machine (load 127–244). Per-reason counters caught
one of those formations (41.9 s, load about 170): an accepting end gave up its half of a handshake on the dialer's
resends (`fleet.accept.stall.repeats`), and the dialer, already past its own side of TLS, waited out its confirmation
deadline twice before it dialed afresh (`fleet.dial.stall.confirm_deadline`, then `fleet.dial.redial`).

- **Repeats are bounded by time.** A resend of a flight this end has already answered is load's to spend: a dialer
  slow to read the reply keeps resending, and each fragment of a resent flight counted as a repeat. So the accepting end
  gave up on a live dialer within a second or two. A turn now gives up on repeats only at its derived deadline (33 × the
  initial probe timeout, about 22 s). It answers them at its own backoff, and counts a resent flight once however many
  fragments it spans (`Reassembly::RepeatRest`). `MAX_HANDSHAKE_RETRANSMITS` now bounds only waits paced by this end's
  own timer.
- **A dialer past its confirmation redials at once.** The second handshake budget on a socket
  (`ESTABLISH_BUDGETS_BEFORE_REDIAL`, 2026-09-14) is for a peer that has not answered: one booting, or starved. A dialer
  waiting on its confirmation has heard from its peer, and its peer's half is what is gone, so a second budget there
  was 22 s more waiting on nothing (`fleet::keeps_its_socket`).
- **An accepting end that abandons tells its dialer** (RFC 9000 §10.2.3, a SHOULD), in a close sealed under the
  Handshake keys (`flight::SEALED_CLOSE_TAG`). The dialer then ends `PeerClosed` and redials within a round trip
  instead of waiting out its deadline. It is sent only once the accepting end holds those keys; before that it has
  answered nothing, and the dialer is still in its first budget, where waiting is right.
  - **Why not the unprotected Initial-level close.** The RFC has a server also send its close in an Initial packet,
    for a client that may not have the Handshake keys yet. In this dialect anyone who can send to a dialer's port could
    forge one and cost the dialer its socket and a fresh dial. A dialer past the point where a close helps it holds the
    Handshake keys already, since it has read the accepting end's sealed flight. So the close is sealed, and a dialer
    ignores any close that does not open under those keys.
  - Within the anti-amplification limit (RFC 9000 §8.1, which has no exemption for a close): the close is 22 bytes,
    against an allowance of three times a received client flight of at least 1,200 bytes.
  - A dialer sends no close: it may still retry on its socket.

Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/transport/src/endpoint.rs`: `HandshakeStall`, `handshake_stall`, `handshake_deadline`, the repeat handling
  in `receive_flight`, `close_abandoned_handshake`, `is_peer_close`, `closes_sent`, and `EndpointError::PeerClosed`.
- `crates/transport/src/flight.rs`: `Reassembly::RepeatRest`, `SEALED_CLOSE_TAG`, `seal_close`, `open_close`.
- `crates/server/src/fleet.rs`: `keeps_its_socket`, and the `fleet.dial.stall.<reason>`, `fleet.accept.stall.<reason>`
  and `fleet.dial.fault.<kind>` counters, `peer_closed` among them.
- Bug record `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-an-accepting-end-gave-up-on-repeats-and-its-dialer-waited-out-two-deadlines.md`;
  GAPS's formation entry.
- Tests, each red-checked: `an_accepted_handshake_is_not_given_up_for_a_dialers_repeats`,
  `a_dialer_that_only_repeats_is_given_up_at_the_handshakes_deadline`, `a_dialer_past_its_confirmation_redials_at_once`,
  `a_dialer_hears_its_peer_abandon_the_handshake_within_a_round_trip` (red with no close sent),
  `a_dialer_ignores_a_close_no_one_sealed` (red with a dialer that believed any close-shaped datagram), and the sealed
  close's hostile-input tests in `flight.rs`.


### A-261 — Stateless reset: a node restarted under its identity ends its peers' old sessions within a round trip (accepted 2026-11-08)

On loadtest-scale's f = 1 primary-kill rung (2026-11-08), a primary restarted under the same member id. The client
node's record session to it stayed in its slot, lent and dead, for 25 to 135 s: nothing told the client node that the
process at the other end no longer held the session. The transport had no stateless reset (RFC 9000 §10.3). A
restarted node's demultiplexer dropped every packet naming a session it did not hold, counted (`unknown_id`) and
otherwise silent.

- **The key** is HKDF-SHA256 over the node's identity's private key, salted and labelled for this use alone
  (`reset::ResetKey`, `Identity::reset_key`). It is secret because only the node holds that key. It is never derived
  from the certificate: every peer sees the certificate, so a key derived from it would let any peer forge a reset and
  end any session.
  - **The same identity must make the same tokens.** A restarted process holds no state for its old sessions. To end
    them it has to recompute their tokens from what survives the restart, which is the identity and not the boot
    (§10.3.2: "an endpoint that loses state can use the same method to generate a valid stateless reset token").
  - **A new identity must not.** It is another node, and a node that could end another node's sessions could end
    anyone's.
- **The token** is HMAC-SHA256 of the session's connection id under that key, truncated to 16 bytes (§10.3.2). Each
  session has one id, which both ends derive from the TLS exporter and which never changes. So each session has one
  token, and connection ids (NEW_CONNECTION_ID, §19.15) are not needed first.
- **Each end issues a token, and only inside the encrypted session.**
  - It sends a `ResetToken` frame (kind 12) once the session's id is bound. The frame is ack-eliciting and retransmitted
    until acknowledged.
  - A token is unforgeable only because it never travels outside the encrypted session. So an end takes its peer's
    token only from that frame. A second token unlike the first is a protocol violation: it is counted, and the first
    token is kept.
  - It is not a transport parameter, as §18.2's server token is: the id comes from the exporter, which exists only once
    the handshake is done.
  - The accepting end's token is the one that matters: its address outlives its restart. A restarted dialer comes back
    on another ephemeral port, so its peer's packets for the old session usually reach a port that nothing holds. The
    dialer's token covers the rare restart that rebinds the old port (below).
- **Compatibility.** The frame goes only to a peer that states transport parameter 3 (`ID_READS_RESET_TOKENS`). An
  older peer skips that parameter (§7.4.2) and is never sent a frame kind it would refuse. Dialect 2 is unchanged, so
  mixed builds still talk during a rolling upgrade.
- **The reset is sent by the demultiplexer.** It answers a 1-RTT packet that names no session, from a source with no
  session there, with a datagram shaped as a short header. The datagram is unpredictable except for its last 16 bytes,
  the token (§10.3), and its length obeys three bounds:
  - it is shorter than its trigger (§10.3.3), so two endpoints cannot loop resets;
  - it is at least 21 bytes, so a trigger of 21 bytes or fewer draws none;
  - it is at most 43 bytes, at least the 41 below which a reset might be told from a short packet.

  Three limits govern when it is sent:
  - **No reset to a source that has a session there.** A dialer's first 1-RTT packet can outrun the binding of its new
    id, and a reset then would end a session about to exist.
  - **At most one reset per source per initial probe timeout (666 ms).** The interval is the transport's initial PTO:
    RFC 9002 §6.2.2's `kInitialRtt` of 333 ms, doubled as the PTO before any RTT sample is
    (`rtt::INITIAL_PTO_NS`). It is the same constant the handshake's own pacing uses, not a separate tuning. A peer
    whose session is gone sends its next packet within its own probe timeout, so the first packet draws a reset at
    once. The interval bounds only a lost reset's repeat and a flood: a flood from one source costs the path at most
    one reset, smaller than its trigger, per 666 ms.
  - **The table of sources answered is no larger than the session pool.**
- **An endpoint on its own socket answers too** (§10.3: any endpoint may answer a packet it cannot associate). A
  dialer's endpoint answers a short-header packet that names another session with a reset under the dialer's identity.
  It sends at most one per initial probe timeout, each shorter than its trigger. So a process restarted onto the port
  its old session's dialer held ends that session at the accepting end within a round trip. Otherwise the accepting
  end would retransmit into it until its own timers gave up. On a shared socket the demultiplexer decides alone.
  - **A session in its handshake is handed no stray.** It has no token to compare one with until its id is bound, and
    a stray there could only be garbage in its reassembly. `a_stray_to_a_session_in_its_handshake_leaves_it_unaffected`
    holds this: strays shaped as resets, from the dialer's address before the handshake completes, reach neither the
    session nor a reset.
- **The receiving end detects it.** When a datagram cannot be opened as the session's packet, its tail is compared with
  the held token in constant time (§10.3.1). A match ends the session `EndpointError::PeerReset`, and every later use
  refuses the same. A tail that matches nothing is discarded like any other stray.
  - Detection sits in the endpoint, not the demultiplexer, because a reset of an accepting end's session arrives at the
    dialer's own socket.
  - The demultiplexer needs no table of tokens. A 1-RTT packet naming no session, from an established session's dialer,
    goes to that session's inbox: the session compares it with the token its dialer issued (§10.3.1, the tokens for
    that remote address). A session still in its handshake is never handed one.
  - This departs from the design as first read (detection in the demultiplexer against a per-source table), as
    confirmed 2026-11-08.
- **The fleet** never puts a reset session back in its slot (`fleet::return_sessions`). It drops the link instead,
  counted as `fleet.link.peer_reset`, and the link task dials the new process at its next pace (one heartbeat). Every
  borrower returns through that one place: the forward lane, live shipping and the coordinator's dispatches.
  loadtest-scale's borrower check stays as the backstop for a lost reset, a silent peer, a peer restarted under
  another identity, and an older build. It is transport-only: at each turn, a session that failed, or one with bytes
  in flight and no authenticated packet for a liveness budget, is judged dead. The membership offers no signal for
  this case: the restarted primary rejoined with the same member id at incarnation 0, and every peer kept it `Alive`.
- **What it does not cover.** An accepting end whose dialer restarted onto another port holds a session no reset can
  end, since nothing answers at the old port. That session ends on its own timers or the link's discovery deadline, as
  before. An accepting end's serve loop counts a reset it does hear (`fleet.serve.peer_reset`).
- **If the transport moves to `quinn-proto`** (`docs/wip/transport-quic.md`), its stateless reset replaces the frame,
  the demultiplexer's sending and the endpoint's detection. The key's derivation and the fleet's handling stay.

Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/transport/src/reset.rs` (new): the key, the token, the datagram and its detection.
- `crates/transport/src/session.rs`: `Frame::ResetToken`.
- `crates/transport/src/params.rs`: `ID_READS_RESET_TOKENS`.
- `crates/transport/src/connection.rs`: `issue_reset_token`, `peer_reset_token`, and the frame's receipt and resend.
- `crates/transport/src/endpoint.rs`: `EndpointError::PeerReset`, the issuing, the detection, `answer_stray`,
  `resets_sent`, `peer_reset` and `holds_reset_token`.
- `crates/transport/src/demux.rs`: `reset_unknown`, the stray handed to an established session, `resets_sent` and
  `resets_withheld`.
- `crates/transport/src/handshake.rs`: `Identity::reset_key`.
- `crates/server/src/fleet.rs`: `return_sessions`, `fleet.link.peer_reset` and `fleet.serve.peer_reset`.
- Bug record `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-restarted-node-left-its-peers-sessions-to-it-in-place.md`; GAPS.
- Tests, each red-checked:
  - `crates/transport/tests/stateless_reset.rs`: `a_session_with_a_restarted_node_ends_within_a_round_trip` (10.0 ms
    against a 10 ms round trip through the relay), `a_reset_from_another_identity_is_ignored`,
    `a_node_resets_only_a_stranger_at_most_once_per_interval_and_shorter_than_it_sent`, and
    `the_reset_key_is_the_private_keys_not_the_certificates`,
    `a_dialer_restarted_onto_its_port_resets_the_accepting_ends_session` and
    `a_reset_from_another_process_on_the_dialers_port_is_ignored`.
  - The reset, frame, parameter and connection unit tests.
  - The process test, loadtest-scale's case: `a_restarted_owner_resets_its_old_session_and_b_reaches_the_new_process`
    (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`).

### A-271 — A live volume's key reaches its successor before a write is durable on it; a successor never makes the key up, and waits for a missing one by event, bounded (accepted 2026-11-09)

A node whose store is destroyed comes back under the same anchor with a new member id and none of its predecessor's
keys. The owner's pair for that anchor had been accepted by the predecessor, and the durability gate counted the
anchor (`covers_candidates`), so writes went durable on a key the replacement never received. As successor, its
rebuild made a key on the spot, failed to open the log, refused the head for good, and kept the made-up key where the
right one would go.

- **Covered means accepted by the current incarnation.** A candidate counts toward a whole entry's cover only when
  this shard's pair to its anchor was accepted by its current member id (`pairs_delivered` keeps the accepting member;
  `covered_anchor`). New writes wait until a replacement accepts its redelivered pair (`fleet::deliver_pairs` already
  owes one to a new incarnation).
- **The pair is per (anchor, owner shard) by design** (`seal_keys::pair_for_delivery` reuses it), so the whole entry
  already written for the anchor opens for the replacement the moment it accepts: no re-seal, no second whole entry. A
  change to per-incarnation pairs must bring back a re-seal on acceptance and a read of the newest whole entry naming
  the current incarnation.
- **A holder's log begins at its newest whole entry or install image** (`live_ship::keep` and `serve_install` drop what
  came before). A successor's fetch therefore reads the newest entry's key from the first payload. Pinned by
  `a_holders_log_begins_at_the_newest_whole_entry_it_holds`; if retention changes, the fetch must read the newest whole
  entry that names the successor (the fallback named here).
- **A reader never makes a key.** Minting belongs to the owner's seal path (`seal_keys::lineage`, `namer`). Every
  rebuild and successor path reads `recorded_lineage` and `recorded_namer`, and a sealed log with no keys recorded is
  refused `no_key`, distinct from `open` (a payload that fails under keys held).
- **A missing key is waited for by event, bounded.** The refusal keeps the head, the whole entry's sealing (a few
  kilobytes, not the log) and when it began. Each attempt checks locally whether the key now unwraps; the log is
  fetched once when it does or when the head moves; past `NO_KEY_WAIT_NS` (ten liveness budgets, `OBSERVE_BUDGET_NS`)
  the takeover is answered `no_key_exhausted`, typed and counted, never waited on. The window this bounds: an owner
  dying after a replacement joined and before it accepted its pair.

Held by `a_pair_accepted_by_a_predecessor_at_the_same_anchor_does_not_cover_its_replacement`,
`a_sealed_log_this_node_holds_no_key_for_is_refused_for_the_missing_key`,
`a_missing_key_is_waited_for_and_the_log_fetched_once_it_comes`, `a_holders_log_begins_at_the_newest_whole_entry_it_holds`
(`crates/server/src/live_ship.rs`) and `a_reader_without_the_key_records_none_and_adopts_the_right_one`
(`crates/server/tests/seal.rs`). Owed: a deterministic skip in ranking computed from the durable whole entry's cover,
model-first, if the bounded wait proves not enough; at `f ≥ 2` A-295 hands the successor the key instead.

**The flow (2026-11-09, diag-live-durability-80).** The store-destroyed takeover (`crates/cli/tests/live_chaos.rs`:
one candidate's node destroyed mid-stream and replaced at its anchor, the fleet recovered, then the owner killed), on
A-271 with main db9c514e and the flows' fixed wait, release, 12 runs a leg, two legs on each Linux arch: 48 of 48
served every acknowledged write. The replacement was the successor in 26 and served 1.997 to 2.481 s after the owner's
kill; the key-wait counters read 0 on every survivor, so no successor lacked the key, the flow killing the owner only
once the fleet has recovered (BENCHMARKS "A live volume taken over by a node replaced at its own anchor"). The
window the bounded wait covers is held by the unit tests above, not by a flow, and the wait does not end it: only the
owner's shard holds the replacement's pair (`fleet::deliver_pairs`), so with the owner dead the key never comes, and
the volume is unserved while the replacement is its successor. So the bounded wait cannot be enough there: the skip in
ranking owed above, or another way for the successor to obtain the key, is what ends it (GAPS "an owner lost before
its replacement candidate accepted the owner's pair", 2026-11-17). A-295 is that other way, at `f ≥ 2`; at `f = 1` the
window leaves the log's recorded holders short of `f + 1` survivors, so no successor adopts it whatever key it holds.

Applied in the same change to: §4.10's status (the cover rule), GAPS (A-271's entry, the recipient fix's, and the
open window above), and BENCHMARKS.

### A-272 — A takeover's line is settled only on evidence; absence leaves it unresolved, and unresolved never reclaims (accepted 2026-11-09)

A holder learns where a retired owner's object went from the configuration (`RegionalConfiguration::lineage`), and a
line read as settled makes every holder reclaim its copy as stale (`takeover::resolve_held_objects`). The line was read
as settled from absence: a retirement no longer kept, or a ranked successor neither a member nor a kept retirement. A
retirement was pruned on its survivors' confirmations, and a survivor confirmed its share even when its round had
declared an object lost (its settled cohort left with fewer members than its recovery quorum). So a takeover that
adopted nothing could have every holder delete the copies the current members still held. The store-destroyed takeover
lost its volume this way: its settled cohort was [owner, A, old B], and the replacement holding the live log was not
in it.

- **A share confirms only when every object its round learned was adopted** (`takeover::share_done`). A round with a
  lost object leaves its retirement kept. A pruned retirement therefore means its objects were adopted.
- **Settled needs that evidence.** A line reads settled only when its retirement was pruned. A ranked successor that
  is neither a member nor a kept retirement, a retirement the bound dropped before every survivor confirmed, and a host
  retired with no neighbourhood to recover through read **unresolved** (`Lineage::Unresolved`,
  `RegionalConfiguration::dropped_unconfirmed`, carried in the configuration's encoding; A-309 replaced it with
  completion records, so settled rests on a record and every other absence reads unresolved).
- **Unresolved never reclaims.** A holder keeps its copy, as for a lost object.
- **Owed (A-272 ii):** kept adoption records, so settled rests on a record rather than on a pruned retirement, and a
  round of the current members for unresolved objects, so `f + 1` counts the members that exist now. A-309 takes it:
  the completion records and the lineage model (piece 1), the recovery by the members that exist now (piece 2), and the
  live takeover past tolerance (piece 3) are built.

Held by `an_absent_ranked_successor_leaves_the_object_unresolved_not_settled` (A-309 renamed it
`an_absent_ranked_successor_settles_the_object_only_on_its_completion_record`),
`a_retirement_dropped_unconfirmed_by_the_bound_leaves_its_objects_unresolved` (`crates/db/src/register.rs`),
`a_round_that_lost_an_object_does_not_confirm_its_share` (`crates/server/src/takeover.rs`; since A-309 nothing is
lost, and it is `a_round_confirms_only_once_every_object_it_learned_is_adopted`), and the store-destroyed
flow's check that no surviving holder reclaims while nobody serves the volume (`crates/cli/tests/live_chaos.rs`). The
§4.8 model (`docs/wip/models/Reconfig.tla`) covers the neighbourhood change, not takeover lineage, and states nothing
here; a lineage model is owed with (ii) (A-309 wrote it: `docs/wip/models/Lineage.tla`, text only, with
`crates/db/tests/lineage_model.rs`).

**The encoding.** `dropped_unconfirmed` is the last field of `raft_wire::encode_regional_configuration`. An entry of
the old encoding read by a new build runs out of bytes there (`RaftWireError::Truncated`), and a new entry read by an
old build has bytes left over (`LengthMismatch`). Every caller refuses rather than defaults:
- a retained council's base and view at restart (`retention::restore`: "invalid retained council base");
- a saved snapshot (`fold::for_saved`: `InvalidSnapshot`);
- an installed snapshot (`fold::install` declines it);
- a learner's fetch and a join (`consensus`).
A fleet that mixes builds therefore stops with a typed refusal; it never reads an old entry as "nothing dropped".
But the refusal comes from the length, not from a version or schema check: the configuration encoding carries
none, so a later field whose absence still parsed would be defaulted. Named as a gap (GAPS), not shimmed here.

> **Status (2026-11-17, g230): the configuration's layout is versioned and refused by name.** A regional configuration
> now begins with a magic ("RCFG") and a layout version (1: the layout with A-272's dropped confirmations and the
> moved-object exceptions last), and a root configuration with its own ("RTCF", 1)
> (`raft_wire::REGIONAL_MAGIC`, `REGIONAL_LAYOUT`, `ROOT_MAGIC`, `ROOT_LAYOUT`). A decoder reads them before any field
> and refuses another kind or an unversioned layout `ForeignLayout { magic }` and another version
> `LayoutVersion { layout }`, so no layout is ever read by another's positions. An unversioned configuration begins
> with its version number, whose low word is the magic only at version 1,195,787,090 (regional) or 1,178,817,618
> (root). A retained council or root whose configuration is another build's layout refuses recovery as a corrupt one
> does (a vote is never forgotten), now by name ("retained council base is another build's layout",
> `retention::configuration_refused`). Every caller above refuses as before; only the reason changed. Held by
> `a_configuration_of_another_layout_is_refused_by_name` (`crates/cluster/src/raft_wire.rs`) and
> `a_retained_council_of_another_layout_refuses_recovery_by_name` (`crates/server/src/retention.rs`). The
> configuration group's commands (`config_group::ConfigCommand`) are told apart by a tag byte and carry no layout
> version: a change to an existing command's fields would be read by position, as the configuration was (GAPS).

### A-251 — A host takeover counts a holder's promise of an object only when the holder spoke for that object, and a holder lists a copy by the authority it was written under (accepted 2026-11-08; steps (a) and (b) built)

A host takeover's phase one (§4.8 "Promotion and takeover") counted a holder's complete paged answer as a promise of
every object of the retired host the holder did not list: listing nothing meant holding nothing. A holder whose page
leaves out a copy it holds therefore reads as holding nothing. Two things left copies out:
- its routing disagreed with the successor's (`takeover::list_page` lists only objects whose owner, by the holder's
  routing, is the asker);
- it could not promise the copy (closed by step (c), `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-holder-that-could-not-promise-a-copy-read-as-holding-nothing.md`).

The successor can then reach an object's recovery quorum with such an empty promise and adopt an older record over a
committed newer one. That breaks NoLoss.

The change, in four steps:
- **(c), landed:** a copy a holder cannot promise is a typed refusal that keeps its answer incomplete
  (`HostPromise::unpromised`).
- **(a), built:** the counting rule is a pure function, `slates_db::takeover::readiness`, under a `CountingRule`.
  `crates/db/tests/takeover_model.rs` models a paged, multi-object takeover:
  - one or two cohorts per object;
  - writes to one cohort (a later owner in the recovery chain) or to all of them (a joint write), each committed by
    `Quorum::committed_within` in every cohort it targets;
  - the successor's own copies behind its lease gate, learned through its routing as any holder's are;
  - pages answered in a generated order;
  - a nemesis that leaves objects out of holders' pages while the pages still end complete.

  Its oracle is NoLoss: an adopted record is at least as new as every committed one. Over 2,000 generated histories,
  today's rule lost 0 records with the nemesis off and 216 with it on. A-251's rule (below) lost none, and 400 of its
  adoptions came only from a holder's answer by name. Each of three mutants of the rule turns the model red:
  - the named rule also counting a complete page;
  - only an object's first cohort judged;
  - the recovery quorum one short. The minimal history is
  `today_s_rule_adopts_an_older_record_when_a_holder_leaves_a_copy_out`.
- **(b), built:** after a holder's pages are complete, the successor asks it by name for each learned object it did not
  list, among the objects whose recovery cohorts it is in. The holder answers from a direct `holder_records` look-up,
  with no routing filter (`takeover::answer_by_name`): its highest record, promised as a page promises it, or "nothing
  held" for that object alone. The rule is now `CountingRule::NamedAnswer`: a member promised an object when it listed
  it or answered for it by name, and a whole answer's silence counts for nothing. The 2026-09-29 empty-promise case (a
  survivor that never received an object) still completes: that survivor answers "nothing held" by name.
  - **The successor answers itself by name too.** It learns its own copies through its routing (`promise_local_copies`),
    which can lose one as any holder's can. So under the named rule its open lease gate is no promise on its own: while
    the gate is open, it answers itself by name for each learned object it has not reported, from its own records
    (`takeover::answer_own_copies_by_name`, at the start of `ready_objects`). With the nemesis also leaving out the
    successor's own copies, a successor that counted its gate instead lost 86 committed records over the 2,000 histories.
  - **What stands in for routing.** A warm-restarted holder loses its routing and its `departed_owners`, so neither can
    decide. A holder answers only when the committed configuration names the asker the object's successor and the
    copy's acceptor serves an owner in the retired host's recovery chain, or the asker already. So a question never
    installs the asker over a live owner's object. Anything else is refused, counted `fleet.takeover.named_refused`,
    and stays unanswered.
  - **The wire.** `HostPrepare::named` and `HostPromise::nothing` are lists appended to the existing messages, written
    only when not empty, so a page request and its answer keep their bytes. Hostile-input tests cover both sides. A
    holder from before A-251 refuses a question that names objects. A successor then waits on that holder's answer as
    on a silent member, which the cohort's quorum tolerates up to `f`: liveness only, until it is upgraded.
  - A by-name answer is bounded by a page's bytes, and a question by the ids that fit one page. What is left out is
    asked again next period.
- **(d), owed:** the process test.

**How a successor learns the names (folded into (b), the supervisor's direction).** Asking by name helps only once
the successor knows the name. An object that every holder leaves out of its pages, the successor's own learning
included, is never learned, so the round confirms without it and NoLoss breaks silently. The model's nemesis now lets
