any holder leave out any object. Over 1,000 histories (2,950 objects), the named rule with today's routing-selected
pages left 620 committed objects unlearned. Two shapes were run against that nemesis, neither a global catalog
(D-14 forbids one for lookups, not a host's own recovery directory):
- **(i), chosen, as one rule with no routing in it: a holder lists a copy by its authority's line, or by the line
  of the owner an install moved that authority from.**
  - **The rule.** A page lists, and a successor learns of its own, every copy whose acceptor's authority, or the owner an
    install last moved that authority from (`Acceptor::moved_from`), has a line in the configuration
    (`RegionalConfiguration::lineage`) that ends in this round with the asker as its successor
    (`slates_db::takeover::copy_falls_to`). Today's routing filter is gone (CLAUDE.md §2.7: one rule, not a rule and a
    second path).
  - **Why the moved-from owner.** The install's authority reconcile moves a retired owner's copies to its successor.
    After a warm restart, such a copy routes to the successor as a live owner, so neither routing nor the authority
    alone names the retired host.
  - **Why not the asker's authority alone.** The asker's own live objects never fall here. Listing one would raise its
    fence to the round's epoch and could refuse the asker's own writes.
  - **Measured over 1,000 histories (2,950 objects).** The model gives copies an authority an install may move, and
    holds the asker's own objects:
    - routing plus a chain path (the first shape (i) built) lost 204 records;
    - the literal "chain or the asker" lost none, but learned the asker's own objects in every history; its minimal
      counterexample is `the_chain_or_asker_rule_learns_the_askers_own_object`;
    - this rule lost none and learned none.
    The first two are rejected.
  - **Cost.** No write: the authority and its last move are kept with the copy.
  - **The field, as bounded.** `Acceptor::moved_from` is set only by an install that moves the authority away from a
    retired owner (`Acceptor::move_authority`, from a takeover's page or answer and from the authority reconcile). It
    holds one owner, overwritten by the next such move, never a list.
  - **The encoding.** `slates_db::register::PersistedAcceptor` is the acceptor's whole durable state, the moved-from
    owner last (`Acceptor::to_persisted`, `Acceptor::from_persisted`). It round-trips canonically. Its hostile-input
    test refuses, each as a typed refusal: a cut at every byte, lengths of `u32::MAX`, a foreign option tag, and a stray
    byte. The layout without the field is refused as truncated, never read as "moved from none".
  - **The image.** The held image's register is its object and this encoding (`HeldRegister`), so a warm restart keeps
    an earlier move. The layout changed, so the image version is 25 and the delta version 8: a delta carries the held
    image whole. Both follow conformance-14 (A-262, image 23 and 24, delta 6 and 7); A-275 (image 26, delta 9) and
    raft-7's A-270 (image 27, delta 10) take the numbers after, in landing order. An image or delta of another version
    is refused by its version. A missing field is never read as none: that would be the compatibility shim §2.7
    forbids.
  - **Counted.** `fleet.takeover.listed_by_moved_from` counts a copy only the moved-from owner placed in the round.
- **(ii), measured and rejected: each host's object directory kept by its recovery cohort at `f + 1`,** as the
  configuration group keeps membership, read by the successor for every name.
  - Measured: 0 records lost over the same histories.
  - Cost: one more committed record for every object created (2,950 over the 2,950 objects), on the create path.
  - It loses nothing more than (i) does and costs a commit per create, so it is rejected.

The successor answers itself by name too: under the named rule its open gate alone is no promise, so a successor
holding nothing of an object in whose cohort it is must say so (`answer_own_copies_by_name`).

Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/db/src/takeover.rs` (new): `CountingRule`, `Heard`, `Readiness`, `readiness`, `promise_object`,
  `falls_to`, `AcceptorStore`, `answer_by_name`, with unit tests.
- `crates/db/src/register.rs`: `HostPrepare::named`, `HostPromise::nothing`, `Acceptor::authority`.
- `crates/db/tests/takeover_model.rs` (new).
- `crates/server/src/takeover.rs`: `ready_objects`, `fold_answers`, `begin_round`, `serve_host_prepare`, `list_page`,
  `promise_local_copies`, `initial_epoch`, `answer_own_copies_by_name`, and the module doc's account of the empty
  promise.
- Bug record `docs/bugs/2026-11-08-a-page-that-left-a-copy-out-read-as-holding-nothing.md`; GAPS's A-251 entry.

### A-232 — A call waits while its daemon lives; a daemon judged stuck is ended by its supervisor, or by its own watchdog when it has none (accepted 2026-11-13, the supervisor's goal 5875dc0c, uniform (a); built 2026-11-14, steps 1 to 6 of plan `01a1d6ca960575d0a36250c5f0a22500`)

Applied in the same change to (step 2): §4.14 (its status on `daemon.alive`), `crates/server/src/watchdog.rs`
(`Supervision`, `Turn`, `Cause`, `decide`, the end, `FAILED_EXIT_CODE`), `crates/server/src/daemon.rs`
(`SegmentSource::supervision`, `Daemon::start`, `starve_control_shard` and `starved_share_ns`), `crates/cli/src/main.rs`
(`EXIT_FAILED` taken from the server), `crates/client/tests/lone_daemon.rs` (new),
`crates/server/tests/common/supervised.rs` (new), the server tests named below,
GAPS, and `docs/bugs/2026-11-13-a-live-starved-daemons-call-was-failed-stalled.md`. Applied in the same change to
(steps 3, 4 and 6): §4.7 (its status), `crates/client/src/driver.rs`, `client.rs` and `error.rs` (the one rule;
`ClientError::Stalled`, `defers_reply`, `Client::defers` and `submit_patient` removed), `crates/client/tests/driver.rs`
and `waits.rs` (new), both SDKs' acceptance tests, READMEs and Node's `index.d.ts`, `sdk-node`'s `async.mjs`,
`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` (`bootstrap_once`), `crates/server/tests/recovery.rs` (`read_answered`),
`crates/client/examples/load_bench.rs`, and `crates/ipc/src/exit_watch.rs`'s module doc.

- **The rule, replacing A-56's.** A-56 said "an overdue call fails `Stalled` while the daemon lives and starts recovery
  when it is gone", and that a stopped daemon's call "stays a stall". Both are replaced by one rule. A call waits while
  its daemon lives. A daemon judged stuck is ended by its supervisor, or by its own watchdog when no other process can
  end it, on the same verdict, window and starved-is-not-stuck rule (A-228). The client then sees the daemon gone: an
  anchored daemon's calls are resent to the daemon the anchor restarts and answered there; a lone daemon's calls end
  `DaemonGone` past the reconnect budget. A stopped daemon has not exited, so its calls wait until it resumes or they
  are cancelled. Every wait a call makes keeps the rule: the async driver's tick, the synchronous round trip, and the
  wait for a slot on a full ring. Each reply deadline that passes asks the daemon's liveness; gone, the client recovers
  or reconnects; alive, the deadline re-arms and the call waits (a full ring's slot is checked at paces doubling from
  the wake estimate, at most a tenth of the deadline, so the wait costs no core beside a starved daemon).
  `ClientError::Stalled` had no other producer and is gone, as are `defers_reply`, `Client::defers` and the driver's
  patient submissions, the rule's earlier exception for long work, which is now every call's rule.
- **The bound, by its terms** (`W` the liveness budget, `B` the beat, `L` the lateness each line names, `t0` a wedge).
  Supervised: `t0 + 2·W + B + L + kill`, `L` the watchdog's first-look lateness plus the anchor's age past the window,
  `kill` the time to the client seeing the daemon gone. Unsupervised: the verdict within `t0 + W + B + L` and the exit
  `end` after it. Step 2 and step 5 below derive each term.
- **Why.** A call to a daemon its own watchdog judged alive failed. Red on main `29ef4521` (`diag-a232-red-4` at
  `e553e306`, a diagnostics probe at `cpu.weight` 1 beside 32 default-weight spinner cgroups): 10 of 10 runs on each of
  ubuntu-latest and ubuntu-24.04-arm, 25 and 19 calls failed `Stalled` 2.152 to 8.929 s after sending, no beat
  withheld, every shard judged starved. On this Mac at nice 19 beside two spinners a CPU, 1 of 3 runs.
- **Evidence, by step** (each in the bug record with its commands, revisions and logs). Step 3, the client's rule: the
  driver's and the waits' tests red on `3c17e017` (every call `Stalled` at its first deadline), green after; each of
  the three waits' mutations red. Step 4, the tests that claimed `Stalled`: both SDKs' stopped-group calls pending past
  3 reply deadlines and answered after the group resumes, red against `3c17e017`; Python 4 of 4 and Node 4 of 4 on each
  Linux runner (`diag-a232-s4-1`). Step 5, live (`diag-a232-starved-2` on `a7c479b3`, 10 runs a shape a runner):
  starved, 0 failed calls of 231; stuck supervised, 20 of 20 within the bound; stuck unsupervised, 20 of 20 verdicts
  within; frozen, 20 of 20 killed. Mutations (`diag-a232-starved-ma`, `-mb`, `-mc-2`): the client's `Stalled` branch
  restored, 10 of 10 red on each runner; the lone self-end removed, 10 of 10 red on each; starved treated as stuck, 7
  and 9 of 10 red.
- **What it does not change.** The watchdog's verdicts and window (A-228), the anchor's lapse rule, the restart
  policy, the wire, the reconnect budget's derivation, and R1 to R10. `W` is still the fixed liveness budget, recorded
  as R3 debt in GAPS. A call cancelled by its caller is still released at once.
- **Open** (GAPS): the first Windows run of the lone daemon and the supervised roles (jupiter was offline); the
  unsupervised bound without its exit term exceeds zero by up to 1.08 ms in 15 of 40 runs; adacachy2's whole-process
  pauses of about 1.16 s, which wake a wedged shard, so no wedge timing can be judged there; and `agents/clients-a232`'s
  `611840a2` (step 2's agent timing the lone daemon's end in two parts), which conflicts with step 5's rework of the
  same test and is not merged here.

The steps' own records follow.

- **Why (this step).** The client's half of A-232 makes a call wait while its daemon lives, and fail `DaemonGone` once
  it is gone. That is safe only if a daemon that will never answer is ended. An anchored daemon is: its watchdog
  withholds the beat on a stuck shard (A-228) and the anchor kills it at its lapse. A daemon run alone
  (`SegmentSource::Create`: `slates daemon` with no anchor) withheld a beat nobody read, and lived on stuck for good.
- **The rule.** The watchdog is told at its start whether an anchor reads its beat (`Supervision`, from the segment's
  source), and each turn decides one of three typed outcomes (`Turn`): beat, withhold, or end. An anchored daemon's turns
  are A-228's, unchanged. A lone daemon's turn ends its own process where an anchored one's withholds the beat: on the
  same verdict (wedged or spinning), the same window (`LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS`) and the same starved-is-not-stuck rule, and
  on a control loop that ended (a refused boot, which nobody would restart). A starved shard ends nothing. Nothing found
  while the daemon stops ends it, since the stop is its end already. The end is a deliberate `std::process::exit` with
  `FAILED_EXIT_CODE` (4, the CLI's code for a failed daemon), never a panic: a stuck shard's thread cannot be joined, so
  an orderly stop would wait on it for good. The end's line is written by a thread of its own, waited for at most one
  beat, since a shard can be wedged in a write to an undrained standard error while holding the lock every log line takes.
  A writer that says the line is written is joined before the exit, so it is owned; one still blocked after the beat is
  ended by the exit (2026-11-18: unjoined, a finished writer was a thread leak to ThreadSanitizer, whose exit report
  held a lone daemon's end 26 s and made its exit code 66, `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-the-watchdogs-end-left-its-writer-unjoined.md`).
- **Decided: only `FromEnv` is supervised; `Handoff` is not** (the plan's choice, recorded here as it asked). `Handoff`
  is an anchor in the daemon's own process: it may read the beat, but it cannot end a stuck daemon without ending
  itself, so nothing would end it, and its watchdog ends the process as a lone daemon's does. Supervision is a fact
  about who can end the daemon, and only another process can. Every in-tree `Handoff` user is a test that plays the
  anchor (the boot tests, the restart oracles, `recovery_slicing`). One that needs a supervised daemon to live on with a
  stuck shard now plays the anchor across a spawn: `crates/server/tests/common/supervised.rs` creates the segment,
  publishes the profile and supervises the test binary's role through the anchor's own `Supervisor`, and the role's
  daemon attaches `FromEnv`. Considered and rejected: treating `Handoff` as anchored, since its holder reads the beat.
  Its holder cannot act on the beat, which is what supervision means, and it would leave an embedding's stuck daemon
  running for good, the defect this amendment removes.
- **The bound, by its terms.** A wedge is judged on the wall clock, from the look that last saw the shard move. The
  watchdog keeps, per shard, the look before that one (`ShardWatch::still_after_ns`). The shard last moved after that
  look, so the wedge did too, and the verdict is due a window and a beat after it. How far past that the verdict came is
  the verdict's lateness `L`, measured by the watchdog and named in its end line. It holds the look's phase against the
  wedge and the lateness of the watchdog's own thread. So a lone daemon exits within `W + B + L` of the wedge, `W` the
  liveness budget and `B` the beat (`HEARTBEAT_NS`). Counted with the thread's lateness alone (also named in the line),
  the same bound reads `W + 2·(B + L_looks)`, since the look that sees the last movement can come a beat after it. The
  rule itself is unchanged. A spin is judged in the shard's own CPU time, which a busy machine hands out slower than the
  wall runs, so its verdict names between a window and a window and one look of CPU.
- **Test fixtures that held a shard stuck in a daemon nobody supervises.** Before A-232 they were harmless, since nobody
  read the beat, and each is now one of two things. A test that watches a daemon go on with a stuck shard (its beat
  stopping, an observation's deadline, a peer's refusal) is about a supervised daemon, the only kind that lives stuck,
  and runs its body as a supervised role: `liveness.rs` (wedged, syscall, spinning, waiting on a blocked thread),
  `observe.rs` (the three wedged control-shard histories and the wedged observation), `cross_shard_wait.rs` (the wedged
  bootstrap and revoke), `nfs_hostile.rs` (the MOUNT to a wedged owner). `Daemon::starve_control_shard` spun its whole
  span, a spinning, stuck shard by A-228's rule that an anchor kills. It now runs as a starved thread runs, a share of
  each beat on the CPU, at most half a window over its span (`starved_share_ns`).
- **Proven** on this Mac (M5 Max, 18 CPUs, macOS 26.4.1), 2026-11-13, at load averages of 40 to 150 from other
  sessions, by `cargo test -p slates-client --test lone_daemon`. A lone daemon whose client's shard was wedged exited
  1.412 s after the wedge, inside `W + B + L` = 1.465 s, the verdict's `L` 365 ms at that load. A spinning shard's
  verdict named 1,157 ms of CPU. Both outstanding calls (`submit_patient`) ended `DaemonGone`, at 4.04 s and 4.06 s.
  Red-checked on a copy of the tree with the self-end removed (a lone daemon's stuck turn withheld): "still running 10s
  after its shard was held; the call: None (None: still pending)". The verdict table is
  `each_verdict_maps_to_beat_withhold_or_end_by_who_reads_the_beat`, and the lateness is pinned by
  `a_wedge_verdicts_lateness_is_measured_from_the_look_before_the_last_movement` and
  `a_shard_found_still_at_the_first_look_is_measured_from_the_watchdogs_start` (16 unit tests in `watchdog.rs`).
- **Found while measuring.** The first lateness the end named counted only how late the watchdog's looks ran, and at
  load 41 to 64 a wedge exited 1.301 s after its hold against `W + B + L` of 1.268 s, 33 ms past. The look that sees a
  shard's last movement can come a beat after it, and that phase was not counted. The verdict's lateness now counts it.
  The child connected and held its shard within a beat of the watchdog's start, and its first look already found the
  hold, so there was no look before it ("not known", 2026-11-13). A watch now begins at the watchdog's own start
  (`ShardWatch::begun_at`).
- **A starved lone daemon is never ended.** Run with `SLATES_STARVE_LONE_DAEMON=1 cargo test -p slates-client --test
  lone_daemon -- --exact a_lone_daemon_starved_beside_spinners_is_never_ended`. On this Mac, at nice 19 beside 36
  spinners (two a CPU), at load 21 to 43: 0 of 10 runs ended it, every call was answered (454 to 990 a run, the
  longest 57 to 386 ms), and each run's watchdog judged a shard starved. On Linux (adacachy2, kernel 7.3.3, through
  kiln), `SLATES_STARVE_LONE_DAEMON=cgroup` in a `systemd-run --user --scope -p CPUWeight=1 -p AllowedCPUs=0-7`
  beside eight weight-100 spinner units on the same CPUs, each a cgroup of its own, started on the test's begin tag:
  0 of 10 runs ended it, every call was answered (57 to 173 a run, the longest 320 to 773 ms), each run judged starved.
- **Every test binary that uses `Handoff`**, and the files changed, this Mac: `liveness` 10/10, `observe` 8/8,
  `cross_shard_wait` 7/7, `nfs_hostile` 20/20, `recovery` 52/52, `recovery_slicing` 1/1, `seal` 2/2, `attach_forms`
  9/9, `green_checkpoint` 6/6, `merge_load` 5/5, `shards` 28/28, `virtiofs` 9/9, fleet's incarnation and two
  starved-hold tests, and in the client crate `client` 35/35, `driver` 2/2, `acknowledge` 2/2, `consumer` 3/3,
  `edit_and_submit` 2/2. No process ended itself. Two fixtures had to change: `recovery.rs`'s stuck-start test, whose
  claim is the anchor's, runs as a supervised role, and its busy start (`BootFaultKind::Busy`, "as a long recovery
  does") runs in the recovery's own slices (`RecoverySlices`). As one poll it was a spinning shard, judged so at 1,093
  ms of CPU, which an anchor would kill too. A fleet test, `a_slow_first_round_candidate_is_hedged_after_the_measured_p95`,
  failed 3 of 3 here at load 57 to 63 with the new starved hold (placed 3.037 to 3.049 s against its 3 s hold), and 3
  of 3 on a copy with the old spinning hold (3.031 to 3.111 s). So it is the base's failure at that load. On CI it was
  this change's: the poll's trace of the held candidate is bounded in that shard's own CPU time, which the starved hold
  spends slowly, so it waited out the 20 s hold (placed at 20.016 s, PR #10's Windows lane, 2026-11-17); the poll now
  leaves the held candidate out. `a_silent_owner_leaves_no_forward_the_lane_admitted_unrun`, which slept a lone
  daemon's shard for two windows and so ended its test binary (exit 4), now starves it, and three siblings that slept
  one for exactly a window starve it or hold half a window, as each one's assertions need. Two more, found by the
  landing's Linux run of every binary: `shards.rs`'s starved hold, a fixed fifth of the CPU for 7.5 s and so a
  spinning shard, now starves by the derived share; and the CLI's frozen-daemon test now waits for the process
  judgment's kill line, which is how this change's anchor kills a frozen daemon (GAPS).
- **Linux (adacachy2, x86_64, 32 CPUs, kernel 7.3.3, 2026-11-13 and -14, through kiln).** Clippy `-D warnings` on
  the three crates; the 16 watchdog unit tests. The wedged lone daemon exited 1.100 s after the wedge, inside
  `W + B + L` = 1.102 s, and the spinning one on 1,003 to 1,098 ms of CPU, both calls `DaemonGone`. `recovery` passed
  56 of 56 and `cross_shard_wait` and `observe` whole. **Open:** run beside their binary's other tests, the supervised
  roles of `liveness.rs` and `nfs_hostile.rs` fail intermittently there. Each passes alone (the MOUNT role 3 of 3, the
  liveness roles 8 of 8 in a systemd unit), and `nfs_hostile` passes whole when its tests run one at a time (2 of 2).
  Measured in a failing run: the shard thread running the hold is the one whose clock the watchdog reads (same tid),
  and it really wakes, its voluntary context switches climbing (12 to 27 in 2.4 s) while it should sit in its blocking
  wait. So the watchdog reads it rightly as moving. What wakes it is not found. It is not this change's: the base
  (`3c17e017`) with the same harness and roles failed 1 of 6 runs in the same period, and 0 of 10 beside the branch's
  0 of 10 later. Tests the change does not touch failed in that period too, in process (a 2.8 s whole-daemon beat gap at
  load 12). GAPS holds it.
- **Not run: Windows.** jupiter was offline. The changed crates pass `cargo xwin clippy -D warnings` for
  x86_64-pc-windows-msvc. The supervised roles and the lone daemon's exit watch on Windows run first on CI's Windows
  lanes.
- **Step 5 (2026-11-14, `agents/clients-a232-s5`): the rule and its bound, live.** Applied in the same change to:
  §4.14 (its status), `crates/server/src/watchdog.rs` (`mark`, `ShardWatch::moved_ns`, `first_look_lateness_ns`,
  `stuck_lateness_words` on the withhold line), `crates/anchor/src/layout.rs` and `segment.rs` (`SUP_LOOKED`, `Supervision::look`, `looked_ns`),
  `crates/cli/src/anchor.rs` (`supervise` split from `run`, `judge_lapse`, `on_lapse`, `Quiet`), `crates/cli/src/daemon.rs`
  (`start` and `serve` split from `run`), `crates/cli/src/liveness_tests.rs` (new),
  `crates/client/tests/lone_daemon.rs`, GAPS, and the bug record's step 5.
  - **The bound, by its terms.** The verdict comes within `W + B + L` of a wedge, `L` the verdict's own lateness (step
    2's rule above). A shard wedged at `t0` is first seen still at the next look `a1`, a beat and that look's lateness
    after the look before it (`still_after_ns`, before `t0`), and the beat is withheld from the first look a whole window
    after `a1`. So an anchored daemon's last beat comes within `W + B + late(a1)` of the wedge, and the withhold line
    names `late(a1)` beside the verdict's lateness (unit test:
    `the_verdict_and_an_anchored_daemons_last_beat_come_within_their_bounds_of_a_wedge`). The anchor kills at its
    logged age past that beat. So the supervised bound is
    `t0 + 2·W + B + L + kill`, with `L` the watchdog's `late(a1)` plus the anchor's age past the window (its p99 and its
    look's overshoot), each read from its own line, and `kill` the measured time to the client seeing the daemon gone.
    With the anchor's p99 alone, as the plan worded it, the bound failed on this Mac 5 of 5 times, the watchdog's looks
    late under kiln's launchd timer policy. On CI the two readings agree to within about a millisecond.
  - **What the client sees.** A supervised daemon's outstanding call is resent to the daemon the anchor restarts and
    answered there, not failed. A lone daemon's call ends `DaemonGone` past the reconnect budget. "DaemonGone time" in
    the bounds is when the client's liveness first answers gone. For a lone daemon that is the verdict plus `end`, the
    exit: 1.7 to 4.6 ms on CI, and the plan's `W + B + L` without it was exceeded by up to 1.08 ms in 15 of 40 runs.
  - **Proven** on both Linux runners (`diag-a232-starved-2`, 10 runs each shape): starved at `cpu.weight` 1, 0 failed
    calls of 231; stuck supervised, 20 of 20 inside; stuck unsupervised, 20 of 20 inside; frozen, 20 of 20 killed by
    the process judgment. On this Mac: supervised 10 of 10, unsupervised 10 of 10, frozen 5 of 5. Mutations each turned
    their own shape red on both runners: the client's `Stalled` branch, the lone self-end, and starved treated as stuck.
    The tables are in the bug record.

### A-277 — A fleet node may bind elsewhere than it advertises (2026-11-17, built for goal g229, chaos across real processes)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.8 "Deployment": the `bind` sentence, and a bound base past the port range refused as an advertised one is.
- `crates/server/src/deploy.rs`: `FleetNodeEntry::bind`; `bind_address` binds the block a node names, else its
  advertised address as before; `validate` and the plan refuse a bind block past the port range
  (`PortBlockOverflows`, naming the bind's base). The tests: `a_node_that_binds_elsewhere_serves_there_and_is_dialed_where_it_advertises`
  and the bind case of `a_bad_manifest_is_refused_by_name`.
- `crates/cli/src/fleet.rs`: the manifest's optional `bind` per node, an IPv4 literal with a nonzero port; a name,
  a missing port, port 0 or a non-string refused naming `nodes[i].bind` (`a_declared_bind_parses_and_a_bad_one_is_named`).
- `docs/cli.md`: the manifest's `bind` field. GAPS: "Chaos from outside the processes", the relay owed.
- **What was there.** A node bound exactly the address it advertised (an IP literal), or every interface on the
  advertised port (a name). Whatever a peer dialed had to be the node's own socket. A node behind a port mapping
  whose outer ports differ from its inner ones (a container runtime's published ports, a NAT's port forward) could
  not join a fleet: it bound the outer port, which is not its to bind. And nothing could stand between two real
  daemons on one machine, since discovery's announcement of a node's own address wins over the manifest's at every
  dial (`fleet::resolve_peer_address`), so every peer reached the node's socket directly.
- **The rule.** `bind` names the IPv4 literal and base port the node's two serve sockets bind; the advertised
  address still names where every peer dials it, and the node still announces only that. The block is the same two
  ports. With no `bind`, nothing changes. The anchor binds and hands over the plan's sockets, so it binds the block
  too, and the daemon's check of an inherited socket compares it with the bind block.
- **Why.** Goal g229 (Ada's chaos directive of 2026-11-04: knock replicas offline, inject latency and loss) owed loss
  across real processes on a developer's machine, where netem needs privileges this project never takes. A relay in
  the test that owns every node's advertised ports and forwards to their bind blocks can drop, delay, duplicate and
  reorder each datagram, and cut a running node off in either direction, with no privilege. Only KIND's netem
  injected loss before, and only on real pods (`cargo xtask kind live`, which no lane runs).

### A-278 — An embedding host drives slates through one library, `slates-api`; the host mount, the issuer and the anchor and daemon roles move into it from the CLI (accepted and built in part 2026-11-18, Ada's goal "slates has a library API for embedding hosts")

Applied in the same change to:
- §2.4 (the surfaces list), §4.12 ("Embedding", its status, and AC-5.12 / T-5.14 in Phase 5's table), Appendix B.6
  (the layout); `docs/library.md` (the user's guide) and the README's documentation table.
- `crates/api` (new): `lib.rs` (the crate doc, `deadlines`, `overlay`, `scratch`), `instance.rs` (`Instance`,
  `LandingPlan`, `Planned`, `Approved`, `LandingRequest`), `issuer.rs` (`Issuer`, `GRANT_TERM_NS`), `mount.rs` (the
  host mount, moved), `error.rs` (`Error`, `MountFault`, `IssuerFault`, `PathFault`), `tests/api.rs`.
- `crates/cli`: `src/mount.rs` deleted; `verbs.rs` mounts, unmounts, exports, grants, enrolls, revokes, runs and
  recovers through the crate; `args.rs` takes the grant's term from it.
- `unsafe-budget.toml` (the macOS `mount(2)` block counted in `slates-api`, `slates-cli` 7 → 6), `xtask/src/main.rs`
  (`slates-api` may name host paths: the mount point's real path, a read), GAPS (the inventory row).
- Piece 2, the same day: `crates/api/src/role/` (`mod.rs`: `Role`, `ProcessOptions`, `FleetSelection`, `serve`,
  `main`, `measure`, `recovery_key`; `anchor.rs`, `daemon.rs`, `parent.rs`, `dumps.rs`, `fleet.rs`,
  `recovery_key.rs` and `liveness_tests.rs` moved from `crates/cli/src/` unchanged in what they do, the anchor's
  daemon started with the executable's prefix; `signal.rs`, the stop flag, moved from the CLI's `signal.rs`, whose
  `slates pmem` relay stays); `crates/api/src/start.rs` (`StartSpec`, `Started`, `Anchor`, `Instance::start`,
  `Instance::wait_for`); `error.rs` (`StartFault`, `Error::Start`, the enums `#[non_exhaustive]`);
  `crates/api/tests/start.rs` (a harness-free test binary that is the host). The CLI's `main.rs` and `args.rs` serve
  `anchor` and `daemon` through `slates_api::role` (its `failure_text`, left unused by piece 1's mount move, removed);
  `unsafe-budget.toml` (the stop flag's three blocks: `slates-api` 1 → 4, `slates-cli` 6 → 3); `xtask/src/main.rs`
  (the fleet manifest and recovery-key reads are `slates-api`'s now) and the host-path table regenerated; `docs/library.md`.

- **Why.** Ada (2026-11-18): kiln invoking slates only through its CLI is wrong; kiln must vendor slates and use a
  library API, as it vendors Shards, Hex and Mantle. Until now kiln ran the `slates` binary for every verb
  (`crates/kiln/src/workspace/slates.rs` at kiln 28b6c8ca): one process per verb, its JSON parsed back, the anchor
  found by a binary on the `PATH`, a landing plan held only while the command that made it ran (so kiln re-planned
  before every grant), one `--exclude` per landing, and a grant possible only by passing on the variables the anchor
  had printed to its log, never on Linux.
- **The rule.** A host product reaches slates through `slates-api` alone. Its name follows the convention of the
  products kiln vendors (`hex-api`, `shards-api`, `quiver-api`): the crate other products reach the product through.
  What a front end needs past the client (a mount, the issuer, the grant's term) lives in this crate once, and every
  front end calls it, the CLI included; no front end keeps a copy (CLAUDE.md §2 item 7).
- **The issuer stays the human's.** The crate's `Issuer` is the same authority `slates grant` holds — the anchor
  segment's handoff, which the anchor's tree inherits and, on macOS and Windows, its user exports — attached for one
  proof at a time and never kept as a secret, so a daemon restart between two grants meets each with its own secret.
  The SDKs and the MCP server do not depend on the crate, so no grant verb reaches them; an embedding host is a
  confirmation surface in §4.13's sense, and `Instance::land_approved` binds its grant to exactly the manifest its
  person approved.
- **No slates binary (piece 2).** The anchor and daemon roles live in the crate (`role`), and any executable whose
  `main` hands the arguments after its prefix to `role::main` serves them: the `slates` binary with no prefix, kiln with
  its own. The anchor's daemon is the anchor's own executable started again with the same prefix, so the prefix and
  `--instance NAME` reach every process of the instance (the e2e contract finds them by it). `Instance::start` spawns
  the anchor and waits for the first answer while it lives: until the anchor holds the rendezvous a connect is refused
  at once and is asked again a heartbeat later (the anchor's own cadence, `HEARTBEAT_NS`); once it holds it, the
  connect waits for the daemon (A-114). An anchor that exits ends the wait with its code. **Changed from the plan:** the
  first draft had the anchor hand its starter the issuer on an inherited channel (the segment's descriptor on Linux).
  Ada's grant decision of the same day (A-285: a grant's proof is a signature by a key only the human holds, with a
  prompt on the anchor's terminal where none is registered) makes that wrong: a host process holding the issuer secret
  could grant without the person. So the starter is handed nothing, and the grant call takes the person's proof.
  (A-285 was revised the same day: write permission follows the agent's mode, and the launcher, the issuer's holder,
  approves.)
- **Piece 3, the same day** (kiln's asks, g263): `mount::available() -> Result<MountKind, MountFault>`, the machine's
  mount mechanism with no daemon (macOS: `mount(2)`, always; the BSDs: `mount_nfs` on the `PATH`; Linux:
  `fusermount3` on the `PATH` and a `/dev/fuse` the user may read and write; Windows: WinFsp's library loads), each
  missing piece refused by its own reason, the macOS mount's own check now the same function; and
  `mount::unmount_lazy(path)`, `fusermount3 -u -z` on Linux, refused `Unsupported` elsewhere. Applied to
  `crates/api/src/mount.rs` (with pure `fuse_available`/`nfs_available` tested on every host), `lib.rs`
  (`MountKind`), `docs/library.md`, §4.12's text and status, GAPS.
- **Owed, in order.** (1) An async form over a host's reactor (R6). (2) A seam trait with a simulator and a
  conformance suite, for hosts whose rules ask for one (Hex's §9, kiln's `kiln-seams`): built 2026-11-18, A-310. A
  landing plan's per-path
  entries, paged, were built by A-287 the same day (`Instance::landing_entries`).
- **Checked.** `crates/api/tests/api.rs` over a daemon in the test process: no daemon is `Unavailable`; a create before
  the group is `ConsensusNotInitialized` and the group is made twice harmlessly; create, snapshot, clone and destroy;
  an overlay's landing with `/.git` left out lands exactly the approved manifest, an approval of another manifest
  writes nothing and returns the plan, and the folder is untouched until then; a file changed on disk after the volume
  changed it is drift and a planned conflict, and a grant id nobody issued lands nothing; the daemon's status and a
  shard's telemetry; and a Shards stream from the crate answers FUSE `INIT` and finds the volume's file (Linux and
  macOS). The CLI's harness verb test runs its enrollment through the crate's issuer.

### A-281 — A Shards guest's run owns what its host made: the stream takes Shards' owner word and shows the volume's owner and the run's swapped (2026-11-18, built for goal g268, what Shards needs from slates)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6, the Shards form: the owner word's bullet and its status. GAPS: the entry of this date. `docs/cli.md`: the
  `slates shards` paragraph.
- `crates/bridge-core`: `OwnerView` (the swap, with its unit test), `Bridge::owner_view` (the identity by default),
  `VolumeBridge::viewing_owners`, and `ScopedBridge` passing its inner bridge's view on.
- `crates/bridge-fuse`: `bridge.rs` shows every `fuse_attr` (an entry, an attribute reply, a READDIRPLUS entry, a
  CREATE's and a TMPFILE's) through the bridge's view, and keeps a creating request's caller and a SETATTR's uid and
  gid through it. `shards_fs.rs` adds `OWNER_WORD`, `OwnerWord`, `owner_word` and `owner_word_reply`. The tests:
  `shards_owner_word_is_taken_from_the_guests_root_on_the_shares_root_alone` and
  `a_streams_owner_view_shows_the_hosts_files_as_the_runs_and_keeps_the_runs_ids_as_the_hosts`.
- `crates/server`: `shards.rs` gives the stream its view (`ShardsStream::owners`), takes the word before any dispatch
  (`take_owner_word`, `root_owner`), and counts it (`shards.owner_named`, and `shards.owner_refused` in the refusal
  ledger). The test: `the_runs_owner_named_on_the_root_owns_what_the_host_made_and_the_host_keeps_its_own`.

- **What was there.** Shards' init names the run's owner on each share's root as it mounts it, with the extended
  attribute `trusted.shards.owner` set to `UID:GID` (Shards' `crates/init/src/setup.rs` `name_owner_as`, D38). Shards'
  own file server takes that word and keeps it on no file, and from then on shows every file the host made as the
  run's (`crates/vmm/src/devices/virtio/fs/server.rs` `set_default_owner`, Shards 183fe264e). slates' dispatch
  answered any attribute outside `user.` with `EOPNOTSUPP`, so the word was refused, and a slates stream showed each
  file's owner as the volume keeps it: the host's user, 501:20 on a Mac. A guest's kernel checks permissions itself
  (Linux mounts virtio-fs with `default_permissions`, as Shards' server's header notes), so a run of user 1000 could
  not write a host-owned volume. Shards'
  coordinator ranked this first of what it needs from slates (2026-11-18): "for a served share, an unprivileged run
  can't write a host-owned volume".
- **The rule.** The stream takes the word before any dispatch, from the guest's root on the stream's root alone, and
  answers it as Shards' server does: taken with nothing written, `EPERM` from any other caller, `EINVAL` on any other
  node or for a value that is not two decimal ids. A body too short for the value it declares is `EIO`, as the
  dispatch answers any body too short for its opcode; a guest's kernel never sends one. From then on the stream shows
  its guest the owner the volume keeps for the stream's root, read as the word came (uid and gid), as the run's owner,
  and the run's owner as that one. The ids the guest names are kept the other way round: a creating request's caller,
  a chown's uid and gid, and the caller of a READLINK, whose answer A-107 bases on whether the caller owns the link.
  A word named again recomputes the swap; a stream that never gets the word shows every owner as the volume keeps it,
  as before.
- **Why a swap, not Shards' own rule.** Shards' server keeps the guest's owner of a file in an attribute beside it on
  the host and shows a file without one, which the host made, as the run's. slates keeps a real owner on every file:
  the host's for a base file, the creator's for the rest. The one-way rule (the host's id shown as the run's) would
  show the run's own files and the host's alike, and would leave nothing for a chown to the host's id to store. The
  swap is the smallest change that shows the host's files as the run's and keeps one owner one owner: it is its own
  inverse, so a chown and the stat after it agree. The volume keeps the host's ids for what the run made, so the
  host's NFS or FUSE mount, the SDK and a landing see the host's user owning it, which is what a person whose agent
  ran in a microVM wants of the files it made. Ids that are neither of the two (root's among them) are shown as they
  are kept, so a file the guest's root makes is root's on every route.
- **Why the stream keeps it, not the volume.** Shards' server keeps the word on no file, and a file holding it would
  show a `trusted.` attribute to every other route. The swap lives with the stream; nothing of a stream survives a
  restart today, and the next stream's guest names its owner again as its init mounts the share. Once a stream may
  outlive a restart (owed: GAPS, Shards' RESEND), the view must be kept with the attachment's record.
- **Where it applies.** Only in the FUSE dispatch's replies and the ids it keeps, on the bridge a Shards stream builds;
  every other transport's bridge answers the identity (`Bridge::owner_view`'s default). slates checks no access by a
  caller's uid but A-107's READLINK rule, so permission is the guest kernel's, against the owners it is shown.
- **Evidence.** The three tests named above: the word read from bytes with every refusal and malformed value; the
  dispatch over a volume holding the host's, the run's and a third owner's files; and a real daemon, whose stream
  takes the word and whose NFS port reads the host's ids for every file the run made or chowned. Owed: Shards' own
  guest test over a slates stream (its `tests/slates_fs.rs` on Linux and macOS), which Shards' coordinator runs after
  its v0.8.0 tag and its bump of the slates revision it pins.

### A-287 — A presentation keeps its manifest's entries, and `LandingEntries` reads them a page at a time to the principal it was presented to (accepted and built 2026-11-18, kiln goal g266: review with no mount of the volume)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.15 step 2 (how the full entry list is read) and its status.
- `crates/ipc/src/protocol.rs`: `RequestBody::LandingEntries { landing, from }` and `ReplyBody::LandingEntries { bytes,
  next, total, manifest }` (both appended); `PlannedEntry`, `PlannedAction`, `PlannedContent`, `ConflictClass`,
  `EntriesCursor` (new).
- `crates/server/src/landing.rs`: `Awaiting::entries` and `Awaiting::conflicts`; `present` takes the plan by value
  and moves the manifest's entries into the presentation. `crates/server/src/landing_entries.rs` (new): the verb, the
  pager and its oracle. `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`: the verb served on the landing's owner shard, as a grant is.
- `crates/client/src/client.rs`: `Client::landing_entries_page` and `Client::landing_entries`; the types re-exported.
- `crates/api`: `Instance::landing_entries(&LandingPlan)` and the types re-exported (A-278's owed item 4), checked in
  `tests/api.rs`'s landing test; §4.12 "Embedding" status; `docs/library.md`.
- `crates/server/tests/presentations.rs`: three tests by use. GAPS: the Landing (4.15) and Embedding library rows.

- **What was there.** §4.15 step 2 promised the full entry list on demand, and a presentation answered the summary's
  counts and the conflicts alone; the manifest was dropped once its hash was taken. So a person granting a landing saw
  how many files it wrote but not which, and a reviewer with no host mount of the volume — kiln's microVM sessions, a
  guest's volume served over virtio-fs — had no way to learn the change it was asked to review.
- **The rule.** A presentation keeps its manifest's entries for as long as A-46 keeps it, and `LandingEntries` reads
  them to the principal it was presented to: to anyone else, and once the presentation has gone, the landing is
  `NotFound`. A page is the bytes of the entries' wire encodings (`PlannedEntry`), one after another in the manifest's
  order, from an (entry, byte) cursor to as many as one reply chunk holds; every page but the last is full, and the
  last names no next cursor. Each create and replace names its bytes' BLAKE3 and length, as the manifest binds them,
  so a reader of the volume's file checks that what it read is what the grant would land. A cursor that names no place
  in the list is refused `BadRequest`.
- **Why bytes and not whole entries.** One reply chunk holds 4,023 bytes of entries, and an entry is its path, plus a
  rename's origin or a symlink's target, plus about 60 bytes. A path near the OS limit, with an origin or a target,
  outgrows a page, and a page of whole entries would have to refuse that landing's list while the landing itself writes
  it (the engine opens each component relative to its parent). Under a cursor into the encodings the entry crosses
  pages; each page still encodes only the entries it carries, so serving the list costs work proportional to the page,
  never to the list, and the server keeps nothing of its readers. The client decodes each entry as its last byte comes,
  so it holds no more than one entry's part between pages.
- **Why the presentation keeps the entries.** The list must be the manifest the grant binds, entry for entry: planning
  again could not promise that (the disk under the preliminary verdicts moves), and planning per page would cost the
  plan per page. The entries are moved from the plan, which had them in memory already; what is new is how long they
  stay, and A-46 bounds that: one presentation a client seat, gone with its landing, its replacement or its client.
- **For a reviewer.** A plain volume reads only at its head (`ReadAt`), so a reviewer snapshots the volume, presents
  the snapshot's landing, reads the list, reads each listed file at the head and checks its BLAKE3 against the entry;
  a mismatch means the volume changed since the snapshot, and the reviewer presents again. The landing of the same
  snapshot later presents the same manifest hash, or the disk changed the plan, which the grant's binding refuses
  (AC-2.8).
- **Checked.** `crates/server/tests/presentations.rs`: over a base, every action a volume can take through the file
  verbs (a directory made, files created, a file replaced, a directory renamed, a file removed), each listed in landing
  order with its bytes' hash and length and its mode, the replaced file's outsider change listed as `ModifyModify`, the
  counts and bytes the summary's; another principal's read and a replaced presentation's are `NotFound`, pages of
  another manifest are never joined; a list whose 3,986-byte entry no page holds whole comes whole and in order, in
  12 pages, 11 of 4,023 bytes and the last of 429, 11 of them ending inside an entry (kiln run r128, macOS arm64,
  2026-11-17); a landed presentation's files hash to what its list named, and its list then is `NotFound`. The pager
  against its oracle: generated lists and page sizes join to the encodings in order with every page but the last
  full; every cursor outside the list refused.

### A-289 — The workload roster runs git's history and maintenance, Mercurial and Subversion on every leg, and a workload that fails alike on both sides fails (accepted 2026-11-17, Ada's goal of 2026-11-18: git, Mercurial and Subversion on slates volumes on every route, byte-identical to the host, covered by workload tests in CI)
Applied in the same change to: Part 6 ("Real workloads" and its status), GAPS, `crates/conformance/src/workload.rs`
(the three workloads, `ENVIRONMENT`, `environment_exports`, `compare`), `crates/conformance/src/record.rs`
(`WorkloadStatus::Failed`, `fails_the_suite`, `failure_note`) and `matrix.rs` (the `FAILED` part of a summary),
`xtask/src/conformance/workloads.rs` and `container.rs` (the shared environment; the host determinism gate; each leg
judged by `fails_the_suite`), `crates/server/tests/virtiofs.rs` (the guest's environment), and CI's `conformance` and
`live-guest` jobs.
- **The decision.** "Byte-identical to the host" is judged as the roster always has been: one script run twice under
  one environment, on the host and over the mount, compared by exit code, output with the two directories as one
  token, and a manifest of the tree under reviewed exclusions. Three workloads join `git`:
  - `git-history`: a bare upstream, a seed that pushes to it, and a local clone whose objects are hard links to the
    upstream's; a branch, a merge, a rebase, a stash, a second worktree made and removed, a tag, a push and a pull;
    then `gc`, a full `repack` and the upstream's `gc` (with its reachability bitmap), `verify-pack` and `fsck`.
  - `mercurial`: a named branch and its merge, a tag and a bookmark; a local clone whose store files are hard links to
    the source's, then a commit in the clone, before which Mercurial copies each store file it appends to and still
    shares, judged by the file's link count; a rebase, a push back, a share of the store, and `verify` of all three.
  - `subversion`: an FSFS repository with a fixed UUID; working copies whose state is SQLite; a commit, a branch by a
    server-side copy, a switch and a commit there, an update back and forward, Subversion's merge into trunk, a tag, a
    cleanup, a second working copy, then `svnadmin verify` and a checksum of the dump.
- **A workload that fails alike on both sides fails.** Part 6 asks exit codes 0 before byte-identity, but `compare`
  asked only that the host's and the mount's exit codes be equal, so a script stopped early on both sides (a tool
  refusing an option, a missing extension) was recorded `Identical` and proved nothing about the mount. A nonzero
  code on both sides is now `WorkloadStatus::Failed`, with the code and the host output's tail; the native,
  container and guest legs all judge through `compare`, and both xtask legs fail their suite by one rule
  (`fails_the_suite`). Red before the change: `a_workload_that_fails_alike_on_both_sides_is_failed_not_identical`
  read `Identical` for two runs that each exited 129.
- **Hard links are counted in the output.** Both clones print how many object or store files have two names, after
  the clone and (Mercurial) after the clone's commit. A mount that cannot link, or that reports a stale or wrong link
  count, differs there; and one that let Mercurial append into a store file it still shared would fail the source's
  `verify`.
- **One environment for every leg.** The host, the container and the guest set `ENVIRONMENT`: the fixed git identity
  and date, Mercurial reading no configuration but a repository's (`HGRCPATH` empty), its plain output and committer,
  and one Python hash seed. Measured on the host gate's first run (2026-11-17, macOS 26, git 2.50.1, Mercurial 7.2):
  Mercurial wrote its store's file list (`fncache`, a set) in a different order in each process until the seed was
  fixed. Commits carry fixed dates; Subversion's revision dates are set to one instant by `svnadmin setrevprop`, which
  runs no hook, before its history is printed; the clones' origins are written back as relative paths.
- **The exclusions, each a file the tool fills with stat data or an absolute path by design.** git's index and
  reflogs (a clone's first reflog entry names its source by absolute path, and gc expires entries by age against the
  clock); Mercurial's dirstate and its transaction copies, and the clone's `undo.desc` (it names the repository a push
  answered by absolute URL); Subversion's `wc.db` and its journal (sizes, modification times and commit times), and
  FSFS's `db/uuid` (a random instance id beside the UUID, which is printed).
- **Locks.** Subversion's working copy and repository take POSIX record locks (SQLite's, and FSFS's `write-lock`),
  and Mercurial's locks are symbolic links made atomically. Every leg runs both sides of a workload under one kernel,
  where the kernel's own locks (macOS `locallocks`, the Linux adapter's `nolock`, FUSE and virtio-fs without served
  locks) bind every process. Served locks (NFSv4.2's) are needed only between kernels.
- **Tools.** The conformance job installs Mercurial and Subversion (Ubuntu's image has Mercurial only and macOS's
  neither); the container and guest images (`rust:1.98.1`, built on `buildpack-deps`'s `scm` layer) carry git,
  Mercurial and Subversion already. The live-guest job requires each new workload's `Identical` line.
- **Owed.** The Windows WinFsp roster: WinFsp's driver has no hard links (its NTFS compatibility page lists them
  unsupported), so a local clone copies there while NTFS links, and a git repository's symbolic-link probe needs
  WinFsp reparse points, which the drive does not serve yet. **Built by A-300 (2026-11-17)**, the drive serving
  reparse points since A-275, and the missing hard links a stated difference of the route. A Linux FUSE leg outside a
  container (the native Linux lane reached the daemon through the NFS adapter): **built by A-293 (2026-11-17)**. The
  runs over each mount are the supervisor's (CLAUDE.md §8); what their first runs found is A-319.

### A-279 — A full control channel tells the senders waiting for its room (2026-11-17, built for goal g239, a kept forward re-sent once the channel has room)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.3: the status of 2026-11-17 (the room wake).
- `crates/rt/src/room.rs` (new): `ShardSet`, the protocol and its three loom models. `crates/rt/src/registry.rs`:
  each entry's `room_wanted` and `room_given`; `give_room`; `note_exited` tells every asker.
  `crates/rt/src/shard.rs`: `want_room`; `drain_control` wakes the tasks a tell names and, after a drain that took a
  message, fences and tells; the counters `room_waits` and `room_wakes`. `crates/rt/src/futures.rs`: `want_room`.
  The tests: `crates/rt/tests/room.rs` and `room_gone.rs`.
- `crates/server/src/daemon.rs` (`serve_loop`) and `crates/server/src/verbs.rs` (`ask_room_for_kept_forwards`,
  `refuse_unsent_forward`): the timed idle while a forward is kept is gone. `Daemon::flood_control_channel_counting`
  and `crates/server/tests/forward_retry.rs`.
- GAPS: the load test's "A kept forward waited for another request". The bug record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-a-kept-forward-polled-for-room-and-its-test-timed-the-owners-queue.md`.
- **What was there.** A shard's control channel is bounded at its admission limit, and a spawn it refuses is kept by
  its sender (§4.3: "backpressure, never a drop"). No message, flag or kick told the sender when the channel had room
  again. The serve loop, while it kept a forward, idled at most one idle window and then tried again (2026-11-07), so
  it armed a timer every window and the forward reached its owner up to a window after the room. The window is the
  shard's measured wake × 100 and has no cap of its own.
- **The rule.** A sender refused `ControlFull` may ask the target to tell it when the channel has room. It marks its
  shard in the target's set, fences `SeqCst`, and tries once more, and it waits only if that try is refused too. The
  target, after every drain that took a message, fences `SeqCst` and tells each shard its set names. A tell marks the
  target in the asker's set, fences `SeqCst`, and publishes the asker's control flag, so a parked asker is kicked as a
  message would kick it. That fence answers the one a drain makes after re-arming its flag with a plain store, which
  ends a publication's release sequence; a message needs none, since the channel claims its slot with a `SeqCst`
  operation. An exiting target tells every asker, and an ask after its exit is refused `ShardGone`. The serve loop asks before it idles with a
  forward kept and then idles with no timer. Asks and the tasks they woke are counted per shard.
- **Why.** Goal g239: the supervisor's runs of main failed `forward_retry.rs` 8 of 30 at load ~35, named a lost wake.
  The test's timeline on this Mac (30 runs beside 36 spinners) found the resend within 21 ms of the room in every run;
  the answer waited for the owner's drain of the 41,125 tasks the test had queued ahead of the forward, which took up
  to 4.33 s. So the test now owes the answer within the liveness budget of the owner's last progress through that
  queue. The exact wake was the 2026-11-07 record's owed sibling. With it, nothing but the owner's word moves a kept
  forward while its shard idles, which the test now proves, and the timer a window is gone.
- **Cost.** The sender pays only on a refusal: a map insert on its own shard, two read-modify-writes and a fence. The
  target pays one `SeqCst` fence and one load for each drain that took a message, nothing when none came, and a fence
  for each tell.

### A-293 — The Linux lane runs the workload roster over the daemon's own FUSE mount (accepted 2026-11-17, Ada's goal of 2026-11-18: git, Mercurial and Subversion on every route, Linux FUSE among them)
Applied in the same change to: Part 6's "Real workloads" status, GAPS, `docs/wip/conformance.md` (§4's Linux row),
`crates/conformance/src/capability.rs` (the cell; `LINUX_NFS_ADAPTER` public), `xtask/src/conformance/slates.rs`
(`Reach`, the FUSE mount), `mod.rs` (`Run::reach`), `bench.rs` and `live_fleet.rs` (their reach named), and the
`conformance` job's comment in CI.
- **The decision.** The native Linux transport is FUSE, and an agent's git, Mercurial and Subversion reach a volume
  on Linux through `slates mount`, the daemon's own FUSE mount. The roster ran there only inside containers
  (`oci-linux`); the native Linux lane ran it through a root `mount -t nfs` of the loopback export, an adapter
  recorded LIMITED. The roster needs no root, and a user's processes reach the user's own FUSE mount without
  `allow_other`, so its cell (`native-linux-fuse` × workloads) now names neither root nor an adapter: tools
  `fusermount3` and `sh`, recorded RAN. The other suites keep the adapter (pjdfstest's root cases need `allow_other`,
  the hermeticity tracer strips `fusermount3`'s setuid unless it runs as root), and over the FUSE mount they run in
  the container lane.
- **How a cell reaches its volume is the table's.** `Reach::of(transport, suite)` reads the cell's adapter from the
  capability table, and `mount_volume` mounts by it: the transport's own mount, or the Linux NFS adapter. A run that
  measures a mount of its own names its reach outright: the NFS bench measures NFSv3 beside NFSv4.2 (it asks for root
  itself rather than borrow the workloads cell, whose reach is now FUSE), and the A-200 live-ship test keeps the soft
  NFS mount it is about. `the_linux_nfs_adapter_is_the_only_adapter` holds every adapter the table names to the one
  the harness can mount.
- **Evidence.** `the_workloads_cell_reaches_linux_fuse_through_the_daemons_own_mount` opens the cell's session as
  `conformance run --suite workloads` does, as a user with no root, and holds the kernel's mount table to a FUSE
  mount and a file's second name to two links (gated on a built CLI, run in CI's Linux conformance step). The roster's
  runs over the mount are the supervisor's (CLAUDE.md §8).

### A-285 — Write permission follows the mode the user gave the agent; signed work is provenance, never the permission gate (accepted 2026-11-18, Ada's decisions; revised the same day)
Applied in the same change to: R10 (CLAUDE.md §1 and Part 1's rule table), D-22 (A-285 line), §4.13 "Grants" (status),
GAPS (2026-11-18 entry), `crates/server/src/grant_signature.rs` (module docs).
Status: a volume's write policy and landing under it are built (2026-11-18): the wire (`WriteAct`, `WriteMode`,
`WritePolicy`, `PolicySubject`, `SetPolicy`, `Policy`, `Refusal::PolicyForbids`), the policy an appended field of the
volume's record (`PolicyRecord.write`, op `VolumeWritePolicySet`), set only under the issuer and never from a
consumer-bound channel; a landing under it, on every Unix host: forbid refuses before any host access, ask answers the
approval request a launcher's grant approves, bypass grants the planned presentation itself (`GrantSurface::Policy`)
and lands it in the same request (`landing::land_under_policy`). Built the same day: `Present`, a landing presented and
never landed whatever the mode (a reviewer's read of a bypass volume's changes writes nothing); merges under the policy,
the stricter of the work's and the green's merge mode, forbid refused before the seal, ask answered
`MergeApprovalRequired` with the increment's identity and its path count and merged by `SubmitApproved` under the
launcher's proof of exactly that identity (`landing::merge_approval_proof`), a volume with no merge mode set merging at
once as every merge did before policies. Built the same day: every launcher-class proof (grant, policy, merge
approval, enroll, revoke) verifies under the daemon's issuer secret or the launcher secret its starter handed the anchor
(`landing::proven_by_launcher`), so a launcher keeps its authority across its own restarts and the daemon's; and a
`SetPolicy` names the policy version it replaces (`PolicyRecord.write_version`, covered by the proof), so a captured
proof sets nothing once the policy has moved (`Refusal::PolicyChanged`). Built the same day: a consumer's own policy,
kept in its record and on every shard's channels bound to it, held on the agent's shard before its request is routed
(forbid refused; ask turns a landing into `Present` and a merge into `SubmitHeld`/`EditSubmitHeld`; bypass leaves the
volume's mode to decide), so the stricter of consumer and volume governs; and the MCP and SDK land verbs, which send
`Land` with no grant, say what the policy does. Built 2026-11-18 with the two-node filesystem-server flow
(`crates/cli/tests/fs_server.rs`, which found it): a landing's grant is refused `Forbidden` on a consumer-bound
channel before anything else, whatever its proof (`landing::grant_verb`, counter `grant_by_consumer`), as a policy
setting and a merge's approval already were, so an agent never approves its own landing
(`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-an-agents-own-channel-could-approve-its-own-landing.md`). Built the same day, its siblings:
`Enroll` and `Revoke` refuse `Forbidden` on a consumer-bound channel before the proof (`enroll_by_consumer`,
`revoke_by_consumer`), so no launcher-class verb answers an agent's own channel (GAPS); `SetSigners` refuses it
alike (A-321). Signed merges built 2026-11-17 (A-321): the statement, the verdict recorded with the version, the
trusted signers and a volume's requirement; signed landings built 2026-11-18 (A-321's second part): the statement each
presentation states, the verdict judged against what is presented and what is written, recorded on the landing's audit
records. The SSH-signature verifier built first (below) is signed work's, its grant statement removed.
- **The rule (Ada, 2026-11-18).** Merging and landing to disk follow the permission mode the user gave the harness or
  agent that asks. Bypass (Claude Code's `bypassPermissions`, Codex's full access): slates merges and writes, no
  prompt. Ask: slates answers a typed approval request (the change's summary and manifest) that the harness presents
  (its own prompt, an MCP elicitation, kiln's presentation), and writes once the approval comes back bound to that
  manifest; a changed manifest is refused. A mode that forbids writing (plan): a typed refusal. The policy is carried
  by the session's consumer or the volume and set by the launcher (kiln passes each agent's mode when it creates the
  workspace) or the harness; the effective mode is the stricter of the two, unset is ask, and an agent can never raise
  its own. The launcher's authority is the instance's issuer, which an agent's consumer channel never holds.
- **Signed work (Ada: "we can (and should) support signed work").** A merge or a landing may carry an SSH signature
  (OpenSSH `PROTOCOL.sshsig`); slates verifies it, records it as provenance and answers a typed check (verified with
  its signer, unsigned, or invalid with its reason), and a volume can require signed merges. It never decides whether
  a write is permitted. Built for merges and landings by A-321 (their statements, the trusted signers, their records).
- **Withdrawn.** The same morning A-285 read R10 as a human-only proof: fs-server's options of 2026-11-05 (A, a prompt
  on the anchor's terminal; B, a same-user socket; C, a separate operator account; D, a signature by a key only the
  human holds; E, standing grants in a file the human writes), of which Ada first chose D with A as the fallback. Ada
  withdrew that reading and the options (2026-11-18): agents can approve merges and landings within the mode their user
  gave them. What was built for it and is withdrawn: the presentation's nonce and the signed `Grant` proof (piece 2,
  d1a46ae9, reverted); never built: key registration and the terminal prompt.
- **Kept.** The verifier (piece 1, 1c31d1c7): an SSH signature under a namespace, `ssh-ed25519` and `sk-ssh-ed25519`
  (the user-presence flag required), `sha512` or `sha256`, Ed25519 and SHA-2 from AWS-LC (A-66), against a set of
  keys; every failure a typed `SignatureRefusal`. Proven by 10 unit tests over a real `ssh-keygen -Y sign` vector
  (OpenSSH 10.0p2): every single-bit flip, an unregistered key, a changed field, another namespace, an expired
  statement, an untouched security key and hostile bytes are refused. Signed work reuses it over its own statement.

### A-299 — The consumer contract: write modes per act, typed outcomes, typed conflicts and drift, signed work, one closed error taxonomy, a contract version a consumer pins (accepted 2026-11-18, Ada's widening of goal g262; piece 4, the contract published, built 2026-11-18)
Applied in the same change to: §4.12 ("Embedding": what a host holds, its refusals and its versioning; "The consumer
contract", new, with its status), GAPS (the A-299 entry and the Embedding library row), `docs/library.md`.
- `crates/api`: `policy.rs` (new: `WriteMode`, `WriteAct`, `WritePolicy`, `PolicySubject`, `PolicyRefusal`,
  `PolicyReason`), `signed.rs` (new: `WorkSignature`, `Verification`, `Signer`, `SignerKey`, `SignatureFault`),
  `outcome.rs` (new: `LandOutcome`, `MergeOutcome`, `RebaseOutcome`, `Approval`, `Awaiting`, `Work`, `Summary`,
  `ActionTally`, `LandingReport`, `LandingState`, `LandingConflict`, `MergeConflict`, `MergeConflicts`), `volume.rs`
  (new: `VolumeSpec`, `Source`, `Provisioned`, `VolumeStatus`, `BaseState`, `DriftReport`, `Drift`, `DriftKind`,
  `Watcher`), `error.rs` (rewritten: the classes and their details, `Note`, `MountMissing`, `Unreported`; every enum
  closed), `instance.rs` (`provision`, `read`, `land`, `plan_landing`, `approval_entries`, `approve`, `merge`,
  `rebase`, `retry_pause_ns`; `create`, `clone_snapshot`, `land` under a grant id, `land_approved`, `LandingPlan`,
  `Planned` and `Approved` removed, replaced), `lib.rs` (`CONTRACT`; `overlay` and `scratch` replaced by
  `VolumeSpec::overlay`, `VolumeSpec::empty`), `grant.rs`, `issuer.rs`, `start.rs` (the launcher's authority),
  `mount.rs` (typed missing pieces), `Cargo.toml` (`slates-merge`), `tests/api.rs`, `tests/start.rs`.
- `crates/cli/src/verbs.rs`: `failure_of_api` maps the taxonomy's classes to the command's exit codes; the Windows
  unmount names each unreported volume from its typed refusal.

- **Why.** Ada (2026-11-18): "merge and write to disk permissions need to reflect those granted by the user to the
  harness/agent seeking to merge their write to disk. Part of your work is figuring out and building a correct, robust,
  performant API with typed responses and errors that consumers can consume (Kiln is a consumer) to act upon this. This
  also applies to handling merge conflicts, permission errors, provisioning/managing volumes, and other interactions."
  And the rule of the same day: agents can approve merges and landings; bypass writes, ask returns a typed approval
  request, forbid a typed refusal; no keys, no signatures, no person-only proofs; the launcher or the harness sets a
  session's or a volume's policy, and an agent can never raise its own. And, later the same day: "we can (and should)
  support signed work (signed merges, etc.)": a merge or a landing may carry a signature, its outcome a typed
  verification, and a volume's policy may require signed merges; signatures never gate permission.
- **Before.** `slates-api` answered the wire's `Refusal` (with free text in a dozen variants), the client's own
  `ClientError`, a landing's plan with its conflicts as `"path (Class)"` strings, a summary counting actions by name,
  an outcome's state as a word, a drift list of `"path (Kind)"` strings with an unreadable base reported as a drift
  entry `"status refused: ..."`, a merge window's class as a byte, and enums a consumer had to match with a wildcard.
  A consumer acting on any of it parsed text.
- **The shape.** One class per thing a consumer does (the table in `error.rs`), with the refusal's own data typed in
  its detail; where the daemon or the OS spoke in prose only, a `Note`, displayed and never matched. The mapping from
  the wire is one exhaustive match, so a refusal added to the wire cannot compile until it has a class. `NotFound`
  names the subject the call named, which the bare wire refusal does not. Outcomes are enums of what happened —
  written, awaiting approval, conflicted, refused — and the refusal a policy makes is an outcome, not an error: in a
  forbid mode it is the expected answer. A landing whose presentation found conflicts answers them typed, read from
  the presentation's own entries (A-287), never parsed. An unreadable base is a state of the status, never a failure of
  it, so a mount still reads the daemon's port.
- **Closed, and versioned for a pinning consumer.** The A-278 crate's enums were `#[non_exhaustive]`, which forces a
  wildcard and lets a new variant fall through it unhandled. Kiln vendors slates at a commit; a new variant should stop
  its build where it must decide, so every contract enum is exhaustive and `CONTRACT` is raised with every change: 1 as
  first published, 2 the same day for `Denied::Policy` (the class `Refusal::PolicyForbids` maps to outside a landing or a
  merge, defined before A-285's owner appends that refusal, so its arm in the exhaustive table is mechanical).
- **Write permission, split between the crate and the daemon.** The modes are enforced where agents reach slates — the
  daemon, through the MCP server, the SDKs and the mounts as much as this crate — so the daemon keeps them (A-285's
  owner). The crate publishes the types now so kiln's agents (g263–g266) build against them. Until the daemon's side
  lands, every landing with something to write asks (today's behaviour, a grant per landing) and `approve` grants it
  with the launcher's issuer, binding exactly the manifest shown; a signed act is refused `Unsupported(SignedWork)`
  before anything is sent, and every outcome reports `Unsigned`, which is true.
- **Rejected.** A merge's conflicts carrying the work's base from the handle a consumer holds: the daemon knows the
  base, a handle can be stale, and the wire carries it next (owed). A paged listing faked over the one-reply list: the
  daemon answers every volume in one reply today, and a page the daemon did not cut would hide that cost; the paged
  verb is owed. Policy verbs that could only refuse until the daemon keeps policies: left out until they work.
- **Piece 5, the same day** (over A-285's policy wire, 203ad8fa): `Instance::set_write_policy` (the launcher's
  `Issuer` proves `slates_server::landing::policy_proof` over the subject and policy) and `Instance::write_policy`;
  `PolicyForbids` answered as a landing's or a merge's `Refused` outcome and as `Denied::Policy` elsewhere (A-285's
  owner added the variant's arm the same hour, and the two definitions were one); the API's policy converted to and
  from the wire's, its signed-merge requirement refused before sending; `plan_landing` refusing a bypass volume until a
  present-only verb exists; `CONTRACT` 3. Applied to `crates/api/src/{policy,issuer,instance,error,lib}.rs`,
  `tests/api.rs` (`a_landing_follows_its_volumes_write_mode`), §4.12's status, GAPS, `docs/library.md`.
- **Piece 6, the same day:** the audit log and the grant listing typed (`observe.rs`: `AuditRecord`, `AuditKind`,
  `LandingStage`, `GrantRecord`, `GrantState`), read from the daemon's closed name tables in one place; `CONTRACT` 4.
  Checked by unit tests over every word and a stranger, and by use: after a landing the audit holds the presentation,
  the issued grant and the landing finished `Done`, and the single-use grant is listed `Consumed`.
- **`CONTRACT` 5, the same day:** `WritePolicy::UNSET` merges at once and asks for landings (it read ask for both).
  The daemon applies an unset policy so (A-285's owner raised it): R10 asks for a write to disk, while a merge changes
  memory, and every submit merged at once before write modes existed, kiln's included.
- **`CONTRACT` 6, the same day** (over A-285's present-only verb and merge approvals, 1242c7d9, whose placeholder in
  `merge` it replaces): `Approval` split into `LandingApproval` and `MergeApproval`, so no outcome can hold an approval
  of the other act; `approve` into `approve_landing` and `approve_merge` (the authority proves the merge with
  `merge_approval_proof`; a changed increment merges nothing and is asked again); `merge` takes evidence;
  `plan_landing` presents through the daemon's `Present`, whatever the mode, and its bypass refusal and
  `Unsupported::WritePolicies` are gone.
- **The launcher secret, piece 1 (the segment's field), the same day.** The launcher's authority must outlive the
  launcher's own restart: handing kiln the anchor segment's descriptor (Linux keeps the segment as a memfd) would die
  with kiln's process, after which no approval or policy could be proven without restarting the instance and losing its
  volumes. So the launcher provides a secret of its own at every start and keeps it; the anchor publishes it into the
  supervision block (`SUP_LAUNCHER_PRESENT` 320, `SUP_LAUNCHER_SECRET` 328, 32 bytes, beside the issuer and session
  secrets; zero in an older anchor's segment, read as none), and the daemon verifies launcher-class proofs under it as
  under the issuer secret (A-285's owner, agreed 2026-11-18). The issuer secret stays minted per boot: the client
  regions' names and the boot incarnation derive from it (A-176). Built here: `AnchorSegment::publish_launcher_secret`
  and `launcher_secret` (`crates/anchor`), with `a_published_launcher_secret_is_read_by_a_later_attachment`. Next: the
  starter's delivery on the anchor's standard input and `Issuer::from_launcher_secret`.
- **The launcher secret, piece 2 (delivery and proofs), the same day; `CONTRACT` 7.** `crates/api/src/launcher.rs`:
  `LauncherSecret` (`generate` from the TLS provider's secure random, `from_bytes` refusing all zero, a redacted
  `Debug`), the record (magic `SLLA`, the secret, CRC32C; 40 bytes) with its typed `LauncherFault`s, and the anchor's
  read. `StartSpec::launcher` / `with_launcher`; `anchor_command` (now fallible, `StartFault::Launcher`) writes the
  record into a fresh pipe, closes its write end before the spawn and hands the read end as the anchor's standard
  input with `SLATES_LAUNCHER=stdin`: never an environment variable, which every process of the user reads, and an
  input that passes unchanged through `systemd-run --scope`'s exec. The anchor reads it before it measures, holds or
  creates anything (a bad record refused `EXIT_REFUSED`) and publishes it before any daemon. `Issuer::from_launcher_secret`
  proves grants, merges, policies, enrollments and revocations with no segment attached; a consensus recovery stays the
  segment's (`IssuerFault::LauncherCannotRecover`). Checked by unit tests (the record whole and as written, each fault;
  two generated secrets distinct) and by use in `tests/start.rs` (an instance started with a secret serves; garbage and
  a short record each refused at the anchor's start). The daemon's verification landed the same hour (A-285's owner,
  0366b68a), and `the_launchers_secret_proves_its_policy_across_a_daemon_restart` proves the whole path by use: the
  daemon killed and restarted by its anchor verifies the launcher's next setting.
- **Typed drift on the wire, the same day; `CONTRACT` 8.** `StatusReport` gains `base: Option<BaseReport>`, appended
  (D-15), filled by the status verb from the base plane's own status and `None` from the merge service; the crate reads
  it and nothing else, and its text reader goes (replaced, not layered). Found by the test first: a green's status
  failed `Protocol(UnknownName { field: "watcher state" })`, since the merge service names a green's watcher `merge`
  (`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-greens-status-failed-in-the-contract.md`). `DriftReport::watcher` is a `Watcher`. Applied to
  `crates/ipc/src/protocol.rs`, `crates/server/src/{verbs,merge_service}.rs`, `crates/api/src/{volume,instance,lib}.rs`,
  `tests/api.rs`.
- **`CONTRACT` 14, the same day (g263's ask; 9 to 13 landed beside it):** `StartSpec::anchor_command_under(wrapper)`, since a host cannot take
  a `Command`'s standard input out to hand its wrapper's: the wrapper's words, then the anchor's program, prefix and
  role, with the launcher's record on standard input, the marker and the process group. Proven by
  `an_anchor_started_under_an_exec_wrapper_keeps_the_launchers_secret` (`/usr/bin/env` execs the anchor; a policy set
  under the launcher's secret verifies; the anchor stops at `SIGTERM`, exit 0).
- **`CONTRACT` 15, the same day: the volume core's refusals typed.** `refusal_of_vfs` (`crates/server/src/error.rs`)
  ended in a catch-all that sent every volume-core error it did not name as `BadRequest { reason: "<its name>" }`, an
  uncategorized refusal (CLAUDE.md §3): `Pinned` (a snapshot a clone holds, a green's origin), `DaxMapped`,
  `NotDirectory`, `NotEmpty`, `StaleHandle` and fifteen more reached every consumer as words. A-310's seam found it
  (its simulator had to answer `Invalid::Request("Pinned")`). The wire appends `Refusal::Volume { refusal:
  VolumeRefusal }`, one variant per volume-core error, with the journal's and the recovery image's numbers; the mapping
  is exhaustive, so a new volume-core error does not compile until it is classified, and `BarrierIncomplete` now
  reaches the wire's own variant. The contract classes each: `Pinned` and `DaxMapped` a holder (`Busy::Volume`), a stale
  handle and a drifted base a moved view (`Stale::Volume`), the volume's rules a denial, its bounds exhaustion, an
  unreadable journal or image unusable, the operations an entry does not take invalid. Applied to
  `crates/ipc/src/protocol.rs`, `crates/server/src/{error,verbs}.rs`, `crates/server/tests/{recovery,fuse_mount}.rs`,
  `crates/api/src/{error,sim,lib}.rs`, `tests/api.rs` (the seam's suite asserts the typed `Pinned`).
- **`CONTRACT` 16, the same day: what an unmount removed, and host refusals in words.** The integrator's Windows lane

  - `a_refused_mount_time_hold_leaves_nothing_mounted` read `Target("...")`, since `Error`'s rendering printed

  - `unmount_releases_every_healthy_drive_beside_a_volume_recovery_could_not_rebuild` exited 0 naming nothing, since

  `HostFault` and `Unreported` now render in words (`TargetUnavailable` named). `Instance::unmount` answers

  the unasked on standard error whether the drive was released or not. Applied to
  `crates/api/src/{error,mount,seam,sim,lib}.rs` and `crates/cli/src/verbs.rs`. The rendering tests are unit tests (`a_host_refusal_is_named_by_its_kind_in_words`,
  red first; `an_unreported_volume_is_named_with_its_refusals_kind`). The two live tests run on CI's Windows runner

- **Checked.** `cargo test -p slates-api` (37 unit, 9 by use, 5 start, 1 doc) and `cargo test -p slates-cli` on
  macOS arm64 (kiln runner, 2026-11-18): the cases in §4.12's status. The Linux and Windows arms of the mount and the
  CLI's Windows unmount are not compiled on this host; the integrator's lanes are their first compiler.

### A-300 — The Windows lanes run git, Mercurial and Subversion over the WinFsp drive, judged against NTFS with the drive's one stated difference: it makes no hard link (accepted 2026-11-17, Ada's goal of 2026-11-18: git, Mercurial and Subversion on every route, WinFsp among them)
Applied in the same change to: Part 6 ("Real workloads": its row and status), §4.6 (the Windows conformance status),
A-289 (its owed Windows roster), GAPS, `docs/wip/conformance.md`, `crates/conformance/src/workload.rs`
(`Workload::runs_on_windows`, the Windows spellings of `normalize_output`, `StatedDifference`, `stated_differences`,
`compare_with`, the Subversion script, `MSYS` in `ENVIRONMENT`), `crates/conformance/src/record.rs`
(`WorkloadStatus::Stated`, `stated_note`), `matrix.rs` (a summary's stated part), `capability.rs` (the Windows
workloads cell runnable), `xtask/src/conformance/workloads.rs` (which workloads a lane runs, the directory's plain
form, the judgment under the route's stated differences), and CI's `windows-lint` and `windows-arm64` jobs.
- **The decision.** The Windows lanes run the roster's version-control workloads (`git`, `git-history`, `mercurial`,
  `subversion`) over the drive (`slates mount ID E:`): each script once in an NTFS folder of the scratch and once on
  the drive, under the shared environment, judged by exit code, output and tree as every leg is. Git for Windows' `sh`
  runs the scripts. The lanes install Mercurial (7.2.4, PyPI's wheel for each architecture) and Subversion (1.15.0,
  VisualSVN's command-line zip, its SHA-256 pinned). The roster's other workloads are owed a Windows form
  (`Workload::runs_on_windows` false): their scripts lean on tools a Windows runner lacks (rsync, rg, sqlite3, vim, a
  watcher's inotify or FSEvents) or have not run there (cargo, npm, python).
- **What Windows needed of the harness**, each a pure function with unit tests:
  - Windows tools print a directory in several spellings: Python's and Mercurial's `D:\a`, git's and a Subversion file
