    URL's `D:/a`, the shell's `/d/a`, a lowercase drive letter, and a canonical path's verbatim `\\?\D:\a`. Each
    becomes the root token (`normalize_output`), the longest first. A POSIX directory gains no Windows spelling, and
    neither does a drive's root, whose shell spelling (`/d`) would match unrelated text. The harness starts each script
    in the directory's plain form (`plain_path`), the one the tools print.
  - A Subversion file URL names a Windows directory as `file:///D:/a`, so the script takes the directory from `pwd -W`
    where the shell has it (other shells refuse the option, and `pwd` answers). Windows' `svnlook youngest` ends its
    line with a carriage return, which the revision loop drops.
  - Git for Windows' shell copies the target for `ln -s` by default. `MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict` in the shared
    environment makes it a Windows symbolic link, and a failure where it cannot make one, as POSIX's `ln -s` does. So
    the `git` workload's link goes through the drive's reparse points (A-275) on one side and NTFS's on the other.
    Every other shell ignores the variable. **Amended by A-327 (2026-11-18):** the variable is set on the workload's
    `ln -s` alone, since git reads it too and then cannot change directory on the drive; and the shared environment
    has the shell hand Subversion's `^/` URLs on as written (`MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL=^/` since the same day's correction
    in A-327; A-327's first form, `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV`, stopped every conversion, and Mercurial's launcher needs one).
- **The drive's stated difference: no hard link.** WinFsp's driver answers `FileLinkInformation` with
  `STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED` itself, before any file system is asked (v2.1, `src/sys/fileinfo.c` 2023-2025); its volume
  parameters' `HardLinks` bit reads "unimplemented; set to 0" (`inc/winfsp/fsctl.h` 213); and its NTFS compatibility
  page lists hard links as unsupported. So a local git or Mercurial clone copies on the drive where NTFS links it.
  `git-history`'s "objects with two names after the clone" line and `mercurial`'s two "store files with two names"
  lines count links on NTFS and none on the drive; every byte the clones hold is the same.
  - The harness states these three lines for the WinFsp route alone (`stated_differences`), each matched by the start
    both lines share. A pair of lines that differ and both carry one stated start is recorded with both sides
    (`WorkloadStatus::Stated`) and does not fail the suite. Any other difference fails it, and so does a stated start
    none of whose lines differed, so the list only shrinks, as an expected-failure list does.
  - Rejected: printing the counts only where the file system can link (it would hide the very difference the goal
    names); and a list kept outside the code (the lines are three and fixed, and their reason belongs beside the
    comparison that applies it).
  - Mercurial on the drive trusts a link count only after its `checknlink` probe makes a link, so there it copies each
    store file before appending to it. The bytes are the same, and `verify` of all three repositories holds them.
  - Hard-linked clones and stores on the WinFsp route need WinFsp's driver to pass hard links to its file system
    (`FileLinkInformation` and the link queries): a change upstream to a signed kernel driver, outward-facing, so it is
    a decision for Ada. Until then the route states the difference.
- **Proven** on this Mac (2026-11-17; the Windows lanes' first run is the supervisor's):
  `a_windows_directory_is_the_root_token_in_every_spelling_its_tools_print`,
  `the_drives_link_count_is_a_stated_difference_on_its_route_alone`, `a_stated_line_excuses_nothing_else` and
  `a_stated_difference_that_no_longer_differs_fails` (`crates/conformance/src/workload.rs`);
  `the_workload_summary_names_a_routes_stated_differences_apart` (`matrix.rs`);
  `windows_runs_fsx_winfstest_and_the_workloads` (`capability.rs`); `the_windows_lane_runs_the_version_control_workloads`;
  and by use `the_drives_stated_differences_name_the_lines_the_real_clones_print` (`xtask/src/conformance/workloads.rs`).
  That last test runs the real `git-history` and `mercurial` scripts on a host whose clones link (git: 5 of 5 objects;
  Mercurial: 7 of 9 store files, 4 after the clone's commit). It judges each against the same run as a copying clone
  prints it: identical but for exactly one and two stated lines; a difference on a route that states nothing; and,
  against itself, refused because no stated line differed.
- **Owed.** The lanes' first run, which is the supervisor's. The Windows workloads cell's record, re-recorded from that
  run (the tracked record is still the owed skip of 2026-11-05). The other workloads' Windows forms.
- **Amended by A-360 (2026-11-18).** The stated difference is WinFsp's driver's as released: a driver carrying
  `docs/wip/winfsp-patches` forwards a hard link, and the drive makes it. Where a lane's driver makes links, the stated
  lines stop differing and the harness fails them, so the list shrinks in that change.
- **Amended by A-498 (2026-11-18).** Both drivers serve one transport, so the list is chosen by the drive the run uses:
  the harness gives one file of the mount's workload root a second name before the workloads run, and the stated lines
  hold only where the drive refused it. A drive that links is held to NTFS's link counts like every other line.

### A-292 — A held durable reply gives up when its holders are silent, not at a deadline (2026-11-17, built for goal g244; found 2026-11-09 by bug-sweep)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.10's status, "The wait is judged by what it hears, not by the clock".
- `crates/bridge-core/src/durable_bound.rs`: the rule, pure (`DurableBound`, `Heard`, `Spans`, `GaveUp`), and its
  unit tests.
- `crates/server/src/live_ship.rs`: `LiveVolume::heard`, counted in `fold_into` and through `fleet::record_acks_in`;
  `begin_durable_bound`, `judge_durable_bound` and `heard_now` (the control shard's driver waits, read off its registry
  pulse); `wait_durable` (an NFS stable write or `COMMIT`, a Shards `FSYNC`) judged a window at a time; and
  `durability_report`, which a give-up logs.
- `crates/server/src/fuse.rs` and `winfsp.rs`: the held `fsync` and the held flush each hold a `DurableBound`.
  `crates/bridge-virtiofs` (the device, its admission and its serve loop) and `crates/server/src/virtiofs.rs`: the
  device's held `FSYNC`, begun and judged through `BridgeAccess::durable_bound` and `durable_heard`.
- Tests: the rule's unit tests; `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/serve.rs`
  (`a_guests_fsync_of_a_live_volume_waits_while_its_volume_keeps_progressing`,
  `a_guests_fsync_is_not_refused_while_its_receiver_has_not_read_what_came`); `crates/cli/tests/live_fleet.rs`
  (`a_fuse_fsync_on_a_live_volume_waits_out_candidates_that_answer_slowly`, gated on `SLATES_TEST_CLI=1`).
- GAPS "2026-11-09: a healthy live `fsync` was refused at a wall-clock deadline under load", and
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-09-a-healthy-live-fsync-was-refused-at-a-wall-clock-deadline.md`.
- **What was there.** A reply held for a live volume's durability (A-200: a FUSE `fsync`, an NFS stable write or
  `COMMIT`, a Shards `FSYNC`, a virtio-fs `FSYNC`, a WinFsp flush) gave up at one wall-clock deadline of the liveness
  budget from its hold. Load that slowed the candidates or the owner spent it, and a healthy `fsync` whose bytes a
  candidate already held was answered `EIO` (1 in 6 runs on main, 2 in 9 on raft-7 at load 36–145).
- **The rule.** The liveness budget is a window, not a deadline. A wait runs in windows: one in which the volume heard
  something on its durability path (a holder's acknowledged position advancing, its head's or catalog's placement
  gaining an acknowledgement) starts the next; one that heard nothing gives up, once the owner has read what its
  candidates sent before it ended. The daemon's control shard, which receives every acknowledgement and hands each to
  the volume's shard, must have waited in its driver twice since the silence was seen, and the verdict comes at a later
  look, the looks a heartbeat apart. Whatever it hears, the wait ends at the failover SLO from the hold, the operator's
  bound on how long an object may go unserved before a takeover serves it (banned item 8). Every transport judges by
  the one pure module.
- **Why.** The budget's own meaning is a holder's silence: past it, "a holder that has not answered is not a live one
  to wait for". Only what the volume hears says whether its holders are speaking; the wall clock also counts the time
  the owner and the candidates spend off their CPUs. The receiver's two waits keep an owner kept off its CPU across a
  window's end from taking its own deafness for its candidates' silence (raft's failing run showed the owner itself
  600 ms late).
- **Evidence.** The slow-candidates flow: 3 of 3 `EIO` at 1.0013–1.0037 s under the old deadline, 6 of 6 answered in
  1.50–1.59 s under the windows (adacachy2, 2026-11-09). The rule's unit tests, including a trickle of other writes'
  acknowledgements ended at the bound after ten windows (red with the bound removed: a thousand windows, no end), and
  a late window's acknowledgements read after its end starting the next (red under the windows alone). The device's
  two tests, each answered `EIO` at one window by the rule before.
- **Owed.** The supervisor's runs of the live FUSE flows under load on main, and a Windows run of
  `crates/cli/tests/live_winfsp.rs`. Open (GAPS): a window can still be silent through the owner's own delay in asking.

### A-311 — Starts that fail in a row are backed off from their own life, however long each takes; the backoff doubles to the failover SLO (accepted 2026-11-12, the supervisor's ruling: "the anchor budget approved, plus serve-then-crash backoff and a derived RETRY_CAP_NS"; built 2026-11-17 for goal g254, the never-served half first and the serve-then-crash half the same day)

Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/anchor/src/supervise.rs`: `RestartPolicy` is the backoff's cap alone (`RestartPolicy::derive(failover_slo_ns)`);
  `crash_loop_backoff`, pure, with its unit tests; the failed starts in a row (`CRASH_LOOP_FAILURES`,
  `Step::Restarted::failed_in_a_row` in place of `in_window`). The restart window, `RETRY_CAP_NS` and
  `Supervisor::set_policy` are removed.
- `crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs`: the policy derived once from the daemon configuration's `failover_slo_ns` and logged
  with its derivation; a measured start no longer re-derives it; the restart line names the failed starts in a row.
- Tests: `crates/anchor/tests/anchor.rs` (`a_crash_loop_of_starts_longer_than_the_window_is_backed_off`, red on main; the
  crash-loop, served-restart, doubling, device-hold, torn-publication and device-refusal fixtures under the rule),
  `crates/anchor/tests/handles_windows.rs` (the prompt fixture's one exit is now a restart), the role harness
  `crates/server/tests/common/supervised.rs` (the role restarted at its exit is stopped at once), and
  `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` (the many-shard start's watch ends at the first start kill; the hold-refusal fixture's
  policy).
- A-119's status, §2.6's status, GAPS, `docs/wip/bench/kill_storm.sh`'s comment, and
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-11-starts-longer-than-the-restart-window-were-restarted-at-once-forever.md`.

- **What was there.** The anchor counted a daemon's failed starts (exits before it served, A-119 as amended 2026-11-09)
  inside a window of the recovery budget, a second, against the starts the budget held at the longest start measured,
  and backed off past that count from the window, doubling to 60 s. A start longer than the window fell in a window of
  its own every time, so it was never a crash loop and was restarted at once for good: B10's Linux gate on adacachy2
  (load 67-73) killed and restarted a 407-shard start every second for 27 minutes.
- **The rule.** A failed start is restarted at once. The second in a row is a crash loop, recorded as `CrashLoop`, and
  restarted after a backoff of at least the failed daemon's own life, spawn to exit: the loop's first backoff that life,
  each next twice the last, doubled no further than the cap and never shorter than the failed start took. A daemon that
  serves resets the count and the backoff. So a loop spends at most half its time starting, however long each start
  takes, and supervision still never gives up (A-119).
- **Why two in a row.** One failure is an event, and restarting it at once is the quickest recovery there is; a second
  in a row is the first evidence that the next start may fail the same way. The window let "budget over start" failures
  through at full speed each second while starts were short, and treated none as a loop once a start outlasted it.
- **The cap, derived.** The operator's failover SLO (`FAILOVER_SLO_NS`, ten seconds until the operator gives one): the
  outage the operator accepts for a failed owner, and the lease the daemon grants every NFSv4 client
  (`crates/server/src/delegation.rs`). Capped there, a looping daemon starts again within one SLO of its last failure, so
  once the loop's cause clears it serves within the bound the operator set, and its NFSv4 clients' leases have not all
  lapsed meanwhile. The old cap was a hard Linux NFS mount's major timeout (`nfs(5)`, `timeo` 600), which no mount slates
  makes sets. The backoff's floor, the failed start's own life, may exceed the cap, and wins: a start longer than the
  SLO still never spends more than half the loop's time.
- **Evidence.** Red on main 29ef4521 (the liveness agent's run, `2a5570e4d`): a child whose every start runs 400 ms and
  fails before serving, under a policy whose window was 200 ms, was restarted at once 4 times of 4, backed off None. On
  this change the same child is a crash loop at its second exit, backed off its own life: 548 ms after starts of 400 ms
  (`cargo test -p slates-anchor --test anchor -- --nocapture a_crash_loop_of_starts_longer`, an 18-core M-series
  MacBook at load 15, 2026-11-17).
- **The serve-then-crash half (built 2026-11-17).** Applied in the same change to: `crates/anchor/src/layout.rs`
  (`SUP_RECOVERED`, the anchor's verdict; the docs of `SUP_SERVING` and `State::CrashLoop`), `segment.rs`
  (`Supervision::mark_recovered` and `recovered_since`, zeroed by `record_start`), `supervise.rs` (`recovered_at`, the
  judgment at every step, `has_recovered`, `start_took_ns`), `crates/api/src/role/anchor.rs` (a daemon looked at every
  beat until it is judged recovered, and the verdict logged once a daemon), the wire's `DaemonReport::recovered`
  (appended; `slates status`, its JSON and MCP's `slates.status`; `slates_api::CONTRACT` raised), and the end-to-end
  flows that kill daemons in a row, which now kill each once it is judged recovered (`crates/cli/tests/support/recovered.rs`,
  used by `held_rendezvous.rs`, `nfs_held.rs`, `merge_kill.rs`, `winfsp.rs` and `guest_vhost.rs`).
  - **The rule.** A daemon's start runs from its spawn to the step that first sees its serving mark, and it has
    recovered once it has served as long again. An exit before then is a failed start, counted as an exit before the
    mark is; after it, the daemon is restarted at once and the count starts again. The anchor publishes the verdict
    when it first holds (`SUP_RECOVERED`), and `slates status` reports it as `recovered`. So a loop of daemons that each
    die a moment after serving is backed off as a loop of failed starts is, and spends at most half its time starting.
  - **Why the anchor's own steps time it.** The supervisor trusts only its own clock, which tests drive with clocks of
    their own; the anchor looks at a daemon every beat until the verdict, so the start's end is late by at most a beat,
    which can only delay the verdict, never grant it early.
  - **Why the kill tests wait for it.** A test that kills daemons one after another to prove something outlives a kill
    is not testing a crash loop. They waited only for a new daemon to answer, and under this rule without the wait
    `held_rendezvous` failed 4 of 4 at load 21-63 (the liveness agent's run of 2026-11-11). Tests that kill once need
    nothing: a first failed start is restarted at once.
- **A long start** that beats per unit of work, so the 407-shard start is not killed in the first place, is A-312.

### A-312 — A daemon's start beats its supervisor at every unit of its work until the watchdog takes the beat over (2026-11-17, built for goal g254: "a long start beats per unit of work")

Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/rt/src/runtime.rs`: `Runtime::start_sized` and `start_with_sized` take a progress hook, called after each
  shard's registration, each pair ring (`connect_pairs`), each worker's spawn and each acknowledged build
  (`await_readiness`); `Runtime::start`, `start_with` and the simulation report to no one.
- `crates/server/src/daemon.rs`: `StartBeat`, the supervision block's heartbeat written by the starting thread from the
  segment's attach, through the runtime's start and each shard's spawn, until the watchdog thread starts;
  `Daemon::start_beats`; a boot line saying how often the start beat.
- Tests: `crates/rt/tests/lifecycle.rs` (`a_start_reports_every_unit_of_its_work_as_it_goes`) and
  `crates/server/tests/daemon.rs` (`a_daemons_start_beats_at_every_unit_of_its_work`). The end-to-end proof is
  `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs` `a_start_whose_shards_sum_past_a_window_comes_up` (gated on `SLATES_TEST_CLI=1`), whose
  watch fails at the anchor's first start kill since A-311.
- §2.6's status and GAPS.

- **What was there.** The anchor judges a start in its own CPU time until its first beat, and kills one whose busiest
  thread runs a liveness window of CPU without beating (§4.14, A-228's rule for a start). Nothing in a daemon beat
  until its watchdog thread ran, at the end of `Daemon::start_with_fleet`, and the work before it grows with the
  shards: a driver and a registration for each, a ring for every ordered pair, N(N-1) of them, and a thread for each.
  At 407 shards on B10's Linux gate (load 67-73) the start's busiest thread ran 1,009-1,037 ms of CPU without a beat,
  and the anchor killed it every time; A-311 backs that loop off, but the start never came up.
- **The rule.** A start beats as it goes. The starting thread writes the heartbeat at the segment's attach, before the
  runtime starts, after each unit of the runtime's work, after each shard's spawn, and once more just before the
  watchdog thread starts, which is the beat's only writer from then on. Each unit is microseconds, so a start that
  keeps progressing keeps beating, however many shards it starts. A start stuck in a unit stops beating: the anchor
  finds the beat lapsed with no watchdog look and judges the process by its CPU from there (A-232's rule for a silent
  watchdog), so a stuck start is still killed, a window later than the start judgment would have killed it. A start's
  beat is the same signal as the watchdog's: the daemon is making progress.
- **Why not start the watchdog first.** It judges shards, and before the runtime there are none, so it would beat
  while the starting thread spun: the case the start judgment exists to catch.
- **Why not only make the rings cheaper.** Each shard could make its own outbound rings on its own thread, spreading
  the quadratic work. That shortens a start but bounds no unit of it: a start is long for other reasons too (a page
  fault cost 128 µs at load 62, `page_fault_ns` in the liveness agent's kill-loop log of 2026-11-11), and a beat at each
  unit holds whatever the start's length.
- **Evidence.** The runtime's hook is called once per unit, `S·(S-1) + 3·S` times for a start of S = 3 shards. A
  daemon's start beats at least once a unit (`Daemon::start_beats`): across `cargo test -p slates-server` on a 32-core
  Mac Studio (2026-11-18, at load 10 to 23) the boot line said 7, 13, 57 and 91 beats for starts of 1, 2, 6 and 8
  shards, `S² + 3·S + 3` each (the hook's units, a beat a shard spawned, and one each at the attach, before the
  runtime and before the watchdog). The attribution of the 407-shard start's long thread to the pair rings is the
  code's arithmetic (165,242 rings), not yet measured.
- **Owed** (GAPS): the supervisor's run of `a_start_whose_shards_sum_past_a_window_comes_up` under load, and the
  starting thread's CPU by phase at 407 shards.

### A-290 — A guest's own attribute namespaces are its data on a guest kernel's route, and no host's route shows or sets them (2026-11-18, built for goal g268, what Shards needs from slates)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.5 "Extended attributes": the namespaces bullet. §4.6, the Shards form: the bullet on the guest's attributes; the
  FUSE extended-attribute status of 2026-10-06, amended. GAPS: A-281's entry, whose owed list loses this item.
- `crates/bridge-core`: `USER_NAMESPACE`, `GUEST_NAMESPACES`, `AttributeNamespaces` (`Host`, `Guest`, `reaches`),
  `guest_only`, `Bridge::attribute_namespaces` (a host's by default), `VolumeBridge::serving_a_guest`, `ScopedBridge`
  passing its inner bridge's kind on; the AppleDouble view (`volume_bridge/view.rs`) shows, removes and sets none of a
  guest's names. The tests: `a_guests_namespaces_are_reached_by_its_route_alone` (unit) and
  `a_hosts_view_neither_shows_nor_sets_nor_removes_a_guests_own_attributes` (`tests/appledouble_view.rs`).
- `crates/bridge-fuse`: `bridge.rs` reaches an attribute through the bridge's kind (`reached_attribute`) in GETXATTR,
  LISTXATTR, SETXATTR and REMOVEXATTR; `needs_barrier` names SETXATTR and REMOVEXATTR. The test:
  `a_guests_own_attributes_are_kept_for_its_route_and_no_hosts_mount_reaches_them` (`tests/shards_fs.rs`).
- `crates/server`: the Shards stream (`shards.rs`) and slates' own virtio-fs device (`virtiofs.rs`) serve a guest;
  `verbs.rs` refuses a declaration of a guest's name on a work `Unsupported`. The tests:
  `a_guests_own_attributes_are_its_data_on_every_stream_and_no_hosts_mount_lists_them` and
  `a_guests_acknowledged_attribute_survives_a_daemon_restart` (`tests/shards.rs`),
  `a_guest_devices_own_attributes_are_kept_and_no_hosts_mount_lists_them` (`tests/virtiofs.rs`), and the work's
  `declare_guest_attribute_part` (`tests/daemon.rs`).

- **What was there.** Every FUSE route stored `user.` names alone and answered any other `EOPNOTSUPP` (§4.6's FUSE
  status of 2026-10-06), since a host's `security.`, `trusted.` and `system.` names belong to its own security modules,
  administrator and ACLs. A microVM's guest kernel keeps its own there: `setcap` sets `security.capability` on a
  binary, and overlayfs keeps `trusted.overlay.*` on an upper directory a guest makes on its share (an image build
  inside the VM). Both failed on a slates stream and succeeded on Shards' own server, which keeps them on a Linux host
  under `user.shards.` and passes them through on macOS (Shards' `server_unix.rs` `host_xattr`, `guest_xattr`, at
  183fe264e). Shards' coordinator ranked this second of what it needs (2026-11-18).
- **The rule.** Each transport's bridge says which namespaces its caller reaches. A host's mount (FUSE or NFS, and the
  AppleDouble view a macOS NFSv3 mount reads) reaches `user.` alone, as before. A guest kernel's route (a Shards stream,
  slates' own virtio-fs device) reaches `user.`, `trusted.` and `security.`, and the volume keeps those like any
  attribute: a snapshot, a clone, an export and a takeover carry them. A host's mount never lists them, reads them
  `ENODATA` and is refused `EOPNOTSUPP` setting or removing one; the AppleDouble view neither shows nor removes them,
  and refuses a sidecar naming one `NotPermitted` whole, so a host never half-writes the guest's attributes. A landing
  writes no attribute at all (its seam has no verb for one, held by `a_landing_never_materializes_a_security_capability_xattr`),
  and the base plane reads none from the host, so nothing of the host's own labels reaches a guest either.
- **No host's channel sets them.** A guest's kernel acts on these names (a capability on a binary its run executes),
  and inside the guest only its privileged processes may set them (xattr(7): `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` for `trusted.`,
  `CAP_SETFCAP` for a capability). A declaration on a work (§4.16, the SDKs' and MCP's `set_xattr` and
  `remove_xattr`) is a host's channel, so it is refused `Unsupported` for a guest's name, as a host's mount is; before
  this change a guest could not see such a name, so the channel's reach mattered to no one.
- **Why not Shards' mapping.** Shards' server must keep the guest's names on a host file, whose `trusted.` and
  `security.` names are the host kernel's, so it renames them into `user.shards.`. A slates volume is no host file:
  it keeps the guest's names as they are, and each route's kind decides who reaches them, so no prefix is reserved
  and nothing is renamed.
- **The durability fix found with it.** `needs_barrier` named every namespace and metadata change but SETXATTR and
  REMOVEXATTR, so on a FUSE mount, a virtio-fs device and a Shards stream an acknowledged attribute change was not
  published before its reply, and a daemon's death after the reply lost it; NFSv4.2's barrier already named its
  attribute calls. `a_guests_acknowledged_attribute_survives_a_daemon_restart` fails without the two opcodes (a
  `user.` attribute set, a capability set and a removal, read back after a second daemon recovers the segment) and
  passes with them: 3 of 3 runs red without them, the second daemon listing nothing (kiln run r423, macOS arm64,
  2026-11-18; the bug record of that date).
- **Not here: POSIX ACLs.** Shards' coordinator ranks them third; A-302 keeps them.

### A-302 — A guest's POSIX ACLs are its data on a guest kernel's route, their named owners kept through the owner view (2026-11-18, built for goal g268, what Shards needs from slates)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.5 "Extended attributes": the ACL bullet. §4.6, the Shards form: the guest's attributes' bullet and the status of
  this date. A-290's entry, whose "Not here" line now points here. GAPS: A-281's entry, whose owed list loses ACLs.
- `crates/bridge-core`: `POSIX_ACL_NAMES` (`POSIX_ACL_ACCESS`, `POSIX_ACL_DEFAULT`) and `is_posix_acl`; a guest's
  route reaches the two names (`AttributeNamespaces::reaches`) and `guest_only` counts them, so a host's mount, the
  AppleDouble view and a work's declaration refuse them as they refuse A-290's names. The unit test
  `a_guests_namespaces_are_reached_by_its_route_alone` asks about both names and about other `system.` names.
- `crates/bridge-fuse`: `posix_acl.rs` (Linux's ACL value checked and its named ids turned each way, with its unit
  tests, the hostile values among them); `bridge.rs` turns an ACL toward the volume's ids at SETXATTR and toward the
  guest's at GETXATTR (`acl_turned`) and refuses a default ACL on anything but a directory (`default_acl_refused`).
  The test: `a_guests_acls_are_kept_through_its_owner_view_and_no_hosts_mount_reaches_them` (`tests/shards_fs.rs`).
- `crates/server`: `a_guests_own_attributes_are_its_data_on_every_stream_and_no_hosts_mount_lists_them`
  (`tests/shards.rs`) sets an access ACL over a real daemon's stream as well.

- **What was there.** A-290 kept a guest's `trusted.` and `security.` names and refused every `system.` name, so a
  guest's `setfacl` failed with `EOPNOTSUPP` on a slates stream, as did `cp -a`, `tar --acls` and `rsync -A` keeping
  one, while Shards' own server keeps them (its `host_xattr` hands every name but `trusted.` and `security.` to the
  host's file as it is, Shards 183fe264e). Shards' coordinator ranked ACLs third of what it needs (2026-11-18).
- **The rule.** A guest kernel's route keeps `system.posix_acl_access` on any node and `system.posix_acl_default` on a
  directory, refusing a default ACL elsewhere `EACCES` as Linux's `set_posix_acl` does. A value is checked as Linux's
  `posix_acl_from_xattr` and `posix_acl_valid` check one, refused whole `EOPNOTSUPP` for another version and `EINVAL`
  for anything else malformed, so nothing half-parsed is kept. Its named users and groups are turned through the
  route's owner view (A-281) toward the ids the volume keeps when set and toward the guest's when read, and put back
  in id order, the order Linux's own ACLs keep and `libacl` expects. A value the volume keeps that no longer parses is
  `EIO` to a reader: the volume's fault, never the caller's. Every route but a guest kernel's refuses both names, as it
  refuses A-290's.
- **Stored, not enforced (superseded the same day by A-314, at Shards' coordinator's ask: enforced).** Neither slates
  nor Shards' own server negotiates `FUSE_POSIX_ACL`, so the guest's kernel
  hands an ACL through and checks the mode bits it is shown (`fs/fuse/acl.c`: a server without the flag "could get
  and set POSIX ACLs without them being used for permission checking by the vfs"). The same guest therefore sees the
  same behaviour whichever server serves its share. Enforcement was weighed and not taken now: the flag makes the
  guest's kernel ask for an ACL on each inode's first permission check (one more round trip per inode on a stream that
  carries one request at a time), and the server would have to keep the mode and the ACL's mask in step on every
  route, a chmod through a host's mount included, and apply a default ACL at every create. Nothing Shards runs asks
  for it; it is recorded here should a consumer need it.
- **Evidence.** The codec's unit tests (the turn both ways with the run, a third user and the host named; the minimal
  and empty ACLs; thirteen refused values and every bit flip of a valid one's tags), the dispatch's test over a volume
  holding the host's and the run's files, and the real daemon's stream, whose second stream reads the ACL as set and
  whose NFSv4.2 port lists no ACL. Owed: Shards' own guest test over a slates stream (`tests/slates_fs.rs`), after its
  v0.8.0 tag and its bump of the slates revision it pins.

### A-303 — A Shards stream hands its device tables at a VM's save and takes them back at its restore (2026-11-18, built for goal g268, what Shards needs from slates; Shards' D176 part 5)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.6, the Shards form: the save-and-restore bullet and the status of this date; A-161's entry, whose control-ask
  bullet is amended. GAPS: A-281's entry, whose owed list loses the tables.
- `crates/vfs`: `Volume::held_by` (one attachment's references and opens, in inode order, the recovery image's own
  record) and `Volume::adopt_held` (a fresh attachment given them, all checked before any is given). The tests:
  `crates/vfs/tests/held.rs`.
- `crates/bridge-core`: `OwnerView::swapped`, the pair a view swaps, which the tables keep.
- `crates/bridge-fuse`: `shards_fs.rs` adds `split_frame_bounded` (a control frame bounded apart from a request),
  `control_answer` and `CONTROL_ANSWER_MOST`.
- `crates/server`: `shards/tables.rs` (the tables, their codec and their bound, with their unit tests, hostile ones
  among them); `shards.rs` answers SAVE (`answer_save`, `save`, held for an ingest by `dax::hold_save_for_ingest`) and
  RESTORE (`answer_restore`, `restore`), counts `shards.saved` and `shards.restored`, and ledgers
  `shards.save_refused` and `shards.restore_refused`; `verbs.rs` lends the snapshot verb's body out as
  `take_snapshot`. The tests: `a_saved_guest_goes_on_over_a_clone_of_its_cut` and
  `a_saved_guest_is_restored_on_its_volume_unchanged_and_refused_otherwise` (`tests/shards.rs`), and the hostile
  control asks' counts by kind.

- **What was there.** Shards' device asks each share's server for its tables while it pauses a VM to save it, keeps
  them in the VM's snapshot, and hands them to the restored VM's server before its first request (Shards' D176 part
  5: each node by the server's id with its lookups, each open handle, and the bytes of files held with no name). A
  slates stream refused both asks, so a VM with a slates share could not be saved, and kiln's plan to move a VM's
  snapshot and its slates overlay together (CP-T4.8) had nothing to stand on. Shards' coordinator confirmed the
  contract (2026-11-18): SAVE answers `[0, tables]`, opaque; SAVE takes a slates snapshot at the cut and names it;
  RESTORE comes on a new stream before any request and accepts the named snapshot, a clone of it, or the live volume
  unchanged since the cut, else `[1, why]`.
- **What the tables hold, and why so little.** The volume and the snapshot the SAVE took, the directory presented, the
  owner view (A-281), and each inode the guest holds with its references and how many are open handles, exactly as the
  volume keeps them for the attachment. A node is an inode number, and a clone shares its origin's numbers (A-166), so
  no translation is needed. No handle table: a request names its node, a READDIR its cookies, and a handle the
  restored stream never issued gives its open back at its release through the takeover path that already exists
  (A-152). No file's bytes either: a file the guest holds with no name left is in the snapshot of the cut, so a clone
  of the snapshot holds it, where Shards' server, keeping no snapshot, must carry the bytes.
- **The cut.** The SAVE first waits for the guest's stores through its DAX maps to reach the volume (the ingest a
  `FSYNC` waits for), since a restored VM refills its maps from the volume and would otherwise lose them. It then takes
  the snapshot with the snapshot verb's own body (its barrier included, so another attachment's request in flight
  refuses the save and it may be asked again), for the attachment's own principal, so a save does nothing that
  principal could not ask itself; and it publishes the shard before answering, so the snapshot the VM's snapshot names
  survives a daemon restart.
- **The restore's checks.** The RESTORE must be the stream's first frame. The tables are bounded before anything is
  allocated for them by the longest a shard could make (its inode slab's capacity, an entry each, from the encoding
  itself), then checked by their CRC-32C, their format and a canonical decode. The stream must present the directory
  the saved one did, and serve either the volume saved, unchanged since the cut (`Volume::unchanged_since`, A-201), or
  a clone of the cut's snapshot (its lineage edge). The volume then checks every entry before giving any: one inode
  once, in rising order, each referenced, no more opens than references, an inode it holds, a count it can take. A
  refused restore changes nothing. The live volume holds no file the saved guest held with no name once the saved
  stream ended (its sweep reclaimed it), so such a guest is restored onto a clone of the cut.
- **Not here.** A SAVE's snapshot is published on the owner shard; a live-shipped volume's candidates (§4.10) are not
  waited for, as a `FSYNC`'s durable reply waits (built since, A-516, 2026-11-19: the tables wait for them). A clone
  keeps no orphan record for a nameless file it carries from its snapshot, so once a restored guest lets such a file go
  nothing reclaims it until the clone is destroyed; that is so for any clone of a snapshot taken while a file was held
  with no name, restored or not (GAPS; built since, A-532, 2026-11-19: the snapshot keeps the orphans it froze, and a
  clone carries each with an orphan record).
- **Evidence.** The tables' unit tests (a round trip, the same bytes twice, every cut, every bit flipped, another
  format, trailing bytes, a vector of `u32::MAX` entries, the bound's arithmetic), the volume's three tests, and the two
  by-use tests over a real daemon named above. Owed on Shards' side: `shards restore` taking a served share and its
  real-VM test of a save and a restore over slates, after its v0.8.0 tag.

### A-310 — slates-api's seam: the volume verbs as a trait an instance and a simulator implement, held to one conformance suite (2026-11-18, built for goal g268, what Hex needs from slates)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.12: "The seam" and its status; the embedding status's owed line, and A-278's owed list, marked built. GAPS: the
  embedding library row. `docs/library.md`: the seam's section and the owed list.
- `crates/api`: `seam.rs` (`Volumes`, implemented by `Instance`), `sim.rs` (`SimVolumes`), `lib.rs` (the modules, their
  exports, the crate's notes, `CONTRACT` 9), `error.rs` (`Error::of_ipc` lent to the crate, for the simulator's pair).
  The tests: `the_seam_conforms` run by `an_instance_answers_the_seams_conformance_suite` and
  `the_simulator_answers_the_seams_conformance_suite`, and `the_simulator_holds_what_it_was_given_room_for`
  (`tests/api.rs`).

- **Why.** Hex, kiln's scheduler and runtime, keeps its volumes on slates (its design's README; kiln's plan T7,
  CP-T7.8 volumes through a CSI-like interface and CP-T7.13 claims on slates), and its rules reach another product only
  through its `-api` crate, "each trait with a simulator implementation and a conformance suite both pass" (Hex
  `CLAUDE.md` §9). Its own simulated cluster (`hex-sim`, after kwok) runs no daemon. A-278 and A-299 left the seam owed;
  their owner (goal g262) handed it to g268 on 2026-11-18, on the condition that it add no type to the contract.
- **The rule.** `Volumes` carries what a scheduler does with volumes and nothing it does not: provision (overlay,
  empty, clone, green, work), snapshot, destroy a snapshot, destroy, list, serve to a Shards VMM, mount, unmount,
  detach, each with the `Instance` verb's own signature and types. Landings, merges and write policy stay on the
  instance. `SimVolumes` answers what an instance answers for every case the suite runs, and documents what it does
  not do (serve bytes, mount anything); its tables are bounded by the caller's own number.
- **Rejected: an associated type for what serving returns.** A simulator could hand out a token instead of a stream end,
  but then the trait's `serve_shards` would not be the contract's, and a host could not move from the simulator to an
  instance without a type changing. The simulator makes a real connected pair (`slates_ipc::stream::pair`, a duplex
  pipe on Windows) and keeps its end unanswered, so a host's plumbing, a VMM's spawn with the end included, runs the
  same over both.
- **Found.** A pinned snapshot's destroy reaches a consumer as `Invalid::Request("Pinned")`: the daemon maps the volume
  core's `Pinned` through its catch-all (`refusal_of_vfs`) to `BadRequest`. The suite asserts the class over both, and a
  typed class is owed to the contract (told to its owner).
- **Evidence.** The suite over an in-process daemon and over the simulator, and the simulator's bound. Owed: Hex's own
  use of it, when Hex takes slates (its agent was idle until 2026-11-19).

### A-306 — A resent forward keeps the place its first send had in the forward lane (2026-11-18, built for goal g245, a dead lent session; finding (b) of the bug record of 2026-11-09)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.8 "Lookup": the status of 2026-11-18.
- `crates/server/src/forward_lane.rs`: `Place`; each ticket's place, and the lane's queue ordered by place, then
  ticket; `ForwardLanes::queue` and `leave` (the queue's discipline apart from the shard's state) and
  `begin_queued_with` (apart from the session); the count `fleet.forward.resent_in_place`; the module doc.
  `crates/server/src/fleet.rs` (`forward_batch_over_leader_session` takes the place) and `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`
  (`resolve_and_forward` keeps one place across its resends; `forward_once` passes it).
- Tests: `a_resend_is_begun_ahead_of_every_forward_first_queued_after_it` and the model test
  `a_lanes_forwards_are_begun_in_the_order_they_were_first_queued` (`forward_lane.rs`), and
  `a_read_through_a_dead_session_keeps_its_place_behind_a_burst` (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`).
- GAPS: the load test's "dead record session" entry. The bug record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-resent-forward-lost-its-place-in-the-lane.md`.
- **What was there.** A forwarder gives its batch up once none of its forwards has progressed for its stall budget,
  queued or begun, and its caller sends the same requests again under their own ids while the owner is not confirmed
  dead and the failover bound allows. Every send was a new batch with fresh tickets, and a lane begins its queue in
  ticket order, so every resend went to the back.
- **The rule.** A forward's place is the ticket its first send was given; a resend is queued at it, each request of a
  batch at its own first ticket. A lane begins its queued forwards in the order of their places: the order of first
  sends, whatever has been given up and sent again since. Its wait is bounded by the forwards first sent before it.
- **Why.** Goal g245, finding (b): behind a 256-client burst a read through a client node whose session to its owner
  died was refused at its failover bound in 1 of 10 runs and answered after 9.2 and 9.5 s in two more (2.3 to 10.5 s
  in all), its every resend given up again behind forwards first sent after it. With its place kept: 4.1 to 6.5 s in
  10 of 10.
- **Cost.** None new: a queued forward's key in the same ordered set is a pair, and a resend's insert and a leave's
  remove are the same logarithmic steps. A forward still queued is given up and resent at its stall budget as before:
  with its place kept that loses it nothing, but it cycles the backlog once a budget on the control shard, which is
  owed apart (GAPS).

### A-315 — A forward lane's silence is judged once its shard has read what came, and a queued forward counts its lane's progress until its failover bound (2026-11-18, built for goal g255; A-306's owed item; supersedes loadtest-scale's lane poll clock, `6da9670d`, never on main)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.8 "Lookup": the status of 2026-11-18 (A-315), and A-306's status, whose owed item this builds.
- `crates/server/src/forward_lane.rs`: `Stall` (pure, with `Heard`, `Verdict`, `GaveUp` and `Noted`), the lane's
  `progress_ns` (a forward begun, a reply taken, bytes of a reply read), `turns_begun` and `drained_turn` (`begin_turn`,
  `mark_drained`: the latest turn that read the session's own socket empty, `left_empty`; `note_sessionless_turn`: a
  driving turn that found the peer with no session at all), `look_in` and `answer_with`
  (the view and the reply's bookkeeping apart from the shard and the session), `failover_bound_from`; the counts
  `fleet.forward.given_up_silent`, `fleet.forward.given_up_at_bound`, `fleet.forward.silence_awaited_receiver`,
  `fleet.forward.held_by_lane` and `fleet.forward.sessionless_turn`; the module doc. `crates/server/src/fleet.rs`
  (`forward_batch_over_leader_session` takes the bound; `forward_over_leader_session` passes one from its own send) and
  `crates/server/src/verbs.rs` (`resolve_and_forward` passes its failover bound, from the first send, to every send
  through `forward_once`).
  `crates/transport/src/endpoint.rs`: `Endpoint::datagrams_received`, the datagrams an established session took, by
  which a lane's turn knows it read the socket empty (stream bytes would not tell: a datagram of acknowledgements alone
  consumes none), and `Endpoint::reads_its_own_socket`, since only a session that reads its own socket proves the
  socket empty by an empty read.
- Tests: in `forward_lane.rs`, `a_silence_is_given_up_only_once_a_turn_begun_after_it_reads_the_socket_empty`,
  `progress_while_a_silence_awaits_its_receiver_starts_the_quiet_again`,
  `a_queued_forward_counts_its_lanes_progress_until_its_failover_bound`,
  `a_silence_past_its_bound_is_given_up_without_its_receiver`,
  `a_batch_whose_own_forwards_progress_is_never_given_up_at_its_bound`,
  `a_queued_forward_behind_a_moving_lane_is_kept_past_its_own_budget` and the model test
  `a_stall_judges_every_history_as_the_rule_reads_it`; in `crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`,
  `a_held_origin_gives_up_no_forward_whose_reply_came_while_it_was_held`, and
  `a_takeover_adopts_the_newest_head_a_holder_left_out_of_its_pages`, which failed without the sessionless turn.
- GAPS: the load test's "dead record session" entry (A-306's open item, closed) and the R3 debt of
  `LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS` (class B, the forward lane). The bug record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-forward-lanes-silence-was-judged-before-its-shard-read-what-came.md`.
- **What was there.** A forwarder looked at its batch whenever it woke, and gave it up once none of its forwards had
  progressed for its stall budget on the wall clock: a liveness budget plus the path's measured round-trip tail. Two
  things counted against a live owner. An origin whose control shard was kept off its CPU past a budget woke with the
  owner's replies unread in its socket, and the waiting forwarders, woken by their timers, ran ahead of the lane's
  driver, which reads one datagram a turn, and gave those batches up. And a forward still queued behind the session's
  stream credit, of which nothing had been sent, was given up at its budget while its lane moved, and resent: behind a
  256-client burst, 17,000 to 52,000 batches a run cycled through the control shard that way (A-306).
- **The rule.** A batch is quiet from the latest of its start, its own forwards' progress and, while one of them is
  still queued, its lane's progress, the last counted only up to the failover bound from the forward's first send. A
  batch quiet for its stall budget before the bound is given up only once a driving turn of its lane, begun after the
  silence was first seen, has read the session's own socket empty (`forward_lane::left_empty`: its drive took no
  datagram, or one more receive that does not wait took none, counted by `Endpoint::datagrams_received`;
  `Lane::drained_turn`) or has found the peer with no session at all (`forward_lane::note_sessionless_turn`), looking
  again every poll interval (`HEARTBEAT_NS / POLL_PER_PERIOD`); progress meanwhile ends
  the confirmation, and a later silence is confirmed afresh. Past the bound a quiet batch is given up at once. A batch
  whose own forwards progress is never given up: a long read stalls only when no byte of it comes for a budget, never
  at a deadline.
- **Why.** The record link's sessions read their own sockets (`Endpoint::client`), so a turn that reads its socket
  empty has read every datagram that reached it before, its settles putting the replies into the lane; begun after the
  silence was first seen, it has read everything that came before the silence was judged. Turns are ordered by the
  lane's own count (`Lane::turns_begun`), exact on the one shard thread, where clock readings within one step need not
  be. A lane whose peer has no session at all has nothing left to read: a dropped session is never put back
  (`fleet::return_sessions` drops a late return), so none of its replies reaches the lane, and a forward begun on it is
  answered unanswered by the next session's settle; one lent to another borrower is not such a lane, since that
  borrower reads the socket and the lane settles it on the session's return. Without the sessionless turn a survivor's
  forward to a stopped owner, whose session its link dropped before the forward's silence was seen, was held to its
  failover bound (`fleet.forward.no_session` and `fleet.forward.given_up_at_bound` 1 each, 3 of 3 runs). Two proofs
  were tried first, and the CI runs refused both. The control shard's two waits in its driver since the
  silence (A-292's receiver rule) gave all 7 waiting batches up in 2 of 18 runs of the held-origin test, each run's lane
  having found its session lent to the link (`fleet.lent_to.link` 1): the shard waits while the link's discovery page
  holds the session, the lane's replies unsettled. And a turn begun after those waits that took nothing kept a forward
  its owner never answered open in 2 of 3 runs of `a_silent_forward_gives_up_while_its_session_carries_others` on
  ubuntu-latest (a session busy with other replies is never found so), while the waits themselves, made the
  precondition of an empty read, held one past its test's window in 1 of 6 on the merged tree, its shard kept busy by
  3,035 other replies. The lane's state lives on its shard, so the verdict needs no further look, as A-292's
  hand-off to a volume's shard does. A queued forward has sent nothing, so its lane moving is the only progress it can
  make; an open one keeps to its own reply's bytes, since bytes of other forwards' replies kept forwards an owner never
  answered open for good (the 298 forwards of 2026-11-07). The failover bound is the operator's bound on how long an
  owner may go unserved, the bound the caller's resends already keep, so nothing here waits past it for a receiver that
  never waits (always busy) or a lane that never begins a forward.
- **Why not loadtest-scale's poll clock.** `6da9670d` counted the quiet on a clock each lane's driving turns credited:
  a turn's wall time up to the larger of a 10 ms poll pace and the CPU its shard ran. It assumed an idle shard's timer
  fires on time. Windows' completion-port wait keeps the system's 15.6 ms tick (`crates/rt/src/iocp.rs` asks no finer
  timer), and Windows charges a thread's CPU time a tick at a time, so by the code an idle origin's clock ran at about
  two thirds of the wall there. The test that wants a forward resent at its budget saw none resent, 5 of 5 on
  `windows-latest` (`an_unanswered_forward_is_sent_again_within_the_takeover_bound`, run 44230887960), and it was
  reverted from the B13 stack (`b458723c9`). The receiver's waits are counted the same way on every platform.
- **Evidence.** `a_held_origin_gives_up_no_forward_whose_reply_came_while_it_was_held` (eight reads through b, a's
  answers delayed half a budget, b's control shard held 1.5 budgets once the forwards were begun), on GitHub's
  ubuntu-latest, macos-latest and windows-latest runners (2026-11-18): main's lane failed 9 of 9, each run giving up
  and resending 7 of the 8 batches (run 44253485264); A-315 as landed passed 16 of 16 on ubuntu-latest and
  windows-latest on the merged tree, none given up, 6 or 7 silences held for the receiver a run (run 44260700333), with
  the lane's other promises kept (the silent forward given up while others flow, 12 of 12; a forward resent at its
  budget, 6 of 6; the dead-session tests, 6 of 6 each). Each of six mutations of the rule turns a unit test red (run
  44260700876). The server suite found the sessionless case before landing:
  `a_takeover_adopts_the_newest_head_a_holder_left_out_of_its_pages` failed 8 of 8 on ubuntu-latest without the
  sessionless turn, its serve poll lasting 10.01 s, the bound (run 44269560693), where main passed it 8 of 8 (run
  44269560657); with it, 8 of 8, and 4 of 4 on windows-latest where it had failed 3 of 3 (runs 44271632046 and
  44271632037), the lane's other tests unchanged, and sixteen runs a side served its volumes in 2.11 to 3.13 s, main
  in 2.15 to 3.37 s (runs 44272364924 and 44272413371). With A-317 over it, the held-origin test passed 3 of 3 on each
  of the three runners, macos-latest among them, and the takeover test 6 of 6 on each (run 44273659893). The bug
  record has the forms that did not land.
- **Cost.** A look reads the lane's two turn counts. A silence awaiting its receiver looks again every poll interval
  while it lasts, and a turn that read a datagram makes one more receive that does not wait. The lane's progress is one
  stored instant per begin, reply and byte-bearing turn.
- **Owed.** The supervisor's runs of the fleet suite under load and on Windows, and the load test's count of batches
  given up behind a burst (A-306's 17,000 to 52,000 a run), which this should bring near none.

### A-317 — A forward's owner location is given the membership horizon, ended by a look begun after it, within the failover SLO (2026-11-18, built for goal g255; clients' class B, `3c072f490`, with the supervisor's derivation)
Applied in the same change to:
- §4.8 "Lookup": the status of 2026-11-18 (A-317).
- `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`: `locate_within_budget` (the give-up counted on the caller's side of the loop) and
  `locate_within_horizon`, and the counts `fleet.owner_location.gave_up`, `.budget_spent` and `.slo_ended`.
- Tests (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`): `a_forward_with_no_owner_to_find_keeps_looking_for_its_location_budget` and
  `the_failover_delay_ends_a_forwards_location_budget` (new), and
  `a_refuted_false_death_keeps_a_forward_out_for_less_than_its_location_budget`, judged by the location's own counts
  (clients' rewrite).
- GAPS: the R3 debt of `LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS` (class B, the location budget).
- **What was there.** A forward with no known owner gave its location one liveness budget of wall time, a fixed
  second: the direct route, then a round, again every poll interval until the second ran out. A control shard kept off
  its CPU ran out of it while the gossip that refutes a false death waited to be read, and its client was refused for
  the machine's load (clients' runs at nice 19 beside two spinners a CPU, 1 or 2 calls in every false death); and with
  silent peers the first round's own wait spent the whole second, so the location never looked again.
- **The rule.** The location looks (the direct route, a round, and the direct route again) every poll interval. It
  gives up once a look begun after the membership horizon, on the wall from its first look, has found no owner, or once
  the operator's failover SLO has passed.
- **Why.** An owner is unfindable while live for the time a false death takes to be gossiped and refuted, which the
  detector's own horizon bounds (the supervisor's derivation of 2026-11-07: the location budget is the membership
  horizon), not for a liveness budget. Ending only with a look begun after it means a round that outlasted the horizon
  is followed by one more look, and the direct route asked after each round sees what the shard read while the round
  waited on its peers.
- **The forms that did not land.** Clients' polls (a liveness budget's worth at the poll interval, capped by the
  failover SLO): a round that waits a liveness budget on a silent peer makes each poll a second, so a forward's
  location runs to the SLO, ten times main's second. And the horizon followed by two waits of the control shard in its
  driver (A-292's receiver rule): a busy shard rarely waits, so it too runs to the SLO (A-315 found the same on the
  forward lane). Built first on main as of `9addf53ef`, each rewrite, this one included, made the five-node takeover test
  `a_survivor_holding_no_copy_of_the_works_catalog_learns_its_green_from_a_location_round` fail there (2 of 6, 4 of 15
  and 8 of 24 GitHub runs, against 0 of 9 on that base's own budget). On main as of `bfc34cace` this form passes it 16
  of 16 on ubuntu-latest and windows-latest, as main does (`diag-g255-a255-green-1`, `-red-1`); what changed between
  the two bases to make the difference was not traced.
- **Evidence.** On GitHub's ubuntu-latest, macos-latest and windows-latest runners (2026-11-18):
  `a_forward_with_no_owner_to_find_keeps_looking_for_its_location_budget` failed 3 of 3 on each over main's budget,
  the location never looking again (`diag-g255-loc-red-1`, `-red-3`), and passed 3 of 3 on each with this form, as did
  `the_failover_delay_ends_a_forwards_location_budget`, the false-death test and the location round's session-out test
  (`-green-4`, run 44260988795); the five-node takeover test, 16 of 16 over main as of `bfc34cace` (above). Over
  A-315 and main as of `1e8f4a49e` (`diag-g255-land2-1`, run 44273659893), on each of the three runners the four
  location tests 3 of 3 each, the five-node takeover test and the left-out-head takeover test 6 of 6 each, and the
  held-origin test 3 of 3; and fmt, clippy and the whole `slates-server` suite pass on ubuntu-latest, `fleet` 157 of
  157.
- **Cost.** None at the location's steady state: one more look at the direct route a round. A location that cannot find
  its owner ends one look past the horizon: about a poll interval when its rounds are answered, and one round's wait
  when they wait on a silent peer.

### A-273 — A shard that holds a green's works keeps a replica of the green, fed the owner's accepted versions in order; a rebase and a read at a named version are served there, over the owner's content in place (2026-11-17; the text first, the code after W1 lands)
Applied in the same change to: GAPS (A-273's entry). Nothing else yet: the tests come first, then the code.

Status: **measured and rejected, and removed whole on 2026-11-19 (A-528, below; BENCHMARKS, "A green's replicas on
the shards that hold its works: measured and rejected"); what follows records what was built.** Step 1 built
2026-11-17 (the owner's frees held for its replicas, below). Step 2 built 2026-11-18 (g083): the
replica and its feed, in `crates/merge/src/replica.rs`. The owner makes a message for each version it commits
(`Green::feed_version`) and for each fold that moves its floor (`fold_and_feed`, `fold_to_budget_and_feed`), at its feed
position, which it then moves past. A replica was built from the owner's checkpoint at its head over the green's origin,
joined at the owner's feed position then, so a base below that version was the owner's to answer (step 3 replaced
this: a replica is now made from the owner whole). It applies the message at its next position through `Green::apply_recorded` or
`fold_history_before`, passes over one below it, and refuses one above it (`FeedRefusal::Gap`), or a version that
would replay as another (`FeedRefusal::Diverged`), before anything changes; its holder then rebuilds it, counted
(`Replica::rebuild`, `Replica::counts`). Proven by `crates/merge/tests/replica.rs`: over generated histories with a
message delivered late, lost, or in flight across a rebuild, the replica is the owner's green at its head after every
step (its identity and every name's bytes), and at the end equals the owner whole (every version both hold, the paths
changed since each, every rebase over each base, and a base below its floor refused). Step 3 built 2026-11-18 (g083):
the green's content in sealed blocks (`slates_mem::sealed`, `crates/merge/src/store.rs`), its current files and its
history chunks alike. The owner seals each run of bytes once and releases what it names no more; a replica is made from
the owner whole (`Green::replica`: every index, history and delta cloned, the content named by the owner's blocks), so
it holds no byte of content of its own and serves every base the owner does, and reads each block in place through its
own live table, which only the owner's messages fill. A replay's seals adopt the blocks the owner sealed in the same
message, in its order, each checked to hold exactly the bytes the replay made, else the message is refused
(`FeedRefusal::NotTheOwners`). The owner frees a released block once every replica has passed the message that
released it (`Fed::Applied`'s `Passed`, `Green::acknowledge_replica`), and nothing for a replica that left
(`Green::leave_replica`); step 1's frees by position now live in the sealed blocks. Proven by the sealed blocks' tests
(a reader on another thread reads in place what its writer frees behind it; generated histories of seals, releases,
joins, passes, late acknowledgements and leaves, every live block allocated and read as sealed) and the replica's
oracle, which now holds every current file's bytes to be the owner's own memory. A replica's lifetime is bounded by
its owner's (2026-11-18, found by Miri): the owner's holder makes every replica leave before it gives the owner up
(`SealedBlocks::end`, refused while a reader is registered); an owner dropped with a replica still registered frees
nothing, since the replica may still read, and is counted (`sealed::dropped_with_readers`; the bug record of
2026-11-18, "a sealed-block writer dropped with a reader kept its blocks"). Step 4 built 2026-11-18 (g083): the
bounds, each derived from the machine by a stated formula its holder applies (`crates/merge/src/replica.rs`) and each a
typed refusal that ends with the replica rebuilt from the owner (`Replica::rebuild`) or given back (`Replica::leave`),
its work going to the owner until one is made again. The replicas an owner takes: `replica_limit` = (shards − 1) × 2,
one on each other shard of its node and beside it the fresh one its rebuild makes before the old one is given back;
none with one shard (R8); past it `ReplicaRefusal::Full`, and a replica makes none (`ReplicaRefusal::NotAnOwner`). A
replica's metadata (`Green::metadata_bytes`: piece lists, change index, IPC history, deltas, accepted record and its
chunk table, running totals all): `replica_budget` = min(the per-green budget its owner's retention is folded to, the
partition's `green_chain_bytes`, the most of its shard's table share one green's history may hold; the room its own
shard has for it now); refused at its making and at a rebuild
(`Unfit::OverBudget`, the fresh green's registration given back) and after a message that takes it past
(`FeedRefusal::OverBudget`). The bytes an owner keeps for its replicas, which are charged to its own per-green budget:
`held_limit` = that budget less the owner's own retention (`Green::retention_charge` less `Green::content_held_bytes`;
`Green::set_replica_held_limit`), so a lagging replica never takes the room of the owner's own work. Past it the owner
evicts its slowest replica, one at a time; every later message names it and it refuses the first it is given
(`FeedRefusal::Evicted`, before any other check), keeping its frees until it leaves, so the bound costs a replica,
never a read of freed bytes (`merge.replica.dropped_lagging`). A change made while the last was still unsent evicts
every replica, which could not be fed in order (`merge.replica.dropped_unfed`), so the owner records one message's
blocks at most. The key indexes, one entry a path, are the owner's own bound; a reader's live table is the owner's live
blocks, and its adoption queue one message's. Proven by the sealed blocks' tests (a join past the limit refused; the
slowest reader evicted past the held limit, reading what it holds until it leaves; a change left unfed evicting every
reader; every writer ended once its readers left) and the replica's (each bound driven to its refusal at its derived
value, the replica rebuilt or given back and made again; one shard takes no replica; an owner with no room beyond its
own retention evicts at its first release; with the eviction past the held limit disabled at a release, both of the
replica's held-limit tests and the sealed blocks' slowest-reader test fail, the unfed one passing: r316 on the Mac
Studio, 2026-11-18). Step 5a built 2026-11-18 (g083, A-457, below): the derivations in the boot profile; a replica on
every other shard of the node, made before the green's first change, fed over the cross-shard carrier and charged to its
own shard; and every replica leaving before its owner is given up. Step 5b built 2026-11-18 (g083, A-465, below): a
work's base reads (its files, a page, every file's length, at its base version) and its rebase answered by its shard's
replica with no hop, by the owner's functions over the replica's engine (byte for byte the owner's, the oracle test);
what the replica cannot serve asked of the owner, counted by why; a replica that left after a refusal or an eviction
made again, counted, never one that left for its budget. The idle give-back built 2026-11-18 (g083, A-473, below): a
replica no work on its shard has used for its idle window, the longest gap it has known between two uses, leaves, its
charge credited, counted; only a recorded use arms the check; work that returns asks for it again, and the owner's next
change remakes it. The supervisor's A/B at 1,000 clients (r406 on the Mac Studio, 2026-11-18) was not green: accepted
submits' p99 at a 20 ms think went from 0.81, 3.88 and 13.61 ms without the replicas to 60.78, 88.90 and 77.99 ms with
them, every message of the feed sent to every replica inside the submit, before its reply, and acknowledged one by one.
A-502 built 2026-11-18 (g083, below): the owner queues a turn's messages and sends each replica's shard one message
with them after the turn's replies, and each replica acknowledges a turn once. The A/B again (r100 on the Mac Studio,
2026-11-19) was not green either: head reads and submits at 26.3 to 56.9 ms p50 with the replicas against 0.09 to 1.27
ms without, and every kind worse at p99 (110 to 302 ms against 0.23 to 32.9 ms). Removed whole by A-528 (below). The
text and its measurements are
perf's (2026-11-11, `agents/perf-a273`, never pushed); the
content question it left open was decided by the supervisor on 2026-11-17 by A-64 and D-7 (below). W1 (A-247), whose
works off the owner it builds on, landed on 2026-11-17 (3c0af9399).

- **Why (measured).** W1 (A-247) moves a work's edits and composition to the work's shard; the verdict and the rebase
  still run on the green's owner.
  - At the 3,000-client load rung (`kernel/` of linux 7.4-rc1, 754 files, 16 MB) the owner spends 51–53% of its wall
    on them (W1, the anchor recipe, 2026-11-11). A verdict is 21.4–21.7 µs of the owner's CPU and a rebase 12.3–12.4.
  - Rebases are the larger share of the owner's merge work: 71,000–72,000 rebases a run against 49,000 verdicts.
  - At 1,000 clients and equal offered load, W1's rebase p99 is worse than main's (rounds' medians 30.7 against 21.2 ms):
    it crosses to the owner and waits in the ask batch, where on main it ran beside its work.
  - A rebase changes nothing on the green. Running it on the work's shard takes it off the owner entirely.
- **The shape.** Each shard that holds a work of a green keeps a replica of the green: the engine's own metadata, built
  from the owner's at a version and kept current by the owner's accepted versions applied in order through the engine's
  own replay (`Green::apply_recorded`, the chain entry's `Applied` over its increment). One code path: a replica at
  version v is the owner's green at v by construction, the property replay already holds for recovery.
  - *The feed.* After a version is committed (A-252: after its quorum), the owner sends its chain entry to each shard
    holding a replica, over the existing bounded control channel, in version order. A fold of the owner's history
    (retention, `Green::fold_history_before`) is a feed message too, in the same order, so a replica keeps no value
    the owner has dropped. Each message has a feed position, one more than the last. A replica that sees a gap (a
    position it lacks before the one it is sent) is rebuilt from the owner, counted.
  - *Served from the replica.* A rebase of a work on that shard, at the replica's head (never below the work's base;
    the work's next submit is judged by the owner against its own head, as every stale base is). A read of the green
    at a named version the replica holds (the 60% of A-247's reads). Everything else is unchanged: the verdict, the
    `Head` read, the merge record, every refusal.
  - *Behind.* A replica whose head is below a work's base (the owner accepted a version the feed has not delivered)
    forwards that rebase to the owner, as today, counted. A read at a version the replica does not hold, above its
    head or below its floor, is forwarded the same way.
  - *Laptop degenerate (R8).* With one shard there is no other shard and no replica: the owner serves, as now.
- **Content: once, in place (the supervisor's decision, 2026-11-17).** A-64 keeps content once in the anchor's RAM, and
  D-7 lets any core read an immutable chunk. So a replica holds no bytes of its own: it names the owner's chunks, and
  reads them where they are. It never copies them and never fetches them through the fleet for a shard of the same node.
  Two things the code does not have today follow, and both are part of this amendment:
  - *Chunks that never move or change.* The engine's content is its owner's heap today (`Green::content`, a map of
    `Vec<u8>`; the history's `Chunks`, a slot vector of `Vec<u8>` reused when freed), so a reference to it from another
    thread is not sound. The owner's current values and history chunks move into blocks of a region the owner allocates
    and seals: a sealed block is never written, moved or reused while any shard can name it (D-6's rule for volume
    chunks, A-64's for the image). A replica's piece names a block by handle and range, as an image's chunk reference
    does.
  - *Frees deferred until every replica has passed them.* A-64's deferral holds a block only until the owner's next
    publication commits, and knows nothing of readers on other shards; alone it would let a replica read a block freed
    and reused under it. So a chunk the owner's last piece leaves is stamped with the feed position of the message
    that carries the change (`Green::feed_position`; the owner moves to the next as it sends one,
    `Green::advance_feed`), and freed only when every replica has acknowledged that position. Positions, not
    versions: a fold releases chunks with no new version, and a replica that had not folded would still read them (the
    text of the same day said versions, and was wrong). A replica acknowledges on the feed's own channel, after its
    turn has applied the message and dropped every piece it released; the acknowledgement is per message (batched to
    the latest), never per chunk, so the cost is one message a feed message a replica and no atomic on any per-item
    path (D-7's quiescent-state rule, made by message). A replica joins at the owner's position then
    (`Green::hold_content`), naming only live chunks. A replica dropped, rebuilt or ended leaves
    (`Green::leave_content`), so a dead replica never holds a free. Built 2026-11-17 in `crates/merge/src/history.rs`
    (`Chunks::hold`, `acknowledge`, `leave`): a held chunk's room is not reused, its bytes are charged to the green's
    retained history (`Green::retained_bytes`) and recounted from the held list, and the frees held are counted
    (`Green::content_frees_held`). With no replica the owner frees at once, as before.
  - *Bounds.* The deferred bytes are charged to the owner's memory class, and they are bounded by the slowest
    replica's lag. A replica more than the derived lag behind (owed: its derivation, from the class's headroom against
    the bytes a version frees) is dropped, counted (`merge.replica.dropped_lagging`), and its rebases and reads go to
    the owner. So no replica can hold the owner's memory past its class.
  - *When this would be wrong.* If a measured fact makes it unsound (a lifetime the acknowledgement cannot hold) or
    slower than a copy (cross-shard reads of the owner's blocks costing more than the copy saves), the numbers and the
    alternative go to the supervisor before code is built another way.
- **What a replica costs, measured** (perf, 2026-11-11). A diagnostic build (never committed) logged the owner's green,
  by kind, at the 3,000-client rung's end: head 9,000, two runs alike to a few hundred bytes. Payload bytes, maps' node
  overhead not counted, so a lower bound:

  | part | bytes | a replica holds it |
  |---|---|---|
  | current file bytes | 16,438,721 | no: the owner's blocks, read in place |
  | history chunks (the current values again, and earlier runs) | 18,859,529 | no: the owner's blocks, read in place |
  | content history index (45,690 entries, their piece lists) | 8,991,756 | yes |
  | deltas (9,000 versions, 44,997 ops) | 4,642,109 | yes |
  | path, last-changed and kind indexes, kind histories | 613,120 | yes |
  | idempotency and rejected-result caches | 4,183,041 | no: the owner's |

  - Metadata is about 14.2 MB a replica at this rung (about 1.6 KB a version kept, until the retention floor folds it),
    about 313 MB at 22 shards. Copying content as well would have been about 49.5 MB a replica, and about 1.3 GB for a
    whole kernel tree, most of a 1.49 GB memory class in every replica: content in place avoids both.
  - Against the budgets, from the measurement's own daemon log (adas-mac-studio.local-2, `effective_capacity_bytes`
    103,079,215,104, 23 shards): a shard's metadata class, `table_bytes`, is 373,475,417 bytes (it already bounds the
    green's chain), and a memory class, `reserve_per_shard`, is 1,493,901,668. A replica's metadata is 3.8% of one
    shard's `table_bytes` (under 8% if the maps' node overhead doubled it), and each shard holds only its own replica.
- **Bounds and outcomes.** A replica's metadata is charged to its shard's metadata budget. At the bound the replica is
  dropped and its rebases and reads go to the owner, counted (`merge.replica.dropped`), never refused to the client.
  A replica no work on its shard has used for the derived idle period (owed: its derivation, from the feed's cost per
  version against the rebases it served) is dropped the same way. The feed rides the control channel's existing bound;
  a full channel delays a version, never drops it (the reply rule since 2026-11-09), and a replica behind forwards.
- **Tests first.**
  - The replica equals the owner at every version over generated histories (files, links, modes, renames, removals),
    the green's identity compared at each version.
  - A lagging replica's rebase is answered exactly as the owner would answer it at the replica's head, and a rebase whose
    base is above the replica's head is forwarded and answered by the owner.
  - A read at a version the replica lacks is forwarded, and its answer equals the owner's.
  - Lifetime (built): a replica holding a piece of a chunk whose last reference the owner has dropped reads the
    chunk's bytes unchanged until it acknowledges, and the owner's free happens at that acknowledgement and not before;
    a replica that leaves releases its hold (`a_chunk_released_while_a_replica_reads_it_stays_until_the_replica_passes_its_release`,
    `a_replica_that_leaves_holds_no_free`, and the generated `no_replica_reads_a_chunk_freed_before_it_passed_the_release`
    in `crates/merge/src/history.rs`). Red with the hold ignored (the owner frees at once).
  - Non-vacuity: counters of rebases and reads served off the owner and of those forwarded, and of frees deferred for
    a replica (`merge.replica.frees_deferred`).
  - Then the A/B the supervisor runs: the anchor recipe, every round, with the owner's utilization before and after.
- **Tried and rejected.**
  - *Copying content into each replica* (perf's option 1) or *for the paths a shard's works touch* (option 2): content
    twice, against A-64, and about 1.3 GB a replica for a whole kernel tree. Rejected 2026-11-17 by the supervisor.
  - *An epoch-published immutable root of the green's metadata* (the owner's maps shared read-only with every shard):
    it needs a persistent map the engine does not use. Rejected 2026-11-11 for a replica fed by message. Its other
    cost, reclaiming what readers may still hold, is paid here for content alone, by acknowledgement.
  - *Shard-count-fixed replicas* (a replica on a literal number of shards): a tuning literal (R3), and a work's shard is
    where its rebases are. Rejected for "every shard holding a work of the green".
  - *Answering the owner's asks in slices of the step budget* (2026-11-09): the step budget, about 4.5 µs, is below one
    ask's cost, so every slice was one ask and every answer a message; SubmitAccepted p99 75.3–493.0 ms against W1's
    53.8–77.2 (BENCHMARKS). It moved no work off the owner.

### A-276 — A heal restores the holders a head names and counts each repair however late its acknowledgement; a holder that left is replaced at the next sequence, recorded with the republished head as one record; every heal ends once its first round's replies have had their whole span (2026-11-17, built for goal g248; the replace is live-fixes' 2026-11-09 work; amends §4.10's healer)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.10: the "Content replication" paragraph's healer sentences.
- GAPS (2026-11-17 entry) and `docs/bugs/2026-11-17-a-heal-miscounted-repairs-and-left-heads-naming-holders-without-the-content.md`;
  the content-replication record's piece 2 (`docs/wip/content-replication.md`).
- `crates/server/src/fleet.rs`: `heal_one_placed_snapshot`, `Heal`, `heal_for`, `heal_decision`, `start_seal`,
  `seal_complete`, `content_work`, `put_seal_content`, `fold_round`, `fold_content_ack`, `fold_late_content`,
  `record_placed_seals`, `record_replacement`, and the test support `injected_content_ack_delay`, with the unit test
  `the_heal_restores_named_candidates_and_replaces_only_a_departed_or_short_placement`; `crates/server/src/head.rs`
  (`SealJob::put_sequence`, `SealJob::republish`, `SealJob::refilled`); `crates/server/src/daemon.rs`
  (`Daemon::inject_content_ack_delay`).
- The tests in `crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`: `a_repair_whose_acknowledgement_outlasts_its_round_is_counted`,
  `a_heal_restores_the_named_holder_and_not_a_candidate_without_the_head`,
  `a_heal_republishes_the_head_once_a_named_holder_has_left`,
  `a_heal_republishes_a_live_volumes_head_once_a_named_holder_has_left` and
  `a_heal_that_cannot_place_ends_at_its_bound_and_the_volume_is_healed_later`; and
  `a_holder_that_lost_placed_content_is_repaired_by_the_healer` now prints whether the holder holds the content and the
  owner's heal counts.

- **The rule amended.** §4.10 said the healer replays puts that never reached f+1 and that anti-entropy repairs only
  differing subtrees between recorded holders. The healer re-opened a placed snapshot as an ordinary seal on the current
  cohort, offered it in rendezvous order, re-recorded whichever holders acknowledged at the head's sequence, and counted
  a repair only for a holder whose acknowledgement its round collected. Three things followed, each measured below:
  - **A late repair was never counted.** A content round stops collecting at the hedge delay (the p95 of the owner's
    put readings, rounded up to the collection poll), and a refill that outlasts it acknowledges as a straggler. The
    straggler was folded into the placement, the job recorded and dropped, and the repair was never counted; every later
    heal found the holder whole. This is how `a_holder_that_lost_placed_content_is_repaired_by_the_healer` failed under
    load (`repairs Ok(0) → Ok(0)`, 2026-11-08, this Mac at load 54).
  - **A restore could place where the head does not name.** A cohort member holding no head for the object (one that
    refused or had not yet received the owner's records, as a restarted holder has not) admits a put at the head's
    sequence as ahead of its records and acknowledged first. The heal placed there, re-recorded that set at the head's
    sequence, and the named holder stayed empty while the head named it.
  - **A departed holder stayed named.** A head is never rewritten at its sequence, so a heal's re-recorded placement
    never reached the head when a holder it named had left the fleet (live-fixes, 2026-11-09).
- **The rule now.**
  - **Restore.** While every holder the placement names is a member, the heal re-offers at the head's sequence to
    exactly the named holders that are candidates, all at once, and ends once every one of them holds the content. It
    records nothing.
  - **Repairs.** A holder whose offer answer named chunks it lacked is remembered on the job (`SealJob::refilled`), and
    its first acknowledgement counts one repair, whether its round collected it or it arrived as a straggler's
    (`fleet.heal.repaired_late`). `fleet.heal.refill_outlasted_round` counts the refills a round did not collect.
  - **Replace.** When a holder the placement names is no longer a member (`fleet.heal.named_gone`), or the placement
