behind `xshard::call_within` with a period's deadline, the held archive copied out whole on the control shard before it,
every period's attempt again. The 1.99 GB, 97,254-file kernel base volume (g232) held its owner shard for seconds.
**Now:** one task of the owner shard (`fleet::make_taken`, generalizing A-374's `make_live`) makes either source
(`fleet::Source::Live` or `Source::Archive`), claiming the volume's record (`ShardState::making_taken_over`) so every
later attempt joins it (`fleet::making_of` for both sources). Before the task, the control shard copies a placed seal's
held archive out of the held store a copy slice of chunks a turn (`fleet::held_archive_in_turns`: `held_manifest`, then
`held_chunk` for each chunk it names) and opens an envelope in turns (A-347). The task: a live log rebuilt in turns
(A-374, `fleet::rebuild_in_turns`) and laid out as an archive, or a placed seal's lineage key adopted; then, unless the
volume is made already, the archive restored a slice a turn (`fleet::restore_in_turns`: A-391's `Planning`, then
`verbs::restore_admitted` at the known need under the pressure hold, this node's candidate claim's bytes counted as
the volume's own (A-401), then `Restoring`); the volume begun (`verbs::begin_making`: this node's candidate claim taken
over, else the admission a create makes, A-401, and the create); its tree laid a
slice a turn (`verbs::Populating`, `verbs::populate_making`: each file checked and each hard link's bytes compared a slice
at a time before the volume is touched, the links counted, the directories made, each file made and its data written a
copy slice of the quantum, a page at least, a write, then the attributes, owners and times, files then directories
deepest first, then the root); then finished (`verbs::finish_making`: the versions hold, the record, the sealed head)
and published before it is served, each a turn. Each turn is held to the seal turns' share of the quantum
(`fleet::making_slice_ns`). The volume being made is held in `ShardState::making_volumes`, not by the task, and a
refusal, a give-up (`fleet.materialize.forgotten`: a turn finds the record the control shard forgot) or any end but its
making discards it and puts its credits back as the candidate claim (`verbs::discard_making`, A-401's
`return_to_claim`), so the next attempt finds the room this one had; a later `begin_making` discards one left over
first.
`verbs::materialize_taken_over`, `restore_taken_over` and `populate_restored` remain, test-only, as the pieces run to
their ends in one call.

Tests: `a_placed_seals_takeover_is_restored_and_laid_in_turns` (three nodes, a sealed volume of 24 distinct files, the
survivors' turns cut to a piece; the held archive copied in turns, more restore turns and more laying turns than files,
one materialization begun and none twice, both survivors' longest steps under the window, every file read back),
`a_tree_laid_a_piece_a_step_is_the_tree_laid_at_once` (a sparse file around a hole, hard links, a symlink, a FIFO,
nested directories and an attribute laid a piece a step and a byte a write equal the tree laid in one call), the live
takeover test and the envelope test unchanged.

Applied in the same change to: §4.10's status (A-397), GAPS (A-347's one-turn walks: the takeover's restore and
population, both sources), `crates/server/src/{fleet,verbs,state,daemon}.rs`, `crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`.

### A-411 — The Windows release builds pin MSVC toolset 14.44 and Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0, so a tag's Windows bytes do not depend on the runner image (2026-11-18, the release goals g236 and g237; settles A-407's owed item)
Applied in the same change to: `.github/workflows/release.yml` (the step "MSVC toolset 14.44 and Windows SDK
10.0.26100.0, pinned", through `ilammy/msvc-dev-cmd`, and the matrix's `msvc_arch`), Appendix B.2 (its recipes),
GAPS (the binary release lane's entry) and `docs/publish.md` ("The binary release").
- **The evidence.** The tag `v0.1.0`'s two x86_64 binaries, from `windows-2025` 20261103.298.1 (871a057d) and
  20261116.315.1 (d3498b4f), differ in 2,559,679 bytes. Their Rich headers, which list every tool build that made
  their objects, differ only in Visual Studio's default toolset: the linker (14.51 build 36260 against 14.52 build
  37029, one entry each), its C runtime objects (build 35721 against 36815: 10 assembled, 16 and 17 C, 40 C++) and the
  objects that toolset compiled (build 36260 against 37029: 4 assembled, 91 C). The Windows SDK's 204 objects are the
  same (build 33145) in both.
- **The decision.** Build with VS 2022 17.14's toolset 14.44, which both `windows-2025` images and the `windows-11-arm`
  image carry beside the default (`Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.14.44.17.14.x86.x64` and `.ARM64`, version
  18.11 and 18.12 of the component on the two images; actions/runner-images' readmes and release notes, 2026-11-18),
  and the one Windows SDK the images carry. A side-by-side toolset is a frozen release serviced apart from the
  default, which moves with every image. Rejected: comparing the two copies' toolsets instead of their bytes, which
  would ship bytes no second runner reproduced; and building both copies in one job, which gives up the separate
  runner AC-9.5 asks for.
- **Owed.** The proof is a release run (a tag or a dry run) whose two copies of a Windows target land on two images
  and match; filed for main. clang-cl, which compiles AWS-LC's C on arm64, still comes from the image.

### A-409 — A lost volume's live log stops by itself, and a holder's refusal names the highest fence it knows (2026-11-18, g230, scale-out; §4.8 "Authority scope", §4.10 "Live shipping"; A-334, A-349, A-382's open item)
Applied in the same change to: §4.8 "Authority scope" (its status), GAPS (A-382's entry: its open item fixed), and the
code below.
- **What was there.** A-349 stopped a fenced log, one a holder had answered with a later fence. A log whose node yielded
  the volume at its re-admission (A-334) was never fenced unless a holder said so, and the holder that refused it as not
  the volume's acting owner answered from its live copy's fence alone. In 2 of 12 runs of
  `every_copy_catches_up_once_the_third_node_takes_the_volume_from_the_adopter` (CI diag 44358084443) the re-admitted
  adopter's log built 119 and 1,714 installs of its whole volume for the creator, each refused `not_the_acting_owner`:
  a storm of the kind A-349 found starving a takeover round's sessions. Why no refusal fenced it is not read from that
  run's counters.
- **The rule.** A yielded volume is lost (`live_ship::lost`: fenced or yielded): its log ships nothing and the period
  only judges what still waits on it; at the yield every verb waiting on its durability is answered `DurabilityPending`
  with the time it was held (`live_ship::yielded`, counted `fleet.live.yield_refused`), since the write it waits for was
  made on a copy the successor's writes have passed and the same request run again goes to the successor; its
  transports' parked replies are woken to meet the yield at their gates. A holder's refusal of a sender that is not the
  acting owner is `StaleEpoch` at the highest fence the holder knows for the volume, its live copy's or its record
  copy's (`known_fence`, the new `Acceptor::fence`), and `Unauthorized` only when the sender's epoch is not below it.
- **Tests.** `a_refused_sender_below_the_fence_a_holder_knows_is_told_that_fence` (`live_ship`'s unit tests: the
  decision over every epoch against a fence). The fleet runs that show the storm gone and every re-admission and
  supersession test still green are filed for main (run-requests.md, A-409).

- **Step two (2026-11-18).** Once a holder keeps a new checkpoint, its ledger drops the positions after version 0 and
  below the checkpoint's own (`Acceptor::compact_ledger_between`: phase one ranks only the highest position, and the
  rebuild still reads version 0's record, which names the origin, and the checkpoint's, whose identity it checks), and
  its retention judges the content placed from version 1 again (`content_retention::retain_object_from`), releasing
  the inputs nothing names now (`merge.replica.compacted_inputs`). A takeover's adoption (A-333) needs nothing below
  the checkpoint: its completions walk passes over the positions it lacks, and its replica is rebuilt from the
  checkpoint and advanced from its records above it. A replica's records and inputs are now bounded by the versions
  its owner has not yet committed. Tests: `a_holder_lets_go_of_the_records_and_inputs_its_checkpoint_stands_for`
  (`merge_origin.rs`: positions 0, 2 and 3 kept, version 1's inputs released, the replica rebuilt to version 3 from the
  checkpoint) and `a_ledger_compacted_between_keeps_its_first_position_and_the_checkpoints_own` (`register.rs`); the
  server's merge, retention, state and takeover unit tests 35 of 35 and the acceptor tests 9 of 9 (kiln, the Mac Studio,
  2026-11-18, debug).

### A-413 — cargo-binstall installs a release binary: the CLI manifest names each shipped target's asset, and the version audit holds it to the shipped targets (2026-11-18, the release goals g236 and g237; B.2's recipe, A-210's "not yet")
Applied in the same change to: `crates/cli/Cargo.toml` (`repository.workspace = true` and
`[package.metadata.binstall]`), the root `Cargo.toml` (`[workspace.package] repository`), `xtask/src/version.rs`
(`Binstall`, `read_binstall`, `audit_binstall`, five findings, and the tests
`the_binstall_table_names_exactly_the_shipped_binaries` and `the_trees_binstall_table_names_the_release_binaries`),
Appendix B.2, GAPS and `docs/publish.md`.
- **What it does.** `cargo binstall --git https://github.com/hyper-light/slates slates-cli` reads the CLI manifest
  and downloads the release binary for the machine's target: `pkg-fmt = "bin"` (a release attaches raw binaries) and
  one override per shipped target naming `{ repo }/releases/download/v{ version }/<asset>`. A target slates does not
  ship has no override, so the default archive names find nothing and cargo-binstall builds from source; quick-install,
  a third party's builds, is off. vorpal's manifest is the model.
- **Held to the shipped targets.** `cargo xtask version`, in `cargo xtask check` on every push and in every tag lane's
  guard, refuses a shipped target with no override, an override for a target slates does not ship, an override
  addressing another asset, an archive format, and a crate with no repository, each as its own finding.
- **Owed.** An install against a published release (run request); publishing the crate to crates.io would let
  `cargo binstall slates-cli` drop `--git`.

### A-410 — Slates' own virtio-fs device keeps each guest write in the write log before its used element: A-358's rule on the vhost-user route (2026-11-18, goal g268; g079's route table, "the vhost-user device neither saves nor logs a write before replying"; §4.6 virtio-fs, §4.8 barrier, D-18; A-63, A-316, A-358, A-379, A-402)
Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/bridge-core`: `VolumeBridge::logging_writes` (a transport's write log, handed each write the volume took;
  one it did not keep makes `awaits_publication` true); `Bridge::awaits_publication`'s doc; the unit test
  `a_bridge_hands_each_write_to_its_log_and_owes_a_publication_for_one_it_did_not_keep`
  (`crates/bridge-core/tests/volume_bridge.rs`).
- `crates/server/src/virtiofs.rs`: `ShardBridge::with_bridge` gives each pass's bridge the shard's write log and
  content object; the module doc. `crates/bridge-fuse/src/bridge.rs`: `needs_barrier`'s doc.
- The test `a_guests_acknowledged_write_outlives_its_daemon_through_the_write_log` (`crates/server/tests/virtiofs.rs`).
- §4.6 (the virtio-fs status after AUD-29-82's); GAPS: the route table in the WinFsp write's entry (2026-11-18), with
  the Windows streams' row brought to A-402, and Phase 8 step 4's owed line.

- **What was there.** The virtio-fs device held a request's used element for the owner's barrier only when
  `needs_barrier` named it (namespace and attribute changes, `fsync`, the `flush` a close sends) or the volume owed a
  publication. A plain `WRITE` was answered with neither a publication nor a log record, so a write acknowledged after
  the last publication was lost at a daemon's death. g079's sibling sweep (A-379) found it; it was safe only while the
  VM died with its device's daemon (crosvm ends the VM at a back end's hangup), and the volume itself outlives the
  daemon, so a write the guest was told succeeded was missing from it afterwards.
- **The rule.** A-358's: a write a client is told succeeded survives the daemon's death before the reply. Here it is
  kept as a FUSE mount and a Shards stream keep it: the bridge appends each write the volume took to the shard's write
  log before the device publishes the used element, and a successor replays the log at recovery. A write the log does
  not keep (no room, or a span the content object refused) makes the bridge owe a publication; the device then holds
  the reply for the owner's barrier, which publishes and answers `EIO` if the publication did not capture the volume. A
  device with no anchor's content object (no log) is a daemon nothing outlives, and owes nothing for its writes.
- **Why not the barrier per write.** A-379 publishes every WinFsp write because Windows had no write log. The log is
  on every platform since A-402, and a logged write costs an append into anchor-held memory, where a publication writes
  the shard's whole recovery image; A-399 measured a stream's close publishing nothing the log held at 15.7-16.0 µs p50
  against 17.5-20.0 µs.
- **Evidence.** The unit test drives a bridge with a keeping log, a refusing log and none. The integration test runs
  the in-process guest seam under a daemon whose anchor the test holds: a guest creates a file (its barrier publishes
  it) and writes into it, the daemon is killed by a fenced stop that publishes nothing, and a successor over the same
  segment reads the bytes back over NFS. Without the change the file comes back empty, as its create's publication left
  it. The vhost-user front end's run on Linux is main's (`run-requests.md`, 2026-11-18).

### A-416 — The many-client bound judges every request and the cycle, and reports the round; the load test's hot set is a set (2026-11-18, built for goals 231 and 257, 1,000 clients under 1 ms; amends A-297's "The judgment")
Applied in the same change to: §1.4 (the status under the table), GAPS (the load test's entry),
`crates/client/examples/load_bench.rs` (`Kind::judged`, `bound_row`, `hot_set`, `plan_round`, `level`'s `refused` row,
the module's "The workload" and "The bound"), and the example's tests below.
- **The round is reported, not judged.** A-297 judged "every kind", and the harness took that as every kind it timed,
  the round among them. §1.4's status names the kinds as each request and a whole edit and merge, which the cycle is (a
  round's first edit to its first verdict). A round is not one: it runs from its first edit to its accept, so it holds
  as many edits and merges as its conflicts make, and its p99 grows with the conflict rate the hot set sets, not with
  any request's time. On the Mac Studio at 1,000 clients and a think mean of 50 ms (1,102 verdicts a second, works on
  their clients' shards, 2026-11-18) every request's p99 was 0.47 to 1.33 ms and the cycle's 104 ms (pauses left out),
  while the round's was 191 ms. The bound now judges every request kind and the cycle; the round stays in the `latency`
  row. This is g231's option (b), whose stated trigger, a measurement with the round alone over the bound, was met;
  decided by the principle above, Ada's to veto.
- **The hot set is a set.** The harness drew `--hot-files` indices with replacement, so a file drawn twice was twice as
  hot as the rest of the set, and 800 draws over `kernel/`'s 700-odd eligible files made every file hot and some three
  to five times hotter: 19 to 28 of 1,000 clients starved (ran out of resolutions) in every run, and the bound requires
  none. The hot set is now `--hot-files` distinct files (a Fisher–Yates shuffle's first places, by the plan's own
  draws), and at most half the files long enough to edit, so a pick from the whole tree misses it at least half the
  time and the tree's picks stay mostly disjoint, as the workload states. A larger one is refused before the level
  runs (`refused`, exit 1), never shrunk to fit; the 1,000-client rung's 800 hot files need a tree of 1,600 eligible
  files or more (`fs/` of linux v7.4-rc1 holds 2,365 files). `--hot-files 0` is a level with no hot set; before, it
  indexed an empty set.
- **Tests** (`cargo test -p slates-client --example load_bench`): a round at 191 ms with every request and the cycle
  under the bound meets it and names the cycle, and a cycle over it fails the level
  (`a_round_is_reported_and_not_judged_and_a_cycle_is_judged`); a hot set names each file once and the same seed draws
  it again (`a_hot_set_names_each_file_once`); a hot set past half the eligible files is refused and exactly half is
  one (`a_hot_set_past_half_the_eligible_files_is_refused`); with no hot set every pick is from the whole tree and no
  shared slot is written (`with_no_hot_set_every_pick_is_from_the_whole_tree`).

### A-415 — The re-admission publishes its let-go of the host's own register copies at once (2026-11-18, g230, scale-out; §4.8 "Authority scope", "Recovery"; A-382's owed item)
Applied in the same change to: §4.8 "Authority scope" (A-382's status), GAPS (A-382's entry), and
`crates/server/src/readmission.rs`.
- **What was there.** A-382's let-go removed the host's own register copies from the control shard's held map, and the
  removals rode the shard's next publication. A warm restart before it restored the copies from the last committed
  image and routed each to the owner it named, this host, so they refused their successors again (A-382's failure)
  until the next re-admission, which a restarted daemon does not see.
- **The rule.** The let-go publishes the shard at once when it let anything go (`readmission::let_go_own_registers`);
  a refused publication is counted `fleet.readmission.registers_let_go_unpublished`, and the removals stay marked
  changed (`crate::tracked`) for the next one.
- **Tests.** `a_readmissions_let_go_is_in_the_journal_a_restart_reads` (`readmission`'s unit tests, on a shard with
  recovery storage): a copy naming the host held and published, the host re-admitted; the journal a restart reads
  (`verbs::committed_held_agrees`) agrees with the shard at once, and with every publication refused around the
  install the let-go is counted unpublished and the next publication carries it. The re-admission flows' fleet tests
  are filed for main (run-requests.md, A-415).

### A-406 — The root group records its voters in the versioned root configuration, so a root learner names who votes from the configuration it fetches (2026-11-18, goal g225: a forming fleet reaches every candidate; §4.8 learners; A-380's root sibling)

- **What was there.** A root learner (every member that is not its region's representative) takes no part in the root
  group's Raft. It knew who votes only from its join state's voters, since a root seat change is a Raft configuration
  entry that moves no root version, and it fetched only when its alive view of the regions differed from the root
  configuration's. Seen on Windows (run 44298844583): after the root moved from its bootstrapper to the regions'
  representatives, three root learners still named the bootstrapper as the only root voter. It asked that voter for
  fetches and kept direct contact with it as a voter, and a representative that died left its region in place, so no
  comparison it made ever moved.
- **The rule.** `RootConfiguration::voters` records the root voters, in id order, and `seat` changes them with the
  version. The root leader proposes `RootCommand::Seat` with the voters in force whenever no change is in flight and
  they differ from the record (`RootGroup::record_voters`, each root leader period). A root learner's `known_voters`
  and `known_voter` read the record of the configuration it holds, its join state's before any record. A root learner
  fetches from the voters it knows, keeps direct contact with them, and fetches also when one of them is no longer
  alive in its membership.
- **Why this and not another.** The same record as A-380's, so the council and the root learn who votes one way. A
  version announced on the probe plane, as the council's is, would be a member-plane wire change, and the root's
  learners need it only when a root voter changes, which a dead voter shows them.
- **What it costs.** One root version per root seat change, and the root configuration's encoding gains the set (layout
  2). A root learner fetches each period while a root voter it knows is dead and not yet replaced, as it already did
  while its regions differed.
- **What it does not change.** The root voters and how they change (Raft §6); the regional council (A-380).
- **Tests.** `a_root_learner_names_the_voters_the_configuration_records_through_a_seat_change`
  (`crates/cluster/src/root_group.rs`),
  `a_root_seat_records_the_voters_in_id_order_and_advances_the_version_only_when_they_change`
  (`crates/db/src/register.rs`), the root round trip and the layout golden in `crates/cluster/src/raft_wire.rs`.

Applied in the same change to: §4.8 (learners), A-380's entry, GAPS (A-380's open sibling),
`crates/db/src/register.rs`, `crates/cluster/src/raft_wire.rs`, `crates/cluster/src/root_group.rs`,
`crates/server/src/fleet.rs`, their tests, and the bug record
`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-root-learner-named-the-root-voters-of-its-join.md`.

### A-412 — A holder behind its own records catches up from them, fetching their inputs from the record's owner (2026-11-18, kiln goal g250; §4.16 "Apply on holders"; A-313, A-333, A-364, A-373)
Applied in the same change to: GAPS (the entry at its head), the bug record of 2026-11-18 on a holder behind its own
records, `crates/server/src/merge_service.rs` (`record_standing`, `catch_up`, `MergeShardState::catching_up`) and
`crates/server/src/fleet.rs` (`fetch_ledger_inputs`, `merge.catch_up.*`).
- **What was there.** A takeover commits the versions it adopted again through the register path, which carries no
  inputs, and the record plane ships a placed version no more, so a holder whose replica had not reached them held their
  records with nothing to apply them by. A record ahead of the replica was out of order, for good.
- **The rule.** A record ahead of the replica's next version looks for the versions between in the holder's own ledger
  (`merge_origin::ledger_unheld`). Held whole, with their inputs, the replica is advanced through them (A-333's
  `advance_replica`) and the record served as the next version, recomputed before it is acknowledged. An input not
  held is fetched by identity from the record's sender, the green's owner, which holds every version's inputs while its
  records name them (A-244), staged as placed for its version, one fetch a green at a time in a detached task of the
  shard, and the owner's next shipment of the record finds it held. A version between whose record the holder lacks is
  out of order, as before.
- **Tests.** `a_holder_behind_its_own_records_after_a_takeover_fetches_their_inputs_and_takes_the_next_version`
  (`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs`): three nodes at `f = 1`, the holder withholding version 3 when the owner dies, the
  successor's version 4 committed with it and recomputed there, version 3's input fetched. Kiln r355, the Mac Studio,
  2026-11-18, debug build: green in 4.4 s; red without the catch-up, version 4 answered out of order 4,865 times in
  405 s. The merge unit tests (`merge_origin`, `merge_service`) 27 of 27.

### A-396 — A live write parks no shard on its path where a held shard polls: the owner holds its idle window while a reply waits for durability, its control shard through an exchange and for its next dispatch, a holder for the owner's next entry; each window learned from the traffic it waits on (2026-11-18, goal g076b: a live write under 50 µs at the median and 1 ms at p999; §4.10 "Live shipping", §4.7 "Wake strategy"; A-200, A-326, A-387)

Applied in the same change to: §4.10 (a status), GAPS (the live entry), `crates/transport/src/rtt.rs`
(`RttEstimator::expected_within`), `crates/rt/src/shard.rs` (`ShardContext::hold_idle_window` says whether it kept the
hold), `crates/server/src/live_hold.rs` (new: `AnswerWindow`, `StreamWindow`, `remaining`, `hold`),
`crates/server/src/live_ship.rs` (`hold_for_answer` from `done_or_park` and `defer`; `hold_for_exchange` and the
exchange's learning in `ship_lane`; the dispatch stream in `send_from_control`; the entry stream in `serve_taken`; the
answer window learned in `count_hops`; `LiveVolume::answers`, `Held::arrivals`, `LiveState::dispatches`;
`count_hold`, `fleet.live.hold.*`), `crates/server/src/state.rs` (`RecordLink::live_answers`),
`crates/server/tests/fleet.rs` (`a_live_write_loop_asks_the_owners_the_control_shards_and_the_holders_shards_to_hold`).
- **What the round cost.** A stable write to a live-shipped volume is answered once a candidate holds it (A-200), so its
  path runs through four shards on three nodes: the owner shard builds and appends the entry, its node's control shard
  sends it and hands the answer back, the holder's control shard keeps it and answers. Each parked in its driver between
  its parts, so a write paid a wake at each: the control shard woken for the dispatch and again for the answer, the
  holder for the entry, the owner for the fold. Measured with the contract command
  (`measure_what_live_shipping_adds_to_a_stable_nfs_write`) on 2026-11-18, before the supervisor's runs:
  - adacachy (Linux, a capped unit, load 45–70): main added 136–182 µs at the median; one shard a daemon (the owner is
    the control shard: no hop at all) 101–163; every shard held for a fixed millisecond (a prototype), one shard 78–107
    and two shards 63–96. Two held shards beat one: the hop between two polling shards is cheap and the shards work in
    parallel. So the hop was not the cost. Held apart at load 55–60, two shards: none 189–291, the owner and its control
    shard 141–221, all three kinds 95–120.
  - The windows of this amendment against main, six rounds alternating at load 78–93: added 86.0–115.2 µs against
    186.0–295.1. Not better in the tails: the live p999 4.2–27.7 ms against 2.6–15.1, and the plain write's p99 293–1,024
    against 132–785 µs. The spinning shards spend the unit's CPU quota (800%), whose throttling stalls every thread of
    the unit; the supervisor's runs read the unit's `nr_throttled` to tell.
  - The Mac Studio (macOS, load 19–24, no hold): main 178–180 µs, the exchange about 130 µs of it with the holder's own
    serve about 7 µs; a macOS thread's wake about 30 µs there.
- **The rule.** Two kinds of wait, each learned by RFC 9002 §5.3's law (the transport's own estimator), held for the bound
  an answer is expected within, `smoothed + 4 · variation` (§6.2.1's terms without the timer granularity and ack delay a
  spinning waiter does not arm):
  - an *answer window*, for an answer a shard's own message caused: the owner's round from a publication to its entry's
    durability, per volume; the control shard's exchange with each holder, kept on its record link;
  - a *stream window*, for the next message of a closed loop: the control shard's dispatches, and each holder's entries
    from one owner's log. A gap within the bound continues the run, a longer one begins a new run; the hold is the
    bound, never longer than the run has lasted, and nothing for a run's first message (A-326's ski-rental rule), so a
    paced sender starts no run and a run's end costs at most the spin the run took.
  Nothing is held before a window is learned. A hold pays only while a held shard sees a message sooner than a kicked
  park would wake for it, and every hold is asked of the runtime, which decides that from the shard's own measurements
  (A-387's predicate, cfg-free since 2026-11-18): it keeps the hold while the idle turn a message lands in is shorter
  than the shard's wake estimate, and declines it otherwise, counted (`fleet.live.hold.declined`). Linux's epoll and
  Windows' completion port answer a zero-timeout poll at once, so their shards hold; a macOS shard's zero-timeout
  `kevent` naps 12–15 µs a turn, longer than its 3–8 µs wake, so it declines; a shard a loaded machine preempts stops
  holding until its turns are cheap again. The windows are learned wherever the holds are declined. The first form of
  this amendment fixed the hold at none on macOS by `#[cfg]`, as A-387's first form did; it now follows A-387's.
- **What was tried and lost.** The owner shipping over sessions of its own, with no hop to the control shard: its proxy
  (one shard a daemon) saved less than the holds, and it needs a session per shard a holder (the transport's
  demultiplexer keeps one session a peer's certificate), so it was not built. The owner and control holds alone, without
  the stream holds, measured as above.
- **Tests.** `RttEstimator`'s bound and the windows' rules are unit-tested (`rtt::tests`, `live_hold::tests`: no window
  before an answer; a stream's first message holds nothing; a run holds no longer than it has lasted; a pause past the
  bound begins a new run). `a_live_write_loop_asks_the_owners_the_control_shards_and_the_holders_shards_to_hold`: a
  closed loop of 32 writes, every one answered at durability, and every site asked its shard to hold with a learned
  window: the owner, its control shard (through an exchange and for a dispatch) and a holder; whether each shard kept
  its holds is A-387's decision, printed with the declines. Landed before its A/B (Ada's rule of 2026-11-18: an agent
  implements, unit-tests, merges and ends). Owed, filed for the supervisor: that test on Linux and macOS, and the A/B
  (main before the holds against main with them; quiet and loaded; Linux and the Studio) with the units'
  `nr_throttled`, which decides whether the holds stay; the answer holds alone are a second arm not built.

### A-417 — A Windows host learns before it mounts whether WinFsp's driver may make the drive (2026-11-18, g085, the Windows leg of kiln's bare-metal goal; amends A-278 piece 3's `mount::available`, follows A-369)
Applied in the same change to: §4.12 (the contract's status, `CONTRACT` = 37), `crates/api/src/mount.rs`
(`available` and the pure `winfsp_available`, with its test), `crates/api/src/error.rs` (`MountMissing::MountManager`
and its words), `crates/api/src/lib.rs` (`CONTRACT`), `crates/bridge-winfsp/src/ffi.rs` (`mount_manager_allowed`, one
`machine_word` reader for it and Developer Mode, so the unsafe count stays 156) and `host.rs`, `docs/library.md`,
README (installing on Windows), GAPS.
- **What was wrong.** Since A-369 every slates WinFsp drive is a Mount Manager drive that WinFsp's driver makes on the
  daemon's request, which it does only where an Administrator set `MountUseMountmgrFromFSD` to 1. `mount::available`,
  the fact a host reads before it mounts (§4.12 "Verbs"; kiln's runner facts), asked only whether WinFsp's library
  loads. So a machine without the setting was told it could mount, and a host that then made a volume and mounted it
  was refused `MountManagerNotAllowed`: kiln's bare-metal engine makes each agent's volume before its mount, and refuses
  a start typed only on what `available` names.
- **The rule, read at its source.** WinFsp's driver reads `MountUseMountmgrFromFSD` under `FSP_REGKEY` at every such
  request (`FspVolumeUseMountmgr`, WinFsp master `src/sys/volume.c`, read 2026-11-18): it refuses `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED`
  when the read fails, the value is not a `REG_DWORD`, or it is anything but 1; `FSP_REGKEY` is
  `\Registry\Machine\Software\WOW6432Node\WinFsp` on every 64-bit Windows, arm64 included (`src/sys/driver.h`).
  Nothing is cached at the driver's load, so `available` reads the same value by the same rule at each call
  (`RegGetValueW` with `RRF_RT_REG_DWORD`, which refuses every other type), and its answer is the one a mount meets.
- **The answer.** `Unsupported { missing: MountMissing::MountManager }`, whose words name the one command that allows
  it. The library is asked first: without it no drive is ever asked for, so `MountMissing::WinFsp` is named alone.
- **Tests.** `a_windows_mount_is_available_only_where_winfsps_driver_may_make_its_drive` (every pair of the two facts,
  and the words), on every host. The registry read itself runs only on Windows: compiled for
  `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`; a Windows run of `available` with and without the setting is filed for main's runners.

### A-418 — The Windows resync wire: a `Resync` names the fresh stream end's handle in its holder's process (2026-11-18, goal 90, item b, piece one: what Shards needs from slates; A-316's and A-339's Windows half)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6, the Shards form's resync bullet; GAPS, A-281's entry (its Windows owed item);
`crates/bridge-fuse/src/shards_resync.rs` (`HandedResync`, `RESYNC_HANDLE_MESSAGE_BYTES`, `ResyncRefusal::NoHandle`, the
module's channel and message paragraphs).

- **What was there.** A-316's and A-339's `Resync` carries the device's end of a fresh stream by `SCM_RIGHTS`. Windows
  carries no descriptor with a message: a handle reaches another process only when a holder duplicates it into that
  process's table (`DuplicateHandle` with the target's process handle), and only its value travels (A-175's route,
  `slates_ipc::handle_route`). So a Windows `Resync` must say where the end was put.
- **The message.** The same 28 bytes as every `Resync` (kind 2, version 1, two zero bytes, the attachment, the token),
  then the id of the process the successor duplicated the fresh end into (`u32`) and the end's handle value there
  (`u64`, never zero: zero names no handle, A-175's convention), little-endian, 40 bytes in all. The `Attached`
  message is the 28 bytes on every platform. The channel on Windows is a message-mode named pipe
  (`slates_ipc::stream::message_pair`, as the anchor's hold channel is), so each message is one read whole and the
  lengths never run together; each form is refused at the other's length, so neither passes for the other.
- **To whom the end goes: the stream's holder, never the confined VM.** Shards' coordinator set condition 4c
  (2026-11-18): a VM process confined in an AppContainer takes handles only through its spawner's grants, so the new
  stream must reach it the way `--slates-fs-handle` does. The process named is therefore the one that holds the stream
  for the VM: the process `slates shards` names with `ShardsHolder` (A-181), else the attaching client. How the device
  takes the end from there is its handle path, which the coordinator specifies with the device's half.
- **Default deny (condition 4a).** The device takes a Windows resync only if it parses at its length, is version 1 and
  kind `Resync` with zero reserved bytes, names a handle, and names the attachment and token of the channel's
  `Attached` (`HandedResync::resyncs`, the token compared over all its bytes).
- **Evidence.** The codec's unit tests (`crates/bridge-fuse`, `shards_resync`): the golden vector, every forgery (each
  token byte, another attachment, an `Attached` in the Windows form, a zero handle), every wrong length to twice the
  message, another version, a reserved byte, and every single-bit flip parsed or refused without a panic.
- **Owed.** The attach's half on Windows (built by A-427, but for `slates shards` handing the end to its command): the
  message-mode resync pipe made at the attach, `Attached` written before the hand-off, the daemon's end held by the
  anchor with the session (token, owner view, form, and the holder's process id and start time, so a successor never
  duplicates into a reused id), the device's end handed beside the stream's (`ShardsHanded`, the client,
  `slates shards`, `serve_shards`). The successor's half: the held end adopted, the
  record kept, a fresh pipe, its client end duplicated into the holder and named in this message, the replies kept for
  a resend and the `FORGET`s logged as on Unix. The anchor's Windows hold needs a kind for the resync end and a
  message that replaces a held entry's record (the session moves as the guest names its owner, its `INIT` is answered,
  a restore runs and its holder changes): built by A-423. And Shards' device half.

### A-420 — A commit times the decode a replay of its record does, and recovery replays a record at a time (2026-11-18, goal 83, g251; A-243's open line)

Applied in the same change to:
- §4.8: the A-243 status blockquote and the Recovery paragraph's account of the measure.
- GAPS: the load-test entry's open line (the commits' measure against the replay's).
- `crates/db/src/record.rs`: `LogRing::encode`, `Encoded::decode_as_replayed` and `LogRing::write` in place of
  `append`; `LogRing::replay` hands each record to its caller's apply before reading the next (`Replayed::records` in
  place of the collected `ops`).
- `crates/db/src/replay.rs`: `append_record` and `timed`; `derive_partition` applies as it walks; the unit test.
- `crates/ipc` (`DbSnapshotReport::tail_replay_ns`'s doc).
- **What was there.** A-243's trigger fires once the tail's replay work, as its commits measured it, reaches the
  recovery budget, so a recovery keeps to the budget only while that measure is at least the replay's own work. The
  commits timed each record's encode, checksum, copy and apply; a replay reads, checksums, decodes and applies, and it
  decoded the whole tail into one list before applying any of it. Where a record's decode costs more than its encode
  the measure fell short: CI's macOS runner measured 0.4x to 1.25x of the replay (run 44260193629's mix test), and a
  record of a thousand one-byte keys (its decode allocates each key, its encode copies five bytes a key) replays in
  more than its commits measured on any machine.
- **The rule.** The measure covers the replay's work, step for step. A commit encodes its record, decodes the body as
  the replay will, writes it (the checksum and the copy) and applies it, and charges all four: the decode is the
  replay's own, the write's checksum and copy are the replay's checksum and copy out of the ring, and the encode (an
  allocation and a write of every byte) bounds the replay's read (an allocation, a zeroing and a copy). So the measure
  errs early only by the encode and a preempted commit's stall. A body that does not decode is refused `Corrupt`
  before anything is written: a replay would cut the record there, and every record after it with it. Recovery
  decodes, applies and drops one record at a time, so it holds one decoded record, never a tail's worth, and repeats
  per record what the commit timed.
- **Rejected.** A per-class model of replay cost learned from recoveries: it learns nothing before a daemon's first
  recovery, which is the one the bound must hold for, and a model by class and bytes misjudges records of one class
  and size with different shapes (a thousand small keys against one large one), the extrapolation A-243 removed.
- **Cost.** One decode a commit, the allocations of the record's decoded fields, beside the clone, encode, checksum,
  copy and apply it already made; the replay saves a tail-sized list.
- **Tests.** `a_tails_measured_replay_work_covers_its_replay_when_its_records_decode_dearer_than_they_encode`
  (`replay.rs`'s unit tests): 64 records of 1,024 one-byte keys, their replay in a recovery past a baseline held to
  what the commits measured. The cadence and cost tests (`snapshot_cadence.rs`, `snapshot_cost.rs`, the model) are
  filed for main.

### A-419 — A DAX fill that fails part-way leaves its range uncleared and counted, cleared before its next fill begins (2026-11-18, goal 83 item B7, g079; §4.6 the backed route; A-163, A-193)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6 (the Shards route's DAX line), GAPS (the 2026-10-25 G-vhost entry's open line and
the backed L1 entry's twin), `crates/vfs/src/shards_backing.rs` (`ShardsBacking::mark_uncleared`, `uncleared`,
`cleared`), `crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs` (a range's fill begins by clearing an uncleared one; a failure and
`abandon_fill` leave it uncleared; `charge_of`; the fill's `range_charge` removed) with three unit tests, and the bug
record `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-dax-fill-refused-part-way-left-its-bytes-for-a-later-fill-to-show.md`.
- **What was there.** A range is marked filled when its fill begins, so write-through reaches it. A fill refused
  part-way (the volume refusing a slice's seek or read, the OS a store or a placement) or given up (the attachment's
  bridge gone) unmarked the range and gave its charge back, while the pages its slices stored stayed in the object. No
  change of the file reached the range from then on, and its next fill copies only the volume's data runs and pages
  that are not zeros, since a range never filled reads zero. So where the file had since become a hole or zeros, the
  guest's map showed the old bytes, and the backings held those pages uncounted. A-193's "placed after the fill"
  reasoned from the old rule.
- **The rule.** A fill that fails or is given up part-way leaves its range uncleared: no longer filled, so no write
  reaches it, and still counted, since its slices may have stored bytes. The next fill of the range clears it before
  it stores anything (`DaxObject::zero`: Linux gives the pages back; macOS and Windows store zeros over what holds
  bytes, within the range's charge), then fills it as a range never filled. A clear the OS refuses refuses that fill,
  and the range stays uncleared and counted. A backing's charge counts its filled and uncleared ranges together, so a
  range moving between them changes no count, and letting the backing go gives both back.
- **Why this and not another.**
  - Clearing at the failure would need a second path for a clear refused there, and on macOS and Windows zeroing gives
    no memory back, so the range would stay counted anyway.
  - Clearing every range as its fill begins costs nothing on Linux, but on Windows a zeroing is stores over the whole
    2 MiB (a section tells no holes), which would make every hole's pages resident. Only a range a fill left part-way
    can hold bytes.
  - Comparing every page with the volume, as a refill does, reads every page of the range, which on Windows faults
    its committed pages in.
- **What it costs.** Nothing on a fill that does not fail. A failed range stays counted until it is filled again or its
  backing goes: at most a range for each fill that failed, within the budget.
- **Tests** (`crates/bridge-core/src/dax_backing.rs`, the lib's unit tests; the refusal injected by a context of
  another volume, which the bridge refuses as any read it cannot serve):
  `a_fill_refused_part_way_leaves_nothing_a_later_fill_shows`, `a_fill_abandoned_part_way_leaves_nothing_a_later_fill_shows`
  and `a_part_way_fill_stays_counted_until_its_range_is_filled_again`. The Mac Studio (d1323898, macOS arm64), debug
  build, 2026-11-18: red without the fix, 3 of 3 failing (kiln r97: the refused and abandoned fills' first slice still
  read `A` after the file was zeroed; 2,097,152 bytes counted where two ranges held bytes); green with it, the module's
  5 of 5.
- **Siblings, reported, not changed here** (each from reading, each owed a failing test; GAPS):
  - a successor's adopted DAX object (A-365) may hold a fill's bytes in a range its range table does not name, since
    a range is recorded only once answered: the one the dead daemon was filling, or one that failed there;
  - on Windows a range is committed (`prepare_range`) before its charge is asked, so a `Budget` refusal leaves a
    committed range uncounted, and Windows gives no committed page of a section back.

### A-414 — The leases off the placeholder take the failover delay as their term, and a write lease stays its holder's while any of its write attachments lives (2026-11-18, built for goal g255; A-363's owed list, the volume's write lease owed since A-384; D-16, §4.15 "The lease keepalive")
- **What was there.** The volume's write lease (D-16), a landing's target lease and the grant a bypass policy issues
  for its landing, and a staging buffer each took the operator's 10 s placeholder (`DaemonConfig::failover_slo_ns`) as
  their term, after A-363 made the failover delay a live output and A-375 moved the waits that bound a failover to it.
  And the write lease ran out at its term whatever its holder still held: it was taken at an attach for writing,
  renewed only by the same principal's next such attach, and released by the reaper at its term, so ten seconds after
  a library client or a mount attached a volume for writing, another principal could attach it for writing too while
  the first still wrote. Writes do not check the lease; its term gates another writer's take.
- **The rule.** Each of these terms is the node's failover delay (`ShardState::failover_ns`, A-363): a holder that is
  gone keeps what it held no longer than a failover would leave it unserved. A write lease is renewed by whatever holds
  it (A-384's rule), and a write attachment is its holder's presence: at the lease's lapse the reaper renews it at its
  epoch while its holder holds a live write attachment of the volume (`verbs::expire_leases`, `lease_kept_until`), to
  that attachment's own expiry for a CLI attachment (its term is its holder's pace, A-384) and a failover delay ahead
  for any other kind, each of which ends by a rule of its own (a library client's at its reap, a mount's at its
  unmount or its daemon's end, a guest device's at its hangup, another host's at that host's reap of its client or its
  retirement, A-222). Another principal's take of a lease past its term whose holder still holds one is refused
  `LeaseHeld` (`verbs::take_write_lease`), so the moment between the lapse and the reaper's pass hands it to no second
  writer. Once the holder's write attachments have ended, the lease lasts one term more, as before: a client reaped
  while paused keeps it (T-2.3). A record the database refuses at the pass is counted (`db.secondary_refused`); the
  pass dropped it silently before.
- **Not a renewal per use.** A CLI attachment's renewals do not renew the lease with them (the first build did, a
  durable record more per renewal, three a second for a held attachment): the lease is renewed once a term, at its
  lapse, and a take between judges the holder's attachments directly.
- **Test support.** `Daemon::inject_failover` now holds the delay on every shard at once: a laptop runs no coordinator
  to fan it, and these terms are read on every shard. The integration tests that shortened a lease through the
  placeholder hold the delay instead (`crates/client/tests/reap.rs`, `crates/server/tests/landing_fairness.rs`).
- **Not moved, owed, each a term of its own:** the NFSv4 and delegation leases (the lease the server advertises, and the
  wait a landing gives a recalled delegation, which must stay equal to it), the anchor's restart cap, and four bounds
  that are not leases: the FUSE mount and unmount helpers' (a helper process's wait), the status capture's (its
  deadline counts from the request, so a scatter on a starved daemon would lose it at a shorter one; it should count
  from the capture), a move's overdue bound and the telemetry freshness horizon (failover-shaped, but their tests run
  in the fleet suites). Then `FAILOVER_SLO_NS` and `with_failover_slo` go.
- **What changes.** On a laptop these terms fall from 10 s to its failover delay, about two seconds (A-405), and in a
  quiet fleet to about four to five: a landing's lease is renewed between its slices at half its term, so a starved
  control shard now has half the delay, not five seconds, to answer a renewal before the landing's entries are fenced
  `LeaseEnded` (filed for main's starved landing lane). A volume a live writer holds is never taken by a second writer,
  however long the first sits idle.
- **Tests.** `a_write_lease_stays_its_holders_while_the_holder_keeps_a_write_attachment` (the reaper's pass past the
  term renews the owner's lease at its epoch; another principal refused `LeaseHeld` past the renewed term with no pass
  between; granted once the owner's attachment ended) and
  `a_cli_attachment_keeps_the_write_lease_to_its_own_term_and_a_read_one_keeps_none` (`crates/server/src/verbs.rs`).
  Run on the Mac Studio (kiln, 2026-11-18, load 19, debug build, `cargo test --locked -p slates-server --lib -- lease
  fanned_the_failover`): 27 of 27, both new tests among them with the landing lease's, the owner lease's and the fan's.
  Red-checked once: with the pass releasing a kept lease, the first test fails at its renewal. The integration tests
  this change edits (the client reap, the landing keepalive) are filed for main's suites.

Applied in the same change to: §4.4 "Derived constants" (its status), GAPS (the `LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS` entry),
`docs/cli.md`, `crates/server/src/{verbs,landing,daemon,remote_attach}.rs`, `crates/db/src/catalog.rs` (the consumers'
lease docs), `crates/client/tests/reap.rs`, `crates/server/tests/landing_fairness.rs`, `crates/cli/tests/fs_server.rs`
(a bound's comment).

### A-421 — The load test's workers park between replies and sends, as the clients they stand for do (2026-11-18, built for goals 231 and 257, 1,000 clients under 1 ms; the harness's half of A-297's measurement)
Applied in the same change to: GAPS (the load test's entry), `crates/client/examples/load_bench.rs` (`drive`,
`Worker::sweep`, `park_until`, `arm_in_flight`, `count_park`, `park_margin_ns`, `next_due`, `park` paired for Unix and
Windows, `park_timeout_ns`, `Parked`, `Connection::completion`, the `harness` row's park columns, the module's "Workers
wait"), and the example's tests below.

Status: **rejected 2026-11-18** by its A/B, and taken back out the same day (g083): the supervisor's run r155 on the Mac
Studio over `fs/` at 1,000 clients (BENCHMARKS, "A load-test worker that parks between replies") found the longest
sweep shorter in 1 pair of 6, the held clients the same (none in any of the twelve runs), and the p99 worse once the box
was loaded (an edit's 26.9 ms against 8.6 ms at load 25 to 28). A dead-even or worse A/B does not land. The workers
spin again; the change's lint fixes stay (the stamp tests' preemption is a yielding wait, D-9; the span drain keeps no
name it never reads), and its two parking tests went with the parking. The text below is the record of what was built.
- **What was measured.** Every worker spun for its whole level, so the harness took a core a worker from the daemon it
  measured: eight on the Mac Studio's 32. On that box under load its sweeps took 25 to 127 ms and held 6.9 clients on
  average, due to send and not yet sent, against 2.2 in flight, at 1,000 clients (g083's trace, 2026-11-18).
- **The rule.** A worker whose sweep took no reply and sent nothing sweeps on for the daemon's published spin window
  (the measured mean cost of a wake), as an async client spins before it parks. Then it arms the completion of every
  connection with a request in flight, drains those once more, which closes the race with a reply that landed before
  its arm, and parks on every connection's completion until a reply makes one readable or its next deadline comes:
  the earliest due send, overdue check or progress report. It wakes early by the spin window and by the mean lateness
  of its timed-out parks, and spins the rest of the way, so a due client is sent on time. Every arm is cleared after
  the park, so a reply taken while the worker sweeps costs the daemon no wake. A worker does not park while a
  connection reconnects or resends: those keep their own pacing. A reply that comes while its worker is parked costs
  the daemon a wake and the worker its wakeup, inside that reply's latency, as it does for an agent's async client.
- **Per platform.** Linux polls the rendezvous's eventfd and macOS each connection's completion bridge pipe, both with
  `poll(2)` (on macOS under a launchd job's timer policy it comes back about 2 ms late where `nanosleep` and `select`
  come back about 76 ms late, 2026-10-26). Windows polls each completion bridge's socket with `WSAPoll`, which waits on
  at least one socket, so every connection's completion is in the set. A connection whose completion is not armed is
  never made readable.
- **Counted.** The `harness` row now ends with the parks, those a reply ended, the worker-nanoseconds parked and the
  mean lateness of the parks that met their deadline.
- **Tests** (`cargo test -p slates-client --example load_bench`): `a_parked_worker_is_woken_by_its_reply` (the daemon's
  one shard held until the worker has armed its connection and found its ring empty; the reply ends the park long
  before its 5 s deadline and is there to be taken; then, with nothing in flight, a park meets its 20 ms deadline less
  its margin and its lateness is kept) and `a_park_wakes_its_margin_before_its_deadline`. The stamp tests now stand in
  for the host's preemption with a yielding wait rather than a blocking sleep (D-9). The A/B is main's: main's harness,
  spinning, against this one at the same daemon, `held`, `max_sweep_ns` and every kind's `latency` and `floor` p99.

### A-423 — The Windows anchor holds a Shards stream's resync end, and a daemon replaces a held entry's record as the stream's session moves (2026-11-18, goal 90, item b, piece two; A-418's owed anchor formats)
Applied in the same change to: A-418's owed list; GAPS, A-281's entry (its Windows item);
`crates/anchor/src/handles.rs` (`WHAT_SHARDS_RESYNC`, `SHARDS_RESYNC_HANDLES`, `admits`, `HandleMessage::Record`, its
encoding and its decoding, the module's notes); `crates/anchor/src/held_windows.rs` (`Held::apply` takes a record's
replacement; `Held::hold` admits each kind at its handle counts); `crates/anchor/src/supervise_windows.rs` (the drain
bound's derivation).

- **What was there.** The Windows hold (A-198) held one kind of entry, a WinFsp mount's handles, and kept each entry's
  record as its hold set it: any other kind was refused `Malformed`, and nothing could change a record once held. A
  Shards stream's resync end needs both: its hold is one handle, the daemon's end of the stream's message-mode resync
  pipe, and its record is the stream's session, which moves while the stream lives (the guest names its owner, its
  kernel's `INIT` is answered, a restore takes a saved guest's tables, a holder is named for the stream), as the Unix
  hold's session does (`crate::held`'s `Session` message, A-281, A-378).
- **The kinds.** `admits(what, count)`: a WinFsp mount one to `MAX_HANDLES` handles, as A-198 left it (its daemon names
  two since A-369; the room stays for a daemon built apart across an upgrade); a Shards stream's resync end
  (`WHAT_SHARDS_RESYNC`, 2) exactly one; any other kind nothing. A record is opaque to the anchor, within `RECORD_CAP`.
- **The record's replacement.** `Record { id, record }` (kind 6), laid out as a hold whose kind, count and handle slots
  are zero, which decoding requires, so the message has one encoding and names no handle; nothing is duplicated for
  it. Answered `Held { id }` once the anchor keeps the new record, the entry's handles as they were held, and refused
  `Malformed` and counted, with nothing changed, for an entry the anchor does not hold or a record past the cap. Its
  answer is a hold's: a daemon runs one exchange at a time, sends a record's replacement only for an entry the anchor
  answered held, and gives the stream's resync up rather than send another after one whose answer did not come, so
  no answer can be taken for another of the same entry. An anchor built before this refuses the kind and the message,
  so a newer daemon's stream is served without a resync there (Shards' option (a)), as when the anchor refuses a hold.
- **Evidence.** The formats' unit tests, on every host (`crates/anchor`, `handles`): the record's golden vector, a
  resync hold and two records round-tripping, a record naming a kind, a count or a handle and one past the cap refused
  with every changed bit, a long record refused at encoding, and `admits` for every count of every kind. Red first: on
  main the tests did not build (no `Record`, `WHAT_SHARDS_RESYNC` or `admits`). The hold's own test
  (`held_windows.rs`, Windows): a resync end held alone and a two-handle one refused, its record replaced and handed to
  the next process under its kind, and a replacement for an entry not held or past the cap refused and counted, with
  nothing changed; compiled clean for Windows (`cargo xwin check`), its run filed for main.
- **Owed.** The daemon's half: its hold of a resync end and its record's replacements over `crate::anchor_hold`'s
  exchange (built by A-427), and a successor adopting a handed resync entry (A-418's successor half).

### A-425 — The NFSv4 lease is derived from the clients it serves, and every wait on a recalled delegation reads it: one number for the lease advertised, the recall's revocation, the quiet period, the NFSv3 gate and a landing (2026-11-18, built for goal g255; A-414's owed list; RFC 8881 §8.3, §10.4, §10.4.5; §4.6 A-35, A-78, A-79)
- **What was there.** The listener granted and advertised (`FATTR4_LEASE_TIME`) the operator's failover SLO, the 10 s
  placeholder, and five places read it each for itself: the session table's limits, the delegation drain's revocation of
  a recall not answered within a lease, the quiet period before a recalled file is delegated again, the NFSv3 write the
  recall gate refused, and a landing waiting on a recall. A failover setting decided an NFS client's lease, and a short
  one broke the clients: an idle Linux client renews no sooner than five seconds after its last renewal whatever lease
  it is told (`nfs4_schedule_state_renewal`, `if (timeout < 5 * HZ) timeout = 5 * HZ;`, fs/nfs/nfs4renewd.c, Linux
  master, read 2026-11-18), so under a lease shorter than that it lapsed between two of its renewals and a full client
  table dropped a live client's opens, locks and delegations.
- **The rule.** The lease is what the clients it serves need, not the failover delay: the longest an idle Linux client
  goes between two renewals (`config::NFS_V4_CLIENT_RENEWAL_FLOOR_NS`, the served client's fact) and a liveness window
  for the renewal's delivery (A-228's lateness), rounded up to the whole seconds `FATTR4_LEASE_TIME` carries, so the
  lease a client is told is the lease it holds: 6 s (`config::NfsV4Caps::lease_ns`, logged with its inputs at boot). The
  failover delay is shorter on a laptop and in a quiet fleet (2 s and 4-5 s), and the lease cannot follow it below the
  clients' renewals; a dead client's delegation now holds a landing or an NFSv3 writer at most 6 s, not 10. Every wait
  on a recall reads the one accessor, `nfs::v4_lease_ns`, so the lease advertised and the waits on it are one number by
  construction (the session table's limits, `delegation::drain`, the quiet period in `nfs_state::file_state`, the NFSv3
  gate in `nfs::serve_local_held`, and `landing::recall_before_finish`).
- **Not changed, owed.** The table's lapse is still one lease for every client; a client slower than Linux's floor (none
  measured) would be judged by its own renewal gaps under A-384's accrual rule, a change of its own. The listener is
  courteous (RFC 8881 §8.3): a lapsed client keeps its state until the table is full, so the lease bounds a dead
  client's hold on a full table and on a recalled delegation, not a live client's.
- **Test support.** The tests that ran a short NFSv4 lease set it on the listener's own knob (`config.nfs_v4.lease_ns`)
  where they set the failover SLO (`crates/server/tests/nfs_mount.rs`, four; `crates/server/tests/recovery.rs`, one).
- **Test.** `an_idle_linux_client_keeps_its_nfs_v4_lease_whatever_the_failover_slo` (`crates/server/src/nfs.rs`): on a
  daemon whose failover SLO is one liveness window, a client table of one under the listener's limits keeps a client
  silent for Linux's renewal floor and a liveness window less a nanosecond (a second client refused `NFS4ERR_DELAY`),
  and makes room once it has been silent a whole lease.
  Run on the Mac Studio (kiln, 2026-11-18, load 5-10, debug build, `cargo test --locked -p slates-server --lib -- nfs
  delegation recall config::`): 22 of 22. Red-checked once: with the limits reading the failover SLO again, the test
  fails at its first ask (the idle client dropped for the second). The NFS suites that run the delegation recall,
  the NFSv3 gate and the landings held for a recall, now on the listener's own knob, are filed for main's run.

Applied in the same change to: §4.4 "Derived constants" (its status), GAPS (the `LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS` entry),
`crates/server/src/{config,nfs,nfs_state,delegation,landing}.rs`, `crates/server/tests/{nfs_mount,recovery}.rs`.

### A-424 — A captured clone lands against its capture, judged by content (2026-11-18, g267, stage 1 of the captured clone's landing; §4.15 `capture_base` and "Plan", A-291)

- **What was there.** A clone of a captured base (A-291) has no base plane: its record is `Scratch` and the capture made
  every body the volume's own, so its landing planned every file as a create. A file its agent changed met the
  target's copy as `CreateCreate`, an outsider's change to a file the agent never touched was a conflict too, a
  removal was never carried, and a landing that did succeed took the target as the clone's base, after which the clone
  no longer moved (GAPS g267, found reading `crates/land/src/verdict.rs`).
- **The rule.** A scratch clone of a snapshot recorded captured lands against that snapshot (`landing::capture_of`, the
  capture on the clone's own shard since a clone shares its origin's store): the manifest is the change of the source
  since the capture (`slates_vfs::captured::ChangedPaths`, stepped a record or a directory a unit, its cost the change
  rather than the tree; `PlanWalk::against_capture`), each entry judged by content (`Judged::Content`): the witness is the
  identity of the captured bytes, a content manifest has its own encoding version so no grant of one binds the other,
  the disk is hashed for every replacement and removal, and `content_verdict` writes or removes only over the captured
  bytes. A removed directory goes only once emptied (`Landing::remove_emptied_dir`, never recursive) and only when it
  held nothing but what the manifest removes at validation (`Ours::removed`). The write is bound to the object the
  validation found (`Landing::observed`, the witness's fingerprint for the write path), so an outsider's change between
  validation and write is a conflict. The finish leaves the clone as it was: a scratch volume that still moves.
- **Tests.** `the_candidates_hold_every_change_and_nothing_untouched`, `a_clone_nothing_changed_has_no_candidates`,
  `held_at_reads_each_kind_and_nothing_beneath_a_file` (`crates/vfs/src/captured.rs`: a full walk of both trees as the
  oracle; an untouched file in a touched directory is no candidate); `the_content_table` (`crates/land/src/verdict.rs`);
  `a_captured_clone_lands_its_change_since_the_capture_and_passes_an_outsiders`,
  `an_outsiders_change_under_the_agents_is_a_conflict_and_nothing_is_written`,
  `a_target_already_holding_the_change_is_accepted_and_written_over_nothing` (`crates/land/src/captured_tests.rs`,
  over the simulated host).
- **Owed.** The advance (a second landing judged against what the first landed); stage 2, a moved captured clone landed
  against its capture (it keeps no lineage on its new node and still lands as a scratch volume); a kind change as one
  entry; the server's own test landing a captured clone into a real directory (filed for main).

Applied in the same change to: `crates/vfs/src/{captured,lib,volume}.rs` (`captured`, `Volume::frozen_tree`,
`Volume::head_tree`, `read_frozen_body`), `crates/land/src/{manifest,verdict,engine,lib,captured_tests}.rs`
(`Judged`, `Manifest::basis`, `PlanWalk::against_capture`, `content_verdict`, `Beginning::against_capture`,
`begin_landing_from`), `crates/server/src/landing.rs` (`capture_of`, `landing_beginning`), §4.15's status, GAPS (g267).

### A-422 — A volume a publication leaves out keeps its logged writes for the next daemon (2026-11-18, goal g268; found by reading in A-410's sibling sweep; §4.8, D-18; amends A-63's clear rule)
Applied in the same change to:
- `crates/server/src/write_log.rs`: `WriteLog::retain` (with `compact` and `restamp`), `owe_restamp`,
  `forgive_restamp`, the overflow word's two bits (`OVERFLOWED`, `RESTAMP_OWED`), `open` and `read` on a stale stamp
  with the restamp owed, the module doc; three unit tests. `log_forgets` and `FORGET_UNLOGGED` are Unix-only, as their
  callers are, and so is `ShardState::writes_lost`: Windows' lint lane found all three dead there.
- `crates/server/src/verbs.rs`: `settle_write_log` replaces `clear_write_log`; `publish_checkpoint` and
  `publish_delta_into` owe the restamp before a commit that leaves a volume out and forgive it on a refusal; the test
  `a_volume_a_publication_leaves_out_keeps_its_logged_writes_for_the_next_daemon`.
- §4.6 (the takeover status, after the volume-naming paragraph); GAPS (2026-11-18); the bug record
  `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-left-out-volumes-logged-writes-were-dropped-at-the-next-restart.md`.

- **What was there.** A-63 emptied and stamped the write log after a publication that captured every volume, and a
  restarted daemon replays the log only when its stamp equals the committed image's generation. A publication that
  cannot image a volume (an overlay whose base host is away or whose base cannot be read) commits a newer generation
  without that volume and left the log under its older stamp. A successor then found the stamp older than the image
  and replayed nothing, and the left-out volume lost every write acknowledged since its last capture, with no loss
  reported.
- **The rule.** After every publication the log holds, for each volume, the records acknowledged since the
  publication that last captured it, under the latest committed generation. A publication that captured every volume
  empties it, as before. One that left volumes out keeps exactly their records and drops the rest, which its image
  carries; replaying those over the image could undo a later change, such as a truncate. The records are kept in
  order and in place, and then the length, the layout and the stamp are stored, in that order.
- **The window.** The restamp follows the commit. So a publication that leaves a volume out first sets the overflow
  word's second bit (the restamp owed), and the retain or a refusal clears it. A successor that finds a stale stamp
  with the bit set cannot tell which records the image carries. It reports the writes lost, as an overflow does, and
  starts its log under the recovered stamp with the loss kept until a publication captures every volume. The bit
  says nothing beside a current stamp, which is what a death before the commit, or after the restamp but before the
  bit is cleared, leaves.
- **Why not per-record generations.** A record stamped with the generation it was appended under would let recovery
  replay a record only past its volume's last capture, with no rewrite. But recovery knows no volume's capture
  generation (`Journal::recover` folds deltas into one image), and a log that only grows while a volume stays left out
  fills, where the retain gives the captured volumes' room back at every such publication.
- **Evidence.** The shard-level test drives a delta that leaves out an overlay whose host was taken and opens the
  log as a restarted daemon does. With the fix it hands back exactly the overlay's logged write, not the plain
  volume's that the delta carries; without it, nothing. The write log's tests cover the retain's order and scrub, the
  owed bit at a death, before a commit and after a refusal, and an overflow kept through a retain. On a Mac Studio
  (2026-11-18, debug) the four new tests pass with the write log's eight others and the two publication tests that
  leave a volume out (`a_streamed_checkpoint_restarts_without_a_volume_it_cannot_capture`,
  `a_publish_leaves_out_a_volume_being_destroyed`), 14 of 14; the shard-level test was red once with both parts
  of the fix removed, the restarted daemon handed nothing (`left: []`). `cargo xwin check -p slates-server
  --all-targets` for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` is clean of the three dead items. The restart through a real daemon
  is main's (`run-requests.md`).

### A-429 — The write log's replay writes an overlay's logged write through its host (2026-11-18, goal g268; found by reading in A-422's sibling sweep; §4.6 "Linux", §4.15 copy-up; amends A-63's replay)
Applied in the same change to: `crates/server/src/verbs.rs` (`replay_one`; the test
`a_replayed_write_into_an_overlays_base_file_keeps_the_disks_bytes_around_it`), §4.6 (the takeover status, after
A-422's paragraph), GAPS (A-422's entry, its second sibling marked fixed) and the bug record
`docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-replayed-write-into-an-overlays-base-file-zeroed-the-bytes-before-it.md`.

- **What was there.** A transport's write reaches an overlay through the overlay's host (`VolumeBridge::write`,
  `host_for`). `Overlay::write` copies a base file up first: it reads the file and records its witness, and for the
  large class it pins each touched window from the disk. Only then does it apply the bytes. The replay of a logged
  write (`replay_one`) called `Volume::write` with no host. For a file the dead daemon had copied up after its last
  publication, which the recovered image still holds as a base file, the write opened its chunk window from the
  window's start with nothing of the disk in it. Every byte of the window before the write then read as zero, and the
  file was left unwitnessed.
- **The rule.** A replayed write is the write the transport made, applied the way the transport applied it. An
  overlay's record goes through `Volume::with_host` and the slot's host, and an overlay whose host is away is refused
  `BaseUnavailable`, as the bridge refuses it. Recovery reopens an overlay's host before it replays the log
  (`build_recovered_volume`), so in a recovery only a volume it could not rebuild lacks one, and that volume is not
  replayed.
- **What remains.** A base file the disk changed between the dead daemon's copy-up and the replay is copied up as the
  disk holds it now. The dead daemon's copy was never published, so the replayed write lands on the newer bytes;
  logging a copy-up's bytes would cost a whole file per first write.
- **Evidence.** The test replays a logged write of eight bytes at byte 10 of an uncopied base file (the server crate's
  `lib.rs`) and reads the file back through the overlay: with the fix it reads as the disk's file with the eight bytes
  in place. It was red once with the replay writing through the volume alone, the first difference at byte 0 (Mac
  Studio, 2026-11-18T20:29Z, debug); with the fix it passes beside the clone replay test and the write log's eleven (13
  of 13).

### A-428 — A holder owed an install is sent the last whole state while the retained tail reaches past it (2026-11-18, g232; §4.10 live shipping, A-344's warm restart; the regression main bisected to A-376)

Applied in the same change to: §4.10's status ("A restarted owner's log shipped nothing once its holders came back"),
GAPS (A-344's entry), `docs/bugs/2026-11-18-a-restarted-owners-log-shipped-nothing-once-its-holders-came-back.md`,
`crates/db/src/live.rs` (`Shipper::retains_after`), `crates/server/src/live_ship.rs` (`reached_volume`), and the test
below.
- **What was there.** A holder that came back to a live volume and was owed an install waited for an image made at the
  log's head whenever the last whole state was behind the head (`reached_volume`, `owes_image`). After an owner's warm
  restart (A-344) the resumed log's first whole entry is made before the owner's pairs are delivered again, so it covers
  no candidate's key, and a write appends after it. Then three rules each waited on another: the image is not made while
  a whole record is owed (`refresh_image`), and the period owes one to cover the candidates' keys once the pairs are
  delivered; that record waits for credit (`Shipper::admits_checkpoint`); and the credit is freed only by the holders
  taking the entries in flight, which needs the installs. Nothing shipped, and every write after the restart was refused
  `DurabilityPending` at the held-reply bound. Main bisected the fleet test's red to A-376 (its cheaper holder
  publications changed the order of the restart's steps); the cause is the live log's.
- **The rule.** A holder owed an install is sent the last whole state while the retained tail still holds every entry
  after it (`Shipper::retains_after`): installed there, it takes those entries from the tail, so its acknowledgements
  free the credit and the owed record follows. Only a whole state behind the tail, which would leave the holder owing a
  second install, waits for an image made at the head, as the rolling partition's installs need
  (diag-live-durability-54).
- **Test.** `live_ship::tests::a_returned_holder_owed_an_install_is_sent_the_last_whole_state_while_the_tail_reaches_past_it`:
  a resumed log past position 5 with its whole entry at 6 and a write at 7, both holders returned: each is sent an
  install of the whole state at 6; past two writes with the tail cut to its newest entry, none is sent. Red on main's
  rule: the first case sent nothing either.
- **Still owed.** With the tail cut past the last whole state, a whole record owed (for the keys, or after a refused
  publication) and a full credit can still meet the same wait; see GAPS.

### A-426 — A scatter's part waits for room, and a batch of asks for its green owner's answer, in the target's own time (2026-11-18, built for goal g255; R3's class A; A-65, A-216, A-228, A-232, A-247, A-388)
- **What was there.** A scatter's part (a listing's, the grants', the daemon's status, an acknowledgement's) that met
  its target shard's control channel full waited for room half a liveness window on the wall, then settled the scatter
  `Overloaded { shard }` (`verbs::PART_ROOM_BUDGET_NS`, "so the typed `Overloaded` reaches the client before it gives
  the reply up"). A batch of asks to a green's owner (`work_home`, A-388) waited for room and for the owner's answer
  within the lease bound on the wall, then answered its asks unanswered. Since 2026-11-13 a client waits for a live
  daemon's answer however long (A-232), so the first reason was gone, and both bounds refused a target that was alive
  and working, starved or slow to drain: the wall judgment class A's other waits gave up (A-65, A-403, A-408).
- **The rule.** One room wait (`xshard::given_room_in_shard_time`), judged at each window's end in the target's own
  time (`RoomRule`): a shard drains its control channel at every step, so its step count says whether room will come,
  not its CPU clock (a shard inside one poll runs, or wakes now and then, and drains nothing until the poll ends). A
  target that stepped in the window is draining and is waited for another whole window; one that took no step but
  waits for a CPU is starved, not stuck (A-228), and is waited for while it has run less than the budget of CPU since
  the wait began (A-318's rule for one poll, the budget held to this build); one that took no step and waits on nothing
  else, or ran its budget in one poll, or cannot be read, ends the wait, and the part is refused typed. The steps are
  read twice around the scheduler's look, as `observe::ShardTime` reads its clock, so a target that stepped between
  the reads is read as draining. The scatter's part's window is `LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS / LATE_BEAT_SHARE`, the gap in
  which the daemon logs one of its own shards as a near miss, so a stuck target is refused typed before the watchdog's
  own judgment would end the daemon (A-232). A batch of asks to a green's owner waits for room the same way and for the
  owner's answer by `within_shard_time` (A-65), both with the lease bound as their window and budget, as before its
  wall deadline (`xshard::call_in_shard_time_given_room`).
- **Tests.** `a_part_waits_for_room_while_its_target_steps` (`crates/server/src/xshard.rs`): a stand-in shard stepped
  once each look's span from a thread of its own, its one-slot channel full, is drained a quarter of a window after the
  room wait's first window; the part is sent and its message is next on the channel. And
  `a_room_wait_goes_on_while_its_target_steps_or_starves_and_ends_when_it_does_neither` (the rule over scripted
  readings: a step, a starved target with CPU left and past its budget, a blocked one, a step between the reads, no
  reading, the mark's move). The four scatter tests of `crates/server/tests/ack_release.rs` hold their target inside one
  poll that sleeps, which takes no step and reads blocked, so each is still refused `Overloaded` at the first window, as
  they assert; the stand-in of `a_bounded_wait_for_room_waits_its_period_in_time_on_a_starved_shard` never steps and has
  no thread to read, so it is given up at its first window too.
  Run on the Mac Studio (kiln, 2026-11-18, load 8-12, debug build, `cargo test --locked -p slates-server --lib -- room
  xshard:: work_home`): 19 of 19, both new tests and every room wait's with them. Red-checked once: with the judge
  never consulted past the first window, the stand-in test fails at its send. The scatter suites of
  `ack_release.rs` and the green owner's batch flows are filed for main's run.

Applied in the same change to: GAPS (the `LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS` entry's class A), `crates/server/src/{verbs,xshard,
work_home,observe}.rs` (`observe::held_to_this_build` shared with the room rule).

### A-427 — A Windows Shards stream's resync channel, the attach's half: made at the attach, held by the anchor before the stream serves anything, its session told before any reply that rests on it, its device end handed beside the stream's (2026-11-18, goal 90, item b, piece three; A-316's and A-339's Windows half; A-418's wire, A-423's hold)
Applied in the same change to: §4.6, the Shards form's resync and death bullets; A-418's and A-423's owed lists; GAPS,
A-281's entry (its Windows item); `crates/api/src/lib.rs` (the `CONTRACT` 12 note: Windows too, the type unchanged, so
no new contract number); `unsafe-budget.toml` (`slates-ipc` 139 → 140); and:
- `crates/server/src/shards/resync_handle.rs` (new, Windows): `establish`, the stream's `HandleResync` (its token, its
  end until the hold is answered, the hold, the holder, the session's version and the version told), `hold`,
  `settle_hold`, `tell`, `settle_tell`, `changed`, `name_holder`, `owed`, `owed_or_wake_me`, `give_up`.
- `crates/server/src/shards/resync.rs`: the session's bytes on every platform; `Holder`, `HANDLE_SESSION_BYTES`,
  `handle_session_bytes` and `from_handle_session` (a successor's, tested now).
- `crates/server/src/shards.rs`: the channel made at a Windows attach; the serve task asks the hold first; a turn
  owing the anchor its session tells it before its reply (`Turned::Session`), and a holder named outside the task wakes
  it (`Woke::Session`); the session moves at `INIT`, the owner word and a RESTORE; the holder is named at the attach's
  hand-off and by `ShardsHolder`; the resync is given up at the end, at the first DAX map, and where the device's end
